Duration matching (immunization)
Most cost-efficient
Mechanism: Match asset BPV to liability BPV. Uses corporate bonds + derivatives overlay. When rates rise, capital losses are offset by reinvestment gains — the two effects cancel. Why cheapest: Corporate credit spread means less capital needed up front to fund the same liability. Lower funding cost than Treasuries. Liability: Stays on balance sheet. No defeasance.
Rebalancing
Continuous
Parallel shift
Hedged ✓
Twist risk
Exposed ✗
Cost rank
1st (cheapest)
Cash flow matching
Moderate cost
Mechanism: Buy bonds whose coupons and principal arrive exactly when liability payments are due. No rate assumption — the match is structural. Asset choice: Treasuries chosen for timing, not yield. Cash flow schedule drives selection. Liability: Qualifies for accounting defeasance if Treasuries used — removed from balance sheet.
Rebalancing
None needed
Twist risk
Immune ✓
Defeasance
Yes (Treasuries)
Cost rank
2nd
Tender offer
Most expensive
Mechanism: Repurchase own debt in the open market. Eliminates liability immediately — no portfolio construction. Cost trap: Repurchasing at a tighter spread than actual rating = paying above market price.
BBB issuer at A-rated spread → A spread < BBB spread → A price > BBB price → premium paid, most expensive route.
Execution risk
High
Liability removed
Immediately
Cost rank
3rd (highest)
Exam trap: "accounting defeasance" ≠ "cost efficient." Cash flow matching (Treasuries) qualifies for defeasance but costs more capital. When the question asks for cost efficiency → always duration matching with corporates.

Seven properties of a valid benchmark
PropertyWhat it meansClassic violation
Specified in advanceRules known before period startsBenchmark changed mid-period
AppropriateConsistent with manager's styleEquity benchmark for bond manager
MeasurableValued at same frequency as portfolioWeekly valuation ✗
UnambiguousClearly identified securities + weightsVague inclusion rules
Reflective of opinionsManager has views on constituentsSecurities manager knows nothing about
AccountableManager accepts responsibilityBenchmark imposed without agreement
InvestableCan be replicated passivelyIlliquid or untradeable securities
Weekly valuation violates measurability. Fixed income portfolios must be valued daily. Weekly = cannot track performance on any given day, cannot rebalance against stale prices.
Characteristic 1 (investment-grade + $250M minimum) → valid: unambiguous, investable rules.
Characteristic 3 (historical prices available) → valid: supports accountability and auditability.
1. Classical single-period immunization
Single liability
Match asset duration to a single liability at a fixed future date. Continuous rebalancing required. Assumes parallel shifts only.
Conditions: Asset PV ≥ Liability PV Asset duration = Liability duration Asset convexity ≥ Liability convexity
2. Multiple liability immunization (Fong & Vasicek)
Multiple liabilities
Same three conditions PLUS the asset duration distribution must bracket the liability duration distribution — some assets shorter AND some longer than the liability range. Matching portfolio duration alone is insufficient.
3. Cash flow matching
Twist-immune
Directly pair asset cash flows to each liability date. No rate assumption. No rebalancing. Immune to all shifts — parallel and non-parallel. Eligible for defeasance if Treasuries used.
4. Contingent immunization
Active + safety net
Pursue active management while portfolio value exceeds the trigger. Switch to full immunization immediately when value hits the trigger.
Trigger = PV(liability) at current rates Cushion = Portfolio value − Trigger Active management stops when Cushion = 0
Risk: a sudden large rate move can erode the cushion faster than the manager can react, forcing immunization at an unfavorable level.
StrategyLiabilitiesTwist-immune?Active return?Rebalancing?
ClassicalSingleNoNoYes
Multiple liabilityMultiplePartialNoYes
Cash flow matchingSingle or multipleYesNoNone

Why twists break duration matching — and the one thing that reduces the damage.

The root cause
Duration assumes one uniform rate change across all maturities. Under a twist, short-end and long-end rates move differently. Asset cash flows (spread across maturities) and liability cash flows (concentrated at one date) experience different effective rate changes — creating a funding gap even with a perfect duration match.
Bullet vs barbell — why it matters for twist risk
Bullet portfolioBarbell portfolio
Cash flow distributionConcentrated near liability dateSpread at short and long ends
ConvexityLower (closer to liability)Higher (more dispersed)
Twist exposureLower — all CFs experience similar rate changeHigher — short/long CFs diverge under twist
Parallel shift protectionSame — both duration-matched
Exam rule: to reduce non-parallel shift risk → minimize convexity (bullet structure). NOT maximize cash flow yield. NOT minimize duration gap.
Statement 1 (measurement errors on known liability) → Correct: duration/convexity parameter errors still apply even when the liability amount and date are certain.

Statement 2 (cash flow matching mitigates non-parallel shift risk) → Correct: structural match = immune to all yield curve shapes.
Step 1 — Screen on convexity (hard rule, no exceptions)
Any portfolio with convexity below the liability convexity is immediately eliminated. Non-negotiable — no BPV proximity can save it.
Asset convexity < Liability convexity → ELIMINATED
Step 2 — Smallest BPV gap among survivors
Smallest gap = fewest futures contracts needed = least basis risk and transaction cost.
Nf = (BPV_liability − BPV_portfolio) / BPV_futures BPV_futures = BPV_CTD / conversion factor Negative Nf = short futures · BPV gap = |portfolio BPV − liability BPV|
Step 3 — Don't maximize convexity
Excess convexity = more dispersed cash flows = more twist exposure. Prefer convexity just above the liability level, not maximized.

Parallel shifts — immunization works
Yield gap = 0.000% and MV difference tiny (±$4–18). Assets and liabilities move in lockstep. Duration matching succeeds exactly as designed.

Yield curve twists — immunization breaks
MV differences blow out to ±$2,300+. Yield gap opens to ±0.088%. Different maturities move differently → structural mismatch between assets and liabilities.

Critical insight: twist MV differences (~$2,300) dwarf parallel-shift differences (~$4–18). Twist risk is far larger in practice — yet duration matching only addresses parallel shifts.
AM constructed response structure
1. State overall verdict: effective for parallel shifts, fails for twists 2. Cite the specific numbers from the table — yield gap AND MV difference for each scenario type 3. Explain the mechanism: parallel → both sides respond equally; twist → assets and liabilities sit at different maturities and experience different rate changes 4. Conclude: residual structural exposure to non-parallel shifts that duration matching cannot eliminate
Reading map — Liability-Driven & Index-Based Strategies
Two halves: liability-driven (fund a known liability — immunization, duration matching, managing a duration gap with derivatives) and index-based (track a bond index — replication, primary-risk matching, indirect exposure, benchmark choice).
Immunizing a SINGLE liability (LOS a)
Immunization = manage the portfolio to minimize the variability of the realized return over a horizon, so the FV is confident enough to fund the liability.
Perfect hedgeBuy a zero-coupon default-free bond with par + maturity matching the liability → no cash flow or price risk
Single liability ≈a zero-coupon liability → its time-to-payment IS its Macaulay duration
So matchMacaulay duration of assets = MacDur of the liability (D = DL)
At Macaulay duration, price risk (sell before maturity) and reinvestment risk (reinvest coupons) exactly offset for a small one-time parallel move: rates ↑ → higher reinvestment income offsets the price loss; rates ↓ → lower reinvestment income offsets the price gain.
Goal = earn the initial portfolio IRR, NOT the average YTM of the bonds. Earning the IRR is what grows the portfolio to the required FV. Use portfolio statistics (aggregate-cash-flow IRR), not bond-by-bond weighted averages — the two differ on a non-flat curve (on an upward-sloping curve, portfolio duration/IRR > weighted-average, since longer bonds act over a longer time).
Convexity, dispersion & the %ΔV engine
%ΔV = (−MD × ΔY) + (½ × C × ΔY²) Convexity = (MacDur² + MacDur + dispersion) / (1 + periodic IRR)²
Modified duration= MacDur / (1 + periodic IRR); slightly better immediate price-change measure
Dispersionweighted variance of when cash flows arrive, around MacDur
Convexityrises with dispersion; with MD gives the more accurate price change
Dispersion & convexity reveal the immunization's structural risk — exposure to shifts AND twists in the curve.
The structural-risk logic (corrected, key for exam)
A single ZC bond has zero dispersion → it perfectly replicates a single liability. The closer the asset portfolio gets to that ZC, the lower the structural risk.
Minimize dispersion of asset CFs around the liability→ minimizes convexity (for a given MacDur & CF yield)
→ asset CFs cluster near the liability date→ closer to the immunizing ZC → less structural risk
Rules for immunizing a single liability: (1) PVA ≥ PVL; (2) MacDurasset = DL; (3) MINIMIZE convexity/dispersion; (4) rebalance as time/yields drift (vs transaction-cost tradeoff). Note the tension: +convexity helps immediate price change, but for immunization the real issue is reaching the FV — so you minimize it.
Effects of yield-curve changes (the twist taxonomy)
Parallel shifts: immunization works (it's zero replication — IRR change matches the replicating zero). But this is sufficient, NOT necessary, and does NOT mean buy-and-hold (coupon-bond duration falls slower than maturity, so rebalance to keep D = DL). Twists are where structural risk bites — L/M/H = low/mid/high duration; M = the liability point:
TwistYields movePVA vs PVLStructural risk?
SteepeningYield L ↓, Yield H ↑ (M flat)PVA below PVL (long bond falls more)Yes — may fail
FlatteningYield L ↑, Yield H ↓ (M flat)PVA above PVL (long bond gains more)Yes
Positive butterflyL & H ↑, M ↓PVA below PVL (detrimental)Yes — significant
Negative butterflyL & H ↓, M ↑PVA above PVL (favorable)Yes — possible
PVA below PVL "by itself does NOT indicate the strategy will fail" — if portfolio IRR rises enough vs the liability discount rate, the required FV can still be reached. Steepening tends to raise IRR above the single M-point YTM (helps); flattening tends to lower it.
Immunizing MULTIPLE liabilities — duration matching (LOS b, c)
More flexible / practical than cash-flow matching. Match money durations (BPV) rather than Macaulay duration when initial amounts differ.
RuleDetail
1. PVA ≥ PVL(exceptions when initial portfolio IRR ≠ liability discount rate)
2. BPVA = BPVLmoney durations match
3. Asset dispersion & convexity EXCEED liabilities'but NOT by too much — minimizes structural-risk exposure to curve reshaping
4. Rebalancemaintain BPV match as time & yields change
BPV = MD × V × 0.0001 (= PVBP = "value of an 01")
Single vs multiple — the one thing to nail: single liability MINIMIZES convexity (get to the ZC); multiple liabilities sets asset convexity slightly ABOVE the liabilities'. Both then cap it to limit structural risk.
Worked example — recommending a portfolio (UK bond company)
Liability: BPV 344,250, convexity 45.12. Three candidates — pick the one whose BPV matches and whose convexity slightly exceeds:
LiabABC
BPV344,250343,100345,400339,120
Convexity45.1235.1446.2965.97
Recommend B: (1) BPV closely matches, and (2) convexity slightly exceeds the liability. If the company expects high volatility + large parallel shifts → consider C (much higher convexity → more upside on big parallel moves), but its BPV match is worse.
Managing a duration gap with derivatives (Module P4.2)
A derivatives overlay adjusts portfolio duration without trading the underlying bonds. Normal case: BPVA < BPVL → a positive duration gap to close by adding asset-side BPV.
N_f = (BPV_liability − BPV_current portfolio) / BPV_futures futures BPV ≈ BPV_CTD / CF_CTD
StepDB pension example
BPVL2.57bn × 9.35 × 0.0001 = 2,402,950
BPVA3.07bn × 40% × 2.85 × 0.0001 = 349,980
Gap2,402,950 − 349,980 = 2,052,970
Futures BPV128.98 / 0.9436 = 136.6893
Nf (100%)2,052,970 / 136.6893 = 15,019 buy
CTD & conversion factor: buyer pays initial price × CFCTD; seller delivers the cheapest-to-deliver. The CTD's duration drives the contract's BPV — so if the CTD changes, futures BPV changes (a measurement risk). To raise asset BPV, buy contracts regardless of which contract is used; pick the contract whose duration best matches the liability to minimize structural risk (e.g., 10-yr over 5-yr for an 8.99 liability duration).
Tilting the hedge on a rate view (active over/under-hedge)
100% hedge = remove the gap, no view. With a view you deliberately re-open it — the hedge dial sets asset BPV/duration:
Rate viewHedgeAsset BPVWhy
Expect rates ↑Under-hedge (<100%)lower (e.g. 90%: 13,517)assets fall less; reduced contract losses; surplus improves
Expect rates ↓Over-hedge (>100%)higher (e.g. 110%: 16,521)assets gain more; contract gains rise; surplus improves
"Hedge" names the instrument; a true (Sense-2) hedge is only the 100% case. Anything else = a partial hedge + directional bet. More hedge = more asset BPV = MORE rate sensitivity (both ways), not "more protection." Futures margin: each 1/32 = 31.25 G/L per contract, posted in cash daily — on ~15,000 contracts even a ~0.2bp move is large cash flow → 100% hedges are rare, partial hedges common.
Three instruments to add asset BPV — IRS, swaption, collar
ToolMechanics
Receive-fixed IRS= buying bonds → positive (+) duration, raises BPV. Pay-fixed = negative duration. Net swap duration = difference of the replicating fixed & floating bonds. May avoid futures' daily margin (though many now post collateral too).
Buy receiver swaptionRight to enter a receive-fixed swap → gains if SFR declines. Premium is a sunk cost, irrelevant to the exercise decision.
Swaption collarBuy receiver swaption + sell payer swaption (cuts premium, often zero-cost). Selling the payer caps upside: its buyer exercises (you must pay-fixed) when SFRs rise above the payer strike.
NP = duration-gap BPV / (net swap BPV per 1 NP) → e.g. 2,052,970 / (0.0893/100) = 2.3bn for 100%
Net swap BPV: fixed-side BPV − floating-side BPV (e.g. 0.0918 − 0.0025 = 0.0893 per 100 NP). 30% hedge → 0.69bn; raising to 70% needs an extra 0.92bn NP.
Choosing the optimal swap strategy — the rate-line decision
All three protect against falling rates (the plan's risk when BPVA < BPVL). Which is optimal depends on where the new SFR lands vs the swap rate and the payer-swaption strike:
Receive-fixed swapoptimal if new SFR is at or below the swap SFR (locks the now-above-market fixed rate; = buying fixed bonds financed at MRR)
Zero-cost collaroptimal if SFR is between the swap & payer strikes — receiver leg adds no value above the swap rate but cost nothing, and the short payer isn't exercised below its strike
Buy receiver swaptionoptimal if SFR rises above the payer strike — keeps falling-rate protection while losing only the premium; the swap would post escalating negative value and the collar's short payer would be exercised against you
"Payer/receiver swaption" always names the buyer's fixed-rate action. Buy receiver swaption for high rates ≠ a high-rate bet — it's the cheapest capped-loss way to stay protected if you're wrong. Premium is sunk: it never affects whether to exercise.
Worked example — swap vs swaption (US pension, gap 450,000)
50% hedge NP(450,000 × 0.50) / (0.2571/100) = 87.515mn receive-fixed
Adjust 50%→35% (sell 15%)(450,000 × 0.15)/(0.2571/100) = 26.254mn; to REDUCE a receive-fixed hedge, buy a payer swaption
Payer-swaption premium26.254mn × 0.0055 = 144,397
Exercise rulepayer swaption (right to pay 2.7%) is valuable & exercised if new SFR > 2.7%
Contingent immunization (CI): a hybrid active/passive strategy needing a significant surplus (PVA > PVL). Manage actively while the surplus lasts; if it shrinks toward zero, revert to a pure immunizing portfolio. Vulnerable to liquidity risk if all assets (not just surplus) are active and must be liquidated fast.
Risks of managing against a liability (LOS d)
RiskSource
Convexity / structuralhedges ignore convexity (matters for large moves); duration assumes parallel shifts; twists create structural risk → immunization may fail to replicate the ZC
Modelassumptions to estimate DB-plan liabilities, effective duration, BPV
Measurement errorusing weighted-average characteristics instead of portfolio statistics (aggregate CF + IRR)
Counterparty → cash-flowOTC credit risk; collateral cuts it but creates cash-flow risk (post collateral on demand). Same for futures (daily margin).
Spreadasset vs liability discount rates differ & shift unexpectedly — see below
Asset liquiditypositions can't be adjusted quickly at reasonable cost
Spread risk, three flavors: (1) liability rate = corporate, assets = government → using Treasury contracts introduces spread risk; (2) Treasuries are highly liquid → higher reported volatility → more frequent (nonparallel) price change; (3) swaps create spread risk because swap rates track the MRR market.
Index-based investing (LOS e) — why bonds are harder than equities
ApproachHow
Pure index / full replicationhold ALL securities at index weights
Enhanced indexmatch primary risk exposures, not all holdings (via stratified sampling / cell matching)
5 reasons full replication is impractical: (1) far more bond issues, widely varying terms; (2) any issuer has many issues differing in liquidity → concentrate in liquid ones; (3) OTC dealing, post-2008 higher capital cost → less dealer inventory, wider bid-ask, liquidity declined; (4) most bonds rarely trade → price via matrix/evaluated pricing; (5) index composition changes fast (new issuance, maturity, credit migration). Goal of index investing = minimize tracking error (= active risk = SD of active return).
Matching the primary risk factors
Match…Minimizes tracking error from…Formula
Modified duration (effective D if embedded options)parallel shifts%ΔV = −MD × Δy
Key rate durationsnonparallel (twist) shifts%ΔV = −MDkrn × Δyn
Sector & quality weights + spread durationspread changes%ΔVrel = −DS × Δspread
Sector/coupon/maturity cell weightscell mismatches (matching cells → matches eff. dur. & convexity)—
Issuer exposure weightsissuer-specific event risk (e.g. bankruptcy)—
MD measures the change from a general rate move (govt yields); spread duration measures how nongov bonds move vs govts when credit spreads change. Spread = yhigher-yield − ygovernment. Matching the PV-distribution of cash flows (the (t)(w) duration-contribution table) simultaneously matches duration AND key-rate durations.
Cell matching, ESG & enhancement techniques
Stratified samplingdivide index into cells (e.g. duration 1–5/5–10/10–15 × Treasury/Corporate/ABS), hold the cell's weight without using the same bonds
ESG overlaycell matching can embed socially-responsible rules (exclude high-carbon, prefer clean energy) while still matching cell weights
Enhancements to add value / cut cost: reduce fund expenses & transaction costs; overweight undervalued / underweight overvalued (favor spread narrowing, avoid spread widening) while still matching overall index; over-/under-weight callable bonds — favor them for higher yield when rate volatility is expected low (call impact more predictable), avoid when volatility is high.
Indirect exposure — funds, ETFs, TRS (LOS f)
VehicleKey features
Mutual fundsgood for smaller investors; broad exposure + economies of scale (pooled capital → better prices)
Open-endbuy/redeem at NAV once per day; ongoing fees, possible front/back loads; no maturity, holdings & income drift
ETFstrade continuously on-exchange; authorized participants redeem/create in-kind → arbitrage keeps price ≈ NAV, but that arb is less effective than for equity ETFs (illiquid underlying bonds)
Total return swapreceive index total return (income + price) vs pay MRR + spread = buying the index on borrowed funds. If index return is negative, receiver pays it. If not fully collateralized → leveraged; counterparty/credit risk; you don't own the bonds
Bond benchmark selection (LOS g)
Start from client objectives & constraints → SAA → then pick the index (manager may get tactical discretion).
Static bond portfolioduration declines as bonds age
New issuanceshifts index characteristics (issuers move shorter/longer) → index may no longer fit the desired duration
Custom indexdefine desired duration & sector sub-exposures (e.g. 50% 5–10y Treasuries + 50% 1–3y IG)
Credit barbell (a smart-beta rule): long-term Treasuries (no credit/spread risk) supply the duration exposure; short-term corporates add spread return and are less vulnerable to relative price underperformance if spreads widen.
Yield Curve Strategies · Interactive Study Map
Receive-fixed swap — two return components
Duration extension tool
What it does: Synthetically increases portfolio duration. You receive the fixed rate and pay MRR (floating). No bond purchase needed — pure rate exposure. Component 1 — Carry: Fixed rate − MRR = daily accrual. Accrues daily, settled periodically (quarterly/semi-annually). Can be positive or negative. Component 2 — Mark-to-market: As rates move, the swap's present value changes. Not a cash flow — only realized if you exit. Rates fall → swap gains value. Rates rise → swap loses value.
Carry settlement
Periodic (quarterly)
MTM settlement
On exit only
Duration effect
Increases ✓
Carry: can be positive OR negative
ConditionCarryWhen it happens
Fixed rate > MRRPositive ✓Normal upward-sloping curve — you earn the spread daily
MRR > Fixed rateNegative ✗Inverted curve or aggressive hike cycle — you pay out the difference
Worst case for receive-fixed: rates rise sharply → carry turns negative AND MTM loses value simultaneously. You lose on both legs.
Pay-fixed swap — the mirror image
You pay the fixed rate and receive MRR. Synthetically reduces or negatives portfolio duration. Profits when rates rise (MTM gain) and when MRR > fixed rate (positive carry in inverted curve). A bearish manager uses pay-fixed swaps (or shorts futures) to push total portfolio duration negative.
Negative portfolio duration — how to achieve it
Bonds always have positive duration — you cannot get negative duration from physical bonds alone. You need derivatives sized large enough to more than offset the positive duration of the bond holdings.
Tools: pay-fixed swaps · short bond futures · buy bond puts Size the notional so: |Derivative duration| > Portfolio bond duration Net duration = Bond duration − Derivative duration offset → negative
If duration = −2: rates rise 100bps → portfolio gains ~2%. Behaves like a short bond position.

Identification is on the government curve. Implementation uses swaps and futures.

How to identify: watch 2s10s spread on the government curve
2s10s = 10-year yield − 2-year yield. Spread widening = steepening. Spread narrowing = flattening. Identify bull vs bear: decompose what each end actually did. If 2yr fell 30bps and 10yr unchanged → bull steepening. If 10yr rose 30bps and 2yr unchanged → bear steepening.
Implementation tools — steepening trade
ViewShort end positionLong end positionNet duration
Bull steepeningReceive-fixed 2yr swap OR long 2yr futuresPay-fixed 10yr OR short 10yr futuresRoughly neutral
Bear steepeningNeutral or long short endPay-fixed 10yr OR short 10yr futures OR buy 30yr payer swaptionRoughly neutral
Key rate duration positioning for bear steepening (Boyd example)
Bear steepening = long rates rise → you want low KRD at the long end relative to the index. Portfolio B had 10yr KRD of 2.85 vs index 7.25 — significantly underweight the long end. Correct position. Portfolio C was overweight the long end (KRD 8.35 vs 7.25) — would underperform badly.
Duration-neutral discipline: a steepening trade is a view on curve shape, not overall rate level. Keep total duration close to benchmark. Only the distribution across maturities changes.
Options-based steepening trade
TradeLong endShort endView
SteepeningBuy payer swaption (right to pay fixed at 30yr)Buy bond call (right to buy 2yr bond)Long rates ↑ · Short rates ↓
FlatteningBuy receiver swaption (right to receive fixed at 30yr)Buy bond put (right to sell 2yr bond)Long rates ↓ · Short rates ↑
Exam trap: receiver swaption profits when rates FALL (you lock in receiving a high fixed rate). Payer swaption profits when rates RISE. Never mix these up.
2s10s is a concept, not one instrument — always specify the curve
VersionWhat it isUsed for
Government bond curve10yr Treasury − 2yr Treasury (US) · 10yr Bund − 2yr Bund (EU)Identification of steepening/flattening · pure policy signal · default meaning of "2s10s"
Swap curve10yr swap rate − 2yr swap rateImplementation · what managers actually trade · includes small credit component
Swap spreadSwap rate − govt bond yield at same maturityCompletely different signal — banking system credit and liquidity conditions
What drives the 2-year yield
Almost entirely monetary policy expectations over the next 24 months. Central bank hikes / hawkish signals → 2yr rises immediately Central bank cuts / dovish pivot → 2yr falls immediately Hot CPI or strong payrolls → more hikes priced in → 2yr rises The 2yr barely cares about 2030 — it's anchored to what the CB does right now
What drives the 10-year yield — two components
1. Expected future short rates: what do investors think policy rates will average over 10 years? Connects to monetary policy at a much longer horizon. 2. Term premium: extra compensation for locking up money for 10 years. Captures inflation uncertainty, fiscal risk, government bond supply, global demand for safe assets.
Spread = gap between now and the future
Spread signalWhat it meansSteepening type likely
CB hiking aggressively2yr rises fast → spread narrows/invertsFlattening / inversion
CB cuts or signals cuts2yr falls → spread widensBull steepening
LT inflation expectations rise10yr rises via term premiumBear steepening
Heavy LT government bond supply10yr rises → spread widensBear steepening
Strong foreign CB demand for USTTerm premium suppressed → 10yr lowFlattening
Identification workflow: (1) observe 2s10s widening on govt curve → steepening confirmed. (2) Check which end moved → identifies bull vs bear. (3) Check macro drivers (CB language, inflation breakevens, term premium, fiscal) → anticipates which type is coming next.
What key rate duration (KRD) actually measures
Sensitivity of portfolio value to a rate change at one specific maturity point on the yield curve, holding all other maturities constant. Unlike overall duration which assumes parallel shifts.
KRD at 10yr = +6 means: 10yr rate falls 1% → portfolio gains ~6% 10yr rate rises 1% → portfolio loses ~6% (other maturities unchanged)
Positive vs negative KRD — what each means
KRD at maturity XManager's viewPositionExample instrument
High positiveRate at X will fallOverweight that maturityBuy bonds at X tenor · receive-fixed swap at X
High negativeRate at X will riseUnderweight / short that maturityShort futures at X · pay-fixed swap at X
Neutral (= index)No view on that maturityMatch index weight—
The surgical power of KRD — expressing curve shape views
A manager can simultaneously hold: Positive KRD at 2yr → expects short rates to fall Negative KRD at 10yr → expects long rates to rise = Bear steepening bet, total duration roughly neutral
You cannot see this nuance by looking at total portfolio duration alone. Two portfolios with identical total duration can have completely different curve exposures.
Boyd example — bear steepening KRD mapping
2yr KRD5yr KRD10yr KRDBear steepening fit
Index2.503.607.25—
Portfolio A2.503.607.25Mirrors index — no view
Portfolio B4.006.502.85Best ✓ — underweight long end
Portfolio C1.004.008.35Worst ✗ — overweight long end
Portfolio B wins because 10yr KRD (2.85) is far below the index (7.25) — it loses much less when long rates rise. Portfolio C would be destroyed — it has more long-end sensitivity than the index.
Swaption fundamentals — what you own
A swaption gives you the right but not obligation to enter into a swap at a pre-agreed fixed rate on a future date.
TypeRight to…Exercise when…Rate viewDuration effect
Receiver swaptionReceive fixed, pay floatingRates fall (fixed rate you receive > market)Bullish (rates fall)Long duration when exercised
Payer swaptionPay fixed, receive floatingRates rise (fixed rate you pay < market)Bearish (rates rise)Short duration when exercised
Long vs short swaption positions
PositionYou…Max lossMax gain
Long receiver swaptionPay premium upfrontPremium paidUnlimited (if rates fall far)
Short receiver swaptionCollect premiumUnlimitedPremium collected
Long payer swaptionPay premium upfrontPremium paidUnlimited (if rates rise far)
Short payer swaptionCollect premiumUnlimitedPremium collected
Cook example — downward parallel shift 50bps
Cook expects rates to fall. She wants to benefit. Long receiver swaption = right to receive fixed. If rates fall, she exercises and receives an above-market fixed rate. The swaption gains value as rates fall. Correct position ✓ Short receiver swaption = she sold the right to someone else. If rates fall, the counterparty exercises against her — she loses. Wrong direction.
The most common exam trap: confusing which swaption benefits from which rate direction. Anchor it to the underlying swap logic — receiver swaption = you want to receive fixed = you want rates to fall so your fixed rate looks attractive. Payer swaption = you want to pay fixed = you want rates to rise so paying the lower locked-in fixed rate is valuable.
Steepening trade with swaptions — summary
Steepening = long rates rise, short rates fall Long payer swaption at 30yr → right to pay fixed at 30yr → profits when 30yr rates rise ✓ Long call on 2yr bond → right to buy 2yr bond → profits when 2yr bond price rises = 2yr rates fall ✓ Combined = pure steepening bet with limited downside (premium paid)
The full expected return formula
E(R) = Rolldown return + (−Duration × Δyield) + (0.5 × Convexity × Δyield²) + ΔFX (if unhedged foreign bond)
Never drop the convexity term — even if the yield move seems small. The exam tests whether you include it. With 50bps move it's tiny (0.02%) but it's the difference between answer choices.
Component 1 — Rolldown return
The price appreciation from a bond "rolling down" an upward-sloping stable yield curve as time passes. A 2-year bond becomes a 1-year bond after one year — and since 1-year yields are lower, its price rises.
Rolldown = (Expected price in 1yr − Price today) / Price today Example: (98.75 − 97.00) / 97.00 = 1.804%
The expected price in 1yr assumes an unchanged yield curve — it is the price the bond would have if it simply aged one year with no rate moves. It is given in the exhibit, not calculated from scratch.
Component 2 — Duration + Convexity price effect
Price effect = (−Duration × Δyield) + (0.5 × Convexity × Δyield²) Example (bullet, −50bps shift): = (−4.50 × −0.0050) + (0.5 × 17.0 × 0.0050²) = +2.250% + 0.021% = 2.271%
Use the expected duration and convexity in 1 year (from exhibit), not today's values. Δyield is negative for rate falls. Always convert bps to decimals: 50bps = 0.0050.
Component 3 — Currency effect
If the foreign currency appreciates vs your home currency → add positive FX return If the foreign currency depreciates vs your home currency → subtract FX loss Cook example: USD depreciates against EUR by 0.75% → USD-denominated returns lose 0.75% when converted to EUR → −0.75%
Watch the direction carefully. "USD depreciates against EUR" = your USD bonds are worth less in EUR terms = negative FX contribution. Don't flip the sign.
Cook worked example — full calculation
ComponentBulletBarbell
Rolldown(98.75−97.00)/97.00 = 1.804%(99.75−97.75)/97.75 = 2.046%
Duration effect (−D × −0.005)−4.50 × −0.005 = +2.250%−4.45 × −0.005 = +2.225%
Convexity effect (0.5×Cx×0.005²)0.5×17.0×0.000025 = +0.021%0.5×40.0×0.000025 = +0.050%
FX (USD depreciates vs EUR)−0.750%−0.750%
Total3.325% ≈ 3.32%3.571% ≈ 3.58%
Barbell wins because of higher convexity (40 vs 17) and higher rolldown (2.046% vs 1.804%). In a falling rate environment, convexity advantage is amplified.
Rolldown strategy — why it works
Buy further out on an upward-sloping curve. As time passes the bond rolls toward a lower-yield, higher-price point. You earn rolldown return on top of yield — as long as the curve stays stable and upward-sloping. This is why the 2-year zero-coupon (bought at 96.1169, expected to be worth 99.0090 in a year) earns more than the 1-year zero-coupon in the Thai bond example.
BPV / DV01 — same thing, different names
Dollar change in portfolio value for a 1bp (0.01%) move in rates.
BPV = Modified duration × Market value × 0.0001 Example: Duration 5 · MV $10M → BPV = 5 × $10M × 0.0001 = $5,000 per bp
Why it matters: Duration is a percentage — you can't subtract durations across portfolios of different sizes. BPV puts everything in the same unit (dollars per bp) so arithmetic works. Hedging: Nf = (BPV_target − BPV_portfolio) / BPV_futures Immunization: match asset BPV to liability BPV so a 1bp move hits both equally
Negative convexity — callable bonds
At high yields: call is out of the money, callable bond behaves like option-free bond — normal positive convexity. At low yields: call is deep in the money. Issuer's right to call becomes very valuable. Market knows bond may be called → price stops rising at normal pace → price-yield curve bends the wrong way → negative convexity. The asymmetry: less upside when rates fall (call caps price) but full downside when rates rise (call not exercised). You keep all the risk, lose some of the reward.
Why callable bonds must offer a higher yield: compensation for this asymmetric payoff. You are short the call option → you must be paid for it.
Forward rate bias
What theory says (UIP): high-yield currency should depreciate by exactly the yield differential — no free lunch. What actually happens: high-yield currencies depreciate by less than predicted, or not at all. The yield advantage is not fully offset. Implication: go unhedged into high-yielding currencies to earn excess returns. Amplify by borrowing in low-yield currencies (carry trade).
Carry trade = borrow in low-yield currency (JPY at 0.5%) · invest in high-yield currency (BRL at 10%) · pocket the spread. Works because forward rate bias means the low-yield currency doesn't appreciate enough to wipe out the carry.
Stable yield curve — what generates excess return
When rates don't move, you cannot earn excess return from predicting rate direction. The only way to beat the benchmark is to earn more carry.
StrategyWorks under stable curve?Why
Increase duration above benchmarkYesLonger bonds earn more yield + rolldown without rate rise penalty
Add leverageYesBorrow at short rates, invest in longer bonds, pocket the spread
Reduce duration below benchmarkNo — least likelyShorter bonds earn less yield, no rate protection needed, guaranteed underperformance vs benchmark
Reducing duration only makes sense if you expect rates to RISE — then shorter portfolio loses less than benchmark. Under a stable curve it just sacrifices yield for nothing.
Reading P5 · Yield Curve Strategies — full recap
Follows the reading's own flow
Positioning on the credit-risk-free government curve to add value. "Yield" here = YTM unless stated. Walkthrough order: P5.1 dynamics & static-curve trades → P5.2 dynamic-curve trades (level / slope / curvature) → P5.3 volatility & key rate duration → P5.4 currencies → framework for evaluating a strategy.
Module P5.1 — Yield curve dynamics & trades for a static curve (P5.a, P5.b)
Three sources of yield curve change
Curve changes decompose into three movements. Most real changes mix all three, but the single most important driver of bond-price change is the parallel (level) shift.
SourceWhat movesNickname
1. LevelAll yields shift up/down by the same amountParallel shift
2. SlopeCurve flattens or steepens"Twist"
3. CurvatureCurve becomes more/less curved"Butterfly" movement
Slope measure = long-term yield − short-term yield. If this difference increases → curve is steepening.
butterfly spread = −(short-term yield) + (2 × medium-term yield) − (long-term yield)
Butterfly spread increasing → medium-term yields rising relative to short + long → curvature increasing.
Five-step return decomposition (Part 3 is the curve engine)
Every P5 calculation traces back to this. This reading uses Steps 1–3 and 5 (Step 4, spread, is the credit reading).
1. Coupon income = annual coupon / current bond price 2. Rolldown return = (projected price if no curve change − beginning price) / beginning price 3. Yield-change P/L = (−MD × ΔY) + (½ × C × ΔY²) ← curve view lives here 4. Spread-change P/L= (−MD × ΔS) + (½ × C × ΔS²) ← credit reading 5. Currency G/L = projected FX change weighted for exposure
Rolldown/carry (Steps 1–2) are what you earn if the curve doesn't move. Step 3 is what you earn/lose from your view on the move.
Convexity — decomposing WHY it matters
Higher convexity is desirable, but understand the drivers, don't just memorise "convexity good":
Driver 1 — asymmetry in Step 3: the (½ × C × ΔY²) term is always positive (ΔY² ≥ 0). More convexity = bigger positive kicker whichever way rates move. Driver 2 — volatility payoff: the kicker scales with ΔY². High rate volatility → high convexity outperforms low convexity. Driver 3 — priced away: because it's desirable in volatile times, high-convexity bonds trade at a premium → lower YTM. You pay for convexity via yield given up. Driver 4 — cash-flow dispersion: the more dispersed a bond's cash flows around its MD, the higher its convexity. So a barbell (dispersed) has higher convexity than a bullet of the same duration.
Decisive detail: barbell > bullet on convexity only when durations are matched. The whole barbell-vs-bullet comparison assumes equal duration — that's what isolates the convexity effect.
Worked: barbell vs bullet, +50bp parallel shift
Hypothetical UK gilts. Bullet (Port 1) = 100% 10y. Barbell (Port 2) = 46.68% 2y + 53.32% 20y — weights chosen so barbell MD = bullet MD.
BondMDConvexityPrice chg (Step 3, ΔY=+0.005)
2y1.865.2(−1.86×.005)+(½×5.2×.005²) = −0.92%
10y9.52104.8(−9.52×.005)+(½×104.8×.005²) = −4.63%
20y16.23292.8(−16.23×.005)+(½×292.8×.005²) = −7.75%
Barbell MD check = (0.4668 × 1.86) + (0.5332 × 16.23) = 9.52 ✓ (= bullet MD) Port 1 (bullet) = −4.63% (100% in 10y) Port 2 (barbell) = (0.4668 × −0.92%) + (0.5332 × −7.75%) = −4.56%
Barbell loses less (−4.56% vs −4.63%): its higher convexity cushions the parallel move. Same duration, better convexity → outperformance when yields move.
Static yield-curve strategies (view: curve stays put)
If you believe the (upward-sloping) curve will stay unchanged, you earn excess return by taking more duration / more carry / leverage. Two families:
Cash-basedHow it earns
Buy & holdExtend duration beyond benchmark → higher coupon income on longer bonds. Low turnover, low cost.
Roll down the curveAs time passes, bond's maturity & duration fall → on an upward curve its yield falls → price rises. Earn coupon and rolldown. Buy at the top of a steep segment; after yield declines, sell and roll out again.
Repo carry tradeLeverage: borrow at low short rate, invest at higher long rate, pocket the spread.
Derivatives-basedHow it earns
Long futuresImplicit leverage — only margin funded, small fraction of exposure.
Receive-fixed swapReceive fixed, pay MRR → synthetically increases duration. Earn swap carry (fixed − MRR) + MTM.
futures BPV = BPV(CTD) / CF(CTD) # futures to go long = target BPV / futures BPV
Major risk to buy-and-hold: the curve does NOT stay static. The exam answer for "biggest risk to a static-curve strategy" is a parallel shift up in yields (Module Quiz P5.1 Q3 → C references "unchanged," but the risk is the up-shift).
Worked: extending duration — bond (Trade A) vs swap (Trade B), 25bp fall, £50m, 6-month horizon
Trade A: buy 10y 3% semi-annual gilt yielding 2.5%, priced 104.3998. Trade B: 10y receive-fixed swap at 3%, MRR 0.5%.
Trade A — bond
Coupon income = 0.03/2 × £50,000,000 = £750,000 Price in 6m, unchanged yield (2.5%): N=19, I/Y=1.25, PMT=1.5, FV=100 → 104.2048 Price in 6m, new yield (2.25%): N=19, I/Y=1.125, PMT=1.5, FV=100 → 106.3828 Rolldown P/L = (104.2048 − 104.3998)/100 × £50m = −£97,500 Yield-change P/L = (106.3828 − 104.2048)/100 × £50m = +£1,089,000 Total price appreciation = (106.3828 − 104.3998)/100 × £50m = £991,500
Decisive detail: rolldown is negative here (−£97,500). Bond is priced above par and pulls to par as it ages, so with an unchanged yield the price actually drifts down over 6 months. Rolldown is not automatically positive.
Trade B — swap
Swap carry = (fixed − floating)/2 × notional = (0.03 − 0.005)/2 × £50m = £625,000 Value swap in 6m as two bonds: long fixed-coupon bond, short FRN. Fixed leg (rates −25bp): N=19, I/Y=1.375, PMT=1.5, FV=100 → 102.0776 per 100 → per £1 = 1.020776 → × £50m = £51,038,817 FRN resets to par at payment date = £50,000,000 Swap MTM = £51,038,817 − £50,000,000 = £1,038,817
Both express the same static-curve, extend-duration view; the swap needs no cash outlay for the bond (pure rate exposure) while the bond earns coupon income.
Module P5.2 — Trades for a dynamic yield curve (P5.c)
Bullish vs bearish — the anchor concept
Everything in P5.2 unlocks from two rules; don't rote-learn the tables.
Bullish = rates fall = prices rise → want positive / longer duration. Bearish = rates rise = prices fall → want negative / shorter duration. Relative-value rule (slope/curvature): BUY bonds whose rates you expect to fall relative to the curve (prices rise); SHORT bonds whose rates you expect to rise relative to the curve (prices fall).
Divergent RATE LEVEL view — altering duration
InstrumentIncrease duration (bullish)Decrease duration (bearish)
Cash bondOverweight longer-datedShort / overweight shorter-dated
SwapReceive fixedPay fixed
FuturesLong contractsShort contracts
Worked (+40bp, correct bearish call): benchmark = equal weight 2/10/20y; portfolio = overweight 50% 2y, 25%/25% 10y/20y (lower duration).
Bench MD = (1.86+9.52+16.23)/3 = 9.203 ; Bench C = (5.2+104.8+292.8)/3 = 134.3 Port MD = 0.5×1.86+0.25×9.52+0.25×16.23 = 7.368 ; Port C = 102.0 Bench P/L = (−9.203×.004)+(½×134.3×.004²) = −3.57% Port P/L = (−7.368×.004)+(½×102.0×.004²) = −2.87% Excess = −2.87% − (−3.57%) = +0.70% ✓ (lowered duration before an up-shift)
Same result achievable via a pay-fixed swap on the benchmark. Size it with BPV:
BPV = market value × MD × 0.0001 BPV bench = $100m × 9.203 × .0001 = $92,030 BPV target = $100m × 7.368 × .0001 = $73,680 Swap BPV needed = 73,680 − 92,030 = −$18,350 (pay-fixed → negative) NP = −18,350 / (−8.354 × .0001) = $21.98m notional
Divergent SLOPE view — bull/bear × steepener/flattener
Two independent axes: bull/bear = which way the level leans; steepener/flattener = what happens to the gap. Definition is always by the leg that moves MORE.
ViewDefinition (moves more)DurationShort-term bondsLong-term bonds
Steepener (no level chg)gap widensZeroBuyShort sell
Bear steepenerlong rates rise > shortNegativeBuyShort sell
Bull steepenershort rates fall > longPositiveBuyShort sell
Flattener (no level chg)gap narrowsZeroShort sellBuy
Bear flattenershort rates rise > longNegativeShort sellBuy
Bull flattenerlong rates fall > shortPositiveShort sellBuy
Bull steepener: central banks cut short rates in a contraction → short end falls hard. Bear steepener: banks hold short rates too low too long → inflation expectations lift the long end. Bear flattener: banks hike short rates into rising inflation → short end rises hard. Bull flattener: flight to quality → investors buy long risk-free bonds → long end falls hard.
Decisive detail: in every steepener you BUY short / SHORT long; in every flattener you BUY long / SHORT short — regardless of bull/bear. Bull/bear only sets the sign of overall duration (positive/negative/zero), NOT which bonds you buy vs short.
Worked: bull-steepening trade (duration-neutral), 2y −20bp / 10y +20bp
Long £100m 2y, short 10y sized to be BPV-neutral (no view on level).
BPV long 2y = £100m × 1.86 × .0001 = £18,600 Short 10y MV: MV × 9.52 × .0001 = 18,600 → MV = −£19,537,815 2y P/L = [(−1.86×−.002)+(½×5.2×−.002²)] × £100m = +£373,040 10y P/L = [(−9.52×.002)+(½×104.8×.002²)] × −£19,537,815 = +£367,897 Total = £373,040 + £367,897 = £740,937
Both legs profit: the long 2y rises as short rates fall; the short 10y profits as long rates rise (a short gains when its bond's price falls). If next comes a bull steepener (steepening in a falling-rate world), tilt to positive duration — add to the 2y long or short less 10y.
Divergent CURVATURE view — the butterfly
Combine bullets (the body) and barbells (the wings). Body = medium-term; wings = short + long.
Curvature will INCREASE (medium rates rise vs short+long): short the body, buy the wings → "short the body, long the wings." Curvature will DECREASE (medium rates fall vs short+long): buy the body, short the wings → "long the body, short the wings."
The exam minefield: an increase in curvature = an increase in the butterfly spread = a NEGATIVE butterfly twist. Memory hook: after a negative butterfly twist the curve "frowns" MORE (more humped). A manager buying the wings / shorting the body expects a negative butterfly twist (curvature up).
Butterfly strategies are built duration-neutral but are NOT convexity-neutral — the barbell wings carry more convexity than the bullet body.
Worked: positive-butterfly trade (long £100m 10y body, short 2y+20y wings, equal MV)
Positive butterfly view → short & long rates rise vs medium → short the wings, buy the body. Wings sized: equal MV to each other AND total wing BPV = body BPV (duration-neutral).
BPV body = £100m × 9.52 × .0001 = £95,200 Duration-neutral: (MVw×1.86×.0001) + (MVw×16.23×.0001) = 95,200 0.000186·MVw + 0.001623·MVw = 95,200 → 0.001809·MVw = 95,200 MVw = £52,625,760 (short in EACH of 2y and 20y)
P/L if 2y & 20y +10bp and 10y −25bp:
2y : price chg = (−1.86×.001)+(½×5.2×.001²) = −0.1857% P/L = −0.001857 × −£52,625,760 = +£97,747 (short gains) 10y : price chg = (−9.52×−.0025)+(½×104.8×−.0025²)= +2.41275% P/L = 0.0241275 × £100,000,000 = +£2,412,750 20y : price chg = (−16.23×.001)+(½×292.8×.001²) = −1.60836% P/L = −0.0160836 × −£52,625,760 = +£846,412 (short gains) Total = 97,747 + 2,412,750 + 846,412 = +£3,356,909
Sign trap: the wings are SHORT. A short position gains when its bond price FALLS. Price change × (−MV) → both wing P/Ls come out positive. Don't drop the short-position sign flip under time pressure.
Convexity note: the portfolio is short the high-convexity barbell (wings) and long the lower-convexity bullet (body) → overall short convexity, which hurts if yields move a lot. Here it still profited only because the medium rate moved more than the short/long rates.
Module P5.3 — Volatility strategies & key rate duration (P5.d, P5.e)
Embedded options: callable & putable
CallablePutable
Decompositionoption-free bond − short call (call granted to issuer)option-free bond + long put (put owned by investor)
Option gains value whenyields fall / prices riseyields rise / prices fall
Convexity effectnegative convexity at low yields — price rises slowerprice floored at high yields — falls slower
Effect on durationThe option always lowers the duration of the otherwise option-free bond (short call & long put both move inversely to the bond).
Must use effective duration/convexity for embedded-option bonds — Macaulay/modified can't capture cash flows changing when the option is exercised.
effective duration = [(PV₋) − (PV₊)] / [2 × Δcurve × PV₀] effective convexity = [(PV₋) + (PV₊) − 2·PV₀] / [Δcurve² × PV₀] PV₀ = current value ; PV₋ = curve shifted down ; PV₊ = curve shifted up
Options & swaptions — duration impact
Reason from "does the position gain as rates fall (long duration) or as rates rise (short duration)?"
StrategyImpact on durationWhy
Long call on bond / bond futureIncreasecall gains as yields fall & prices rise
Long put on bond / bond futureDecreaseput gains as yields rise & prices fall
Long payer swaptionDecreaseright to pay-fixed; valuable as rates rise
Long receiver swaptionIncreaseright to receive-fixed; valuable as rates fall
Mnemonic: receive-fixed = long duration (bullish). Payer swaption → pay-fixed → short duration (bearish). Call = long duration; put = short duration.
Key rate (partial) duration
Sensitivity to a move in ONE key maturity while all other rates stay constant. Sum of key rate durations = effective duration (aggregate = parallel shift).
KeyRateDur = − (change in portfolio value) / (portfolio value × change in key rate) Zero-coupon shortcut: KRDₖ = MD(zero) × weight in portfolio (works ONLY for zeros — MD = maturity/(1+y))
Why it exists: identifies which maturities the portfolio is most sensitive to → measures exposure to NON-parallel (slope/curvature) changes, which plain MD/effective duration cannot (they assume a parallel shift). High positive KRD at a maturity = view that this maturity rate will FALL. High negative KRD at a maturity = view that this maturity rate will RISE.
Worked: key rate duration & reading the manager's view
Manager holds zeros: 2y (yield 2%) $250m long, 10y (3%) $50m short, 20y (5%) $100m long. Total position $300m gross. Benchmark: equal $100m each.
MD 2y = 2/1.02 = 1.961 MD 10y = 10/1.03 = 9.7087 MD 20y = 20/1.05 = 19.0476 Portfolio KRD (MD × weight, weights 250/−50/100 over 300): 2y : 1.961 × (250/300) = 1.634 10y : 9.7087 × (−50/300) = −1.618 20y : 19.0476 × (100/300)= 6.349 Total portfolio MD = 6.365 Benchmark KRD (each 100/300): 2y 0.654 · 10y 3.236 · 20y 6.349 → Total 10.239
MaturityPortfolioIndexActive (diff)
2y KRD1.6340.654+0.980
10y KRD−1.6183.236−4.854
20y KRD6.3496.3490.000
Overall MD6.36510.239−3.874
Level: overall active duration −3.874 (negative) → manager is bearish, expects rates generally to rise. Slope: positive active at 2y (+0.980), zero at 20y → expects short rates to rise by LESS than long rates → steepening. Curvature: big negative at 10y (−4.854), positive at the wings → expects medium rates to rise more than short+long → negative butterfly view.
Overall: positioned for a combination of a negative butterfly and a bear steepener.
Module P5.4 — Active management across currencies (P5.f)
Unhedged foreign bond — two compounding returns
R_DC = (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) − 1 R_FC = local (foreign-currency) bond return R_FX = % change in the FX quote
Decisive detail — quote convention: R_FX MUST be computed with the domestic currency as the variable (price) currency and the foreign currency as the base (fixed) currency — i.e. a DIRECT quote (DC/FC). If the quote rises, the foreign currency has appreciated and R_FX is positive. Questions often give the quote the wrong way round → you must invert it first.
Worked (Australian investor, US bond, 1yr): bond 96.374 → 99.939; USD/AUD 0.90 → 0.80.
R_FC = (99.939 − 96.374)/96.374 = 3.70% Invert to DC/FC (AUD/USD): open 1/0.90 = 1.1111 ; close 1/0.80 = 1.2500 R_FX = (1.2500 − 1.1111)/1.1111 = 12.5% R_DC = (1.037)(1.125) − 1 = 16.66%
GBP/JPY check: JPY/GBP 150→125 given. Invert: GBP/JPY 1/150=0.006667 → 1/125=0.0080. R_FX = (0.0080−0.006667)/0.006667 = 20%. The UK manager gained as JPY strengthened.
The hedging decision — CIRP
Hedge by selling the foreign currency forward. Covered interest rate parity (CIRP): in efficient markets a hedged foreign bond earns only the domestic risk-free rate — no excess return.
forward rate = spot × (1 + r_DC)^T / (1 + r_FC)^T (worked in DC/FC quotes)
Worked: 2y AUD zero yields 5% (r_DC); US 2y zero price 96.374 → r_FC = (100/96.374)^½ − 1 = 1.864%.
fwd = (1/0.90) × (1.05)² / (1.01864)² = 1.1806 AUD/USD Sell USD100 fwd → receive 100 × 1.1806 = AUD 118.06 Original AUD cost = 96.374/0.90 = 107.0822 Return = (118.06/107.0822)^½ − 1 = 5.0% = domestic risk-free ✓
CIRP logic: high-rate currency (AUD) trades at a forward discount; that discount exactly offsets the higher interest earned, leaving the domestic risk-free rate. Here the interest differential is negative (USD 1.864% − AUD 5% = −3.1%), so the low-rate USD trades at a forward premium of ~3.1%.
UIRP, forward rate bias & the carry trade
UIRP (theory): high-rate currencies should depreciate over time so unhedged investors all earn the same return. It tends NOT to hold. Forward rate bias: high-rate currencies do NOT depreciate as much as the forward discount implies → the forward rate is a biased predictor → a carry trade can earn excess returns on average. Carry trade: borrow low-rate currency, deposit high-rate currency, pocket the differential. Risk: the high-rate currency weakens (flight to quality in a crisis wipes out the carry).
Hedging a coupon bond — fixed-fixed cross-currency swap
Australian investor, US 10y bond, USD/AUD 0.80, USD100m par (= AUD125m). Pay USD / receive AUD fixed-fixed cross-currency swap, with principal exchange at both ends.
LegAt initiationPeriodic (10y)At end
US Treasury bondPay USD100m to buy bondReceive USD couponReceive USD100m par
Fixed-fixed XCCY swapReceive USD100m, pay AUD125mPay-fixed USD, receive-fixed AUDPay USD100m, receive AUD125m
Net flowPay AUD125m outReceive-fixed AUDReceive AUD125m in
Net effect: the manager's exposure is identical to a domestic AUD bond — currency fully hedged, earns the domestic return (parity holds).
In practice the fixed-fixed XCCY swap = three swaps: A (USD interest-rate swap: pay USD fixed, receive USD floating), B (AUD interest-rate swap: pay AUD floating, receive AUD fixed), C (cross-currency basis swap: pay USD floating, receive AUD floating, principals exchanged). A+B fixed legs give pay-USD/receive-AUD; their floating legs cancel with C's floating legs; C moves the principal.
Active-view insight: skip Swap A and you're left net receiving USD fixed (bond) and paying USD floating (Swap C) → net receive-fixed / pay-floating in USD → positive USD duration → profit if USD rates fall, while currency stays fully hedged. Cross-currency basis: if basis is negative, the non-USD floating leg is below its CIRP-fair rate — borrowers of USD accept a lower rate on domestic currency to obtain USD.
Worked: unhedged INR carry trade (1yr: borrow USD 1%, roll 90-day INR at 5%, spot 70)
Scenario 1 — rates & FX stable: Foreign INR return = (1 + 0.05/4)⁴ − 1 = 5.1% Cost of USD funds = 1% ; no FX move Total = 5.1% − 1% = 4.1% Scenario 2 — 90-day INR rates evolve 5%,6%,4%,3% ; INR/USD 70 → 85: Foreign INR = (1+.05/4)(1+.06/4)(1+.04/4)(1+.03/4) − 1 = 4.6% FX: base-currency = INR. USD/INR 1/70 = 0.014286 → 1/85 = 0.011765 FX P/L = (0.011765/0.014286) − 1 = −17.6% Total = 4.6% − 1.0% − 17.6% = −14.0%
Carry-trade risk crystallised: a big depreciation of the high-rate currency (INR 70→85) wiped out the rate differential many times over → −14%. Classic flight-to-quality / market-crisis outcome.
Swaps for cross-currency views: receive-floating where you expect floating rates to rise, pay-floating where you expect them to fall; receive-fixed where you expect rates to fall, pay-fixed where you expect them to rise (basic duration comment). Watch FX risk doesn't exceed the rate advantage.
A framework for evaluating a yield curve strategy (P5.g)
Worked: CAD bullet vs barbell, US-based manager, 1yr
Ties Steps 1–3 + 5 together. Canadian zero-coupon bonds; expected stable curve.
BulletBarbell
Avg bond price96.7597
Expected price in 1yr (stable curve)98.7598.95
Expected effective duration4.894.92
Expected convexity28.543
Expected CAD bond yield change+0.25%+0.25%
Expected CAD vs USD−0.50%−0.50%
Step 1 Coupon: zeros → 0 for both Step 2 Rolldown: Bullet (98.75−96.75)/96.75 = 2.067% ; Barbell (98.95−97)/97 = 2.010% Step 3 Yield chg (ΔY=+.0025): Bullet (−4.89×.0025)+(½×28.5×.0025²) = −1.214% Barbell (−4.92×.0025)+(½×43×.0025²) = −1.217% Step 4 Spread: no info → 0 both Step 5 Currency (compound −0.50%): Bullet (1+.02067−.01214)(1−.005)−1 = 0.35% Barbell (1+.02010−.01217)(1−.005)−1 = 0.29%
Bullet outperforms by ~6bps. Driver: higher rolldown on the bullet (it sits on a steeper part of the curve → larger yield fall as it ages), not convexity — under a near-stable curve the convexity kicker (½·C·ΔY²) is tiny.
Exam note: this reading compounds Step 5 (multiplicative currency) whereas the earlier FI reading simply added it. Kaplan recommends the multiplicative approach here but says examiners are unlikely to penalise the additive one given the earlier reading used it.
Quiz decisive-detail bank
Trap isolation
Barbell outperforms bullet under BOTH up and down shifts (same duration, higher convexity) — Quiz P5.1 Q1 → C. Stable curve → receive-fixed swap to add duration/carry (Quiz P5.1 Q2 → A). "Least likely" under stable curve = reduce duration. Downward-shift view → receive-floating swap is the trade to AVOID; the manager wants long duration (receive-fixed / long call / long receiver swaption). Buys wings + sells body → expecting a NEGATIVE butterfly twist / curvature increase (Quiz P5.2 Q3 → C). Long short-term + short long-term, negative overall duration → bear steepener (Quiz P5.2 Q2 → B). Expecting upward shift → least likely to buy a putable bond? No — a putable is MOST attractive when rates rise (put floors the price). Least likely = the bond with no protection given the direction; know the callable/putable/option-free ranking (Quiz P5.3 Q1 → B putable is what you'd WANT, so "least likely to invest in" is the option-free/callable per the framing). Downward-shift view → long a call on bond futures or long receiver swaption; short a receiver swaption and long payer swaption are bearish (Quiz P5.3 Q2 → C).
Highest-frequency slip for you: under pressure, don't collapse "which bonds to buy/short" into "bull vs bear." Slope trades fix buy/short by steepener-vs-flattener; bull/bear only sets the overall duration sign. Curvature trades fix buy/short by body-vs-wings; the butterfly-spread/twist sign is the separate decisive detail.

Two approaches to credit risk modelling
Both estimate probability of default (POD) and derive fair credit spreads — from different angles.
StructuralReduced form
Core ideaAsset value falls below default thresholdMacro + financials → default intensity
Also calledDistance to default modelsIntensity models
Data sourceEquity market data (price, vol, mkt cap)Financial ratios, macro variables
OutputDaily POD + implied fair spreadDefault intensity → fair spread
ExamplesMoody's EDF, Bloomberg DRSKAltman z-score
Core intuition
A firm defaults when asset value falls below liabilities. Structural models track the asset value process and estimate the probability it crosses below the default threshold.
Why "distance to default"?
The model measures how far asset value is from the default threshold, in units of asset volatility.
Distance to default = (Asset value − Default threshold) / Asset volatility Higher distance → lower POD → tighter credit spread Lower distance → higher POD → wider credit spread
Inputs — inferred from equity markets
Asset value and volatility are unobservable. Equity = call option on firm assets → infer from equity data.
Market capitalization → proxy for asset value Equity price volatility → proxy for asset volatility
Examples
Moody's EDF — Expected Default Frequency, daily POD estimates Bloomberg DRSK — daily POD + implied fair credit spreads
Core intuition
Rather than modelling asset value, reduced form models look at statistical relationships between macro conditions, issuer financials, and observed defaults. Default is a surprise event whose intensity varies with observable inputs.
What they estimate
A default intensity — probability of default per unit time — as a function of observable variables.
Fair credit spread ≈ Default intensity × LGD
Inputs used
Macroeconomic conditions (GDP growth, credit conditions) Issuer financial ratios (leverage, coverage, profitability) Industry and sector characteristics
Key difference: reduced form models don't need equity market data — works for private firms, sovereigns, any issuer without listed equity.
Altman z-score formula
z = (1.2×A) + (1.4×B) + (3.3×C) + (0.6×D) + (0.999×E) A = Working capital / Total assets B = Retained earnings / Total assets C = EBIT / Total assets D = Market value of equity / Total liabilities E = Sales / Total assets
Interactive z-score calculator
A (WC/TA)0.20
B (RE/TA)0.20
C (EBIT/TA)0.10
D (MVE/TL)1.00
E (Sales/TA)1.00
Exam note: the formula is always given in the question. Focus on plugging in the inputs correctly and interpreting the z-score against the three bands.
Standardized fixed coupon
CDS contracts pay a standardized fixed coupon — makes settlement operationally straightforward. This is NOT the fair spread.
IG issuers → fixed coupon = 1% (100bps) per year HY issuers → fixed coupon = 5% (500bps) per year
The fixed coupon ≠ fair CDS spread. The difference is settled via an up-front payment at initiation.
Who pays whom at initiation?
Fair spread > fixed coupon → buyer pays up-front to seller (buyer pays below-market coupon, compensates upfront) Fair spread < fixed coupon → seller pays up-front to buyer (seller receives above-market coupon, compensates upfront) Fair spread = fixed coupon → no up-front payment
Inverse price / spread relationship
Spreads rise → protection more expensive → old contract (low fixed coupon) worth less → CDS price falls Spreads fall → old contract worth more → CDS price rises
Same logic as bonds: price and yield move in opposite directions.
Up-front premium formula
CDS spread > fixed coupon: Up-front = (CDS spread − fixed coupon) × EffSpreadDur → paid by protection BUYER to seller CDS spread < fixed coupon: Up-front = (fixed coupon − CDS spread) × EffSpreadDur → paid by protection SELLER to buyer
Intuition: up-front payment = PV of the difference between what you pay (fixed coupon) and what is fair (CDS spread), scaled by duration.
Interactive calculator

Fixed coupon
EffSpreadDur4.0
CDS price formula
CDS price ≈ 1 + [(fixed coupon − CDS spread) × EffSpreadDur]
Expressed as % of notional. Same inverse spread/price relationship as bonds.
Spread rises → (coupon − spread) more negative → price falls below 1 Spread falls → (coupon − spread) more positive → price rises above 1
