*Note: in the textbook table, "Source of risk: styles" is listed as Lower for Factor Diversified — this is because each individual style exposure is moderate (balanced across many factors). The factor RISK comes through clearly, but no single style dominates as a risk source.
Memory hook: think "where does the volatility live?" For Factor Diversified, it lives in MARKET beta (close to 1, broad exposure). For Sector Rotator, it lives in SECTOR bets and IDIOSYNCRATIC risk from concentrated names.
Why this matters — the alignment principle
✓ Risk budget allocated correctly: the sources of risk match the stated strategy ✗ Misallocation: e.g., a "factor diversified" fund whose risk comes mostly from sectors or single positions → the manager is making bets they didn't advertise → potential style drift
Diagnostic check (factor diversified fund): - Most active risk should come from factor exposures - Sector and idiosyncratic contributions should be LOW - Number of securities should be HIGH (hundreds) - Position concentration should be LOW → If any of these are off, the manager has a misalignment. Diagnostic check (sector rotator): - Most active risk from sector bets & concentrated positions - Style/factor contributions should be LOW - Number of securities LOW (tens) - Cash positions can be HIGH (tactical) → If factor risk dominates, the manager is closet factor-betting.
The 2 archetypes side by side — visual summary
Factor Diversified
Broad · diversified · factor-driven
  • Hundreds of securities
  • Low position concentration
  • Market beta ≈ 1
  • Active Share LOW, Active Risk LOW
  • Risk source: market & factors
  • Cash: very low
Sector Rotator
Concentrated · tactical · sector-driven
  • Tens of securities
  • High position concentration
  • Beta >1 or <1 (depends on tilt)
  • Active Share HIGH, Active Risk HIGH
  • Risk source: sectors & idiosyncratic
  • Cash: high when tactical (defensive)
Exam-ready cheat sheet
"Hundreds of securities, low concentration, beta ≈ 1" → Factor Diversified profile "Tens of securities, high concentration, high cash, sector bets" → Sector Rotator profile Active risk source dominated by SECTORS → Sector Rotator (or misaligned Factor Diversified) Active risk source dominated by MARKET → Factor Diversified (broad exposure) Active risk source dominated by IDIOSYNCRATIC/UNEXPLAINED → Sector Rotator (concentrated positions)
Common trap: confusing "high active risk" with "high factor exposure". A Sector Rotator can have very high active risk WITHOUT taking factor bets — the risk comes from idiosyncratic concentration, not from style tilts.
What makes a portfolio "well-constructed"
A well-constructed portfolio delivers the characteristics promised to investors in a cost-efficient and risk-efficient way. Four requirements:
✓ A clear investment philosophy and a consistent investment process ✓ Risk and structural characteristics as promised to investors (no style drift) ✓ Achieving desired risk exposures in the most efficient manner ✓ Reasonably low operating costs, given the strategy
"Risk-efficient" means you get the targeted exposures with as little extra (unintended) risk as possible. "Cost-efficient" means low fees AND low operating expenses for the type of strategy.
Comparing portfolios with the SAME desired characteristics
When two portfolios target the same exposures, three tie-breaker rules tell you which one is better-constructed:
ScenarioWhich portfolio wins?
Same desired exposures, but achieved with FEWER positions The one with fewer positions — more focus on risk management. Doesn't guarantee higher excess return, but indicates higher risk efficiency.
Similar risk factor exposures + similar costs Lower absolute volatility & lower active risk wins — same exposure, less noise.
Similar active risk + absolute risk + costs + alpha skill HIGHEST Active Share wins — leverages the manager's alpha skill more; higher expected return.
Memory anchor for the 3 tie-breakers: fewer positions → lower risk → higher Active Share. Each applies when EVERYTHING ELSE is equal.
Exam trap: the highest Active Share isn't always preferable. It's only preferable when the manager has REAL alpha skill AND when other risks/costs are similar. Without alpha skill, higher Active Share just means more uncompensated risk.
Part 2 · Long-Only, Long Extension, Long-Short, Market-Neutral
The four construction styles — at a glance
StyleLongShortNet exposureTypical
Long-only100%0%100%Traditional mutual funds, most active managers
Long extension130%30%100%130/30 funds — constrained long-short
Long-shortvariesvariesvariesGeneral — any portfolio that can short
Market-neutralvaries≈ longs≈ 0% (net beta ≈ 0)Stat arb, pairs trading, equity market neutral
Gross vs Net exposure — the two key metrics
Gross exposure = |Long| + |Short| (as % of capital) Net exposure = |Long| − |Short| (as % of capital)
Worked example (textbook): fund raises $100M. Invests $80M long, shorts $30M.
Long position: $80M = 80% of capital Short position: $30M = 30% of capital Gross exposure = 80% + 30% = 110% Net exposure = 80% − 30% = 50% Cash balance = $20M uninvested + $30M short sale proceeds = $50M
The short sale proceeds sit as cash (collateral with the lender). The "uninvested" portion is what wasn't put into longs. Both contribute to the cash balance.
The 130/30 long extension — the classic example
A long extension portfolio is a long-short fund constrained to 100% net exposure. The most common version: 130% long + 30% short = 130/30 fund.
→ Net exposure: 100% (130 − 30) — same market beta as a long-only fund → Gross exposure: 160% (130 + 30) — higher than long-only's 100% → Manager has no discretion over net exposure (it's fixed at 100%) → But can use 30% shorting to express negative views & finance the 130% long
Who picks 130/30? Investors who want full market exposure (100% beta) AND want the manager to be able to short. They get the upside of shorting without giving up the market risk premium.
Market-neutral portfolios — net beta ≈ 0
Market-neutral funds aim to remove market exposure by balancing long and short positions. Two ways to think about this:
Net beta zero: weighted average of long and short betas cancels out Equal beta-weighted longs & shorts: not just $-equal, but β-equal
Textbook example: Long $200M of assets with β = 0.9 → β-weighted long = $180M Short $150M of assets with β = 1.2 → β-weighted short = $180M → Net market beta = 0 ✓ → Gross exposure = $350M (much larger than longs alone) → If positions had EQUAL betas (size/value/etc.), net exposure = 0
Market-neutral isn't $100M long + $100M short. It's β-weighted long = β-weighted short. The example shows you can be net-beta-zero with UNEQUAL dollar amounts when betas differ.
In practice it's hard to maintain a zero beta over time because correlations between exposures change continually. Market-neutral funds rebalance frequently.
Market-neutral construction methods — pairs trading & stat arb
Pairs trading: buy and short securities of similar companies to exploit perceived mispricings (the relative bet hedges market exposure) Statistical arbitrage (stat arb): quantitative pairs trading — same idea but driven by quantitative signals across many pairs
Market-neutral funds are often used for diversification (low correlation with other strategies), not for high returns. They should have lower volatility than long-only strategies.
Part 3 · Benefits & drawbacks of long-short
Benefits of long-short strategies
BenefitWhy it matters
Express negative viewsLong-only manager: max underweight = security's benchmark weight. Long-short: no cap on negative bets → higher transfer coefficient (TC) → higher IR (fundamental law)
Leverage long ideasShort proceeds finance additional long positions → gear into high-conviction longs
Remove market riskMarket-neutral construction → diversifying investment against other strategies (low correlation)
Better control of factor exposuresMost rewarded factors (size, value, momentum) are long-short by construction. Shorting allows cleaner factor exposures.
The transfer coefficient point is key for the fundamental law of active management: IR ≈ IC × √breadth × TC. Removing the long-only constraint raises TC.
Drawbacks of long-short strategies
DrawbackWhat it means
Unlimited losses on shortsStock prices have NO upper bound → potential losses are unlimited; also reduces long-term exposure to market risk premium
Leverage magnifies lossesSome long-short strategies require significant leverage → both gains AND losses are amplified
Borrowing costsCost of borrowing securities can be high — especially for hard-to-borrow names
Collateral & forced liquidationLosses on shorts → lender demands more collateral → may force liquidation at unfavorable prices. Short squeeze risk: heavily-shorted stocks rise sharply, forcing covers that push prices even higher. Lenders can also recall shares at inopportune times.
RegulationsSome countries ban short selling in periods of financial instability
Transactional complexitySource borrow + post collateral + manage recalls + prime broker counterparty risk (if PB goes bankrupt, collateral may be lost)
Higher costsManagement fees + operational expenses higher than long-only
Personal ideologySome investors morally object to profiting from another company's failure
Exam trap: forgetting that short squeezes and share recalls are SEPARATE risks. Squeeze = price action forces you out. Recall = lender pulls the shares back. Both can disrupt the strategy at the worst moment.
Part 4 · The merits of long-only investing
Why some investors stay long-only
FactorLong-only advantage
Long-term risk premiumsMarket risk premium is earned by NET LONG investors. Long-term holders should be net long; short sellers suffer negative expected returns over long horizons. Long-only naturally captures the equity risk premium.
Capacity & scalabilityLong-only capacity = liquidity of underlying securities. Short strategies' capacity is limited by availability to borrow — typically much smaller than long-only capacity, especially for large-cap funds.
Limited legal liabilityMax loss for long investor = price paid (stock falls to zero, you lose 100%). For short seller: unlimited loss since prices have no ceiling. "Naked" short selling (no hedge) is riskier than long-only by definition.
Regulation & restrictionsMany institutional mandates and retail products don't permit shorting at all
Lower costs & complexityNo borrowing fees, no collateral, no prime broker counterparty risk
Short horizon investors worried about negative returns may PREFER strategies with short exposure (market-neutral, long-short). Long horizon investors should generally lean toward long-only or constrained long-short (130/30) to retain equity risk premium exposure.
Part 5 · Which approach for which investor?
Decision matrix — matching strategy to investor profile
Investor characteristicBest suited to...
Long-term horizon, wants market risk premiumLong-only (or 130/30 if wants shorting flexibility with full market exposure)
Wants 100% net market exposure + manager flexibilityLong extension (130/30)
Wants alpha without market risk; diversifierMarket-neutral
Short horizon, downside-sensitiveMarket-neutral or long-short
Moral / ideological objection to shortingLong-only
Strong manager alpha skill + similar risks across optionsHigher Active Share variant (long-short usually allows higher AS than long-only)
When selecting equity managers for a multi-asset fund: combine managers so the overall equity allocation is well-constructed. A risk factor exposure that's desired but missing in one manager can be added via a different manager that specializes in that factor.
The scale problem — why size impairs strategy
As a fund's AUM grows, the manager must own more dollars of each name. But each security has limits:
Index weight floor: strategy may forbid investing in tiny index names (below e.g. 0.02%) Position weight cap: maximum portfolio weight a single security can have (e.g. 10× index weight or +100bps) Liquidity cap: can't own more than X% of a security's average daily volume (ADV) without crippling market impact
When the fund grows large enough that the dollar position dictated by the weight cap exceeds the dollar amount allowed by the liquidity cap, the strategy is impaired — you can't fill the position without moving the price.
Small-cap focused funds hit this wall earlier than large-cap funds (smaller ADV, smaller market cap). Solutions: limit AUM, diversify further, lower turnover, or change trading style.
Worked example — Issues of Scale (textbook)
A diversified multifactor fund: $200M AUM, 350 positions. Benchmark = large-to-mid-cap index, 1,000 constituents, total market cap ≈ $20 trillion. Smaller index securities trade ~1.5% of shares daily.
#Constraint
1No investment in any security with index weight < 0.02%
2Max fund position = lesser of (10 × index weight) or (index weight + 100 bps)
3Absolute position size cannot exceed 5% of ADV (trailing 12 months)
Question: at what AUM is the strategy impaired by illiquidity?
Step-by-step walkthrough — click "Next step" to animate
Step 0 / 5
1What's the SMALLEST market cap I'm allowed to invest in?
Constraint 1 says: no security with index weight < 0.02%. The smallest allowed has weight exactly 0.02% of the index.
Smallest mkt cap = 0.02% × total index mkt cap = 0.0002 × $20 trillion = $4 billion
→ Smallest allowed market cap = $4 billion
2What's the ADV of that smallest name?
The smaller securities trade 1.5% of shares outstanding daily. For a $4bn cap stock:
ADV = 1.5% × $4 billion = 0.015 × $4,000,000,000 = $60 million
→ Daily trading volume ≈ $60 million
3What's the MAX dollar position I can hold (liquidity limit)?
Constraint 3 caps the position at 5% of ADV — beyond this, market impact becomes punishing.
Max position $ = 5% × ADV = 0.05 × $60 million = $3 million
→ Max dollar position in the smallest cap holding = $3M
4What does the STRATEGY tell me to hold (weight cap)?
Constraint 2: max position weight = lesser of (10 × index weight) or (index weight + 100 bps). For the smallest stock at 0.02% index weight:
Option A: 10 × 0.02% = 0.2% Option B: 0.02% + 1.00% = 1.02% Lesser of the two = 0.2%
→ Strategy wants up to 0.2% of fund in the smallest holding
5At what AUM does the strategy break?
Set the two binding constraints equal: the dollar position the strategy wants (0.2% × AUM) cannot exceed the $3M liquidity cap.
0.2% × AUM ≤ $3,000,000 0.002 × AUM ≤ $3,000,000 AUM ≤ $3,000,000 / 0.002 AUM ≤ $1.5 billion
→ Strategy is impaired when AUM exceeds $1.5 billion
Above $1.5bn, the manager is constrained by small-cap illiquidity and CAN'T hold the maximum 0.2% weight allowed by the strategy. They'll have to underweight small caps relative to the model — style drift.
Visual logic chain
Interactive — change the parameters
Adjust any input below. The maximum AUM updates live.
Total index mkt cap ($T)$20T
Min index weight (%)0.02%
Daily volume (% of shares)1.5%
Max position vs ADV (%)5%
Weight cap multiplier (× idx)10×
Weight cap bps add-on100 bps
Try lowering total mkt cap to $5T (e.g. an emerging market index) — the AUM ceiling drops dramatically. Or raise the daily volume to 5% (more liquid market) and watch capacity expand.
Exam-ready memory anchors
The chain: min index weight × total mkt cap = smallest stock's mkt cap → × daily volume % = ADV → × position-vs-ADV cap = max $ position Then: max $ position ÷ max portfolio weight = AUM ceiling Why this matters: if a fund's AUM exceeds this ceiling, it physically can't hold its smallest names at the weight the strategy specifies → style drift forced by liquidity Small-cap funds hit the ceiling EARLIER than large-cap funds because ADVs are smaller and prices move more on the same trade size Solutions for funds approaching capacity: limit AUM (close fund to new investors) · diversify into more names · lower turnover · adapt trading strategy (slower execution, dark pools)
Exam trap: "higher market impact cost is associated with lower AUM" → FALSE. Higher AUM = need to trade more $ at once = more market impact. Also: large-cap securities have LOWER impact cost (more liquid). Higher portfolio TURNOVER = more trades = more impact cost.
Three sources of active return
SourceDriven byBuilding block
1. Strategic exposure to rewarded factors (beta, size, value, liquidity…)Risk premia — now cheap via rules-based index, so no longer alphaFactor weightings
2. Tactical exposure to mispricings (securities, sectors, factors)Alpha → manager skillAlpha skills
3. Idiosyncratic risk from concentrated positionsLuckPosition sizing
Active return is positive when you overweight outperformers and underweight underperformers — it's driven by the differences in weights vs the benchmark.
The building blocks + breadth
BlockWhat it is
Factor weightingsRewarded-factor exposures that differ from benchmark (active return from Δbeta). Maps to source #1.
Alpha skillsSkill — esp. factor timing (when a factor will out/underperform), incl. unrewarded factors (geography, sector, commodities, security selection). Maps to source #2.
Position sizingBalances conviction vs idiosyncratic risk. Smaller positions in more names → diversify away idiosyncratic risk → lower vol.
Breadth of expertise ties them together — the fundamental law of active management: more independent decisions (higher breadth) → higher active return. Factor manager spreads wide (minimizes idiosyncratic risk); stock-picker concentrates (deliberately takes idiosyncratic risk).
Active Share vs Active Risk — the key comparison
Active ShareActive Risk (tracking error)
Definition½ Σ|wp − wb| (0 to 1)SD of (pf − benchmark) returns
MeasuresHow different the holdings are from the benchHow consistent performance is vs bench
Affected by correlations?NOYES (cross-correlations, variances)
Manager controlFull (controls weights)Not full (predicted risk needs estimates that may not realize)
Active Share = ½ Σ |w_p − w_b|
Same bench, both invest only in bench securities → the pf with fewer/more concentrated positions has higher Active Share. Active Share is used to judge fee-per-unit-of-active-management: AS 0.2 is "expensive" vs AS 0.5 at the same fee. Factor bets necessarily raise Active Share, but high Active Share does NOT imply factor bets were taken.
Active risk composition + manager-style fingerprints
Research conclusion on active return
High net factor exposure → high active risk
No net factor exposure → active risk attributed entirely to Active Share
Active risk from Active Share is inversely proportional to # of securities
Active risk rises as factor & idiosyncratic risk levels rise
StyleConstraint fingerprint
Sector rotatorLarge permitted sector-weight deviations
Stock pickerLarge permitted individual-security deviations
Diversified multifactorModerate flexibility (not large) — moderate active risk
Closet indexerLow targeted active risk + low deviation
Risk budgeting — absolute vs relative
Process: (1) pick the right risk measure for the mandate → (2) understand each strategy's risk contribution → (3) set the overall budget level → (4) allocate risk across positions/factors.
Absolute riskRelative / active risk
WhenObjective in total returns (e.g., L/S vs cash + margin)Objective is to beat an index
Contribution of asset iCVi = wi·Cip (= Σ wiwjCij)CAVi = (wpi − wbi)·RCip
Sums toPortfolio varianceActive variance (AVp)
CVi = wi · Cip (absolute) CAVi = (wpi − wbi) · RCip (active) RCip = Σ(wpi − wbi)RCij
Active variance uses active risk, not absolute SD. Cash has tiny SD but ~2× the active risk of the indexes (low correlation to the bench) → cash can contribute 100% of active variance. And if the bench = equal-weight of Index A & B, the active returns of A and B are correlated −1 (one above bench ⇒ the other below).
Determining the appropriate level of risk
FactorEffect
Implementation constraintsShort/leverage limits cap under/overweights; liquidity costs rise with active risk → degrade the info ratio
Limited diversificationConcave efficient frontier — higher risk/return targets run out of high-return ideas → falling Sharpe
LeverageFixes diversification in one period, but in multi-period too much leverage lowers compounded return
Rg ≈ Ra − vol² / 2
Leverage raises both Ra and vol, but the vol² term means past a point, more leverage reduces geometric compounded return over time.
Risk measures — heuristic vs formal
Heuristic (experience-based)Formal (statistical)
Limits on position / sector / region exposure, leverage, liquidity, turnoverLimits on vol, active risk, skewness, drawdown, VaR-family
No return-distribution forecast neededRequire forecasts → estimation error
VaR familyMeaning
CVaRExpected loss given VaR is exceeded (expected tail loss / shortfall)
IVaRChange in VaR from adding a new position
Marginal VaRImpact of a very small change in a position size on VaR
Leverage magnifies the cost of bad risk estimates — tail events can force liquidation at the worst time. Few-position pfs have higher estimation error → formal measures are harder to apply. Style matters: absolute-return/benchmark-agnostic manager cares little about drawdown; market-neutral manager targets a tight absolute-vol band.
Implicit costs — market impact & slippage
Market impact = the price move your own trade causes. Driven by: AUM vs security cap (small-caps = liquidity barrier for big AUM), higher turnover / shorter horizon, and trades that signal "information" to others.
Slippage facts
= execution price − midpoint of bid-ask when the trade was entered
Usually higher than explicit costs
Greater for small-cap than large-cap
NOT necessarily greater in EM
Substantially higher in high volatility
Small-cap strategy hitting capacity from rising slippage → manager should close the fund to new money or warn that the strategy may change. Broadly: a small-cap firm must limit AUM, diversify, limit turnover, or adapt trading as AUM grows.
Your errors are not 11 isolated mistakes — they're 4 patterns
I analyzed your 11 wrong answers. They cluster into 4 recurring error types. Fix the patterns, fix the questions.
Pattern 1 · Confusing similar-sounding concepts
You mix up concepts that look alike but mean different things.
ConfusionAffected Qs
Alpha vs Active ReturnQ19 (Fraser, you said −0.17%, correct = −0.20%)
Active Risk vs Active Share vs Total VolatilityQ14 (Fund A/B), Ash/Blue/March
What reduces volatility vs what reduces active riskAsh/Blue/March — low covariance reduces volatility but you need HIGH covariance to reduce active risk
Top-down vs Bottom-up when description has BOTHQ Soar (occasional macro doesn't make it top-down)
Diagnostic: when you see two words that "feel close" in a question, STOP and write the formula or definition for each before answering.
Pattern 2 · Variance/Covariance contribution formula
You missed the multi-factor variance decomposition 3 times — same formula, different vignettes.
QuestionWhat was askedCorrect answer
Q20 HerrickCountry A's contribution to portfolio variance47.5%
Q25 LSMEMarket factor's contribution to variance9%
Q30 Fund 1Market factor's contribution to total risk87%
The formula every time: Contribution of factor k = w_k × Σ_j (w_j × Cov(k, j)) (sum across ALL other factors, including itself) Then: Proportion = Contribution / Total portfolio variance (= σ²_portfolio)
Memory anchor: it's a row of the covariance matrix × the weight vector, then × the weight of factor k again. Never just w_k × Cov(k,k) — that's the trap that gives wrong answers.
Pattern 3 · Classifying a strategy from a description
You misclassify fund descriptions when the wording is ambiguous.
FundYour answer (wrong)CorrectThe key signal
SoarTop-down systematicBottom-up systematic"Security-specific factors" = bottom-up. Low idiosyncratic + low concentration = systematic.
FraserBalanced factor exposureFirm-specific (pricing power)"Discretionary" → firm-specific. Balanced factor = systematic.
AE vs CCMomentum tiltAE = concentrated stock-picking, CC = concentrated factor-bettingCC has R²=0.98 (factors dominate). AE has R²=0.72 + 42 names (idiosyncratic dominates).
Decision tree: (1) Does it use security-specific or macro factors? → bottom-up vs top-down. (2) Rule-based or judgement? → systematic vs discretionary. (3) Concentrated or diversified? → tells you stock-picker vs factor-better.
Pattern 4 · Scale & liquidity arithmetic
You got the chained calculations right (40 days for Reed) but you missed the strategic ANALYSIS in the Voyager question.
For Voyager: 2 concerns were (1) cash size vs total market cap of holdings ($1.1bn vs $800M), (2) daily volume vs shares outstanding (<0.1% means high impact for any large trade) You said "cash has low correlation with benchmark" — that's not a recognized issue. Cash is uninvested capital; the issue is whether you can DEPLOY it without market impact.
Memory anchor: when you see new contributions vs current holdings, ALWAYS compare to (a) total market cap of current positions and (b) average daily volume of those positions. These are the two capacity constraints.
Pattern 1 deep-drill · The concept confusions
a. Alpha vs Active Return
DefinitionFormula
Active ReturnPortfolio return minus benchmark returnR_A = R_p − R_b
AlphaReturn NOT explained by rewarded factorsα = R_p − Σ(β_k × F_k)
Q19 Fraser walkthrough: R_p = 0.55%, R_b = 0.72%. Factor return = (0.91×0.61) + (0.15×0.17) + (0.60×0.18) + (0.08×0.72) = 0.75%. So active return = 0.55 − 0.72 = −0.17% BUT alpha = 0.55 − 0.75 = −0.20%. Different concepts, different math.
b. Active Risk vs Active Share vs Volatility
What it measuresReduces if...
Active ShareWeight difference vs benchmarkPortfolio weights closer to benchmark
Active Risk (tracking error)Volatility of (R_p − R_b)Higher COVARIANCE with benchmark
Total Volatilityσ(R_p) — standalone portfolio riskLower correlation between holdings
Ash/Blue/March walkthrough: To minimize ACTIVE risk of total Amity fund after substitution → pick fund with HIGH covariance with Amity (Ash). Low covariance (Blue, March) reduces total volatility but NOT active risk.
c. Sector bets affect which?
Sector bets → Active Risk (yes) → Active Share (yes, only if weights differ) But: same Active Share + very different Active Risk = different sector/idiosyncratic profile Fund A active risk 3× Fund B with same Active Share → A makes sector bets, NOT B
Pattern 2 deep-drill · The variance contribution formula
This formula appears in 3 different forms but it's always the same logic. Learn it once.
FORMULA: Contribution of factor k to portfolio variance = w_k × [w_k × Var(k) + Σ_{j≠k} w_j × Cov(k,j)] = w_k × [Σ_j w_j × Cov(k,j)] ← combines into one clean form Where the bracket [...] is the covariance of factor k with the WHOLE portfolio: Cov(k, portfolio) = Σ_j w_j × Cov(k,j) So: Contribution_k = w_k × Cov(k, portfolio) Proportion_k = Contribution_k / Var(portfolio)
Q20 Herrick worked example: For Country A with weight 30%, the covariance with portfolio (given) = 0.0276. Contribution = 0.30 × 0.0276 = 0.00828. Portfolio variance = 0.132² = 0.01742. Proportion = 0.00828 / 0.01742 = 47.5%.
Q30 Fund 1 worked example: Market factor β = 1.080. Sum all 4 covariance terms (×βs):
1.080×0.00109×1.080 = 0.001271
1.080×0.00053×0.098 = 0.000056
1.080×0.00022×(−0.401) = −0.000095
1.080×(−0.00025)×0.034 = −0.0000092
Sum (Contribution) = 0.001223
Total variance = 0.0374² = 0.001399. Proportion = 0.001223 / 0.001399 = 87%.
Common errors: (a) using just w_k² × Var(k) without the cross-terms → wrong. (b) Forgetting to multiply by w_k at the end → gives the bracket value alone. (c) Forgetting to square σ → gives wrong denominator.
Pattern 3 deep-drill · Fund classification decision tree
Signal in descriptionPoints to
"Security-specific factors / individual securities first"Bottom-up
"Macro / sectors / countries first"Top-down
"Occasionally considers macro" + bottom-up primaryStill bottom-up
"Discretionary / judgement / firm-specific (e.g., pricing power)"Discretionary
"Systematic / rule-based / broad universe / formal optimization"Systematic
"Low idiosyncratic risk + low concentration"Systematic (high N, diversified)
"Concentrated + high Active Share + low R²"Concentrated stock-picking
"Concentrated + high R² (factors dominate)"Concentrated factor-betting
AE vs CC walkthrough: AE has R²=0.72 (factors explain only 72% of variance, idiosyncratic dominates) + 42 names + Active Share 0.92 → concentrated stock-picking. CC has R²=0.98 (factors explain 98%) + 124 names + Active Share 0.71 → concentrated factor-betting. The R² is the deciding signal.
Pattern 4 deep-drill · Capacity & cash deployment
Two questions you have to ask when new contributions arrive:
Q1: Is the new cash large relative to the total market cap of current holdings? → If yes, the strategy might not be able to deploy the cash within its current universe Q2: Is the daily trading volume large enough to absorb the deployment? → If daily volume is <0.1% of shares outstanding, even modest position sizes will move the price
Voyager numbers: Current portfolio holdings total mkt cap = 500 + 200 + 100 = $800M New cash contribution = $1,100M (= $1.1bn) → New cash > total mkt cap of existing holdings ✗ capacity issue → ADV of A,B,C all < 0.1% of shares outstanding ✗ impact issue
When asked "discuss concerns about new contributions", the 2 answers should always be: (1) size relative to holdings' market cap (can you deploy?) and (2) liquidity relative to ADV (can you trade without impact?). Don't reach for "correlation" or "active variance" — those aren't the structural issues.

Reference prices — what they are and why we need them
A reference price is a benchmark price used to (1) determine expected trading costs before trading, (2) select the optimal trading strategy, and (3) calculate the actual cost of trading for post-trade evaluation.
A trade's "cost" = execution price minus reference price. Choice of reference price drives what you measure. 4 categories based on WHEN the reference is set: Pre-trade, Intraday, Post-trade, Price target.
The category dictates the manager's INTENT: pre-trade = "what did I expect when I decided?", intraday = "how well did I participate?", post-trade = "tracking the close", price-target = "earn alpha vs fair value".
Animated trading day — click "Reveal next" to see each benchmark in order
0 / 8 benchmarks shown
PRE-TRADEDecision price
Price of the security at the moment the portfolio manager made the investment decision. The earliest "anchor" in the workflow.
Use case: standard benchmark for measuring implementation shortfall.
PRE-TRADEPrevious close
Yesterday's closing price. A proxy for decision price often used by quantitative systematic managers running rule-based, data-driven strategies (decisions are made overnight from data ending at prior close).
Use case: quant funds where the decision is generated by the data of D−1.
PRE-TRADEOpening price
Today's open. Often used as a proxy for decision price by subjective fundamental managers chasing long-term alpha — it doesn't punish or reward traders for overnight news.
Use case: long-term fundamental managers who want a "neutral" reference unaffected by overnight news.
Trap: if the TRADE itself goes into an opening auction, then the opening auction price IS affected by the trade → opening price is NOT a good benchmark in that case.
PRE-TRADEArrival price
Price at the exact moment the order is sent to the market for execution. Active managers trying to generate alpha will often pick arrival price as the benchmark.
Use case: alpha-driven active managers; tightest implementation shortfall measure.
INTRADAYVWAP — Volume-Weighted Average Price
Average price of all trades, weighted by volume, over the trading horizon. Managers use VWAP when they want to participate with normal volume patterns.
Use case: rebalancing over a day · using sell-side cash to fund buy-side · low-information urgency trades.
Why VWAP fits rebalancing: you're not pursuing alpha, you're trying to be representative of how the market actually traded that day.
INTRADAYTWAP — Time-Weighted Average Price
Equal-weighted average price across the trading horizon — ignores volume. Managers use TWAP to remove the impact of outlier trades (large blocks at highs/lows) and during highly volatile volume conditions.
Use case: thinly traded names · highly fluctuating volume · when manager can't participate in extreme block trades.
VWAP vs TWAP: same averaging idea, but VWAP weights by volume, TWAP weights by time. If volume is steady, they converge. If there's a giant block, VWAP gets pulled toward it; TWAP doesn't.
POST-TRADEClosing price
End-of-day price. Most frequent post-trade benchmark. Often used by managers who execute AT the close to reduce tracking error vs the benchmark index (which is also marked to close).
Use case: index funds / index-tracking strategies that fundamentally want zero tracking error.
Drawback: the closing price isn't known until AFTER trading is done → manager cannot assess trading performance DURING the day. Post-trade only.
PRICE TARGETPrice target benchmark
A price reflecting the manager's view of fair value. Profit-seeking managers chasing short-term alpha will use a price target benchmark.
Example: Current price: $10 Manager's fair value: $10.50 Strategy: buy as many shares as possible BELOW $10.50
Use case: short-term alpha extraction · "buy under fair value" or "sell over fair value" tactical strategies.

Exam traps to remember
Opening auction trap: opening price is normally a good pre-trade benchmark, but if the trade is executed AS PART of the opening auction, the trade itself moves the auction price → it's no longer a clean benchmark.
Closing price post-trade drawback: the closing price benchmark is unknowable until trading ends → managers can't evaluate trading performance during the horizon, only after.
VWAP vs TWAP confusion: VWAP weights by volume; TWAP weights equally over time. TWAP is the right choice when you want to avoid being dragged by large blocks at the highs/lows.
Memory anchor for category → use: Pre-trade = "how good was my decision-vs-execution?" · Intraday = "how well did I participate?" · Post-trade = "where did the day close?" · Price target = "did I beat fair value?"
The selection framework — match trading strategy to the trade's purpose
Every trade has a purpose. The trading strategy (urgency level, reference price benchmark, execution method) should fit that purpose.
Urgency is not a single number — it's the result of 4-5 underlying drivers. Each card below shows the drivers so you see WHY each trade type has its urgency level.
The 5 urgency drivers — what makes a trade urgent or not
DriverRaises urgency when...Lowers urgency when...
Market liquidityLiquid market (you can move fast)Illiquid market (forces patience to avoid impact)
Time horizonShort window (intraday, fixed deadline)Long window (weeks, months)
Directional exposureOne-sided trade (open risk during execution)Two-sided rebalance (no directional risk)
Alpha decay riskFast decay (mispricing closes in minutes)Slow decay (thesis plays out over months) or N/A
Information leakage costLiquid market absorbs your trades anonymouslyDealers see your size and front-run you
Drivers can conflict (e.g. illiquid market raises leakage cost AND raises impact cost — both push toward LOW urgency / slow execution). The dominant driver determines the overall urgency.
Reveal the 5 trade types one by one
0 / 5 trade types shown
URGENCY: HIGH Short-term alpha
Objective: Trade short-term mispricing in a liquid equity market (e.g. overreaction to news flow).
⚙️ Why urgency is HIGH — the drivers
Market liquidity→HIGH (liquid equity)
Time horizon→VERY SHORT (intraday)
Directional exposure→YES — one-sided alpha bet
Alpha decay risk→FAST — minutes to hours
Information leakage cost→Tolerable (liquid market absorbs)
Reference price: Price target benchmark (manager's fair value) + Arrival price for orders placed in the market
Execution method: Computer algorithm (fast, automated, low-latency)
URGENCY: LOW Long-term alpha
Objective: Trade over the long term due to changes in fundamental conditions (e.g. sell average-sized positions in illiquid bonds expected to experience deteriorating credit over the next year).
⚙️ Why urgency is LOW — the drivers
Market liquidity→LOW (illiquid bonds)
Time horizon→LONG (weeks to a year)
Directional exposure→YES but slow-moving thesis
Alpha decay risk→SLOW — months
Information leakage cost→HIGH (dealers move prices on you)
Reference price: Difficult to use in practice (no clean anchor over weeks/months)
Execution method: Sell securities gradually over a few weeks in small parts to avoid information leakage and pressure on dealer's prices
Key tension: liquidity is LOW (which would normally raise urgency to "do it quickly before market moves") but leakage cost is HIGH (which forces patience). Patience wins → low urgency, slow execution.
URGENCY: LOW Risk rebalance
Objective: Rebalance or hedge risk exposure (e.g. reduce risk in liquid FX markets by liquidating long AND short positions to bring fund volatility down to a target level).
⚙️ Why urgency is LOW — the drivers
Market liquidity→HIGH (liquid FX markets)
Time horizon→FLEXIBLE (a couple of days)
Directional exposure→NO — both buying AND selling
Alpha decay risk→N/A — not an alpha trade
Execution risk→LOW (two-sided neutralizes risk)
Reference price: TWAP
Execution method: Algorithmically target TWAP over the next couple of days
Key insight: even though it's a "trade", a two-sided rebalance has NO directional exposure → very low execution risk. One-sided rebalances would carry higher urgency because the trader IS exposed during execution.
URGENCY: DAY-END DEADLINE Cash flow driven · Client redemption
Objective: Liquidate holdings to meet client redemptions (e.g. liquidate small-cap fund to meet redemptions calculated using the closing prices of portfolio securities). The fund bears the risk that liquidations are NOT made at the closing prices used to calculate the redemption.
⚙️ Why urgency is DAY-END — the drivers
Market liquidity→VARIABLE (small-cap → low)
Time horizon→FIXED to TODAY's close
Directional exposure→YES — must SELL to fund payout
Alpha decay risk→N/A — not an alpha trade
NAV tracking risk→HIGH if missing close price
Reference price: Closing price
Execution method: Execute a reasonable amount of liquidity in the closing auction; execute the remainder before the close of trading (e.g. at VWAP)
Risk to watch: if the close auction can't absorb all the volume, the rest is traded earlier in the day → may not hit the close benchmark → tracking error to NAV calculation.
URGENCY: IMMEDIATE EXPOSURE Cash flow driven · New trade mandate
Objective: Invest new client funds (e.g. invest large amount with a mandate to track a small-cap index with 3% tracking error). Performance measurement begins at today's closing price.
⚙️ Why urgency is IMMEDIATE — the drivers
Market liquidity→LOW in underlying (small-cap)
Market liquidity (futures)→HIGH (index futures)
Time horizon→EXPOSURE: NOW · Build: weeks
Directional exposure→YES — must BUY the index
Cash drag risk→HIGH if uninvested
Tracking error budget→3% (limits how slow you can go)
Reference price: Closing price
Execution method: (1) Obtain immediate exposure to the index via a LONG position in index futures to eliminate cash drag; (2) build underlying stock positions OVER TIME to reduce market impact; (3) simultaneously unwind the futures position as cash is deployed
Two issues: (1) there may not be a closing auction for the futures contract, so the futures trade has to be done as close to the market close as possible; (2) the mandate must allow derivatives positions.
The split urgency is the key insight: the EXPOSURE is immediate (so futures bridge), but the underlying BUILD is slow (small-cap illiquidity). Two different speeds, one trade.

If the trade description says...Driver signal→ Urgency→ Strategy hint
"Exploiting overreaction / mispricing in liquid market"High liquidity + fast alpha decayHIGHAlgorithm + arrival/price target

Exam traps for trading strategy selection
High urgency ≠ always bad: short-term alpha REQUIRES high urgency. Slowing down kills the alpha. Don't recommend TWAP for an alpha-extraction trade.
Rebalance ≠ urgent: even though it's a "trade", a two-sided risk rebalance has LOW urgency because there's no directional exposure. Recommending arrival-price aggressive execution would be wrong.
Long-term alpha has NO clean reference price: this is intentional — over weeks, no single benchmark works. The strategy is about avoiding leakage, not about hitting a price.
Cash flow redemption AND new mandate both use closing price but for different reasons: redemption = NAV strike, new mandate = performance start. Same benchmark, different urgency profiles.
Memory anchor by urgency level: High → short-term alpha · Low → long-term alpha + risk rebalance · End-of-day → cash flow redemption · Immediate via derivative → new mandate.
Two big families of trade execution
Once you've picked the strategy (urgency + reference price), you still need to choose HOW to execute. Two broad approaches: high-touch (human-intensive) vs electronic (computer-driven).
High-touchElectronic
Human involvementHIGH — traders, dealers, brokersLOW — algorithms + systems
Best forLarge trades (block trades), illiquid marketsMore liquid markets, smaller trades
Why high-touch?Finding the OTHER side of large/illiquid trades requires discretion + relationshipsOrder book + algos can find counterparties efficiently
Market typeQuote-driven (dealers post quotes)Order-driven (limit orders in CLOB)
Same trade, two paths: large illiquid → high-touch. Small liquid → electronic. The trade size relative to market liquidity is the master variable.
High-touch sub-types — Principal vs Agency
When you go high-touch, there are 2 ways the broker can act:
PRINCIPAL · BROKER RISK Principal trade (broker risk trade)
Mechanism: The dealer/market maker takes the OTHER side of your trade onto their own book — they assume the risk. Their compensation is baked into the bid-ask spread.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Market structure→Quote-driven · OTC · off-exchange
Urgency→HIGH (need immediate fill)
Liquidity→LOW or fragmented
Risk transfer→Broker absorbs execution risk
Also used in: Request-for-quote (RFQ) markets — market makers don't post continuous quotes but provide them on request
AGENCY Agency trade
Mechanism: The broker SEARCHES for the other side of the trade. They earn a commission but the execution risk stays with the portfolio manager/trader.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Urgency→LOWER (can wait for natural counterparty)
Risk transfer→PM still bears execution risk
Cost structure→Commission (often tighter than spread)
Discretion→Broker uses judgement / network
Memory anchor: PRINCIPAL = broker BUYS your risk (urgent, illiquid). AGENCY = broker FINDS your buyer (patient, less urgent).
Electronic trading basics
Order-driven markets: buyers and sellers post limit orders to a Central Limit Order Book (CLOB). Trades match when orders cross. Limit order: trade only at a specific price OR BETTER. Buy with limit $20 → execute up to $20. Sell with limit $20 → execute at $20 or higher. Direct Market Access (DMA): buy-side traders access the order book DIRECTLY through a broker's technology infrastructure (no broker manual intervention). Algorithmic trading: programmed rules execute orders electronically (covered in the next tab).
Why electronic dominates in liquid markets: low cost, fast, transparent, scalable. Why it fails for blocks: a large limit order on the book reveals your hand and moves the price against you (information leakage).
Quick decision matrix
Trade profileApproachSub-type
Large block, illiquid market, urgentHigh-touchPrincipal (broker risk)
Large block, illiquid market, can waitHigh-touchAgency
Small order, liquid market, urgentElectronicArrival price algo or SOR
Small order, liquid market, can waitElectronicScheduled algo (VWAP/TWAP/POV)
OTC derivatives, FX dealer marketHigh-touchPrincipal (RFQ)
Algorithmic trading — the 2 big purposes
Algorithmic trading = programmed rules to electronically trade orders. Two purposes:
Profit-seeking algos: use real-time market data to decide what to buy/sell. Used by electronic market makers, quant funds, HFTs. Execution algos: trade according to manager rules to meet the manager's objectives. This is what the exam focuses on.
All 5 algo types below are EXECUTION algos. They don't decide WHAT to trade — the manager already decided. They decide HOW to slice it.
The 5 execution algorithm types — animation
0 / 5 algorithms shown
SCHEDULED Scheduled algorithms — POV, VWAP, TWAP
Execute according to rules based on historical volumes or specified time periods. Trade passively throughout the day.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Order size→SMALL relative to ADV
Market liquidity→HIGH (liquid market)
Urgency→LOW (longer horizons tolerated)
Concern→Minimize market impact
3 sub-types:
POV (Percent of Volume / participation): send orders to be e.g. 5% of traded volume. Advantage: auto-exploits liquidity when available. Disadvantage: trades at any (potentially adverse) price; may not fill if volume is low.
VWAP (time-slicing on volume profile): carves up trade based on HISTORICAL intraday volumes — more at open/close, less midday. Advantage: ensures specified shares executed in specified time. Disadvantage: may force trades in low liquidity, miss high liquidity windows.
TWAP (time-slicing equal): equal shares per time period (e.g. each hour). Same advantage/disadvantage as VWAP but volume-insensitive.
LIQUIDITY-SEEKING Liquidity-seeking algorithms (opportunistic)
Take advantage of favorable liquidity when it's offered. For a buyer: wait until a large seller appears, then enter a market order. Use BOTH lit and dark venues.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Order size→LARGER
Market liquidity→LESS LIQUID (sporadic episodes)
Urgency→HIGHER
Information leakage concern→HIGH (don't want to display limit orders)
Market impact concern→Mitigated by trading only when liquidity is offered
Memory anchor: "I'm hungry, I'll wait for the buffet" — only trades when the other side shows up.
ARRIVAL PRICE Arrival price algorithms
Seek to trade close to market prices prevailing at the time the order is entered. Trade MORE AGGRESSIVELY (faster) than other algos, with more shares executed close to the arrival price.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Order size→SMALL (less than 15% of expected volume)
Market liquidity→HIGH (liquid market)
Manager view→Prices likely to MOVE AGAINST during horizon
Profile→Profit-seeking OR risk-averse minimizing execution risk
Memory anchor: "lock in the price NOW before it gets away" — aggressive, frontloaded execution.
DARK / AGGREGATOR Dark strategies / liquidity aggregators
Execute trades in dark pools with aggregator algorithms optimizing across multiple dark venues. No order book exposure → no information leakage.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Order size→LARGE
Market liquidity→ILLIQUID lit markets
Execution speed→LOWER probability of immediate fill
Urgency→CAN WAIT (no need for immediate full fill)
Alternative algos→Arrival/scheduled would cause high impact
Memory anchor: "hide and seek in private rooms" — patience trades anonymity for completion risk.
SMART ORDER ROUTER Smart Order Routers (SORs)
Determine the BEST DESTINATION (lit or dark venue) to route an electronic order. For market orders → best price. For limit orders → highest probability of execution.
⚙️ When this is the right choice — the drivers
Order size→SMALL
Market impact→LOW
Market dynamics→Fast-moving market (for market orders)
Multi-venue→Multiple potential execution venues
Info leakage→LOW concern (small orders don't move markets)
Memory anchor: "GPS for your order" — find the cheapest/fastest route across many venues.

SFDL → Liquidity-seeking algorithm
⚙️ Why — the drivers
Order size vs ADV→50% (HIGH — big order)
Liquidity→LOW (ADV 20k is small)
Urgency→HIGH
Market impact concern→HIGH (must minimize)
Why this algo: trades only when liquidity is offered by the other side → minimizes market impact for a large order in a thin market. High urgency means execution should still occur relatively quickly when liquidity appears.
TWEL → Scheduled algorithm (POV, VWAP, or TWAP)
⚙️ Why — the drivers
Order size vs ADV→5% (LOW)
Liquidity→RELATIVELY HIGH
Urgency→LOW
Adverse price concern→LOW (long horizon OK)
Why this algo: low urgency means we can tolerate longer trading horizons. Low order size + high liquidity means a scheduled algo can passively trade throughout the day → minimizes market impact cost. Perfect fit.
UDSL → High-touch principal approach
⚙️ Why — the drivers
Order size vs ADV→100% (= entire daily volume)
Information leakage→EXTREME risk if displayed
Market impact→PROHIBITIVE for any algo
Discretion needed→YES — find a natural counterparty
Why this approach: 100% of ADV = an algorithm would either dump the price (information leakage) or take days to fill (and still leak). Need a human intermediary with relationships to find the other side of a block trade discreetly. The dealer takes on the principal risk and prices it into the spread.

Recent developments — ML in algorithmic trading
Clustering
Machine learning technique where a computer learns to identify which algorithm is optimal for different trade types, based on key features.
How it works: groups trades together with similar attributes (e.g. order size as a fraction of ADV). Then quantitatively tests factors for their impact on the performance of different algorithms.
Key value: clustering can identify features that a human manager hadn't previously considered important.
High-frequency market forecasting
Attempts to model short-term market direction. Challenge: too many potential explanatory variables.
LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) = machine learning technique that reduces the number of explanatory variables to a manageable number of significant ones.
Memory anchor: LASSO = "shrink the variable list to the ones that matter".
5 key markets — each with its own trade implementation pattern
Different asset classes have different market structures → different ways trades get done. The exam asks you to know what's typical for each.
Equity markets
Venues: stock exchanges (lit markets) + dark pools Tech level: MOST advanced of all asset classes Execution: mostly electronic; algorithmic trading is commonplace Order type: order-driven (CLOB)
Memory anchor: equities = the gold standard for electronic + algorithmic execution.
Fixed-income markets
Structure: large number of heterogeneous securities (many issues per issuer) Liquidity: generally LOW per security, but typical order size is LARGE Market type: dealer-based, quote-driven Electronic RFQ: growing, but algorithmic trading is mostly limited to on-the-run U.S. Treasuries + futures contracts Corporate bonds: electronic trading is growing but still a small fraction
⚙️ Execution method depends on urgency
Urgent trades→Principal (broker risk) trade
Less urgent→Broker-agent approach
Exchange-traded derivatives (options & futures)
Electronic trading: COMMON Algorithmic trading: NOT as common as in equities — and is used MORE for futures than for options DMA: buy-side traders generally use Direct Market Access
Memory anchor: futures > options for algo adoption (futures are simpler, more standardized).
OTC derivatives
Market type: dealer quote-driven Execution: implemented through high-touch approaches Regulation shift: since 2008 credit crisis, regulators pushed for transparency + central clearing of basic OTC derivatives (e.g. interest rate swaps via Dodd-Frank Act 2010 in the US)
OTC = the most "high-touch" asset class. Discretion + dealer relationships matter more here than in any other market.
Spot foreign exchange (FX)
Venue: OTC market Execution: BOTH electronic AND high-touch broker approaches
3-tier structure (decreasing trade size, increasing spreads):
1. Interbank — largest trades, tightest spreads 2. Interdealer — middle tier 3. Bank-to-client — smaller trades, widest spreads
⚙️ FX execution method by trade type
Large urgent→RFQs with brokers
Large non-urgent→Scheduled algorithms OR high-touch agency
Small trades→DMA
5 markets side by side — quick comparison

Exam traps for key markets
Trap 1: "Algorithmic trading is widespread in fixed income" → FALSE. Only on-the-run U.S. Treasuries and futures contracts. Corporate bonds are still mostly high-touch.
Trap 2: "OTC derivatives are quote-driven order book markets" → FALSE. Quote-driven, yes. But NOT an order book — dealers quote on request, no CLOB.
Trap 3: "Options have more algo adoption than futures" → FALSE. Reversed: futures > options for algos.
Trap 4: "FX spot is purely electronic" → FALSE. It's BOTH electronic AND high-touch. Large urgent trades use RFQs with brokers.
Memory anchor: liquidity + standardization drive algo adoption. Equity wins on both → most algo. OTC derivatives lose on both → least algo.
Trade Governance — why it exists
Asset managers must have a formal written trade policy that clearly spells out trade procedures. This is BOTH good practice AND usually required by regulation. The policy protects clients from conflicts of interest and ensures consistent execution.
Trade policy has 4 key areas. Each is examinable on its own. Together, they describe how the firm finds, evaluates, and monitors execution.
The 4 pillars of trade policy — animation
0 / 4 pillars shown
PILLAR 1 Meaning of best execution
Definition: "Best execution" is a regulatory term — the duty of asset managers to seek the best possible RESULT for clients when trading. The trade policy must define best execution within the applicable regulatory framework.
⚙️ Factors that determine best execution
Execution price→Achieved vs benchmark
Trading costs→Explicit + implicit
Speed & likelihood of execution→Settlement included
Order size & liquidity→Size relative to ADV
Nature of the trade→Urgency, motivation
Critical exam point: Best execution does NOT simply mean seeking the best price or trading at the lowest cost. It means the best RESULT for the client overall.
Example: a manager with a large stake in a company they expect to file for bankruptcy might get a better RESULT by selling a BLOCK to a trusted dealer at a discounted price — even if there are higher bids for small quantities on lit venues. Why? Because hitting lit bids would cause information leakage and adverse market movements that would tank the bigger position.
PILLAR 2 Factors that determine the optimal execution approach
The trade policy needs to communicate the criteria that determine HOW each trade gets executed. These factors:
⚙️ The criteria the policy must spell out
Urgency & size of order→From the PM's mandate
Liquidity of security (ADV)→+ standardized vs customized
Characteristics of venues→Lit / dark / quote-driven
Investment strategy objectives→Long-term vs short-term
Reason for the trade→Alpha / rebalance / cash flow
Regulatory context: different asset classes have different trading conventions. The policy must reflect both the relevant regulations AND the conventions used by the manager.
MiFID II trap: Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (MiFID II) in Europe has effectively prohibited soft-dollar arrangements.
Soft-dollar arrangements = an asset manager pays for goods or services using REBATES from client commissions in return for executing high volume with a broker. This may jeopardize best execution if the manager uses the client's soft dollars for the manager's OWN benefit (e.g. buying research that helps the manager, not the specific client).
Memory anchor: asset classes match methods. Equities + exchange-traded derivatives = algorithms. Fixed income = high-touch. The policy must reflect these conventions.
PILLAR 3 List of eligible brokers and execution venues
The policy includes a list of approved brokers + the process used to create it. Best practice = establish a Best Execution Monitoring Committee (BEMC).
⚙️ BEMC composition
Portfolio execution→Traders / PMs
Compliance→Regulatory oversight
Risk personnel→Counterparty risk view
BEMC duties: maintaining, updating, and distributing the list to all parties involved in trade execution.
Why due diligence matters MOST for OTC trades: no exchange rules protection, low transparency, no central clearing → counterparty risk is huge.
6 principles for broker approval:
⚙️ Criteria the BEMC checks
Service quality→Execution price, speed, capacity
Financial stability→Mitigates counterparty risk
Ethical reputation→Good behavior history
Settlement facilities→Adequate infrastructure
Explicit costs→Competitive commissions
Capital commitment→Willing to take principal risk in illiquid trades
PILLAR 4 Process for monitoring execution arrangements
The approved broker list must be constantly monitored. Brokers that fail the standard are removed promptly.
⚙️ What's monitored continuously
Reputational issues→News, allegations, regulatory actions
Trading error frequency→Mistakes that cost clients
Criminal actions→Investigations, charges, convictions
Financial stability→Ongoing creditworthiness
Execution quality→vs benchmarks, ongoing
Record-keeping: trading records must be kept to (1) facilitate execution quality analysis, (2) address client concerns, (3) respond to regulator inquiries about executions and trade allocations.
Memory anchor: pillar 3 = onboarding (who's allowed in). Pillar 4 = ongoing surveillance (are they still good enough?). Both work together to enforce best execution.

#PillarWhat it covers
1Meaning of best executionDefine best RESULT (not lowest price) + the 5 factors that determine it
2Factors determining optimal approachUrgency, liquidity, venue, strategy, reason for trade + MiFID II / soft dollars
3Approved broker list + BEMCComposition (PM/compliance/risk) + 6 approval criteria + OTC due diligence
4Monitoring processContinuous tracking + record-keeping for regulators/clients
"Best execution" — the most misunderstood concept
Best execution ≠ Best price Best execution ≠ Lowest cost Best execution = Best RESULT for the client The "best result" is a function of: Execution price + Trading costs + Speed + Likelihood of fill + Order size + Liquidity + Nature of the trade A worse price can be the BEST execution if: - Selling a small piece at a high lit bid would leak info - The lit market would move against the larger remaining position - A block trade with a trusted dealer protects the bigger value
This is a classic CFA exam construction: "manager A got a worse price but better best execution because..." The right answer is the manager who protected the client's overall position, not the one who hit the highest visible bid.
Exam traps for Trade Governance
Trap 1 · "Best execution = best price". FALSE. Best execution = best RESULT for the client. A worse price can be the right choice if it preserves overall value.
Trap 2 · Soft dollars allowed everywhere. FALSE. MiFID II in Europe effectively PROHIBITED soft-dollar arrangements. The exam might test US vs EU regulatory differences.
Trap 3 · BEMC = just the PM. FALSE. BEMC = portfolio execution + compliance + risk personnel. It's cross-functional by design to prevent conflicts of interest.
Trap 4 · Due diligence equally important everywhere. FALSE. Due diligence on brokers is PARTICULARLY important for OTC trades (no exchange protection, low transparency, no central clearing).
Trap 5 · One-time broker approval. FALSE. Approved broker list must be CONSTANTLY monitored and updated. Pillar 4 = ongoing surveillance.
Memory anchor: governance has 4 verbs — DEFINE (pillar 1) → DETERMINE (pillar 2) → APPROVE (pillar 3) → MONITOR (pillar 4).
Your 13 errors cluster into 4 patterns
Fix the patterns, fix the questions. Each pattern has its own drill section.
Pattern 1 · IS & cost calculations (the BIG one — 7 errors)
You miss the sign convention for SELL orders and you mix up the components of expanded IS.
CalculationWhat you missed
Arrival cost (SRM)132 bps. Formula : Side × [(Avg − Arrival)/Arrival] × 10,000
IS for TS sell$35,450 (you picked $21,650 — forgot opportunity cost or sign for sell)
IS for West Commerce206 bps (you picked 139)
Delay cost (West Commerce)$1,800 (you picked $2,700)
Expanded IS favorable (UPX)Trading cost is most favorable (you picked delay)
Market-adjusted cost (TEXX)−44.6 bps wins vs TWAP/VWAP
Delay cost (LIM)Calculated arrival − decision price × shares
Decision price for ACME$79.90 (Tuesday close), NOT $80 (limit) — decision is observed, not chosen
The key trap: for SELL orders, shares are NEGATIVE. If you forget the sign, your numbers will be wrong but plausible-looking.
Second key trap: the decision price ≠ limit price. Decision price is the market price OBSERVED at the moment of decision (previous close if before open, arrival if intraday, today's close if after close). Limit price is just an execution constraint chosen by the PM.
Drill: 4 separate interactive calculators (Arrival Cost / IS / Expanded IS / Market-Adjusted) preset with each question's numbers.
Pattern 2 · Trade urgency drivers (3 errors)
You confuse execution risk (price moves against you while you trade) and market impact (you push the price). They move in OPPOSITE directions with speed.
StatementTruth
"Trading with greater urgency → lower execution risk"✓ TRUE (faster = less time exposed to volatility)
"Wide bid-ask spread + longer time → lower execution risk"✗ FALSE (longer = MORE exposed to vol)
"Larger size + higher urgency → reduces market impact"✗ FALSE (urgency + size → MORE impact)
"High alpha decay → less aggressive trading"✗ FALSE (high decay = MUST trade fast, accept impact)
"Info leakage minimized by fast exchange execution"✗ FALSE (info leak → dark pools + limit orders)
Memory anchor — the inverse relationship: FASTER trading → LOWER execution risk → HIGHER market impact SLOWER trading → HIGHER execution risk → LOWER market impact You can't minimize BOTH simultaneously. You pick which to prioritize.
Pattern 3 · Algo selection (3 errors)
You pick the wrong algo when the dominant driver isn't "urgency" but something else (info leakage, completion guarantee).
CaseYour wrong pickCorrectDecisive driver
Music Plus (20% vol, urgent, leakage concern)POV or arrival priceLiquidity-seekingOrder size > 15% of volume + leakage concern
Dynopax (illiquid, must complete in 1 day)VWAP or POVTWAPCompletion guarantee in time window
Music Plus open marketClosing auction or passiveOpen market (active)HIGH urgency on intraday alpha
Decision tree: Order size > 15% of vol? → Liquidity-seeking. Must complete in fixed window? → TWAP. High intraday urgency? → Active open market (NOT closing auction).
Pattern 4 · Trade policy themes (mineur — 2 erreurs)
You miss what's INAPPROPRIATE in a trade policy.
Theme statementAppropriate?
"Disclose ALL trade errors to clients"✗ INAPPROPRIATE — errors go to compliance, priority = no adverse impact for client
"Lowest possible trading cost only"✗ INAPPROPRIATE — best execution ≠ lowest cost
"Same execution approach for all asset classes"✗ INAPPROPRIATE — depends on asset class & market structure
"Pre-approved broker list, reviewed regularly"✓ APPROPRIATE
"Pro-rata allocation for partially-executed pooled orders"✓ APPROPRIATE
Trap: "treatment of trade errors" policy is NEEDED (errors must be documented in trade error log + reported to compliance) — but NOT necessarily disclosed to clients. Two different things.

Market-Adjusted Cost calculator
Market-adjusted cost = Arrival cost − (β × Index arrival cost) This isolates the cost CAUSED BY the trade (vs cost caused by general market movement). Step 1: Compute trade's arrival cost (in bps) Step 2: Compute index's arrival cost (in bps) over the trade horizon Step 3: Market-adjusted cost = Step 1 − (β × Step 2) A NEGATIVE market-adjusted cost = the trade looks BETTER than the index move suggests. The trade outperformed the broader market move.

Urgency drivers drill — true or false?

The fundamental tradeoff — memorize this
FASTER trading → LOWER execution risk → HIGHER market impact SLOWER trading → HIGHER execution risk → LOWER market impact You can't minimize BOTH simultaneously. Which to prioritize depends on: • Alpha decay rate (fast decay → trade fast → accept impact) • Information leakage concern (high → use dark pools, NOT exchanges) • Bid-ask spread (wide spread + long horizon = high execution risk) • Order size vs ADV (large = unavoidable impact)
The exam frames the same idea 5 different ways. Once you know the tradeoff, you can spot any reformulation.

QuestionIf YES

Common mistake: defaulting to POV when "volume" is mentioned. POV chases volume but CAN'T guarantee completion. Use TWAP if completion in a window matters.
Why you panic on essays — and how to stop
You don't panic because you don't know the content. You panic because you have NO PROCEDURE. Once you have a 4-step procedure, the page is never blank.
The 4-step universal procedure: 1. SCAN the question → identify the instruction KEYWORD 2. HUNT the vignette → underline 2-4 signal facts the examiner planted 3. PICK the concept(s) the question refers to → define them in 1 line each 4. WRITE the 3-block answer: CHOICE → DEFINITION → APPLICATION
When you can write definitions in 5 seconds and you've highlighted your signals, the writing starts immediately. No more blank page.
The 3-block answer template
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ BLOCK 1 · DIRECT CHOICE │ │ One bold sentence that answers the question. │ │ Don't preamble. Don't hedge. State the answer. │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ BLOCK 2 · DEFINITION │ │ One or two sentences defining the concepts named │ │ in the question. Shows theoretical mastery. │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ BLOCK 3 · APPLICATION (the most important) │ │ 2-3 reasons drawn FROM THE VIGNETTE. │ │ Each reason: [vignette fact] → [theoretical effect] │ │ Examiners reward you for connecting facts to theory.│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
If you skip Block 2, you sound like you guessed. If you skip Block 3, you sound like you wrote a textbook. You need BOTH.
Quality checklist — before you stop writing
✓ Did I make a clear choice in the first sentence? ✓ Did I define the key concept(s) named in the question? ✓ Did I cite at least 2 specific facts from the vignette? ✓ Did each fact connect to a theoretical effect (driver → consequence)? ✓ Did I close with a synthesis sentence?
If you can't answer YES to all 5, your essay is incomplete. Add what's missing before moving on.
Common reasons you block (and the fix)
Block reasonFix
"I don't remember the definition perfectly"Write what you DO remember + apply the procedure. Partial definition + good application beats no answer.
"I'm searching for the 'right' wording"There's no right wording. There's a right STRUCTURE. Use the 3-block template.
"I don't know which concept they want"The question NAMES the concept(s) explicitly. "Trade urgency and alpha decay" = those are the two concepts.
"I don't have enough to say"Re-read the vignette. Each unusual detail is a planted signal. 3-year holding, persistent mispricing, etc.
"I want to write more but I'm not sure if it adds points"Stop. Concise + structured beats long + rambling. The graders use a rubric.
Decode the instruction keyword first — it dictates your format
Different keywords expect different response formats. Mismatching = lost points even if your content is correct.
Determine / Identify
Examiner wants: one clear choice in the first sentence, then justification.
Format: "X is the [most likely / most appropriate / correct] choice because..." [2-3 reasons drawn from vignette]
Examples: "Determine the most appropriate algorithm." "Identify which fund has higher trade urgency."
Calculate
Examiner wants: formula + numbers + result with units.
Format: Formula: [write the formula clearly] Substitution: [plug in numbers from vignette] Result: [final answer with currency or bps unit]
Show your work even if you have it right — partial credit if final number is wrong but steps are correct.
Discuss / Justify
Examiner wants: 2-3 reasons with evidence from the vignette.
Format: [Topic sentence stating the position] Reason 1: [vignette fact] → [theoretical consequence] Reason 2: [vignette fact] → [theoretical consequence] (Reason 3 if relevant)
"Justify" = give reasons FOR something already chosen. "Discuss" = present analysis (often pros AND cons or multiple sides).
Recommend
Examiner wants: a specific choice + at least 2 justifications based on vignette evidence.
Format: "I recommend [X] because..." Justification 1: [vignette evidence] Justification 2: [vignette evidence] (Optionally: "[X] is preferred over [alternative] because...")
Compare / Contrast
Examiner wants: a side-by-side comparison, ideally as a table.
Format: Build a 2-column or 2-row structure. For each dimension: state the difference clearly. Example dimensions: urgency, liquidity, risk appetite, time horizon
If a table isn't feasible, use parallel sentences: "X has [feature A], while Y has [feature B]."
Evaluate / Critique
Examiner wants: your assessment with reasoning — often "is X appropriate / correct?"
Format: "X is [appropriate / inappropriate / incorrect] because..." [Reason 1] [Reason 2] [What should be done instead, if relevant]
For "evaluate the firm's trading policy" or similar, scan for the LOS-required components and check each.
Drill Mode — build your essay step by step
For each question: read the vignette, then progressively reveal the signals, structure, and full answer. Train yourself to spot signals BEFORE reading the answer.
