Yield Curve Transitions Drill
15 scenarios drilling the most common exam patterns on curve transitions. Read carefully — the direction of change matters as much as the current shape.
Decision tree for curve scenarios
Step 1: What is the curve's CURRENT shape? (steep / flat / inverted) Step 2: What DIRECTION is it moving? (steepening / flattening / re-steepening) Step 3: What are RATES doing? (short rising/falling? long rising/falling?) Step 4: What is the central bank doing? (easing / tightening / on hold) Map to phase: STEEPEST → Initial Recovery (or just before) Steep, flattening → Early Expansion FLAT → Late Expansion Inverted → Slowdown (peak inversion) Re-steepening from inverted → Contraction (in progress)
Reading 1 · Capital Market Expectations, Part 1 — Framework & Macro
Full-reading recap, module by module. CME = risk, return, and correlation expectations by asset class. Combined with the investor's objectives & constraints, they drive the strategic asset allocation. No single technique works consistently — know each one's issues.
Module 1.1 · Formulating Capital Market Expectations
LOS 1.aRole & framework for CME
Set long-term expectations for every allowable asset class in the IPS; optionally set short-term expectations for active decisions. A disciplined approach improves security selection, asset allocation, and risk management.
Two consistency requirements on any set of forecasts:
Cross-sectionalConsistency across asset classes regarding portfolio risk & return characteristics. IntertemporalConsistency across investment horizons — portfolio decisions over time.
Exam trap: cross-sectional = across classes at one time; intertemporal = across time horizons. MCQ swaps the two.
The 7-step CME process
1
Determine needs
Specify the asset classes and investment horizon(s) required. Time horizon is particularly important in setting the expectation set.
2
Investigate history
Study historical performance and the drivers behind it → establish a plausible future range and sanity-check forecasts against the past.
3
Identify the valuation model
Pick the model & its requirements. A comparables/relative-value approach used in the US may be hard to apply in an emerging market.
4
Collect the best data
Faulty data → faulty conclusions. Financial publications & commercial databases are usually the best sources.
5
Apply experience & judgment
Interpret current conditions, assign input values, and verify inputs are consistent across classes.
6
Formulate the expectations
Record all assumptions and rationales used.
7
Monitor & refine
Compare realized vs forecast. If actual varies significantly, refine the process and the model.
Supporting info categories: Geography (countries, blocs like EU, domestic vs nondomestic, regional, global) · Major asset classes (fixed income, equity, real assets) · Sub-asset classes (equity by industry/sector/size/style; FI by nominal vs TIPS, floating vs fixed, credit quality, maturity; real assets like commodities, real estate, timber).
Good forecasts are: unbiased · objective · well-researched · efficient (small forecast error) · internally consistent. Rule of thumb: ≥30 observations to test a hypothesis.
LOS 1.bThe 9 problems in forecasting
Poor forecasts → inappropriate asset allocation. Nine problems in data, models, and the resulting expectations:
1 · Economic data limitsCollection→publication lag (IMF up to 2 yrs); revisions after release (CPI basket, methodology change); rebasing of indexes (unaware analyst mis-computes % changes). 2 · Measurement error/biasTranscription errors (worst if biased); survivorship bias (poor performers deleted → upward bias); appraisal (smoothed) data → path looks smoother, σ biased down, correlations look closer to 0 (a real-estate / alternatives problem). 3 · Historical estimate limitsValues must be adjusted forward as economic/political/regulatory/tech environments change. Regime changes → nonstationary data (e.g. 2007–09 GFC). Different subperiods have different statistical properties. 4 · Ex post → ex anteUsing after-the-fact data to set before-the-fact risk/return. Post-risk-event high returns make the analyst blind to the risk that existed → underestimate risk, overestimate return. Outliers/rare events also distort VaR upward. 5 · Data biasesData mining (5% significance × 40 vars → ~2 spurious "significant" relations); time-period bias (small-cap "premium" vanishes if 2000–2010 excluded). 6 · Conditioning informationRelationship of returns to the economy is not constant over the cycle. A firm's β = 1.2 historically may be 1.0 in expansions, 1.4 in recessions → use the beta matching the expected regime. 7 · Misinterpreting correlationCausality direction (rain→corn, not corn→rain; rain exogenous, corn endogenous); spurious correlation; a third variable; nonlinear links missed by (linear) correlation. 8 · Psychological biasAnchoring (cog) · status quo (emo) · confirmation (cog) · overconfidence (emo) · prudence (cog) · availability (cog). See table below. 9 · Model uncertaintyWhich model (DCF vs relative value)? Parameter uncertainty (estimation error in params) · input uncertainty (correct input values). Model uncertainty is the MOST serious — a wrong model → invalid conclusions.
Decisive detail: among the three uncertainties (model / parameter / input), model uncertainty is the most serious. Appraisal-data smoothing biases σ downward (not up) and pushes correlations toward 0.
Psychological biases (Problem 8) — cognitive vs emotional
BiasTypeWhat happensCounter
AnchoringCognitiveFirst info overweighted (first debate speaker's recession call gets extra credence).Consider a range of outcomes.
Status quoEmotionalPrediction = recent past (inflation 4% now → forecast 4%); avoids active error of commission.Challenge the default.
ConfirmationCognitiveSeek only supporting evidence; ignore the rest.Give all evidence equal scrutiny; seek contrary views.
OverconfidenceEmotionalIgnore past mistakes; treat others' comments as agreement; overstate forecast accuracy.Consider a range of outcomes.
PrudenceCognitiveOverly conservative to avoid regret from extreme (wrong) forecasts.Consider a range of outcomes.
AvailabilityCognitiveEasiest-to-recall (often extreme) event overweighted (1929 crash suppressing equity values for 30 yrs).Base predictions on objective data, not emotion/recollection.
Anchoring vs status quo — anchoring locks onto the first piece of info received; status quo locks onto the recent past / current level. Confirmation vs overconfidence — confirmation is about which evidence you consider; overconfidence is about certainty in your own view.
Module Quiz 1.1
Q1. Analyst uses inconsistent valuation across classes: low discount rates for equity (overstates equity value) and high discount rates for fixed income (understates FI value). Effect on allocation?
Answer (reasoning): Inputs are not internally consistent across asset classes (violates Step 5). Overvaluing equity and undervaluing fixed income biases the analyst toward over-allocating to equities and under-allocating to fixed income — an inappropriate SAA driven by inconsistent inputs, not by true relative value.
Module 1.2 · The Trend Rate of Growth
LOS 1.cExogenous shocks & growth trends
Economic growth splits into cyclical variations (short-term focused) and growth trends (relevant for long-term return expectations).
Exogenous shockUnanticipated event outside the normal course of the economy → NOT already built into market prices. Likely produces a statistical regime change. Endogenous (contrast)Normal trends arising within the economy → ARE built into current market prices.
Causes of exogenous shocks (drivers, each with direction on growth):
Govt policiesSound fiscal policy, minimal interference w/ free markets, competition, infrastructure & human capital, sound tax policy → ↑ long-term growth. Political eventsGeopolitical tension diverts resources to less productive uses → ↓ growth; peace dividend / defense cuts → ↑ growth. Technological progressNew markets/products/tech → ↑ growth potential. Natural disasters↓ short-term growth; may ↑ long-term if more efficient capacity replaces old (counter: owners already replace when optimal). Resource discoveryNew resources / cheaper recovery → ↑ growth; higher production costs / lower supply → ↓ growth. Financial crisesCrisis of confidence → ↓ output short-term AND ↓ trend growth.
LOS 1.dApplying trend growth to CME
Why the trend rate matters (drivers of its relevance):
DCF disciplineDCF forecasts incorporate trend growth → keeps forecasts consistent w/ long-term growth; trend rate anchors long-term bond & equity returns. Equity linkHigher trend growth → potentially higher stock returns, if not already reflected in prices. Inflation headroomHigher trend growth = economy can grow faster before inflation is a concern → influences monetary policy & bond yield levels. Bond yieldsHigher trend growth → higher government bond yields.
Trend growth is relatively stable in developed economies; in emerging economies it is less predictable and can include longer catch-up periods of rapid growth.
Basic growth model — three inputs:
Labor inputLabor-force growth (population + demographics) + labor participation (real wages, work/leisure, social factors). Capital per workerRaises labor productivity. Total factor productivityTechnological progress + government-policy changes.
Worked example · long-term growth rate (verified 5.25%)
Population +2%, labor-force participation +0.25%, capital spending +2.5%, TFP +0.5%. Long-term projected growth = sum of components.
g = 2% + 0.25% + 2.5% + 0.5% = 5.25%
Worked example · long-run equity return (Navaro) (verified 8.2%)
Equity return decomposition = nominal GDP growth ± Δ(profit share of GDP) ± Δ(P/E) + dividend yield. Long run: profit share and P/E cannot grow forever, so their long-run Δ is applied to the capital-gains component only (not the dividend yield).
InputValue
Annual labor input growth0.4%
Annual labor productivity growth1.4%
Annual inflation3.8%
Dividend yield2.6%
Δ profits as share of GDP0%
Δ P/E multiples0%
Real GDP growth = 0.4% + 1.4% = 1.8% Nominal GDP = 1.8% + 3.8% = 5.6% Capital gains = %ΔnomGDP + %Δprofits/GDP + %ΔPE = 5.6% + 0% + 0% = 5.6% Equity return = capital gains + div yld = 5.6% + 2.6% = 8.2%
Trap: the profit-share & P/E changes attach to capital gains, then you add the dividend yield last. Don't add the dividend yield into GDP.
LOS 1.eThree approaches to economic forecasting
ApproachAdvantagesDisadvantages
Econometric modeling
Structural (theory-based) & reduced-form (compact); OLS most common		 Incorporates many variables · reusable once specified · quantified output on a consistent set of relationships. Complex & time-consuming to build · data hard to forecast & relationships can change · output may need interpretation or be unrealistic · poor at turning points.
Economic indicators
Leading / coincident / lagging; Conference Board 10 leading; composite; diffusion index		 Simple, intuitive, easy to interpret · data readily available from third parties · lists can be tailored. Results have been inconsistent · have given false signals · revised frequently (fit past cycles better in hindsight than at release).
Checklist approach
Series of questions → judgment + some modeling		 Less complex than econometrics · flexible in mixing objective analysis with judgment to capture changing relationships. Subjective & time-consuming · complexity limited by the manual process.
Indicator vocabulary: Leading = move ahead of the cycle (predict); coincident/lagging = move with/after the cycle (confirm). Traditionally 3 consecutive months of the leading index rising (falling) signal the start of an expansion (contraction). A diffusion index counts how many indicators point toward expansion vs contraction.
Module 1.3 · The Business Cycle
LOS 1.fBusiness cycles & short-/long-term expectations
Trend growth guides long-term expectations; deviations from trend cancel over the long run but are useful for shorter-term projections. Economic activity is cyclical because decision-makers act on imperfect information, adjustments take time, and reversing wrong decisions is costly.
Why the cycle↔CME relationship is not straightforward:
1 · Duration/intensity varyTurning points hard to predict; cycles = interaction of many subcycles across frequencies. 2 · Trend vs cycleHard to separate short-term (business-cycle) effects from long-term (trend-growth) effects. 3 · Markets ≠ only economyCapital-market returns also depend on investors' expectations & risk tolerances, not just the real economy.
Business-cycle analysis is most useful within one typical cycle's horizon. For long horizons spanning multiple full cycles, current-state info is less valuable.
The 5 business-cycle phases
PhaseDurationConfidence / gap / inflationShort ratesBond yieldsStocks
1 · Initial recoveryA few monthsConfidence rising; large output gap; decelerating inflation; govt stimulus (low rates / deficits).Low or fallingBottoming outRising; cyclical/riskier assets (small-cap, high-yield) do well.
2 · Early expansion1 yr → several yrsIncreasing confidence & growth; low inflation; output gap narrowing.RisingStable or risingRising
3 · Late expansion—High confidence & employment; output gap eliminated, overheating risk; increasing inflation; CB limits money growth.RisingRisingRising/peaking; ↑ risk & volatility.
4 · SlowdownFew months → yr+Declining confidence; inflation still rising; short rates at a peak.At a peakPeaking, possibly falling → prices rising; possible inverted curve.Falling
5 · Contraction12–18 monthsDeclining confidence & profits; ↑ unemployment & bankruptcies; inflation topping out.FallingFalling → prices risingIncreasing during latter stages (anticipating end of recession).
Decisive detail (LOS 1.f MCQ): the phase with rising short-term rates AND stable bond yields is early expansion (late expansion has rising short AND rising long; initial recovery has low/falling short with bottoming yields).
LOS 1.gInflation vs the business cycle
InflationGenerally rising prices. CPI 100→105 = +5%. Typically accelerates late in the cycle (near the peak). DisinflationDeceleration of inflation (still positive). CPI 105→108 ≈ +3%. Typically decelerates as the economy approaches / enters recession. DeflationGenerally falling prices. CPI 108→106 ≈ −2%. Severe threat.
Why deflation is dangerous: (1) encourages debt default — home $100k / mortgage $95k → equity only $5k; a >5% price fall → negative equity → panic sales & default; (2) with negative inflation, nominal rates hit ~0 → limits central banks' ability to cut & stimulate (post-2007–09 → QE).
QE: after the GFC, with rates near zero, CBs bought high-quality (and later MBS/corporate) fixed income. QE differed from ordinary open-market ops in being larger in scale and intended as a long-term increase in bank reserves. CBs target a slightly positive inflation rate; investors expect equity & bond prices to reflect some positive inflation.
Figure 1.1 · Inflation & the business cycle (markets)
PhaseInflationEcon policyMarkets
Initial recoveryInitially decliningStimulativeShort rates low/declining; long rates bottoming & bond prices peaking; stocks ↑.
Early expansionLow inflation, good growthBecoming less stimulativeShort rates ↑; long rates bottoming/↑ with bond prices beginning to decline; stocks ↑.
Late expansionInflation rate increasingBecoming restrictiveShort & long rates ↑ with bond prices ↓; stocks peaking & volatile.
SlowdownInflation continues to accelerateBecoming less restrictiveShort & long rates peaking then declining with bond prices starting to ↑; stocks declining.
ContractionReal activity declining, inflation peakingEasingShort & long rates declining with bond prices ↑; stocks begin to ↑ later in the recession.
Figure 1.2 · Inflation expectations & asset classes
ScenarioCashBondsEquityReal estate
Inflation within expectations real rate earns the real rate of interest. Shorter-term yields more volatile than longer-term. no impact given predictable growth. neutral at typical rates of return.
Inflation above/below expectations + / − positive (negative) with increasing (decreasing) yields. Longer-term yields more volatile than shorter-term. negative (CB action / falling prices) — some firms may pass costs on. positive real asset values rise with inflation.
Deflation positive if nominal rates bound by 0%. positive fixed cash flows gain purchasing power (assuming no default). negative as activity & business decline. negative property values generally decline.
Volatility flip (memorize): inflation within expectations → short-term yields more volatile; inflation above/below expectations → long-term yields more volatile.
Professor's note: these generalizations don't hold in every case — they're a starting point. Even if they always held, it's hard to know when a phase starts, how long it lasts, or when it ends.
Module Quiz 1.2 / 1.3
Q1. Analyst believes GDP is best forecast with a system of equations capturing GDP as a function of many current & lagged variables. Most-likely method?
Answer: Econometric modeling — statistical methods / systems of equations with current & lagged variables (e.g. GDP from consumption & investment); OLS most common.
Q2. Phase where we most likely see rising short-term rates AND stable bond yields? (A) late expansion (B) initial recovery (C) early expansion
Answer: C · early expansion. Rising short rates with stable/rising (still-bottoming) bond yields. Late expansion → short and long both rising; initial recovery → low/falling short with bottoming yields.
Q3. Describe how bonds & equities typically perform during deflationary periods.
Answer: Bonds — positive: fixed future cash flows gain purchasing power as prices fall (assuming no default). Equities — negative: economic activity and business decline, depressing earnings and prices.
Module 1.4 · Monetary & Fiscal Policy
LOS 1.hMonetary policy
Central banks use monetary policy as a countercyclical force, balancing price stability against economic growth. Goal: keep growth near its long-run sustainable rate — growth persistently above it → inflation. Late-expansion inflation → CBs turn restrictive; risk: overtighten and cause a recession.
Lower rates →↑ consumer spending, ↑ business spending, ↑ stock prices, ↑ bond prices, lower domestic currency → ↑ exports. Level matters tooRates raised 4%→6% to fight inflation may still be low vs the country's average → still growth-permissive. Direction ≠ whole story. Neutral rateEquilibrium rate balancing growth & inflation = real growth component + inflation component (+ judgment). e.g. inflation target 3% + growth 2% → neutral 5%.
The Taylor rule
Prescriptive target for the nominal short-term rate using the neutral rate, expected GDP relative to trend, and expected inflation relative to target.
n_target = r_neutral + i_expected + [ 0.5·(GDP_expected − GDP_trend) + 0.5·(i_expected − i_target) ] r_neutral = neutral real short-term rate i_expected = expected inflation i_target = target inflation GDP_expected= expected GDP growth GDP_trend = long-term GDP growth trend
Rearranged form (Prof's note): move expected inflation to the LHS → n_target − i_expected = r_neutral + [0.5(GDP_exp − GDP_trend) + 0.5(i_exp − i_target)], i.e. the real adjusted target.
Worked example · Taylor-rule target (verified 7%)
InputValue
Neutral rate3%
Inflation target2%
Expected inflation4%
GDP long-term trend2%
Expected GDP growth0%
n_target = 3% + 4% + [0.5(0% − 2%) + 0.5(4% − 2%)] = 7% + ( −1% + 1% ) = 7%
Interpretation: weak growth alone would call for cutting rates (target 1% below neutral), but expected inflation is 2% above target. The two offset in the bracket (−1% + 1% = 0), so the inflation concern overrides the weak-growth concern → target = 7%.
Negative interest rates
A negative rate = a net payment made to keep money on deposit, or a net fee to invest in short-term instruments. A pre-2007–09 curiosity.
Why 0 seemed the floorInvestors could hold physical cash (0 interest) instead → withdrawals shrink bank balance sheets → less lending → higher borrowing rate (simple supply/demand). Why it was wrongNo big move into physical cash — daily fund flows are too large; the convenience of deposits for settling transactions outweighed the explicit cost → negative rates proved sustainable for extended periods. Intended effectLike QE: holders spend/invest in longer-term stocks & bonds (↑ prices, wealth effect) or borrow & spend now → stimulate activity.
Negative rates complicate CME: (1) risk-free rate anchors buildup models — when it's negative, use a sustainable expected risk-free rate (e.g. the policy neutral rate in the Taylor rule); that rate isn't fully risk-free, so a modest default premium can be removed. (2) Must forecast the path back to a long-run sustainable risk-free rate (use multiple path projections). (3) Alternatively read negative risk-free rates as consistent with the contraction or early-recovery stages. (4) Historical data is more problematic — few comparable periods, regime change, + untested QE → more subjective assessments.
Fiscal policy
To stimulate: loose fiscal policy = ↓ taxes or ↑ spending → larger budget deficit. To rein in growth: fiscal tightening.
It's the CHANGE, not the levelThe level of the deficit doesn't stimulate — an increase in the deficit does. A steady deficit is not stimulative. Cyclical ≠ policyDeficit changes that occur naturally over the cycle are neither stimulative nor restrictive (expansion → deficits fall as tax receipts ↑ & transfers ↓; recession → opposite). Only policy-directed changes influence growth.
Exam trap: a large deficit by itself does not stimulate; only a discretionary increase in the deficit does. Automatic-stabilizer swings don't count as stimulus/restraint.
LOS 1.iThe yield curve as an economic predictor
The yield curve = relationship between interest rates and maturity. Sensitive to government actions and current/expected conditions.
Both expansiveSharply upward-sloping (short < long) → economy likely to expand. Both restrictiveDownward-sloping / inverted (short > long) → economy likely to contract. Monetary restrictive + fiscal stimulativeYield curve flat → implications less clear. Monetary stimulative + fiscal restrictiveYield curve moderately steep → implications less clear.
Curve over the cycle: typically steep at the bottom of the cycle; flattens toward expansion; flat→inverted at the top; re-steepens during contraction. Analysts can use the curve to read the state of the economy and the future path of rates — but the relationships may not always hold.
Two "less clear" cases (memorize the pairing): M-restrictive + F-stimulative → flat; M-stimulative + F-restrictive → moderately steep. Both-same-direction cases give the clean steep(expand) / inverted(contract) signals.
Module 1.4 · International Considerations
LOS 1.jMacro, interest-rate & exchange-rate linkages
Economic links between countries matter more with globalization — especially for small countries with undiversified economies. Large diversified economies (e.g. US) are less affected but still influenced.
Macro linksCan produce convergence in business cycles. Trade: a country's economy is depressed by a slowdown in a trading partner (exports ↓, imports ↓). Capital flows: cross-border investing declines as a partner's economy contracts. Current vs capital accountCurrent account ≈ net exports; capital account ≈ net investment flows. They are opposites — a surplus in one produces a deficit in the other.
Current-account identity: net exports = net private saving + government surplus (X − M) = (S − I) + (T − G) X=exports M=imports S=private saving I=investment spending T=tax G=govt spending
Currency pegs & interest-rate differentials
Peg = strong linkSmaller economy unilaterally pegs its currency to a larger, more developed one → business cycles converge because the pegging country must follow the anchor country's economic policies. If it doesn't, investors favor one currency → peg fails. Rate differentialPegged-currency rates generally exceed the anchor's rates; the differential moves with market confidence in the peg. High confidence → small differential; doubt → larger differential (compensation for risk). Defending the pegIf investors lose confidence & the currency starts to fall, the pegging country must raise short-term rates to attract capital & hold the peg.
Without pegging, interest-rate differentials & currency movement reflect:
Overvalued currencyIf substantially overvalued & expected to decline → bond rates likely higher to compensate foreign investors for the expected currency decline. Relative bond yieldsBoth nominal & real yields rise with strong economic activity & increasing demand for funds. Real ratesDriven by savings/investment decisions & capital productivity. Real rates differ across countries but tend to move together — global saving & investing are linked through the current account.

LOS 2.a · Three approaches to forecasting FI returns
Forecasting fixed-income returns can be done through:
1. DCF method — uses YTM as estimate of expected return (this tab) 2. Risk premium / building block approach — stack premiums on a risk-free base (next tab) 3. Equilibrium model — assumes supply and demand in global asset markets are in balance
DCF Analysis — YTM as expected return
DCF is useful when future cash flows are KNOWN or can be estimated reasonably accurately. It supports YTM as the estimate of expected return.
YTM = the discount rate that makes PV of future bond cash flows = bond's price. It's an IRR calculation → it is the realized return IF (a) cash flows reinvested at the YTM AND (b) bond held to maturity.
Zero-coupon bonds: no cash flows to reinvest, but held-to-maturity assumption still applies Bond portfolios: YTM = weighted average of individual bonds' YTMs (generally a good approximation)
Why realized return DEVIATES from initial YTM
Even if all expected cash flows are received, realized return can differ from YTM. Two main reasons:
1. Investor may SELL the bond before maturity → capital gain or loss 2. Rising/falling rates change REINVESTMENT returns. Falling (rising) rates DECREASE (increase) reinvestment returns.
Also: holding to maturity does NOT factor in optionality → cash flows may not be received as expected (e.g. callable bonds).
Interactive · Horizon vs Macaulay Duration
This is the most testable concept in 2.1. The relationship between your investment horizon and the bond's Macaulay duration determines whether capital gain/loss or reinvestment risk dominates. Enter the values and rate direction.
Investment horizon (years)
Macaulay duration (years)
Modified duration (optional → Macaulay)
Interest rates are expected to:
Exam shortcut: Macaulay duration = modified duration × YTM. (e.g. mod dur 5 × YTM 1.055 ≈ Macaulay 6.6... actually mod × (1+YTM). For the exam Kaplan uses Macaulay = modified × YTM as the quick conversion.)
The logic, in words
Horizon SHORTER than Macaulay duration: → CAPITAL gain/loss effect DOMINATES → Falling rates = HIGHER realized return (price gain wins) → Rising rates = LOWER realized return (price loss wins) Horizon LONGER than Macaulay duration: → REINVESTMENT effect DOMINATES → Falling rates = LOWER realized return (reinvest at less) → Rising rates = HIGHER realized return (reinvest at more) Horizon ≈ Macaulay duration: → The two effects roughly OFFSET (immunization) → Realized return ≈ initial YTM
The Building Block (Risk Premium) Approach
Start with a risk-free rate, then ADD compensation for additional risks. The required return stacks up as:
Liquidity premium compensation for illiquidity
Credit premium compensation for expected risk of default
Term premium compensation for duration / maturity risk
Short-term default-free rate the risk-free base (≈ central bank policy rate)
= Required Return on the bond
Read bottom-up: Required return = short-term default-free rate + term premium + credit premium + liquidity premium.
Block 1 · Short-term default-free rate
The base of the stack.
• Matches the FORECAST HORIZON; closest to the government zero-coupon yield • Closely tied to the CENTRAL BANK POLICY RATE • Observed risk-free rate is typically sufficient; may need to NORMALIZE it
When horizon >> short instrument maturity: alternatives may be optimal — (a) use yield of a longer-maturity zero-coupon bond, or (b) take the return realizable by ROLLING OVER the short-term instrument over the horizon. Futures contract rates provide useful proxies for the expected path of short-term rates.
The full stack — what each block compensates for
BlockCompensates forKey detail
Short-term default-free rateTime value (risk-free)≈ central bank policy rate; futures for path
Term premiumDuration / maturity risk4 drivers; positive & related to duration
Credit premiumExpected RISK of defaultSeparate from expected default LOSSES
Liquidity premiumIlliquidityHighest at earliest stages of bond's life
Subtle distinction (credit): the credit premium compensates for the expected RISK of default — which is SEPARATE from the additional compensation for the expected LEVEL of default losses. Both are components of the credit spread.
Term Premium — 4 primary drivers
Real term premium CANNOT be derived from the yield curve alone (though spot-curve implied rates give useful info). Empirically, term premiums are POSITIVE and related to duration. The 4 primary drivers:
DriverMechanism / sub-drivers
1. Inflation uncertainty Higher inflation levels → higher inflation uncertainty → nominal yields rise → term premium INCREASES.
sub-driver: level of inflation → uncertainty about inflation → nominal yield level
2. Recession hedge Depends on the SOURCE of inflation:
• Inflation from strong aggregate DEMAND → nominal bond returns NEGATIVELY correlated with growth → bonds are a good hedge → LOW term premiums
• Inflation from aggregate SUPPLY → nominal bond returns POSITIVELY correlated with growth → bonds are a poor hedge → HIGHER term premiums
3. Supply and demand Relative supply of short- vs long-term default-free bonds → determines slope of the yield curve → influences the level of term premiums.
4. Business cycles The slope of the yield curve and the level of term premiums are related to the business cycle (links back to Reading 1, Module 1.3).
Recession hedge trap (very testable): DEMAND-driven inflation → bonds hedge → LOW term premium. SUPPLY-driven inflation → bonds don't hedge → HIGH term premium. The source of inflation flips the sign.
Other term-premium indicators
Beyond the 4 drivers, these also influence term-premium forecasts:
• Ex ante (forecast) real yield • Cochrane and Piazzesi curve factor — captures both slope AND curvature of the yield curve • Kim and Wright premium — a three-factor model of the term structure • Slope of the yield curve • Supply indicator — proportion of debt with maturity > 10 years • Cyclical proxies — corporate profit-to-GDP ratio, business confidence, unemployment rate
Credit Premium
Compensates for the expected RISK of default — separate from the additional compensation for expected default LOSSES. Both are components of the credit spread.
Key fact: the yield spread is typically NOT a good predictor of future default rates. Spreads are affected primarily by FINANCIAL MARKET CONDITIONS and the credit premium, and only to a LESSER extent by expected default losses.
Predictors of the credit spread — what works, what doesn't
Strong predictors ✓Weak predictors ✗
• Stock returns
• Stock volatility
• Risk-free rate		 • GDP growth
• Default rate changes
Memory anchor: credit spreads track the EQUITY market and rates (financial conditions) far better than they track the real economy (GDP) or actual defaults.
Credit quality — high grade vs low grade
AAA / AA (high grade): extremely low default rates → credit premium & spreads mainly driven by DOWNGRADE BIAS — an asymmetrical risk (a downgrade is more likely than a credit improvement/upgrade) Lower-rated / non-IG: credit premium & spreads reflect much HIGHER compensation for credit risk
Steep Treasury curves → high credit premiums AND high term premiums → both are BULLISH indicators (they imply larger compensation for credit losses).
Credit premium & maturity — the counterintuitive bit
Credit premiums are NOT positively related to maturity. In fact, credit premiums tend to be HIGHER at SHORTER maturities, possibly due to:
• Event risk — large credit-negative events (a bond won't pay more than face value, so upside is capped)
• Illiquidity — bonds with short time to maturity tend to be illiquid older bonds that aren't actively traded
Barbell strategy: to exploit these credit features, PMs often take ON credit risk from SHORTER-maturity bonds and take DURATION risk from LONGER maturities.
Liquidity Premium
Liquidity tends to be HIGHEST at the earliest stages of a bond's life — typically the first few weeks only. Securities with the highest liquidity: sovereign bond issues, current-coupon mortgage-backed securities, high-quality corporate bonds.
6 features that make a bond MORE liquid
As a general rule, liquidity is higher for bonds that are:
1. Issued at close to PAR or market rates 2. NEW (recently issued) 3. LARGE in size 4. Issued by a FREQUENT and WELL-KNOWN issuer 5. SIMPLE in structure 6. HIGH credit quality
Mnemonic: "Par, New, Large, Known, Simple, Quality" — the more a bond drifts AWAY from these features, the larger the liquidity premium.
How to gauge the "true" liquidity premium
Compare the yield spread between the HIGHEST-quality issuer (usually the sovereign) and the NEXT-highest-quality issuer. The analyst then makes adjustments to this spread as the bond moves further away from the 6 liquidity features above.
LOS 2.b · Emerging Market Bond Risk
EM debt offers HIGH expected returns at the expense of HIGHER risk. Many EM countries depend on foreign borrowing, which can create crisis situations. The most significant risk for the bond investor is credit risk — does the country have the ABILITY and WILLINGNESS to pay back its debt? Economic, political, and legal risks also matter.
Signs an EM is MORE susceptible to risk
• Wealth concentration • Income concentration and a less diverse tax base • Greater dominance of cyclical industries / commodities / less pricing power • Restrictions on capital flows, trade, and currency • Inadequate fiscal and monetary policies • Poor workforce education / infrastructure / weak technology • Large foreign borrowing in foreign currencies • Less developed and smaller financial markets • Exposure to volatile capital flows
EM health thresholds — MEMORIZE these numbers
Potential bond investors should check these factors before committing funds:
MetricThresholdSignal
Fiscal deficit-to-GDP> 4%Substantial credit risk
Debt-to-GDP70% – 80%Troublesome for EM
Real growth rate< 4%Growing too slow (want ≥ 4%)
Current account deficit> 4% of GDPWarning sign of difficulty
Foreign debt> 50% of GDPOverleveraged
Foreign debt> 200% of current account receiptsHigh risk
FX reserves< 100% of short-term debtSign of trouble
FX reserves> 200% of short-term debtConsidered strong
The "4% club": deficit-to-GDP >4%, real growth <4%, current account deficit >4% — three different 4% thresholds all signal trouble. Plus the debt ratios: 50% (foreign/GDP), 70-80% (debt/GDP), 200% (foreign/CA receipts AND FX reserves strong), 100% (FX reserves floor).
Government & structural factors
Hospitable: government supportive of structural reforms; committed to responsible fiscal policy, competition, privatization of state-owned businesses Hazard signs: weak enforcement laws, weak property rights laws, nationalization of property, corruption Coalition governments seen as riskier due to inherent political — and therefore policy — instability

📝 Essay gap · "Discuss the statement" on EM/frontier debt risk
Prompt: an adviser says "ALL emerging and frontier market fixed income securities pose economic, political and legal risk" — then lists poor fiscal discipline, foreign-borrowing reliance, narrow tax base, industry dependence, capital-flight susceptibility, limited ability to pay, weak property rights, weak contract enforcement, political instability. Discuss.
Your answer: "the statement is correct and reflects the risks of investing in EM; this risk is usually offset by high expected return." → graded as a MISS.
What "discuss" wanted — the flaw in the word ALL:
Concede what's right: the adviser correctly identifies economic, political and legal risks, and the listed characteristics genuinely affect governments' and corporate borrowers' ABILITY and WILLINGNESS to pay bondholders Attack the overstatement: the assertion that ALL EM/frontier securities pose such risk is INCORRECT — many countries classified as "emerging" are healthy, prosperous economies
Pattern — the "ALL / ALWAYS / NEVER" overstatement trap: when a "discuss" prompt contains a universal quantifier, the answer is almost always: concede the substance, then reject the universal. The "offset by high return" point wasn't asked and earned nothing. Discuss = find the flaw, not agree.
Likely problem areas to watch on this reading:
• Horizon vs Macaulay duration direction (which effect dominates)
• Recession hedge: demand-driven (low term premium) vs supply-driven (high term premium)
• Credit premium higher at SHORTER maturities (counterintuitive)
• Yield spread NOT a good predictor of default rates
• EM thresholds (the 4% / 50% / 200% / 100% numbers)
• Building block: which premiums stack and in what order
LOS 2.c · DCF for equity — Gordon → Grinold-Kroner
DCF says intrinsic value = PV of future cash flows; advantage = correct emphasis on future cash flows + ability to back out a required return. Best for LONG-TERM valuation. Applied to equity markets, the most common application is the Gordon (constant) growth model, where the growth rate is proxied by nominal GDP growth (real GDP + inflation), adjusted for differences between the economy's growth and that of the equity index.
Grinold-Kroner (2002) takes Gordon one step further by adding: (a) a variable for stock repurchases (cash transferred to shareholders), and (b) changes in market valuation (the P/E ratio).
The Grinold-Kroner model
E(R_e) ≈ D/P + (%ΔE − %ΔS) + %ΔP/E where: E(R_e) = expected equity return D/P = dividend yield %ΔE = expected % change in total earnings %ΔS = expected % change in shares outstanding %ΔP/E = expected % change in the P/E ratio
Regrouped into 3 components:
ComponentFormulaMeaning
1. Expected cash flow (income) returnD/P − %ΔSDividend yield adjusted for share count changes
2. Expected nominal earnings growth%ΔE = real earnings growth + inflationThe growth engine
3. Expected repricing return%ΔP/EChange in market valuation multiple
The %ΔS sign trap (Professor's Note)
Candidates get confused on when to add or subtract %ΔS.
• A share REPURCHASE (buyback) = REDUCTION in shares outstanding = company pays cash to investors → a form of POSITIVE return.
• Mathematically, a buyback is a NEGATIVE %ΔS term. Since the model SUBTRACTS %ΔS, subtracting a negative becomes a POSITIVE contribution.
• A share ISSUANCE = positive %ΔS → subtracting it REDUCES return (dilution).
Interactive · Grinold-Kroner calculator
Enter the inputs. Use the toggle to specify whether shares are being repurchased (buyback) or issued — the calculator handles the %ΔS sign automatically. "Preset 9.0%" loads the textbook example.
Dividend yield (D/P) %
Real earnings growth %
Inflation %
Change in shares outstanding (magnitude) %

Change in P/E ratio (%ΔP/E) %
Grinold-Kroner — assumptions & shortcomings
The model's assumptions may lead to irrational results because it IGNORES an investor's time horizon.
The P/E growth shortcoming (very testable):
Because the model assumes an INFINITE time horizon, an investor who selects ANY positive %ΔP/E growth rate is implicitly assuming an infinitely rising P/E ratio — an implausible result.

For very long-term horizons, the theoretically appropriate value is:
%ΔP/E = 0  (and  %ΔS = 0)
Why %ΔS = 0 too: over an infinite horizon, you can't keep buying back (or issuing) shares forever — the share-count change must also settle to zero.
P/E mean reversion — long-term vs short-term
It is relatively easy to observe the model's inputs (from published statistical data). It's more challenging to estimate the change in the P/E ratio.
• The assumption of the P/E (or price relative to other metrics like cash flow or sales) is that it has an observable long-term mean • The ratio will revert to this mean • Empirical evidence: mean reversion is true in the LONG term, but NOT in the SHORT term
Memory anchor: over an infinite/very-long horizon → assume %ΔP/E = 0 (P/E reverts to its long-run mean, so no net change). Over short horizons, P/E can deviate substantially and persistently from its mean.
Three approaches to equity returns
Same family as fixed income, applied to equity:
1. DCF (Gordon / Grinold-Kroner) — most suitable for LONG-TERM valuation 2. Risk premium approach — equity risk premium = amount equity return exceeds risk-free rate (Module 2.4) 3. Equilibrium (Singer-Terhaar) — international CAPM blending integrated + segmented (Module 2.4)
Long-horizon data & shrinkage estimators
When looking at a very long time horizon — over 100 years — mean real returns of equity markets in various countries do NOT show statistically meaningful differences.
The problem: these sample averages tend to be IMPRECISE, unless the volatility of the data is small.
The solution: shrinkage estimators are typically MORE RELIABLE as predictors of equity returns. (Shrinkage = combine the sample estimate with a target/prior to reduce estimation error.)
Equity risk premium vs the building block
Key distinction (LOS 2.c/2.d):
• For bonds: the approach relative to the risk-free rate uses a BUILDING BLOCK (stack term + credit + liquidity premiums).
• For equity: the approach relative to the risk-free rate uses a SINGLE premium for equity (the equity risk premium).

Forecasting the equity premium is generally quite challenging regardless of the approach. An analyst must supplement forecasts with other methods of analysis.
LOS 2.d · The Equilibrium Approach — Singer-Terhaar
The financial equilibrium approach assumes financial models value securities correctly. Singer-Terhaar is based on the international CAPM, using TWO versions: one where global asset markets are fully INTEGRATED, and another where markets are fully SEGMENTED. It then takes a weighted average of the two.
CAPM: R_i = R_f + β_i,M (R_M − R_f) or alternatively RP_i = β_i,M × RP_M where: R_i = expected return on asset i R_f = risk-free rate β_i,M = sensitivity (systematic risk) of asset i to the global investable market R_M = expected return on the global investable market RP_i = the asset's risk premium RP_M = the market's risk premium
The 4-step process
StepWhat you do
Step 1β_i,M = Cov(R_i,R_M) / Var(R_M) = ρ_i,M × (σ_i / σ_M)
Step 2Rearrange CAPM → RP_i = β_i,M × RP_M = ρ_i,M × σ_i × (RP_M / σ_M)
i.e. RP = correlation with global × own SD × global Sharpe ratio
Step 3Fully SEGMENTED: asset is its own market portfolio → perfectly correlated with itself (β = ρ = 1) → RP_i^S = σ_i × Sharpe. If no local Sharpe given, use global Sharpe.
Step 4Weighted average of the two: RP = φ·RP^G + (1−φ)·RP^S
φ = degree of integration; G = globally integrated, S = segmented
Step 2 in words: the risk premium for an asset = the product of its correlation with the global market portfolio AND the standard deviation of the asset (in parentheses with the global Sharpe ratio). From this we forecast the risk premium and expected return for a market.
Integration vs Segmentation
INTEGRATED: capital flows freely across borders → use the asset's ACTUAL correlation with the global market (ρ < 1) → LOWER risk premium SEGMENTED: government restrictions block capital flow → asset is its own market → ρ = 1 → HIGHER risk premium. Investment barriers INCREASE the risk premium.
Integration estimates: developed-world equity markets ≈ 75%–90% integrated; emerging market equities ≈ 50%–75% integrated.
The key driver: segmented markets always produce a HIGHER risk premium than integrated (because ρ=1 > actual ρ). The more segmented (lower φ), the higher the blended RP.
Interactive · Singer-Terhaar calculator
Computes the integrated RP and segmented RP side-by-side, then blends by the degree of integration φ. "Preset" loads the Module Quiz 2.4 Market A example.
Global Sharpe ratio (RP_M / σ_M)
Asset standard deviation (σ_i) %
Correlation with global market (ρ_i,M)
Degree of integration (φ) %
Note: this computes only the risk PREMIUM. To get expected return, add the risk-free rate (e.g. Market A example uses rf = 4.5%).
Worked example — Country X (from the reading)
Given: bonds σ=10%, ρ=0.40; equities σ=15%, ρ=0.70; market Sharpe = 0.35 RP_bonds = 10% × 0.40 × 0.35 = 1.40% RP_equities = 15% × 0.70 × 0.35 = 3.68% (This is the fully-INTEGRATED case using actual correlations.)
LOS 2.d · Emerging Market Equity Risk
Emerging markets are often characterized by:
• Fragile economies • Political and policy instability • Weaker legal protections — including weak property rights • Weak disclosure and enforcement standards
Key consequence for forecasting: EM equities tend to exhibit IDIOSYNCRATIC risks where LOCAL country effects tend to be MORE important than GLOBAL effects. Emerging markets tend to be LESS FULLY INTEGRATED than developed markets.
Ties to Singer-Terhaar: because EM markets are less integrated (φ ≈ 50–75% vs 75–90% for developed), the SEGMENTED component carries more weight → higher risk premium. Local effects dominating = lower correlation with the global market.
EM equity vs EM bond risk — connect the readings
EM Bonds (2.b)EM Equity (2.d)
Primary riskCredit risk (ability + willingness to pay)Idiosyncratic / local country effects
Key metricsDeficit/GDP, debt/GDP, FX reserves, current accountIntegration level, property rights, policy stability
Integration—50–75% (vs developed 75–90%)

❌ Error · Singer-Terhaar: which way to shift on integration
Q (Bader): Country A = developed, stays HIGHLY INTEGRATED. Country B = EM, becoming MORE SEGMENTED. Country C = EM, becoming MORE FULLY INTEGRATED. Singer-Terhaar implies Bader should shift capital from Country A to…?
Your pick: B (only Country B) ✗ Correct: C (only Country C) ✓
Why you were wrong — the "higher premium" trap: a segmented market DOES end up with a higher risk premium, so it FEELS like you'd want it. But you trade the price re-rating during the transition, not the destination yield.
The re-rating mechanic:
Integration ↑ → required return FALLS → price RISES now (markup) → buy C to capture the gain Segmentation ↑ → required return RISES → price FALLS now (markdown) → avoid B; you'd ride the loss down Country A already integrated → no re-rating left to harvest → this is the funding source
Memory hook: the risk-premium level is the DESTINATION; the price move during the trip is what you TRADE. Buy the market whose required return is about to FALL (integration), sell/avoid the one about to RISE (segmentation). Shift = A → C only.
❌ Error · EM risk — apply the threshold before naming the driver
Q (Bader): Country B is (i) experiencing declining per-capita income, (ii) running a persistent current account deficit BELOW 2% of GDP, (iii) transitioning to IFRS with full convergence in 2 years. Which area most signals INCREASING risk?
Your pick: B (Competitiveness) ✗ Correct: A (Politics) ✓
Why you were wrong: you flagged the current account as a competitiveness risk WITHOUT applying the threshold. A persistent deficit signals a lack of competitiveness only when it's > 4% of GDP. Country B's is BELOW 2% → NOT a competitiveness concern.
SignalReads asRisk?
Declining per-capita incomeSource of POLITICAL stress✓ YES
CA deficit < 2% of GDPBelow the >4% competitiveness threshold✗ no
IFRS convergence in 2 yrsBETTER accounting standards✗ positive
Threshold to memorize: CA deficit becomes a competitiveness red flag at > 4% of GDP (see EM Bond Risk thresholds). Below that, look elsewhere — here, falling per-capita income → politics.
📝 Essay (got it right — lock the formula) · Singer-Terhaar integrated RP
Prompt: market PERFECTLY INTEGRATED with world markets. GIM risk premium 3.5%, GIM σ 8.5%. Estimate each industry's expected risk premium given its σ and correlation with the GIM.
RP_i = σ_i × ρ_(i,GIM) × (RP_GIM / σ_GIM) Sharpe of GIM = 3.5 / 8.5 = 0.412
Industryσ × ρ × 0.412RP
Swiss Healthcare12 × 0.7 × 0.4123.46%
Swiss Watch6 × 0.8 × 0.4121.98%
Swiss Consumer Products7.5 × 0.8 × 0.4122.47%
Why no risk-premium split here: "perfectly integrated" → use the integrated form ONLY (full Sharpe of the GIM). No segmented component, no φ blend. The degree-of-integration blend only appears when the market is PARTIALLY integrated.
📝 Essay (subtle point worth keeping) · "Most attractive on valuation?"
Prompt: given the RPs above, judge which industry is most attractive from a VALUATION perspective.
The trap: Healthcare has the HIGHEST expected return (3.46%) → tempting to call it "most attractive."
Correct answer: that higher expected return is purely COMPENSATION FOR SYSTEMATIC RISK (higher σ × ρ). Based on the data provided, you CANNOT conclude which industry is most attractive from a valuation standpoint — you'd need to compare expected return to a REQUIRED/fair return (i.e. find mispricing).
Memory hook: highest expected return ≠ most attractive. A higher CAPM/S-T return is the hurdle, not alpha. Valuation attractiveness = expected return ABOVE the required return, which this data doesn't give.
📝 Essay gap · EM equity risks ABOVE fixed-income risks
Prompt: identify risks faced by EM EQUITY investors OVER AND ABOVE those faced by fixed-income investors in the same markets.
Your answer: fragile economies, political instability, weaker legal protection, weak disclosure/enforcement. → graded a MISS — these are the SAME economic/political/legal risks bondholders already face, not the ADDITIONAL ones.
The keyword the rubric wanted — CORPORATE GOVERNANCE RISK:
• Ownership claims may be EXPROPRIATED by corporate insiders, dominant shareholders, or the government • Interested parties may MISUSE the company's assets • Weak disclosure & accounting standards → limited transparency that FAVORS INSIDERS • Weak checks/balances on government → regulatory uncertainty, seizure of property, NATIONALIZATION
Pattern: the question said "over and above" fixed income → equity holders are RESIDUAL claimants, so the extra risk is about who controls the firm and its assets = corporate governance. Don't re-list the shared economic/political/legal risks.
Likely problem areas to watch on equity:
• Grinold-Kroner %ΔS sign (buyback = negative %ΔS = positive contribution)
• P/E growth assumption over infinite horizon (%ΔP/E = 0, %ΔS = 0)
• Singer-Terhaar segmented (ρ=1) vs integrated (actual ρ) — segmented gives HIGHER premium
• The weighted blend RP = φ·RP^G + (1−φ)·RP^S
• Shrinkage estimators for long-horizon equity returns
• EM equity: local effects > global effects, less integrated
LOS 2.e · What makes real estate different
Unlike traditional asset classes (equities, bonds, cash), real estate is:
• Immobile and illiquid • Part of a heterogeneous group — each property has unique characteristics • Requires maintenance → operating costs can be significant
Appraisal smoothing (very testable): RE returns are often calculated through APPRAISALS, which are subject to time lags and data smoothing because they're done infrequently. As a result, appraised values may differ SIGNIFICANTLY from market values. This smoothing artificially LOWERS measured volatility and correlation.
Real Estate Cycles
RE values are subject to business cycles, but they also DRIVE business cycles. Because supply is FIXED at any given point, property values exhibit cyclicality, and demand is strongly influenced by the quality and type of property available.
Quality matters: HIGH-quality properties fluctuate LESS with business cycles. LOW-quality properties show MORE cyclicality.
PhaseWhat happens
Boom↑ demand → ↑ property values + lease rates → induces CONSTRUCTION activity → stronger economic activity
BustFalling demand → overcapacity + overbuilding → values + lease rates DOWN. Leases lock tenants in for long terms + high moving costs → excess supply CAN'T be absorbed quickly.
Note from the reading: the 2008 US commercial RE collapse was caused by leverage and speculation, NOT by business cycle movements.
Capitalization Rate (Cap Rate)
The cap rate is a commercial RE property's earnings yield:
cap rate = current NOI / property value (NOI = net operating income)
It's similar to the denominator of the Gordon growth model (expected return less the NOI growth rate). The cap rate is used as a long-term measure of the risk/discount rate for RE property valuations — analogous to "expected return net of growth rate" for equities.
Expected return formulas
INFINITE time period: cap rate = E(R_re) − NOI growth rate → E(R_re) = cap rate + NOI growth rate FINITE time period (subtract change in cap rate): → E(R_re) = cap rate + NOI growth rate − %Δcap rate
Grinold-Kroner parallel: NOI growth is a NOMINAL measure incorporating real growth + inflation — just like %ΔE in Grinold-Kroner. During stable periods, long-run NOI growth ≈ GDP growth.
Interactive · Cap rate → expected return
Toggle between infinite and finite horizon. In finite mode, the change in cap rate is subtracted.
Cap rate %
NOI growth rate %
Time horizon:
Expected %Δ cap rate %
What drives the cap rate
Positively related to changes in interest rates and vacancy rates (higher rates/vacancy → higher cap rate → lower property value) Inversely related to the availability of credit and debt financing (lenders less willing to extend credit when risk is perceived higher → higher cap rates) Credit spreads (which are countercyclical) MITIGATE the cyclical sensitivity of cap rates
Competitive pressure example: with the rapid growth of online retailers, the cap-rate difference between high- and low-productivity US malls grew from 1.2% (2008) to 3.2% (2018) — cap rates are sensitive to competitive pressures.
Risk Premiums on Real Estate
RE assets require several risk premiums to compensate for their higher risk:
PremiumCompensates for
Term premiumHolding LONG-TERM assets
Credit premiumRisk of tenant NONPAYMENT
Equity risk premiumFluctuation in RE values, leases, and vacancies (above corporate bond returns)
Combined risk premium ranking (memorize): the combined RE risk premium is HIGHER than corporate bonds but LOWER than equities.

Bonds < Real Estate < Equities
Liquidity risk on real estate
Liquidity risk is also important:
• Publicly traded RE (incl REITs): liquidity risk = risk the asset cannot be sold quickly at a reasonable price • RE as an asset group: liquidity risk reflects an inability to sell the asset except at periodic times
Liquidity premium for commercial RE is between 2% and 4%.
Two adjustments for equilibrium models (Module Quiz 2.5)
Once the appropriate risk premiums are calculated, RE can be used in equilibrium models like Singer-Terhaar. BUT analysts must make two adjustments:
1. Adjust for the impact of SMOOTHING — the smoothing must be removed from the data (appraisal smoothing understates true volatility) 2. Adjust for ILLIQUIDITY — incorporate a liquidity premium
Also consider: the LOCAL rather than global nature of real estate should be considered (similar to EM equities — local effects dominate).
Public vs Private Real Estate
Wealthy individuals and large institutions can create diversified RE portfolios. Investors with less wealth can choose publicly traded RE (including REITs) to benefit from diversification.
Correlation with equities:
• REITs are generally STRONGLY correlated with equities in the SHORT term
• Direct real estate shows LOW correlation — BUT this low correlation is partly due to the SMOOTHING of returns data
• Over LONG time horizons, REITs have a relatively HIGH correlation with direct real estate
Unlevering REITs for comparison
Key step: REITs use significant LEVERAGE, so their returns and risks must first be UNLEVERED to provide an appropriate comparison with direct real estate holdings.
When adjusted for leverage, REITs as an asset class historically show:
• HIGHER return and LOWER volatility than direct real estate
Why? This difference may be due to REITs capturing much of the liquidity risk premium of direct investments, while ALSO profiting from professional management.
Property-class rankings (memorize)
CategoryHighest returnVolatility note
REITs (by class)RETAIL REITs — highest returnRetail: 2nd-LOWEST volatility
REITs (worst)INDUSTRIAL REITs — lowest returnIndustrial: HIGHEST volatility
Directly-owned REAPARTMENTS — highest returnOFFICES — lowest return
Memory anchors: RETAIL wins among REITs (high return, low vol). INDUSTRIAL is worst among REITs (low return, high vol). Among direct RE: APARTMENTS best, OFFICES worst.
Residential Real Estate Returns
Residential is the LARGEST class of developed properties, accounting for ~75% of global values.
Overall: residential RE outperformed equities on an inflation-adjusted basis with LOWER volatility. But return performance differed before and after WWII, with relatively weaker postwar returns.
PeriodResidential RE vs equities
1950–1980Strongest postwar — generally OUTPERFORMED equities
1980–2015Comparably WEAKER returns
Diversification — the key fact
Important for diversification: after the war, residential RE returns were UNCORRELATED across countries, while equity returns showed RISING correlations.
Why this matters: as equity markets became more globally correlated (less diversification benefit), residential RE retained its cross-country diversification value — making it attractive in a global portfolio.

📝 Essay gap · Main issues in historical analysis of RE returns
Prompt: describe the main issues that arise when conducting historical analysis of real estate returns.
Your answer: appraisal smoothing — subject to time lag and data smoothing, differs significantly from MV, artificially lowers measured volatility and correlation. → you had the CONSEQUENCE but the rubric wanted the CAUSES too.
The full set of issues (causes → consequences):
1. Infrequent trading: properties trade infrequently → NO data on simultaneous periodic transaction prices for a selection of properties → analysis must rely on APPRAISALS 2. Heterogeneity: each property is different (heterogeneous) — not interchangeable like shares 3. Appraisal = weighted average: returns calculated from appraisals represent weighted averages of UNOBSERVABLE returns → Consequence: the published return series is too SMOOTH → sample volatility UNDERSTATES true volatility AND distorts estimates of CORRELATIONS
Pattern (completeness): "describe the issues" wants the chain — WHY appraisals are used (infrequent trading + heterogeneity), WHAT appraisals are (weighted averages of unobservable returns), and the EFFECT (too smooth → understates vol, distorts correlation). You jumped to the effect and skipped the first two links.
Likely problem areas to watch on real estate:
• Cap rate formula: E(R_re) = cap rate + NOI growth (infinite); − %Δcap rate (finite)
• Cap rate positively related to rates/vacancy, inversely to credit availability
• Combined RP ranking: bonds < RE < equities
• Liquidity premium 2–4% for commercial RE
• The 2 equilibrium-model adjustments (smoothing + illiquidity)
• Unlever REITs before comparing to direct RE
• Property rankings: Retail REIT best, Industrial REIT worst; apartments best / offices worst direct
• Appraisal smoothing → understates volatility & correlation
• Residential uncorrelated across countries (diversification)
LOS 2.f · Why exchange rates matter & are hard to forecast
Currency exchange rate forecasting is particularly DIFFICULT → managers either FULLY HEDGE currency exposure or ACCEPT the volatility. Currencies are the units of account in which asset prices are quoted, so FX movements change the value of ALL assets denominated in one currency relative to all others.
Exchange rates are determined by factors influenced by trading, governments, financial systems, geographies, laws, regulations, and customs of a country.
Trade in goods/services — 3 channels affecting FX
Trade affects exchange rates through three channels:
1 · Trade flows
The impact of NET trade flows (gross trade flows less exports) tends to be relatively SMALL on exchange rates — ASSUMING they can be financed.
Crisis signal: large trade flows WITHOUT large financing flows in FX markets likely indicates a CRISIS.
2 · Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)
PPP implies prices of goods/services in different countries should reflect changes in FX. Therefore:
• Expected FX movement should follow expected INFLATION RATE DIFFERENTIALS
• Expected change in REAL exchange rates should be ZERO (real FX = ratio of price levels converted through a common FX rate)
3 · Competitiveness & sustainability of the current account
Covered in detail in the Current Account sub-tab.
PPP — when it works and when it doesn't
PPP works BETTER when: long-term horizon, inflation differences are LARGE and determined through money supply.
PPP does NOT work well for: short-term FX changes. Actual real FX may differ from PPP predictions because of:
• Trade barriers
• Certain goods may not be traded (non-traded goods)
• PPP does NOT account for CAPITAL FLOWS (which can exert significant influence)
• FX may also be influenced by economic development independent of PPP
Exam application (PPP): if Country A has HIGHER expected inflation than Country B, PPP predicts Country A's currency will DEPRECIATE. An investor would favor assets in the LOWER-inflation country's currency (it appreciates), OR — for an investor whose home currency appreciates — domestic assets become relatively more attractive.
Current account & exchange rates
When restrictions are placed on capital flows, exchange rate sensitivity tends to INCREASE relative to the current account balance.
Key nuance (very testable): current account balances have the largest influence on FX when they are PERSISTENT and SUSTAINED. It is NOT the SIZE of the current account balance that matters as much as the LENGTH of the imbalance.
5 sources of structural current account imbalances
Structural imbalances in the current account can exist from:
1. Fiscal imbalances that persist over time 2. Demographics and trade preferences that impact savings decisions 3. How abundant or scarce resources are 4. Availability (or lack) of viable investment opportunities 5. The terms of trade
Adjustments to capital flows → 3 considerations
Adjustments to capital flows place substantial pressure on exchange rates. Three important considerations look at the implications on:
1. Capital mobility — see Capital Flows sub-tab (the formula) 2. Uncovered interest rate parity (UIP) — see UIP & Hot Money sub-tab 3. Portfolio balances and compositions — see Portfolio Balance sub-tab
Capital mobility — the FX change formula
The expected % change in the exchange rate = the difference between nominal short-term interest rates AND the risk premiums of the domestic portfolio over the foreign portfolio:
E(%ΔS_d/f) = (r^d − r^f) + (Term^d − Term^f) + (Credit^d − Credit^f) + (Equity^d − Equity^f) + (Liquid^d − Liquid^f)
Reading the formula: a positive E(%ΔS_d/f) means the DOMESTIC currency is expected to DEPRECIATE by that percentage (in d/f quote convention, the domestic price of foreign currency rises). Each bracket is a domestic-minus-foreign differential.
Interactive · Capital mobility calculator
Enter the domestic and foreign values for each component. The calculator computes each differential and the total expected FX change.
ComponentDomestic %Foreign %
Short-term rate (r)
Term premium
Credit premium
Equity premium
Liquidity premium
The 3-phase overshooting mechanism
When there is a relative IMPROVEMENT in investment opportunities in a country, the currency initially appreciates but "OVERSHOOTS" and eventually depreciates. Three phases:
① Initial appreciation: the exchange rate will initially SIGNIFICANTLY APPRECIATE as capital flows in to capture the improved investment opportunities.
② Reversal expectation: following an extended level of stronger exchange rates in the intermediate term, investors will start to EXPECT A REVERSAL.
③ Long-run reversion: the exchange rate will tend to start REVERTING (DEPRECIATE) once the investment opportunities have been realized. This third phase is shown in the formula with a POSITIVE E(%ΔS_d/f) — the domestic currency depreciates by that percentage.
Uncovered Interest Rate Parity (UIP)
UIP states that exchange rate changes should EQUAL differences in nominal interest rates.
UIP vs the capital mobility formula: UIP implies that in the formula, ONLY the interest rate differential (r^d − r^f) matters — NOT the premium differentials (term, credit, equity, liquidity).
Carry trades — why they contradict UIP
In contrast to UIP, carry trades involve:
• BORROWING in a LOW-rate currency • LENDING in a HIGH-rate currency
Why carry trades work: they are considered successful because they include a RISK PREMIUM. This CONFIRMS the validity of the risk premiums in the capital mobility equation.

If UIP held perfectly, carry trades would NOT be profitable (the high-rate currency would depreciate exactly enough to offset the rate advantage). The fact that carry trades earn returns is evidence that the premium differentials matter.
Hot Money
When capital flows into a country given exchange rate differentials, this is referred to as HOT MONEY. Hot money creates monetary policy issues:
1. Central banks' ability to use monetary policy effectively is LIMITED 2. Firms use SHORT-TERM financing to fund LONG-TERM investments → increases financial market risk 3. Exchange rates tend to OVERSHOOT → creating business disruption
Central bank response: central banks may try to COUNTER the effects of hot money flows through INTERVENTION in currency markets, including:
• Selling government securities to limit the growth of bank reserves
• Maintaining interest rate targets
Portfolio balance and composition
Strong economic growth in a country tends to correspond to an INCREASING share of that country's currency in the global market portfolio.
The mechanism: investors need to be INDUCED to increase their allocations to that country/currency — which WEAKENS the currency and INCREASES the risk premiums of that country and currency.
Mitigating factors — why the currency may NOT weaken
A few factors could mitigate this weakening impact:
1. Home country bias: investors tend to have a strong home-country bias, which leads them to absorb a LARGER share of the new assets (less inducement needed → less weakening) 2. Productivity-driven growth: if growth is due to productivity gains, investors may fund it with financial flows AND foreign direct investment 3. High-trend-rate countries: countries that experience high trend rates tend to be smaller EMERGING markets — increasing the weight in these countries generally does NOT weaken their currency
Current account deficits — also weaken FX, with mitigants
Similarly, LARGE current account deficits also weaken exchange rates, but several mitigating factors exist:
1. Current account deficits due to large INVESTMENT spending are easier to finance if they are expected to be PROFITABLE 2. SMALL current account deficits in global RESERVE currencies (including the US dollar) help provide global LIQUIDITY and are beneficial to the financial system

⚠ Pattern · Directional Inversions (your recurring trap)
On the Bader set you flipped the DIRECTION on three otherwise-correct concepts. The concept was right; the side it pointed to was backwards.
Integration trade: bought the segmenting market instead of the integrating one Sterilization: matched "buys domestic bonds" to the inflow country instead of the outflow country Crisis vulnerability: picked the MOST-supportive holding (private equity) as the most vulnerable instead of the LEAST (public debt)
Drill habit: after you choose, say out loud which way the arrow points and why. If you can't state the direction in one sentence, you're guessing.
❌ Error · Sterilization — who BUYS domestic bonds?
Q (Bader, Exhibit 1): which country's central bank is most likely to BUY domestic bonds near term to sterilize the impact of money flows on domestic liquidity? (Country B: hot money flowing OUT. Country C: hot money flowing IN.)
Your pick: C ✗ Correct: B ✓
Why you were wrong: you matched the action to the inflow country. Trace it step by step — the BUY-bonds action belongs to the OUTFLOW country.
Country B · hot money OUTCountry C · hot money IN
FX defenseSELL foreign currency to defend domestic FX (drains domestic liquidity)(currency under upward pressure)
Sterilize viaBUY government bonds → re-injects liquidity ✓SELL government securities → drains excess reserves
GoalOffset the liquidity drain, hold rate targetLimit growth of bank reserves, hold rate target
Direction hook: outflow → CB SELLS FX, BUYS bonds. Inflow → CB BUYS FX, SELLS bonds. The question said "buys domestic bonds" → that's the OUTFLOW country (B). Sterilization always = the OFFSETTING open-market trade to neutralize the liquidity effect.
❌ Error · Currency crisis — supportiveness ranking of holdings
Q (Bader): which country is MOST vulnerable to a potential crisis based on its currency-portfolio composition? (A = majority private equity. B = majority public equity. C = majority public debt.)
Your pick: A ✗ Correct: C ✓
Why you were wrong — exact inversion: you picked the MOST-supportive composition (private equity) as the most vulnerable. The vulnerability ranking is the reverse of the supportiveness ranking.
HoldingSupportivenessWhy
Private equity (Country A)MOST supportiveLong-term committed capital — doesn't flee
Public equity (Country B)MiddleMore mobile than private, less than debt
Public debt (Country C)LEAST supportive → MOST vulnerableMust be SERVICED + repaid/refinanced → can trigger a crisis
Ranking hook (most → least supportive): Private equity > Public equity > Public debt. "Most vulnerable" = LEAST supportive = the majority-public-debt country (C). Debt has to be paid back; equity doesn't.

📝 Essay (got it right — lock the logic) · Fip & PPP
Prompt: 3 years ago the Fip was at PPP. Since then Fap inflation exceeded other countries' by ~5%/yr, but the Fip stayed broadly unchanged. What should PPP have shown, and is the Fip over- or undervalued?
PPP expectation: to offset the higher Fap inflation, the Fip should have DEPRECIATED against the other currencies by ≈ the inflation difference (~5% per annum) Verdict: since it did NOT depreciate as PPP required, the Fip is OVERVALUED
Logic: higher domestic inflation should weaken the currency under PPP. A currency that "should have fallen but didn't" is sitting ABOVE its PPP value → overvalued.
Likely problem areas to watch on exchange rates:
• PPP: higher inflation → currency depreciates; favor lower-inflation currency
• PPP works long-term / large inflation differences, NOT short-term; ignores capital flows
• Current account: LENGTH of imbalance matters more than SIZE
• Capital mobility formula: positive E(%ΔS_d/f) = domestic DEPRECIATES
• 3-phase overshooting: appreciate → expect reversal → revert (depreciate)
• UIP: only interest rate differential matters (not premiums)
• Carry trades confirm risk premiums exist (contradict UIP)
• Hot money 3 issues + central bank intervention
• Portfolio balance: growth → currency share up → currency weakens (unless home bias / productivity / EM)
LOS 2.g · The VCV Matrix
Estimating the variance for a SINGLE asset is relatively EASY. Estimating variances for MANY assets is more COMPLEX → requires a variance-covariance (VCV) matrix or other forecasting tools.
Professor's note: there are many formulas in this module, included to explain the underlying concepts. It is UNLIKELY you'll be required to do these calculations on the exam — the LOS only asks you to DISCUSS methods of volatility forecasts.
Sample VCV Matrix
A constant VCV matrix is most easily estimated from sample statistics (deriving variances and covariances from the sample).
Sample size is critical for large portfolios: the number of assets CANNOT exceed the number of historical observations. If the sample size is small relative to the number of assets, outcomes may be MEANINGLESS — e.g. the matrix may show that a large portfolio is RISKLESS.
Rule of thumb (testable): the number of observations should be at least 10× larger than the number of portfolio assets.
Sample VCV — the key advantage
Consistent AND unbiased: unlike the factor-based matrix, the sample VCV matrix is both CONSISTENT (converges to the true matrix as the sample grows) and UNBIASED (a predictor of true returns, on average). This is the benchmark the factor model fails against.
Factor-Based VCV Matrices
Main advantage: using multifactor models for VCV matrices significantly REDUCES the number of required observations. Correlations can be estimated from a few common factors, while variances require factors related to specific assets.
Return of the ith asset in a multifactor model:
r_i = α_i + Σ(k=1 to K) β_ik · F_k + ε_i
K = number of common factors α_i = intercept β_ik = ith asset's sensitivity to the kth factor F_k = kth factor return ε_i = factor term unique to asset i (zero mean)
Variance & covariance formulas
Variance of asset i: σ²_i = ΣΣ β_im · β_in · ρ_mn + ν²_i Covariance between i and j: σ_ij = ΣΣ β_im · β_jn · ρ_mn
ρ_mn = covariance between the mth and nth factors ν²_i = variance of the unique factor ε_i
Assuming these factors are NOT redundant and do NOT have zero terms → ensures matrix outcomes are not meaningless and portfolios don't incorrectly appear riskless.
Interactive · Why factor models need fewer estimates
Enter the number of assets (N) and common factors (K). Compare the number of estimates for a full sample VCV vs a factor-based model.
Number of assets (N)
Number of factors (K)
Textbook example: N=50, K=6 → sample VCV needs 1,225 covariances (50×49/2), while the factor model needs only 300 sensitivities (50×6) + 21 factor elements (6×7/2).
2 shortcomings of factor-based VCV
1 · BIASED
Matrix inputs need to be estimated, so the matrix will be biased (misspecified). As a result, it will NOT be a predictor of the true returns — not even on average.
2 · INCONSISTENT
As the sample size increases, the model does NOT converge to the true matrix.
Contrast: the SAMPLE VCV matrix is both CONSISTENT and UNBIASED — the two properties the factor-based matrix lacks. (This contrast is the testable point.)
Shrinkage Estimates
Combining information in the SAMPLE VCV matrix with a TARGET matrix (e.g. the factor-based VCV matrix) results in more precise data and reduced estimation error.
shrinkage estimate = weight × sample + (1 − weight) × target (same weights used for ALL elements of the matrix, including variance and covariance factors)
Why it helps: the resulting figures are more EFFICIENT because they have smaller error terms. Even though shrinkage estimates may be biased, MORE PRECISE (less biased) target matrices will result in greater improvement.
Interactive · Shrinkage estimate
Replicates the textbook example: sample covariance 180, target 220, weight 60% sample / 40% target → 196.
Sample covariance
Target covariance (factor-based)
Weight on SAMPLE %
Smoothed Returns to Estimate Volatility
The core effect (very testable): smoothing of data leads to:
• UNDERESTIMATING risk
• OVERSTATING returns
• OVERSTATING diversification benefits

Not adjusting for smoothing → distorted portfolio analysis and suboptimal asset allocation decisions.
Adjust by taking a weighted average of the current "true" returns and previously observed returns:
R_t = (1 − λ)·r_t + λ·R_t−1 (λ = weight between 0 and 1)
Variance inflation formula
var(r) = ((1 + λ) / (1 − λ)) · var(R) > var(R)
The TRUE variance var(r) is always GREATER than the observed (smoothed) variance var(R) — confirming that smoothing UNDERSTATES risk.
Interactive · Variance inflation from smoothing
Replicates the textbook example: λ = 0.6 → true variance is 1.6/0.4 = 4× the observed variance, and 2× the standard deviation.
Smoothing weight λ (0–1)
Shortcoming of the smoothing model
One shortcoming: the true CURRENT return (r_t) is NOT directly observable.
Remedy: proxies for estimating the true return include using an asset INDEX.
ARCH Models
Asset returns generally show periods of HIGH and LOW volatilities, leading to VOLATILITY CLUSTERING. These volatilities can be addressed through autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH) models, used for portfolios with multiple assets in VCV matrix estimations.
Professor's note: you encountered ARCH at Level II — use that knowledge to your advantage.
The simplest ARCH formula
σ²_t = γ + α·σ²_t−1 + β·η²_t equivalently: σ²_t = γ + (α+β)·σ²_t−1 + β·(η²_t − σ²_t−1)
α, β, γ = nonnegative parameters (α + β) < 1 — required constraint η_t = random variable indicating the unexpected return component
Interpreting α + β
Key relationship (testable): HIGHER α + β terms indicate HIGHER emphasis on PAST information, leading to more VOLATILITY CLUSTERING.
Intuition: the more weight placed on the prior period's variance (σ²_t−1) and the prior shock, the more today's volatility "remembers" yesterday's — so high-volatility periods follow high-volatility periods (clustering).
