Module Quiz 2.7 · Q1 framework (the recurring essay setup)
Setup: manager needs 17 asset classes; has weekly sample data over the last 6 months; uses a factor-based matrix but NO shrinkage. Determine strengths and shortcomings.
Strengths to cite: factor model needs FEWER observations (key, because 6 months of weekly data ≈ 26 observations < 10×17 = 170 needed for a sample VCV → a sample VCV here would be MEANINGLESS / could appear riskless).
Shortcomings to cite: factor-based matrix is BIASED (not a predictor even on average) and INCONSISTENT (won't converge to true matrix as sample grows).
Q2 remedy: use SHRINKAGE — combine the factor-based (target) matrix with the sample VCV to reduce estimation error and improve efficiency.
Likely problem areas to watch on volatility:
• Sample VCV: observations ≥ 10× assets; too few → appears riskless
• Sample VCV is consistent AND unbiased (the benchmark)
• Factor model advantage = fewer observations
• Factor model 2 shortcomings: BIASED + INCONSISTENT
• Shrinkage = weighted avg sample + target (ex: 180×0.6 + 220×0.4 = 196)
• Smoothing → underestimates risk, overstates returns + diversification
• Smoothing variance: ((1+λ)/(1−λ))·var(R); λ=0.6 → 4× variance, 2× SD
• Smoothing shortcoming: true return not observable → use asset index proxy
• ARCH: volatility clustering; (α+β)<1; higher α+β → more clustering
LOS 2.h · The goal of this module
Recommend and justify changes in the component weights of a global investment portfolio based on TRENDS and EXPECTED CHANGES in macroeconomic factors. The focus is on HOW to adjust a portfolio, not on the particular forecast details.
Starting from a typical equities/bonds portfolio, an analyst may change weights between:
• Equities vs bonds
• Domestic vs international
• Credit quality, duration, yield curve positioning, or currency exposures of the underlying assets
The 5 questions to keep in mind
To aid the decision-making process, keep these five questions in mind:
1. Have the drivers of trend growth changed significantly? 2. Are markets becoming more or less integrated? 3. Where is the country positioned within the business cycle, and are fiscal and monetary policies consistent with the business cycle phase? 4. What is the trend in current account balances? 5. Are currencies strong or weak, and how are currencies affecting economic growth and competitiveness?
Mnemonic: Trend → Integration → Cycle → Current account → Currency. Each question maps to one of the other sub-tabs in this module.
Trend Growth → equity vs bond tilt
Trend growth is…EffectWhy
FAVORABLE to equities↑ equity weightImplies long-term EARNINGS GROWTH
UNFAVORABLE to bonds↓ bond weightTypically results in HIGHER interest rates
The analyst can use country-specific and global expectations through VCV matrices to adjust the allocations between equities and bonds.
Market Integration → required returns
Key relationship (from Singer-Terhaar): as markets become MORE integrated globally, required returns will FALL. Lower required returns → higher current prices → lower future expected returns.
The reallocation rule:
INCREASE allocations toward emerging markets EXPECTED to see INCREASED integration (they'll re-rate up as required returns fall) DECREASE / move AWAY from markets that are ALREADY highly integrated (the re-rating benefit is already captured)
The intuition: you want to OWN the market BEFORE its required return falls (capturing the price appreciation), not AFTER. Already-integrated markets have already had their required returns fall.
Trough vs Peak — the reallocation playbook
The business cycle position drives the entire reallocation. Each lever is decomposed below.
LeverTROUGHPEAK (reverse)
Equity weightINCREASEREDUCE
Bond weightREDUCEINCREASE
Bond durationREDUCE (shorten)INCREASE (extend)
Curve structureBARBELL (short + long, less medium)Reverse of barbell
Why the TROUGH playbook — decomposed
Equities perform well at the trough: valuation ratios AND earnings growth are expected to INCREASE. The analyst could use the Grinold-Kroner model to compute the required equity risk premium → INCREASE equity weights.
At the trough, the yield curve is STEEP with high credit and term premiums. So why reduce bonds and shorten duration?
Driver 1 — rising rates expected: the expectation of RISING interest rates means bonds tend to UNDERPERFORM → reduce bond allocation Driver 2 — duration risk: rising rates hurt long-duration bonds most → REDUCE overall bond duration Driver 3 — curve positioning: a BARBELL may be optimal — increased short-term exposure (rolls up as rates rise) + long-term exposure, with reduced medium-term exposure
PEAK — the reverse strategy
At the peak, follow the REVERSE strategy:
• REDUCE equity exposure
• INCREASE bond exposure AND durations

(Slowing growth + expected rate cuts → bonds outperform, long duration captures the rally.)
Monetary & Fiscal Policy — focus on STRUCTURAL changes
The key nuance: the analyst should focus LESS on monetary and fiscal policy ACTIVITIES — these are expected to be ALREADY REFLECTED in asset values. Focus instead on STRUCTURAL changes in policy direction.
Examples of structural changes that CAN influence portfolio reallocation:
• Changes in the tax code • Changes from standard interest rate targeting to other policies, including quantitative easing (QE)
Current Account — the LONG-TERM TREND matters
Current account balances fluctuate with business cycles, but it is the LONG-TERM TREND in current account balances that is more important in setting portfolio expectations.
Rising current account deficits tend to be associated with:
• RISING required returns (and therefore FALLING asset prices)
• INCREASED capital flows to the deficit country to fund its deficit
Capital Flows → Currency: is it at its PEAK?
Capital flows also influence currencies. If assets in a particular currency offer HIGHER risk-adjusted return potential than in other currencies, capital will flow to that country and put UPWARD pressure on its currency.
The analyst's judgment call: determine whether the currency STILL HAS POTENTIAL to appreciate, or whether it is at its PEAK (links to the 3-phase overshooting in the Exchange Rate module — appreciation eventually reverses).

Pick a scenario signal. The drill reads the signal → infers the cycle phase → recommends the reallocation across every lever, with reasoning. Includes the two Module Quiz 2.8 country scenarios.

Likely problem areas to watch on portfolio adjustments:
• The 5 questions (trend / integration / cycle / current account / currency)
• Trend growth: favors equities, hurts bonds (higher rates)
• More integration → required returns FALL → tilt toward EM gaining integration, away from already-integrated
• TROUGH: ↑equity, ↓bond, ↓duration, BARBELL; use Grinold-Kroner for ERP
• PEAK: reverse — ↓equity, ↑bond, ↑duration
• Inverted/downward curve → late cycle/peak signal → reduce equity, extend bond duration
• Policy: focus on STRUCTURAL changes (tax code, QE), not already-priced activities
• Current account: LONG-TERM TREND matters; rising deficit → rising required returns, falling prices
• Currency: judge whether still appreciating or at PEAK
Reading 2 · Capital Market Expectations, Part 2 — Forecasting Asset Class Returns
Full-reading recap, module by module. Builds on Part 1 by setting expectations per asset class: fixed income, equity, real estate, and currencies — plus risk analysis for developed vs emerging markets, volatility forecasting, and portfolio adjustments. Core idea: investments revert to fundamental levels over time (central tendency).
Introduction · Approaches to Forecasting CME
Three approaches: formal tools, surveys, judgment
Formal toolsGive forecasts replicable by other analysts when applied to reputable data. Three types below. SurveysPoll experts (economists, analysts) for opinions — useful to gauge consensus. E.g. the Philadelphia Fed's ongoing CPI/GDP survey. JudgmentQualitative, experience-based. Even with quantitative models, an analyst must sometimes adjust the numbers with insight.
The three formal tools:
Statistical methodsSample statistics (means, variance, correlation from known data — clearest, but can be imprecise); shrinkage estimate (weighted average of historical estimate + another projection); time-series estimate (forecasts a variable from its own lagged values + lags of others, incorporating volatility dynamics). DCF modelsIntrinsic value = PV of future cash flows. Advantage: correct emphasis on future cash flows and ability to back out a required return. Best for long-term valuation. Risk premium / buildupStart with a risk-free rate, add compensation for priced risks. Used for FI and equity. Includes equilibrium models (e.g. CAPM), factor models, and building blocks.
Module 2.1 · Forecasting Fixed-Income Returns
LOS 2.aThree approaches to FI returns
DCF method, risk-premium (building block) approach, and the equilibrium model (assumes global supply & demand in asset markets are in balance).
DCF analysis & the YTM
Useful when future cash flows are known or reasonably estimable. Uses YTM as the estimate of expected return — YTM is an IRR, so it's the realized return only if cash flows are reinvested at the YTM and the bond is held to maturity. For zero-coupon bonds there are no coupons to reinvest, but the hold-to-maturity assumption still applies. For a portfolio, the YTM is the weighted average of the bonds' YTMs (a good approximation).
Why realized return deviates from initial YTM: (1) hold-to-maturity ignores optionality → cash flows may not arrive as expected; (2) sell before maturity → capital gain/loss; (3) rate changes alter reinvestment: falling (rising) rates decrease (increase) reinvestment returns.
Horizon vs Macaulay duration — the decisive rule
Horizon < Macaulay durCapital gain/loss dominates. Falling (rising) rates → higher (lower) realized return. Horizon > Macaulay durReinvestment risk dominates. Falling (rising) rates → lower (higher) realized return.
For the exam: Macaulay duration = modified duration × (1 + YTM).
Worked example · Turk bond portfolio (Macaulay verified 6.6)
$200M portfolio, YTM 5.5%, modified duration 6.25, investment horizon 4 years, yields expected to fall 25 bps/yr. Higher or lower realized return than initial YTM?
Macaulay duration = mod dur × (1 + YTM) = 6.25 × 1.055 = 6.6 Horizon (4 yrs) < Macaulay (6.6) → capital-gain effect dominates. Falling yields → HIGHER realized return than the initial YTM. (Price gain outweighs the decline in reinvestment yield.)
The building block (risk premium) approach
Required return = one-period default-free rate + term premium + credit premium + liquidity premium.
4 · Liquidity premium newest / off-the-run & less-liquid issues
3 · Credit premium expected risk of default (separate from expected default losses)
2 · Term premium positive, related to duration
1 · Short-term default-free rate ≈ central bank policy rate / govt zero-coupon
= Required return on the bond
1 · Short-term rateMatches the forecast horizon; closest to the government zero-coupon yield, tied to the central bank policy rate. If horizon ≫ instrument maturity → use a longer-maturity zero yield, or the roll-over return (futures rates proxy the expected short-rate path). 2 · Term premiumPositive, related to duration. The real term premium can't be derived from the yield curve alone. Four primary drivers below. 3 · Credit premiumCompensates for expected risk of default — separate from compensation for expected default losses (both are in the credit spread). 4 · Liquidity premiumHighest at a bond's earliest stages (first few weeks). Most liquid: newest issues, current-coupon MBS, some sovereigns.
Term premium — 4 primary drivers + other indicators
Inflation uncertaintyHigher inflation → higher inflation uncertainty → nominal yields rise and the term premium increases. Recession hedgeInflation from strong aggregate demand → nominal bond returns negatively correlated with growth → low term premiums. Inflation from aggregate supply → positively correlated with growth → higher term premiums. Supply & demandRelative supply of short- vs long-term default-free bonds sets the curve slope, which influences the term-premium level. Business cyclesCurve slope & term-premium level are also tied to the business cycle.
Other term-premium indicators: ex-ante (forecast) real yield · Cochrane-Piazzesi curve factor (slope + curvature) · Kim-Wright premium (3-factor term-structure model) · slope of the yield curve · supply indicator (% of debt with maturity > 10 yrs) · cyclical proxies (corporate profit-to-GDP, business confidence, unemployment).
Credit premium — behavior & predictors
Uneven / clusteredPremiums earned are uneven, with clustering of persistent high/low default rates → the yield spread is NOT a good predictor of future default rates. Strong spread predictorsStock returns, stock volatility, and the risk-free rate. Weak predictors: GDP growth and default-rate changes. High-quality (AAA/AA)Extremely low default rates → premium/spread driven mainly by downgrade bias (asymmetric: downgrade more likely than upgrade). Low(er)-rated / HY bonds carry much higher credit-risk compensation. Maturity relationCredit premiums are NOT positively related to maturity — often higher at shorter maturities (event risk: defaults are large credit-negative events; older short bonds tend to be illiquid).
Steep yield curve = bullish: high OAS → higher credit premium; steep Treasury curve → declining default rates. Steep curves imply large compensation for credit losses (high credit AND term premiums). Managers exploit these with a barbell — take credit risk from shorter maturities, duration risk from long maturities.
Module Quiz 2.1
Q1. Bond portfolio: YTM 4, modified duration 5, held ≥6 years, yields rise +100 bps total over horizon. Higher or lower realized return than initial YTM?
Answer: Macaulay = 5 × 1.04 = 5.2. Horizon (6 yrs) > Macaulay (5.2) → reinvestment effect dominates. Rising yields → reinvestment at higher rates → higher realized return than the initial YTM.
Q2–Q3 (Lou Bee): 1-yr govt (rf 2.5%) & 5-yr AA corp. Term premium 60 bps, credit premium 30 bps, liquidity premium 25 bps. Equal-weight.
Component1-yr govt5-yr AA corp
Risk-free rate2.50%2.50%
+ Term premium—0.60%
+ Credit premium—0.30%
+ Liquidity premium—0.25%
Expected return2.50%3.65%
Total risk premium0.00%1.15%
Q2 (expected return, EW): (2.50% + 3.65%) / 2 = 3.075% → closest to 3% (B).
Q3 (total risk premium, EW): (0% + 1.15%) / 2 = 0.575% → closest to 0.6% (A). The govt bond's risk premium above rf is 0.
Module 2.2 · Emerging Market Bond Risk
LOS 2.bEM fixed-income risks & country analysis
EM debt offers high expected returns at the cost of higher risk. Many EMs depend on foreign borrowing → later crises in economy, currency, and financial markets. Often unstable political/social systems, undiversified economies. For the bond investor the key risk is credit risk — does the country have the ability AND willingness to repay? Economic, political, and legal risks matter too.
Signs an EM is more susceptible to risk
ConcentrationWealth concentration; income concentration & a less diverse tax base. Economic structureGreater dominance of cyclical industries (incl. commodities) & less pricing power. RestrictionsRestrictions on capital flows, trade, and currency. Policy & capacityInadequate fiscal/monetary policies; poor workforce education, infrastructure, weak tech advancement. External fragilityLarge foreign borrowing in foreign currencies; small/underdeveloped financial markets; exposure to volatile capital flows.
EM health checklist — the decisive thresholds
Deficit-to-GDP> 4% indicates substantial credit risk (fiscal-policy gauge). EMs borrow short and refinance periodically → debt buildup raises non-payment likelihood. Debt-to-GDP70%–80% has been troublesome for EMs. Real growth rateInvestors should expect ≥ 4% to compensate for higher risk; below that may signal a slowing economy. Current account deficit> 4% of GDP is a warning sign of potential difficulty. Debt levelsForeign debt > 50% of GDP, or growing beyond the country's ability to service it, indicates overleverage. Foreign debt as a large share of short-term debt is a trouble sign. FX reserves / short-term debtReserves relative to short-term debt: < 100% important; > 200% considered strong.
Government stance: support for structural reforms, responsible fiscal policy, competition, and privatization → better growth prospects & a more hospitable environment. Weak enforcement of property-rights laws, nationalization, and corruption are hazard signs. Coalition governments are riskier due to inherent political/policy instability.
Module Quiz 2.2
Q1. Analyst evaluating an EM notices the country's current account deficit is growing. Sign of increasing risk? Explain.
Answer: Yes. A rising current-account deficit is a warning sign — especially once it exceeds 4% of GDP. It signals the country increasingly relies on foreign financing; if foreign capital flees, the result is currency devaluation and declining asset values (a financial crisis). Growing deficits are associated with rising required returns and falling asset prices.
Module 2.3 · Forecasting Equity Returns
LOS 2.cApproaches to equity returns
Over 100+ years, mean real equity returns across countries don't show statistically meaningful differences (sample averages are imprecise unless volatility is small) → shrinkage estimators are typically more reliable predictors of equity returns.
Two main tools: DCF (most suitable for long-term valuation) and the risk-premium approach (Module 2.4).
Gordon growth (constant)Most common DCF for equities; often applied to whole markets. Backs out expected return; growth proxied by nominal GDP growth (real GDP + inflation), adjusted for any gap between the economy's growth and the equity index's growth. Grinold-Kroner (2002)Extends Gordon: adds a variable for share repurchases and for P/E changes. Below.
The Grinold-Kroner model
E(Re) ≈ D/P + (%ΔE − %ΔS) + %ΔP/E D/P = dividend yield %ΔE = expected % change in total earnings %ΔS = expected % change in shares outstanding %ΔP/E = expected % change in the P/E ratio
Regroup into three components:
1 · Income returnD/P − %ΔS. Current yield adjusted for repurchases/issues. 2 · Nominal earnings growth%ΔE = real earnings growth + expected inflation. 3 · Repricing return%ΔP/E = expected change in the P/E multiple.
Sign of %ΔS (Prof's note): a share repurchase reduces shares outstanding → it is a negative %ΔS term. Subtracting a negative makes income return larger — repurchases raise EPS, cash flow to investors, and expected return.
Infinite-horizon shortcoming: G-K ignores the investor's time horizon. Any positive assumed %ΔP/E growth rate implies an infinitely rising P/E — implausible. For very long horizons the theoretically appropriate assumption is %ΔP/E = 0 (and %ΔS = 0), i.e. P/E reverts to its long-term average. Empirically the P/E has an observable long-term mean it reverts to in the long term, but not the short term.
Worked example · Grinold-Kroner (verified 9.0%)
Dividend yield 2.1%, real earnings growth 4.0%, long-term inflation 3.1%, share increase +0.5%, P/E expansion +0.3%.
Income return = D/P − %ΔS = 2.1% − 0.5% = 1.6% Nominal earnings= real growth + inflation = 4.0% + 3.1% = 7.1% Repricing return= %ΔP/E = 0.3% ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── E(Re) = 1.6% + 7.1% + 0.3% = 9.0%
Module Quiz 2.3
Q1 (Tel-Pal). Price $75, next-year dividend $3, 2M shares outstanding, firm issues 40,000 new shares, expected inflation 3.5%, P/E stays the same, nominal earnings +6.8%. Expected return next year?
D/P = 3 / 75 = 4.0% %ΔS = 40,000 / 2,000,000 = +2.0% (issue → positive) Income = D/P − %ΔS = 4.0% − 2.0% = 2.0% %ΔE (nominal earnings) = 6.8% %ΔP/E (P/E unchanged) = 0.0% ────────────────────────────────────────────── E(Re) = 2.0% + 6.8% + 0.0% = 8.8%
Note: here the firm issues shares, so %ΔS = +2% and income return is reduced (the opposite of a repurchase). Inflation of 3.5% is already embedded in the given nominal earnings growth, so it is not added again.
Q2. Analyst uses G-K with an infinite horizon and a P/E growth rate of 2%. Discuss one shortcoming of the P/E-growth assumption.
Answer: A positive P/E growth over an infinite horizon implies an infinitely rising P/E ratio — implausible. Over long horizons the P/E should revert to its long-term average, so the appropriate long-run assumption is %ΔP/E = 0. A permanent +2% repricing return is not sustainable.
Module 2.4 · The Risk Premium Approach
Equity risk premium — two definitions
Relative to risk-freeThe amount equity return exceeds the risk-free rate → a single premium for equity. Relative to bondsThe amount equity return exceeds the expected return on a default-free bond → uses a building-block approach.
Forecasting the equity premium is challenging regardless of approach — supplement with other analysis.
The equilibrium approach — Singer-Terhaar (CAPM-based)
Assumes financial models value securities correctly. Based on the international CAPM under two versions: one where global markets are fully integrated, another where they are fully segmented; then a weighted average of the two.
CAPM: Ri = Rf + βi,M (RM − Rf), i.e. RPi = βi,M × RPM Step 1: βi,M = Cov(Ri,RM)/Var(RM) = ρi,M (σi / σM) Step 2: RPi = βi,M · RPM = ρi,M · σi · (RPM / σM) → RPi = ρi,M · σi · (market Sharpe ratio)
Reading of Step 2: an asset's risk premium = its correlation with the global market × its own σ × the global market's Sharpe ratio. The global investable market = all investable assets, traditional + alternative.
Segmentation (adjustment)The model adjusts CAPM for market imperfections. Segmented: capital does NOT flow freely across borders (govt restrictions on investing are a frequent cause) → two same-risk assets can have different expected returns; investment barriers increase the risk premium. Integration (contrast)Capital flows freely; same risk → same expected return. RealityMost markets are partial. Developed equity ≈ 75%–90% integrated; emerging equity ≈ 50%–75% integrated. Investors have a home-country bias, preventing full exploitation of overseas opportunities.
Singer-Terhaar — the 4-step procedure
Step 1 · ββi,M = Cov(Ri,RM)/Var(RM) = ρi,M(σi/σM). Step 2 · RP (integrated)RPi = ρi,M · σi · (market Sharpe ratio) — the fully integrated premium (uses the global correlation). Step 3 · RP (segmented)If ρi,M = 1 → RPiˢ = σi · (RPiˢ/σi) = σi × Sharpe. Under full segmentation the asset is its own market, so it is perfectly correlated with itself (β = ρ = 1). If no local Sharpe is given, use the global market Sharpe. Step 4 · Weighted RPRP = φ·RPG + (1 − φ)·RPS, where φ = degree of integration with global markets (G = globally integrated, S = segmented).
Illiquidity premium: for emerging / illiquid markets, add an illiquidity risk premium to the CAPM-derived risk premium (in BOTH the integrated and segmented calculations) before taking the weighted average.
Worked example · Country X (verified 1.40% / 3.68%)
Market Sharpe ratio 0.35. Bonds: σ 10%, correlation w/ global 0.40. Equities: σ 15%, correlation w/ global 0.70.
RP_bonds = σ × ρ × Sharpe = 10% × 0.40 × 0.35 = 1.40% RP_equities = σ × ρ × Sharpe = 15% × 0.70 × 0.35 = 3.68% (3.675, rounded)
Worked example · Markets A (developed) & B (emerging) (all verified)
Horizon 5 yrs. Global market Sharpe 0.29. Risk-free 5.0%. EM illiquidity premium 2.30%.
InputMarket AMarket B
Volatility σ17%28%
Correlation w/ global0.820.63
Degree of integration80%65%
Illiquidity premium0%2.3%
FULL INTEGRATION RPi = ρ · σ · Sharpe (+ illiq for EM) RP_A = 0.82 × 0.17 × 0.29 = 4.04% RP_B = 0.63 × 0.28 × 0.29 + 0.0230 = 7.42% FULL SEGMENTATION RPi = σ · Sharpe (ρ = 1, local = reference) RP_A = 0.17 × 0.29 = 4.93% RP_B = 0.28 × 0.40 + 0.0230 = 13.50% (Market B uses its own Sharpe 0.40 under segmentation) WEIGHTED RP = (integ)(RP_int) + (1 − integ)(RP_seg) RP_A = 0.80 × 4.04% + 0.20 × 4.93% = 4.22% RP_B = 0.65 × 7.42% + 0.35 × 13.50% = 9.55% EXPECTED RETURN = Rf + RP R_A = 5% + 4.22% = 9.22% R_B = 5% + 9.55% = 14.55%
Segmentation detail: under full segmentation the local market is the reference (ρ = 1.0), and — if given — the local Sharpe ratio is used (here Market B's 0.40), not the global 0.29.
LOS 2.dEmerging market equity risk
EMs: fragile economies, political/policy instability, weaker legal protections (incl. weak property rights), weak disclosure & enforcement. Idiosyncratic (local) risks tend to matter more than global effects, and EMs tend to be less fully integrated than developed markets.
Module Quiz 2.4 mirrors the A/B worked example (global Sharpe 0.29, σ_global 8%, rf 4.5%, integration A 80% / B 65%, σ_A 18% / σ_B 26%, ρ_A 0.87 / ρ_B 0.63) — asks to calculate the risk premiums and expected returns for both markets using the same 4-step Singer-Terhaar procedure above.
Module 2.5 · Forecasting Real Estate Returns
LOS 2.eEconomic & competitive factors in RE
Unlike traditional asset classes, real estate is immobile, illiquid, heterogeneous, and has significant operating/maintenance costs. Returns are often computed via appraisals → subject to time lags and data smoothing (done infrequently) → appraised values can differ significantly from market values.
Real estate cycles
Supply is fixed short-runProperty values exhibit cyclicality; demand depends on quality & type. High-quality properties fluctuate less with the cycle; low-quality show more cyclicality. BoomRising demand → higher values & lease rates → induces construction → stronger economic activity. BustFalling demand → overcapacity & overbuilding → values & lease rates fall. Long leases lock in tenants & high moving costs → excess supply can't be absorbed quickly.
A recent study suggests the U.S. commercial RE collapse after the GFC was caused by leverage and speculation rather than business-cycle movements.
Capitalization (cap) rates
The cap rate = current NOI ÷ property value (an earnings yield). Analogous to the Gordon-model denominator (expected return − NOI growth rate).
cap rate = E(R_re) − NOI growth rate E(R_re) = cap rate + NOI growth rate (infinite horizon) E(R_re) = cap rate + NOI growth rate − %Δcap rate (finite horizon)
NOI growth ≈ GDPDuring stable periods the long-run NOI growth rate should be close to GDP growth. Like G-K, NOI growth is a nominal measure (real growth + inflation). Competitive pressureCap rate is sensitive to competition — e.g. the mall cap-rate gap between high- and low-productivity malls grew from 1.2% (2008) to 3.2% (2018) with the rise of online retail. Rates & vacancyCap rates are positively related to interest rates and vacancy rates (used as a long-term risk discount rate). Credit availabilityLenders less willing to extend credit → higher perceived risk → cap rates inversely related to credit/debt-financing availability. Credit spreads (countercyclical) mitigate the cyclical sensitivity of cap rates.
Risk premiums on real estate
Term premiumFor holding long-term assets. Credit premiumFor risk of tenant nonpayment. Equity risk premiumAbove corporate-bond returns, for fluctuation in RE values, leases, and vacancies. Liquidity premiumRE (incl. REITs) can't always be sold quickly at a fair price — sellable only at periodic times. 2%–4% for commercial real estate.
Combined RE risk premium is higher than corporate bonds but lower than equities. Using equilibrium models (e.g. Singer-Terhaar) for RE requires two adjustments: remove the impact of smoothing from the data, and incorporate a liquidity premium. Also consider RE's local (not global) nature.
Public vs private RE · residential
REITs vs directREITs strongly correlated with equities short-term; direct RE shows low correlation (partly smoothing). Over long horizons REITs have relatively high correlation with direct RE. Leverage adjustmentREITs use significant leverage → must be unlevered for a fair comparison with direct holdings. Adjusted for leverage, REITs historically show higher returns & lower volatility — capturing the liquidity premium of direct investment plus professional management. By class (REITs)Retail REITs: highest return, second-lowest volatility. Industrial REITs: lowest return, highest volatility. Directly-owned: apartments highest return, offices lowest. ResidentialLargest class (~75% of global developed-property value). Outperformed equities on an inflation-adjusted basis with lower volatility; strongest postwar returns 1950–1980, weaker 1980–2015. Postwar residential returns were uncorrelated across countries (good for diversification) while equity returns showed rising correlations.
Module Quiz 2.5: the two adjustments analysts must make to RE risk premiums from equilibrium models — (1) remove the impact of smoothing from the data, and (2) incorporate a liquidity premium (also consider the local rather than global nature of RE).
Module 2.6 · Exchange Rate Forecasting
LOS 2.fApproaches to forecasting exchange rates
FX forecasting is particularly difficult — managers either fully hedge or accept the volatility. Currencies are the units of account for asset prices; exchange-rate moves reprice all assets in one currency relative to others. Rates are influenced by trading, governments, financial systems, geographies, laws, and customs.
A. Trade in goods & services — 3 channels
1 · Trade flowsNet trade flows have a relatively small impact on FX (assuming they can be financed). Large trade flows without large financing flows → likely a crisis. 2 · Purchasing power parityExpected FX movement follows expected inflation-rate differentials; expected change in the real rate should be zero. PPP works poorly short-term, better long-term and when inflation differences are large (money-supply driven). Doesn't hold with trade barriers, non-traded goods, or capital flows; FX also moves with economic development independent of PPP. 3 · Competitiveness / current accountSee capital-mobility channels below — current-account sustainability drives FX.
B. Capital flows — 3 considerations
1 · Capital mobilityExpected % FX change = difference between domestic & foreign nominal short-term rates AND risk premiums:
E(%ΔS_d/f) = (r^d − r^f) + (Term^d − Term^f) + (Credit^d − Credit^f) + (Equity^d − Equity^f) + (Liquid^d − Liquid^f)
Overshooting (3 phases)When investment opportunities improve, the currency (1) initially appreciates significantly; (2) in the intermediate term investors expect a reversal; (3) long-run it reverts / depreciates once opportunities are realized. Positive E(%ΔS_d/f) → domestic currency depreciates by that %. 2 · Uncovered interest rate parity (UIP)FX changes should equal differences in nominal interest rates → only the interest-rate differential matters, not the premium differentials. In contrast, carry trades (borrow low-rate, lend high-rate currency) are considered successful because they include a risk premium — confirming the risk premiums in the equation. 3 · Portfolio balance & compositionStrong economic growth → an increasing share of that country's currency in the global market portfolio; investors must be induced (higher returns) to raise allocations.
Hot money: capital flowing in on rate differentials. Creates monetary-policy problems: (1) limits central banks' policy effectiveness; (2) firms use short-term financing for long-term investment → ↑ financial-market risk; (3) FX tends to overshoot → business disruption. Central banks may counter via currency-market intervention: selling government securities to limit bank-reserve growth, or maintaining interest-rate targets.
Current account & FX — mitigating factors
Current-account balancesHave the largest FX impact when persistent and sustained; the length of the imbalance matters more than its size. Structural imbalances arise from: (1) fiscal imbalances, (2) demographics/trade preferences, (3) abundant/scarce resources, (4) availability (or lack) of viable investment opportunities, (5) terms of trade. High trend rate mitigantsWeakens currency & ↑ risk premiums, BUT: home-country bias (investors absorb more new assets); if growth is from productivity gains, funded by financial flows & FDI; high-trend countries tend to be smaller EMs (raising their weight generally doesn't weaken the currency). Large deficit mitigantsDeficits from large investment spending are easier to finance if expected profitable; small deficits in global reserve currencies (incl. USD) provide global liquidity and benefit the financial system.
Module Quiz 2.6
Q1. Japanese cumulative inflation projected 8.2% over 5 yrs; U.S. 13.2% over the same period (U.S. 5% higher). Stock prices just started rising and will continue. Assuming PPP holds, which asset class should a Japanese-asset investor favor?
Answer: Under PPP, the currency with lower inflation appreciates — so the yen appreciates ~5% vs the dollar over the period. For an investor in Japanese assets, favor equities: stock prices are rising and set to continue, and the appreciating yen enhances the (yen-denominated) return relative to dollar assets. Rising prices/growth also favor equities over bonds.
Module 2.7 · Volatility Forecasting
LOS 2.gMethods of forecasting volatility
Estimating variance for a single asset is easy; for many assets it requires a variance-covariance (VCV) matrix or other tools. Four methods below.
1 · Sample VCVDerive variances & covariances from sample statistics. Sample-size rule: number of observations should be ≥ 10× the number of assets; the number of assets cannot exceed the observations or outcomes are meaningless (a large portfolio can appear riskless). 2 · Factor-based VCVMultifactor models reduce the required observations — correlations from a few common factors, variances need asset-specific factors. 3 · ShrinkageWeighted average of the sample VCV and a target (e.g. factor-based) matrix → more precise, reduced estimation error. 4 · Smoothed returnsAdjust for data smoothing that understates risk & overstates diversification.
Factor-based VCV — the count advantage
Return: r_i = α_i + Σ β_ik F_k + ε_i (k = 1..K) Variance: σ²_i = ΣΣ β_im β_in ρ_mn + ν²_i (m,n = 1..K) Covariance: σ_ij = ΣΣ β_im β_jn ρ_mn (m,n = 1..K) where ρ_mn = covariance between factors m and n, ν²_i = variance of asset i's unique factor ε_i.
Element count (N = 50 assets, K = 6 factors): a full sample VCV needs N(N−1)/2 = 1,225 covariance terms, whereas the factor model needs only N×K = 300 sensitivities plus K(K+1)/2 = 21 factor variance/covariance elements. Factors must not be redundant and must have no zero terms, so portfolios don't incorrectly appear riskless.
Two factor-VCV shortcomings: (1) biased — factor inputs must be estimated, so the matrix will be biased and won't be the true predictor even on average; (2) inconsistent — the model does not converge to the true matrix as sample size grows. In contrast, the sample VCV is both consistent and unbiased.
Shrinkage & smoothed returns
Shrinkage combines the sample VCV with a target (e.g. factor-based) matrix using the same weights for all elements → smaller error terms. Even if the target is biased, its lower variance can yield greater overall improvement (bias-variance trade-off).
Shrinkage example: sample covariance = 220, target = 180, weights: 60% target / 40% sample (well-chosen) shrinkage estimate = 180 × 0.60 + 220 × 0.40 = 196
Smoothed returns understate risk and overstate diversification benefits → distorted portfolio analysis and suboptimal allocation. Adjust via a weighted average of current "true" and prior observed returns:
R_t = (1 − λ) r_t + λ R_(t−1) (0 ≤ λ ≤ 1) var(r) = [(1 + λ) / (1 − λ)] · var(R) > var(R) Example λ = 0.6: (1 + 0.6)/(1 − 0.6) = 1.6/0.4 = 4× → true variance = 4× observed variance, 2× the observed SD.
Shortcoming: the true current return isn't directly observable — proxies include using an asset index.
ARCH models
Asset returns show periods of high & low volatility → volatility clustering, addressed via autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH). Can be used for multi-asset VCV estimation. Simplest form:
σ²_t = γ + α σ²_(t−1) + β η²_t = γ + (α + β) σ²_(t−1) + β (η²_t − σ²_(t−1)) α, β, γ ≥ 0 and (α + β) < 1; η_t = unexpected return component.
Higher (α + β) → higher emphasis on past information → more volatility clustering.
Module Quiz 2.7
Q1. Manager needs a VCV for 17 asset classes, has weekly data over the last 6 months, decides to also use a factor-based matrix but does NOT use shrinkage. Strengths & shortcomings?
Answer: Sample-size problem — 17 assets need ≥ 170 observations (10×), but 6 months of weekly data ≈ 26 → far too few → the sample VCV is unreliable and can appear riskless. Factor-based strength — it dramatically cuts the required observations. Factor-based shortcomings — it is biased and inconsistent (won't converge to the true matrix). Not using shrinkage forgoes the error-reduction from blending sample + target matrices.
Q2. One potential remedy to the shortcomings.
Answer: Use a shrinkage estimate — a weighted average of the sample VCV and the factor-based (target) matrix. This reduces estimation error and offsets both the small-sample noise of the sample matrix and the bias of the factor matrix.
Module 2.8 · Global Portfolio Adjustments
LOS 2.hRecommending portfolio weight changes
Apply everything learned to adjust allocations — the focus is how to adjust, not the forecast mechanics. Five guiding questions:
1 · Trend growthHave the drivers of trend growth changed significantly? 2 · IntegrationAre markets becoming more or less integrated? 3 · Business cycleWhere is the country in the cycle, and are fiscal/monetary policies consistent with that phase? 4 · Current accountWhat is the trend in current-account balances? 5 · CurrenciesStrong or weak, and how are they affecting growth & competitiveness?
The adjustment playbook
Trend growth ↑Favorable to equities (implies long-term earnings growth); unfavorable to bonds (higher interest rates). Use country-specific & global VCV to shift equity↔bond weights. Integration ↑Required returns fall as markets integrate (Singer-Terhaar). Increase allocations to EMs expected to see more integration; decrease from already-highly-integrated markets. Trough of cycleEquities perform well; valuation ratios & earnings growth rising → increase equity weights (use G-K for ERP). Curve is steep w/ high credit & term premiums, but rising-rate expectation → bonds underperform → reduce bond allocation & duration; a barbell may be optimal (↑ short + long, ↓ medium). Peak of cycleReverse the trough strategy: reduce equity, increase bond exposure & duration. PolicyFocus on structural changes (tax code, QE), not policy activities already reflected in prices. Current accountThe long-term trend matters. Rising deficits → rising required returns → falling asset prices, and increased capital flows to fund the deficit (also moving currencies). CurrencyHigher risk-adjusted return potential → capital inflow → upward currency pressure. Judge whether the currency still has room to appreciate or is at its peak.
Module Quiz 2.8 — applied reallocations
Q1 · Country A — yield curve is downward sloping (inverted); current portfolio 60% stocks / 40% bonds.
Answer: An inverted curve signals late cycle / approaching contraction (restrictive policy, likely peak). Reverse the trough playbook: reduce equity exposure and increase bond exposure & duration — shift away from 60/40 toward a more bond-heavy, longer-duration stance.
Q2 · Country B — declining prices (deflation) expected to continue; no funds invested yet; considering bonds, equity, real estate.
Answer: Deflation → favor bonds (fixed cash flows gain purchasing power, assuming no default). Avoid equities (economic activity & business decline) and avoid real estate (property values fall). Allocate primarily to high-quality bonds.
Q3 · Countries C vs D — government-bond purchase decision:
MetricCountry CCountry DRead
FX reserves / short-term debt147%78%C stronger (D < 100% = weak)
Debt-to-GDP42%84%C safer (D in the troublesome 70–80%+ zone)
Answer: Favor Country C's government bonds. C has FX reserves > 100% of short-term debt (D's 78% is a weakness) and low debt-to-GDP of 42% (D's 84% exceeds the troublesome 70–80% range). C shows greater ability to service & refinance its debt → lower credit risk. Underweight/avoid Country D.

LOS 3.b · Traditional vs Economic Balance Sheet
Balance sheetWhat it contains
Traditional (accounting)Assets, liabilities, and owner's equity. Used by accountants to illustrate the financial position of an organization.
EconomicContains the financial assets/liabilities PLUS any NON-financial assets and liabilities applicable to the asset allocation decision.
Those non-financial items are called extended portfolio assets and liabilities — they are NOT included on traditional balance sheets.
Why it matters for asset allocation
Investors making appropriate asset allocation decisions should recognize assets and liabilities in BOTH the financial portfolio AND the extended portfolio.
The point of the economic balance sheet is that your "true" wealth and obligations include things like future earnings and future consumption — and your asset allocation should reflect them, not just your brokerage account.
Extended portfolio ASSETS — decomposed
Investor typeExtended assets
IndividualPV of expected future earnings = HUMAN CAPITAL
InstitutionalPV of intellectual-property royalties · PV of underground mineral resources
Extended portfolio LIABILITIES — decomposed
Investor typeExtended liabilities
IndividualPV of expected future CONSUMPTION
InstitutionalPV of expected foundation payouts
Memory hook: individuals → earn (human capital) & spend (consumption). Institutions → royalties/minerals in, payouts out. Each is a PV of a future cash-flow stream.
Figure 3.1 · Economic Balance Sheet (institutional example)
AssetsLiabilities & Net Worth
Financial AssetsFinancial Liabilities
Domestic equity400Short-term borrowing100
Real estate250Mortgage obligations200
Extended AssetsExtended Liabilities
PV of expected royalties150PV of expected payouts300
Economic Net Worth
Economic assets − Economic liabilities200
Total800Total800
Economic net worth = total economic assets − total economic liabilities. Here: 800 − (100+200+300) = 200. It is the balancing figure that makes both sides equal 800.
Interactive · Economic net worth
Enter the four economic items. The tool sums assets and the two liability types, then computes economic net worth as the plug.
Financial assets
Extended assets
Financial liabilities
Extended liabilities
Life-cycle balanced fund (target-date / target-retirement fund)
A practical application of including HUMAN CAPITAL in an investment. These funds adjust the asset mix over time, accounting for the changing levels of human capital vs financial capital for an individual.
Young (workforce entry): human capital >> financial capital Aging: financial capital begins to outweigh human capital (PV of future earnings declines) Retirement: total wealth is made up of FINANCIAL capital
Human vs financial capital over the life cycle
Equity/bond glide path: at age 25 a target-date fund may hold 85% equity / 15% bonds — because human capital has significant bond-like characteristics, so the financial portfolio tilts to equity to balance total wealth. As the investor ages and human capital declines, the mix shifts toward bonds; at retirement (~65) it may be closer to 50% equity / 50% bonds.
Why equity-heavy when young: a stable salary (human capital) acts like a big bond position on the economic balance sheet. To keep TOTAL wealth balanced, the financial portfolio overweights equity early on, then de-risks as that "bond" (human capital) shrinks.

LOS 3.c · Three asset allocation approaches
All three attempt to match investors' goals with their optimal level of risk: (1) asset-only, (2) liability-relative, (3) goals-based.
1 · Asset-only
Basis: decisions based SOLELY on the investor's assets Example: mean-variance optimization (MVO) — uses expected returns, volatilities, correlations Objective: maximize expected return per unit of risk (e.g. maximize the Sharpe ratio) Constraints: consider IPS constraints + investor risk tolerance
2 · Liability-relative
Basis: decisions based on FUNDING LIABILITIES Objective: pay liabilities when they come due Example: surplus optimization (from MVO principles). Surplus = investor assets − PV of investor liabilities Modeling liabilities: short an amount of bonds matching the duration & PV of liabilities, OR build a portfolio designed to hedge the liabilities Also known as: liability-driven investing (LDI)
3 · Goals-based
Basis: asset allocations for SUB-PORTFOLIOS that help individuals/families meet lifestyle & aspirational goals Specify per goal: type of cash flows needed (even / uneven / bullet), the time horizon(s), and the risk tolerance (probability of attaining the goal) Construction: each sub-portfolio has a unique allocation; summing them produces the overall portfolio SAA Also known as: goals-based investing (GBI)
Liability-relative vs Goals-based — both focus on meeting liabilities
The main difference: liability-relative focuses on liabilities of INSTITUTIONAL investors; goals-based focuses on liabilities/goals of INDIVIDUAL investors.
Institutional (liability-relative)Individual (goals-based)
Obligation typeLegal obligations / debtsSpecific lifestyle goals
Penalty for missingMuch HIGHERLower
ObligationsConstant & numerous (insurance, pension payments)Much less predictable
ForecastabilityMore confidently forecast (large number of obligations → average more certain)Uncertain time-horizon needs of ONE individual
Why institutional liabilities forecast better: the average of a large number of obligations is more certain than the uncertain time-horizon needs of one individual investor.
LOS 3.d · Risk concepts by approach
Asset-only risk
Focus on asset class risk + constructing effective asset-class combinations.
Relevant measure (MVO): standard deviation of portfolio returns (incorporates asset-class volatilities + correlations) Relative risk: can be modeled with tracking error Downside risk: value at risk (VaR), semivariance, or maximum drawdown
Monte Carlo simulation complements MVO: pick optimal portfolios via MVO, then simulate multiple paths to see performance over time → reveals downside risk in market-stress scenarios → refine allocation.
Liability-relative risk
Focus: NOT having enough assets to pay liabilities when they come due Also a risk: the volatility of contributions used for funding liabilities Relevant measure: standard deviation of the SURPLUS
Main drivers of risk: the differences between asset and liability characteristics (e.g. size, sensitivity to interest-rate changes).
Goals-based risk
Focus: the risk of NOT being able to achieve the stated financial goals Multiple goals: risks encompass multiple future time periods Portfolio risk: the WEIGHTED SUM of the risk attached to each goal
Quick contrast (the testable summary)
ApproachRisk = Relevant measure
Asset-onlyAsset-class riskSD of portfolio returns (+ tracking error, VaR)
Liability-relativeCan't pay liabilities when dueSD of the surplus
Goals-basedCan't achieve goalsWeighted sum of per-goal risk

LOS 3.e · Asset classes & systematic risk
An asset class is a group of assets with similar investment characteristics. Each asset class has its own quantifiable systematic risk.
The key link: SAA is a conscious effort to gain the DESIRED exposure to systematic risk via specific weights to individual asset classes. In other words, SAA reflects the investor's desired systematic risk exposure.
The 3 "super asset classes"
Super asset classSource of valueExample
Capital assetsProvide a CONTINUOUS source of valueDividends (stocks, bonds)
Consumable / transformableCan be CONSUMED or TRANSFORMED into a source of valueCommodities
Store-of-valueProvide value when EXCHANGED or SOLDCurrencies, art
Memory hook: Capital = pays you continuously · Consumable = use it up / convert it · Store-of-value = worth something when you sell it.
5 criteria for specifying an asset class
Combining classes with obviously different risk/return (e.g. EM equities + domestic equities into one "equities" class) is only appropriate from a general-description standpoint. Use these criteria to specify classes properly:
1. Assets in a class should have similar attributes from both a DESCRIPTIVE and STATISTICAL perspective 2. Assets cannot be classified into more than one asset class (if they can, the class descriptions are too vague) 3. Classes should NOT be highly correlated (high correlation defeats the purpose of holding separate classes for diversification) 4. Classes should cover all possible investable assets (increases the investable set AND pushes up the efficient frontier — higher expected return at all risk levels) 5. Classes should contain a sufficiently large percentage of LIQUID assets (if liquidity/transaction costs are significant, the class may not be ideal)
Well-accepted asset classes: domestic equity, domestic fixed income, global equity, global fixed income, cash & equivalents, and alternatives (real estate, private equity, etc.).
Figure 3.2 · Asset classes & sub-asset classes
Asset classSub-asset classSegment
Global equityU.S. equitiesLarge-cap equities
Small-cap equities
Non-U.S. equitiesDeveloped countries
Emerging countries
Global fixed incomeU.S. debtInvestment-grade debt
High-yield debt
Non-U.S. debtDeveloped countries
Emerging countries
Granularity: SAA vs TAA
Too much granularity (number of subdivisions) makes it difficult to construct an optimal portfolio based on the investor's required return and risk. Within each class, sub-asset classes are LESS distinct than their broad parent classes.
SAA should focus primarily on asset-class divisions that are distinctly different and provide diversification (e.g. global equity vs global fixed income) As you move DOWN in granularity, the differential between classes SHRINKS (US vs non-US equity are less distinctly different than equity vs fixed income) TAA (tactical) → decisions may focus more on the sub-asset classes
Rule of thumb: SAA = broad, distinct classes. TAA = finer sub-classes. More granularity ≠ better; it can make optimization harder.
LOS 3.f · Asset-based vs Factor-based allocation
Asset classes have traditionally been the units of analysis → asset-based asset allocation (e.g. MVO using expected return, volatility, correlation of the selected classes).
The problem: using asset classes this way can be problematic due to OVERLAPPING risk factors among asset classes.
Risk factors & overlap
An investor selects asset classes based on desired exposure to common risk factors. Examples:
volatility · liquidity · inflation · interest rates duration · foreign exchange · default risk
Overlap example: domestic equity AND domestic fixed income BOTH share exposure to foreign-exchange (currency changes affect issuer profitability + returns), liquidity, and volatility risk factors. Examining overlapping risk factors helps identify the CORRELATIONS among asset classes.
Factor-based asset allocation
Because factors overlap, it may be insightful to focus on RISK FACTORS rather than asset classes as the units of analysis: identify the factors + the desired exposure to each. Multifactor models then create factor portfolios that isolate systematic (nondiversifiable) risk exposures → factor-based asset allocation.
Not inherently superior — it has limitations: investors may not be able to directly invest in all risk factors. But it can offer additional insight, and factors often correspond to expected-return premiums.
Some factors ARE investable via spread positions (long/short) or derivatives:
• Isolate inflation: go LONG Treasuries (compensation for consensus-expected inflation) and SHORT inflation-linked bonds (adjust for actual future inflation)
• Isolate volatility: invest in VIX futures with payoffs based on actual change in volatility
LOS 3.g · Strategic Asset Allocation (SAA)
SAA combines capital market expectations (expected return, volatility, correlation) with the investor's risk, return, and investment constraints (from the IPS). SAA is LONG-TERM in nature.
Vocabulary: the SAA weights are called targets, and the portfolio represented by the SAA is a policy portfolio (= target portfolio = benchmark).
Utility-theory foundation
Most quantitative approaches are based on utility theory: a utility function incorporates investor risk aversion. Expected utility for an allocation is determined with a distribution of ending-wealth values (based on asset-class weights, returns, and beginning wealth). The maximum utility, subject to asset-class constraints, represents the investor's optimal allocation given the investment horizon.
The 9 steps to select & justify an SAA
1. Determine investor objectives — how will they use the assets? Liabilities/goals? How measured? 2. Determine investor tolerance for risk — sensitivities to risk? How is risk measured? 3. Determine investor time horizon(s) — horizon to evaluate objectives AND risk tolerance 4. Determine investor constraints — tax situation, ESG considerations, legal/regulatory/political, any IPS constraints 5. Select the asset allocation approach — asset-only / liability-relative / goals-based 6. Specify the asset classes — once specified, capital market expectations can be established 7. Develop potential asset allocations — optimization produces candidate allocations 8. Simulate results — test whether results align with objectives + risk tolerance over the chosen horizon 9. Repeat step 7 until the optimal asset allocation is discovered
The loop: steps 7 → 8 → 9 iterate — develop, simulate, refine — until the optimal allocation is found. Steps 1–4 profile the investor; step 5 picks the approach; step 6 sets the classes; 7–9 optimize.

LOS 3.h · The global market portfolio as a baseline
Financial theory proposes that the FIRST asset allocation to consider should be the global market portfolio.
Contains ALL available risky assets (global equity, global FI, real estate, etc.) in proportion to their total market values It is the portfolio that MINIMIZES diversifiable risk — the most diversified portfolio possible Found on the efficient frontier by drawing a line from the risk-free asset tangent to the frontier (the capital market line); the point of tangency = the global market portfolio
Using it in practice
The global market portfolio's weights serve as a good STARTING POINT. The weights can then be adjusted to meet specific investor objectives, constraints, and desires (e.g. a home-country or small-cap bias).
Hard to invest in some classes: residential real estate or private equity may not be practical for individual investors. For this reason, investors often use a PROXY to represent the global market portfolio — such as a portfolio of exchange-traded funds (ETFs).
Professor's note · risk vocabulary
Nondiversifiable riskDiversifiable risk
market risk · priced risk · systematic risknonmarket · nonpriced · company-specific · unsystematic
The compensation rule: you should expect compensation (higher expected returns) for taking NONDIVERSIFIABLE risk — but NOT for taking diversifiable risk (you could have diversified it away for free).
LOS 3.i · Passive/active choices for asset class weights
Once the SAA is constructed, implementation choices must be made regarding passive/active management for (a) asset-class weights AND (b) allocations within asset classes. First aspect: should the investor DEVIATE from the SAA by adjusting the asset mix?
TAA — Tactical Asset Allocation
Active strategy that DEVIATES from the SAA to exploit perceived SHORT-TERM opportunities Introduces additional risk, seeking incremental return — often called ALPHA Deviations restricted by risk budgets / rebalancing ranges that control the amount of deviation May be based on forecasted asset-class valuation, business-cycle state, or stock-price momentum
TAA tradeoff: potential outperformance vs tracking error. Key limitation = additional trading/monitoring costs + possible capital gains taxes → the decision to implement TAA should be evaluated under a COST-BENEFIT approach.
DAA — Dynamic Asset Allocation
A MULTIPERIOD view of the investment horizon Recognizes that asset (and liability) performance in ONE period affects the required rate of return and acceptable level of risk for SUBSEQUENT periods
Changes to the SAA may be limited to simply adjusting the mix between stocks, bonds, and cash. Conversely, global TAA may involve a broader and more complex multiasset approach.
Passive vs Active within asset classes
PassiveActive
Insights impact composition?NO — investor insights/expectations do not impact compositionYES — composition changes when expectations change
ExamplesIndexing, holding bonds to maturitySecurity selection, style tilts
GoalTrack the indexEarn risk-adjusted returns > passive benchmark
The passive → active spectrum
Most passive: buy & hold a self-rebalancing broad index of risky assets (e.g. global market portfolio) Tilt toward a style index (e.g. growth equity) — slightly more active (active decision, but still passive indexing implementation) Growth approach + security selection to enhance returns — more active Most active: unconstrained mandates, NOT managed with regard to traditional benchmarks
Indexing costs: low-cost overall, but some transaction costs (adjusting to index changes; equal-weight tracking costs MORE than market-cap weight; FI indexes incur costs as bonds mature/are called/default). As a portfolio moves from passive → active, tracking error AND expected active return increase — these measures quantify the degree of active management.
4 factors driving the active/passive choice
1. Availability of appropriate investments (e.g. a relevant index) 2. Active management scalability — value added from each active decision 3. Investor constraints (e.g. social/environmental concerns when using a passive approach) 4. Investor belief in efficient markets (would discourage active management)
Also: the cost-benefit tradeoff (additional transaction costs needed for excess returns) and the tax status of investors (differs between taxable and tax-exempt).
Risk Budgeting
Asset allocation can be conducted with a RISK perspective. The types of risk to take — and the amount — are addressed with risk budgeting.
Measuring risk varies by focus: volatility → standard deviation of returns; tail risk → value at risk (VaR) Quantified in either RELATIVE or ABSOLUTE terms; stated in either money or percentage terms (e.g. 10% return volatility)
Key point: risk budgets specify how RISK should be distributed among portfolio assets — WITHOUT regard to asset expected returns.
Active risk budgeting
In the passive/active context, active risk budgeting determines how much ADDITIONAL risk relative to the benchmark the investor is willing to take. Objective: outperform the benchmark while sticking to the risk budget.
Decision levelActive risk measured relative to…
Asset-class MIX (weights)the SAA benchmark
Allocation WITHIN asset classesthe asset-class benchmark
LOS 3.j · Why rebalance
SAA responds to long-term strategic (policy) needs + long-run CME, expressed via IPS objectives/constraints. The allocation is typically specified as a RANGE (e.g. domestic equity 30%–40%); if the actual % wanders outside the range, rebalance. Triggered by normal asset price changes.
Primary benefit: maintaining the investor's desired exposure to systematic risk factors. If allowed to drift, the riskier assets take over (equities grow → portfolio risk grows). Only rebalancing (sell equities / buy debt) returns the portfolio to its original IPS risk/return.
Discipline: rebalancing avoids the "let it ride" temptation after strong equity gains. But "letting it ride" can also fail to realize gains from temporarily overvalued securities before they fall back — a potential COST of NOT rebalancing.
Costs of rebalancing — liquidity demand vs supply
Trade DEMANDS liquidity (selling when others are selling) → transaction cost (bid-ask spread) can be SUBSTANTIAL Trade PROVIDES liquidity (selling when others are buying) → costs may be MINIMAL
Plus: realized capital gains create a tax liability, and transaction costs apply.
Two rebalancing approaches
CalendarPercentage-range
TriggerPredetermined date (monthly/quarterly)Change in VALUE (tolerance bands / corridors)
Related toPassage of TIMEPortfolio VALUE
BenefitDiscipline without constant monitoringMinimizes how far classes violate corridors
DrawbackCan stray considerably between datesConstant monitoring cost + more frequent trading
Corridor example: 50% ± 5% → the class must stay within a band of 45%–55%. Calendar frequency generally depends on portfolio volatility; sometimes scheduled to coincide with review dates.
4 questions for range-based rebalancing
1. Who is ultimately RESPONSIBLE for rebalancing the portfolio? 2. How FREQUENTLY should the portfolio be monitored? 3. What is the SIZE of the rebalancing corridors? 4. Should rebalancing to target weights be FULLY or only PARTIALLY corrected?
Strategic considerations · optimal corridor WIDTH (7 drivers)
Each driver pushes the corridor wider or tighter. Memorize the DIRECTION and the why.
DriverEffect on corridorWhy
Transaction costsHigher costs → WIDERExpensive/illiquid to trade → rebalance less often → wider corridor
Risk toleranceMore risk-averse → TIGHTERLess risk-averse → wider (willing to let it drift)
CorrelationsHigher correlation → rebalance LESSIf assets move together, weights stay within ranges (both ↑20% → stay in band; one ↑20%/other ↓20% → both breach)
MomentumTrends continue → WIDERIf mean reversion anticipated → TIGHTER corridors
LiquidityIlliquid → WIDERPE/real estate → larger trading costs → wider corridors
DerivativesOverlay → can rebalance syntheticallyLower transaction costs/taxes, quicker/easier; tradeoff = needs additional risk management
TaxesTaxable → WIDER than tax-exemptRealized gains/losses hit taxes; corridors may be ASYMMETRIC (loss harvesting → e.g. 48%–55% for a 50% target)
Volatility — the nuanced one
Most likely: higher volatility → NARROWER corridors to control risk.
The complication: higher volatility (in the absence of high positive correlation between classes) makes weights shift MORE quickly. But more frequent rebalancing increases transaction costs (argues for WIDER corridors). So: higher volatility argues for narrower; substantial transaction costs argue for wider.
Most likely conclusion (exam): higher volatility → NARROWER corridors. Ultimately the choice is a tradeoff between risk control, transaction costs, and correlations — in complex situations, a quantified cost-benefit analysis is required.
Errors & Mastery — ready for your wrong answers
This tab will hold the other-approaches/rebalancing questions you get wrong.
When you miss a question, send: the question + your wrong pick + correct answer.
Watch areas:
• Global market portfolio = all risky assets at market value; minimizes DIVERSIFIABLE risk; CML tangency; use ETF proxy
• Compensated for nondiversifiable (systematic) risk only, NOT diversifiable
• TAA = short-term, alpha, deviates from SAA, cost-benefit; DAA = multiperiod
• Passive→active spectrum; tracking error + active return rise toward active
• 4 active/passive factors (availability, scalability, constraints, market efficiency belief)
• Risk budgeting ignores expected returns; active risk vs SAA benchmark (weights) / asset-class benchmark (within)
• Rebalancing maintains systematic risk exposure; liquidity demand (costly) vs supply (cheap)
• Calendar (time-based) vs percentage-range (value-based); the 4 range questions
• Corridor: costs/illiquid/momentum-trends/taxable → WIDER; risk-averse/mean-reversion/volatility → TIGHTER; high correlation → rebalance less
Reading 3 · Overview of Asset Allocation
Full-reading recap, module by module. Big-picture view of asset allocation and its link to investor objectives & constraints. SAA is often considered the single most important decision in the portfolio management process. Covers investment governance, the economic balance sheet, three allocation approaches (asset-only, liability-relative, goals-based), passive vs active implementation, and rebalancing.
Module 3.1 · Investment Governance
LOS 3.aElements of effective investment governance
Governance ensures the appropriate individuals/groups make informed decisions and conduct oversight. Objective: match the investor's objectives with constraints while complying with laws/regulations, and improve performance by aligning asset allocation with implementation.
Effective governance models do the following (6):
1 · ObjectivesEstablish long-term and short-term investment objectives. 2 · Rights & responsibilitiesAllocate rights and responsibilities within the governance structure. 3 · IPS processSpecify processes for creating an investment policy statement. 4 · SAA processSpecify processes for creating a strategic asset allocation. 5 · Reporting frameworkApply a reporting framework to monitor progress toward stated goals & objectives. 6 · Governance auditPeriodically perform a governance audit.
Investment objectives & the required return
Pension fundPlan assets meet current & ongoing plan liabilities. EndowmentAchieve a rate of return that exceeds the return required to fund current & ongoing distributions. Individual investorSufficient assets for retirement while adhering to constraints & risk preferences.
At the core of the objective statement is the return requirement. Context includes the investor's willingness & ability to tolerate risk, the funding obligations, and cash-flow timing. Overall goal: discover the optimal risk-return combination given the investor's constraints & risk tolerance.
Risk sensitivities drive required return: beyond liquidity risk (illiquid assets are hard to fund obligations during market stress → risk of selling at the worst time), governance must weigh volatility risk — high-risk allocations with high expected returns bring greater price swings.
Rights & responsibilities · IPS · SAA · reporting · audit
Rights & responsibilitiesDelegate decision-making to the best-qualified individuals (knowledge, experience, capacity, timely execution). Allocation varies with program size, internal-staff availability, and staff skill. Small programs → simpler options; large programs → more complex strategies (if robust internal controls), but can hit capacity constraints when too many managers are involved. IPSAn effective program begins with a well-developed IPS — a roadmap for portfolio management giving stakeholders confidence the program is managed with due diligence & care. SAAThe investment committee (highest governance level) typically approves the SAA. Developed after (1) the IPS is constructed, (2) results are simulated over the appropriate horizon(s), and (3) risk/return attributes of all possible allocations are considered. Good governance also specifies rebalancing decisions & responsibilities. Reporting frameworkLets stakeholders evaluate performance, guideline compliance, and progress. Proper benchmarking is key for evaluating managers/staff; shows which parts of the portfolio are ahead/behind schedule; governance reporting done regularly to address strengths/weaknesses. Governance auditAn independent third party audits structure, policies, procedures — examines governing documents, capacity to execute, and portfolio efficiency given constraints.
Key term — decision-reversal risk: effective governance aims to minimize the risk of reversing investment decisions at the worst possible time (creating the maximum loss) — helping the program survive market-stress periods. Governance also provides durability (evaluates staff/committee turnover & overreliance on one member; new members properly trained).
Module 3.2 · Economic Balance Sheet
LOS 3.bEconomic balance sheet (EBS)
The traditional accounting balance sheet has an organization's assets, liabilities, and owner's equity. An economic balance sheet adds any nonfinancial (extended portfolio) assets and liabilities relevant to the asset-allocation decision that don't appear on traditional sheets.
Extended assetsPV of expected earnings / human capital (individuals); PV of pension income (individuals); PV of intellectual-property royalties & underground mineral resources (institutions). Extended liabilitiesPV of expected consumption (individuals); PV of expected foundation payouts (institutions).
Figure 3.1 · Economic balance sheet example (balances 800 / net worth 200 — verified)
AssetsLiabilities & net worth
Financial assetsFinancial liabilities
Domestic equity400Short-term borrowing100
Real estate250Mortgage obligations200
Extended assetsExtended liabilities
PV of expected royalties150PV of expected payouts300
Economic net worth
Economic assets − economic liabilities200
Total800Total800
Life-cycle balanced funds (target-date): a practical application including human capital. When an individual enters the workforce, human capital ≫ financial capital, so the fund holds more equity (e.g. at age 25, ~85% equity / 15% bonds — human capital acts bond-like). As the investor ages, human capital declines and total wealth becomes mostly financial → the mix shifts toward bonds (e.g. at retirement ~age 65, closer to 50% equity / 50% bonds).
Module 3.3 · Approaches to Asset Allocation
LOS 3.cAsset-only vs liability-relative vs goals-based
ApproachObjectiveExample methodAlso known as
Asset-onlyDecisions based solely on the investor's assets. Maximize expected return per unit of risk (e.g. maximize the Sharpe ratio), subject to IPS constraints & risk tolerance.Mean-variance optimization (MVO) — uses expected returns, volatility, correlations of asset classes.—
Liability-relativeDecisions based on funding liabilities; pay liabilities when they come due.Surplus optimization (MVO-based; surplus = assets − PV of liabilities). Also: short bonds matching liability duration/PV, or a hedging portfolio.Liability-driven investing (LDI)
Goals-basedSub-portfolios to achieve lifestyle & aspirational goals. Specify cash-flow type (even/uneven/bullet), horizon(s), and probability of attaining each goal.Each sub-portfolio has a unique allocation for its goal; sum of sub-portfolios = overall SAA.Goals-based investing (GBI)
Liability-relative vs goals-based (both liability-driven): liability-relative focuses on institutional liabilities (legal obligations/debts); goals-based focuses on individual lifestyle goals. Penalties for missing liabilities are much higher for liability-relative. Institutional obligations are constant & numerous (insurance/pension payments) → more confidently forecast (law of large numbers); individual goals are less predictable (uncertain single-investor horizon).
LOS 3.dRelevant risk concepts by approach
Asset-onlyFocus on asset-class risk & effective combinations. Primary measure for MVO = standard deviation of portfolio returns (uses volatilities + correlations). Other sensitivities: relative risk vs benchmark → tracking error; downside risk → VaR, semivariance, or maximum drawdown. Monte Carlo simulation complements MVO — simulate multiple return paths to see downside risk under market stress and refine the allocation. Liability-relativePrimary risk = not having enough assets to pay liabilities when due. Volatility of the surplus (and volatility of contributions used for funding) is the relevant measure. Liability characteristics (size, interest-rate sensitivity) are the main drivers of risk. Goals-basedRisk = not achieving the stated financial goals. With multiple goals over multiple horizons, total portfolio risk = the weighted sum of the risk attached to each goal.
Module 3.4 · Allocation by Asset Class or Risk Factor
LOS 3.eAsset classes & systematic-risk exposure
An asset class = a group of assets with similar investment characteristics. Each class has its own quantifiable systematic risk. SAA is a conscious effort to gain the desired exposure to systematic risk via specific weights to individual classes → SAA reflects the investor's desired systematic-risk exposure.
Three "super asset classes":
1 · Capital assetsProvide a continuous source of value (e.g. dividends) — stocks, bonds. 2 · Consumable / transformableCan be consumed or transformed into a source of value — e.g. commodities. 3 · Store-of-valueProvide value when exchanged or sold — e.g. currencies, art.
Criteria for specifying an asset class
Similar attributesAssets in a class should be similar descriptively AND statistically. Mutually exclusiveAn asset cannot be classified into more than one class — if it can, the class descriptions are too vague. Low correlationClasses should not be highly correlated, to provide diversification. High correlation → classes are related on risk/return → defeats the purpose of separate classes. Cover investable universeClasses should cover all possible investable assets — increases the investable set and pushes up the efficient frontier (more expected return at every risk level). Sufficient liquidityContain a sufficiently large percentage of liquid assets — if liquidity/transaction costs are significant, the class may not be ideal.
Granularity trap: too much granularity (too many sub-divisions) makes it difficult to construct an optimal portfolio for the investor's required return & risk. Sub-asset classes are less distinct than broad classes (Fig 3.2: global equity → US/non-US → large/small-cap, developed/emerging; global FI → US/non-US → IG/HY, developed/emerging). SAA focuses primarily on divisions with distinctly different characteristics (global equity vs global FI); moving down in granularity, differences shrink. Progressing from SAA to policy implementation & TAA, decisions focus more on sub-asset classes.
LOS 3.fRisk factors & factor-based allocation
Asset-based allocationTraditional units of analysis are asset classes (e.g. MVO uses expected return, volatility, correlation of selected classes). Problem: overlapping risk factors across classes. Common risk factorsVolatility, liquidity, inflation, interest rates, duration, foreign exchange, default risk. Exposures overlap — e.g. domestic equity & domestic FI both share FX, liquidity, and volatility exposures. Examining overlaps helps identify correlations among classes. Factor-based allocationFocus on risk factors as the units of analysis: identify factors + desired exposure, then use multifactor models to build factor portfolios that isolate systematic (nondiversifiable) risk. LimitationsNot inherently more useful. Investors may not be able to invest directly in all factors. But factors offer added insight and often correspond to expected-return premiums; some are investable via spread positions (long/short) or derivatives.
Isolating a factor (examples): to isolate inflation risk — go long Treasuries (compensation for consensus-expected inflation) and short inflation-linked bonds (adjust for actual future inflation); or invest in VIX futures with payoffs based on actual change in volatility.
