US equities: MCTR = 1.300 × 12.00% = 15.60% ACTR = 0.60 × 15.60% = 9.36% % contribution = 9.36% / 12.00% = 78.00% ER/MCTR = 6.5% / 15.60% = 0.417 Portfolio Sharpe = 5% / 12% = 0.417
Optimal check: ER/MCTR = 0.417 for both US equities and US bonds, and equals the portfolio Sharpe (5%/12%). Therefore the 60/30/10 allocation is optimal from a risk-budgeting perspective.
LOS 4.h / 4.iClient preferences & investment factors
LOS 4.h — incorporating client risk preferences (three ways):
Additional constraintsLimits on risky classes or a ceiling on portfolio risk (Plowshare example). Risk-aversion factor λe.g. average investor Bronsten with λ = 4. Monte Carlo simulationIllustrate the wealth outcomes possible under allocations with different risk levels.
LOS 4.i — factor-based allocation: instead of asset classes, define the opportunity set as factors (market exposure, size, valuation, momentum, liquidity, duration, credit, volatility). Consistent with fundamental factor models like Fama-French (market, size, value-growth).
Factors are zero-dollarLong the better-performing attribute, short the underperforming attribute. Fama-French three factors: long small / short large (size); long value / short growth (value-growth); and the market portfolio. Why it helpsFactors are not highly correlated with each other or the market → improves the risk-return tradeoff and expands the efficient frontier. Once factor returns/variances/covariances are identified, MVO is used the same way. Class vs factorResearch: when the two opportunity sets broadly reflect the same underlying exposures, the resulting efficient frontiers are not significantly different (neither is clearly superior). Choice depends on how you form CME: think in asset classes → allocate risk by class; think in risk factors → allocate risk by factor.
Module Quiz 4.5
QQuestionAnswer
1Canadian equities: weight 50%, excess return 8.25%, beta 1.19; portfolio σ 10%. Closest ratio of excess return to MCTR?MCTR = 1.19 × 10% = 11.90%. Ratio = 8.25% / 11.90% = 0.693 → C.
2Most accurate re using investment factors to form an allocation?C · factor exposures may be investable by forming a series of zero-dollar long/short portfolios. (Not clearly superior to class-based — A wrong; won't necessarily replicate class-based results — B wrong.)
Module 4.6 · Asset-Liability Management
Liability-relative asset allocation (DB pension context)
Addresses MVO's ignore-liabilities criticism. Focus: institutional investors (pension funds, insurers, banks) with liabilities they're obligated to meet under strict regulation. A DB plan has two components: the pension liability (PV of future retirement obligations) and the investment portfolio managed to meet the liability's cash flows.
plan surplus = market value of assets − PV of pension liabilities funding ratio = market value of assets / PV of liabilities Fully funded → funding ratio = 1 (surplus = 0) Underfunded → funding ratio < 1 Overfunded → funding ratio > 1
The pension liability's characteristics drive the return & risk requirements of the portfolio; asset & liability values are driven by some of the same factors, so the correlations between changes in the two matter.
LOS 4.jCharacteristics of liabilities relevant to allocation
Fixed vs contingentFixed: cash flows & timing specified in advance (like a fixed-rate corporate bond). Contingent: cash flows depend on uncertain future events (DB pension liability). Legal vs quasi-legalLegal: obligations defined in a legal agreement. Quasi-legal: not legal obligations but expected cash outflows essential to the mission (university endowment payouts). Duration & convexityMeasure the change in a liability's value for a change in interest rates (concept applies to any liability, not just fixed income). Liability vs sponsor sizeA large liability relative to the sponsor must be accounted for; a small one can usually be ignored (minimal effect on the optimal allocation). Factors affecting cash flowsInflation, interest rates, risk premiums, other economic conditions (DB obligations influenced by the discount-rate choice). Timing considerationsInclude longevity risk. RegulationsAffecting how the liability's value is determined (typically in insurance).
LOS 4.k / 4.lThree approaches to liability-relative allocation
1 · Surplus optimizationAn MVO extension: build an efficient frontier based on the surplus, with surplus volatility as the risk measure (money or % terms). Include the liabilities' expected returns & variances; correlations reflect how well assets hedge liabilities. 2 · Two-portfolio (hedging + return-seeking)Split assets into a hedging portfolio (hedges the liabilities) and a return-seeking portfolio (managed independently via MVO). 3 · Integrated asset-liabilityIntegrates assets AND liabilities in a joint optimization.
Surplus optimization: R_s,m = surplus return = (Δ asset value − Δ liability value) / initial asset value U_m = E(R_s,m) − 0.005 × λ × Var_s,m
Two-portfolio & integrated approaches in depth
Hedging portfolio buildVia fixed-income techniques: cash flow matching, duration matching, immunization. Estimate liability inputs by (1) assuming liabilities behave like corporate bonds (use corporate-bond expected return & volatility), or (2) a factor approach identifying common factors driving both assets & liabilities. When usedMost often for insurance companies and overfunded pension plans that want to minimize underfunding risk. More aggressive variants(1) Only partially hedge liabilities → allocate more to the return-seeking portfolio; (2) increase the hedge as the funding ratio & surplus rise. Both trade higher expected return for higher risk. Two limitations(1) If funding ratio < 1, it's difficult to fully hedge the liabilities. (2) A hedging portfolio may not be available for certain risks (e.g. earthquakes). Integrated distinctive featureTwo-portfolio & surplus optimization assume the liability composition is already in place when the asset allocation is decided (two independent decisions). Banks, hedge funds (short positions), insurers decide liability composition jointly with asset allocation → a continuous feedback loop → a multiperiod integrated model. Example: a highly leveraged bank stress-tests both sides of the balance sheet.
Module Quiz 4.6
QQuestionAnswer
1Which is best described as a contingent liability?B · An insurance company's obligations to pay policyholders. (Cash flows depend on uncertain future events. A fixed-coupon debt is fixed; foundation distributions are quasi-legal but planned.)
2A bank is most likely to use which liability-relative approach?B · Integrated asset-liability approach. (Banks decide liabilities jointly with assets → integrated/multiperiod.)
Module 4.7 · Goals-Based & Heuristic Approaches
LOS 4.mGoals-based asset allocation
Useful for individuals with multiple (sometimes conflicting) objectives across different horizons & urgency levels, measured as required probabilities of success. Example: college tuition in 10 yrs at 90% probability (more urgent) vs $1,000,000 in 30 yrs to fund a foundation at 60% probability.
Sub-portfoliosThe portfolio is composed of sub-portfolios; each goal addressed individually with its own sub-portfolio. Taxable & tax-exempt investments are both in the opportunity set. Minimum expectationsInstead of an average expected return, identify a "minimum expectation" for each goal — the minimum expected return needed to provide the required probability of success over the horizon. ModulesAdvisers often select from pre-established sub-portfolios (modules) distinguished by risk-return tradeoffs, liquidity, and class inclusion/exclusion. Selection & sizingFor each goal, pick the module with the highest expected return at the specified probability over the horizon. Investment size = PV of the future goal discounted at that module's expected return. Total portfolio = sum of the individual investments.
Worked example · goals-based module selection (verified $372,047 / $1,311,231)
Goal 1: $500,000 in 10 yrs, 90% required success. Goal 2: $6,000,000 in 30 yrs, 75% required success. Modules A/B/C.
Minimum-expectation returnModule AModule BModule C
10-yr @ 90%3.0% ←2.4%−2.2%
10-yr @ 75%3.6%3.8%1.7%
30-yr @ 90%4.0%4.3%4.7%
30-yr @ 75%4.1%4.8%5.2% ←
Goal 1 (10yr, 90%): highest return = Module A at 3.0% Invest = 500,000 / 1.03^10 = $372,047 Goal 2 (30yr, 75%): highest return = Module C at 5.2% Invest = 6,000,000 / 1.052^30 = $1,311,231
Rule: at each goal's (horizon, required-success) cell, pick the module with the highest minimum-expectation return, then discount the future goal at that return to size the investment. Treat each goal separately.
LOS 4.nHeuristic & other approaches (ad hoc, not theory-based)
120 − ageEquity % = 120 − age; remainder to fixed income. (40-yr-old → 80/20; 50 → 70/30.) Consistent with declining human capital → shift equity to FI as you age; comes close to mimicking target-date funds. 60/40 splitMaintain 60% stocks / 40% bonds. Not far-fetched — the global financial asset portfolio has historically been ~60/40. Endowment / Yale modelAllocate more to alternatives (PE, real estate, natural resources) than strict MVO recommends. Rationale: these markets are less informationally efficient (skilled managers outperform), and long-horizon institutions can bear liquidity risk for a liquidity premium. Popular with university endowments. Risk parityEach asset class contributes the same amount to total portfolio risk → addresses the MVO criticism that class diversification ≠ risk-source diversification. Criticism: it ignores expected returns and focuses only on risk. 1/N ruleEqual weight — each of N classes gets 1/N (8 classes → 12.5% each), commonly rebalanced quarterly. Despite its simplicity, empirical evidence shows it performs better than expected.
Module 4.8 · Rebalancing Policy
LOS 4.oFactors affecting rebalancing policy
Rebalancing (CFA definition) = adjusting allocations to move back toward the originally defined strategic allocation goal. Percentage-range rebalancing sets trigger points around the optimal allocation and rebalances back to target (or partially) when triggers are hit.
Key factors affecting the optimal corridor width (rebalancing range):
Transaction costsHigher costs → wider corridor (benefits of rebalancing must "pay" for higher costs). Risk toleranceHigher risk tolerance → wider corridor (less concerned about deviations from optimal). Correlation with rest of portfolioHigher correlation → wider corridor (the portfolio moves with the class → allocation strays more slowly from target). Volatility of the classHigher volatility → narrower corridor (higher volatility ↑ the likelihood the actual allocation diverges from target).
Ultimately the choice of corridor width is a tradeoff between risk control, transaction costs, and correlations. In complex situations a quantified cost-benefit analysis is required.
Module Quiz 4.7 / 4.8
QQuestionAnswer
1Most accurate re sub-portfolios in the goals-based approach?C · The size of the investment in a particular sub-portfolio is the present value of the future goal discounted by [that module's return]. (The most significant difference between sub-portfolios is not solely return-risk — A overstated; higher-priority goals don't inherently require higher-return assets — B wrong. C states the sizing rule correctly.)
2Most correct re the 120-minus-your-age heuristic?B · A 60-year-old should have 60% (=120−60) in equities → 40% in fixed income. (A 70-yr-old → 50% equity, not "50% invested" ambiguously stated in A; the approach actually comes close to mimicking target-date funds, so C is wrong.)
3Rebalancing corridor for Asset Class Z will be wider if?B · the correlation of Z with the rest of the portfolio is highly positive. (High volatility → narrower, so A wrong; low transaction costs → narrower/tighter, so C wrong.)

Covered: 4.1 basic MVO (utility/certainty-equivalent, efficient frontier, MVO process, budget/nonnegativity constraints, 6 criticisms) · 4.2 reverse optimization, Black-Litterman, adding constraints, resampled MVO, nonnormal/CVaR · 4.3 Bronsten & Plowshare worked examples · 4.4 individual economic balance sheet, MCS, liquidity, Quiz 4.1–4.4 · 4.5 risk budgeting (MCTR/ACTR, Fig 4.5), client preferences, investment factors, Quiz 4.5 · 4.6 ALM (surplus optimization, two-portfolio, integrated, liability characteristics, funding ratio, Quiz 4.6) · 4.7 goals-based (module selection + verified example) & heuristics (120−age, 60/40, Yale, risk parity, 1/N) · 4.8 rebalancing corridor factors, Quiz 4.7/4.8.
LOS 5.a — Why size constrains the optimal allocation
Asset allocation is not abstract math. Beyond MVO inputs, four practical considerations restrict which allocations are actually achievable for a given owner: asset size, liquidity needs, time horizon, and regulatory/external constraints. Size is the first.
The core idea: there is a "sweet spot" of fund size. Too small → can't diversify or access complex assets. Too large → can't deploy capital into capacity-constrained strategies.
Small funds — the diversification problem
▪ Lack expertise & governance to invest in complex strategies → struggle to reach adequate diversification. ▪ Local legislation may restrict some assets to investors with a minimum capital / experience level (accredited-investor style rules). ▪ Solution: commingled (pooled) accounts — pool money from a small group of investors to reach the size needed to diversify. ▪ Families may pool assets to meet minimum-investment thresholds set by local legislation.
Large funds — the advantages
▪ Greater governance capacity & expertise → can consider complex strategies smaller funds can't. ▪ Meet high minimum-investment requirements → access more asset classes → higher diversification. ▪ Economies of scale: cost savings on internal management + greater negotiating power on fees → higher allocations to alternatives. ▪ As fund size ↑, the per-participant cost of governance infrastructure ↓ → competitive advantage in PE, hedge funds, infrastructure.
Too-large funds — the diseconomies of scale
Funds that are too large may not be able to use asset classes that lack the capacity to absorb large amounts (e.g. active small-cap equity). A small-cap manager suffers diseconomies of scale because:
(1) Larger trades have increased price impact. (2) Capital inflows may push managers to abandon their core strategy (style drift). (3) More staff needed → slower decision-making.
Solution & its cost: split the allocation among several managers — but identifying and monitoring them is an added burden/cost. Result: large funds often go passive in such situations.
Very large funds & FoF: may find too few alternatives (e.g. too few hedge funds) and choose a fund-of-funds (FoF). But FoF carries a double fee structure (FoF manager + underlying managers), and one HF manager's strategy may be offset by another's.
Liquidity Needs — match owner to asset class
The key: integrate the needs of the owner with the characteristics of the asset class. High-liquidity owners → high-quality, short-term, liquid assets. Owners with low needs + long horizons → can harvest the illiquidity premium in alternatives (real estate, infrastructure).
Typical liquidity needs by portfolio owner
Portfolio OwnerTypical Liquidity Needs
BanksHigh — support day-to-day operations, stand ready to repay deposits
SWFs, endowments, pension plans, foundationsLow — longer time horizons and lower liquidity needs
Property & casualty insuranceRelatively high — unpredictability of claims
Life & auto insuranceRelatively low — predictability of claims
IndividualsVaries by individual circumstance
Case-specific exceptions exist: e.g. a bank with a highly liquid loan portfolio; or a foundation funding unpredictable breakthrough research that needs high liquidity. Don't apply the table mechanically.
Extreme conditions & governance
▪ Plan liquidity for extreme market conditions — investor behavior changes under stress. ▪ Portfolio governance matters: unsophisticated investors may panic-sell in times of stress → permanent losses and lower total returns when prices revert to pre-crisis levels.
Time Horizon
A portfolio's time horizon is defined by a liability to be paid or a goal to be funded at a future date. Allocations must consider the horizon of each liability/goal and adapt as the mix of assets & liabilities changes over time.
▪ Human capital declines over time → allocation shifts toward lower-risk assets such as fixed income as the investor ages. ▪ Changing nature of liabilities: a pension fund with a young workforce → heavily in long-term bonds; a mature scheme → moves to intermediate & short-term bonds.
Time diversification
Time horizon is also linked to the ability to take risk. Portfolios with longer horizons are often invested in higher-risk assets.
Time diversification: evidence suggests risky-asset returns mean-revert over time, evening out below- and above-average periods of return. Longer horizon → more capacity to ride out volatility.
EXAMPLE — Older retired individual (Barry Garland)
Barry is 70, recently retired, with two goals:
Goal 1: maintain constant standard of living to age 85 — fully funded. Goal 2: maintain constant standard of living age 85→100 — partially funded. Life expectancy at 70 = 17.5 yrs.
Logic: Goal 1 is higher priority (his chances of living decline as he ages) AND fully funded → subportfolio emphasizes conservative investments. Goal 2 is lower priority + not fully funded → can be invested more aggressively with more growth potential.
EXAMPLE — Family with multiple funding goals (Bigstones)
Jane & Arthur (both 52, lawyers). Daughter Alice (16, college). Son Mark (27, future mayoral run in ~8 yrs). Want a scholarship at age 80. Four goals → lifestyle split into worst-case / baseline / aspirational → six subportfolios.
Figure 5.1 — Subportfolios (today)
GoalRiskAllocation% Total
MinimumConservative100% bonds & cash65%
MaintainModerate60% equity / 40% bonds12%
AspirationalAggressive100% equity8%
College fundConservative100% bonds & cash6%
Campaign donationAggressive100% equity6%
ScholarshipAggressive100% equity3%
Aggregate—25% equity / 75% bonds100%
Figure 5.2 — Subportfolios 15 years later
GoalRiskAllocation% Total
MinimumConservative100% bonds & cash60%
MaintainModerate60% equity / 40% bonds10%
AspirationalAggressive100% equity6%

What changed: college & campaign goals were funded and dropped out; only scholarship remains as the aspirational goal (now 24%). Fewer consumption years left → minimum subportfolio shrinks 65%→60%, aggregate equity rises 25%→35%.
Professor's note: the specific allocations are somewhat arbitrary — there is no formula. Your task is to see the logic behind choosing higher/lower equity, bond, cash in one subportfolio vs another.
Regulatory & External Constraints — Insurance Companies
Investment returns are a large contributor to insurer performance. The largest allocation is fixed income, reflecting the need to match assets to projected cash flows of the risks insured.
Book-value accounting: Local accounting laws often allow assets stated at book value, so the insurer focuses primarily on the pattern of cash-flow receipts rather than the volatility of market value.
Main risk considerations — maintaining enough capital to meet policyholder claims + factors affecting financial-strength metrics:
▪ Risk-based capital measures ▪ Liquidity ▪ Yield levels ▪ Credit ratings ▪ Potential to liquidate assets to meet claims
Allocation caps: local legislation often limits allocations — equity may be limited to as little as 10%, with caps also on private equity and high-yield bonds.
Pension Funds
Beyond capping allocations to certain asset classes, local legislation places a wide range of tax, accounting, reporting, and funding constraints on pension funds.
▪ Tax incentives may encourage investing in domestic assets. ▪ Accounting rules may allow deferred recognition of losses. ▪ Final allocation considers anticipated funding cost + the pension expense reported in financial statements.
Funding as a constraint — the risk/return trade-off
The fund compares the risk of funding cost exceeding a threshold (to minimize) against the PV of expected contributions (also to minimize).
The tension: higher allocation to equities (vs bonds) → ↑ volatility of returns → ↑ risk that low returns increase required contributions. But the higher expected return decreases the PV of expected contributions.
The fund decides the optimal combination of risk (contributions exceed a level) and return (measured by PV of expected contributions), subject to external regulatory requirements and allocation limits.
Endowments & Foundations
▪ Assumed infinite time horizon → very few regulatory constraints vs other entities. ▪ Some countries: a minimum required annual distribution or socially responsible investing requirement to keep tax-exempt status. ▪ Long horizon usually allows investing in risky assets. ▪ Caveat: if the endowment funds an organization, lender covenants on that organization may constrain the portfolio's activities.
Sovereign Wealth Funds
▪ Government-owned entities investing on behalf of the state. ▪ Typically not looking to match assets and liabilities (unlike insurers/pensions). ▪ But: subject to scrutiny from citizens → this may reduce the level of risk their long horizon would otherwise allow.
Self-governance: each fund self-governs by capping allocations. Constraints may include: minimum investment in socially/ethically acceptable assets; maximum in risky assets such as alternatives; limits on investment in certain currencies. ESG investing is usually not part of the initial allocation — rather, an allocation is set aside and invested in acceptable assets.
LOS 5.b — Tax considerations in allocation & rebalancing
With taxation, pretax vs after-tax risk and return characteristics may differ significantly. Taxable entities should use after-tax characteristics during allocation — adjusting for taxes after the fact may lead to suboptimal allocations.
Common tax characteristics
▪ Interest income — usually taxed at the highest rate, often progressively. → tax-exempt bonds (e.g. US munis) may form a large part of a taxable investor's fixed-income allocation. ▪ Dividends — usually taxed lower than interest. → some investors hold preferred stock instead of bonds. ▪ Capital gains — usually taxed lower than income; capital losses can offset capital gains elsewhere. ▪ Tax-deferred / tax-exempt accounts — place the least tax-efficient (most heavily taxed) assets in the most tax-advantaged accounts.
Key: Return & risk must be considered on both a pretax and after-tax basis — but correlations are unaffected by taxes.
EXAMPLE — Simple after-tax return (bond held to maturity)
Investor taxed 40% on interest, considering a 5% coupon bond held to maturity. Input for allocation:
After-tax = 0.05 × (1 − 0.40) = 0.03 = 3%
EXAMPLE — Multi-step after-tax return (equity)
Stock: 16% pretax return, of which 10% is dividend income and 90% is price appreciation. Dividend tax 30%, capital gains tax 20% (realized annually).
Pretax dividend income: 16% × 0.1 = 1.6% After-tax dividend income: 1.6% × (1 − 0.3) = 1.12% Pretax capital gain: 16% × 0.9 = 14.4% After-tax capital gain: 14.4% × (1 − 0.2) = 11.52% After-tax return: 1.12% + 11.52% = 12.64%
Equity returns include both dividend income and capital gains → the after-tax calc must adjust each component with its own tax rate, then sum.
Embedded gains / losses — cost basis ≠ market value
Cost basis below market value → unrealized gain (embedded tax liability). Cost basis above market value → unrealized loss (embedded tax asset). Three ways to adjust current market value:
(1) Subtract the embedded capital-gains tax from current market value as if sold today. (2) Assume sold in the future, discount the tax liability to PV using the asset's after-tax return as the discount rate. (3) Assume sold in the future, discount the tax liability to PV using the after-tax risk-free rate.
After-tax standard deviation
Risk must also be adjusted for tax. Capital gains tax reduces gains on price appreciation, and the ability to use losses to offset gains reduces losses on price declines → use a posttax standard deviation as the allocation input.
σAT = σPT × (1 − t)
EXAMPLE
Pretax σ = 12%, capital gains tax = 20%.
σAT = 12% × (1 − 0.20) = 9.6%
Effect on the frontier: using after-tax return + after-tax risk shifts the efficient frontier. Allocations to tax-inefficient assets (e.g. high-yield bonds) usually decrease — but they can still feature in the optimal allocation if they have low correlations with other assets.
Portfolio rebalancing under tax
To maintain the SAA, all portfolios rebalance periodically. Taxable owners realize taxable gains at each rebalancing → must balance maintaining the SAA against avoiding taxable gains via frequent rebalancing.
Rebalance less frequently in taxable portfolios — taxation reduces volatility (while correlations remain unaltered), so the allowable deviation band can be wider.
Two distinct tax effects — don't confuse them
Effect on σ of return: taxes cushion the upside & downside → decrease after-tax σ of the asset.
σAT = σPT × (1 − t)
Effect on allowable deviation from target weight: because taxes lower return volatility, they increase the allowable deviation band.
deviationAT = deviationPT / (1 − t)
Trap: one effect multiplies by (1−t) [σ shrinks], the other divides by (1−t) [band widens]. Opposite directions.
EXAMPLE — Pretax vs after-tax rebalancing range
Tax-exempt-style SAA: 40% fixed income, ±5% → range 35%–45%. Fixed-income returns taxed 30%. Equivalent after-tax range?
Pretax allowable deviation = 45% − 40% = 5% Posttax deviation = 5% / (1 − 0.30) = 7.14% Range = 40% ± 7.14% = 32.86% – 47.14%
Two strategies to reduce the impact of taxation
▪ Tax loss harvesting — deliberately realizing losses to offset gains elsewhere. ▪ Strategic asset location — most efficient use of tax-advantaged accounts.
Two tax-advantaged account types:
Tax-exempt accounts — assets not subject to taxation. No adjustment to market value before inclusion in allocation; use pretax risk/return inputs. Tax-deferred accounts — assets appreciate tax-free but are taxed upon distribution. (grow tax-free → use pretax inputs.)
Strategic asset location — general rules:
▪ Assets subject to the lowest tax rates (typically equity) → first allocated to taxable accounts.
▪ Assets subject to frequent trading & high tax rates → allocated to tax-advantaged accounts.
▪ Inputs: tax-deferred/tax-exempt (grow tax-free) → pretax; taxable vehicle → after-tax.
Account-expansion logic: 2 accounts (1 taxable, 1 tax-deferred) × 2 asset classes (FI + equity) → the optimization should use four account "types," depending on whether each class sits in the taxable or tax-deferred account.

Income tax rate (%)
Multi-step after-tax return (equity)
Pretax total return (%)

Dividend tax rate (%)

LOS 5.c — Revising the strategic asset allocation
The initial optimal allocation is unlikely to be applicable for the entire lifetime of any portfolio. In practice it is reevaluated annually, or whenever a change in goals, constraints, or beliefs suggests a revision is required.
Three triggers for revision: change in goals · change in constraints · change in beliefs.
1 · Change in Goals
▪ For institutions, the business cycle may trigger goal changes. ▪ Example — airlines: facing competition from low-budget rivals + uncertain revenue → may reduce risk exposure in their pension fund to smooth the volatility of contributions. ▪ Pension funds facing increasing deficits in recent years → triggers reexamination of the allocation. ▪ Individuals: change in employment status or starting a family → impacts both willingness and ability to take on risk.
2 · Change in Constraints
A change in any constraint discussed earlier necessitates a review. Examples:
▪ Government regulations requiring increased distributions to maintain tax-exempt status. ▪ Large unexpected cash flows to cover one-off events. ▪ Increased funding requirements for the beneficiary of an endowment. ▪ Forced early retirement of an investor due to illness.
The liquidity rule: any change requiring increased cash outflows → shift to more liquid assets. Conversely, a large inflow (e.g. donation to a foundation) → more flexibility to take on risk.
3 · Change in Beliefs
Investment activities are guided by a set of principles/beliefs — no guarantee these stay fixed.
▪ Investment committee: a change in committee makeup can change beliefs. New members are walked through an asset allocation study to understand the adopted approach. ▪ Economic environment: changes have a major impact on optimization. Key inputs = expected returns, volatility, and correlation. If macro forecasts for a major asset class change → the optimal allocation will likely change.
Example: an allocation exercise on fixed-income performance done pre-2008 would use very different expectations than one done post-2008 (interest-rate environment shift).
Predetermined revisions — target-date funds
Allocations may also change at predetermined dates without detailed reexamination. Target-date mutual funds adjust by investor age using a glide path — shifting from equity to more conservative investments (nominal and inflation-protected bonds) as the target date approaches.
LOS 5.d — SAA vs TAA
SAA (strategic): the long-term allocation specified in the IPS — target asset weightings for the portfolio. TAA (tactical): short-term deviations used to exploit cyclical conditions or a perceived mispricing in an asset class.
Objective
Increase risk-adjusted returns by exploiting short-term opportunities.
Key assumptions: TAA assumes short-term returns are predictable (rather than a random walk, as assumed for long-term returns). Success depends on market or factor timing — NOT individual security selection.
TAA still respects the risk constraint in the IPS, but does not consider specific goals or liabilities.
Constraints
▪ Success judged against the SAA benchmark. ▪ Size of deviations often limited to a range around the SAA. ▪ May also have an allowable range of predicted volatility or a tracking-error budget vs the SAA.
Evaluation — measuring TAA success
▪ Compare Sharpe ratios under TAA vs SAA. ▪ Information ratio or t-statistic of excess realized returns relative to the SAA. ▪ Compare realized risk/return of TAA to portfolios on the SAA's efficient frontier (may be less optimal than other frontier portfolios). ▪ Attribution analysis on excess return → identify contribution of specific under/overweightings.
Drawbacks
▪ Additional trading costs and taxation (for taxable investors). ▪ Overweighting concentrates risk within the portfolio and reduces diversification benefits.
Discretionary TAA — qualitative interpretation
Relies on qualitative interpretation of macroeconomic variables. A skillful manager aims to enhance returns in a rising market and hedge risks in a falling market by forecasting short-term deviations from expected returns. Uses a combination of macroeconomic, fundamental, and sentiment indicators.
Data inputs
▪ Macroeconomic: bond yields & credit spreads, monetary policy, GDP growth, earnings & inflation predictions, leading economic indicators. ▪ Fundamental: deviation of P/E, P/B, dividend yield from their historic means. ▪ Sentiment: consumer confidence index.
Market sentiment indicators
1 · Margin borrowing — ↑ purchases on margin drives up prices → bullish. BUT if margin buying gets too high → bearish sign (investors overenthusiastic). 2 · Short interest (aggregate short selling) — the opposite. ↑ short interest drives prices down → bearish. BUT very high levels could indicate the market is at/near a low. 3 · Volatility indexes — level of fear in the market, from bid-ask spread on index options. ↑ with more put purchases, ↓ with more call purchases.
Note: although the data is quantitative in nature, the individual manager decides which indicators to use and how to prioritize/interpret them — hence "discretionary."
Systematic TAA — quantitative
A more quantitative view. Attempts to capture excess returns using strategies that have historically been predictable and persistent. Two main exploitable factors: value and momentum.
Value approach
Exploits the excess return of value stocks over growth stocks. Value measured by dividend or cash-flow yields.
▪ Equities: Shiller's earnings yield (E/P) — 10-year average inflation-adjusted earnings vs market price. ▪ Currencies: short-term interest-rate differentials. ▪ Commodities: roll yields. Backwardation → positive roll yield to the long; contango → negative. ▪ Fixed income: yield spreads over risk-free rates identify value.
Momentum approach
Assumes trends will persist → recent price movements indicate whether to overweight/underweight an asset class.
▪ Most recent 12-month trend — assumed to persist for the next 12 months. ▪ Moving-average crossover — shorter-term MA crossing above longer-term MA → uptrend (and vice versa).
LOS 5.e — Behavioral biases in asset allocation
Behavioral biases cause problems during the allocation process. Awareness that the bias exists is crucial to dealing with every bias.
Loss aversion
Investors dislike losses more than they like gains → hard to maintain discipline when returns are negative; strong temptation to alter the allocation.
Overcome: goals-based investing. Goals are prioritized & subportfolios used — high-priority goals funded with less-risky assets; riskier assets used as goal priority declines. Risk analysis focuses on downside measures such as shortfall risk.
Illusion of control (+ overconfidence)
Tendency to overestimate the ability to control events. Combined with overconfidence → investors fail to diversify, trade too frequently, or both. Common signs:
▪ Frequent trading & tactical shifts attempting market timing (over-confidence after correctly calling one reversal). ▪ Active security selection by institutions believing their resources give superior selection skills. ▪ Above-average use of short selling and leverage. ▪ Shifting allocations despite lack of consensus (an individual trustee thinks they know better than the market). ▪ Concentrated positions exposing the portfolio to diversifiable risk. ▪ Biased risk/return forecasts → allocations inappropriately different from the market portfolio → undiversified extreme corner portfolios (too heavy in 1-2 classes).
Hindsight bias exacerbates it: looking back at past strategies as having led to predictable outcomes.
Overcome: use the market portfolio (CAPM mean-variance) as the starting point; shifts away from it should be subject to a formal review process.
Mental accounting (+ endowment effect)
Separating assets & liabilities into different "buckets" based on subjective criteria → suboptimal allocations. E.g. spending a tax refund on luxury goods while savings are inadequate; keeping low-interest savings while paying high credit-card interest; an entrepreneur emotionally attached to a founded company, irrationally holding it in a high-risk aspirational bucket even after losing control.
Endowment effect also leads to mental accounting: ownership of an asset causes an investor to overvalue it.
Overcome: goals-based investing.
Professor's note: mental accounting ≠ goals-based investing. Goals-based has some elements of mental accounting, but it is primarily a rational effort to differentiate goal priority and use subportfolios to increase the chance of meeting goals.
Representative / recency bias
Attaching more importance to recent data than old data. Result: shift allocations toward assets that performed well recently. E.g. 1990s real-estate "flipping" by a generation who had only experienced rising house prices — the past trend can and did change.
Overcome: strong governance & objective asset allocation processes.
Framing bias
The way information is presented affects the decision. If risk is presented as standard deviation, most prefer the lower risk — but downside risk measures may be more useful in specific situations:
▪ VaR — amount of loss at some probability over a time. ▪ Conditional VaR — average loss within the VaR tail. ▪ Shortfall probability — directly states the probability of an adverse outcome occurring.
Overcome: provide a full range of relevant information, not selectively framed information.
Availability bias (+ familiarity & home bias)
Personally experienced or easily recalled events disproportionately influence decisions. E.g. an investor who lost heavily in the tech bubble won't buy tech / high-P/B stocks again. Also: benchmarking your portfolio to other investors without regard to whether they have comparable goals & constraints.
▪ Familiarity bias — offshoot: what is familiar/easy to recall is given too much weight. ▪ Home bias — offshoot: overallocate to domestic securities, missing international diversification.
Overcome: start the allocation process with the global market portfolio.
Investment Governance
Investment governance is essential to keeping behavioral biases under control. An effective framework should incorporate:
▪ Clearly stated long-term and short-term objectives. ▪ Logical allocation of responsibility for allocation decisions based on skills and workload. ▪ Documented processes for developing and approving the investment policy statement. ▪ Documented processes for developing and approving the SAA. ▪ A framework to monitor and report performance relative to specified goals and objectives. ▪ Periodic audits.
THE TRIAD — lock this distinction
Goals = change in risk appetite / risk capacity (employment status, starting a family, illness affecting willingness/ability to take risk). Constraints = change in time horizon, liquidity needs, asset size, or regulatory/external limits. Beliefs = change in optimization inputs or guiding principles (macro forecasts, committee makeup, expected returns/vol/correlation).
You missed this triad in opposite directions (Phase 4 → called beliefs "goals"; Young → called constraints "goals"). Drill the table above until the mirror-image trap disappears.

Reading 5 · Asset Allocation with Real-World Constraints
Full-reading recap, module by module. Asset allocation is not an exercise in abstract math — this reading is about the practical constraints that shape a real client's allocation: asset size, liquidity, time horizon, regulatory/other constraints (5.a); taxes in allocation & rebalancing (5.b); revising the SAA when goals/constraints/beliefs change (5.c); tactical (short-term) shifts (5.d); and behavioral biases (5.e). Be ready to recognize the impact of an issue on a particular client's allocation.
Module 5.1 · Real-World Issues
LOS 5.aConstraint 1 — Asset Size
Fund size creates opposite problems at each extreme. The tension is between too small to diversify and too large to deploy.
Small fundsLack the expertise & governance to run complex strategies → struggle to reach adequate diversification. Local legislation may restrict some assets to investors above a capital/experience threshold. Fix: commingled accounts (pool a small group) or families pooling to hit minimum-investment levels. Large fundsAccess more expertise & complex strategies; meet high minimum-investment requirements → higher diversification. Economies of scale: lower per-participant governance cost + negotiating power on fees → competitive edge in PE, hedge funds, infrastructure. Too-large fundsCan't use classes that lack capacity (e.g. small-cap). Diseconomies: (1) larger trades → more price impact; (2) capital inflow tempts managers to abandon core strategy; (3) more staff → slower decisions. Splitting among managers adds monitoring burden/cost → large funds often go passive. Very-large fundsMay find too few alternatives available (e.g. too few hedge funds) → choose a fund-of-funds (FoF). Cost: double fee layer (FoF + underlying) and one manager's strategy may offset another's.
Trap: "bigger is always better" is wrong. Both very small and very large funds face diversification/deployment problems — small-cap and niche alternatives are where the too-large fund is constrained, not the small one.
Constraint 2 — Liquidity Needs
Key: integrate the owner's needs with the asset class characteristics. High-need owners hold high-quality short-term liquid assets; low-need, long-horizon owners can harvest the illiquidity premium (real estate, infrastructure).
Portfolio ownerTypical liquidity need
BanksHigh — fund day-to-day operations & stand ready to repay deposits
SWFs, endowments, pension plans, foundationsLower — longer time horizons
Property & casualty insuranceRelatively high — claims are unpredictable
Life & auto insuranceRelatively low — claims are predictable
IndividualsVaries by individual circumstance
Case-specific exceptions break the pattern: a bank with a highly liquid loan portfolio (liquidity from the loan book, not the investments); or a foundation funding unpredictable breakthrough research (needs high liquidity despite the "low" endowment label).
Twist — extreme conditions: plan liquidity for stress. In a crisis, unsophisticated investors may panic-sell → permanent losses & lower total returns from the capital base when markets revert to precrisis levels. Good portfolio governance guards against this.
Constraint 3 — Time Horizon
A portfolio's horizon is defined by a liability to be paid or a goal to be funded at a future date. Allocation must consider the horizon of each liability/goal and adapt as the asset/liability mix changes over time.
Human capital ↓The value of human capital declines over time → allocation shifts toward lower-risk classes (fixed income) as the investor ages. Changing liabilitiesA pension for a young workforce → heavily long-term bonds; a mature scheme → moves to intermediate/short-term bonds. Time diversificationLonger horizons → often more higher-risk assets. Evidence: risky returns mean-revert over time, evening out below-/above-average returns. That is time diversification.
EXAMPLE — Barry Garland (older retired, age 70). Two goals: G1 = constant standard of living to 85; G2 = constant standard 85–100. Life expectancy at 70 = 17.5 yrs (→ ~age 87.5). G1 is fully funded & higher priority (survival probability falls as he ages) → its subportfolio is conservative. G2 is lower priority & only partially funded → invested more aggressively for growth.
Priority rule: higher-priority / fully-funded goals → conservative subportfolio; lower-priority / underfunded goals → aggressive subportfolio. This is the goals-based logic reused throughout the reading.
Time Horizon in action — the Bigstone family (Fig 5.1 → 5.2)
Jane & Arthur Bigstone (both 52, lawyers) have four goals → split into six subportfolios. The lifestyle/consumption goal splits into worst-case (Minimum), baseline (Maintain), aspirational cases.
GoalRiskAllocation% Total (Fig 5.1)15 yrs later (Fig 5.2)
MinimumConservative100% bonds & cash65%60%
MaintainModerate60% equity & 40% bonds12%10%
AspirationalAggressive100% equity8%6%
College fundConservative100% bonds & cash6%— (funded)
Campaign donationAggressive100% equity6%— (funded)
ScholarshipAggressive100% equity3%24%
Aggregate—Fig 5.1: 25% equity & 75% bonds
Fig 5.2: 35% equity & 65% bonds		100%100%
15 years later: fewer consumption years → less needed for future consumption; college & campaign are funded and drop out; only the scholarship remains aspirational (now 24%). Aggregate equity rises 25% → 35%. New goals (e.g. a Congress run for Mark) could later replace the scholarship.
Prof's note trap: the specific percentages are arbitrary — there is no formula. Don't try to compute them. The exam skill is the logic: why one subportfolio gets more equity/bond/cash than another (priority + funded-status + horizon).
Constraint 4 — Regulatory & Other External Constraints
Each portfolio faces its own regulatory/external set. Know the entity-by-entity pattern:
Insurance cos.Largest allocation = fixed income (match assets to projected cash flows of insured risks). Local accounting often lets FI be held at book value → insurer focuses on cash-flow pattern, not market-value volatility. Risk considerations: risk-based capital measures, liquidity, yield levels, credit ratings, ability to liquidate to meet claims. Local law may cap equity to as little as 10%, with caps on PE & high-yield. Pension fundsLaw caps classes & adds tax/accounting/reporting/funding constraints; tax incentives to invest domestically; accounting may allow deferred loss recognition. Decision weighs anticipated funding cost & reported pension expense. Trade-off: more equity → more volatility → risk low returns raise required contributions; but higher expected return lowers PV of expected contributions. Optimize risk (contributions exceed a threshold) vs return (PV of expected contributions) within regulatory limits. Endowments & foundationsInfinite horizon, very few regulatory constraints. Some countries: minimum annual distribution or socially-responsible investment to keep tax-exempt status. Long horizon allows risky assets — but if the endowment funds an organization, lender covenants may constrain the portfolio. Sovereign wealth fundsGovernment-owned, investing for the state; typically not matching assets & liabilities. Subject to citizen scrutiny → may reduce risk below what the long horizon would otherwise allow.
Self-imposed (self-governance) caps each fund may add:
Min in SRIMinimum investment in socially/ethically acceptable assets. Max in riskyMaximum in risky assets such as alternatives. Currency limitsLimits on investment allowed in certain currencies.
ESG timing: investing in ethically acceptable assets (E/S/G goals) is usually NOT part of the initial allocation — rather, an allocation is set aside and invested in acceptable assets.
Module 5.1 · Tax Considerations
LOS 5.bTax in allocation & rebalancing — the four characteristics
Under taxation, pretax vs after-tax risk/return characteristics can differ substantially → taxable entities must use after-tax inputs during allocation. Adjusting for tax after allocating leads to suboptimal allocations.
InterestUsually taxed at the highest rate, often progressively → tax-exempt bonds (e.g. US munis) can form a large part of a taxable investor's FI allocation. DividendsUsually taxed lower than interest → some investors hold preferred stock in place of bonds. Capital gainsUsually taxed lower than income; capital losses can offset gains elsewhere in the portfolio. Account typeSome accounts are tax-deferred / tax-exempt → place the least tax-efficient (most heavily taxed) assets in the most tax-advantaged accounts.
Trap: taxes complicate optimization — return and risk must be considered on both a pretax and after-tax basis, but correlations are UNAFFECTED by taxes.
Worked example 1 — after-tax return (interest)
Investor pays 40% income tax; bond with a 5% coupon, held to maturity. What return goes into the allocation process?
After-tax return = 5% × (1 − 0.40) = 3%
This is the Calculators → "Simple after-tax return (interest)" widget with its default inputs (5%, 40%). Verified: matches textbook 3%.
Worked example 2 — multi-step after-tax return (equity)
Income tax 30% on dividends, 20% on capital gains. Stock: pretax return 16%, of which 10% is dividend income and 90% is price appreciation (capital gains realized annually).
Pretax dividend income: 16% × 0.1 = 1.6% After-tax dividend: 1.6% × (1 − 0.3) = 1.12% Pretax capital gain: 16% × 0.9 = 14.4% After-tax capital gain: 14.4% × (1 − 0.2) = 11.52% After-tax return: 1.12% + 11.52% = 12.64%
Why splitEquity return has two components taxed at different rates — dividends (30%) and gains (20%). You must tax each piece separately then add. Decisive detailThe 10%/90% split of the return (not of the tax) is what's easy to drop. Apply the split to the 16% first, then the respective tax rate.
Calculators → "Multi-step after-tax return (equity)", defaults 16 / 10 / 30 / 20. Verified: matches textbook 12.64%.
Worked example 3 — after-tax standard deviation of return
Security with pretax σ = 12%, capital-gains tax 20%. Capital-gains tax reduces gains on appreciation and (via the ability to use losses to offset gains) reduces realized losses → a posttax σ should be the input.
σAT = σPT × (1 − t) = 12% × (1 − 0.20) = 9.6%
Calculators → "After-tax standard deviation", defaults 12 / 20. Verified: matches textbook 9.6%. Note: taxes cushion both upside & downside → decrease after-tax σ.
Embedded gains/losses & effect on the frontier
When an asset's cost basis differs from market value: cost basis below market → unrealized gain (embedded tax liability); cost basis above market → loss (embedded tax asset). Three ways to adjust market value to reflect the liability/asset:
Method 1Subtract the embedded capital-gains tax from current market value as if sold today. Method 2Assume sale in the future & discount the tax liability to PV using the asset's after-tax return as the discount rate. Method 3Assume sale in the future & discount the tax liability to PV using the after-tax risk-free rate.
Frontier effect: using after-tax returns & after-tax risk shifts the efficient frontier — allocations to tax-inefficient assets (e.g. high-yield bonds) usually DECREASE. But such assets can still earn a place if they have low correlations with other portfolio assets.
Portfolio rebalancing under tax
To maintain the SAA all portfolios rebalance periodically. Taxable owners realize taxable gains at each rebalancing → must balance "maintain the SAA" against "avoid taxable gains." Because taxes lower return volatility (correlations unaltered), rebalance less frequently in taxable portfolios.
after-tax deviation from target = pretax deviation / (1 − t)
Prof's note — DO NOT confuse the two "(1−t)" formulas:
• After-tax σ of return: σAT = σPT × (1−t) → taxes DECREASE it (multiply).
• Allowable deviation from target weight: devAT = devPT / (1−t) → taxes INCREASE it (divide). Because lower volatility means the weight drifts less, so a wider band is tolerable.
Worked example 4 — pretax vs after-tax deviation from target weight
Tax-exempt investor's SAA: 40% fixed income, ±5% (range 35%–45%). If FI returns were subject to a 30% tax, find the equivalent after-tax rebalancing range.
Pretax allowable deviation = 45% − 40% = 5% Posttax deviation = 5% / (1 − 0.30) = 7.14% Range = 40% ± 7.14% = 32.86% – 47.14%
Calculators → "After-tax rebalancing range" (defaults 40 / ±5 / 30 → 7.14%, 32.86–47.14). Verified: matches textbook 7.14% and 32.86–47.14%.
Decisive detail: the range widens (divide by 1−t), it does not shrink. Higher tax → wider tolerable band → rebalance less often.
Two strategies to reduce tax impact + asset location
Tax loss harvestingDeliberately realize losses to offset gains elsewhere. Strategic asset locationMake the most efficient use of tax-advantaged accounts. Two advantaged types: Tax-exempt (assets not subject to tax) and Tax-deferred (appreciate tax-free, taxed on distribution).
Value adjustmentAssets in tax-exempt accounts need no market-value adjustment. Assets in tax-deferred & taxable accounts are reduced by the tax burden before entering allocation. Inputs by vehicleRisk/return inputs for assets in the tax-deferred vehicle (grow tax-free) should be pretax; inputs for assets in the taxable vehicle should be after-tax. Account multiplierThe optimization uses both classes and locations: 2 asset classes × 2 account types → the process uses 4 "account types" (each class in taxable vs tax-deferred).
Two asset-location rules (don't swap them):
• Assets subject to the lowest tax rates (typically equity) → allocated first to taxable accounts.
• Assets subject to frequent trading & high tax rates → allocated to tax-advantaged accounts.
Liquidity for consumption should always be considered (pension assets may not be reachable without penalty).
Module 5.2 · Adjusting the Strategic Asset Allocation
LOS 5.cRevising allocation for changes in goals / constraints / beliefs
The initial optimal SAA is unlikely to last a portfolio's whole life — reevaluate annually or when goals, constraints, or beliefs change. Three triggers:
Change in goalsBusiness cycle can shift institutional goals. A business downturn → higher cash-flow needs from the portfolio (e.g. airlines under low-budget competition reduce pension risk to smooth contributions; pension deficits force reexamination). For individuals: employment change or starting a family shifts willingness & ability to take risk. Change in constraintsExamples: govt regs requiring increased distributions to keep tax-exempt status; large one-off cash flows; increased funding for an endowment beneficiary; forced early retirement due to illness. Direction: a change needing increased cash outflows → shift to more liquid assets; a large inflow (e.g. donation) → more flexibility to take risk. Change in beliefsOwner's activities follow a set of principles/beliefs that can change — e.g. a new investment-committee makeup (new members walked through an allocation study). Economic-environment change → new expected returns/volatility/correlations → new optimal allocation (pre-2008 vs post-2008 rate regimes give very different FI expectations).
Predetermined changes: some allocations shift on schedule with no reexamination — target-date funds use a glide path, moving from equity to more conservative investments (nominal & inflation-protected bonds) as the target date approaches.
LOS 5.dShort-term shifts — Tactical Asset Allocation (TAA)
SAA = the long-term target weightings in the IPS. TAA = short-term deviations to exploit cyclical conditions or a perceived mispricing in a class.
ObjectiveIncrease risk-adjusted returns by exploiting short-term opportunities. Assumes short-term returns are predictable (not a random walk). Success depends on market/factor timing, NOT security selection. ConstraintsStill respects the IPS risk constraint, but ignores specific goals/liabilities. Judged against the SAA benchmark; deviations often limited by a range of predicted volatility or a tracking-error budget vs the SAA. DrawbacksExtra trading costs & taxes (for taxable investors); overweighting a class concentrates risk & reduces diversification.
Evaluation — measuring TAA success:
SharpeCompare Sharpe ratios under the TAA vs the SAA. IR / t-statInformation ratio or t-statistic of the excess realized returns relative to the SAA. vs frontierCompare realized risk/return of the TAA to portfolios on the SAA's efficient frontier (TAA may be less optimal than other frontier portfolios). AttributionAttribution analysis on the excess return → identify the contribution of specific under-/over-weightings.
Approaches to TAA — discretionary vs systematic
DiscretionaryQualitative interpretation of macro variables. Skilled manager enhances returns in a rising market & hedges in a falling one by forecasting short-term deviations. Uses macro data (bond yields, credit spreads, monetary policy, GDP, earnings & inflation predictions, leading indicators), fundamental data (deviation of P/E, P/B, dividend yield from historic means), and sentiment (consumer confidence index). Data may be quantitative, but the manager decides which indicators to use & how to weight them. SystematicQuantitative; captures returns from historically predictable & persistent patterns. Two main factors: value & momentum.
Market sentiment (used in discretionary TAA) can be assessed with:
Margin borrowingRising margin purchases drive prices up → bullish; but too high → bearish sign (over-enthusiasm). Short interestAggregate short selling. Rising short interest drives prices down → bearish; but very high levels could mark a near-low (opposite of margin). Volatility indexesLevel of fear; from bid-ask spread on index options. Rises with more put buying, falls with more call buying.
Value (systematic)Exploits excess return of value over growth. Equities: dividend/cash-flow yields, Shiller E/P (10-yr avg inflation-adjusted earnings vs price). Currencies: short-term interest-rate differentials. Commodities: roll yields — backwardation → positive roll yield (long), contango → negative. Fixed income: yield spreads over risk-free. Momentum (systematic)Assumes trends persist → recent price moves signal over-/under-weighting. Indicators: most recent 12-month trend (assumed to persist next 12 months); moving-average crossover (shorter-term MA crossing above longer-term → uptrend, and vice versa).
Backwardation vs contango — don't flip it: backwardation = positive roll yield (go long); contango = negative roll yield. And for the VIX-type index: puts ↑ volatility ↑, calls ↑ volatility ↓.
Module 5.3 · Behavioral Issues
LOS 5.eBehavioral biases in asset allocation & how to overcome them
Awareness that a bias exists is crucial to dealing with every bias. Learn each bias with its signature symptom and its fix.
Loss aversionDislike losses more than equivalent gains → hard to keep discipline when returns are negative; tempted to alter the allocation. Fix: goals-based investing — prioritize goals, fund high-priority goals with less risky assets, use riskier assets as priority declines; focus risk analysis on downside measures (shortfall risk). Illusion of controlOverestimate ability to control events; with overconfidence → fail to diversify &/or trade too much. Signs: frequent trading/TAA market-timing; institutions doing active selection believing resources give superior skill; above-average short selling & leverage; shifting allocations despite no consensus (trustee "knows better"); concentrated positions exposing diversifiable risk; biased forecasts → extreme corner portfolios. Fix: start from the CAPM market portfolio; subject shifts to a formal review. Hindsight biasExacerbates illusion of control — looking back at past strategies as if outcomes were predictable. Mental accountingSeparate assets/liabilities into subjective "buckets" → suboptimal allocations (e.g. spend a tax refund on luxuries while under-saved; keep low-interest savings while paying high credit-card interest; hold a founded company in a high-risk bucket). Endowment effect (ownership → overvalue an asset) also feeds it. Fix: goals-based investing. Representative / recencyOver-weight recent data vs old → shift toward recent winners (e.g. 1990s house "flipping" by a generation that only saw rising prices). Fix: strong governance & objective allocation processes. FramingThe way information is presented changes the decision (risk as σ → most pick lower risk; downside measures may be better: VaR = loss amount at a probability over time; CVaR = average loss within the VaR tail; shortfall probability = probability of an adverse outcome). Fix: present a full range of relevant information, don't selectively frame. AvailabilityPersonally-experienced or easily-recalled events dominate (e.g. tech-bubble victim avoids tech forever); benchmarking to other investors regardless of comparable goals. Familiarity (offshoot): over-weight the familiar. Home bias (offshoot): over-allocate domestic, miss international diversification. Fix: start allocation from the global market portfolio.
Fix pattern to memorize: loss aversion & mental accounting → goals-based investing; illusion of control, availability/familiarity/home → start from the (global) CAPM market portfolio + formal review; representative → governance & objective process; framing → full information, not selective framing.
Prof's note: mental accounting is NOT the same as goals-based investing. Goals-based investing has some elements of mental accounting, but it is a rational effort to differentiate goal priority and then use subportfolios to raise the chance of meeting the goals.
Investment Governance
Essential to keeping behavioral biases under control. An effective framework incorporates:
ObjectivesClearly stated long-term & short-term objectives. ResponsibilityLogical allocation of decision responsibility based on skills & workload. Documented IPSDocumented processes for developing & approving the investment policy statement. Documented SAADocumented processes for developing & approving the SAA. MonitoringA framework to monitor & report performance relative to specified goals & objectives. AuditsPeriodic audits.
Module Quizzes · verified reasoning
Quiz answers & the decisive detail
Answer keys were not in the uploaded photos; the answers below are my verified reasoning from the reading, not a copy of the official key.
QuizQuestionAnswerWhy
5.1 · Q1Extremely large fund seeking a large allocation → liquidity constraint when investing in?A. Hedge fundsAlternatives (hedge funds) have limited capacity; a huge allocation can't be absorbed. Global equity & IG bonds are deep/liquid.
5.1 · Q2SAA 60/40, after-tax rebal range ±12.5% (tax 20%); current 71/29. Which is most accurate?C. Neither fund is outside its rangeEquity drift = 71−60 = 11%. The ±12.5% band is stated as the after-tax range and applies to both funds; 11% < 12.5% → both within. Verified.
5.2/5.3 · Q1Target-date fund, retire at 65 → most likely?A. Increase inflation-protected bonds later in the glide pathGlide path shifts equity → conservative (nominal and inflation-protected) bonds as the date approaches (i.e. later), not earlier.
5.2/5.3 · Q2TAA vs SAA relative success — most likely correct?B. TAA is unsuccessful if the information ratio is negativeA negative IR means TAA underperformed the SAA per unit of active risk. A positive Sharpe alone (A) or lower σ (C) doesn't establish success vs the SAA benchmark.
5.2/5.3 · Q3Rotheram: aggressive side portfolio in home-state REITs + equity of her ex-employer. Which bias?B. Familiarity biasShe over-weights what she knows (home-state property, former employer) — an availability offshoot. Not mental accounting (that's the two-portfolio split, which is rational goals-based here) and not framing.
Refresher — calls, puts, parties
▪ Call = a right to buy the underlying. ▪ Put = a right to sell. ▪ Buyer (long) pays the premium and holds the right. ▪ Seller (short) receives the premium as payment for taking on the contingent liability: a short call must deliver the underlying if exercised (receiving the strike); a short put must take delivery (paying the strike). ▪ European = exercisable only at expiration. ▪ American = exercisable any trading day up to and including expiration (the labels are not about geography).
Symbols (curriculum notation)
X = exercise (strike) price S = underlying (stock) price c, p = call premium, put premium subscripts: 0 = position entry, T = expiration e.g. S_T = underlying price at expiry
Intrinsic value + time value
An option's total premium decomposes into two parts:
▪ Intrinsic value = value of immediate exercise; the degree to which the option is in-the-money (ITM). Zero if not ITM. ▪ Time value = the extra value reflecting what might happen over the option's remaining life. Driven by volatility, time to expiry, the risk-free rate, and any yield — which is why the first pricing formula (BSM, 1973) was needed.
Two principles to remember (all else equal): higher volatility → higher premiums (calls AND puts); less time to expiry → lower premiums (calls AND puts).
Trap: intrinsic value is NOT profit. An option can be ITM yet still produce a loss for the long if intrinsic value < premium originally paid. "ITM" only means exercise (ignoring premium) would yield a gain.
Implied vs historical volatility
▪ Implied volatility = the consensus volatility backed out of the current option price through a pricing model (forward-looking). ▪ Historical (realized) volatility = the square root of the actual realized variance of returns to date (backward-looking). The two are not the same.
ITM / ATM / OTM and intrinsic value
OptionITM whenIntrinsic value (if ITM)OTM when
CallS > XS − XS < X
PutS < XX − SS > X
▪ ATM: S = X (zero intrinsic value). ▪ OTM: zero intrinsic value as well.
Call ITM logic: the right to pay less than market for the underlying; gain = S − X (buy at X, sell at market S). Put ITM logic: the right to receive more than market; gain = X − S (buy at market S, sell at X).
Twist: at expiration there is only intrinsic value (no time value) — that intrinsic value is the option's payoff. Before expiry, even an OTM option has positive value (all time value).

The golden rule of payoff diagrams
Profit line = value line shifted by the net initial premium: down if the net premium was an outflow (you paid), up if it was an inflow (you received). The profit line always has the same shape as the value line. Long and short of the same option have identical breakevens; their max profit/loss just swap (zero-sum).
Long call  |  Short call
Long call: max loss = premium paid (expires OTM); breakeven = X + c₀; unlimited max profit. Motivation: profit from a rise, downside limited to the premium. Short (naked) call: max profit = premium received; breakeven = X + c₀; unlimited max loss. Limited upside (premium) balanced against unlimited loss if the underlying rises.
XYZ MAY 50 call, c₀ = 6.26 S=40 → value 0, profit = 0 − 6.26 = −6.26 (max loss) S=60 → value 10, profit = 10 − 6.26 = +3.74 Breakeven = 50 + 6.26 = 56.26
Long put  |  Short put
Long put: max profit = X − p₀ (when S→0); breakeven = X − p₀; max loss = premium paid. Note max profit equals breakeven here. Short put: max profit = premium received; max loss = X − p₀ (= breakeven); large but limited downside (stock can't fall below zero). Profile looks like a covered call.
XYZ JUN 50 put, p₀ = 4.88 Max profit = max loss of the short = 50 − 4.88 = 45.12 Breakeven = 50 − 4.88 = 45.12 (= max profit for the long put)

Synthetic long forward (LOS 16.a)
Long call + short put (same underlying, same strike, same expiration) = a synthetic long forward position. Value at expiration = S_T − X.
Above X: the long call is ITM (positive value); the short put is OTM. Below X: the short put is ITM — exercised by the counterparty (negative value); the long call is OTM.
Either way the position ends as if you bought the stock for X — the same payoff as a long forward struck at X. (A cash-secured short put deposits X; a naked short put does not.)
Put–call parity
Buying the call & selling the put must cost the same as buying the stock and borrowing PV(X), since both end with value S_T − X:
c₀ − p₀ = S₀ − PV(X) rearranged: S₀ + p₀ = c₀ + PV(X) XYZ check (MAY 50, rf 3%, 61 days): c₀ − p₀ = 6.26 − 3.87 = 2.39 PV(50) = 50 / 1.03^(61/365) = 49.75 S₀ − PV(X) = 52.14 − 49.75 = 2.39 ✓
Put–call FORWARD parity: substitute PV(F₀(T)) for S₀ → PV(F₀(T)) + p₀ = c₀ + PV(X). For an underlying paying no yield, the fair forward = FV(S₀), so it's just a restatement of standard parity.
Note: this parity assumes the underlying pays no yield over the life. If PV(X) exactly equalled S₀, call and put would have identical premiums and X would be the fair forward price.

Covered call (LOS 16.b)
Structure: long stock + short call. The short call is hedged by ownership of the stock. Above the strike, the increasingly negative call value exactly offsets the stock's gain, capping the upside.
Max profit at expiry = X − S₀ + c₀ Breakeven = max loss basis = S₀ − c₀ (loss increases one-for-one below breakeven; stock floored at 0)
Three motivations — told apart by strike vs spot
UseStrike vs spotIdea
Yield enhancementOTM (possibly far)Stock has limited upside; pocket premium as extra yield.
Reduce position at favourable priceITMPlan to sell; if exercised, sell at strike + keep premium → more than selling at market now.
Target price realizationmarginally OTMHappy to sell slightly higher; calls struck just above market.
Exam hook: the observable difference between the three uses is purely the strike relative to the current stock price. A question describing intent (income vs disposal vs target) is testing whether you map it to OTM / ITM / marginally-OTM.
Example (yield enhancement)
Long XYZ @ 52.14, short APR 55 call, c₀ = 2.52 Max profit = 55 − 52.14 + 2.52 = 5.38 (cap at 55: stock gain 2.86 + premium 2.52) Breakeven = max loss basis = 52.14 − 2.52 = 49.62 Worse off than just holding only if S_T > 55 + 2.52 = 57.52

Protective put (LOS 16.c)
Structure: long stock + long put. The classic options hedge for a long position — protects against the underlying falling while retaining full upside.
Max loss at expiry = S₀ − X + p₀ Breakeven = S₀ + p₀ Max profit = unlimited (stock keeps rising; put just expires)
XYZ example: long @ 52.14 + MAY 50 put @ 3.87. Stock loss capped at 52.14 − 50 = 2.14; net max loss = 2.14 + 3.87 = 6.01. Breakeven = 52.14 + 3.87 = 56.01.

Options as a hedge of a SHORT position (LOS 16.e)
A short seller gains if the price falls, loses if it rises. The two option overlays mirror the long-position hedges:
Buy a call (likely OTM): hedges the short against the price rising — the positive call value above the strike offsets short-stock losses. Analogous to a protective put on a long position. Caps the loss, keeps downside gain. Sell a put (likely OTM): sells off part of the benefit of the price falling, in the same way a covered call sells off the upside of a long position. Collects premium, caps the gain.
Underlying positionHedge upside-cap (sell premium)Hedge protect (buy insurance)
Long stockCovered call (short call)Protective put (long put)
Short stockShort putLong call
Mirror map: short-stock ↔ long-stock swaps calls and puts. Buy-call-on-short ≙ buy-put-on-long (protection); sell-put-on-short ≙ sell-call-on-long (income, capped benefit).
The Collar — protective put + covered call
A collar is best thought of as a combination of a protective put and a covered call, held on an existing long position in the underlying. Also known as a fence or a hedge wrapper.
▪ Long the underlying + buy a put (usually OTM) → hedges the stock's downside. ▪ Sell a call (usually OTM) → sells off the upside and subsidizes the cost of the put.
Zero-cost collar
Usually the put strike is set first, then an appropriate call strike is chosen so the call and put have the same premium.
If the options are OTC (rather than exchange-traded), matching premiums is easy → no net inflow or outflow at initiation → a zero-cost collar.
Profile (LOS 16.f)
Objective: hedge an existing long position cheaply by giving up upside. Structure: long stock + long put (OTM) + short call (OTM). Max profit: rise from initial price up to the call strike. Max loss: fall from initial price down to the put strike. Breakeven: the initial stock price (for a zero-cost collar — no net premium).
The stock value is hedged beyond the strikes — value capped above the call strike, floored at the put strike.
EXAMPLE — XYZ zero-cost collar (20 March, price = $52.14)
Buy a June 50 put (premium $4.88) and sell a June 55.87 call (premium $4.88). Same premium → zero net cost.
Max profit
$3.73
Max loss
$2.14
Breakeven
$52.14
Max profit = call strike − initial price = $55.87 − $52.14 = $3.73 Max loss = initial price − put strike = $52.14 − $50.00 = $2.14 Breakeven = initial stock price = $52.14 (zero net premium)
Chart note: the "stock profit + option values" line is the same as the net profit line because the zero net initial premium means there's nothing to subtract.
Payoff regions
Stock at expirationOutcome
Below put strike ($50)Floored — put protects; loss capped at $2.14
Between strikes ($50–$55.87)Profit/loss tracks the stock; both options expire worthless
Above call strike ($55.87)Capped — short call caps upside; profit capped at $3.73

The Straddle — the classic volatility play
A long straddle involves the purchase of an equal number of calls and puts on a given underlying. All options have the same expiry date and strike.
Distinction: unlike covered call / protective put / collar, the straddle (and the spreads) do not involve a position in the underlying — they use options only.
Strangle (currency reading): like a straddle, but the call and put have different strikes.
At expiration — only one leg is ITM
Either the call or the put will be ITM, but not both. With strike 52.50: call is ITM for prices above 52.50, put is ITM for prices below 52.50.
The value line is always V-shaped, centered on the strike, where both options expire worthless so total value = 0.
EXAMPLE — Long XYZ June 52.5 straddle
Stock at $52.14 → go long both the June 52.5 call and June 52.5 put (strike close to ATM). Call premium $6.22 + put premium $6.19, both paid at initiation.
Total outlay = Max loss
$12.41
Upside breakeven
$64.91
Downside breakeven
$40.09
Total outlay = $6.22 + $6.19 = $12.41 (max loss, at the strike) Upside BE = strike + outlay = $52.50 + $12.41 = $64.91 Downside BE = strike − outlay = $52.50 − $12.41 = $40.09
Profit profile: larger profits the further the underlying moves either way. No maximum profit on the long call (unlimited upside). Max profit on the long put = strike price − cost of the options.
Short Straddle — the neutrality play
A short straddle involves selling instead of buying — it is a neutrality play.
▪ Makes more profit the closer to the strike the underlying ends up. ▪ No limit on potential loss (mirror of the long straddle's unlimited profit).
Trap: long straddle = volatility play (wants a big move, either way); short straddle = neutrality play (wants the underlying to stay near the strike). Loss is unlimited on the short.

Spreads — the building blocks
Bull and bear spreads are positions with equal numbers of long options on one strike and short options on a second strike. A spread is constructed using either calls or puts.
▪ Bull spreads = "Buy Low" — long options on the lower strike, short options on the higher strike. ▪ Bear spreads = short options on the lower strike, long options on the higher strike.
Key identity: a bear spread is just a short bull spread.
Debit vs Credit
TypeStrategiesNet premiumWhy
DebitBull call · Bear putNet outlay (pay)The bought (more valuable) option costs more than the sold one
CreditBear call · Bull putNet inflow (receive)The more valuable option is sold
Professor's note: by default assume a bull spread uses calls and a bear spread uses puts (debit spreads preferred over credit spreads) unless the question states otherwise.
Bull Call Spread (debit) — bullish, limited
Buy XYZ June 50 call ($7.40), sell XYZ June 55 call ($5.20). Net outlay = $7.40 − $5.20 = $2.20.
Max loss
$2.20
Breakeven
$52.20
Max profit
$2.80
At 55+: value = diff between strikes = $5 (max value; further upside hedged by short call) Max loss = net premium paid = $2.20 (value = 0, below lower strike) Breakeven = lower strike + net premium paid = $50 + $2.20 = $52.20 Max profit = diff strikes − net premium paid = $5 − $2.20 = $2.80
Below 50 → both OTM, value = 0. Between strikes → only long call ITM, value = stock − lower strike. Similar to a covered call, but with a long call taking the place of the stock.
Bear Put Spread (debit) — bearish, limited
Sell a lower-strike put, buy a higher-strike put. Buy XYZ May 55 put ($6.61), sell XYZ May 50 put ($3.87). Net outlay = $6.61 − $3.87 = $2.74.
Max loss
$2.74
Breakeven

$2.26
Max loss = net premium paid = $2.74 Breakeven = higher strike − net premium paid = $55 − $2.74 = $52.26 Max profit = diff strikes − net premium paid = $5 − $2.74 = $2.26
Both OTM above the higher strike → value 0. Between strikes, value reflects the moneyness of the long 55 put. At the lower strike (50), value is maxed and hedged for any lower price. Exposure is bearish but limited vs just a long put at 55.
Bear Call Spread (credit) — using calls for a bear position
Short XYZ June 50 call ($7.40), long XYZ June 55 call ($5.20). Net initial inflow = $7.40 − $5.20 = $2.20.
Max profit = net premium received = $2.20 (at 50 and below) At 55+: net intrinsic value = −$5 Max loss = diff strikes − net premium received = $5 − $2.20 = $2.80 Breakeven = lower strike + net premium received = $50 + $2.20 = $52.20
Bull Put Spread (credit) — using puts for a bull position
Reverse of the bear put spread: short XYZ May 55 put ($6.61), long XYZ May 50 put ($3.87). Net inflow.
Max profit = net premium received Breakeven = higher strike − net premium received Max loss = diff strikes − net premium received
Beware credit spreads with American-style options: the short option may go ITM while the long option is still OTM → the counterparty might exercise early, disrupting the strategy.
Generalized at-expiration formulas
"Net premium" = absolute value of the difference between the premiums.
Debit spreads (bull call & bear put)
Max loss = net premium paid Max profit = difference between strikes − net premium paid
Credit spreads (bear call & bull put)
Max profit = net premium received Max loss = difference between strikes − net premium received
Breakeven (by option type)
Call spreads: breakeven = lower strike + net premium Put spreads: breakeven = higher strike − net premium
