The Greeks — each is a ratio of absolute changes
So far we considered values/profits at expiration (simple one-for-one with intrinsic value). During their lives, options respond to changes in the underlying (and other factors) in a more complex way. The Greeks describe that.
You won't be asked to calculate the Greeks — if needed they'd be provided. What matters is the meaning and significance of each.
The four Greeks
GreekDefinitionSign (long call)Sign (long put)
Delta (Δ)Δ option price per +1 change in stock pricepositivenegative
Gamma (Γ)Δ option delta per +1 change in stock pricepositivepositive
Theta (θ)daily change in option price (effect of time passing)negativenegative
Vega (ν)Δ option price per +1% change in volatilitypositivepositive
Memory anchor: long options are long gamma and long vega (both positive), but short theta (time decay hurts). Delta is the only one whose sign flips between calls (+) and puts (−).
Delta — slope of the value line
Delta measures the change in option price for a +1 change in the underlying (all else constant — the change must be instantaneous).
XYZ stock $52.14. MAY 55 call delta = 0.47. If stock rises $1 to $53.14, the call rises ~$0.47: $4.02 + $0.47 = $4.49 (predicted).
Why the pricing model gives $4.51, not $4.49: the option price line is curved (except at expiration), with curvature measured by gamma — so delta itself varies with the underlying. Delta is only accurate for infinitesimal moves.
Time value
The vertical distance between the (total) value line and the intrinsic value line = time value. It is greatest around ATM and diminishes the more an option is ITM or OTM (time value reflects uncertainty about whether the option expires ITM/OTM — deeply ITM/OTM = less uncertainty).
Delta sign & magnitude rules
▪ Long calls: positive delta. ▪ Long puts: negative delta (line slopes downward).
Simple rule (ignoring the sign), all else equal:
▪ The more ITM an option → the higher its absolute delta (closer to 1). ▪ The more OTM an option → the lower its absolute delta (closer to 0).
Delta ranges: Long call 0→+1 · Short call 0→−1 · Long put 0→−1 · Short put 0→+1.
Gamma — curvature of the value line (slope of delta)
Gamma = change in delta per +1 change in the underlying. It's the slope of the line representing delta, and changes with the underlying too.
MAY 55 call gamma = 0.031. If the share price rises $1, the call's delta rises 0.031: 0.470 + 0.031 = 0.501.
Gamma adjustment improves the delta estimate: if delta is 0.470 at $52.14 and 0.501 at $53.14, the average delta = (0.470 + 0.501)/2 = 0.486. Predicted call value $1 up = $4.02 + $0.486 = $4.506 — much closer to the model's $4.51 than using initial delta alone.
When is gamma highest?
Gamma tends to be higher the closer an option is to ATM, and is at its greatest for ATM options close to expiration.
Why: with little time left, the option premium line is crammed into a narrow range either side of the strike (low time value), so delta swings sharply from ~0 to ~1 across that range → gamma is highest there. ATM + near expiry = max gamma.
Gamma table — XYZ at $52.14 (20 March)
StrikeCall γ (APR/MAY/JUN)Put γ (APR/MAY/JUN)
500.041 / 0.030 / 0.0240.041 / 0.030 / 0.024
52.50.044 / 0.031 / 0.0250.044 / 0.031 / 0.025
550.043 / 0.031 / 0.0260.043 / 0.031 / 0.026
Note gamma is higher for the nearer expiry (APR > MAY > JUN) and peaks around the ATM strike (52.5). Call gamma = put gamma at the same strike/expiry.
LOS 16.d — Position (portfolio) delta
The overall delta for a combination of options and positions in the underlying = sum of the individual deltas (being careful with signs).
▪ Long position in 1 unit of the underlying: delta = +1. ▪ Short position in 1 unit of the underlying: delta = −1. ▪ Futures/forwards on a no-yield underlying are proxies → delta +1 (long) / −1 (short).
Contract multiplier: a traded option contract is usually a right over 100 shares. A long XYZ call with delta +0.65 → position delta = 100 × +0.65 = +65.
Worked examples
100 shares of XYZ → delta = 100 × +1 = +100 (stock +$1 → value +$100) 1,000 shares + 10 long put contracts (put delta −0.6): = (1,000 × +1) + (10 × 100 × −0.6) = 1,000 − 600 = +400 → stock falls $1: shares lose $1,000, but net position only falls $400
Full forward hedge: long stock + short forward on the same number of shares → delta = shares × (+1 + −1) = 0 → completely hedged against price moves.
Position delta calculator

Option delta
Protective put pre-expiry
At expiration we thought of a protective put as retaining full stock exposure above the strike and fully hedging below it. Before expiration, it's better seen as modifying the delta of the long stock from its unhedged +1.
▪ Large stock rises → put moves substantially OTM → position delta → +1 (almost same as unhedged stock). ▪ Large stock falls → put moves substantially ITM → position delta → 0 (downside protected).
Stock + protective put has a net exposure equivalent to a long call.
Contrast — forward hedge: a forward-based hedge (short forward on the same shares) gives position delta = shares × (+1 + −1) = 0 → completely hedged. The put hedges asymmetrically (keeps upside), the forward hedges both directions.
Covered call pre-expiry
As with the protective put, the covered call's position delta varies with the underlying:
▪ Call deeply OTM (stock low) → position delta close to +1 (you still have nearly full stock exposure). ▪ Call deeply ITM (stock high) → position delta close to 0 (virtually all the stock's upside is hedged away by the short call).
Both covered call and protective put mute the exposure of the underlying — the bull/bear spread pre-expiry behaves similarly (highly muted vs the at-expiration profile).
MQ 16.9 #1 — likely deltas just after establishment (3 months out)
A covered call (long stock + short OTM call) and a protective put (long stock + long OTM put), both newly established with time to expiry.
▪ Covered call: long stock (+1) + short OTM call (small negative, e.g. −0.55) → net position delta around +0.4 to +0.45 (positive, <1). ▪ Protective put: long stock (+1) + long OTM put (small negative) → net positive but <1 as well.
Trap: both deltas are positive and between 0 and 1 just after establishment — neither is zero, and the protective put's delta is NOT negative (the long-stock +1 dominates the small negative put delta).
Theta — speed of time-value decay
Theta measures how quickly an option loses value as time passes (all else equal). For a long option position theta is always negative: less time to expiration means less time value.
Call ThetaStrikePut Theta
APRMAYJUNPriceAPRMAYJUN
−0.058−0.042−0.03550−0.054−0.038−0.031
−0.061−0.043−0.03652.5−0.056−0.039−0.031
−0.059−0.043−0.03655−0.055−0.039−0.031
▪ All negative: long calls AND long puts both lose time value as expiry nears. ▪ Shorter-dated = larger |theta|: APR (nearest) thetas are more negative than JUN (furthest) — the near-dated option bleeds time value fastest. This is the engine behind calendar spreads.
ATM behaviour: options close to ATM have the highest |theta|, and |theta| increases (becomes more negative) as expiration approaches → ATM options lose time value at an increasing rate. A 1-month-to-expiry ATM option loses far more time value over a month than an otherwise-identical 3-month option does over the same period.
Contrast — deep OTM / deep ITM: for options far from the money, the decline in time value slows down as maturity approaches (the curve flattens), the opposite of ATM. Don't assume "closer to expiry → faster decay" universally; it's true for ATM, false for deep OTM/ITM.
Calendar Spreads (LOS 16.g)
Calendar spreads are the only strategy where the two options have different expirations (same underlying, same strike). The motivation: exploit the difference in theta between a close-to-expiry and a more-distant option.
For options near ATM, the nearer-dated option has a higher absolute theta (more negative) than the longer-dated one. The calendar spread monetises that gap.
Long calendar spread
Structure: buy longer-dated option + sell shorter-dated option (same strike & underlying). Logic: shorter-dated premium falls faster than longer-dated → more value gained on the short leg than lost on the long leg → net profit. Conditions: options near ATM (so thetas are the right way round); want little movement in the underlying over the near option's life (large moves undermine profit). Calls or puts? reflects longer-term view — calls if bullish, puts if bearish. Benefits from: a stable market or an increase in implied volatility.
Short calendar spread
Structure: reverse — sell longer-dated + buy shorter-dated. Vulnerable when: the underlying stays still so the options end up ATM as the short-dated option expires → longer-dated premium rises (a loss, since we're short it) unless implied vol also falls. Benefits from: a big move in the underlying or a decrease in implied volatility.
Unifying idea: in both cases the strategy sells the option expected to lose value (theta) relatively faster as time passes.
Example — Jenkins long calendar spread
20 March, XYZ = $52.14. Long-term bullish but expects little movement next month.
Buy 4 XYZ June 52.5 calls @ 6.22 Sell 4 XYZ April 52.5 calls @ 3.53 Net premium outlay = 2.69 × 4 × 100 = $1,076 At April expiry, stock still $52.14: • Both calls OTM → April call expires worthless (good, we're short it) • June call now worth $5.00 (from pricing model) Position value = 5.00 × 400 = $2,000 (paid $1,076 a month earlier)
Profit would be even higher if implied volatility rose — that drives the June call value up.
Vega — sensitivity to a +1% change in volatility
Vega measures the effect of a 1% increase in implied volatility on the option's value. Vegas are always positive: a more volatile underlying makes every option on it more valuable (more uncertainty about the expiry outcome → more time value).
Call VegaStrikePut Vega
APRMAYJUNPriceAPRMAYJUN
0.0570.0810.098500.0570.0810.098
0.0600.0840.10252.50.0600.0840.102
0.0590.0840.103550.0590.0840.103
▪ More time → higher vega: JUN vegas > MAY > APR. Longer-dated options are more sensitive to vol. ▪ Diminishes deep ITM / deep OTM: vega peaks near ATM and falls away as the option moves far in- or out-of-the-money. ▪ Call vega = put vega at the same strike/expiry (put–call parity).
Aside — converting volatility between periods
To convert a volatility (standard deviation) from one period to another, multiply by the square root of the ratio of the period lengths.
σ(target) = σ(source) × √(days_target / days_source) Annual 57% → two-monthly (42 trading days, 252-day year): 57% × √(42 / 252) = 23.27% Monthly (21 days) → annual: σ_monthly × √(252 / 21)

Straddle value before expiration
At expiry a long straddle has the familiar V-shape. Before expiry the value curve is smoother (U-shaped) but the same idea holds: value increases the further the underlying moves from the strike.
▪ Delta near the strike ≈ 0 (the curve is flat at the bottom). ▪ Delta → +1 as the underlying rises far above strike; → −1 as it falls far below.
Long volatility: at a given underlying price, a higher level of volatility lifts the whole curve — the long straddle gains value even if the underlying doesn't move. This is the real reason a long straddle is called "going long volatility."
Long straddle — Greeks profile
Delta: long call (+δ) + long put (−δ) → delta-neutral (≈0 near strike) — we don't much care about small moves in the underlying. Vega: positive — value rises if vol rises. Theta: negative — two long options bleed time value. Vol must rise quickly enough to offset the decay.
Short straddle — Greeks profile
Delta: delta-neutral as well. Vega: negative — a bet on falling volatility. Theta: positive — collects time decay.
Twist: "delta-neutral" describes BOTH long and short straddles — the distinguishing Greek is vega (long = +vega = long vol; short = −vega = short vol). A question that hinges on delta to tell them apart is a trap.
Volatility Skew & Smile (LOS 16.h)
The XYZ option prices throughout this reading assumed a single volatility of 30% for all strikes and expirations — a simplification. In practice, implied volatility computed from actual traded options varies by strike and by expiration (and differs between calls and puts). Holding expiration constant, two patterns appear:
Smile vs Skew
▪ Volatility SMILE: further-from-ATM options (both sides) have higher implied vol → a U-shaped (smiling) curve when IV is plotted against strike. Less common. ▪ Volatility SKEW: implied vol increases for more OTM puts and decreases for more OTM calls. Explanation: OTM puts are desirable as insurance against market declines, so they're bid up by higher demand (higher value ⇒ higher implied vol); demand for OTM calls is comparatively low. More common.
Memorise the skew direction: OTM puts → IV UP; OTM calls → IV DOWN. The reversed wording ("IV up for OTM calls, down for OTM puts") is a classic distractor (it describes neither standard pattern).
Reading sentiment from skew deviations
▪ Bearish signal: a sharp increase in the level of the skew plus a surge in the absolute level of implied vol → market sentiment turning bearish. ▪ Bullish signal: higher implied vols (vs historical) for OTM calls → investors bullish, demand to take on upside exposure is strong.
Deviations expected to correct can form the basis of trading strategies — which might use risk reversals (next tab).
Two more terms
▪ Term structure of volatility: implied vols differ across maturities. Contango (longer-dated options having higher implied vol) is quite common. ▪ Implied volatility surface: a 3-D graph examining the joint influence of maturity (x-axis) and strike price (y-axis) on implied volatility (z-axis).
Risk Reversal
A long (short) risk reversal combines long (short) calls and short (long) puts on the same underlying. It's used to exploit a skew that has deviated anomalously from historical levels.
Long risk reversal: if a trader believes put implied vol is relatively too high vs calls → buy the OTM call (seen as relatively underpriced) + sell the OTM put (seen as relatively overpriced), same expiration. Aim: profit if the anomalous IV relationship corrects — long the options that should gain value, short those that should lose. NOT a directional bet on the stock.
Problem: long call + short put both create long exposure to the underlying → the position is "broadly long" the stock, which is problematic if you didn't want directional risk.
Example — PQR risk reversal & delta hedge
PQR = $50. Buy call (strike 60, IV 50%) + sell put (strike 40, IV 70%). The 20-point IV differential is substantially greater than seen in the past → trade the anomaly.
At the current price ($50) the risk reversal delta ≈ 0.3 (well below 1). Position = 10 call contracts + 10 put contracts (each on 1,000 shares). For each $1 fall in the stock: loss ≈ $1 × 0.3 × 1,000 = $300 (the net long exposure)
To remove the unwanted long exposure → delta hedge: sell 300 shares. Why 300? A short position of that size produces equal-and-opposite P&L to the risk reversal's stock exposure.

1,000 shares' worth of options with delta 0.3 are delta-hedged by 1,000 × 0.3 = 300 shares. (The hedge size = the other side's notional × its delta.)
Dynamic hedge: the delta of the risk reversal does not stay constant — it changes as the stock price moves and as time passes. So the size of the delta hedge must be adjusted periodically (rebalanced). This is typical of all delta hedges.

Master summary — max profit, max loss, breakeven & P&L
Every formula in curriculum notation: X = strike, S₀ = entry stock price, S_T = stock at expiry, c₀ / p₀ = premiums paid (+) or received (−) at entry. "Net" = net premium of a multi-leg position. All per share, transaction costs ignored.
Single options

Stock + option overlays (single-stock hedges)
StrategyStructureMax profitMax lossBreakeven
Covered calllong stock + short callX − S₀ + c₀S₀ − c₀S₀ − c₀ (= max loss)
Protective putlong stock + long putUnlimitedS₀ − X + p₀S₀ + p₀
Collarlong stock + long put (lower X_p) + short call (higher X_c); net premiumX_c − S₀ − netS₀ − X_p + netS₀ + net (net = p₀ − c₀)
Short-stock mirror (16.e): short stock + long call ≙ protective put; short stock + short put ≙ covered call. Calls and puts swap when the underlying is short.
★ Two-leg decomposition — why stock+option formulas look the way they do
The #1 trap on stock+option strategies: forgetting the stock leg. Profit always = (stock leg) + (option leg). The stock you bought at S₀ contributes its own gain/loss separately from the option. Always split them before reaching for a formula.
Master identity: at any expiry price, total profit = (S_T − S₀) from the stock + option payoff ± premium. The maxima below are just this, evaluated at the best/worst S_T.
Covered call — long stock + short call (strike X, receive c₀)
LegContribution at expiry
Stock legS_T − S₀
Short call leg+c₀ − max(S_T − X, 0)
BEST CASE: stock ends at (or above) X — say S₀=52.14, X=55, c₀=2.52, S_T=60 Stock leg : 60 − 52.14 = +7.86 Call leg : +2.52 − (60 − 55) = 2.52 − 5 = −2.48 Total : 7.86 − 2.48 = 5.38 Above X the two legs cancel $1-for-$1 → profit is CAPPED. At the cap, S_T = X, so plug in: (X − S₀) + c₀ = (55 − 52.14) + 2.52 = 2.86 + 2.52 = 5.38
Why NOT just c₀? c₀ alone ignores the stock gain from S₀ up to the strike (the 2.86). You bought at 52.14 and effectively sold at 55 — that appreciation is yours, PLUS the premium. c₀ would be the answer only for a naked call (no stock leg).
Max profit = (X − S₀) + c₀ → stock gain up to strike + premium kept.
Max loss / breakeven = S₀ − c₀ → stock falls to 0; effective cost was S₀ minus the cushion c₀.
Protective put — long stock + long put (strike X, pay p₀)
LegContribution at expiry
Stock legS_T − S₀
Long put legmax(X − S_T, 0) − p₀
WORST CASE: stock ends at (or below) X — say S₀=52.14, X=50, p₀=3.87, S_T=40 Stock leg : 40 − 52.14 = −12.14 Put leg : (50 − 40) − 3.87 = 10 − 3.87 = +6.13 Total : −12.14 + 6.13 = −6.01 Below X the put gain offsets further stock losses → loss is FLOORED. At the floor, S_T = X, so plug in: (S_T − S₀) + (X − S_T paid premium) = (X − S₀) + p₀ as a loss S₀ − X + p₀ = 52.14 − 50 + 3.87 = 2.14 + 3.87 = 6.01
Max loss = S₀ − X + p₀ → stock fall down to strike (S₀ − X) + premium spent on insurance.
Breakeven = S₀ + p₀ → stock must rise to cover the put's cost.
Max profit = unlimited → you still own the stock; the put just expires.
Collar — long stock + long put (X_p) + short call (X_c), net = p₀ − c₀
LegContribution at expiry
Stock legS_T − S₀
Long put leg (X_p)max(X_p − S_T, 0) − p₀
Short call leg (X_c)+c₀ − max(S_T − X_c, 0)
The collar is just covered call + protective put on the same stock. • Below X_p: put protects → floored. • Above X_c: call caps → ceilinged. • Net premium = p₀ − c₀ (a cost if put dearer than call). CEILING (S_T = X_c): (X_c − S₀) − net FLOOR (S_T = X_p): (S₀ − X_p) + net (as a loss) BREAKEVEN: S₀ + net
Sign of "net": net = p₀ − c₀. If the put costs more than the call you collect (net > 0) it's a debit — it lowers max profit and raises max loss. A zero-cost collar picks strikes so c₀ ≈ p₀ → net ≈ 0, and the formulas collapse to (X_c − S₀) and (S₀ − X_p).
The reconstruction habit (use this when you blank)
1. Write the stock leg: S_T − S₀. Never skip it. 2. Write each option leg: payoff ± its premium (− if you bought, + if you sold). 3. For max profit, push S_T to the helpful extreme and add the legs. For max loss, push it the other way. 4. For breakeven, set total profit = 0 and solve for S_T.
Do this once on scratch paper and you'll never confuse "c₀" with "(X − S₀) + c₀" again — the stock leg is right there in front of you.

Universal identities worth memorising
▪ Profit line = value line shifted by net premium (down if paid, up if received); same shape as value. ▪ Put–call parity: c₀ − p₀ = S₀ − PV(X)  ⇔  S₀ + p₀ = c₀ + PV(X). ▪ Synthetic long forward = long call + short put (same X, same expiry); value = S_T − X. ▪ Long & short of the same option share a breakeven; max profit/loss swap (zero-sum).

Module 16.1 · Options Basics — Value & Profit at Expiration
Terminology, moneyness, intrinsic vs time value
Call / PutCall = right to buy; put = right to sell. Buyer (long) pays the premium and holds the right; seller (short) receives it as payment for the contingent liability. European / AmericanEuropean: exercisable only at expiration. American: any trading day up to and including expiration. Labels only — nothing to do with where they trade. MoneynessCall ITM if S > X; put ITM if S < X. ATM: S = X. Call OTM if S < X; put OTM if S > X. Not-ITM ⇒ zero intrinsic value. Premium splitPremium = intrinsic value + time value. Intrinsic = value of immediate exercise (degree ITM). Time value = what might happen over remaining life; greatest near ATM; zero at expiration. Value driversStrike; underlying level; time to expiry; volatility (expected, annualized); risk-free rate; yield on underlying; style. Holding all else constant: higher vol ⇒ higher premiums (calls & puts); less time ⇒ lower premiums (both). Implied volBacked out of the market price via a pricing model — the consensus forward-looking vol estimate. Not the same as historical (realized) vol = √ of actual realized variance to date.
⚠ ITM ≠ profitable. Intrinsic value ignores the premium originally paid — an option can expire ITM and still lose money for the long (intrinsic < initial premium). ITM only means exercise beats non-exercise.
The four basic positions (XYZ numbers, node-verified)
Profit line = value line shifted down by premium paid (long) or up by premium received (short). Same shape, always.
Long call (MAY 50, c₀=6.26)Value = max(ST−X, 0). Max loss = c₀ = 6.26 (ST≤50). Max profit unlimited. BE = X+c₀ = 56.26. At $60: 10−6.26 = +3.74; at $40: −6.26. Short call (MAY 50)Mirror image. Max profit = c₀ = 6.26; unlimited max loss; BE = 56.26 (same as long). Sold with no hedge = naked (uncovered) call. Long put (JUN 50, p₀=4.88)Value = max(X−ST, 0). Max loss = p₀ = 4.88 (ST≥50). Max profit = X−p₀ = 45.12 (stock → 0), identical number to BE = 45.12. Short put (JUN 50)Max profit = p₀ = 4.88; max loss = 45.12 = BE. Writing a put + depositing X in a designated account = cash-secured put; without = naked put.
Long & short of the same option share ONE breakeven; their max profit / max loss just SWAP (zero-sum game, ignoring transaction costs).
Payoff shapes at expiration (profit lines)
Module 16.2 · Synthetic Positions Using Options
LOS 16.aReplicating an asset’s returns with options
Synthetic long forwardLong call + short put, same X, same expiry. Value at expiration = ST − X whatever happens (above X the call is ITM, below X the short put is exercised against you — either way you buy at X). MAY 50 numbersPay c₀ = 6.26, receive p₀ = 3.87 → net outlay 2.39. Profit line sits 2.39 below value line; BE = 50 + 2.39 = $52.39 (call is $2.39 ITM there, just covering the net premium). Put–call paritySame payoff as buy stock + borrow PV(X), so same cost: c₀ − p₀ = S₀ − PV(X) ⇔ S₀ + p₀ = c₀ + PV(X). Check: PV(50) = 50/1.0361/365 = 49.75; 52.14 − 49.75 = 2.39 = 6.26 − 3.87 ✓. Assumes no yield on the underlying. Put–call FORWARD paritySubstitute PV(F₀(T)) for S₀: PV(F₀(T)) + p₀ = c₀ + PV(X). Since fair F₀(T) = FV(S₀) for a no-yield underlying, this is just standard parity restated. Special caseIf PV(X) = S₀ exactly ⇒ c₀ = p₀ (identical premiums); that X is the fair forward price. Ennis example: dealer short a 4-month forward at 179.59 hedges by buying the 179.59 call + selling the 179.59 put (net premium zero since both trade at 16.34) — buys 1,000 shares at 179.59 at expiry whichever leg is exercised.
⚠ Synthetic SHORT exposure = short call + long put (same X/expiry), possibly + lend PV(X) for the full synthetic short stock. Quiz trap: watch borrow vs lend in the answer choices — replicating short stock means you receive today, i.e. positions equivalent to lending arithmetic, and the long-put/short-call combination is the defining pair.
Module 16.3 · Covered Calls
LOS 16.bCovered call = long stock + short call
Construction / viewOwn the stock, sell a call against it (short-call risk is hedged by the shares). View: neutral-to-mildly-bullish, willing to cap upside for premium income. At-expiry formulasMax profit = X − S₀ + c₀ · Max loss = S₀ − c₀ (stock to zero) · BE = S₀ − c₀ (same number as max loss). APR 55 exampleSell APR 55 call @ 2.52 vs stock @ 52.14. Max profit = 2.86 + 2.52 = 5.38; BE = 52.14 − 2.52 = 49.62 = max loss. Only worse off than plain stock if ST > 55 + 2.52 = 57.52. Shape = short put. Motivation 1 — yieldYield enhancement: calls are OTM (possibly substantially). Cash in the upside you don’t believe in. Motivation 2 — reduce positionReducing a holding at a favorable price: calls are ITM. Jenkins sells 15 APR 50 calls (1,500 sh) @ 4.80 → premium $7,200; if ST ≥ 50 delivers at 50 → 75,000 + 7,200 = $82,200 > $78,210 outright — captures time value 4.80 − 2.14 = $2.66/sh (×1,500 = $3,990). Risk: ST < 50 → calls lapse, shares unsold. Motivation 3 — target priceTarget price realization: calls marginally OTM, strike just above spot. Perkins writes APR 52.5 @ 3.53; if exercised realizes 52.50 + 3.53 = $56.03. Dangers: stock soars (regret) or falls (sale missed).
Strike vs spot tells you the motivation: OTM (well above) -> yield enhancement ITM (below spot) -> reduce position at favorable price marginally OTM -> target price realization
Module 16.4 · Protective Puts
LOS 16.cProtective put = long stock + long put
Construction / viewOwn the stock, buy a put as insurance: hedged below the strike, full upside retained. Classic options hedge of a long position. At-expiry formulasMax loss = S₀ − X + p₀ · BE = S₀ + p₀ · Max profit = unlimited. MAY 50 examplePut @ 3.87 vs stock @ 52.14. Net max loss = 2.14 + 3.87 = 6.01; BE = 52.14 + 3.87 = 56.01 (must recoup the premium). Shape = long call.
⚠ CC vs PP breakevens move in opposite directions: covered call BE is below S₀ (S₀−c₀, premium cushions), protective put BE is above S₀ (S₀+p₀, premium must be earned back). Mixing these up is a free mark lost.
Module 16.5 · Options as a Hedge of a Short Position
LOS 16.eBuying a call vs selling a put on a short underlying
Short position exposureShort stock gains if price falls, loses (without limit) if price rises. Buy a call(Probably above spot.) Hedges the stock rising — positive call value caps the loss above the strike. Analog of the protective put on a long position. Sell a put(Probably below spot.) Sells off part of the benefit of the stock falling, in exchange for premium. Analog of the covered call on a long position.
Module 16.6 · Collars
LOS 16.fCollar = protective put + covered call
ConstructionLong stock + buy put (most likely OTM, hedges downside) + sell call (most likely OTM, sells upside & subsidizes the put). A.k.a. fence or hedge wrapper. Zero-cost collarSet the put strike first, then pick the call strike so call premium = put premium → no net inflow/outflow at initiation (easy OTC, approximate with exchange-traded). XYZ exampleBuy JUN 50 put (4.88) + sell JUN 55.87 call (4.88), zero net premium. Max profit = 55.87 − 52.14 = 3.73 (rise to call strike); max loss = 52.14 − 50 = 2.14 (fall to put strike); BE = S₀ = 52.14 exactly (zero-cost ⇒ profit line = stock-plus-options value line, unshifted). General formulasMax profit = Xcall − S₀ − net premium · Max loss = S₀ − Xput + net premium · BE = S₀ + net premium (net premium = 0 for zero-cost).
Pre-expiry, the collar dampens position variability to roughly 15–20% of the unhedged level (delta well below 1 between the strikes) — that is the practical point of collaring.
Module 16.7 · Straddles
LOS 16.fStraddle = call + put, same strike & expiry
Long straddleBuy equal numbers of calls and puts, same strike (typically near ATM), same expiry. Classic long-volatility play — no position in the underlying. Value line is a V centered on the strike (both legs worthless there). JUN 52.5 numbersc = 6.22 + p = 6.19 → outlay = max loss = 12.41 (at the strike). BEs: 52.50 ± 12.41 = $64.91 and $40.09. Upside unlimited via the call; downside max profit = strike − cost via the put. Short straddleSell both: neutrality play. Max profit = total premium at the strike; unlimited potential loss; same two breakevens. Strangle (footnote)Like a straddle but call and put strikes differ (met again in the currency reading). BEs: put strike − total cost / call strike + total cost.
⚠ “Expensive vol” check (16.12 KH scenario): if a news story bids up implied vol before you trade, re-derive the move needed to reach the new breakevens. KH expected ±10% but the pricier straddle needed >±12% → don’t enter. Vega estimates the repricing: Δstraddle ≈ vega × Δvol-points = 0.468 × 15 = $7.02.
Module 16.8 · Spreads
LOS 16.fBull & bear spreads (calls or puts)
DefinitionsBull = long the lower strike, short the higher (“Buy Low”). Bear = short the lower, long the higher. Equal numbers each leg; bear spread = short bull spread. Debit spreads (net outlay): bull call, bear put. Credit spreads (net inflow): bear call, bull put. Bull call 50/55Buy JUN 50 call 7.40, sell JUN 55 call 5.20 → debit 2.20 = max loss. BE = 50 + 2.20 = 52.20. Max profit = 5 − 2.20 = 2.80 (value maxes at strike difference above 55). Bullish but capped. Bear put 55/50Buy MAY 55 put 6.61, sell MAY 50 put 3.87 → debit 2.74 = max loss. BE = 55 − 2.74 = 52.26. Max profit = 5 − 2.74 = 2.26. Bearish but capped. Bear call 50/55Short JUN 50 call 7.40 + long JUN 55 call 5.20 → credit 2.20 = max profit (at 50 and below). At 55+ net intrinsic = −5 → max loss = 2.80. BE = 52.20. Bull put 55/50Short MAY 55 put 6.61 + long MAY 50 put 3.87 → credit 2.74 = max profit; max loss = 5 − 2.74 = 2.26; BE = 55 − 2.74 = 52.26. Adding a leg laterThe two legs need not be simultaneous: long an Oct 30 call bought at S=28, stock now 38.5 → sell an Oct 40 call to cash in upside no longer believed in (covered-call motivation, done with options).
GENERALIZED AT-EXPIRY FORMULAS (net premium = |difference of premiums|) Debit spreads (bull call, bear put): max loss = net premium paid max profit = strike difference - net premium paid Credit spreads (bear call, bull put): max profit = net premium received max loss = strike difference - net premium received Breakeven, CALL spreads: lower strike + net premium Breakeven, PUT spreads: higher strike - net premium
⚠ Two traps. (1) Professor’s note: unless a question says otherwise, assume bull spread = calls, bear spread = puts (prefer debit spreads). (2) American-style credit spreads: the short leg can go ITM while the long leg is still OTM → early exercise by the counterparty can disrupt the strategy.
Module 16.9 · Delta and Gamma
LOS 16.dThe Greeks; position deltas; pre-expiry behavior
Delta (Δ)Change in option price per +1 in stock. + for long calls, − for long puts. |Δ| → 1 the more ITM; |Δ| → 0 the more OTM (all else constant). = slope of the value line at the current price. Gamma (Γ)Change in delta per +1 in stock. Positive for long calls AND long puts. Highest near ATM, and greatest for ATM options close to expiration (premium line crammed around the strike). Theta (θ) / Vega (ν)θ = daily price change from time passing — negative for long calls & puts. ν = price change per +1% vol — positive for long calls & puts. Greeks are given if needed, never calculated. Delta in actionMAY 55 call: Δ = 0.47 → stock 52.14→53.14 predicts 4.02 + 0.47 = 4.49; model says 4.51. Gap = curvature (gamma = 0.031): new delta 0.470 + 0.031 = 0.501; using the average delta 0.486 → 4.02 + 0.486 = 4.506, much closer. Time value = vertical gap between value and intrinsic lines; greatest near ATM. Underlying & forwardsΔ of one unit of underlying: +1 long / −1 short. Futures & forwards on no-yield underlyings are proxies → also ±1. A traded stock option contract = right over 100 shares (long call, Δ=0.65 ⇒ position delta +65). Position deltaSum the individual deltas, watching signs. 1,000 sh + 10 put contracts (Δ = −0.6): (1,000×+1) + (10×100×−0.6) = +400 → stock −$1 costs $400, not $1,000. Forward hedge, same size: N×(+1 + −1) = 0, fully hedged. Pre-expiry shapesProtective put delta: →+1 for big rises (put deep OTM), →0 for big falls (put deep ITM, downside protected) — net exposure ≈ long call. Covered call: ≈+1 deep-OTM call, →0 deep-ITM call (upside all hedged away). Collar / bull spread pre-expiry: delta muted between strikes — the two look alike.

⚠ MQ 16.9 pattern: just-established covered call and protective put both have deltas between 0 and +1 (e.g. CC 0.4 / PP 0.45-ish) — never 0, and the protective put’s delta is positive (stock +1 dominates put’s −Δ). An answer giving the PP a negative delta is wrong.
Module 16.10 · Theta and Vega; Calendar Spreads
LOS 16.gTime decay, vega, and calendar spreads
Theta patternAll thetas negative (less time = less time value). XYZ 52.5 calls: APR −0.061 / MAY −0.043 / JUN −0.036 — near-dated ATM options decay fastest, and ATM theta gets more negative as expiry approaches. Deep ITM/OTM: decay slows near maturity. Vega patternVegas always positive (more vol = more time value). Higher with more time to expiry (JUN > MAY > APR: e.g. 52.5 strike 0.102 / 0.084 / 0.060); diminishes the further ITM/OTM. Long calendar spreadBuy longer-dated, sell shorter-dated, same strike (≈ATM) & underlying. Exploits |θnear| > |θfar|: the short leg decays faster than the long leg loses. Needs little movement over the near option’s life. Calls if long-term bullish, puts if long-term bearish. Benefits from a stable market or rising implied vol. Jenkins exampleBuy 4 JUN 52.5 calls @ 6.22, sell 4 APR 52.5 @ 3.53 → net 2.69 × 4 × 100 = $1,076. S unchanged at April expiry: April lapses, June call worth $5.00 → position $5 × 400 = $2,000 vs $1,076 paid. Higher IV would add more. Short calendar spreadSell longer-dated, buy shorter-dated. Used when options are sufficiently ITM or OTM (there the longer-dated theta is relatively higher). Benefits from a big move in the underlying or a fall in implied vol. Both variants: sell whatever is expected to lose time value relatively faster. Vol √-time conversionScale vol by √(period ratio): annual 57% → 2-month (42 of 252 trading days): 57% × √(42/252) = 23.27%. Monthly (21d) → annual: multiply by √(252/21).
⚠ MQ 16.10 pattern: long-term bearish + short-term flat ⇒ long calendar spread with puts: sell near-dated ATM puts, buy longer-dated ATM puts — after the short leg expires you are left holding the bearish exposure you wanted.
Module 16.11 · Volatility Skew and Smile
LOS 16.hImplied-vol patterns; straddle pre-expiry; risk reversals
Straddle pre-expiryValue curve is a smooth U (not the V of expiry). Near the strike delta ≈ 0 (delta neutral), tending to +1 far above / −1 far below. Long straddle = positive vega, negative theta — vol must rise fast enough to beat decay. That is the real sense of “going long volatility.” Short straddle: delta-neutral, negative vega = bet on falling vol. SmileFurther-from-ATM options have higher implied vols → U-shape of IV vs strike. Less common than skew. SkewIV increases for more-OTM puts, decreases for more-OTM calls. OTM puts are bid up as insurance against market declines; OTM call demand is low. Sentiment readsSkew jumps + surge in absolute IV ⇒ sentiment turning bearish. Higher-than-historical IVs on OTM calls ⇒ investors bullish (demand for upside exposure). Risk reversalLong RR = long call + short put (short RR = reverse), same underlying/expiry. Trade skew deviations expected to correct: put IV looks too rich vs calls → buy the “cheap” OTM call, sell the “rich” OTM put. Side effect: net long exposure to the underlying. Delta hedgePQR RR: delta 0.3, 10+10 contracts on 1,000 sh → $1 fall costs 1 × 0.3 × 1,000 = $300 ⇒ hedge = sell 300 shares (1,000 × 0.3). Delta drifts with price & time → delta hedges are dynamic, needing periodic rebalancing. Term structure / surfaceTerm structure of vol: IV differs across maturities; contango (longer-dated higher) is common. IV surface: 3-D graph — maturity (x), strike (y), implied vol (z).
⚠ MQ 16.11 wording trap: skew = IV up for OTM puts, down for OTM calls. Answers that flip puts/calls are the standard distractor. And a long straddle is a play on realized movement/vol, not on the “smile.”
Module 16.12 · Applications
LOS 16.i / 16.jChoosing the strategy; targeted equity exposures
Covered call (cash)Client needs cash, advisor bearish 6 months, stock @ 169. Sell 170 calls (50 contracts vs 5,000 sh): premium meets the cash target & cuts delta. ITM calls raise the most cash but risk the shares being called away; deep-OTM raise too little. Risks: ST > 170 caps gains; stock may fall (cushioned by premium). Put writingOQ wants the shares but only at 165 (spot 169): write 165-strike OTM puts — paid to wait. If ST < 165 the put is exercised and OQ buys at 165. Risk: shares fall below X − p₀ → outright purchase later would have been cheaper by more than the premium. If ST − 169 > p₀, buying at 169 would have beaten the premium. Long straddle checkKH expects ±10%; news bids IV up before the trade. New BEs need > ±12% → straddle no longer worthwhile; don’t enter. Vega pre-check: 15 IV pts × 0.468 = $7.02 straddle repricing ≈ actual. Zero-cost collarLow-cost-basis stock → selling ruled out (tax); need downside protection. Zero-cost collar: short calls sell the right tail and fund puts that remove the left tail. Calendar spread (index)ID: flat EURO STOXX 50 near-term (3,500), bearish long-term. Sell 3-month 3,500 put (€119), buy 6-month 3,500 put (€173), net €54. Short put lapses ATM; long put keeps time value > €54 → net profit; then keep the long put as the bearish bet. Puts, not calls, because the residual exposure wanted is bearish. Worst case: entire net premium lost; big move either way hurts; IV up helps / IV down hurts. Vol hedge (VIX)JW fears a correction + vol spike: buy ATM VIX-futures call; fund it by selling an OTM VIX put (collar-like, but vs an effective short-vol book, since equity portfolios are short vol). Sizing: regress portfolio P&L on vol changes. Alternative: buy VIX futures (less flexible). Long call as proxyAS expects £60→£70 in 3m, IV unchanged: choose the call maximizing [70 − (X + c₀)] / c₀ (profit-to-premium). Auto-exclude any call with BE (X + c₀) above £70. If closing early, the winner has lower |delta| but higher gamma, which more than compensates. Risk: share ends elsewhere than £70. Protective put pickEM expects ≤10% drop (€42 → €37.80) in a week: maximize [(X − p₀) − 37.8] / p₀; exclude puts with BE (X − p₀) below €37.80. Hedge closed by selling the put after the danger passes → what matters is how the premium changes; again lower |Δ| + higher Γ wins.
Figure 16.1 · Strategy selection: direction × implied volatility
Logic: direction picks the leg you are long/short (calls bullish, puts bearish); the vol view decides whether you buy options (IV up → long vega) or write them (IV down → short vega / harvest premium). Neutral + unchanged IV lands on the theta play: calendar spread.
Module Quizzes · Answer Keys (reasoning-derived — not visible in source photos; all numbers node-verified)
MQ 16.1–16.3
Q1 — synthetic shortA. Synthetic short exposure to PQR needs long 100 put + short 100 call; A is the only choice with that pair (B buys both; C’s long call/short put + short forward nets to flat). PV(100) at 2% for 6m ≈ 99 explains the “99” leg. Q2 — covered call (43 stock, short 45 call @ 2.10)a) Max profit = (45−43)+2.10 = 4.10; max loss = 43−2.10 = 40.90 = BE at $40.90. b) Profit at ST: $0 → −40.90; $35 → −5.90; $40 → −0.90; $45 → +4.10; $50 → +4.10 (capped).
MQ 16.4–16.5
Q1 — protective put (37.50 stock, long 35 put @ 1.40)a) Max loss = (37.50−35)+1.40 = 3.90; BE = 37.50+1.40 = 38.90; max profit unlimited. b) $30 → −3.90 (floor); $35 → −3.90; $40 → +1.10; $50 → +11.10. Q2 — Jones short @ 220C. October 200 puts. Short stock + flat near-term + bearish long-term → harvest yield by selling OTM puts below spot (covered-call analog for a short). 240 calls would be bought as a hedge, not sold; 240 puts are ITM.
MQ 16.6–16.7
Q1 — collar (29 stock, 27.50 put @ 0.20, short 30 call @ 0.20)Zero net premium. a) Max profit = 30−29 = 1.00; max loss = 29−27.50 = 1.50; BE = 29.00. b) $15 & $20 → −1.50 (floored at 27.50); $23.50... note prices below 27.50 all floor at −1.50; $28.50 → −0.50; $25 → −1.50; $30 → +1.00; $100 → +1.00 (capped). Q2 — straddle (45 strike, c 3 + p 2)a) Max loss = 5 (at 45); BEs 40 and 50; max profit: unlimited up, 40 down. b) $0 → +40; $35 → +5; $40 → 0; $45 → −5; $47 → −3; $55 → +5; $100 → +50. Q3 — EUR vol tradeExpecting vol > priced → buy the OTM pair = long strangle: buy 0.98 put @ 0.005 + buy 1.04 call @ 0.004, cost 0.009. BEs: 0.98 − 0.009 = 0.971 and 1.04 + 0.009 = 1.049.
MQ 16.8
Q1 — bull call (long 45 @ 2.10, short 50 @ 0.50)Net debit 1.60. a) Max loss = 1.60; BE = 46.60; max profit = 5−1.60 = 3.40. b) $35 → −1.60; $45 → −1.60; $48 → +1.40; $50 → +3.40; $55 → +3.40. Q2 — bear put (long 25 @ 4.00, short 20 @ 1.80)Net debit 2.20. a) Max loss = 2.20; BE = 25−2.20 = 22.80; max profit = 5−2.20 = 2.80. b) $15 → +2.80; $20 → +2.80; $23.50 → −0.70; $25 → −2.20; $30 → −2.20. Q3 — bear spread (stock 51; calls 47 @ 5.25, 53 @ 0.75)Bear call spread: short 47 call, long 53 call → initial inflow 4.50 (“initial investment” = net credit of 4.50; no outlay). BE = 47 + 4.50 = 51.50. Max loss = 6 − 4.50 = 1.50; max profit = 4.50.
MQ 16.9 – 16.12
16.9 Q1 — deltasB. Just-established, 3 months out: both CC and PP have deltas strictly between 0 and 1 (CC 0.4 / PP 0.45 plausible). A (zero) is the fully hedged forward case; C’s negative PP delta is impossible for stock+put. 16.10/16.11 Q1 — calendarB. Long-term bearish + short-term flat ⇒ long calendar spread in puts: sell 2-month ATM puts, buy 5-month ATM puts. A is a short calendar in calls; C is a risk-reversal-style directional trade. 16.10/16.11 Q2 — skewC. Skew: IV up for more-OTM puts, down for more-OTM calls. B flips it; A misdescribes the straddle (payoff from movement, not the smile). 16.12 Q1 — Austin, up 3%B. Protective put. Objective: keep a positive stock position AND retain upside → only the protective put keeps unlimited upside while flooring the downside. Bull call/bull put cap the upside. 16.12 Q2 — Austin, up 16%, needs 15%Long straddle (A). Scenario is large gains OR large losses (big move either way) → long vol. Short straddle is the opposite bet; calendar wants a flat market. 16.12 Q3 — oscillating, drifting downA. Sell call options. Range-bound with mild downside → harvest premium via covered calls; buying puts spends premium on protection the oscillation view doesn’t justify; C double-spends. 16.12 Q4 — hedging naked callsB. Buy the underlying asset. Short calls lose when the price rises → long stock offsets (turns them into covered calls). A long put adds to the downside bet; shorting the stock doubles the upside risk.
Every quiz answer above is reasoning-derived (the answer pages were not photographed). Numeric parts are node-verified; MCQ letters follow directly from the module logic recapped above — re-derive rather than memorize.
LOS 6.a — Four roles of equities in the overall portfolio
Equity securities play several beneficial roles. Each role is a separate driver — keep them distinct under exam pressure.
RoleDriver / mechanismDetail to remember
Capital appreciationGrowth in cash flows, revenues, and/or earningsThe main driver of long-term equity returns. Over the last 50 years, equities > bonds & bills on average. Equities outperform in strong growth, underperform in weak growth.
Dividend incomeExcess cash flows distributed instead of reinvestedRecent annual yields ~1%–3%. Dividend yield is more stable than price-change return. Not guaranteed to increase or continue.
DiversificationLess-than-perfect (< +1.0) correlation with other asset classesPortfolio σ < weighted sum of individual σ. Benefit shrinks in a crisis (see trap below).
Inflation hedgeFirms that pass input-cost increases to customers; commodity producersRecord is mixed: positive equity/inflation correlation usually, but negative in hyperinflation; equity = leading indicator, inflation = lagging → less-than-perfect correlation.
Diversification breaks down in a crisis — the two reasons
Quiz 6.1 Q1 lives here. Risk reduction from diversification is not constant. In a financial crisis:
1. Correlations rise toward +1.0 → the cross-asset offset that lowers portfolio σ shrinks → less diversification exactly when needed.
2. Asset-class σ rise → even at fixed correlation, higher component volatility feeds through to higher portfolio σ → further reduces the expected risk reduction.
Client investment considerations (IPS)
High risk tolerance → prefer growth-oriented companies Low risk tolerance → prefer stable, well-established dividend payers Constraints may include ESG considerations and religious beliefs
Two screening tools for ESG/values constraints:
ApproachWhat it doesExample
Negative (exclusionary) screeningExcludes companies/sectors that fail client standardsExclude oil & gas investments
Positive (best-in-class) screeningSeeks/overweights companies ranking most favorablyOverweight firms with strong governance
ESG approaches beyond screening: ESG integration (now the dominant strategy — analyze valuation, expected returns, risk, build sustainable portfolio); thematic investing (screen on a theme, e.g. climate change); impact investing (active engagement / direct investment for explicit social-environmental impact alongside return).
Size & Style — the 3×3 style box (Figure 6.1)
Size = market capitalization (large / mid / small-cap). Style = value / blend (a.k.a. core) / growth, determined by metrics: P/E, P/B, dividend yield, earnings &/or book-value growth. Tap a cell:

Tap any cell to see the box. A style box ranks/scores companies; managers can scatterplot holdings across the nine boxes (and add finer classes like micro-cap growth).
Advantages & the disadvantage of size/style
+ Better address client risk/return considerations + Greater diversification across sectors/industries + Construct relevant benchmarks for size/style-specific funds + Analyze how company characteristics change over time (e.g. small-cap growth → matures to mid/large & blend)
The twist: that last advantage is also the disadvantage — categories are not stable over time. Examiners love "which is both an advantage and a drawback?" → style drift.
Geography — by stage of economic development
StageExamples
DevelopedUnited States, United Kingdom, Germany, Australia, Japan
EmergingBrazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa
FrontierIceland, Estonia, Nigeria, Jordan, Vietnam
Advantage: investors with heavy domestic exposure learn to diversify across international markets Disadvantage 1: international equities introduce currency risk Disadvantage 2: overestimation of diversification benefit — foreign large-caps may already be internationally diversified and even earn much of their income in the investor's own country
Economic Activity — sector/industry grouping
Two ways to group companies into sectors/industries:
Four primary classification structures:
StructureApproach
GICS — Global Industry Classification StandardMarket-oriented
ICB — Industry Classification BenchmarkProduction-oriented
TRBC — Thomson Reuters Business ClassificationProduction-oriented
RGS — Russell Global SectorsProduction-oriented
Professor's note (top-level naming): GICS, TRBC, RGS call the top level sectors then subdivide into industries. ICB is the odd one — starts with industries, then subdivides into sectors.
GICS hierarchy (Figure 6.2, Consumer Staples) — tap to drill:
+ Advantage: analyze/compare & build performance benchmarks by sector/industry; diversification enhanced across sectors/industries − Disadvantage: some firms (esp. larger ones) have operations not easily assigned to one sector/industry
Equity indexes & benchmarks
Indexes combine size/style + geography, and can be subdivided by economic activity (sector/industry) or by client considerations (e.g. ESG).
IndexBuilt from
MSCI Europe Large Cap Valuesize/style + geography
MSCI China Small Capsize/style + geography
MSCI World Energyeconomic activity (sector)
S&P Global Natural Resourceseconomic activity (sector)
LOS 6.c — Ways to earn current income from an equity portfolio
SourceMechanismDetail / trap
Dividend incomeMost obvious & often largestMay be taxed (income and/or withholding). Growth-focused investors are LESS likely to seek dividend income.
Optional stock dividendInvestor chooses cash OR new sharesThe "option" has value — can even be sold to another investor.
Special dividendOne-time cash paymentAs opposed to the regular periodic dividend.
Securities lendingLend out shares (often for short-sellers)Lender earns a fee + can reinvest cash collateral. See dedicated card.
Writing optionsSell options to earn premiumsCovered call / cash-covered put. See card.
Dividend captureBuy before ex-date, hold through, then sellProfitable if price falls by less than the dividend. See card.
Securities (stock) lending — the details
Short sale = sale of a security not owned; seller borrows it to deliver to the buyer Lender is paid a fee and may receive cash/collateral on which it earns a return; gets the security back at a future date Fee ~0.2%–0.5% annually in developed markets; much higher for in-demand stocks called specials Common in index funds, large institutional portfolios (pensions), endowments
Issues it introduces: short selling drives the price down (bad for the lender who still owns it) — more of a concern for an active manager expecting outperformance than a passive index manager. Lender must watch borrower quality (return ability). Borrower must compensate the lender for dividends during the loan. Lender generally loses the right to vote the shares during the loan. Reinvesting collateral carries market/credit/operational risk + admin costs.
Option-writing & dividend capture
StrategyWhat you doRisk / payoff
Covered callWrite a call on a stock you ownEarn premium; lose the upside above the strike.
Cash-covered put (cash-secured put)Sell a put + set aside cash to buy the stock if exercisedEarn premium; buyer exercises only if the stock declines — you get assigned at a loss-ish level.
Dividend captureBuy just before ex-date, hold through ex-date, then sellProfit if price drops by less than the dividend. Theory: price should drop by the full dividend, but supply/demand & taxes make it differ.
LOS 6.c — Fees & costs of an equity portfolio
CostWhat it covers
Management fees (ad valorem)Compensate manager + research/analysis, hardware/software, compliance, trade processing. % of AUM, charged at intervals (e.g. annually). Higher for active (more analysis + turnover). Negotiable.
Performance / incentive feesWhen the portfolio beats a stated objective; common for hedge/alternative funds. Often 10%–20% of appreciation above the threshold.
Administration feesRisk/return measurement, voting; if external: custody, depository, registration fees.
Marketing & distribution feesSales/client-service teams, advertising, conferences, brochures, platform fees, intermediary commissions.
Trading costsExplicit + implicit (see below).
Investment strategy costsImplicit cost of the chosen strategy (incl. predatory trading on index funds).
Incentive fees — two protections to remember
One-sided: manager shares in outperformance but is NOT penalized for underperformance High-water mark: stops paying twice for the same performance — after a peak then a decline, incentive fee only on future appreciation above the previous compensated level
Trading costs — explicit vs implicit
ExplicitImplicit
Broker commissions, stock-exchange fees, taxesBid-ask spread, price impact, delay/slippage costs from not completing a trade (illiquidity)
Liquidity demand by strategy: Momentum demands liquidity (buy rising / sell falling) → high market-impact cost. Contrarian supplies liquidity (buy falling / sell rising) → low market-impact cost. Passive index replication falls in the middle.
Predatory trading: even passive index funds face hidden costs — predatory traders buy (sell) shares about to be added (removed) from an index, creating price-impact cost for the fund and profit for the predator.
LOS 6.d — Shareholder engagement
Engagement = investors/managers interacting with companies to favorably impact the stock price and improve corporate governance (via calls and voting at general assemblies). Topics discussed:
Corporate strategy — objectives, constraints, growth, resources, culture, sustainability, stakeholder balance Capital allocation — new-project selection, M&A, capex, leverage, dividends, equity financing Corporate governance — audit/risk committees, regulatory & political risk management Compensation structures — top-management remuneration & alignment Board composition — experience, competence, diversity, succession planning
Benefits — incl. the free-rider point (Quiz 6.2 Q2)
Active managers engage more (want to influence & improve performance); passive focus on minimizing the cost Larger investors absorb the cost more easily (spread over more assets)
Free riders: successful engagement raises the stock price — that benefit reaches ALL shareholders, including those who never engaged. This is exactly how engagement benefits investors not actively involved.
Can address nonfinancial concerns (ESG), though benefits are harder to quantify Affects other stakeholders (employees, customers, creditors, regulators); can be influenced by academic research / media
Costs & limitations (Quiz 6.2 Q3 menu)
Not free — requires time & resources Short-termism — may push near-term cash flow / price at the expense of long-term goals Insider-trading risk — may acquire material nonpublic information Conflicts of interest — e.g. an engaged PM backs management because management invests in the PM's fund
Manager's role: may assign specific employees, consult outside experts on voting/governance; some countries set legal requirements + written documentation. Activist investing goes further: propose shareholder resolutions, media campaigns, seek board seats, launch proxy fights (persuade other shareholders to back their proposals).
LOS 6.e — Active vs passive rationale
Passive = replicate an index/benchmark. Active = outperform the benchmark & add value (riskier — can also underperform). The line blurs (e.g. closely tracking with limited deviations).
Rationales for shifting to ACTIVE:
Confidence the manager has expert knowledge/skill to add value Mandates (e.g. ESG) requiring screening & active techniques Client preferences & enough assets to cover active costs — growth styles often suit active; value may be more passive
Active management caveats: manage investor expectations (unreasonable → dissatisfied); strategies that get too popular attract capital → harder to add value; need an appropriate broad, liquid benchmark — narrow/limited benchmarks give little room to deviate → support passive.
Two extra risks of active management (Quiz 6.2 Q5)
Key person risk — individuals essential to the fund's success may leave the firm Higher portfolio turnover → higher tax burden; tax-limiting techniques are themselves costly, risky, and need tax expertise (varies by country)
Beyond these two: active results are less certain and costs are higher (the given facts) — Q5 asks for the additional risks, so name key-person and turnover/tax, not cost again.
Passive-vs-active decision (Quiz 6.2 Q4 logic)
Client concernPoints toward
Low feesPassive (active is costlier)
Narrow, limited large-cap benchmarkPassive (little room to deviate)
Wants substantial value-add vs benchmarkActive (only active seeks to outperform)
Numerous ESG restrictionsActive (mandates need screening / active techniques)
LOS 6.f — Three required characteristics of a benchmark index
Must be...Meaning
Rules-basedInclusion/exclusion rules, weighting scheme, and rebalancing frequency are consistent, objective, predictable — so investors can replicate performance.
TransparentThe underlying rules are public, clearly stated, understandable to investors.
InvestableInvestors can actually replicate the return & risk of the index.
Quiz 6.3 Q1 trap: the answer is Investable. "Selective" and "Flexible" are NOT requirements — "selective" is lifted from the index-construction discussion (exhaustive vs selective inclusion), a different concept entirely. Memorize the trio: rules-based, transparent, investable.
Two considerations when choosing a benchmark
1. Determine desired market & risk exposures 2. Identify the methods used to construct & maintain the index
Market exposure choices:
Broad market vs focused exposure to certain sectors Domestic vs international exposure Among developed / emerging / frontier markets
Risk-factor exposure = expected sensitivity of portfolio returns to risk factors: market risk (beta), firm size, style (growth vs value), prior returns (momentum), plus liquidity, volatility, and firm "quality."
Index construction — inclusion method
MethodDefinitionExample
ExhaustiveEvery stock in a defined universeCRSP U.S. Total Market Index
SelectiveA subset of stocks within a universeS&P 500, Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA)
Four index-weighting methods
MethodHow weightedNotes
Market-capEach stock by its total cap as % of all stocks' capCAPM market portfolio; S&P 500. In practice uses free-float shares (excludes closely-held). Rebalance when firms issue/repurchase significant shares.
Price-weightedEach stock by its priceHigher-priced stocks get larger weight; DJIA. Adjusted for stock splits (complicates calculation).
Equal-weightedEqual $ in each stockReduces concentration risk & sector exposure; factor-indifferent (randomizes mispricing); small-cap bias → returns more volatile; needs frequent rebalancing.
FundamentalBy share of a fundamental factor (sales, income, dividends)e.g. a firm paying 3% of all dividends gets 3% weight in a dividend-weighted index.
Equal-weight edge: can produce marginally better returns before transaction costs when prices oscillate around intrinsic values (rebalancing sells winners / buys losers).
Rebalancing triggers differ by scheme: equal-weight drifts as soon as prices move; price-weight changes on splits & stock dividends; market-cap changes on significant share issuance/repurchase.
Stock concentration — HHI & effective number of stocks
HHI = Σ wᵢ² (sum of squared portfolio weights) effective number of stocks = 1 / HHI HHI range: 1/n (equally weighted) → 1 (single stock) As HHI ↑, concentration risk ↑.
Enter weights (comma-separated, as decimals or %) to get HHI + effective N:
Weights
Benchmarks: equal-weighted 500 stocks → HHI = 1/500 = 0.002 → effective N = 500. A market-cap index of 500 stocks might have HHI = 0.01 → effective N = 100 — the 100 < 500 shows the disproportionate effect of the largest-cap names.
Rebalancing vs Reconstitution
RebalancingReconstitution
WhatAdjust portfolio weights as index weightings changeRemove & replace stocks that no longer fit the index's market exposure
TriggerPrice moves (equal-wt), splits/dividends (price-wt), share issuance/repurchase (cap-wt)e.g. a small-cap whose cap grows into mid-cap is dropped from a small-cap index
EffectIncurs trading (and possibly tax) costs → decreases returns; done periodically (often quarterly)Incurs trading costs → also reduces returns
Buffering vs Packeting — cutting migration costs
PracticeMechanism
BufferingSet a threshold (buffer zone) for the change in cap rank before a stock migrates between indexes. Example: large-cap = top 200, mid-cap = next 300. A mid-cap firm rising into the top 200 is NOT moved until its rank passes the buffer — e.g. reaches rank 150 or higher at the next reconstitution.
PacketingMove the position in halves. When a mid-cap rises to qualify as large-cap, half the position moves to the large-cap index at reconstitution. If it still qualifies at the next reconstitution, the remainder moves over.
Memory hook: Buffering = delay the move (wait for a rank threshold). Packeting = split the move (half now, half later). Both cut the trading costs of reconstitution.
1 — Four roles
Capital appreciation - MAIN long-term return driver (>bonds/bills 50y) Dividend income - 1-3% yield; MORE STABLE than price return Diversification - corr < +1.0; breaks down in crisis Inflation hedge - MIXED record; negative in hyperinflation
2 — Diversification fails in crisis (2 reasons)
1. Correlations RISE toward +1.0 -> offset shrinks 2. Asset-class sigma RISE -> portfolio sigma up Both reduce the expected risk reduction.
3 — Three segmentation approaches
SIZE & STYLE 3x3 box; metrics P/E, P/B, div yield, growth twist: categories NOT stable (adv = disadv) GEOGRAPHY developed / emerging / frontier disadv: currency risk + overstated diversification ECONOMIC ACTIVITY sector/industry; GICS/ICB/TRBC/RGS
4 — Classification structures
GICS = market-oriented (sector -> industry) ICB = production-orient (INDUSTRY -> sector) <- odd one TRBC = production-orient (sector -> industry) RGS = production-orient (sector -> industry) GICS hierarchy: Sector > Industry group > Industry > Subindustry
5 — ESG screens & approaches
Negative/exclusionary - exclude failing firms (e.g. oil&gas) Positive/best-in-class - overweight top rankers (e.g. governance) ESG integration (dominant) | thematic | impact investing Client: high risk tol -> growth; low -> stable dividend payers
6 — Income sources (6.c)
Dividends (growth investors seek LESS) | optional stock div | special div Securities lending - fee 0.2-0.5%; "specials" higher; lose VOTE; borrower pays divs Write options - covered call (lose upside) | cash-covered put Dividend capture - buy pre-ex, sell after; profit if drop < dividend
7 — Costs & fees (6.c)
Mgmt fee (ad valorem, %AUM) - HIGHER for active (analysis+turnover) Performance/incentive 10-20% - ONE-SIDED; high-water mark stops double pay Trading: explicit (commission/exch/tax) | implicit (spread/impact/slippage) Momentum DEMANDS liq (high impact) | Contrarian SUPPLIES (low) | index middle Predatory trading hits index funds on add/remove
8 — Engagement (6.d)
Topics: strategy | capital allocation | governance | comp | board Benefit: FREE RIDERS gain too (price rises for all holders) Active engage more; passive minimize cost; large investors absorb cost Limits: time/cost | short-termism | insider risk | conflicts of interest Activist: resolutions, media, board seats, PROXY FIGHT
9 — Active vs passive (6.e)
Active rationale: skill confidence | ESG mandates | client pref (growth=active) Caveats: manage expectations | too-popular strategy | need broad liquid benchmark (narrow benchmark -> passive) Extra active risks: KEY PERSON | higher turnover -> TAX burden
10 — Benchmark & indexing (6.f)
Benchmark MUST be: rules-based | transparent | INVESTABLE (NOT "selective"/"flexible" - selective = index construction) Weighting: market-cap (free-float) | price (DJIA, splits) | equal (small-cap bias, factor-indifferent) | fundamental HHI = Sum w_i^2 ; effective N = 1/HHI ; HHI up = concentration up Rebalance = adjust WEIGHTS | Reconstitute = swap STOCKS Buffering = delay move (rank threshold) | Packeting = split move (half now/half later) Inclusion: exhaustive (CRSP) vs selective (S&P500, DJIA)

QCommandFull-credit answer

Module Quiz 6.2
QCommandFull-credit answer
1Explain why active > passive on fees/costsActive needs more investment analysis and higher portfolio turnover → higher management fees (ad valorem) + higher trading costs; may also carry performance/incentive fees.
2Explain how engagement benefits non-involved investorsFree-rider effect: successful engagement lifts the stock price, and that gain reaches all shareholders — including those who never engaged or bore the cost.
3Identify two disadvantages of engagementAny two: costs time/resources • short-termism vs long-term goals • insider-trading risk (material nonpublic info) • conflicts of interest. Identify = name two, no essay needed.
