Module Quiz 6.3
QAnswerWhy
1B — InvestableThe three required benchmark traits are rules-based, transparent, investable. "Selective" is a distractor from the index-construction topic (exhaustive vs selective inclusion); "Flexible" isn't a requirement at all.
High-probability traps
Style drift: "which advantage is also a disadvantage?" → categories not stable over time ICB inversion: ICB goes industry→sector; the other three go sector→industry Market vs production: only GICS is market-oriented; ICB/TRBC/RGS are production-oriented Geography diversification: the benefit is overestimated — foreign large-caps may already be global / earn income in your home country Growth investors & income: growth-oriented investors are less likely to seek dividend income Dividend stability: dividend yield is more stable than the price-change component of return Benchmark traits: rules-based / transparent / investable — NOT "selective" (that's index construction) Buffering vs packeting: buffering DELAYS the move (rank threshold); packeting SPLITS it (half now, half later) Rebalance vs reconstitute: rebalance = adjust weights; reconstitute = swap stocks in/out
Reading 6 · Overview of Equity Portfolio Management
Full-reading recap, module by module. Covers the roles of equities (6.a), how a manager's universe is segmented (6.b), the income & costs of managing equity (6.c), shareholder engagement (6.d), the active/passive spectrum (6.e), and benchmark selection (6.f) including index weighting & the HHI. Mostly conceptual — the one calculation is HHI / effective number of stocks (see the Benchmark tab's live calculator).
Module 6.1 · Equity Investment Roles
LOS 6.aFour roles of equities in the overall portfolio
Capital appreciationThe main driver of long-term equity returns (price growth from rising cash flows, revenues, and/or earnings). Ranges from small growth-tech to large well-established value firms. Over the last 50 years, equity returns > bonds & bills on average. Equities outperform in strong economic growth, underperform in weak growth. Dividend incomeExcess cash flows distributed rather than reinvested. Recent yields ~1%–3%. Dividend yield is more stable than the price-change return. Dividends are not guaranteed to rise or continue. DiversificationEquities have < +1.0 correlation with other classes → portfolio σ is lower than the weighted sum of individual σ. Twist: the benefit is not constant — in a financial crisis correlations rise (benefit shrinks) and class σ can rise too, further cutting the risk reduction. Inflation hedgeA firm that can raise prices when input costs rise passes inflation into cash flow/earnings; commodity producers (e.g. oil) benefit directly. Record is mixed: generally positive real-return/inflation correlation, but it varies by time & country; equities & inflation can turn negative in hyperinflation; equity prices lead while inflation lags → a less-than-perfect correlation.
Trap: equities are only an imperfect inflation hedge (leading vs lagging, hyperinflation flips the sign). Don't overstate it as a reliable hedge.
Client investment considerations & ESG constraints
Risk tolerancePer the IPS: high risk tolerance → growth-oriented companies; low risk tolerance → stable, well-established dividend payers. Negative screening(= exclusionary screening) excludes companies/sectors that fail client standards (e.g. exclude oil & gas). Positive screening(= best-in-class screening) uncovers/overweights the most favorably ranked companies (e.g. overweight strong-governance firms). ESG integrationThe dominant sustainable strategy — embed ESG throughout valuation, expected returns, risk analysis, and portfolio construction. Thematic investingScreens equities on a specific theme (e.g. climate change). Impact investingMeets objectives by becoming actively engaged and/or directly funding company projects with the explicit intention of a positive social/environmental impact alongside a financial return.
Don't confuse: negative = exclusionary; positive = best-in-class. Thematic = theme screen; impact = active engagement + intended real-world impact.
Module 6.1 · Equity Investment Segmentation
LOS 6.bThree ways to segment the investment universe
Three main approaches: size & style, geography, and economic activity. Segmentation improves understanding of how equities fit the overall portfolio and enhances diversification.
1 · Size & style. Size = market cap (large / mid / small). Style = value / growth / blend (a.k.a. core), determined by metrics like P/E, P/B, dividend yield, and earnings/book-value growth. A style box (3×3) ranks companies:
Size ↓ / Style →ValueBlendGrowth
LargeLarge-cap valueLarge-cap blendLarge-cap growth
MediumMid-cap valueMid-cap blendMid-cap growth
SmallSmall-cap valueSmall-cap blendSmall-cap growth
Advantages(1) Better address client risk/return considerations; (2) greater diversification across sectors/industries; (3) build relevant benchmarks for a specific size/style fund; (4) analyze how company characteristics change over time (a small-cap growth firm may mature into mid/large and drift toward blend). DisadvantageThe last advantage is also the drawback: categories are not stable over time (style drift).
2 · Geography. Categorizes markets by stage of economic development:
DevelopedUS, UK, Germany, Australia, Japan. EmergingBrazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa. FrontierIceland, Estonia, Nigeria, Jordan, Vietnam. AdvantageDomestically-concentrated investors learn to diversify internationally. Disadvantages(1) Currency risk; (2) overestimated diversification — a large foreign firm may already be globally diversified and even earn much of its income from the investor's own country.
3 · Economic activity. Groups firms into sectors/industries via a market-oriented or production-oriented approach:
Market-orientedSegments by markets served, how products are used by consumers, and how cash flows are generated. Used by GICS. Might classify a coal company in energy. Production-orientedSegments by products manufactured & inputs required in production. Used by ICB, TRBC, RGS. Might classify the same coal company in basic materials. Four structuresGICS (market-oriented) · ICB · TRBC · RGS (production-oriented).
Prof's note — sector vs industry ordering: GICS, TRBC, RGS start at the top with sectors then subdivide into industries. ICB is the exception — it starts with industries then subdivides into sectors. GICS example (Consumer Staples): Sector → Industry group (Food, beverage & tobacco) → Industry (Beverages) → Subindustry (Soft drinks).
Adv (econ activity)Analyze/compare & construct performance benchmarks by sector/industry; diversification enhanced across sectors/industries. DisadvantageSome firms (esp. larger ones) have operations not easily assigned to one sector/industry.
Indexes combine approaches: MSCI Europe Large Cap Value & MSCI China Small Cap mix size/style + geography; MSCI World Energy & S&P Global Natural Resources track by sector/industry. Indexes can also track ESG.
Module 6.2 · Portfolio Income & Costs
LOS 6.cWays to earn current income from an equity portfolio
Dividend incomeMost obvious & often largest. Watch taxation (income and/or withholding). Growth-focused investors are less likely to seek dividend income. Optional stock dividendInvestor chooses cash or new shares. The "option" itself has value & can be sold to another investor. Special dividendA one-time cash payment (vs the regular periodic dividend). Securities lendingLend stock (often to enable a short sale) for a fee; may also earn a return reinvesting posted cash collateral. Common in index funds, large institutional portfolios (pension funds), endowments.
Lending issuesShort selling drives the price down (bad for the lender, who still owns it) — concerns an active manager more than a passive one. Watch borrower quality & return ability. Borrower must compensate the lender for dividends during the loan; lender generally loses voting rights during the loan. Lending fee~0.2%–0.5% annually in developed markets; much higher for EM loans or high-demand stocks (specials). Cash-collateral reinvestment adds market/credit/operational risk + admin costs. Writing optionsSell options for premium. Covered call = write a call on a stock owned (lose upside above strike). Cash-covered / cash-secured put = sell a put & set aside cash to buy the stock if exercised (risk: buyer exercises only if the stock falls). Dividend captureBuy just before the ex-dividend date, hold through it (earn the dividend), then sell. Profitable if the price declines by less than the dividend. Theory says price drops by the dividend, but market forces & taxes can differ.
Equity portfolio fees & costs
Management (ad valorem)Pay the manager + research, hardware/software, compliance, trade processing. Based on % of AUM, due at intervals. Higher for active (more analysis & turnover). Usually a standard schedule but negotiable. Performance (incentive)Earned when the portfolio beats a stated objective; common for hedge/alternative funds, e.g. 10%–20% of appreciation above a threshold. One-sided — manager shares upside, not penalized for underperformance. A high-water mark stops paying twice for the same gains. AdministrationCorporate-activity services (risk/return measurement, voting). May be inside the mgmt fee or separate if external. Sub-types: custody (independent custodian holds assets), depository (segregate assets + verify compliance with limits like leverage/cash), registration (register mutual-fund share ownership). Marketing & distributionSales/client teams, advertising, conferences, brochures, online platform fees, sales commissions to intermediaries (e.g. financial planners/brokers). Trading costsExplicit: broker commissions, exchange fees, taxes. Implicit: bid-ask spread, price impact, and delay/slippage costs (trade not completed due to illiquidity). Investment strategyImplicit cost of the chosen strategy. Active > passive cost, but even passive index funds face predatory trading — traders buy/sell shares soon to be added/removed from an index → price-impact cost to the fund, profit to the predator.
Liquidity demand vs supply: momentum strategies demand liquidity (buy rising / sell falling) → high market-impact cost. Contrarian strategies supply liquidity (buy falling / sell rising) → low impact cost. Passive index replication falls in the middle.
Prof's note: a manager may bundle all of these into one management fee, break some out separately, or a third party may charge them. Bottom line — services aren't free; consider total cost regardless of how the bill is presented.
Module 6.2 · Shareholder Engagement
LOS 6.dBenefits of engagement & the equity manager's role
Engagement = investors/managers interacting with companies (calls, voting at general assemblies) to favorably influence the stock price and improve corporate governance. Meetings may cover:
Corporate strategyObjectives, constraints, growth opportunities, resources; research, culture, products, competitive environment, sustainability; balancing short-term obligations with long-term goals. Capital allocationNew-project selection, M&A, capex, use of leverage, dividends, equity financing. Corporate governanceInternal controls, audit & risk committees, regulatory & political risk management. CompensationTop-management remuneration/incentives & alignment with shareholders; larger shareholders may influence future comp structures. Board compositionBoard experience, competence, diversity, culture, effectiveness; succession planning for departing members.
Benefits & economics of engagement:
Active vs passiveActive managers engage to improve performance; passive managers focus on minimizing engagement costs. ScaleLarger investors absorb costs more easily (spread over more assets). Free ridersSuccessful engagement benefits all shareholders, including free riders who don't engage but reap the same stock-price gain. NonfinancialCan address ESG concerns, though benefits are harder to quantify. Other stakeholders (employees, customers, creditors, regulators, governments) are also affected.
Limitations / disadvantages (isolated): engagement is not free (time + resources); it may (1) focus on short-term goals at the expense of long-term ones; (2) lead to acquiring material nonpublic information → insider-trading risk; (3) create conflicts of interest (e.g. an engaged manager backs management because management invests in the manager's fund).
Manager's roleEquity managers play a key role & may have staff assigned; firms may consult outside experts. Some countries set legal/regulatory rules on voting & monitoring, requiring written documentation. Activist investingGoes further: propose shareholder resolutions, launch media campaigns, seek board representation, and launch proxy fights (persuading other shareholders to back their proposals).
Module 6.2 · Active / Passive Management
LOS 6.eRationales across the active-management spectrum
Passive = replicate an index/benchmark; Active = outperform & add value (riskier — can also underperform). Real strategies blur the line (closely tracking with limited deviations). Rationales for shifting toward active:
Manager skillConfidence the manager has expert knowledge/skill to add value. Client mandatesMandates to invest in certain companies (e.g. ESG) may require active screening techniques. Client preferencesNeed enough interested investors to cover active costs. Growth styles are more likely to benefit from active; value may be more passive.
ExpectationsManage what investors should reasonably expect; unreasonable expectations → dissatisfaction. CapacityStrategies that get too popular are a problem — too much capital makes it harder to find value. Benchmark breadthActive needs a benchmark with a broad range of liquid equities. Narrow/limited benchmarks give little room to deviate → favor a passive approach.
Active management risks (isolated): results are less certain and costs higher. Key-person risk (a person essential to the fund's success leaves the firm) and higher portfolio turnover → higher tax burdens (tax-mitigation techniques are themselves costly/risky and need extra knowledge of country-specific tax rules).
Module 6.3 · Benchmark Selection
LOS 6.fChoosing a benchmark for an equity portfolio
A usable equity-index benchmark must be (1) rules based, (2) transparent, (3) investable:
Rules basedInclusion/exclusion rules, weighting scheme & rebalancing frequency are consistent, objective, predictable → investors can replicate performance. TransparentRules are public, clearly stated, understandable. InvestableInvestors can actually replicate the index's return/risk.
Two considerations when choosing: (1) determine desired market & risk exposures; (2) identify the construction/maintenance methods of the index.
Market exposureBroad vs focused (sectors); domestic vs international; developed vs emerging vs frontier. Risk-factor exposureSensitivity to factors: market risk (beta), firm size, style (growth vs value), prior returns (momentum); also liquidity, volatility, firm quality. Inclusion methodExhaustive (every stock in a universe, e.g. CRSP US Total Market) vs selective (a subset, e.g. S&P 500, DJIA).
Index weighting methods
Market-capWeight each stock by its cap as a % of total. CAPM market portfolio & most indexes (S&P 500) are cap-weighted; practice uses free-float shares (exclude closely-held). PriceWeight by price → equivalent to holding an equal number of shares; higher-priced stocks get larger weights (e.g. DJIA). Stock splits complicate the calculation. EqualInvest equal amounts → reduces concentration risk vs cap-weighting (esp. large-cap). Small-cap bias vs cap-weighting; factor-indifderent (randomizes factor mispricing); returns more volatile; can earn marginally better returns before costs when prices vary around intrinsic value; higher transaction costs. FundamentalWeight by a fundamental factor's share of the index total (sales, income, dividends). E.g. a firm paying 3% of all index dividends gets a 3% weight in a dividend-weighted index.
Stock concentration — Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI): HHI = Σᵢ₁ⁿ wᵢ² (wᵢ = weight of stock i, n = number of stocks) Range: 1/n (equal-weighted, lowest concentration) → 1 (single stock) Higher HHI → higher concentration risk Effective number of stocks = 1 / HHI
Example (cap)A cap-weighted index of 500 stocks might have HHI = 0.01 → effective number = 1/0.01 = 100. That 100 < 500 reflects the disproportionate weight of the largest-cap stocks. Verified. Example (equal)An equal-weighted 500-stock index has HHI = 1/500 = 0.002 → effective number = 1/0.002 = 500. Verified. See the Benchmark → HHI Calculator tab.
Decisive detail: effective number of stocks ≤ actual number; they're equal only when equally weighted. A large gap signals heavy concentration in the biggest names.
Index maintenance — rebalancing, reconstitution, migration
RebalancingAdjust weights as weightings change. Equal-weight drifts as prices move; price-weight changes on splits/dividends; cap-weight needs rebalancing when firms issue/repurchase significant shares. Incurs trading (and possibly tax) costs → done periodically, often quarterly. ReconstitutionRemove & replace stocks that no longer fit the index's market exposure (e.g. a small-cap grows to mid-cap and leaves a small-cap index). Also incurs trading costs → lowers index returns. BufferingReduces migration trading costs via a threshold (buffer zone) a firm's rank must cross before switching indexes. E.g. large-cap = top 200, mid-cap = next 300; a rising mid-cap isn't moved to large-cap until its rank reaches, say, 150 or higher. PacketingAlternative: when a mid-cap grows into large-cap, move half the position to large-cap on the reconstitution date; if it still qualifies at the next reconstitution, move the remainder.
Rebalance vs reconstitute: rebalance = adjust weights; reconstitute = swap stocks in/out. Buffering (rank threshold) and packeting (move in halves) both cut migration costs.

Quiz answers & the decisive detail
Quizzes 6.1 & 6.2 are constructed-response (no MCQ key). Quiz 6.3 Q1 is MCQ; its answer key was not in the photos, so the answer below is my verified reasoning, not a copy of the key.
QuizTaskFull-credit / verified answer
6.1 · Q1Discuss two reasons a crisis affects diversification's risk reductionTwo labeled chains: (1) correlations rise toward +1.0 → cross-asset offset shrinks; (2) asset-class σ rise → portfolio σ climbs even at fixed correlation. Both erode the benefit.
6.1 · Q2Describe two advantages of economic-activity segmentation(1) Analyze/compare & build performance benchmarks by sector/industry; (2) diversification enhanced across sectors/industries. (Don't borrow size/style advantages.)
6.2 · Q1Explain why active portfolios have higher fees/costsMore investment analysis + higher turnover → higher management fees & trading/tax costs than passive.
6.2 · Q2Explain how engagement benefits non-engaged investorsFree-rider effect: successful engagement raises the stock price, benefiting all shareholders including those who didn't engage.
6.2 · Q3Identify two disadvantages of engagementAny two of: costly (time/resources); short-termism; risk of acquiring MNPI (insider-trading risk); conflicts of interest.
6.2 · Q4Low fees + big value-add + many ESG restrictions + narrow large-cap benchmark: two reasons each for passive vs activePassive: low-fee preference; narrow/limited benchmark gives little room to deviate. Active: wants substantial value-add vs benchmark; numerous ESG restrictions require active screening.
6.2 · Q5Identify & describe two additional active-manager/investor risksKey-person risk (essential person leaves) and higher turnover → higher tax burden (mitigation techniques costly/risky).
6.3 · Q1Necessary characteristic for an equity index used as a benchmark?B. Investable — the three requirements are rules-based, transparent, and investable. "Selective" and "flexible" are not requirements.
LOS 7.a — Three roles of fixed income in a portfolio
Each role is a separate driver. Under exam pressure, name the role AND its mechanism — don't collapse them.
RoleDriver / mechanismDetail to remember
1. DiversificationLow (often < +1) correlation to equities → improves risk-adjusted returnLower the correlation, greater the benefit. 2000–2019: ranged −0.30 (10y US Treasury) to +0.63 (US high-yield) vs S&P 500.
2. Regular cash flowPredictable coupon/principal to meet future obligationsSuits individuals (living expenses, tuition) & insurers (policyholder payouts). Build a buy-and-hold laddered portfolio: no sales planned, ~equal par maturing periodically.
3. Inflation hedgeSome structures pass inflation through to coupon and/or principalNot the first thing investors think of. Standard nominal (fixed-coupon) bonds do NOT protect. Linked & floating do (different ways — see comparator).
Diversification — decomposed drivers
Cross-asset: adding a low-correlation class to a portfolio raises risk-adjusted return; numbers vary by period & instrument type. Internal (within FI): achievable too — driven by credit-spread changes causing IG vs HY (below-IG) performance to diverge. Not stable over time: a particular problem is flight to quality.
Flight-to-quality trap. In market stress, all lower-quality / riskier assets (HY bonds + equities) decline together → their correlation approaches +1 (diversification evaporates when you need it). Meanwhile investors buy high-quality developed-market government bonds for safety → government-bond correlation to risky assets falls and may go negative. Also: bond-return volatility rises over time, especially HY in a crisis.
Inflation protection — the 3 structures (interactive)
Pick a structure. Watch which leg moves: par, coupon, or neither. This is the single most tested distinction in 7.a.
Principal (par) leg
Coupon leg
Worked example — inflation rises 3% → 5% (par = 1,000,000)
Inflation-linkedFloating-coupon
ParAdjusts +5% → 1,050,000Unchanged 1,000,000
Coupon rulereal rate × adjusted par(MRR + spread) × par
First coupon0.5% × 1,050,000 = 5,250(3.5%+1%)×1m = 45,000
After +2% inflationpar & coupon keep adjusting +5% each periodMRR → 5.5%; coupon = (5.5%+1%)×1m = 65,000
Coupon changetracks cumulative inflation45,000 → 65,000 = +44.4%
What's protectedCoupon AND principalCoupon only — NOT principal
Prof's note: In a fully efficient market, NR / linked / floating from the same issuer & maturity are priced to the same expected return (small differences from differing inflation-risk response). If realized inflation > (<) initial consensus, linked & floating returns beat (lag) the NR bond. Which of linked vs floating wins depends on the actual path of inflation. Accept the reading's conclusions — they're correct.
Fixed-income mandates — two major types
First branch in the classification tree. Liability-based = fund a liability; total return = beat/match a benchmark.
Liability-basedTotal return
GoalManage assets solely to meet expected future liability payoutsNot funding liabilities; target an absolute return OR (more commonly) match/outperform a benchmark
MechanismAll asset cash flows reinvested until paid out → immunizationMeasured by active return (= value added / alpha) & active risk (= tracking error / tracking risk)
Sub-typesCash flow matching · Duration matching · Contingent immunization (CI) · Derivatives overlaysPure indexing · Enhanced indexing · Active management
Liability-based — immunization variations
Cash flow matching — simplest. Assets selected so cash flows occur when & in the size the liabilities need. Duration matching — match asset duration to liability duration so ending values move similarly as rates change → values stay matched. Contingent immunization (CI) — hybrid of active + immunization. Funded with more than required; PVA − PVL = surplus. Derivatives overlays — futures/swaps to implement duration matching or CI.
CI surplus logic (decomposed):
• Surplus = PVA − PVL; while positive, manager can run the assets actively any way they believe adds value.
• If active mgmt succeeds → surplus grows → ultimate cost of CI < cost of initially immunizing.
• If surplus declines to zero → portfolio must be immediately immunized → ultimate cost of CI > initial immunization, but by a known amount.
Total return — the indexing spectrum
TypeActive return targetDuration vs indexTurnover
Pure indexing~Zero active return & riskMatch all risk factors (duration, credit/quality, sectors, prepayment); leeway on individual bondsLow, similar to index
Enhanced indexingModest active returnDuration still matched; small sector/quality over/underweights allowedSlightly higher
Active managementLarger active returnDuration can be mismatched; large deviations from index risk factorsMuch higher
Pure indexing trap (Quiz Q2). Most pure bond indexing does NOT literally replicate (hold every issue at index weight) — the huge number of bonds & their illiquidity make that impractical. It instead exactly matches the index risk factors while allowing leeway on the individual bonds selected. "Allows large deviations / high active return" = active mgmt, not pure indexing.
LOS 7.b — Key bond risk & return measures
Exam framing: L3 is less about calculation, more about interpretation & use in a PM situation. Know what each measure tells you.
MeasureDefinitionInterpretation
Macaulay durationWeighted-avg time to receive cash flows; weights = PV of cash flowsHigher → investors wait longer → higher price volatility when yields change
Modified durationMacaulay ÷ (1 + periodic yield)Approx % price change for a 1% yield change. ModDur 7 → price ≈ −7% if yields +1%
Effective durationPrice sensitivity to a parallel shift in benchmark curve (modeled, not formula)Approx % change for 1% benchmark-curve change. Used for complex bonds (uncertain CF, embedded options)
Key rate (partial) durationSensitivity to a change at one specific maturity, others held constantAssesses nonparallel curve exposure. 10y key-rate dur 7 → −7% if 10y yield +1% while others unchanged
Empirical durationInterest-rate sensitivity from regressing bond returns vs benchmark yield changesSame idea as effective duration, but from past observed market behavior rather than modeling
Money (dollar) durationModified duration × market valueAbsolute (currency) value gain/loss for a 1% yield change. Higher → larger absolute P&L
PVBP / DV01 / BPVMoney duration × 0.0001Absolute currency change for a 1 basis point move
ConvexityExtent price–yield relationship is nonlinear; positive for option-free fixed-coupon bondsPrice rises more than duration implies when yields fall, falls less when yields rise
Effective convexityNonlinear price–curve relationship via modelingUsed for complex bonds (uncertain CF, embedded options)
Convexity — three key facts
1. Valuable when yields are expected to change — positive convexity = up more / down less than duration predicts → investors pay higher prices (accept lower yields) for higher-convexity bonds. 2. Second-order measure — measures how price-vs-yield sensitivity itself changes as yields move. Approx ∝ duration²: dur-20 bond ≈ 4× the convexity of a dur-10 bond (20² = 4 × 10²). 3. Related to cash-flow dispersion — directly tied to dispersion of CFs in time around Macaulay duration. For a given Macaulay duration, the lowest-convexity bond is a zero-coupon (one CF at maturity).
Effective duration & convexity calculator
effective duration = (PV₋ − PV₊) / [2 · Δcurve · PV₀] effective convexity = (PV₋ + PV₊ − 2·PV₀) / [Δcurve² · PV₀]
PV₀ = current value · PV₋ = value if curve shifts down · PV₊ = value if curve shifts up · Δcurve = size of the shift (decimal, e.g. 0.01 for 1%).
PV₀ PV₋ (down) PV₊ (up) Δcurve
Combining bonds into a portfolio
Macaulay duration of a portfolio = cash-weighted (market-value-weighted) duration of the individual assets. Applies to all basic duration measures. Modified duration & convexity of a portfolio = cash-weighted of the individual assets (same process). Effective duration & convexity of a portfolio = use the PV₋ / PV₊ / PV₀ formulas on the whole portfolio value. Spread duration = portfolio % sensitivity to a 1% change in credit spreads. Duration times spread (DTS) = spread duration × the bond's credit spread. Gives higher sensitivity when spreads are already high (spread changes tend to be proportional to spread levels).
Cash-weighted portfolio duration calculator
Enter weight,duration pairs (one per line, e.g. 0.4,10). Weights normalize automatically. Textbook check: 0.4,10 & 0.6,15 → 13.
DTS calculator
Spread duration Credit spread (bps)
Active management moves (decomposed)
ViewActionWhy
Rates expected to fallIncrease portfolio durationAmplify the price rise as yields drop
Rates expected to riseLower portfolio durationCushion the price fall as yields climb
Spreads expected to narrowIncrease spread duration / DTS; lower avg credit rating (hold riskier bonds)Capture the larger price rise from spread tightening
Spreads expected to widenDecrease spread duration; increase avg credit ratingReduce loss from spread widening
Bond selectionUse relative value (valuation, issuer traits, technicals) to rank bondse.g. expecting narrowing → pick bonds with DTS > benchmark's
Correlations between fixed-income sectors
Same market → correlations likely high (shared overarching macro conditions). Investment-grade (low credit risk) → returns driven primarily by the benchmark sovereign yield curve. High-yield → more affected by spread changes than benchmark rates.
The negative rate–spread relationship (decomposed): in poor economic conditions, interest rates tend to be low but credit spreads high (and vice versa) → benchmark rates & spreads move oppositely. Because HY is spread-driven, this makes HY behave more like equity → HY shows higher correlation with equities.
LOS 7.c — What bond liquidity is
Liquidity = ability to transact in relatively large size, quickly, with minimal deviation from market price. In bonds: most recently issued (on-the-run) developed-market govt bonds are quite liquid; other bonds may be quite illiquid — trading rarely or at very wide bid-ask spreads.
Why bonds are illiquid — the drivers
Huge number of issues — one issuer can have dozens of separate bonds (different maturity, coupon, call features); each issue is small. Vs equity: one issuer usually has one class of common stock. Heterogeneous — bonds of one issuer differ; stock is homogeneous. OTC trading — raises search cost to find a counterparty; less transparent (hard to find past price/volume). Dealer inventory — recently issued bonds more liquid (dealers hold inventory). Over time bonds settle into buy-and-hold portfolios. On-the-run → off-the-run — when a new similar-maturity issue arrives, the older one becomes off-the-run, liquidity drops, trades at higher YTM = a liquidity premium.
Prof's note: "illiquidity premium" and "liquidity premium" mean the same thing; L3 calls it liquidity premium = extra yield compensation for lack of liquidity. As liquidity falls, the premium and yield rise.
Liquidity by bond market subsector
SubsectorLiquidityDrivers
On-the-run sovereign (high quality)HighestLarge size, homogeneous, used as pricing benchmarks & repo collateral. Declines somewhat for older off-the-run.
Corporate bondsVaries widelyFalls with lower quality (riskier) and smaller issue size. Small issuers also often excluded from indexes. Same analysis effort for small vs large issuer, but harder to build a large holding.
Quiz Q3: highest liquidity = on-the-run sovereign government debt. A small corporate issue or a below-investment-grade issue would be less liquid.
Effects of liquidity on bond portfolio management
Pricing data — OTC trades historically unreported → hard to find prices. Absent reporting / with infrequent trading, use matrix pricing: infer price from YTM of recent trades in bonds with similar maturity, quality, coupon. Portfolio construction — buy-and-hold investors need less liquidity (no plan to sell) → may prefer less liquid bonds for the higher yield. Active investors / those who may need to sell → prefer more liquid bonds. Dealer bid-ask — most trading is in dealer markets; dealers widen bid-ask on less liquid bonds (longer to resell → more compensation for inventory risk).
Bid-ask trading cost calculator
cost ≈ bond duration × (ask yield − bid yield)
Textbook: duration 10, bid-ask spread 20 bps → 10 × 0.002 = 0.02 = 2% (if bought at ask & immediately sold at bid).
Duration Bid-ask spread (bps)
Alternatives to direct investment in bonds
VehicleWhat it isKey point
Fixed-income ETFsReplicate many FI sectors; listed on an exchangeEasily traded throughout the day → high liquidity
Open-end mutual fundsSubscribe / redeem units dailyDiversification & economies of scale smaller investors can't get directly
DerivativesExchange-traded bond futures & options; OTC interest-rate swaps & total return swaps (TRS)See TRS decomposition below
Total Return Swap (TRS) — decomposed
Total return receiver pays
Interest rate + a spread
Total return receiver gets
Total return on a reference bond portfolio
Advantage: only a relatively small amount of capital posted as collateral vs fully funding an ETF position to access bond-market returns. Drawback 1: counterparty risk of the total-return payer. Drawback 2: rollover risk — renewing contracts at maturity. Drawback 3: potential regulatory reform requiring higher collateral & raising contract costs.
LOS 7.d — Expected fixed-income return = sum of 5 components
Can be projected (expected return) or computed after the fact (decompose realized return). For a portfolio it uses aggregate data. Each component is a separate slot — name all five, don't merge.

Rolling yield = #1 + #23.86%

Assumes no reinvestment of cash flow (so semiannual vs annual coupon timing doesn't matter — 1.50 at 6m + 1.50 at 12m = 3.00 per 100 par).
What's solid vs what's a projection
Near-certain: #1 coupon income (the yield income), if no default. Assumption-based: #2 rolldown assumes the yield curve is unchanged; curve plotting varies (on-the-run vs off-the-run, which carry a liquidity premium). Pure predictions: #3 (ΔY) & #4 (ΔS) price changes, and #5 currency G/L. Not captured: shifts in individual bonds' relative valuation, and credit losses. Predicted price change rests only on duration & convexity.
5-component return calculator

Rolldown direction rule
Flat curve, bond at a premium → projected end price lower than start (price pulled toward par as maturity nears). Flat curve, bond at a discount → projected end price higher than start (pulled up toward par). Upward-sloping curve → rolldown return is higher than the start-of-period YTM: as the bond ages it "rolls down" the curve to a lower YTM → higher price at horizon end. Downward-sloping → opposite (lower rolldown, higher YTM at horizon end).
"Rolldown" = projecting bond prices with the yield curve held unchanged; the bond simply gets shorter in maturity and re-prices off the (assumed unchanged) curve.
Convexity is a second-order effect
In the example the convexity term added only +0.041% to Component 3. For option-free bonds it's often insignificant unless ΔY is large. Bonds with embedded options → must use effective duration & convexity. Floating-rate securities complicate it: their duration is low, but they still have spread sensitivity.
Prof's note — which duration in Component 4?
Technically Component 4 (ΔS) should use SPREAD duration, not modified duration. The CFA-curriculum example uses MD, assuming spread duration ≈ modified duration. That's a fair approximation for a fixed-coupon bond, but NOT for floating-rate bonds — there MD is low (coupons reset with benchmark rates) while spread duration stays high (spread increases don't flow through to higher coupons).
Exam rule: if a question gives you BOTH effective duration/convexity AND spread duration/convexity → use effective for Part 3 (ΔY) and spread for Part 4 (ΔS).
Why this framework matters
This return decomposition is the framework used to analyze returns from active strategies across the next several readings — a very important series of calculations. Know the five slots cold.
LOS 7.e — Leverage: the core idea
Leverage = borrow funds to increase portfolio return (return on investor's equity). Particularly attractive in periods of low interest rates (and low expected return).
If rI > rB (asset return > borrow cost) → leverage enhances portfolio return. If rI < rB (asset return < borrow cost) → leverage amplifies losses. Duration note: borrowing is normally at shorter-term rates, whose cost can rise faster than asset returns → in a leveraged portfolio asset duration normally EXCEEDS liability duration. Leverage also raises exposure to interest-rate risk.
Leveraged return formula + calculator
r_p = r_I + [ (V_B / V_E) × (r_I − r_B) ] r_p = portfolio (equity) return r_I = return on invested assets r_B = rate paid on borrowings V_B = amount of leverage (borrowed) V_E = amount of equity invested
r_I (%) r_B (%) V_B (borrowed) V_E (equity)
Four ways to achieve leverage
MethodHow it leveragesKey detail
1. Repurchase agreements (repos)Sell a security for cash + agree to buy it back later; assets = collateral → explicit borrowingUsually overnight (can renegotiate daily / longer). Functionally a loan secured by the security.
2. Futures contractsSmall initial margin controls the full contract value (price × multiplier)leverage = (notional − margin) / margin
3. Swap agreementsReceive-fixed / pay-MRR swap ≈ buy bonds + borrow floating → raises bond exposure & duration, no explicit fundsReceive-floating / pay-fixed = opposite. Post-2007–09 many cleared centrally.
4. Securities lendingLend securities for collateral; supports short selling (sell what you don't own, borrow to deliver)Open-ended (no maturity). Earnings depend on how badly the borrower needs the specific collateral.
Repo mechanics — decomposed
Repo rate math: $100m overnight at 2.5% → dealer receives 100m, repays 100m × [1 + (0.025 / 360)] next day (standard repo-rate convention, 360-day). General collateral — any previously agreed securities can be delivered (e.g. any domestic govt bond). Security-driven (specific) — lender wants a specific security (hedging/arb) → offers a lower repo rate; this is a form of securities lending. Haircut — collateral worth MORE than the loan (e.g. market value = 102% of repo amount → 2% haircut) protects the lender; larger for riskier / less-liquid collateral. Cash- vs security-driven: cash-driven = borrower wants cash, any collateral; security-driven = lender wants a specific security. Bilateral vs tri-party: tri-party uses an intermediary (usually a bank) to hold collateral & record ownership → cheaper than physically exchanging; repo rate may not need adjusting since the bank manages collateral quality.
Futures leverage calculator
leverage = (notional value of contract − margin amount) / margin amount
Notional value Margin amount
Securities lending — rebate rate
rebate rate = collateral earnings rate − security lending rate
Lender of securities can take cash collateral and invest it to earn interest (usually > value of securities lent). A portion of those earnings may be rebated to the securities borrower. If the borrower badly needs the specific collateral, the lender can demand an explicit fee, more cash collateral, or more general collateral — all raise lender earnings.
Open-ended risk: unlike repos, securities-lending agreements usually have no specified maturity — they continue until one party requires settlement (return of collateral). This creates risk if the counterparty isn't prepared to reverse.
Risks created by leverage
Obvious risk: if borrowing cost rises ABOVE earnings on the assets → loss (magnified by the leverage ratio). Rate increase → value decline: rising rates lower the value of the leveraged portfolio AND its collateral. Forced liquidation / fire sale: lenders demand repayment → assets sold when DOWN in value (distressed conditions). Vicious cycle: if liquidations are widespread, each round of sales drives prices down → other credit providers, repo participants & securities lenders demand repayment and/or stop lending → cascade.
Why asset duration > liability duration matters here: borrowing is short-term (low liability duration) while assets are longer (high asset duration). When short rates rise, borrowing costs reprice fast while the long assets fall in price — squeezing the leveraged equity from both sides.
LOS 7.f — Taxable vs tax-exempt: the core difference
Both seek the highest risk-adjusted return net of fees & transaction costs, consistent with objectives/constraints. It's more complex for taxable investors — taxes must be factored into after-tax return AND risk. Rules differ by jurisdiction.
Tax factDetail
Two return sources taxed differentlyIncome (coupon) vs capital gains (price change), usually at different rates
Gains taxed when realizedUsually only at sale. Exception: zero-coupon imputed income (accretion toward par) may be taxed yearly even with NO cash flow
Holding periodLong-term gains often taxed LOWER than interest income; short-term holdings often higher
Capital lossesOffset capital gains (not other income). Excess losses may be carried FORWARD; sometimes carried BACK for a refund on a prior year
Tax-sheltered accountsMay be possible to hold some of the portfolio in tax-advantaged accounts
Strategies for taxable accounts
Realize LOSSES to offset gains — incl. selective tax-loss harvesting on partial sales when bought at multiple prices (lots). Extend holding periods to realize long-term rather than short-term gains (lower rate). Extend holding periods to DEFER taxes. Consider income-vs-gain rate differentials when selecting investments.
Quiz 7.3 Q3 traps: it's realize LOSSES (not gains) to offset gains; and EXTEND (not shorten) holding periods for long-term treatment. The correct general strategy is considering income-vs-gain rate differentials.
Funds vs separately managed accounts (SMA)
Mutual / collective funds: income is taxable to the fund regardless of payout or reinvestment. Gains treatment varies: pass-through (investor taxed when the fund realizes the gain; that payment then reduces tax when shares are sold) vs deferred (investor taxed on all gains only when fund shares are sold). SMA: when a client hires a manager for a separately managed account, all income, gains & losses pass to the client and are reported on the client's tax return.
Worked example — which bond to sell (taxable vs tax-exempt)
Raise EUR 5m. Income tax 38%, cap gains 15%. Bond A = unrealized GAIN; Bond B = unrealized LOSS; otherwise identical except B has a slightly higher yield. Sell all of one.
InvestorSellWhy
1. TaxableSell Bond BAvoid realizing the gain (and paying tax now) on Bond A — defer the tax. Selling the loss bond is tax-friendlier.
2. Tax-exemptSell Bond ATaxes are irrelevant, so retain Bond B for its slightly better yield.
LOS 7.g — Liability-driven investing (LDI)
Used when there are definable future liabilities to be paid from portfolio assets. Classified as passive total return — but "passive" does NOT mean do nothing: it still requires continual monitoring & adjustment. (Active management = outperform a benchmark.) Mostly institutional; the specific LDI approach depends on the nature of the liabilities.
Trap: LDI is passive total return, yet still needs ongoing monitoring/adjustment. Don't equate "passive" with "no action."
Three related terms — what's taken as given
TermWhat's GIVENWhat's MANAGEDExample / when
ALM (asset-liability mgmt)Neither — considered togetherAssets in relation to liabilitiesAppropriate when BOTH asset PV and liability PV change with interest rates
LDI (liability-driven)Liabilities givenAssets managed to meet liability valuesInsurer, DB pension funding payouts. This reading's focus.
ADL (asset-driven liabilities)Assets givenLiability structure managed/designed to match assetsLeasing company structuring floating/fixed-rate liabilities to match its assets
LDI for individuals: e.g. a married person retiring in 12 years, planning to use a bond portfolio to fund an annuity purchase — reinvests bond cash flows and adds a regular amount each year to meet the goal.
Four types of liabilities (interactive)
Classified on two axes: is the future amount known? is the payout date known? Tap a type:
Amount
Payout date
Reference grid
TypeAmountDateExamplesModeling
IKnownKnownOption-free fixed-rate bondSimple duration (Macaulay/modified) adequate
IIKnownUncertainCallable/putable bond; term life insurance (date uncertain, but law of large numbers estimates payouts/period)Effective duration
IIIUncertainKnownFloating-rate instruments; real-rate bonds (TIPS)Effective duration
IVUncertainUncertainProperty & casualty; some DB plan liabilitiesEffective duration
Modeling rule: only Type I can use simple (Macaulay/modified) duration. Types II–IV need effective duration — modeled to reflect the initial yield-curve shape PLUS assumed up/down curve shifts, to estimate the amount & timing of payouts.
LOS 7.h — Cash flow matching
Simplest but least flexible approach to immunizing.
Single liability: buy a zero-coupon bond with par & maturity matching the liability → no cash flow to reinvest, no bonds to sell → no reinvestment or price risk. Bonds must be default-free. Accounting defeasance: assets legally set aside & dedicated to meet the liabilities → both assets AND liabilities can be removed from the organization's balance sheet. Multiple liabilities (recursive): buy a bond maturing on/with par + final coupon to exactly fund the LONGEST liability; its earlier coupons partially meet earlier liabilities. Then recursively fund the next-longest (net of coupons from bonds already bought for longer liabilities), and so on backward.
Cash-in-advance constraint: perfect-matching coupon bonds are unlikely to exist. So require the funding bond to mature BEFORE the liability's payout date. This exposes the portfolio to reinvestment risk in an upward-sloping curve — cash arrives early and must be reinvested short-term at the lower rates at the short end of the curve.
LOS 7.i — Laddered bond portfolio
Roughly equal par amounts purchased across different maturities. Can also be used to cash-flow-match multiple liabilities.
StructureHoldingsSame duration?
LadderEqual par across many maturitiesIf all three share the same duration → same price sensitivity to a parallel shift
BulletConcentrated in a single middle duration
BarbellShort + long duration holdings combined
Ladder advantages — decomposed
Regular liquidity: some bonds mature each year → less need to sell at large bid-ask (esp. for less-liquid corporates). Near-maturity bonds are good collateral → borrow at favorable rates. Broad cash-flow diversification across time: less concentrated exposure to nonparallel curve changes at specific maturities. Price-risk vs reinvestment-risk diversification: long-dated bonds carry price risk, short-dated carry reinvestment risk. Maturing bonds reinvested long-term (typically higher rates) → keeps overall duration stable over time. More convexity than a bullet: benefit in large parallel shifts (convexity ∝ dispersion of cash flows across time). BUT a ladder is NOT as convex as a barbell.
Convexity ranking (decisive): Barbell > Ladder > Bullet. The ladder beats the bullet on convexity but loses to the barbell.
Building ladders without individual bonds
Target-date (fixed-maturity) bond ETFs: each ETF has a designated year when it matures & is paid off; passively managed to replicate a bond maturing that year. Often cost advantages vs individual bonds + more liquidity if unanticipated sales are needed. Disadvantage: for some investors an ongoing (no target date) passive index or active bond fund may be better — larger, greater diversification of credit risk, more liquid than directly holding the underlying bonds.

Tax (7.f)Taxable more complex (after-tax). Income vs gains taxed differently; gains taxed at realization (zero-coupon imputed yearly); long-term lower than short; losses offset gains (carry fwd/back). Strategies: realize LOSSES, EXTEND holding (long-term/defer), income-vs-gain differentials. Sell: taxable→loss bond; tax-exempt→gain bond (keep higher yield). LDI (7.g)Passive total return but needs monitoring. ALM (both together) · LDI (liabilities given→manage assets) · ADL (assets given→manage liabilities). CF match (7.h)Simplest, least flexible. Single liability: default-free zero matching par+maturity → no reinvest/price risk. Defeasance removes assets+liabilities from B/S. Multiple: fund longest first, coupons cover earlier, recurse. Cash-in-advance (mature before payout) → reinvestment risk in upward-sloping curve.
Ladder (7.i)Equal par across maturities. Ladder/bullet/barbell same duration → same parallel-shift sensitivity. Advantages: regular liquidity (collateral), CF diversification across time, price-vs-reinvestment risk diversification, more convexity than bullet (but < barbell). Build via target-date bond ETFs (cost/liquidity); ongoing index/active fund may be better (bigger, more credit diversification, more liquid).
Formula strip
Modified duration = Macaulay / (1 + periodic yield) Money duration = modified duration × market value PVBP / DV01 / BPV = money duration × 0.0001 DTS = spread duration × credit spread eff. duration = (PV₋ − PV₊) / (2 · Δcurve · PV₀) eff. convexity = (PV₋ + PV₊ − 2·PV₀) / (Δcurve² · PV₀) portfolio duration = Σ wᵢ · durationᵢ (cash/MV weighted) bid-ask trade cost ≈ duration × (ask yield − bid yield)
Module Quiz 7.1 — worked
QAnswerWhy
1
Which security protects both coupon AND notional principal from inflation?		B — Inflation-linked bondsLinked bonds adjust par for inflation, and the coupon = rate × adjusted par → both protected. Fixed-coupon (A) = no protection. Floating-coupon (C) protects the coupon only — principal is unchanged. The word "principal" is the decisive slot.
2
Which most accurately describes a pure indexing strategy?		C — exactly match index risk factors, leeway on individual bondsPure indexing targets ~zero active return; literal replication is impractical (too many illiquid bonds), so it matches all risk factors with leeway on bond selection. A (large deviations / high active return) = active mgmt. B (duration matched but sector/quality mismatches allowed) = enhanced indexing.
3
Which issue leads to higher liquidity?		B — on-the-run sovereign government debtOn-the-run sovereigns are large, homogeneous, benchmark/collateral bonds → most liquid. A small corporate & C below-IG both reduce liquidity (small size, lower quality).
Module Quiz 7.2 / 7.3 — worked
QAnswerWhy
1
25m notional, 5% coupon, duration 8, convexity 0.5, expected ΔY +0.35%, no spread change. Expected price change?		B — −2.799%Price Δ = (−MD×ΔY) + (½×C×ΔY²) = (−8×0.0035) + (½×0.5×0.0035²) = −0.028 + 0.0000031 = −2.7997% ≈ −2.799%. Notional & coupon are distractors — only duration, convexity & ΔY enter the price-change formula. Convexity term is tiny here.
2
Most correct statement on leverage & its risks?		C — leverage enhances return as long as funds are borrowed at rates below the return earned on investmentsThis is the core leverage principle (rI > rB). B is wrong — in a leveraged portfolio asset duration normally EXCEEDS liability duration (borrowing is short-term). A (rates up → portfolio & collateral decline) is a true risk but isn't the "most correct" statement about how leverage works.

Module Quiz 7.4 — worked
QAnswerWhy
1
Issuer wants a liability that's easily managed with known future amounts AND payout dates. Which type?		B — Option-free fixed-rate bondsKnown amount + known date = Type I (easiest to model, simple duration works) = option-free fixed-rate bond. A callable = uncertain DATE = Type II. C TIPS = uncertain AMOUNT = Type III.
2
Most correct on laddered-portfolio construction/advantages?		A — the investor is diversified between price risk and reinvestment riskLong-dated bonds bring price risk, short-dated bring reinvestment risk → a ladder diversifies between the two. B wrong — a ladder spreads cash flow, so it has less concentrated reinvestment risk in any single year, not more vs a barbell. C wrong — more distributed cash flows give MORE convexity than a bullet (convexity ∝ CF dispersion), not less.
High-probability traps
Linked vs floating principal: BOTH protect the coupon — only inflation-linked protects the principal. Floating par is unchanged. Nominal bonds: standard fixed-coupon (nominal-rate) bonds give no inflation protection — don't let "fixed income" imply "inflation safe." Pure vs enhanced indexing: pure = duration matched + match ALL risk factors; enhanced = duration still matched but small sector/quality mismatches allowed. Active = duration CAN be mismatched. CI cost direction: succeed → CI cost < immunizing; fail (surplus→0) → must immunize, cost > immunizing but by a KNOWN amount. Effective vs modified duration: effective = benchmark curve shift (complex/optioned bonds); modified = own yield change. DTS direction: expecting spreads to NARROW → INCREASE spread duration/DTS & LOWER credit rating (hold riskier). Widen → opposite. Rates vs spreads (active): rates fall → raise duration; spreads narrow → raise spread duration. Two different levers. Convexity ∝ dur²: dur-20 ≈ 4× convexity of dur-10, not 2×. Zero-coupon = lowest convexity for a given Macaulay duration. Liquidity premium sign: less liquid → HIGHER YTM (premium), so off-the-run trades at higher yield than on-the-run. Buy-hold vs active liquidity preference: buy-hold prefers LESS liquid (higher yield); active prefers MORE liquid. Leverage duration: in a leveraged portfolio asset duration normally EXCEEDS liability duration (borrowing is short-term) — NOT the reverse. Leverage benefit condition: leverage enhances return only when rI > rB; if borrow cost exceeds asset return it AMPLIFIES losses. Repo direction: the security OWNER sells & agrees to buy back = the borrower of cash. Specific-collateral (security-driven) repo carries a LOWER repo rate. Haircut: collateral value > loan (102% = 2% haircut); bigger for riskier/less-liquid collateral — protects the LENDER. Tax — realize which?: realize LOSSES to offset gains (not gains); EXTEND holding periods for long-term treatment / deferral (not shorten). Which bond to sell: taxable → sell the LOSS bond (defer the gain's tax); tax-exempt → sell the GAIN bond, keep the higher-yield bond (taxes irrelevant). Zero-coupon tax: imputed accretion income can be taxed yearly even with NO cash flow. LDI is passive: LDI = passive total return, but still requires ongoing monitoring/adjustment — "passive" ≠ "do nothing." ALM vs LDI vs ADL: ALM = both together; LDI = liabilities given, manage assets; ADL = assets given, manage/design liabilities. Liability types: I = known amt + known date (only one that uses SIMPLE duration); II = known amt, uncertain date (callable, term life); III = uncertain amt, known date (floaters, TIPS); IV = both uncertain (P&C, some DB). Convexity ranking: Barbell > Ladder > Bullet. Ladder beats bullet but is NOT as convex as a barbell. Cash-in-advance constraint: bond matures BEFORE the payout → reinvestment risk in an upward-sloping curve (reinvest early cash short at lower rates). Cash flow matching single liability: a default-free ZERO-COUPON matching par & maturity removes BOTH reinvestment and price risk.

Full-reading recap, module by module: roles of FI + two mandate types (7.a), risk/return measures (7.b), bond liquidity (7.c), the five-component return model (7.d), leverage (7.e), taxable vs tax-exempt (7.f), and LDI: liability types, cash-flow matching & ladders (7.g–i). All worked figures below are node-verified against the textbook and reproduced by the widget's live calculators.
Module 7.1 · Role of Fixed Income
LOS 7.aThree roles of FI + how mandates are classified
The FI market is highly varied: public bonds & money-market, plus nonpublic loans & private placements; varies by maturity, credit quality; structures include straight bonds, embedded prepayment options, variable coupons, inflation adjustment. Three portfolio roles:
DiversificationLow correlation to equity. 2000–2019 correlations to S&P 500 ranged −0.30 (10-yr UST) to +0.63 (US high-yield). Flight to quality: in stress, HY & equities fall together (corr → +1) as investors buy high-quality developed-gov bonds → those gov bonds' corr to risky assets falls, may go negative. Bond-return volatility also rises for HY in a crisis. Regular cash flowPredictable coupons fund future obligations (living expenses, tuition, insurer payouts). Buy-and-hold laddered portfolio = no planned trading + roughly equal par maturing periodically. Assumes no significant credit risk & all payments made. Inflation hedgeStandard fixed-coupon (nominal) bonds do NOT hedge inflation — if inflation rises, fixed coupon loses real value & price must fall. Two that DO: inflation-linked & floating-rate.
Inflation-linked (real-rate) bond: PAR adjusts for inflation. 1M par, inflation 5% → par = 1.05M ; coupon = rate × adjusted par. Real rate 0.5% → first annual coupon = 1,050,000 × 0.005 = 5,250. → BOTH coupon & principal inflation-protected. Floating-coupon bond: coupon = MRR + spread; PAR unchanged. MRR 3.5% + 100bp on 1M → 45,000. Inflation +2% → MRR 5.5% + 100bp → 65,000 (par stays 1M). → COUPONS inflation-protected, principal is NOT.
Decisive detail: inflation-linked adjusts par (so coupon & principal both protected); floating adjusts the coupon rate only (principal unprotected). The floating coupon jump 45k→65k is a +44.4% rise while the linker's par/coupon rose only 5% — different mechanics, same "full protection" idea. In an efficient market all three (nominal/linked/floating, same issuer/maturity) price to the same expected return; realized winners depend on the actual inflation path.
Fixed-income mandates — the two types
Liability-basedAssets managed solely to meet expected future liability payouts; all asset cash flows reinvested until paid out — often called immunization. Forms below. Total returnDon't fund liabilities; target an absolute return OR (more commonly) match/beat a benchmark. Key metrics: active return (= value added = alpha) and active risk (= tracking error/tracking risk = σ of active return).
Cash flow matchingSimplest immunization — assets' cash flows occur when & in the size needed to meet payouts. Duration matchingMatch asset & liability duration so both move alike as rates change → ending values stay matched. Contingent immun. (CI)Hybrid of active + immunization. Fund with more than required (PVA > PVL → positive surplus). While surplus > 0, manage actively. Success → ultimate cost less than initial immunizing; if surplus hits zero → immediately immunize & cost is more than initial immunizing but by a known amount. Derivatives overlayFutures or swaps to implement duration matching or CI.
Pure indexingReplicate a bond index; zero active return/risk. Full replication is impractical (huge # of illiquid bonds) → instead match all risk factors (duration, credit/quality, sectors, prepayment) with some leeway on individual bonds; low turnover ~ index turnover. Enhanced indexingModest active return; duration still matched to index but small risk mismatches (over/underweight sectors & quality) allowed → slightly higher turnover. Active managementLarge deviations from index risk factors, greater active return sought; duration can be mismatched; turnover much higher.
Module 7.1 · Fixed-Income Portfolio Measures
LOS 7.bRisk & return measures — interpretation focus
L3 tests interpretation & use, not calculation. Know what each measure tells you:
MeasureWhat it is / tells you
Macaulay durationWeighted-avg time to receive CFs (weights = PV of CFs). Higher → wait longer → higher price volatility when yields change.
Modified durationMacaulay / (1 + periodic yield). Approx % price change for a 1% yield change (MD 7 → −7% if yields +1%).
Effective durationPrice sensitivity to a parallel benchmark-curve shift, by modeling prices. Used for complex bonds (embedded options, uncertain CFs).
Key rate (partial) durationSensitivity to a change at a specific maturity, others held constant → assesses nonparallel curve shifts.
Empirical durationInterest-rate sensitivity from regressing bond returns vs benchmark-yield changes — same interpretation as effective duration but from past observed behavior, not modeling.
Money (dollar) duration= MD × market value. Absolute currency gain/loss for a 1% yield change.
PVBP / DV01 / BPV= money duration × 0.0001. Absolute value change for a 1 bp yield move.
ConvexityNonlinearity of price-vs-yield; positive for option-free bonds. Positive convexity → price rises more than duration implies when yields fall & falls less when yields rise.
Effective convexityNonlinear version modeled from curve shifts; for complex/embedded-option bonds.
Spread duration% price sensitivity to a 1% credit-spread change.
Duration times spread (DTS)= spread duration × credit spread. Higher sensitivity when spreads are higher (spread changes tend to be proportional to spread levels).
Convexity factsValuable when yields expected to change → investors pay higher prices / accept lower yields for more convexity. Second-order: ~proportional to duration² (dur-20 bond has ~4× the convexity of a dur-10 bond). Directly related to dispersion of CFs in time — for a given Macaulay duration, the lowest-convexity bond is a zero-coupon (single CF at maturity). Portfolio aggregationPortfolio Macaulay/modified duration & convexity ≈ cash-weighted average of the individual bonds. Ex: 40% dur-10 + 60% dur-15 → (0.4×10)+(0.6×15) = 13. Effective duration/convexity of a portfolio use the PV₃/PV₋/PV₊ curve-shift formulas. Manager useExpect rates to fall → raise duration (bigger price gain); expect rates to rise → lower duration. Expect spreads to narrow → raise spread duration (may lower credit rating / buy higher-DTS bonds); expect spreads to widen → lower spread duration / raise average credit rating. Relative-value techniques rank bonds to pick the best expression of the view.
Portfolio effective duration & convexity (see Risk-Measures calculator): eff duration = (PV₋ − PV₊) / (2 · Δcurve · PV₀) eff convexity = (PV₋ + PV₊ − 2·PV₀) / (Δcurve² · PV₀)
Module 7.1 · Bond Liquidity
LOS 7.cBond liquidity, subsector differences & effect on PM
Correlations between FI sectors: bonds in the same market are highly correlated (shared macro). IG returns driven mainly by the benchmark sovereign curve; HY driven more by spread than rates → usually a negative rate–spread relationship (bad economy: low rates but high spreads) → HY correlates more with equity.
Liquidity = transact in large size, quickly, with minimal price deviation. On-the-run developed-gov bonds are very liquid; other bonds may trade rarely / at wide spreads.
Why illiquid(1) Huge number of bond issues (one issuer has many bonds, each unique in maturity/coupon/call — heterogeneous) vs one homogeneous common stock; (2) bonds trade OTC → higher search cost, less transparent past price/volume. On/off-the-runRecently-issued (on-the-run) is more liquid (dealer inventory). Over time bonds get locked in buy-and-hold portfolios; a new similar issue makes the old one off-the-run → liquidity falls → higher YTM = liquidity premium (extra yield for lack of liquidity; "illiquidity premium" = same thing). By subsectorSovereign on-the-run high-quality: high liquidity, large, homogeneous, used as benchmarks & repo collateral. Corporate: varies with quality & issue size → liquidity falls with lower quality & smaller size; small issuers harder to build a large holding & may be excluded from indexes.
Pricing dataOTC + infrequent trading → hard to price. Use matrix pricing — infer price from recent trades of bonds with similar features (maturity, quality, coupon). Portfolio constructionBuy-and-hold investors need less liquidity → accept less liquid bonds for higher yield. Active investors prefer more liquid bonds. Those anticipating possible early sales avoid illiquid (long-maturity, small issuers, private placements). Bid-ask costCost of crossing the spread ≈ duration × (ask yield − bid yield). Ex: duration 10, 20 bp spread → 10 × 0.002 = 0.02 = 2% if bought at ask & instantly sold at bid. Less-liquid, dealer-market bonds trade at wider bid-ask (dealers widen to be paid for holding harder-to-resell inventory).
Alternatives to direct bond investment:
Fixed-income ETFsReplicate many FI sectors; exchange-listed → traded intraday, high liquidity. Open-end mutual fundsDaily subscribe/redeem; diversification & economies of scale small investors can't get directly. Derivatives / TRSExchange bond futures/options & OTC swaps. Under a total return swap (TRS), the total-return receiver pays an interest rate + spread for the total return of a reference bond portfolio. Prefer TRS: needs little collateral vs fully funding an ETF. Drawbacks: counterparty risk of the payer, rollover risk at maturity, potential regulatory reform raising collateral/cost.
Module 7.2 · Modeling Return
LOS 7.dThe five-component fixed-income return model
Expected FI return = sum of five components. Same worked example throughout (par 50M, coupon 3.0%, price 101.50, projected price 102.419, C=28, MD=5.60, ΔY=−0.54%, Δspread=−0.06%, currency +3.925% on 40% foreign). See the Return-Model calculator.
1. Coupon income = annual coupon / current price = 3.0 / 101.50 = 2.956% 2. Rolldown return = (projected price − begin price) / begin price = (102.419 − 101.50) / 101.50 = 0.905% Rolling yield = #1 + #2 = 2.956 + 0.905 = 3.86% 3. Δ price from Δ benchmark yield (ΔY = −0.54%): (−MD × ΔY) + (½ × C × ΔY²) = (−5.60 × −0.0054) + (½ × 28 × (−0.0054)²) = 0.03024 + 0.00041 = 3.065% 4. Δ price from Δ credit spread (ΔS = −0.06%): (−MD × ΔS) + (½ × C × ΔS²) = (−5.60 × −0.0006) + (½ × 28 × (−0.0006)²) = 0.00336 + 0.000005 = 0.337% 5. Currency G/L = FX change × foreign weight = 3.925% × 0.40 = 1.570% TOTAL expected return = 2.956 + 0.905 + 3.065 + 0.337 + 1.570 = 8.833%
Rolling yield= coupon income + rolldown (components 1+2 combined). Rolldown assumes an unchanged yield curve. Rolldown signFlat curve, premium (discount) bond → price pulled to par → projected price lower (higher). Upward- (downward-) sloping curve → rolldown higher (lower) than start YTM (bond ages into a lower/higher point on the curve). Convexity effectSmall (only +0.041% here) — often insignificant for option-free bonds unless ΔY is large. Embedded-option bonds → use effective duration & convexity; floaters have low duration but still sensitivity to spreads. What's projectedOnly coupon income is (nearly) certain. Rolldown assumes an unchanged curve; the ΔY, Δspread & currency pieces are pure predictions. Model uses only duration & convexity — ignores relative-valuation shifts across individual bonds.
Prof's-note trap (Part 4): technically spread duration should be used for the spread component, but the curriculum example uses modified duration (a fair approximation for a fixed-coupon bond, but poor for floaters, where MD is low yet spread duration is high). In a question: use effective duration/convexity for Part 3 and spread duration/convexity for Part 4 when both are given.
Module 7.3 · Leverage & Tax
LOS 7.eLeverage — use, methods & risks
Leverage boosts return, attractive when rates/expected returns are low. As long as funds borrow at a rate below the return earned (rᵢ > rᲲ), leverage enhances return; it also raises interest-rate risk & losses if the asset return falls below the borrow rate. Borrowing is usually short-term → asset duration normally exceeds liability duration in a leveraged portfolio.
Leveraged portfolio return (return on equity): r_p = r_I + [(V_B / V_E) × (r_I − r_B)] r_I = return on invested assets ; r_B = borrow rate V_B = amount of leverage (borrowed) ; V_E = equity invested
Repo (repurchase)Owner "sells" a security for cash & agrees to "buy" it back later — functionally a collateralized loan; assets are collateral. Usually overnight, renegotiated daily. Ex: 100M overnight at 2.5% → pay back 100,000,000 × [1 + (0.025/360)]. Haircut: dealer delivers collateral worth >100% (e.g. 102% = 102M, a 2% haircut) → extra security for the lender; bigger haircut for riskier/less-liquid collateral. General collateral (cash-driven, any agreed gov bonds) vs security-driven (lender wants a specific bond → offers a lower repo rate). Bilateral vs tri-party (a bank holds & records the collateral). Repo rate may be adjusted for collateral quality instead of the haircut. FuturesSmall initial margin controls full contract value → leverage = (notional value − margin) / margin. SwapsA receive-fixed / pay-MRR swap ≈ buying fixed-rate bonds funded by floating borrowing → increases bond-market exposure & duration with no explicit funds. Receive-floating/pay-fixed = opposite. Post-2007–09 crisis, many swaps clear through a central clearinghouse. Securities lendingRelated to repo but supports short selling (short seller borrows the security to deliver). Lender takes collateral (often >100%, e.g. 105%) & can reinvest cash collateral. rebate rate = collateral earnings rate − security lending rate. Usually open-ended (no set maturity) → extra risk if a counterparty won't reverse. Lender earns more when the borrower badly needs that specific security.
Risks created by leverage: beyond the obvious, if borrowing cost rises above portfolio earnings (or rates rise → leveraged portfolio & collateral fall in value), lenders demand repayment & force liquidation. Selling under distress = fire sale; if widespread it drives a vicious cycle (each sale lowers prices → more repayment demands & halted lending).
LOS 7.fManaging taxable vs tax-exempt portfolios
Both seek the highest risk-adjusted return net of fees & costs; taxable is more complex because after-tax return & risk matter. Two return sources taxed differently: income vs capital gains (price change).
Tax factsIncome & gains usually taxed differently. Zero-coupon: imputed income (accretion to par) taxed yearly even with no cash flow. Gains usually taxed only at sale & at a lower rate than income; long-term (longer hold) often taxed below short-term. Capital losses may offset gains (sometimes carried forward, sometimes back for a refund). Taxable strategies(1) Realize losses to offset gains (selective tax-loss harvesting for partial sales / multiple lots); (2) extend holding to get long-term vs short-term rates; (3) extend holding to defer taxes; (4) weigh income-vs-gain rate differentials when selecting investments; (5) use tax-sheltered/advantaged accounts where possible. Funds vs SMACollective funds: income usually taxed to the fund/investor when earned; gain taxation varies — pass-through (taxed when fund realizes; that payment cuts later tax when shares sold) vs deferred (taxed only when fund shares are sold). A separately managed account (SMA) passes all income/gains/losses straight to the client's return — taxable to the client.
EXAMPLE — taxable vs tax-exempt (sell decision). Two substantially identical bonds, same market value; Bond A has a big unrealized gain, Bond B a big unrealized loss; B has a slightly higher yield. (1) Taxable investor: sell Bond B (realize the loss / avoid triggering a taxable gain now &mdash the reading frames it as avoiding realizing a gain and paying tax now). (2) Tax-exempt investor: sell Bond A, keep Bond B for its slightly better yield (taxes irrelevant).
PWM cross-check: the tax-drag intuition here is the same one the private-wealth tax calculator captures — the accrual-tax regime example returns a 39.7% tax drag on the stated inputs. Deferral & loss-harvesting are the levers that reduce that drag.
Module 7.4 · Liability-Driven Investing
LOS 7.gLiability-driven investing & the four liability types
LDI applies when there are definable future liabilities paid from portfolio assets — classified as passive total return, but "passive" doesn't mean do nothing (many strategies need continual monitoring). Mostly institutional (insurers, DB pensions), also individuals saving for retirement. Key terms:
ALMAsset-liability management — strategies considering assets in relation to liabilities; appropriate when PV of both assets & liabilities change with rates. LDITakes liabilities as given, manages assets to meet them (this reading's focus). ADLAsset-driven liabilities — takes assets as given, structures/adjusts the liabilities (e.g. a leasing company designs its debt to match its financial assets).
TypeAmountDateExampleModeling
Type IKnownKnownOption-free fixed-rate bondSimple duration (Macaulay/modified) is adequate — easiest to model
Type IIKnownUncertainCallable/putable bond; term life insurer (amount known, date not — law of large numbers estimates)Effective duration
Type IIIUncertainKnownFloating-rate instruments; real-rate bonds (TIPS)Effective duration
Type IVUncertainUncertainProperty & casualty; some DB plan liabilitiesEffective duration
Modeling rule: only Type I is simple enough for Macaulay/modified duration. Types II–IV need effective duration — model the initial curve shape plus assumed up/down shifts to estimate the amount & timing of payouts.
LOS 7.hCash flow matching (incl. multiple liabilities)
Single liabilitySimplest but least flexible immunization. Buy a zero-coupon bond with par & maturity matching the liability → no cash flow or price risk. Bonds must be default-free. May allow accounting defeasance (assets legally set aside & dedicated → both assets & liabilities removed from the balance sheet). Multiple liabilitiesCan use coupon bonds, built recursively from the longest liability backward: buy a bond whose par + final coupon exactly funds the longest liability; its earlier coupons partially meet earlier liabilities; then fund the next-longest with another bond's par+final coupon (crediting coupons of bonds already bought), and so on. Cash-in-advancePerfect matching is unlikely in practice. A cash-in-advance constraint requires the funding bond to mature before the liability date → exposes the portfolio to reinvestment risk: with an upward-sloping curve, cash received early must be reinvested at the lower short-end rates until payout.
LOS 7.iLaddered bond portfolios — construction, benefits, limits
A ladder holds roughly equal par across different maturities. Same duration could instead come from a bullet (concentrate at one middle maturity) or a barbell (short + long holdings); all three with the same duration share roughly the same price sensitivity to a parallel shift.
Benefit — liquidityRegular liquidity as bonds mature each year (matters when less-liquid bonds like corporates are used → less need to sell at wide bid-ask). Near-maturity bonds are less risky collateral & can borrow at favorable rates. Benefit — diversificationBroad diversification of cash flow across time & less concentrated exposure to nonparallel curve changes at specific maturities. Benefit — risk balanceDiversifies price risk (long-dated bonds) against reinvestment risk (short-dated); maturing bonds reinvest at long-term (typically higher) rates → keeps overall duration stable over time. Benefit — convexityMore convexity than a bullet (convexity relates to CF dispersion in time) — helpful under large parallel shifts. But the ladder is not as convex as a barbell. Target-date ETFsAlternative to individual bonds: a ladder of fixed-maturity (target-date) bond ETFs, each maturing in a designated year, passively managed. Often cheaper & more liquid than buying individual bonds if unanticipated sales are needed. DisadvantageFor some investors an ongoing (no target-date) passive index or active bond fund is better — larger, greater credit-risk diversification, more liquid than direct bonds.
