High-probability traps (9.4)
Average rate < marginal rate under any progressive system. Accrual tax drag > tax rate; increases with higher returns & longer horizons. Deferred-CG drag = tax rate (when basis = current value); the lowest-drag regime. Low cost basis raises drag — the embedded gain is a stored-up tax liability. Tax hits NOMINAL gains → inflation exacerbates tax erosion; worst for fixed income. More income (vs deferred CG) → higher tax drag at the same total return. Capital gains are taxed only when REALIZED.
What the IPS does
The Investment Policy Statement documents a private client's investment objectives, risk tolerance, time horizon, liquidity preferences, and other preferences/constraints. The manager uses it to construct the portfolio given prevailing capital-market conditions.
The six IPS sections (private client)
#SectionHolds
1Client Background & ObjectivesBackground (personal/financial/tax), outside assets, external cash flows; planned/unplanned goals; quantify, reconcile, prioritize (primary/secondary).
2Key Investment ParametersRisk tolerance, time horizon, asset-class preferences, liquidity preferences, other preferences, constraints.
3Portfolio Asset AllocationStrategic AA (targets) vs tactical AA (ranges).
4Portfolio Mgmt & ImplementationDiscretionary authority, rebalancing approach, tactical changes, implementation vehicles.
5Duties & ResponsibilitiesOf the private wealth manager (formulate/review, construct, monitor, report, vote proxies).
6IPS AppendixFrequently-changing items: modeled portfolio performance, capital market expectations.
1 · Client background & investment objectives
Background from personal, financial & tax information; identify ALL portfolio components + assets held outside (e.g. with another manager) + external cash flows (e.g. DB pension). Goals can be planned/unplanned, ongoing or one-off. Manager works to quantify objectives, reconcile competing ones, and prioritize into primary & secondary. Use capital sufficiency (capital needs) analysis to test feasibility and, where needed, revise objectives to be realistic.
Exam note: investment OBJECTIVES are prepared separately from risk tolerance — risk tolerance lives under Investment Parameters (section 2), not here.
2 · Key investment parameters
ParameterDetail
Risk toleranceWillingness + ability. Low for important goals, higher for low-priority; near-term goals → lower tolerance. Assess via questionnaires + conversations.
Time horizonDescribed as a range (e.g. >15y long, <10y short) — not a specific length. Multiple objectives → a different horizon each.
Asset-class preferencesAcceptable (or unsuitable) classes + their risk-return characteristics.
Liquidity preferencesNeeds not stated in background (e.g. cash reserve); preferences that restrict certain classes (e.g. dividend preference precludes small-growth stocks).
Other preferencesConcentrated single-stock position (past employment/inheritance); ethical investing.
ConstraintsRestrict the manager's choices (e.g. ESG / ethical investing).
Exam note: in THIS reading, risk tolerance / time horizon / liquidity / other preferences / constraints are investment parameters; taxes are part of the client's financial background, not a parameter here.
3 · Portfolio asset allocation
Strategic AA — long-term TARGET allocation per class; rebalanced periodically to maintain the target. Tactical AA — active strategy; normally specifies a range per class rather than a single target.
4 · Portfolio management & implementation
ItemDetail
Discretionary authorityManager acts without prior client approval. Full vs limited (e.g. only rebalance to agreed ranges). Nondiscretionary = can recommend but NOT act without approval.
RebalancingTime-based (quarterly/semiannual/annual — ignores deviations) vs threshold-based (rebalance once weights deviate by a set amount).
Tactical changesIPS states if manager may do tactical AA + acceptable weight ranges + how far beyond bounds.
ImplementationAcceptable vehicles (in-house/external managers, ETFs, mutual funds) + due-diligence process.
5 · Duties & responsibilities of the manager
Formulating & reviewing the IPS (incl. review frequency) Recommending/selecting investments & constructing the asset allocation Monitoring & rebalancing the portfolio; monitoring implementation costs Monitoring third-party service providers Reporting portfolio performance; reporting taxes & financial statements Voting proxies
6 · IPS Appendix (frequently-changing items)
Modeled portfolio performance — range of possible outcomes over different horizons + a distribution of returns at specific percentiles. Capital market expectations — expected return, risk & correlations of the asset classes available.
Reflex: capital market expectations & modeled portfolio behavior belong in the Appendix — NOT the portfolio-management section. Rebalancing methodology belongs in Portfolio Management.
"Which section?" — the exam's favourite trap
ItemSection
A specific funding goal / purchase / bequestObjectives
Risk tolerance, time horizonParameters
Cash reserve / need to sell quicklyParameters → Liquidity preferences
Acceptable / unsuitable asset classesParameters → Asset-class preferences
ESG / ethical restrictionParameters → Constraints
Concentrated single stockParameters → Other preferences
Strategic vs tactical targets/rangesAsset Allocation
Discretion · rebalancing method · vehiclesPortfolio Management
Modeled performance · capital market expectationsAppendix
TaxesFinancial background (NOT a parameter)
Elam — preparing investment objectives
William Elam, 30, inherited $750k; factory worker $50k, wife Elizabeth teacher $38k, 3 kids; DB pension (not vested), her 403(b); $20k credit-card debt. Stated: salaries/expenses grow only with inflation; don't improve lifestyle — grow the portfolio for college + retirement in 30y; set up a trust for the kids.
Purpose: pay children's college, fund the couple's retirement, set up a trust for children. Cash flows: salaries cover living costs (inflation-adjusted) → portfolio distributions begin when college starts in ~10y (pay off the credit card immediately). Manager's job: help quantify & prioritize the competing objectives; use capital sufficiency analysis to test feasibility & revise if unsupported.
Time horizons (multiple): college >10y · trust for children after college likely >20y · retirement >30y. Expressed as ranges/"exceeding", not exact figures.
DuBois — revising an existing IPS
DuBois, 65, retired 5y; son no longer needs support (both got promotions); modest lifestyle unchanged; equities should be domestic only; portfolio $2M; horizon >15y; withdraw $75k/yr inflation-adjusted (highest priority); cash reserve up to $25k; bequest $1.2M each to son & museum ($2.4M total) at death.
IPS sectionChange
ObjectivesPrimary is now retirement lifestyle (son support removed); add bequest $1.2M each to son & museum; distribute $75k/yr inflation-adjusted; quantify museum gift over time.
Risk toleranceNo change — still able/willing to accept short-/medium-term volatility.
Time horizonNo change — still reasonable to exceed 15 years.
Asset-class preferencesEquities = domestic only; manager advises on the return & diversification cost; MVO must incorporate the no-foreign-equities constraint.
Liquidity preferencesCash reserve raised $10k → $25k.
Other preferencesNo change (keeps Chic Apparel — not a concentration risk, actively traded).
ConstraintsEquities domestic-only; note Chic Apparel has significant embedded capital gains.
The teaching points: (1) a circumstance change reorders priorities (retirement becomes primary). (2) A domestic-only equity preference is an asset-class preference + constraint and must flow into the MVO. (3) Portfolio management / responsibilities / review sections need no change — only objectives & parameters.

High-probability traps (9.5)
Objectives = goals; risk tolerance / liquidity / asset-class are parameters — don't put them in objectives. ESG / ethical = constraint; single-stock concentration = "other preferences". Capital market expectations & modeled performance → Appendix; rebalancing/discretion/vehicles → Portfolio Management. Need to sell quickly = liquidity (a parameter), goes in liquidity preferences. Time horizons are RANGES, not specific lengths; multiple objectives → one horizon each. Strategic AA = targets; tactical AA = ranges. Nondiscretionary = recommend but can't act without client approval. Taxes = financial background, NOT an investment parameter (this reading).
The command word dictates the answer SHAPE
Most lost marks come from answering a different question than the one asked. Match the verb to the shape before you write a word.
CommandRequired shapeMark-killer
Identify / State / ListJust name it — a label, one line.Padding with explanation wastes time, earns nothing extra.
Identify and discuss / describe / explainLabel + mechanism/consequence. The "discuss" half is ~half the marks.Stopping at the label — the #1 leak.
Determine … JustifyState the answer + the reason(s) FROM the vignette that drive it.Bare conclusion with no justification = the conclusion mark only.
Justify which / RecommendPick one + why it wins + why the others fail.Leaving the pick bare, or not dismissing the alternatives.
Calculate / Determine (numeric)Show the working line, not just the final number.Skipping the formula → losing method marks even if blank.
Two / at least oneThe grader has a slot per point. "At least one" still rewards two.Writing one point when two are asked = half marks max.
Other than YY is forbidden — answer with something else.Naming Y scores zero for that part.
Your pattern (from your 6 attempts): you consistently nail the label/conclusion but stop one sentence short of the "discuss" mark, and you write ONE point when TWO are asked. Fixing just those two habits recovers most of your lost marks.
The 3-step drill — run it on every part
1. Read the command word first. Underline it. How many points? What shape? 2. Mine the vignette for the planted facts that answer THIS exact command (see next tab). 3. Write label + mechanism per point. For each point ask: "Have I said WHY / SO WHAT?" If not, add the sentence.
Read the vignette twice: stated vs missing/implied
These stems plant facts on purpose. Every number, every "he is concerned about…", every "highest priority" is there to be used. Many PWM questions ask what is missing or what a planted fact implies — not what's plainly stated.
Pass 1 — what's stated: list the hard facts (ages, salary, portfolio, goals, horizons, risk comments). Pass 2 — what's missing or implied: what would a complete IPS background need that ISN'T here? What does a planted concern imply for risk tolerance / priority / section placement?
Worked: "missing component of Cree's financial background"
A complete financial background needs personal, financial AND tax info, all assets, and external cash flows. Pass-2 scan of Cree finds:
Candidate gapScores?
Tax status of the portfolio (taxable vs tax-deferred)YES — drives after-tax return needed for capital-sufficiency analysis.
Pension / employer retirement incomeYES — a future cash-flow component of his background.
Current expenses (your answer)Defensible, but the book wanted the two above. Expenses are partly implied ("salary provides for expenses").
Lesson: the question said "at least one" but the model gives TWO — and the strongest gaps are tax status and pension income because the curriculum literally lists "personal, financial, and tax" as the background inputs. Scan for those named categories first.
The "test it against the command" check
Before committing a point, ask: does this item actually answer the exact command?
Cree goal-quantification trap: you picked "retirement" (already quantified → scores 0) and "antiques priority" (not an unquantified goal). The command wanted goals that are UNQUANTIFIED and COMPETE for funds → university expenses and the apartment-building scope. A point that is already-quantified, not-a-goal, or off-command earns nothing — even if true.
Your biggest leak: stopping one sentence short
You repeatedly reach the right conclusion and the first reason, then stop. The mark for "discuss/justify" lives in the second and third reasons — usually the time horizon, the competing goal, or the specific planted fact.
Side-by-side: Cree retirement risk tolerance (Determine + Justify)
Your answerFull-mark answer

(2) He'll accept a 10% drop in planned spending → willing. (3) Even the linked medical-expense concern carries higher tolerance because retirement is 17y away AND he views the rental property as a stable income stream to cover it."
What you missed: the time horizon (the single most important justification for risk tolerance) and the medical-expense/rental-income reasoning. The conclusion was right; the marks were in the reasons you didn't write.

Your answerFull-mark answer

She has NOT retired yet (retiring in coming months), so she can't be in early retirement (which is ~65–75, the active retirement period). Peak accumulation (~50–60) precedes this."
What you missed: the discriminator is "has not retired yet" → pre-retirement. The phrase "retiring in coming months" is the trap — it points at retirement, but until she actually retires she's pre-retirement. Always pick the PRECISE label, and justify by ruling out the neighbours.
The "so what?" test
After each point, force one more sentence answering "why does this matter for the IPS / the decision?" If your point is "tax status is missing," the so-what is "→ because it drives the after-tax return needed for capital-sufficiency analysis." That second clause is the mark.
You left every calculation essay blank — these are the most learnable marks
They reuse the same formulas as Module 9.4. Always write the formula line first (method marks), then plug in.
Patel — after-tax distribution vs shortfall
Shortfall = need − pension − business = 200,000 − 50,000 − 120,000 = 30,000
After-tax annual distribution = B × [1 + r(1 − tₓ)]^T − 1, with T = 1 = 4,000,000 × [0.02 × (1 − 0.40)] = 48,000
Distribution 48,000 > shortfall 30,000 → more than sufficient. (Ignores capital-appreciation return, which only adds to the surplus.)
Patel — retirement needs in 10y after inflation (5%)
Needs 200,000 real; pension 50,000 is inflation-linked → need 150,000 real from business + portfolio.
Real business income (10y) = 120,000 / (1.05)¹⁰ = 73,670 Subtotal still needed from portfolio = 150,000 − 73,670 = 76,330 Real after-tax growth factor = (1 + r)/(1 + π) ^T = (1.065 / 1.05)¹⁰ = 1.1524 Real portfolio value (10y) = 4,000,000 × 1.1524 = 4,609,598 Real cash distribution = 1.2% × 4,609,598 = 55,315 (1.2% = 2% pre-tax × (1 − 0.40)) Shortfall in 10y = 76,330 − 55,315 = 21,015
→ Patel faces a ~21,015 real income shortfall in 10y; he may liquidate small portions of the portfolio (which then lowers future distributions — note the trade-off).
Patel — sell securities to buy the vacation home? (method)
Comparative FV: compute the after-tax future value of keeping the securities vs selling to buy the home, over the holding period, then pick the higher.
Keep path: grow securities at 6.5% capital + reinvest dividends net of 40% tax (= 1.2%); track the rising cost basis each year; liquidate at the end and pay 20% CG on the gain over basis. Buy-home path: grow the home at 8%, pay 20% CG on sale; the remaining securities grow likewise. Conclusion (book): NOT buying the home is the better value strategy — the securities' after-tax compounding beats the home, before even considering property taxes / leverage.
Exam tip: even if you can't finish every year's arithmetic, writing the two FV structures + the comparison logic earns most of the method marks.
Desai — current average tax rate (progressive bands)
Taxable income = salary + RE income + taxable dividends + interest = 550,000 + 60,000 + (10% × 700,000) + 15,000 = 695,000 (retirement-account dividends are tax-deferred → excluded; only the 700k brokerage yields taxable dividends) Tax = 120,000 (on first 500k) + 35% × (695,000 − 500,000) = 188,250 Average tax rate = 188,250 / 695,000 = 27.09%
Two planted traps: (1) only the brokerage account's 10% dividend is taxable — the tax-deferred retirement account's dividends are NOT taxed annually; (2) use the cumulative band figure (120,000) then the marginal 35% on the excess — don't tax the whole 695k at one rate. Average (27.09%) < marginal (35%), as always.
Cree 1 — missing financial-background component (Identify & discuss, ≥1 → give 2)
Tax status of the portfolio (taxable vs tax-deferred) — drives the after-tax return needed for capital-sufficiency analysis; without it the real return objective can't be set. Employer pension (does it exist, expected amount) — a future cash-flow component that materially changes what the portfolio must fund.
Your answer (current expenses): defensible but partly implied by "salary provides for expenses"; weaker than the two named-category gaps. Fix: give TWO points, lead with tax status.
Cree 2 — two areas to improve goal quantification
Children's university expenses — start in 10y for 12–15y; unquantified and competes with retirement (17y). Quantifying tests consistency between the two. Apartment-building scope — how much to spend + expected rental income + maintenance; a near-term (3y) need that must be reconciled with the long-term goals.
Your answer: retirement (already quantified → 0) and antiques priority (not an unquantified competing goal → off-command). Fix: pick UNQUANTIFIED goals that COMPETE for funds.
Cree 3 — how capital sufficiency analysis aids prioritization
It tests whether current + future capital resources can support all goals. Once university & the apartment are quantified, it estimates the likelihood of achieving each goal (retirement, education, apartment, philanthropy, antiques). If resources are insufficient, Cree can prioritize — adjust down or eliminate lower-priority goals and protect the most important. (You left this blank; the structure is: define it → apply it to his goals → say what he does if it falls short.)
Cree 4 — retirement risk tolerance (Determine & justify)
Higher. 17-year horizon (time to recover) + accepts a 10% spending drop (willing) + the medical-expense concern is offset by the rental property as a stable income source.
Your gap: had the conclusion + 10% reason; missing the horizon and the rental-income reasoning. (See "The Discuss Half" tab.)
Sili — HC / FC / total wealth across the life cycle
Financial assets & real estate rise over time to OFFSET the decline in human capital as her career matures → protect total future wealth. 28→35 assumptions: illiquid start-up stakes become valuable (the ~$80m gap between net worth $100m and investable $20m); financial assets keep growing to reach $20m investable; real-estate equity rises. Retirement / decumulation: HC declines as she does fewer advisory roles; FC keeps growing while she invests well; eventually she converts FC into philanthropic donations → total wealth finally declines (decumulation).
All three you left blank — but they're pure life-cycle logic (Module 9.2): HC falls with age, FC rises with saving/investing, total wealth peaks near retirement then draws down.
Desai — missing investment parameter
Risk tolerance (the vignette says Zhong failed to ask about volatility preferences) — the client's ability AND willingness to withstand portfolio volatility.
Your answer: listed risk tolerance + time horizon + liquidity. The stem specifically said she missed volatility preferences → only risk tolerance is correct. Lesson: a planted "failed to ask about volatility" points at ONE parameter — don't over-list.
Silva — life-cycle stage (Determine & justify)
Pre-retirement — few years before retiring; max income, highest accumulation. She has NOT retired yet, so not early retirement (~65–75); peak accumulation (~50–60) precedes this.
Your answer: "early retirement" off the phrase "retiring in coming months." Fix: hasn't-retired-yet → pre-retirement; justify by ruling out the neighbouring stages.
Reading 9 · An Overview of Private Wealth Management
Full-reading recap, module by module: wealth types & distribution (9.a), human/financial capital across the life cycle (9.b), returns, risks, objectives & constraints vs. HC/FC (9.c), taxation & inflation (9.d), and private clients & the IPS (9.e). Every calculation — progressive tax, employment+investment tax, tax drag (accrual/deferral/basis), inflation adjustment, the combined income+CG comprehensive example, and the holistic balance sheet — is node-verified against the textbook figures and reproduced by the widget's Tax & Wealth Calculator.
How to read the driver rows: the left label is the lever; the right side is what that lever does to the value. Focus on why a number lands where it does, not just the label — that's where marks are dropped under time pressure.
Module 9.1 · Wealth Across the World
LOS 9.aTypes of individual wealth & how it is created / distributed
Key wealth definitions (Figure 9.1). The one that trips people up is net worth vs. aggregate vs. economic net worth — know which items each includes.
MeasureWhat it is / the decisive detail
Aggregate wealthTotal value of all assets owned (personal property, financial, real, productive, rights). Asset-only — stated BEFORE subtracting liabilities.
Net worthAssets − liabilities, using values easy to measure (listed securities, real estate, debts). Excludes complex intangibles like copyrights.
Financial wealthAll financial assets (funds, stocks, bonds, hedge funds) + accrued pension rights. Excludes stakes in family businesses → those are productive wealth.
Real wealthTangible assets: real estate + commodities. Not personal property or financial assets. Primary residence is often the biggest piece.
Personal propertyCars, clothes, furniture. Not expected to appreciate; may be worth more to the holder than fair market value.
Productive wealthAssets used to generate wealth via production/business (e.g. a direct shareholding in a family business).
Liquid wealthEasily converted to cash (listed securities). A subset of the above.
Investable wealthFinancial & other assets readily available for investment; usually a subset of financial wealth. This is the main focus of private wealth management.
Economic net worthNet worth extended: assets also include pension benefits + human capital; liabilities also include PV of future consumption + bequests. HC = PV of future earnings.
Real wealth creationEntrepreneurship + asset-price appreciation = primary sources in most economies. Global stock-market cap & global GDP both grew ~7%/yr, 1970–2021, and are highly correlated. NOT new wealthGambling wins, inheritances, lottery, sudden fame — only a transfer of wealth within a country, not an increase in overall net wealth. (Quiz 9.1 Q4 → none of lottery/inheritance/fame create new wealth.) Long-term growth driversMarket-oriented policies & competition, shift to free-market capitalism (privatization), lower regulatory barriers, global connectivity, entrepreneurship, asset-price appreciation. Long-term DRAGState ownership of major industries decreases long-term growth (Quiz 9.1 Q2 → A). Foreign investment & competition increase it.
Regional drivers (know the one-liner for each):
North AmericaBusiness formation & entrepreneurship + productivity + financial-asset appreciation. Uneven — benefits professionals/executives with equity & business-sellers. EuropeSimilar to NA (economic growth) but more wealth in privately-held family business & inherited real estate. E. Europe: post-Soviet market transition; some oil/mineral wealth to politically-connected oligarchs. (EU+NA ≈ 57% of global wealth.) Asia-PacificAgrarian → manufacturing/services; heavy education & training investment, high entrepreneurship, inward FDI. Latin AmericaModernized but persistent inequality & instability; Argentina hyperinflation (ARS near parity 2012 → 175/USD 2022). Middle EastPetroleum wealth, very concentrated in inheriting families; diversifying away from oil (Saudi ~40% of GDP oil-related). AfricaRising commodities revenue + inward FDI; high inequality, wealth concentrated in ruling elite/executives/professionals.
Inequality & the Gini coefficient (Figures 9.2–9.3):
Gini = 0Perfect equality. Each 10% of population holds 10% of wealth; mean = median; Lorenz curve = 45° line. Gini → 1Maximum inequality. Wealth in the hands of very few; mean » median (positive skew). Higher Gini = higher skew & more Lorenz bowing. Rises whenSevere economic contraction / recession (GFC 2007–09, COVID), greater income variability, fewer safety nets. (Quiz 9.1 Q6: 0.5→0.6 → A, contraction.) Russia ≈0.9, China ≈0.82. Mean vs medianGini 0.5 → positive skew → mean > median (Quiz 9.1 Q7 → C). Lorenz curve = area under the cumulative wealth-vs-household curve.
Global stats to anchor (Credit Suisse 2022): 53% of adults had wealth < USD 10k; only 1% > USD 1m. Median USD 8,360 vs mean USD 87,489 (positive skew). Bottom 50% held <1%; top decile held 82% of global wealth.
HNW / UHNW & family offices: no precise cutoff, but complexity rises with wealth. UHNW = tens of millions USD (centimillionaires >$100m, billionaires) often use family offices. Family-office primary objective preserve & grow wealth across generations, aware of the family's unique opportunities/challenges (multiple tax & legal jurisdictions). Tax havens vs. ethics/political-risk trade-off for cross-border moves.
Quiz 9.1 traps. Q1 → B: a savings account & a tax-advantaged investment account are both investable assets. (A is false — vested DB benefits are in aggregate wealth; C is false — family-business shares are productive, not financial, wealth.) Q3 → B is least accurate: it's the Middle East / oligarchs (E. Europe), not Asia-Pacific, that concentrate natural-resource wealth. Q5 (hyperinflation) → A: currency weakens & nominal local-currency GDP per capita rises. (Circled/verified from photos: Q2→A, Q6→A. Others reasoning-derived; official keys not in photos.)
Module 9.2 · Life-Cycle View of Human Capital
LOS 9.bHow HC, FC & economic net worth change across the seven stages
The seven financial stages of life — and the key fact attached to each:
1. EducationBefore the workforce; financially dependent on parents; little FC. 2. Early careerEnters workforce, starts a family, begins to save, takes on debt (house). 3. Career development~ages 35–50; income growth but rising responsibilities/outgoings limit ability to save. 4. Peak accumulationMaximum earnings. Retirement planning & tax minimization a key focus. 5. PreretirementFew years before retiring; may adjust lifestyle expectations to match wealth. 6. Early retirementMost active retirement period; keep some risk in the portfolio to ensure asset growth. 7. Late retirementComplex, unknown duration; longevity risk = outliving financial assets; health care a concern.
Human capital (HC) = PV of expected future employment income. Conceptually simple, practically un-valuable exactly. Exam-relevant inputs:
Future incomeCurrent income × assumed growth rate × remaining years of employment. Survival prob.Weight each future year by probability of survival (actuarial tables — may not fit an individual's risk profile). Discount rateNominal risk-free rate + risk premium for earnings-stream uncertainty. Volatile professions (investment banker) → higher premium → discounted more heavily than a stable government worker/teacher.
Holistic (economic) balance sheet — extends net worth to include HC & pensions as assets, and PV of future consumption + bequests as liabilities. The worked example (all figures in 000s) is the calculation to lock:
Assets (000s)Liabilities (000s)
Current assets500Short-term debt175
Investment assets1,500Home mortgage500
Home750PV of future consumption3,500
DC plan balance1,450Planned bequests1,000
Private pension40
Government pension450
Future labor income (HC)250
Total assets4,940Total liabilities5,175
Traditional BSAssets 4,200 (500+1,500+750+1,450) vs explicit debt 675 (175+500) → looks healthy (+3,525). Holistic BS4,940 − 5,175 = −235 net worth. The italic items (pensions, HC, PV consumption, bequests) flip the picture. InterpretationNegative economic net worth → consumption/bequest plans are unrealistic & must eventually change. Caveats: harder to value the extra items; could be estimation error; may be a missing asset (e.g. expected inheritance). Low HC (250) relative to pensions signals the individual is near retirement.
HC composition over the life cycle & entrepreneurship:
YoungHC is the dominant asset; FC small. Over timeRemaining work-life shortens → HC declines; savings/investment build → FC rises. Total wealth (HC+FC) & FC peak near retirement, then draw down. EntrepreneurGives up stable employment income for volatile business cash flows. Unlike HC, business value can be turned into FC when the owner liquidates the stake → entrepreneurship adds to total wealth & offsets the HC decline.
Diversification rule (very testable): use pension & financial assets to diversify the risk embedded in HC.
• Government employee / stable salary → can take MORE equity risk in the financial portfolio (bond-like HC) → greater growth. (Quiz 9.2 Q3 → B: more of FC to equities vs an entrepreneur.)
• Entrepreneur / volatile HC → portfolio should be more fixed-income-heavy & include industries not correlated with the business; trade-off is lower returns may pressure meeting objectives.
• Pensions carry risk too (private-pension failure, government-pension shortfall) — less concern for the very wealthy but real for pension-reliant clients.
Quiz 9.2 keys (reasoning-derived; official keys not in photos). Q1 least accurate → A: the discount rate uses the nominal (not real) risk-free rate + risk premium. (B & C are true.) Q2 least likely a liability on a holistic BS → A: human capital is an ASSET; planned bequests & PV of future consumption are the liabilities. Q3 → B (above).
Module 9.3 · Individual Investor Considerations
LOS 9.cReturns, risks, objectives & constraints vs. human & financial capital
Returns — think in inflation-adjusted (real) terms. Inflation erodes purchasing power & compounds; objectives need returns that outpace inflation, not just nominal returns. Distinguish outpacing inflation vs. hedging against inflation:
EquitiesOutpace inflation over the long term (above-inflation real return), but volatile short-term & may NOT outpace persistent/rising inflation short-term. → long-term outpacer, not a reliable short-term hedge. CommoditiesOil/gold prices can outperform during inflationary periods (commodity prices may cause inflation) → short-term hedge. But don't always beat persistent inflation; prices volatile. Real estateHedge — property prices track the general price level; rents may be pegged to inflation indexes. But can stagnate/drop in inflationary times if economic uncertainty is high. Fixed incomeMost bonds are NOT inflation-linked → suffer in real terms. Inflation-linked govt bonds keep pace but offer low real returns.
Risks individuals face:
Return volatilityFluctuations in value & returns. Drawdown riskDifference between the investment's peak value and its lowest point over a period. Not a realized loss unless forced to liquidate at that low. Missing objectivesFailing to meet financial objectives — from market conditions OR under-allocating capital to the goal. MitigantVolatility & drawdown risk are reduced by diversification across asset classes.
Four ways to describe a client's risk orientation — keep tolerance, capacity, and perception distinct:
Risk toleranceBoth willingness AND ability to take risk. Opposite = risk aversion. Risk capacityAbility only — based on wealth, income, horizon, liquidity needs, importance of goals. Higher capacity = portfolio can sustain losses without jeopardizing goals. Risk perceptionSubjective view of investment risk; varies by client; the wealth manager can influence it via education. EvaluationQuestionnaires + conversations. Conversations surface past successes/failures, perception & background hard to get from a questionnaire (Quiz 9.3 Q2 → C: capacity AND perception).
Risk capacity is DECREASED by (drivers of lower ability to bear risk):
Shorter horizonLess time to recover from losses. Large critical goalsGoals large relative to portfolio size. Important / non-deferrable goalsGoals that matter or can't be postponed. High liquidity needsMore cash demands on the portfolio. Sole source of supportPortfolio is the only support, or client can't tolerate value losses.
Objectives & constraints — goal categories:
Planned goalsReasonably estimated within a specified time horizon. Retirement, specific purchases (residence), education of dependents, family events (weddings), charitable giving, wealth transfer during life or at death. Unplanned goalsUnexpected expenditures — harder to deal with due to uncertain amount and/or timing. E.g. property repairs, medical costs not covered by insurance, long-term care.
Wealth-manager's role in formulating goals: Quantifying (make vague goals specific & realistic), Prioritizing (into primary vs. secondary when goals compete — higher priority need not be the earliest-in-time), and Changing (revise goals & strategy as circumstances change). Use capital sufficiency (capital needs) analysis to test whether goals are achievable and revise if not.
Risk tolerance by goalLow risk tolerance for more important goals; higher tolerance for lower-priority goals. Near-term goals → lower tolerance than long-term goals. Sample question"When you invest, do you focus on: A always gain / B usually gain / C always loss?" Answer C → strong risk aversion → indicates the client's risk perception.
Quiz 9.3 keys (reasoning-derived; official keys not in photos). Q1 most accurate on inflation protection → B: equities give a long-term above-inflation return and a short-term hedge. (A false — FI suffers, esp. short run; C false — inflation-linked bonds protect short and long run.) Q2 → C: a questionnaire helps understand capacity + perception. DuBois goals worked example lives in Module 9.5 recap below.
Module 9.4 · Impact of Taxation & Inflation
LOS 9.dHow different taxes & inflation influence investment decisions
How each return source is taxed (drives the whole module):
Interest incomeTaxed in the year received (accrual). Some jurisdictions exempt some interest or apply favorable rates. Dividend incomeTaxed in the year received (accrual). Often favorable — the company already paid tax on profits. Capital gainsLevied on realized gains (asset must be sold/transferred) → deferral basis. Rate varies by asset type/holding period; longer-term gains taxed favorably to encourage long-term investment & saving. Wealth taxesAnnual tax on wealth in some systems; unusual; excluded from this module's calcs. Accrual vs deferralAccrual = taxed annually (dividends, interest). Deferral = tax postponed to realization (capital gains). "Deferred" here has no link to the accounting concept of deferred tax.
Calc 1 — Progressive tax. Each slice of income taxed at its band rate; investment income sits on top of employment income. Baghurst, taxable income EUR 600,000:
Bands: 0–10k @10% | 10–40k @20% | 40–100k @30% | 100–500k @40% | 500k+ @50% Cumulative tax to 500k (Column 3) = 185,000 Tax = 185,000 + (600,000 − 500,000) × 50% = EUR 235,000 Average rate = 235,000 / 600,000 = 39.17% | Marginal rate = 50%
Why avg < marginal: lower slices are taxed at lower band rates, so the blended (average) rate is always below the top (marginal) band in a progressive system. (Quiz 9.4 Q3 → A.)
Calc 2 — Employment + investment income. Emp 450k, interest 60k, dividends 100k.
Case 1 (all income treated equally) — total 610,000: Tax = 185,000 + (610,000 − 500,000) × 50% = EUR 240,000 Average = 240,000 / 610,000 = 39.34% Case 2 (25k interest EXEMPT; dividends 20% flat): Taxable interest = 60,000 − 25,000 = 35,000 Progressive base = 450,000 + 35,000 = 485,000 → cumulative to 100k = 25,000; + (485,000 − 100,000) × 40% = 25,000 + 154,000 = 179,000 Dividends 100,000 × 20% = 20,000 Total tax = 179,000 + 20,000 = EUR 199,000 Average = 199,000 / 610,000 = 32.62%
Driver: Case 2 is lower purely because 25k interest is exempt and dividends get a flat 20% (vs the 40–50% top bands they'd otherwise hit). Same gross income, different tax treatment → 6.7pp lower average rate.
Calc 3 — Tax drag (accrual). 50k, 8%/yr, 25% tax annually. FV = [1 + R(1−t)]T per unit.
20y: FV = 50,000 × [1 + 0.08(1−0.25)]20 = EUR 160,357 No-tax: 50,000 × 1.0820 = 233,048 Tax drag = (233,048 − 160,357) / (233,048 − 50,000) = 72,691 / 183,048 = 39.7% 30y: FV = 50,000 × [1.06]30 = EUR 287,175 | No-tax = 503,133 Tax drag = 215,958 / 453,133 = 47.7%
Decisive detail (Quiz 9.4 Q4 → A): with accrual tax, the tax drag EXCEEDS the tax rate (39.7% > 25%) because you lose 25% of the gain every year and forgo compounding on it. Tax drag rises with a longer horizon (39.7% → 47.7%) and with a higher pretax return. So Q4's B ("decreases for higher returns") & C ("increases for shorter periods") are both backwards.
Calc 4 — Tax deferral (capital gains realized at end). Same 50k, 8%, 25%, 20y, all gain realized at end.
FV = 50,000 × 1.0820 − (50,000 × 1.0820 − 50,000) × 25% = EUR 187,286 Tax drag = (233,048 − 187,286) / (233,048 − 50,000) = 45,762 / 183,048 = 25.0%
The key contrast: under pure deferral (all return taxed once at the end) the tax drag = the tax rate exactly (25% = 25%). Deferral lets gains compound tax-free until realization → far lower drag than accrual (25% vs 39.7% for the same inputs). Tax-advantaged retirement accounts are a further deferral example → drag reduced to the tax rate.
Calc 5 — Impact of cost basis on CG. Low basis = a stored-up untaxed liability. Baghurst: 50k value, cost basis 20k, 8%, 20y, 25% deferred.
FV = 50,000 × 1.0820 − (50,000 × 1.0820 − 20,000) × 25% = EUR 179,786 (using basis factor B = 20,000/50,000 = 0.25) Tax drag = (233,048 − 179,786) / (233,048 − 50,000) = 53,262 / 183,048 = 29.1%
Why drag (29.1%) > deferral (25%): the 30,000 embedded gain above cost basis (50k − 20k) gets taxed on top of future gains → a low basis raises the effective drag. Formula: FV = (1+R)T(1−tcg) + B×tcg.
Calc 6 — Inflation adjustment. Take the nominal after-tax 179,786 to real terms at 3% over 20y:
FV(real, after-tax) = 179,786 / 1.0320 = EUR 99,543
Inflation + tax interaction (Quiz 9.5 Q6 context). Taxes are levied on nominal gains, so inflation exacerbates the tax erosion on long-term gains — an asset merely keeping pace with inflation is still taxed on the nominal "gain." Inflation has a GREATER eroding impact on after-tax gains than on annual income, and tax-advantaged accounts protect against tax but not against inflation's loss of purchasing power. The least accurate claim (Quiz 9.5 Q6 → B) is that "as long as the nominal-vs-inflation gap is the same, the impact is the same" — false, because the nominal base being taxed differs.
Calc 7 — Comprehensive (income + capital gains combined). 200,000 portfolio, 3% dividend income + 6% price appreciation, both taxed 20%, dividends on accrual, CG realized at 15y.
Case 1 (as stated): Annual return = 6% + 3%×(1−0.2) = 8.4% First term = 1.08415 = 3.353 | CG ratio = 6% / 8.4% = 71.4% Growth 3.353 − 1 = 2.353 ; net CG tax = 71.4% × 2.353 × 20% = 0.336 After-tax factor = 3.353 − 0.336 = 3.017 → FV = × 200,000 = EUR 603,379 Case 2 (swap: 6% dividend, 3% appreciation): Annual return = 3% + 6%×(1−0.2) = 7.8% ; first term 1.07815 = 3.085 CG ratio = 3% / 7.8% = 38.5% ; net CG tax = 38.5% × 2.085 × 20% = 0.160 After-tax factor = 3.085 − 0.160 = 2.925 → FV = EUR 584,958 Tax drag (no-tax factor = 1.0915 = 3.642, gain 2.642): Case 1 drag = (3.642 − 3.017)/2.642 = 23.7% Case 2 drag = (3.642 − 2.925)/2.642 = 27.2%
Why Case 2 drag > Case 1: Case 2 has a higher proportion of return as income (6% vs 3%), which is taxed annually on accrual → loses compounding → higher drag, even though total pretax return (9%) is identical. More income share → more accrual tax → more drag.
Module Quiz 9.4 answers (reasoning & node-verified; official keys not in photos).
Q1 (emp 150k + realized CG 100k + div 25k, all equal, bands 5/10/20/30/40%): total 275k → 59,500 + (275−250)k×40% = 69,500; avg 69,500/275,000 = 25.3% → A (25%). (A circled in photo.)
Q2 (dividends exempt, CG 20% flat): prog on 150k emp = 14,500 + (150−100)k×30% = 29,500; + CG 100k×20% = 20,000 → total EUR 49,500 → B. (✓ in photo.)
Q3 → A: progressive avg rate < marginal rate. (A circled.)
Q4 → A: accrual tax drag > the applied tax rate. (A circled.)
Q5 (MV 80k, basis 20k, 7%, 30% CG, 10y deferred): 80k×1.0710 − (80k×1.0710 − 20k)×30% = ~116,000 → B (GBP 116,000). (B circled.)
Q6 (inflation, least accurate) → B (same gap ≠ same impact). (B circled.)
Q7 (500k, 3% income + 5% appr, 25% both, income accrual, CG at 20y): using the book's combined method, after-tax factor 3.53 vs no-tax 1.0820=4.66 → drag ≈ 30.9% → A. (Reasoning-derived; not circled in photos. This matches the curriculum's Comprehensive-Example structure.)
Module 9.5 · Individual Investors & the IPS
LOS 9.ePrivate vs. institutional clients & formulating a private-client IPS
The IPS documents a private client's objectives, risk tolerance, horizon, liquidity preferences & constraints; the manager builds the portfolio given prevailing capital-market conditions. A private-client IPS covers five areas — and the exam constantly tests which item belongs in which section:
1. Background & objectivesClient background (personal, financial & tax info; assets in & outside the portfolio; external cash flows like a DB pension) + quantified & prioritized investment objectives (primary vs secondary). Taxes live here, in financial background. 2. Key investment parametersRisk tolerance, time horizon, asset-class preferences, liquidity preferences, other investment preferences, constraints. In this reading, risk tolerance/horizon/liquidity/other-prefs/constraints are all parameters (not "objectives"). 3. Portfolio asset allocationStrategic AA = long-term targets, rebalanced to maintain. Tactical AA = active, usually a range per class rather than a point target. 4. Portfolio management & implementationDiscretionary authority (full / limited / nondiscretionary), rebalancing (time-based vs threshold-based), tactical-change authority & bounds, implementation (in-house/external managers, ETFs, funds, due diligence). 5. Duties & responsibilitiesFormulate/review IPS, select investments & build AA, monitor & rebalance, monitor costs & third-party providers, report performance, report taxes/financials, vote proxies. IPS AppendixItems that change more often: modeled portfolio performance (range of outcomes/distribution of returns at percentiles) & capital market expectations (expected return, risk, correlations).
Section placement — the recurring MCQ pattern:
Risk tolerance→ Key investment parameters. Time horizon→ Key investment parameters. Described as a range (e.g. ">15y long", "<10y short"), not a precise length; multiple goals → multiple horizons. Liquidity preferences→ Key investment parameters. A cash reserve, or a constraint on asset selection because the portfolio may need to be sold quickly, goes HERE (Quiz 9.5 Q4 → A). Constraints (e.g. ESG)→ Key investment parameters. ESG/ethical-investing restrictions are a constraint (Quiz 9.5 Q2 → A). A specific purchase / goal→ Investment objectives (Background & objectives). E.g. a $2m holiday-apartment purchase in 2y is an objective, not a parameter (Quiz 9.5 Q1 → B). Rebalancing methodology→ Portfolio management section (Quiz 9.5 Q3 → C). Capital-market expectations & modeled behavior sit in the Appendix, not here.
Discretionary authority spectrum: full discretion → act without prior approval; limited → only prespecified actions (e.g. rebalance within agreed ranges); nondiscretionary → can recommend but cannot act without client approval. Rebalancing: time-based (quarterly/semiannual/annual — ignores drift) vs threshold-based (rebalance once weights drift a preset amount from target).
Worked example A — Elam (preparing objectives). William & Elizabeth, both 30, three kids (8/5/3), salaries cover living expenses, $20k credit-card debt, $750k inheritance.
Portfolio purposePay children's college, fund retirement, set up a trust fund for the kids — NOT to improve current lifestyle. Distributions begin~10y (college), apart from paying off the credit card immediately. Then trust + retirement funding. Manager's jobQuantify & prioritize the competing objectives; use capital-sufficiency analysis to test feasibility & revise if unsupported. Time horizonsMultiple: college >10y; trust for children (post-college) likely >20y; retirement >30y. State each separately.
Worked example B — DuBois (formulating goals). 60, retired 35-yr fashion career, $2m portfolio, paid-off house, needs $60k/yr (inflation-adjusted), comprehensive health insurance but worries about long-term care; supports son Barry's family $30k/yr for 5y (top priority, proximity); wants a vacation property in 5y (funding unsure); estate gifted to a museum at death.
Planned goals(1) fund retirement lifestyle, (2) support son's family 5y, (3) purchase vacation property, (4) gift estate to museum at death. Unplanned goalsLong-term-care costs if health deteriorates, and property repairs on the house & (if bought) the vacation property. QuantifyRetirement & son-support are already quantified; manager must help quantify the vacation-property goal & funding, and the museum bequest. PrioritizeClient says supporting the son is top priority (proximity in time). Timing should NOT be the primary reason for priority — manager helps rank which goals truly matter most; if son-support competes with the vacation property & a meaningful bequest, she should reevaluate priorities.
Worked example C — DuBois IPS revision (IPS Appendix example). A year later: son & wife promoted → no longer need support. Now she'll plan bequests ($1.2m each to son & museum = $2.4m), keeps her modest lifestyle, and the equity sleeve must be domestic only. Withdrawals now $75k/yr → $90k/yr inflation-adjusted; cash reserve $10k → $25k. Horizon still >15y. What changes to each IPS section:
IPS SectionChange
Background & objectivesNew primary objective = retirement lifestyle (son-support dropped); add bequests of $1.2m each to son & museum ($2.4m total). Distribution need rises to $90k/yr inflation-adjusted. Manager works to keep the rate sustainable & reevaluate other goals via capital-sufficiency analysis.
Risk toleranceNo change.
Investment horizonNo change — still reasonable to exceed 15 years.
Asset-class preferencesEquities now domestic only; advise her on the return & diversification implications; mean-variance optimization must incorporate the no-foreign-equity constraint. (Full asset-class list otherwise unchanged.)
Other investment preferencesNo change (concentrated Chic Apparel position — not a significant concentration risk; actively traded).
Liquidity preferencesCash reserve $10,000 → $25,000 (unexpected expenses likely to rise).
ConstraintsAdd the domestic-equities-only constraint; note the Chic Apparel position has significant embedded capital gains.
Portfolio mgmt / responsibilities / reviewNo changes required.
DuBois strategic AA (with rebalancing ranges) for reference: Cash 5% (4–6), Domestic govt bonds 10% (8–12), Domestic corp bonds 10% (8–12), Global govt bonds 10% (8–12), Domestic equities 40% (35–45), Global equities 10% (8–12), Domestic real estate 10% (8–12), Commodities 5% (4–6). Ranges in brackets = threshold-rebalancing bounds.
Module Quiz 9.5 keys (reasoning-derived; official keys not in photos, except where noted circled).
Q1 (low risk tol / $2m holiday-apartment in 2y / no commodities&HF): the item for the objectives section is the $2m vacation-apartment purchase → B. (Risk tolerance & asset-class exclusions are parameters.)
Q2 most likely a constraint → A (ESG investing). (Time horizon & liquidity are parameters, not constraints.)
Q3 item in the portfolio-management section → C (rebalancing methodology). (Capital-market expectations & modeled behavior are Appendix items.)
Q4 cash reserve / must-sell-quickly constraint → A (liquidity preferences). (A circled.)
Q5 Collins (45, retire 20y; college 3–6y = top priority; gifting at death): multiple horizons stated as ranges → C (college exceeding 3y, retirement exceeding 20y, gifting exceeding 35y). (Photo: B first circled then struck, C circled — horizons are ranges per the curriculum, so C.)
Portfolio Management for Institutional Investors
READING 10 · Portfolio Construction
Scope & exam focus
Institutional investor types covered: DB & DC pension plans, sovereign wealth funds (SWFs), university endowments, private foundations, banks, insurance companies. The exam gives a case study and asks you to prepare/evaluate parts of an IPS — focus on what each institution is trying to achieve and which risk considerations & constraints apply.
LOS 10.a — Five characteristics: institutional vs individual investors
#CharacteristicWhat it means
1Scale (size)Institutions tend to be larger. The largest may be too big for low-capacity investments (small-cap equity, VC). Large institutions can directly access & manage in-house high-minimum classes (PE, real estate). Smaller institutions struggle to diversify & hire talent → outsource to external managers/consultants.
2Long-term horizonGenerally longer than individuals, because they're driven by the need to meet specific liabilities that are relatively low.
3Regulatory frameworkDifferent legal/regulatory/accounting/tax rules vs individuals; differs by national jurisdiction. Tightened since the 2007–2009 GFC to lower leverage, increase centralized clearing, improve reporting transparency.
4Governance frameworkFormal: board of directors + investment committee (often a board subcommittee). Board sets long-term strategic AA; board/IC establishes IPS & monitors performance; IC oversees policy. Strategy run by an investment office under a CIO; in-house or outsourced.
5Principal-agent issuesConflict when the asset owner (principal) appoints an agent whose interests aren't aligned. Internal (IC/staff) & external (outsourced managers). Classic external example: high management fee paid regardless of performance.
Quiz reflex: scale tends to WIDEN an institution's investable universe (access to PE, RE, in-house) — a claim that scale narrows the universe is false (only the very largest are excluded from tiny low-capacity assets).
LOS 10.b — The institutional IPS should include
The institution's mission & investment objectives (return and risk tolerance). Discussion of the investment horizon & liabilities to be paid. External constraints affecting asset allocation: legal, regulatory, tax, accounting. An asset allocation policy (portfolio weights) with ranges & asset-class benchmarks. A rebalancing policy. Reporting requirements.
Review the IPS annually; revise when there are material changes in investor circumstances and/or the market environment.
Four general asset-allocation models (Figure 10.1)
ModelAsset allocationAdvantagesDisadvantages
Norway (SWF)Passive; public equities & bonds (trad. 60/40 base case); little/no alternatives; tight tracking-error limitsLow costs/fees; easy for board to comprehendNo opportunity for outperformance
Yale endowmentHigh allocation to alternatives; significant active mgmt; EXTERNALLY managedPotential for outperformanceHard for small institutions lacking alts expertise; capacity issues for large managers; high fees/costs
Canada Pension PlanHigh allocation to alternatives; significant active mgmt; INTERNALLY managed; reference portfolio of passive public assets as benchmarkOutperformance potential + builds internal capabilitiesPotentially expensive & difficult to manage
Liability-driven (LDI)Focus on maximizing expected surplus (assets − liabilities) & managing surplus volatilityExplicitly recognizes liabilities in the investment processCertain liability risks (e.g. longevity) hard to hedge
The discriminator that's always tested: Yale vs Canada are nearly identical (high alts, active) — the difference is Yale = EXTERNAL managers, Canada = INTERNAL management. Norway = passive/no alts. LDI = surplus focus (assets − liabilities).
Module Quiz 10.1 — worked
QAnswerWhy
1
How many statements correct? (EPW)		A — only oneS1 wrong: a larger scale tends to WIDEN the investable universe (access to PE/RE/in-house), not narrow it. S2 correct: institutional governance is more formal than an individual's. → one correct.
2
SJT Foundation: alts + outsource external + active outperformance		B — Yale endowment modelHigh alts + active + EXTERNAL managers = Yale. Canada would be INTERNAL management; Norway is passive with no alternatives.
High-probability traps (10.1)
Scale WIDENS the universe for institutions (only the very largest lose access to tiny low-capacity assets). Yale = external, Canada = internal — same high-alts/active profile otherwise. Norway = passive 60/40, no alts, no outperformance chance. LDI = maximize surplus (assets − liabilities) & manage surplus volatility. Classic principal-agent example = high fee paid regardless of performance. Institutions: longer horizon, driven by specific liabilities; review IPS annually.
Reading LOS (apply across all institution types)
10.c — stakeholders, investment time horizons, liquidity needs of different institutional types. 10.d — focus of legal/regulatory/tax constraints by type. 10.f — evaluate the IPS of an institutional investor. 10.g — evaluate the investment portfolio of a private DB plan, SWF, university endowment, private foundation.
General outline used for each institution type
main features / mission stakeholders (parties impacted by success / failure) key elements of the IPS, in order: 1. liabilities & investment horizon 2. liquidity needs 3. external constraints 4. investment objectives 5. asset allocation
Pension funds — main features / mission
Pension funds save & invest to provide retirement income for beneficiaries. The entity that sets up the plan = plan sponsor (usually an employer). Two major types:
DB (defined benefit) — sponsor defines the benefit paid to beneficiaries at retirement. DC (defined contribution) — contributions to assets today are defined; no guarantee of ultimate benefits.
Move DB → DC over recent decades: sponsors prefer lower financial risk + DC is portable (moves with beneficiary on job change). Hybrid (e.g. cash balance): sponsor defines contributions which are then pooled; sponsor faces some investment risk, as in DB.
Figure 10.2 — DB vs DC
FeatureDefined BenefitDefined Contribution
Benefit paymentsContractually defined (usually dependent on final salary); creates a measurable liability for the sponsorDepends on investment performance; once promised contributions met, no liability for sponsor
ContributionsPrimarily by employer (employee may also)Primarily by employee (employer may also)
Investment decision-makingPension fund (sponsor + investment staff)Sponsor provides suite of funds; employee decides level of investment & asset allocation
Investment riskFaced by sponsorFaced by beneficiary
Mortality / longevity riskPooled at fund level (long-lived funded by early-dying); risk of general life-expectancy increase faced by sponsorEmployee faces longevity risk of outliving own savings
Spine of the table: in DB the sponsor bears benefit/investment/longevity risk; in DC the beneficiary bears it. Contributions flip employer↔employee.
DB stakeholders
Plan sponsors (employers) — must contribute; poor performance → extra contributions to an underfunded plan (assets < liabilities). Plan beneficiaries (employees & retirees) — face ultimate risk the employer defaults on contributions. Investment staff / investment committee / board — directly impacted by success or failure. Governments — provide tax incentives; taxpayers bear costs for those who under-save. Shareholders of the corporate employer — underfunded plan = balance-sheet liability + lower income → higher financial risk → ↑ share-price volatility.
Liabilities & investment horizon
DB liabilities = PV of future benefits promised to participants. Employees qualify only after vesting conditions (typically a minimum number of years of service).
funded ratio = fair value of plan assets / PV of DB obligations
Figure 10.3 — DB liability factors (impact of an INCREASE in the factor)
Factor ↑LiabilityWhy
Service / tenure (years worked)IncreasesBenefits linked to years of service
SalaryIncreasesBenefits linked to final salary
LongevityIncreasesBenefits paid every year alive in retirement
Employee turnoverLowersFewer employees reach the vesting requirement
Additional / matching contributionsIncreasesUsually increases benefits promised
Expected investment returnPotentially lowersMay raise the discount rate used → lowers liability
Discount rateLowersHigher discount rate → lower PV of benefits
Active vs retired lives: active = still employed, earning benefits; retired = receiving payments. Higher proportion of retired lives → shorter horizon → lowers risk tolerance. Frozen plans (closed to new participants) have shorter horizons (no new active lives).
LOS 10.e — Figure 10.4: DB risk considerations (drivers of risk tolerance)
ConsiderationEffectRationale
Plan funded statusHigher → ↑ tolerancePlan can absorb short-term losses
Sponsor financial statusStronger → ↑ toleranceLower debt / higher profitability → capacity to contribute on losses
Size of plan vs sponsorSmaller plan → ↑ toleranceSponsor can tolerate volatility in contributions if assets underperform
Common risk exposuresLower correlation → ↑ toleranceLow corr of sponsor results & pension-asset returns → sponsor likely profitable & able to contribute when plan underperforms
Provision for early retirement / lump-sum distributions→ lower toleranceShorter horizon → less time to recover from short-term losses
Workforce characteristicsYounger / more active lives → ↑ toleranceGreater duration of liabilities → time to recover from short-term losses
Prof note (ability vs willingness): higher funded status = greater ability to take risk, but willingness may stay low — e.g. a plan in surplus where the sponsor wants to stay in surplus to minimize contributions → minimize surplus volatility via LDI. Read the case. Figure 10.4 factors are a recent source of constructed-response IPS questions.
Example — Viewpoint Research Corp (DB plan)
UK market-research firm. All participants still working or in alternative employment (zero retired lives); plan in a small deficit; no early-retirement / lump-sum options; rapid earnings growth, ROE above industry, debt-to-assets 50% above competitors. Discuss two factors that increase and two that decrease the plan's ability to take risk.
↑ Ability to take risk↓ Ability to take risk
1. Zero retired lives → long-duration liabilities → time to recover from short-term underperformance.1. Higher debt than industry → lowers sponsor's ability to top up contributions if performance is poor → lowers tolerance.
2. No early-retirement / lump-sum options → longer & more predictable liabilities → time to recover from short-term falls in funded status.2. Plan in deficit → further underperformance could significantly hurt ability to meet future liabilities.
Prof-note trap: do NOT cite high ROE / profitability as an increase. It's stated for the last year only, during high leverage — so it may just reflect leverage, with no guarantee it persists. The two case-specific answers above are better.
Liquidity needs (DB)
Function of benefits paid to retired lives and sponsor contributions. Higher when:
Higher proportion of retired lives (frozen > nonfrozen — benefits exceed contributions). Older workforce (shorter time to pay benefits). Higher funded status (lower sponsor contributions → more paid from existing plan assets). Participants able to switch / withdraw (triggers payments).
Lower liquidity needs → can invest more in risky asset classes.
External constraints (DB)
Regulation (varies by country): extensive fee/cost reporting; increased personal liability for trustees. Europe = IORP II (governance, risk mgmt, disclosure). US = ERISA 1974 (regulates investing/funding/payouts; created the PBGC protecting beneficiaries of terminated plans); Pension Protection Act 2006 set minimum DB funding ratios; later revision lets corporations discount liabilities at a 25-yr average high-grade bond yield (lowers liabilities, but can push more risk-taking to maintain funded status). Tax: funds often tax-favored; taxable funds consider tax (lower LT cap-gains → lower-turnover strategies; high tax on derivative returns may preclude derivatives; watch double-taxation treaties & domestic credits for foreign withholding). Accounting: US corporate DB → GAAP ASC 715 (funded status on balance sheet). US public plans → GASB (assets at market value; liabilities via a blended rate — expected return on assets for the funded portion, tax-exempt muni yield for the unfunded portion).
Prof note: exam is portfolio-management-focused and led by the case — a significant external constraint will be referenced in the case.
Investment objectives (DB)
Primary — achieve a target return over a specified long-term horizon while assuming risk consistent with meeting contractual liabilities. Secondary — minimize (in PV terms) the cash contributions the sponsor must provide.
Target return should reflect that plan assets must grow in line with liability growth (≈ the discount rate applied to liabilities). If in deficit, the split between investment-return growth and extra contributions is driven by the plan's ability to take risk and the sponsor's ability to contribute.
DC stakeholders
Plan sponsors (employers) — do not face investment or longevity risk, but retain fiduciary responsibilities: contributing, overseeing investments, offering suitable options. Plan beneficiaries (employees & retirees) — face investment risk (contributions + returns not meeting needs) and longevity risk of outliving savings. The board — communicate with participants at their sophistication level; may select a default option when participants are disengaged (make no explicit choice). Governments — tax incentives; taxpayer welfare cost for under-savers.
Liabilities & investment horizon (DC)
DC sponsor's only liability = required contributions; no liability for future benefits (unlike DB). Via pooling / scale, DC can access alternatives not usually available to retail. Sponsor bears the liquidity risk of any event causing participants to exit.
Individual horizon is linked to age — older participants → shorter horizon (retiring & drawing sooner). Many DC plans offer a default life-cycle / target-date option:
Participant-switching option — automatically switches members to a more conservative allocation as they age. Participant / cohort option — pools the participant with others of similar retirement date; the fund is managed more conservatively as that date approaches.
Liquidity needs (DC)
Primary drivers = age of the workforce + ability of participants to switch / withdraw. If these are high, liquidity needs are high (as in DB).
External constraints (DC)
Regulation: regulators recognize many DC participants have low investment understanding → sponsors must educate participants on default options for the disengaged. Australia & US require the plan to offer a diversified default option. This does not absolve trustees of their fiduciary duty to run the plan in beneficiaries' best interests. Tax: US DC (401(k)) is tax deferred — pretax contributions, untaxed earnings; benefits taxed as ordinary income; withdrawals before age 59½ incur an extra 10% tax. Similar deferral in the UK (first 25% of benefits tax-free). ERISA (US) and IORP II (Europe) are relevant to both DB and DC.
Investment objectives (DC)
Main — prudently grow assets to meet retirement spending needs; onus on the sponsor to provide cost-efficient default options for the disengaged. Secondary (if active funds offered) — outperform the passive default's strategic asset allocation. Where participants can voluntarily switch between competing DC providers, outperforming other DC plans may be an objective.
Asset allocation by DB & DC (aggregate data)
Asset allocation varies by region — driven by differences in external constraints, risk appetite, and stakeholder preferences. Past decade: rotation from equities into alternatives & fixed income to lower volatility of funded ratios. Within equities, some home bias to domestic markets.
Module Quiz 10.2 — worked
QAnswerWhy
1
↑ which factor most likely DECREASES DB liabilities?		C — employee turnoverHigher turnover → fewer employees reach vesting → lowers liability. A life expectancy & B years of service both INCREASE liability.
2
which change most likely INCREASES DB risk tolerance?		C — ↑ allocation to low-correlation assetsLow correlation of pension assets with sponsor operating results → sponsor likely profitable & able to contribute when plan underperforms → ↑ tolerance. A older workforce = shorter horizon (lower); B overfunded→underfunded = lower funded status (lower).
High-probability traps (10.2)
DB = sponsor bears risk; DC = beneficiary bears risk. Higher discount rate / turnover / expected return → LOWER liability; service, salary, longevity, contributions → higher. More retired lives → shorter horizon → lower risk tolerance AND higher liquidity needs. Low correlation (sponsor results vs pension assets) → HIGHER risk tolerance. Ability ≠ willingness — surplus plan may still choose low risk (LDI) to protect surplus. 401(k) = tax deferred, 10% penalty before 59½; ERISA & IORP II apply to both DB & DC. funded ratio = plan assets / PV of DB obligations.
SWFs — main features / mission
SWFs = investment funds owned by a government. The IMF defines five categories, each with a different mission:
#TypeMission
1Budget stabilizationSet up when revenues are heavily linked to a natural resource / cyclical industry — insulate (protect) the government budget from commodity-price volatility & economic cycles.
2DevelopmentPrioritize national socioeconomic projects — usually infrastructure or supporting key industries.
3SavingsInvest revenues from nonrenewable assets for the benefit of future generations.
4ReserveEarn returns on excess foreign reserves held by central banks. FX reserves are low-yielding vs the bonds CBs issue to fund them → reduce this negative cost of carry by boosting returns.
5Pension reserveSave & invest to meet future pension liabilities of governments.
SWF stakeholders
Current & future citizens — benefit directly (payments) or indirectly (lower taxation / increased domestic investment). Investment offices — invest SWF assets directly in-house or appoint external managers. The board — fiduciary duty to the ultimate beneficiaries of the fund. Governments — may rely on SWF returns to balance budget deficits.
Figure 10.5 — SWF liabilities & time horizons
SWF liabilities are linked to mission and are generally less well defined than other institutions.
TypeLiabilities & horizon
Budget stabilizationUncertain liabilities linked to commodity prices / cyclical industries; short-term horizon (budget support needed short-term)
DevelopmentLiabilities linked to socioeconomic investments made by the fund; some long-term (infrastructure), some medium-term (medical research)
SavingsLinked to future generations → long term
ReserveTechnically the yield promised on bonds issued by governments/central banks, but funds target higher returns; horizons very long, typically no near-term liabilities
Pension reserveLinked to future pension payments → long term; may have an accumulation stage (contributions) & a decumulation phase (benefits drawn) — horizon depends on when these occur
Liquidity needs (ranked)
Budget stabilization — HIGHEST; low-risk assets, to meet short-term deficits from negative economic/commodity events. Reserve — lower than stabilization but higher than savings; liquid fixed-income, sellable if reserves change dramatically. Development — low (infrastructure & R&D are long-term). Savings — LOWEST (accumulate for future generations); rise as resources deplete & government withdraws. Pension reserve — varies: lower in accumulation, higher in decumulation.
External constraints (SWF)
Legal / regulatory — SWFs established by laws giving mission & structure (clear governance rules, especially for development funds with a specific socioeconomic mission). To avoid political influence: governance, independence, transparency, accountability are crucial → the Santiago Principles (best-practice framework by the International Forum of SWFs / IFSWF) cover these plus ethics, risk mgmt, compliance monitoring. Tax — SWFs generally tax exempt; this may void the ability to claim withholding-tax credits available to taxable investors. Watch double-taxation treaties when investing internationally; avoid being seen as using status to dodge foreign-jurisdiction taxes.
Figure 10.6 — SWF investment objectives
TypeInvestment objectives
Budget stabilizationCapital preservation; returns above inflation with low probability of losses; should avoid assets correlated with the source of government revenues
DevelopmentSupport economic development & long-run growth; implicit objective = real return > real domestic GDP / productivity growth
SavingsMaintain purchasing power of assets over time while making ongoing spending on government budgetary needs
ReserveEarn a return in excess of the yield the government/central bank pays on bonds it has issued
Pension reserveEarn returns to meet future unfunded pension & social-care payments promised by the government
Prof note: savings funds share very similar objectives to endowments & foundations (next module).
Asset allocation by SWF type
Budget stabilization — mostly fixed income & cash (defensive nature). Development — driven by socioeconomic mission (e.g. local infrastructure). Savings — long horizon → relatively high equities & alternatives. Reserve — similar to savings but lower alternatives allocation (higher potential liquidity needs). Pension reserve — high equities & alternatives (long horizon, low liquidity needs in accumulation phase).
Savings & pension reserve funds typically follow the endowment model; some adopt the Canadian model. Theme: fewer constraints → broader mandate & longer horizons → higher allocation to alternatives than most institutions.
Module Quiz 10.3 — worked
QAnswerWhy
1
SAA 10% eq / 60% FI / 30% cash → which SWF?		C — budget stabilizationVery defensive (90% FI + cash) = capital preservation, highest liquidity. A savings & would be high equity/alts; B development is mission/infrastructure-driven.
2
BoC buys USD to boost FX reserves — reserve funds, most accurate?		A — excess FX reserves invested in riskier, higher-yielding assetsReserve funds offset the negative cost of carry (low-yield FX vs higher-yield issued bonds) by investing in higher-yielding assets. B wrong — buying USD injects domestic currency (not deflationary); C wrong — issuing bonds while holding low-yield FX = negative carry, not positive.
High-probability traps (10.3)
Budget stabilization = short-term, highest liquidity, defensive FI+cash, avoid assets correlated with govt revenue source. Savings = lowest liquidity, longest horizon, high equity/alts (endowment model). Reserve = negative cost of carry; beat the yield on bonds the govt/CB issued; liquid FI, lower alts than savings. Pension reserve = accumulation (low liq) vs decumulation (high liq); meet unfunded pension/social-care. Santiago Principles / IFSWF = governance best-practice; SWFs generally tax exempt (may lose withholding credits).
SWF master matrix — five types × five dimensions
TypeHorizonLiquidityObjectiveAsset allocation
Budget stabilizationShortHighestCapital preservation; > inflation, low loss prob; avoid revenue-correlated assetsMostly FI & cash (defensive)
DevelopmentMedium–long (mission)LowEconomic development; real return > real GDP growthMission-driven (local infrastructure)
SavingsLongLowestMaintain purchasing power + ongoing budget spendingHigh equities & alts (endowment model)
ReserveVery long (no near-term)Med (> savings)Beat yield on bonds govt/CB issuedLiquid FI; lower alts than savings
Pension reserveLongVaries (accum low / decum high)Meet unfunded pension & social-careHigh equities & alts
Memory hook: Stabilization is the defensive outlier (short/high-liq/FI); Savings & Pension reserve are the aggressive long-horizon pair (low-liq/equity+alts); Reserve sits between (long but more liquid FI); Development follows the mission.
University endowments — features & mission
Funds set up by gifts & donations, invested to earn returns that provide ongoing support to the university's operating budget.
Main objective = balance the needs of the university today against its needs in the future → intergenerational equity.
Scale anchor: Harvard ≈ $30B (2016) — one of the largest endowments.
Stakeholders
StakeholderInterest
Current + future studentsOngoing support of university operations & intergenerational fairness
Alumni / donorsContribute gifts & donations; often sit on the board / IC (esp. those who are investment professionals)
University employeesLivelihoods depend on the university
Endowment boards often have professional investment experience via alumni — a key contrast vs foundations (see Matrix tab).
Spending policy — the endowment's "liability"
Liabilities = future payouts promised to the university, set in an official spending policy. Goal: ensure intergenerational equity while smoothing payouts to insulate the university from market volatility.
spending(t+1) = w × [ spending(t) × (1 + inflation) ] + (1 − w) × ( spending rate × average AUM ) w = weight on the PRIOR year's spending amount
Smoothing logic: the first term anchors to last year's payout (predictable); the second term ties to current asset levels. w dials between certainty and market-responsiveness.
Three spending rules — by value of w
RulewMechanicsTrade-off
Constant growthw = 1Fixed REAL payout, grown by HEPI (Higher Education Price Index). Often has caps & floors = max/min % of AUM over 1 or 3 yrs.+ Most certainty for the university
− % of endowment paid out fluctuates with endowment value
Market valuew = 0Payout = spending rate (4–6%) × 3-to-5-yr moving avg of asset values.Procyclical — spending fluctuates in line with the moving average of assets
Hybrid0 < w < 1Weighted average of the previous two rules.Blends certainty & market-responsiveness
w-direction trap: w = 1 is the constant-growth rule (all weight on prior spending → smooth/certain); w = 0 is the market-value rule (all weight on current AUM → procyclical). Don't invert them. Also: constant-growth grows by HEPI, NOT CPI.
Other liability-related factors
FactorEffect on risk tolerance
Fundraising from donorsGifts flow IN → net spending rate ≈ 2–4% of assets (below the 4–6% spending rate applied) → supports higher risk tolerance
Reliance of university on the spendingBigger share of the operating budget funded by the endowment → LOWER risk tolerance
Capability to issue debtAccess to debt markets → HIGHER risk tolerance (can borrow to meet spending in poor-performance years)
Liabilities & investment horizon
Intergenerational equity + unlimited life of the university → PERPETUAL investment horizon.
Liquidity needs
Annual spending net of gifts & donations is very low (≈ 2–4% of assets).
Low liquidity needs + perpetual horizon → HIGH risk tolerance → can absorb relatively high short-term volatility in pursuit of longer-term returns.
External constraints — legal / regulatory / tax
ConstraintDetail
Total-return basisLaws require investing on a total-return basis (income + capital gains, not income only) + diversification per MPT
Fiduciary duty of careInvestment committees / boards & staff oversee investments with a duty of care
US — UPMIFAUniform Prudent Management of Institutional Funds Act: allows flexibility in spending + enforces adoption of MPT
UK — Trustee Act 2000Similar role; relevant because UK endowments are often structured as trusts
TaxTax-exempt on investment returns; universities not taxed on payouts; donors can deduct gifts from taxable income
UPMIFA & the Trustee Act also apply to private foundations (next module tab).
Investment objectives
Primary: preserve purchasing power in perpetuity (grow with inflation) + earn returns adequate to fund spending → typical target = real return ≈ 5% (after HEPI, measured over 3-to-5 yrs).
Volatility limit: typically 10–15%.
Secondary: outperform a passive benchmark. Tertiary: outperform a peer group of similar endowments.
Peer-group objective risk: chasing a peer benchmark can dislocate decisions from the core mission (funding unique liabilities) and cause herding by managers into similar investments.
Real assets: endowments need to beat inflation → significant allocation to real assets. GFC 2007–09 lesson: analyze liquidity risk via detailed cash-flow modeling; some use a liquidity risk band = upper bound on illiquid exposure (incl. uncalled commitments in alt funds).
Asset allocation by university endowments
Large US endowments → the endowment (Yale) model: majority (>50%) to alternatives — share has risen over the past two decades.
Smaller US endowments → less to alternatives, more to domestic equities & fixed income; home bias → US equities overweighted vs non-US.
Calculator — Capital University endowment
4% spending on 5-yr avg assets; vol limit 15%. CPI inflation 1%/yr; HEPI = CPI + 100bp. Defaults = textbook. Edit the allocations to test.
Required nominal return = spending rate 4% + HEPI inflation 2% = 6% Current AA: 30% US eq / 70% FI New AA: 25 FI / 35 US eq / 20 Intl / 10 RE / 10 PE
Asset classExp return %Current %New (SAA) %
Fixed income37025
US equities63035
International equities7020
Real estate8010
Private equity10010
Why accept the new SAA (return alone): current AA earns 0.3×6 + 0.7×3 = 3.9% → fails the 6% nominal required. New AA earns 0.25×3 + 0.35×6 + 0.20×7 + 0.10×8 + 0.10×10 = 6.05% → meets 6%.
Factor that could make the new SAA inappropriate: the investment office is small with no alternatives experience → lacks skills/contacts for due diligence on PE & real assets. Also the new mix must still be checked against the 15% volatility limit — return-adequacy alone isn't sufficient.
Quiz 10.4 — Q1
Endowment: spending policy 5% of 3-yr rolling assets; CPI 3%/yr; HEPI 2.5%/yr. Investment objective = achieve a total real rate of return of at least:
A. 5.0%   B. 7.5%   C. 8.0%
B — 7.5%. To preserve purchasing power AND fund spending, the endowment must earn its spending rate plus its own cost inflation (HEPI): 5% + 2.5% = 7.5%.
Trap C (8.0%): uses CPI 3% instead of HEPI. An endowment maintains real value against its OWN index (HEPI), not general CPI. Trap A (5.0%): spending only — ignores maintaining purchasing power.
Private foundations — features & mission
Nonprofit institutions set up to make grants to specified charitable causes. This reading focuses on private foundations (individual donors + families, e.g. the Gates Foundation).
Other foundation typesSet up by / for
CommunityFor the good of the local community
OperatingTo fund a specific not-for-profit business
CorporateFrom the profits of an existing company
Objective = maintain purchasing power in perpetuity + earn returns sufficient to support grant-making → same as a university endowment's objective.
Stakeholders & the board-experience trap
Stakeholders: founding family, donors, grant recipients, wider community. Government = stakeholder (favorable tax treatment). Intergenerational tensions (current vs future recipients), as with endowments.
