Key endowment-vs-foundation difference: foundation board members are LESS likely to have professional investment experience than endowment-board alumni → less rigorous oversight / greater delegation to staff → may hurt decision quality in sophisticated markets (alternatives).
Mission-related investing (a.k.a. impact investing): investing in projects that promote the foundation's mission. Challenge = maintaining a sufficient return to meet long-term objectives.
Liabilities & investment horizon
Typically perpetual horizon. Trend toward limited-life foundations — mandated to spend down assets within a set time frame of the founder's death → shortens the horizon.
US tax law payout: must pay out a minimum 5% of assets (12-month trailing) + investment expenses.
Flow-through: must spend any donations in the year received.
Reliance: unlike universities (which have other revenue), foundations rely almost exclusively on the portfolio to meet budgets. Higher liquidity requirement + heavy reliance → LOWER risk tolerance than university endowments.
Liquidity needs & external constraints
Liquidity needs — keep sufficient liquidity for: near-term spending (5%), capital calls from PE/limited-partnership funds, and margin calls on derivatives.
ConstraintDetail
Same laws as endowmentsUPMIFA (US) / Trustee Act (UK): total-return basis, diversification, duty of care from board & staff
Tax-exemptSimilar status to endowments — but conditional on meeting the spending rule
30% taxOn undistributed income if the foundation FAILS the minimum-spending requirement
2% taxOn net investment income (most US foundations)
Penalty traps: 30% = on UNDISTRIBUTED income (failure to meet the 5% payout). 2% = on NET INVESTMENT income (general). Don't swap the two rates or bases.
Investment objectives & AA
Objective: real return over CPI ≥ spending rate (min 5%) + investment expenses; expected volatility 10–15% over 3-to-5 yrs. Secondary: beat a policy benchmark on a tracking-error budget.
AA: lower risk tolerance than endowments (higher liquidity + heavy reliance) — but overall risk tolerance remains high (beat-inflation objective + long horizon).
Larger US foundations → ≈ half to alternatives. Smaller foundations → more to domestic equities & fixed income.
University endowment vs private foundation — master matrix
DimensionUniversity endowmentPrivate foundation
MissionSupport university operating budget; intergenerational equityGrant-making to charitable causes; intergenerational equity
ObjectiveMaintain purchasing power in perpetuity + returns sufficient to fund spending (same)
HorizonPerpetualPerpetual (trend to limited-life → shorter)
Min payoutNo legal min; spending rate 4–6% (HEPI rules)Legal min 5% of assets + expenses; flow-through on donations
Net spending2–4% (gifts offset)≈ 5%+ (relied on almost exclusively)
Other revenueYes (tuition, research, etc.)No — portfolio is the main funding source
Liquidity needsLowHigher (spending + capital calls + margin calls)
Risk toleranceHighLower than endowment (but still high overall)
Board expertiseOften investment-pro alumniLess investment experience → more delegation to staff
TaxTax-exempt; donors deduct giftsTax-exempt IF meets payout; 30% on undistributed, 2% on net inv. income
Vol limit≈ 10–15% over 3-to-5 yrs (same)
AALarge → endowment model >50% alts; small → more domestic eq/FILarge → ≈ half alts; small → more domestic eq/FI
Memory hook: foundation = endowment's objective + stricter payout (5% legal) + no backup revenue + weaker board → net effect = lower risk tolerance & higher liquidity needs, despite the same long-horizon, beat-inflation mandate.
Banks & insurers — what makes them different
Both are financial intermediaries run for profit — unlike the other institutions in this reading.
Scope reminder: we advise on the institution's investment portfolio, NOT its core business of being a bank/insurer — though the two are interlinked.
Banks — main features / mission
Primary function = earn profits by taking deposits from savers + making loans to borrowers.
Other functions: safeguarding assets; executing securities & derivatives transactions; investing in securities; advising.
Banks — stakeholders & the balance sheet
StakeholderRole
Shareholders (external)Most large intl banks publicly listed → want profit maximization
Depositors (external)Expect protection of assets; make up most of the bank's LIABILITIES
Borrowers (external)Retail (home purchase) + commercial (fund operations); their loans = most of the bank's ASSETS
Creditors, rating agencies, regulators, communitiesOther external stakeholders
Employees, managers, directorsInternal stakeholders
Balance-sheet anchor: deposits = liabilities; loans = assets. This is the heart of the bank's asset/liability mismatch.
Liabilities & investment horizon
LiabilityNature
Demand depositsWithdraw without notice → deemed short-term in duration
Time / term depositsRequire advance notice before withdrawal
OtherShort-term wholesale funding; long-term debt; trading/securities payables; repo finance payables
Assets: mostly longer-term illiquid mortgage & commercial loans.
Horizon logic: driven by the difference between long-term illiquid assets and short-term liquid liabilities. Bank is a perpetual org, but the investment-portfolio instruments are very short → manage shareholder-capital volatility on a medium- to short-term basis.
Perpetual-but-short trap: the bank itself is perpetual, yet its investment portfolio is run short-term. Don't say the portfolio horizon is long just because the institution is perpetual.
Liquidity needs & post-GFC ratios
Deposits = short-duration liabilities + possible need to raise liquidity in adverse conditions → liquidity management is a key focus.
RatioWhat it requires
LCR (liquidity coverage ratio)Sufficient liquid assets to cover near-term expected cash outflows
NSFR (net stable funding ratio)Adequate capital from stable sources
Effect: bank investment portfolios are more liquid + rely less on wholesale interbank funding.
Retail vs commercial: commercial-lending banks use wholesale funding more; retail banks use more deposits (cheaper, more stable) → retail banks have a BETTER liquidity position than commercial banks.
External constraints — regulators
Systemic-failure risk to critical functions (payments, credit) → regulators intensely focus on capital adequacy, liquidity, leverage.
Goal: banks adequately capitalized to absorb losses themselves — not customers, creditors, or taxpayers. Via diversification, asset quality-based reserves, stable funding, LCR/NSFR.
Quality-based reserves (Prof note): riskier assets → higher risk-weighted assets → higher required reserves. e.g. switching IG bonds → HY bonds raises required reserves.
SIFIs — systemically important financial institutions
Economies of scale + diversification benefits push banks to grow → largest = SIFIs. Post-GFC, SIFI rules:
RuleDetail
↑ Capital requiredMore capital to absorb losses on assets
Limit dividends & buybacksThese payouts effectively INCREASE leverage → limiting them retains capital
Restrict subordinated-debt / preferred claimsLimit their ability to claim in bankruptcy → forces them to bear more risk
Restrict derivativesPlus prop trading + off-balance-sheet liabilities & guarantees
Leverage-direction trap: dividends/buybacks INCREASE leverage (cash out, equity shrinks). Regulators LIMIT them to reduce leverage. Don't invert.
Three accounting systems (banks & insurers)
SystemUsed forIncome volatility
Standard financial reporting (GAAP/IFRS)Communicate results to shareholders; accruals processSmoothest
Statutory accountingUsed by regulators; more conservative (removes intangibles, accelerates expenses, recognizes reserves vs large losses/guarantees)Middle
True economic accountingMarket value for all assets & liabilitiesMost volatile
Volatility ranking trap: Standard = smoothest (accruals); True economic = most volatile (mark-to-market). Statutory sits between (conservative, not smoothest).
Banks are fully taxable → must consider after-tax returns.
Investment objectives & ALMCo
Primary objective: manage liquidity + reduce risk mismatches between the bank's NONINVESTMENT assets & liabilities.
ALMCo (asset-liability management committee) oversees: sets the IPS, monitors performance, sets risk limits (market / credit / liquidity / solvency), with authority to require changes on both sides of the B/S. Then sets policy benchmarks, monitors, reports to management & board.
"Noninvestment" trap: the goal is to offset mismatches vs the bank's CORE-business (noninvestment) assets & liabilities — the investment portfolio is a tool, not the thing being matched to itself.
Insurers — two broad categories
TypeWrites
Life insurersWhole/term life (fixed payments); variable life (payouts linked to policyholder-chosen funds); annuities; health; universal life (flexible premiums & benefit payouts)
P&C insurersProperty & liability; surety; commercial property/liability; home ownership; marine; legal liabilities
Stakeholders — listed vs mutual
StructureOwner / interest
Publicly listedShareholders → long-term maximization of capital value WHILE honoring policyholder obligations
MutualOwned by policyholders; profits retained as a surplus vs potential losses, or distributed via dividends / premium reductions
Other external: derivatives counterparties, creditors, regulators, rating agencies. Internal: employees, management, board.
General account vs separate account — who bears the risk
AccountFundsWho bears investment risk
General accountTraditional life (incl. universal life) + fixed annuityINSURER
Separate accountVariable life + variable annuities (invested per policyholder choices)POLICYHOLDER
Risk-bearer trap: general account → insurer bears risk (fixed/traditional). Separate account → policyholder bears risk (variable). "Variable" = variable for the policyholder, who carries the market outcome.
Liabilities & investment horizon — life vs P&C
Life insurersP&C insurers
DurationLong (varies by product line)Shorter
CertaintyMore predictableHigher uncertainty — claims tied to unlikely, unpredictable, high-payout events (e.g. natural disasters)
Historic horizon20–40 yearsShort
Like banks: the institution has a perpetual time horizon, but the nature & timing of policy claims strongly affect the investment horizon.
Underwriting cycle (key for both): competition-driven swings in profitability over the business cycle. Intense competition & low underwriting profit → insurers bear less underwriting risk → may increase appetite for investment risk (all else equal).
Liquidity needs
Manage internal liquidity (cash from operations & investing) + external liquidity (ability to borrow in debt markets).
Interest rates & lapses: ↑ interest rates → ↑ lapses/surrenders. Policyholders holding low-yielding contracts surrender (cash in) to reinvest at higher yields → increases the life insurer's net cash outflows.
P&C: significant cash-flow uncertainty → portfolios need ample liquidity of high-grade short-term fixed income.
General account split — reserve vs surplus portfolio
PortfolioPurposeManagement
Reserve portfolioCapable of meeting policy liabilities (regulation requires it)Conservative
Surplus portfolioGenerate higher returnsAssume liquidity risk + allocate to alternatives
Reserve vs surplus trap: reserve = conservative (must meet liabilities); surplus = aggressive (return-seeking, alts, liquidity risk). Don't swap which one takes the risk.
External constraints
Like banks: crucial intermediary roles → can be large enough to be classed as SIFIs; regulators ensure sufficient capital to absorb business & investment losses.
RegionRegulator / framework
United StatesNAIC (National Association of Insurance Commissioners) — association of state regulators setting accounting & reporting policies
EuropeSolvency II — framework standardizing regulation across member states
Same 3 accounting systems as banks (standard / statutory / true economic). Insurers are fully taxable → after-tax returns.
Investment objectives
Primary (like banks): manage liquidity + reduce risk mismatches between the institution's assets & liabilities. Must consider general business conditions + expected external economic conditions.
Oversight: a board committee responsible for all investment policies & procedures; reports to regulators & external stakeholders. (Banks → ALMCo; insurers → board committee.)
Bank vs insurer — master matrix
DimensionBankInsurer
NatureFinancial intermediary run for profit (both)
Core liabilitiesDeposits (demand + time/term)Policy claims (life: long; P&C: short/uncertain)
Core assetsLoans (mortgage + commercial)Investment portfolio backing reserves
Institution horizonPerpetual (portfolio run short-medium)Perpetual (claims drive portfolio horizon)
Liability durationShort (deposits)Life 20–40 yr; P&C short
Key cycle/riskLiquidity runs; LCR/NSFRUnderwriting cycle; ↑IR → ↑lapses
Primary objectiveManage liquidity + reduce risk mismatches btwn assets & liabilities (same)
Oversight bodyALMCoBoard committee
US regulatorBanking regulators (capital/liquidity/leverage)NAIC
EU frameworkBasel-style capital rulesSolvency II
SIFIBoth can be SIFIs → ↑capital, payout limits, derivative restrictions (same)
AccountingStandard (smoothest) / statutory (conservative) / true economic (most volatile) (same)
TaxFully taxable → after-tax returns (both)
Isolated traps — drill these
ConceptCorrect direction
Demand vs time depositDemand = no notice, short-term; time/term = advance notice
Retail vs commercial liquidityRetail = better (cheap stable deposits); commercial uses wholesale funding more
Dividends/buybacks & leveragePayouts INCREASE leverage → regulators limit them
Accounting income volatilityStandard smoothest < statutory < true economic most volatile
General vs separate accountGeneral → insurer bears risk; separate → policyholder bears risk
Life vs P&C durationLife long (20–40 yr); P&C short + uncertain
Reserve vs surplus portfolioReserve = conservative; surplus = return-seeking + alts
Interest rates & lapses↑IR → ↑lapses → ↑ insurer cash outflows
Primary objectiveManage liquidity + reduce mismatch vs noninvestment (core) assets/liabilities
Overall objective & the %ΔE equation (LOS 10.h)
For both banks & insurers: maximize the market value of equity capital, with high assurance that depositor/creditor/policyholder claims can be met.
%ΔE = %ΔA × M − %ΔL × (M − 1) M = leverage multiplier = A / E %ΔA, %ΔL = % change in value of assets, liabilities
Intuition: term 1 = asset returns magnified by leverage M; term 2 has a negative sign — rising liabilities cut equity. M−1 = size of liabilities vs equity. e.g. M=4 → $4 assets per $1 equity → $3 liabilities (M−1=3).
Calculator — %ΔE, Dₒ and σₒ
One panel drives all three balance-sheet equations. Defaults below = the %ΔE textbook example (E/A 5%, liabilities +1.5%, assets flat).
% change inputs (for %ΔE):
Duration inputs (for Dₒ):
Volatility inputs (for σₒ):
To reproduce the textbook checks: %ΔE → E/A 5, %ΔA 0, %ΔL 1.5 = −28.5%. Dₒ → E/A 12.5, Dₐ 3, Dₗ 2, Δi/Δy 0.70 = 14.2. σₒ → E/A 12.5, σₐ 7, σₗ 4, ρ 0.3 = 54.6%.
Worked example — %ΔE
Bank E/A = 5% → M = 1/0.05 = 20. Liabilities +1.5%, assets stable.
%ΔE = (0% × 20) − (1.5% × 19) = −28.5%
M−1 trap: liabilities are weighted by M−1, NOT M. With M=20, the liability term uses 19. Using 20 here would overstate the hit.
Modified duration of equity capital
Sensitivity of the institution's equity capital to a unit change in the asset reference yield y:
Dₒ = Dₐ × M − Dₗ × (M − 1) × (Δi / Δy) Dₒ/Dₐ/Dₗ = modified duration of equity / assets / liabilities Δi/Δy = est. change in LIABILITY yield i per unit change in ASSET yield y
Same M and M−1 roles as %ΔE. The only extra term is Δi/Δy — how the liability yield moves relative to the asset yield. Modified duration = % value change per 1% yield change.
WellLife Holdings — worked example
E/A = 12.5% → M = 1/0.125 = 8. Dₐ = 3, Dₗ = 2, Δi/Δy = 0.70.
Dₒ = (3 × 8) − (2 × 7 × 0.70) = 24 − 9.8 = 14.2
25bp FALL in asset yield: Dₒ=14.2 → Δequity ≈ +0.25 × 14.2 = +3.55%.
Raise E/A to 10% → M = 10: Dₒ = (3 × 10) − (2 × 9 × 0.70) = 30 − 12.6 = 17.4.
Leverage & equity duration: LOWERING E/A from 12.5% to 10% RAISES leverage (M: 8 → 10), which RAISES Dₒ (14.2 → 17.4). Higher leverage magnifies equity duration. Track the direction of M, not E/A — a smaller equity ratio means more leverage.
Volatility of equity capital (σₒ)
Expected SD of % changes in the market value of equity:
σₒ² = M²σₐ² + (M−1)²σₗ² − 2(M)(M−1)σₐσₗρₐₗ σₐ/σₗ = SD of % change in assets / liabilities ρₐₗ = correlation of % value changes in assets & liabilities
It's the two-asset variance formula you've used all over the CFA curriculum — a portfolio with weight M on assets and weight −(M−1) on liabilities. The minus-sign cross term comes from that negative liability weight.
WellLife Holdings — worked example
E/A = 12.5% → M = 8. σₐ = 7%, σₗ = 4%, ρₐₗ = 0.3.
σₒ² = (8² × 0.07²) + (7² × 0.04²) − (2 × 8 × 7 × 0.07 × 0.04 × 0.3) = 0.298 σₒ = √0.298 = 0.546 = 54.6%
New regs: raise E/A to 20% → M = 5; lower σₐ to 5%.
σₒ² = (5² × 0.05²) + (4² × 0.04²) − (2 × 5 × 4 × 0.05 × 0.04 × 0.3) = 0.0641 σₒ = √0.0641 = 0.253 = 25.3%
Two levers cut σₒ here: (1) lower leverage (M 8→5) and (2) lower asset volatility (σₐ 7→5%). Both reduce equity-capital volatility 54.6% → 25.3%. Don't forget to square M and (M−1), and keep the cross term NEGATIVE.
Figure 10.7 — strategies for changing σₒ
StrategyImpact on factorσₒWhy
Hold diversified FILowers σₐFallsDiversified FI has lower SD than riskier classes
Hold high-quality FILowers σₐFallsLower chance of significant loss in asset value
Match A/L durations + borrower/claimant optionsIncreases ρₐₗFallsRegulators penalize high A/L mismatch
Hold common stockIncreases σₐ; lowers ρₐₗRisesMost regulators require ~100% reserves vs common stock
Derivatives transparency & collateralizationLowers σₐ & σₗ; increases ρₐₗFallsMore protection vs counterparty default → fewer unexpected losses
Hold more liquid portfolio investmentsLowers σₐFalls—
Surrender penalties (insurance)Lowers σₗFallsCushion losses when policyholders cash in after rates rise
Prepayment penalties on debtIncreases ρₐₗFallsPrepays happen in LOW-rate env; penalties offset rising liabilities in FALLING-rate env
Catastrophic insurance riskIncreases σₗRisesLarge unpredictable losses → regulators demand higher reserves, liquid assets, robust reinsurance
Predictability of underwriting lossesDecreases σₗFallsTotal insurance liabilities less uncertain
Diversifying insurance businessDecreases σₗFallsTotal insurance liabilities less uncertain
Variable annuitiesIncreases ρₐₗFallsAsset gains/losses passed through to policyholders
Only TWO strategies RAISE σₒ: holding common stock (↑σₐ, ↓ρ) and catastrophic insurance risk (↑σₗ). Everything else lowers σₒ. Memory: anything that lowers σₐ/σₗ or raises ρₐₗ (better A/L matching) cuts equity volatility.
Direction map: ↓σₐ → falls · ↓σₗ → falls · ↑ρₐₗ → falls (assets & liabilities move together = natural hedge) · ↑σₐ or ↑σₗ → rises · ↓ρₐₗ → rises.
Asset allocation for banks & insurers
Optimize the investment portfolio + the business liabilities simultaneously, within external economic conditions + regulatory reserve requirements; stay conscious of the drivers of shareholder-equity volatility & optimal leverage.
Exam focus (Prof note): usually a basic grasp of duration, credit risk, liquidity of fixed income — and the impact of changing these on earnings, volatility of shareholder capital, and regulatory reserves.
SJT Bank case — switching to safer investments
ALMCo findings: (1) corporate spreads below historical norms, expected to widen; (2) loan-book liquidity expected to fall, depositor withdrawals larger & less predictable. Plan: switch HY corporate floating-rate → IG government fixed-rate; enter a plain-vanilla pay-fixed / receive-floating swap.
QAnswer
1. Addresses findings?Widening spreads → HY corporate prices fall more than IG govt → switch lowers exposure to widening credit spreads. IG govvies more liquid than HY → improves portfolio liquidity, offsetting the business-liquidity deterioration.
2. Regulatory risk-based capital?Falls. IG govt = lower credit risk → lower risk weighting than HY → lower risk-weighted assets → regulator requires less equity capital.
3. A/L duration mismatch?Floating→fixed raises asset duration. Pay-fixed/receive-floating swap = synthetic liability that raises liability duration (fixed leg paid has higher duration than floating leg received). If tailored, the two offset → mismatch unchanged.
4. Earnings & volatility?Govvies yield less (no credit spread) → earnings fall. More-liquid IG govt has lower volatility → lower volatility of shareholder equity.
Swap-duration trap: pay-fixed/receive-floating ADDS duration on the LIABILITY side (you owe the high-duration fixed leg). It offsets the asset-duration rise from floating→fixed. Don't treat the swap as adding asset duration.
Quiz 10.5/10.6 — Q1
Capital requirements for banks & insurance companies are typically set with reference to:
A. statutory reporting   B. true economic reporting   C. standard financial reporting
A — statutory reporting. Regulators set capital requirements using statutory accounting (conservative adjustments). Standard financial reporting (GAAP/IFRS) is for shareholders; true economic uses market value.
Quiz 10.5/10.6 — Q2 (SAJ excerpt)
SAJ splits its general account into a reserve portfolio (provide liquidity to pay claims) and a surplus portfolio (stated objective: "hedge interest rate mismatches between the reserve portfolio and the liabilities"). The excerpt is best described as:
A. correct   B. incorrect — it's the SEPARATE account that splits, not the general   C. incorrect re the surplus-portfolio objective
C. The general account IS the one split into reserve + surplus (so B is wrong). Reserve = conservative liquidity for claims (correct). But the surplus portfolio objective is wrong: it should be run to take higher risk for higher returns to grow surplus over the long term — not merely to hedge IR mismatches.
Quiz 10.5/10.6 — Q3 (σₒ calc)
Bank equity-capital ratio 20%. σₐ = 7%, σₗ = 5%, ρₐₗ = 0.5. Volatility of shareholder capital is closest to:
A. 9.3%   B. 16.3%   C. 30.4%
C — 30.4%. E/A 20% → M = 1/0.2 = 5.
σₒ² = (5² × 0.07²) + (4² × 0.05²) − (2 × 5 × 4 × 0.07 × 0.05 × 0.5) = 0.1225 + 0.04 − 0.07 = 0.0925 σₒ = √0.0925 = 0.304 = 30.4%
Trap: must apply weights M (=5) on assets and M−1 (=4) on liabilities, square them, and SUBTRACT the covariance term. Forgetting leverage or flipping the sign gives the distractors.
Pattern 1 — "source of risk / significant risk" questions
When asked which item is LEAST likely a source of risk, the answer is usually the option with no actual adverse indicator in the vignette.
Don't manufacture a risk where the facts show stability. If the sponsor is BBB+ / investment-grade, 82 years in business, no signs of decline → that is NOT the risk. The risks are the options carrying concrete red flags (illiquid+volatile assets vs old workforce; sponsor stock in the plan).
Mirror pair: Tucker Q (answer = sponsor financial health is fine) and Pure deferred-comp Q (answer = no sponsor/plan correlation). Both test "pick the non-risk."
Pattern 2 — sponsor × plan correlation risk
Correlation between the sponsor and plan assets is a real, heavily-tested risk — but ONLY when the plan assets are tied to the sponsor.
CaseCorrelation risk?Why
TuckerYES~18–19% of plan assets in Tucker's OWN stock → sponsor weakens → assets fall AND contributions rise at the same time
PureNOSponsor = banking; plan assets = fixed income → no meaningful link
The danger in the Tucker case: poor sponsor health hits the asset value precisely when the sponsor is least able to fund the larger required contribution → raises insolvency risk.
Pattern 3 — DB required return is liability-driven
A DB plan's required return is about funding the change in liability cash flows AND their valuation — not a generic real-return target.
Two errors to never make: (1) double-counting inflation — salary growth already embeds inflation, so "inflation + salary growth" counts it twice; (2) ignoring the market discount-rate dimension — required return must reflect IG long-term bond yields used to value liabilities, and should generally exceed the discount rate on liabilities.
Q1 — Investment approaches (Canadian model)
Picked A (correct). Answer: B — she's wrong on the Canadian model.
The return logic is fine (alternatives suit long-horizon / low-liquidity clients), but the Canadian model runs alternatives in-house → needs scale to build/hire that expertise. Clients of USD 20–100M are too small. Also Chattahoochee is an external manager → wouldn't recommend an in-house approach. LDI half = correct.
Lesson: a model's return logic can be sound while its operational/scale fit fails. Check whether the institution is big enough to RUN the approach.
Q2 — Least likely a risk source (Tucker)
Answer: B — the sponsor's financial health.
OptionRisk?
Workforce characteristicsRisk — many retirees + old long-tenured actives near retirement, vs illiquid (new PE, undeveloped land) + volatile (small-cap growth) assets
Common risk exposureRisk — ~18–19% in Tucker stock (correlation trap)
Sponsor financial healthNOT a risk — BBB+, 82 yrs, no decline signals
Q3 — Proposed investment objective (Tucker)
Answer: C — the proposed required return is inappropriate.
Her formula = inflation + salary growth. Double-counts inflation (salary growth already embeds CPI) and has no market-rate component (should reflect IG long-term bond yields; required return should exceed the liability discount rate).
Distractor B (secondary objectives incompatible) is wrong: "avoid underfunding" + "don't raise contributions" are routinely pursued together — just balanced against each other.
Q4 — Rising rates & checking clients (Pure)
Answer: C — an increase in residual equity.
Clients are rate-insensitive, non-interest-bearing → deposits stay put at ~zero cost. Pure's variable-rate loans reprice UP with rates → asset yield rises, funding cost flat → margin widens → equity (A−L) rises.
Why not B: variable-rate loans REPRICE — they don't lose value like fixed-rate would. Sticky zero-cost deposits + floating-rate assets → rising rates are GOOD for bank equity.
Q5 — Deferred-comp least significant risk (Pure)
Answer: C — correlation between sponsor's business and plan investments.
Sponsor = banking; plan assets = fixed income → no meaningful correlation, and Li never flagged one. Plan-design (forfeitures fund contributions; short tenures cap growth) and workforce (withdrawal-on-separation, vesting schedule) ARE relevant considerations.
Direct mirror of Q2 — same "pick the non-risk," same correlation principle, opposite outcome from Tucker because Pure's assets aren't tied to its business.
The big one — IPS investment objectives template
For ANY endowment/foundation "construct/formulate the investment objectives" prompt, open with the mission, THEN the quantified return. Don't lead with a tiered list.
MISSION: provide [X] while maintaining purchasing power of assets IN PERPETUITY. OBJECTIVE: achieve a TOTAL REAL rate of return of [spending rate]% (after inflation), at a reasonable level of risk.
What costs marks: (1) skipping the mission sentence; (2) omitting "in perpetuity / purchasing power"; (3) over-tiering with benchmark/peer outperformance — those are approach considerations, NOT IPS investment objectives. (4) If the vignette gives a specific provision (e.g. Melrose "up to 30% of operating budget"), cite it in the mission.
Melrose: mission = maintain purchasing power while financing up to 30% of the operating budget in perpetuity; objective = real return of 4% (inflation 2%). Prometheo: mission = provide scholarships, maintain purchasing power in perpetuity; objective = total real return ≥ 6% (the spending rate).
DB plan objective — anchor to the actuarial rate
When a DB vignette hands you the actuary's required return, the objective MUST cite that number.
Burger Shack: not just "maintain 100% funded ratio / align assets with liabilities" — say "grow assets in line with liabilities, achieved at the 7% annual return that matches the actuaries' rate."
Return-adequacy test — return vs (spending + inflation)
Build the hurdle by ADDING inflation to the spending rate, then compare to the portfolio return. Don't subtract inflation from the return and compare to spending alone.
Required nominal return = spending rate + inflation Melrose: 4% + 2% = 6% hurdle Portfolio = 5.70% < 6% -> NOT appropriate
Why the wording matters: "5.7% − 2% = 3.7% vs spending 4%" compares a REAL return to a NOMINAL spending rate — a mismatch a grader can ding. State it as return vs (spending + inflation).
Endowment-model disadvantage — lead with ACCESS, not just cost
"Higher fees/costs" scores, but the discriminating disadvantage is manager access.
SizeAccess problem
Small institutionCan't reach top-tier hedge fund / PE managers
Very large institutionSuffers from its own large footprint
You already used this correctly on the Prometheo REJECT answer — deploy the same access logic on adv/disadv prompts. Advantage is always: high potential for value-added / above-market returns.
Four-model drawbacks — tighten each
ModelSharp drawback
NorwayNo alpha / no outperformance opportunity
EndowmentCost + manager access (small can't reach top managers; very large footprint)
CanadaNeeds internal teams / large scale to run alternatives in-house
LDILow return / growth potential — not for a perpetual-horizon, equity-tilted fund
Avoid vague phrasing like "difficult to manage" or "some liabilities hard to manage" — name the specific mechanism (scale, access, alpha, growth potential).
Recommendation REJECT answers — frame the magnitude first
Open with: this is a significant departure from current practice entailing much higher risk — THEN give your access/expertise reasons.
Prometheo: (1) departure + higher risk; (2) four-person staff lacks alternatives expertise/access; (3) small AUM → unlikely access to top HF/PE managers. Your two reasons were right — the magnitude framing is a free half-mark.
DB risk tolerance — pick the HIGHEST-signal reasons
When a vignette lists many drivers and asks for two, lead with sponsor/asset correlation and sponsor financial health — these are first-pick.
Antiliaro driverSignal
High correlation sponsor results × pension assetsMarquee — company struggles → assets fall AND can't fund contributions
Deteriorating sponsor (losing sales, flat earnings, rising debt)Top — constrains contribution ability
Underfunded + aggressive 6% discount rateValid
Older workforce / many retireesValid — liquidity need
Same correlation principle as the Tucker MCQ. Whenever a vignette explicitly states sponsor×asset correlation, that's a flashing signal → pick it. All five Antiliaro drivers point to below-average risk tolerance.
Mastery — ready for re-test
Quick self-check prompts built from the misses above. Reveal only after answering aloud.
When the institution lacks the scale to manage alternatives in-house, or when the adviser is an external manager (the model pushes assets in-house). Return logic alone isn't enough — check operational fit.
Only when plan assets are tied to the sponsor (e.g. holding sponsor stock). Then a sponsor downturn cuts assets exactly when larger contributions are needed. Banking sponsor + FI plan assets = no risk.
(1) Double-counting inflation (salary growth already includes it); (2) omitting the market discount-rate dimension (IG long-term bond yields; required return should exceed the liability discount rate).
Equity RISES. Loan yields reprice up, deposit cost stays ~zero → margin widens → residual equity increases. Floating-rate assets reprice (don't lose value like fixed-rate).
Pick the option with no adverse indicator in the vignette. Don't invent a risk where the facts show stability (healthy sponsor, uncorrelated assets).
Reading 10 · Portfolio Management for Institutional Investors
Full-reading recap, module by module: common characteristics (10.a), IPS & the four AA models (10.b), stakeholders / liabilities / horizons / liquidity (10.c), legal-regulatory-tax constraints (10.d), DB risk considerations (10.e), IPS evaluation (10.f), portfolio evaluation of DB / SWF / endowment / foundation (10.g), and balance-sheet management for banks & insurers (10.h). Every calculation — the endowment required return & SAA, the equity-sensitivity %ΔE, equity duration DE, and equity volatility σE — is node-verified against the textbook and reproduced by the widget's calculators.
The master framework (memorize the running order): for every institution — Mission → Stakeholders → Liabilities & horizon → Liquidity → External constraints → Investment objectives → Asset allocation. The exam gives a case; you slot facts into these buckets.
Module 10.1 · Overview of Institutional Investors
LOS 10.aFive common characteristics of institutional investors
1. Scale (size)Larger than individuals. Too large for low-capacity investments (small-cap, VC) → direct-access & in-house. Too small → can't diversify into high-minimum assets (PE, RE) & can't hire skilled staff → outsource to external managers/consultants. 2. Long horizonLonger than individuals (with exceptions) — driven by meeting specific liabilities and relatively low liquidity needs. 3. Regulatory frameworkDifferent legal/regulatory/accounting/tax rules by jurisdiction. Tightened since the 2007–09 GFC to lower leverage, increase centralized clearing, improve reporting transparency. 4. Governance frameworkFormal structure: board of directors + investment committee (may be a board subcommittee). Board sets long-term SAA; board/IC establish the IPS & monitor performance. Strategy implemented by an investment office headed by a CIO; management in-house or outsourced. 5. Principal-agentConflict when a principal (asset owner) appoints an agent whose interests diverge. Internal: appointing the IC & staff. External: outsourced managers. Classic external example → high management fee paid regardless of performance.
LOS 10.bInvestment policy of institutional investors & the four AA models
The IPS should include: mission & investment objectives (return & risk tolerance); investment horizon & liabilities; external constraints (legal, regulatory, tax, accounting); an asset-allocation policy (weights, ranges, benchmarks); a rebalancing policy; reporting requirements. Reviewed annually; revised on material changes in circumstances/market.
Model (Fig 10.1)Asset allocationAdvantages / Disadvantages
Norway (SWF)Passive public equities+bonds (base 60/40); little/no alternatives; tight tracking-error limits.+ Low cost/fees, easy for board. − No chance to outperform markets.
Yale (endowment)High alternatives, significant active management, externally managed assets.+ Potential to outperform. − Hard for small institutions w/o alts expertise; capacity issues for large managers; high fees/costs.
Canada Pension PlanHigh alternatives, significant active, internally managed; uses an easily-communicated reference portfolio of passive public assets as benchmark.+ Outperformance potential + builds internal capability. − Potentially expensive & difficult to manage.
Liability-driven (LDI)Maximize expected surplus (assets − liabilities) & manage surplus volatility.+ Explicitly recognizes liabilities in the process. − Some liability risks (e.g. longevity) are hard to hedge.
Quiz 10.1 keys. Q1 (Statement 1: different scale narrows the universe / Statement 2: institutional governance more formal): both true → C (both correct). Scale does narrow the universe (too big for small-cap/VC, too small for high-minimum alts); institutional governance is more formal than an individual's. Q2 (SJT Foundation: aggressive alts to hedge inflation, outsource due to no internal alts experience, active outperformance) → B (Yale). Yale = high alts + active + external management. (Canada would be internal; Norway is passive with no alts.) (Reasoning-derived; official keys not in photos.)
Module 10.2 · Pension Funds (DB & DC)
LOS 10.c/e/gDB vs DC — the distinctions that carry the marks
Feature (Fig 10.2)Defined Benefit (DB)Defined Contribution (DC)
Benefit paymentsContractually defined (usually on final salary) → creates a measurable liability for the sponsor.Depend on investment performance. Once promised contributions are met, no liability for sponsor.
ContributionsPrimarily by employer (employee may too).Primarily by employee (employer may too).
Decision-makingPension fund (sponsor + staff).Sponsor offers a suite of funds; employee decides level & AA.
Investment riskFaced by sponsor.Faced by beneficiary.
Mortality/longevityPooled at fund level (early deaths fund those who live long); general life-expectancy rises fall on sponsor.Employee faces longevity risk of outliving own savings.
Trend DB→DC (sponsors want lower financial risk; DC is portable). Hybrid = e.g. cash-balance plan (sponsor defines contributions, then pooled; sponsor bears some investment risk like DB).
DB Pension Plan — stakeholders, liabilities, risk
StakeholdersSponsors (must top up an underfunded plan), beneficiaries (risk of sponsor default), investment staff/IC/board, governments (tax incentives; taxpayers bear the welfare cost of under-saving), shareholders of the corporate sponsor (underfunding → balance-sheet liability → lower income → higher financial risk & share-price volatility). Liability = PV(benefits)PV of future benefits promised. Employees qualify after vesting (minimum years of service). Funded ratio = FV of plan assets / PV of DB obligations.
Liability factors (Fig 10.3) — know the direction each pushes the liability:
Service/tenure ↑Increases liability (benefits linked to years of service). Salary ↑Increases (benefits linked to final salary). Longevity ↑Increases (more years of benefits paid). Employee turnover ↑Lowers (fewer reach vesting). Additional/matching contributions ↑Increases (usually raises promised benefits). Expected investment return ↑Potentially lowers (may raise the discount rate used). Discount rate ↑Lowers (higher rate → lower PV of benefits). Quiz 10.2 Q1 → the factor that DECREASES liability = none of life-expectancy/service; among A/B/C, C (employee turnover).
Active vs retired lives: a higher proportion of retired lives (drawing benefits) → shorter horizon & lower risk tolerance. Frozen plans (closed to new active lives) also have shorter horizons.
DB risk considerations (Fig 10.4, LOS 10.e) — each drives plan risk tolerance:
Funded status ↑↑ risk tolerance (can absorb short-term losses). But if the plan is in surplus & sponsor wants to stay there, willingness may stay low → LDI to minimize surplus volatility. Sponsor financial strength ↑↑ (lower debt / higher profitability → capacity to contribute after losses). Plan small vs sponsor↑ (sponsor can tolerate more contribution volatility). Common risk exposures ↓↑ — lower correlation between sponsor results & pension assets = greater risk tolerance (sponsor likely profitable & able to contribute when plan underperforms). Quiz 10.2 Q2: change that INCREASES risk tolerance → C (allocate to assets with low correlation to sponsor operating results). A (older workforce) & B (overfunded→underfunded) both LOWER it. Early-retirement / lump-sum provisions↓ (shorter horizon → less time to recover). Younger workforce / more active lives↑ (greater liability duration → more time to recover).
Viewpoint Research (10.g worked example). Factors that INCREASE ability to take risk: (1) zero retired lives (all still working/left) → long-duration liabilities, time to recover; (2) no early-retirement / lump-sum options → longer, more predictable liabilities. Factors that DECREASE: (1) higher debt than industry → sponsor less able to top up after poor performance; (2) plan running a deficit → further underperformance threatens meeting liabilities. Trap: don't cite the one-year high ROE/profitability as increasing risk — it's a single year at high leverage, not sustainable.
DB liquidity higher when: more retired lives (frozen > nonfrozen), older workforce (shorter time to pay), higher funded status (lower sponsor contributions → benefits met from assets), ability to switch/withdraw. Lower liquidity needs → can hold more risky/illiquid assets.
DB external constraints: regulations tightened post-GFC (fee/cost reporting; personal liability for trustees). US: ERISA (regulates investing/funding/payouts; created the PBGC protecting beneficiaries of terminated plans); Pension Protection Act 2006 set minimum funding ratios (a later revision let firms discount liabilities at an average high-grade bond yield over 25y → lower liabilities, but may push more risk-taking to grow assets at the higher discount rate). Europe: IORP II. Tax: pensions often favorably treated; consider CGT on turnover, derivatives, double-taxation treaties. Accounting: US corporate DB → GAAP ASC 715 (funded status on the balance sheet); public plans → GASB (assets at market; liabilities via a blended rate — expected return on assets for the funded portion, muni yield for the unfunded).
DB investment objectives: primary = achieve a target return over a long horizon consistent with meeting contractual liabilities; secondary = minimize (PV) the sponsor's cash contributions. Target return should let assets grow in line with liabilities (the discount rate); a deficit means assets must grow faster — split between investment return and extra contributions per the plan's risk tolerance & sponsor's ability.
DC Pension Plan — the contrasts to lock
StakeholdersSponsors (no investment/longevity risk, but keep fiduciary duties: contribute, oversee investments, offer suitable options); beneficiaries (bear investment + longevity risk); board (communicate to participants at their sophistication level; select a default option for disengaged members); governments. Liabilities/horizonSponsor liability = required contributions only — no future-benefit liability. Pooling/scale can access alternatives not open to retail. Sponsor bears liquidity risk of member exits. Individual horizon tied to age (older → shorter). Life-cycle / target-dateDefault option managed to a retirement date. Participant-switching: auto-switch a member to more conservative AA as they age. Participant/cohort: pool members with a similar retirement date; fund managed more conservatively as the date nears. Liquidity / constraintsLiquidity driven by workforce age & switch/withdraw ability. Regulators require participant education (default options for disengaged); AU & US require a diversified default (doesn't absolve trustees of fiduciary duty). Tax: US 401(k) = tax-deferred (pretax contributions, earnings untaxed, benefits taxed as ordinary income; <59½ penalty +10%). ERISA/IORP II apply to both DB & DC. ObjectivesPrudently grow assets to meet retirement spending; onus on sponsor for cost-efficient default options; secondary = outperform the default's passive SAA (or outperform competing DC providers where members can switch).
Aggregate DB+DC AA data: varies by region (external constraints, risk appetite, stakeholder prefs); past decade shows a rotation from equities into alternatives & fixed income to lower funded-ratio volatility; some home bias to domestic equity.
Module 10.3 · Sovereign Wealth Funds
LOS 10.gFive IMF categories of SWF — mission drives everything else
SWF typeMissionLiabilities / horizonLiquidityObjective & typical AA
Budget stabilizationInsulate govt budget from commodity-price / cyclical volatility (revenues tied to a natural resource).Uncertain, tied to commodity prices; short-term horizon (budget support needed short-term).Highest liquidity; low risk of short-term loss.Capital preservation; beat inflation with low loss probability; avoid assets correlated with the revenue source. AA: mostly fixed income & cash (defensive).
DevelopmentPrioritize national socioeconomic projects (infrastructure, key industries).Linked to socioeconomic investments; some long, some medium (e.g. medical research).Low (long-term infrastructure/R&D).Support economic development; implicit = real return > real GDP/productivity growth. AA driven by the socioeconomic mission (local infrastructure).
SavingsInvest nonrenewable-resource revenues for future generations.Linked to future generations → long term.Lowest (rises as resources deplete & govt withdraws for budget needs).Maintain purchasing power while funding budget needs. AA: high equities & alternatives (PE, real assets) (long horizon).
ReserveEarn returns on excess FX reserves held by central banks (reduce the negative cost of carry).Technically the yield promised on govt/CB-issued bonds; funds target higher; horizon very long, no near-term liabilities.Lower than stabilization but higher than savings; hold liquid FI that can be sold if CB reserves change dramatically.Earn a return > the yield the govt/CB pays on its bonds. AA similar to savings but lower alts (higher liquidity needs).
Pension reserveSave & invest to meet future govt pension liabilities.Linked to future pension payments → long term; may have accumulation & decumulation phases.Vary: lower in accumulation, higher in decumulation.Earn returns to meet unfunded pension/social-care payments. AA: high equities/alts due to long horizon & low liquidity in accumulation.
StakeholdersCurrent & future citizens (direct payments / indirect via lower tax or more domestic investment); investment offices (invest in-house or appoint external); the board (fiduciary duty to ultimate beneficiaries); governments (may rely on SWF returns to balance deficits). External constraintsEstablished by laws giving mission & structure (esp. development funds with a socioeconomic mission). To avoid political influence: governance, independence, transparency, accountability — the Santiago Principles (IFSWF best-practice framework). Generally tax-exempt → may void ability to claim withholding-tax credits; watch double-tax treaties abroad; avoid being seen to dodge foreign taxes. Savings ≈ endowmentsSavings funds & pension reserve funds typically follow the Canadian model; savings funds share very similar objectives to endowments & foundations (broader mandate, longer horizon → higher alts).
Quiz 10.3 keys. Q1 (SAA of 10% equities / 60% FI / 30% cash) → C (budget stabilization) — the defensive, FI-and-cash-heavy profile matches the highest-liquidity stabilization fund. Q2 (BoC buys USD from exporters to boost FX reserves; reserve-fund context) → B: financing the USD purchase (issuing local-currency debt / creating reserves) can cause deflationary pressures is the accurate one relative to A (reserves aren't put in the riskiest assets — they stay liquid) and C (stabilization bonds create a negative, not positive, carry). (Reasoning-derived; official keys not in photos.)
Module 10.4 · University Endowments & Private Foundations
LOS 10.gUniversity endowments
MissionFunds from gifts/donations, invested to give ongoing support to the operating budget. Main objective = balance the university's needs today vs the future → intergenerational equity. StakeholdersCurrent & future students, alumni donors, employees whose livelihoods depend on the university. Alumni (often investment professionals) frequently sit on the board/IC. HorizonPerpetual (unlimited university life + intergenerational equity). LiquidityLow — net spending only ~2–4% of assets (gifts & donations offset the 4–6% gross). Low liquidity + perpetual horizon → high risk tolerance, can absorb short-term volatility for long-term returns. Analyze liquidity risk with cash-flow modeling; some use a liquidity risk band capping illiquid exposure (incl. uncalled commitments). External constraintsTotal-return investing + diversification (MPT); fiduciary duty of care. US: UPMIFA (flexibility in spending + adoption of MPT); UK: Trustee Act 2000 (endowments often structured as trusts). Generally tax-exempt on returns; donors can deduct gifts. ObjectivesPreserve purchasing power in perpetuity (grow with inflation) while funding spending. Real return target typically ~5% over HEPI over 3–5y; volatility ~10–15%. Secondary = beat a passive benchmark; tertiary = beat a peer group (peer-benchmarking risks herding & dislocating from the core mission).
Spending-policy formula — smooths payouts to insulate the university from market volatility:
spendingt+1 = w × [spendingt × (1 + inflation)] + {(1 − w) × (spending rate × avg AUM)} where w = weight on the prior year's spending amount
Constant-growth (w=1)Fixed real payout, grown by HEPI. Certain for the university, but the % of AUM paid fluctuates with value. Often has caps & floors (max/min % of AUM over 1 or 3 years). Market-value (w=0)Payout = prespecified spending rate (4–6%) × a 3–5y moving average of asset values. Procyclical — spending tracks the moving average. Hybrid (0<w<1)Weighted average of the two rules. FundraisingGifts/donations mean the net spending rate is closer to 2–4% vs the 4–6% gross applied. Reliance & debt accessHigher endowment share of the operating budget → lower risk tolerance. Ability to issue debt → higher risk tolerance (can borrow to cover spending in downturns).
Endowment AA: large US endowments follow the endowment model — majority (>50%) to alternatives (risen over two decades). Smaller endowments hold less alts, more domestic equity & FI, with home bias overweighting US equities.
Capital University endowment (10.g worked example) — the required-return + SAA calc:
Nominal required return = spending rate + HEPI HEPI = CPI (1%) + 100 bps = 2% → required = 4% + 2% = 6% (volatility cap 15%) Current AA (30% US eq @6%, 70% FI @3%): 0.30×6% + 0.70×3% = 3.9% → FAILS the 6% target New SAA: FI 25%@3 + USeq 35%@6 + Intl 20%@7 + RE 10%@8 + PE 10%@10 = 0.75 + 2.10 + 1.40 + 0.80 + 1.00 = 6.05% → MEETS 6%
Answers. (1) Objective: maintain purchasing power in perpetuity while funding 10% of the operating budget; nominal required = 6%. (2) Accept the shift on return grounds — current 3.9% fails, new 6.05% meets 6%. (3) Concern making it inappropriate: the investment office is small & inexperienced in alternatives (new allocations to PE & real assets need due-diligence skill), and the new SAA must still be checked against the 15% volatility cap.
Private foundations — vs endowments
MissionNonprofits making grants to charitable causes. Types: private (donor/family, e.g. Gates), community, operating (fund a specific not-for-profit), corporate. Objective similar to endowments: maintain purchasing power in perpetuity & fund grant-making. StakeholdersFounding family, donors, grant recipients, wider community, government (favorable tax). Board members less likely to have professional investment experience than endowment alumni boards → less rigorous oversight / more delegation → may hurt decision quality in sophisticated markets (alts). Mission-related (impact) investing promotes the mission but challenges maintaining sufficient returns. HorizonPerpetual (trend toward limited-life foundations that spend down within a set time of the founder's death → shorter horizon). Liabilities / spendingUS: minimum 5% of assets (12-month trailing) + investment expenses; must spend donations in the year received (flow-through). Unlike universities, foundations rely almost exclusively on the endowment/spending to meet budgets → higher liquidity needs → lower risk tolerance than university endowments. LiquidityMust fund the 5% near-term spend + capital calls from LP fund investments + margin calls on derivatives. External constraintsSame laws as endowments (UPMIFA / Trustee Act): total-return, diversification, duty of care. Tax-exempt status depends on meeting the minimum spending rule — failing it → 30% tax on undistributed income; most US foundations also pay a 2% tax on net investment income. Objectives / AAReal return over CPI of the spending rate (min 5%) + investment expenses; volatility ~10–15% over 3–5y; secondary = beat a policy benchmark on a tracking-error budget. Overall risk tolerance still high (beat inflation, long horizon) → larger US foundations put ~half in alternatives; smaller ones tilt to domestic equity & FI.
Quiz 10.4 Q1. Endowment spends 5% of a 3y rolling value; CPI 3%, HEPI 2.5%. Objective total real rate of return → B (7.5%): to maintain purchasing power (measured by HEPI 2.5%) and fund the 5% spend, the return objective = spending 5% + HEPI 2.5% = 7.5%. (Reasoning-derived; official key not in photos.)
Module 10.5 · Banks & Insurers
LOS 10.gBanks & insurers — profit-seeking intermediaries (advise the investment portfolio, not the core business)
Banks. Primary function = earn profits by taking deposits & making loans (also safeguarding assets, executing securities/derivatives, advising/investing).
StakeholdersShareholders (profit max), depositors (most of liabilities; want asset protection), borrowers (loans = most of assets), creditors, rating agencies, regulators, communities; internal = employees/managers/directors. Liabilities / horizonDeposits dominate liabilities: demand deposits (withdrawable without notice → short duration) & time/term deposits (advance notice). Also short-term wholesale funding, long-term debt, repo. Assets = longer-term illiquid mortgage & commercial loans. Horizon driven by the long-illiquid-asset vs short-liquid-liability gap; though perpetual, the investment portfolio holds short instruments to manage shareholder-capital volatility short/medium-term. LiquidityKey focus (short-duration deposits + need to raise liquidity in stress). Post-GFC: LCR (cover near-term outflows with liquid assets) & NSFR (adequate stable funding) → more liquid portfolios, less wholesale reliance. Retail banks (stable, low-cost retail deposits) > commercial banks (wholesale-reliant) on liquidity. External constraintsRegulators focus on capital adequacy, liquidity, leverage (systemic-failure risk). Goal: adequate capital to absorb losses (not customers/creditors/taxpayers) via diversification, asset-quality-based reserves, stable funding. Largest banks = SIFIs → higher capital, dividend/buyback limits, restricted subordinated-holder claims & derivatives/off-balance-sheet use. Quality-based reserves: switching to riskier assets (IG→HY) raises risk-weighted assets → higher required reserves. Accounting (3 systems)(1) Standard (GAAP/IFRS) → smoothest income (accruals). (2) Statutory (regulators) → more conservative (removes intangibles, accelerates expenses, recognizes reserves). (3) True economic → market value for all → most volatile income. Banks are fully taxable → consider after-tax returns. ObjectivesPrimary = manage liquidity & reduce risk mismatches between the bank's noninvestment assets & liabilities. An ALMCo sets the IPS, monitors, sets market/credit/liquidity/solvency risk limits with authority over both sides of the balance sheet.
Insurers. Two types: Life (whole/term with fixed payments; variable life & annuities with policyholder-chosen funds; annuities; health) & P&C (commercial property/liability, home, marine, surety, legal).
Stakeholders / accountsPublicly listed → shareholders want long-term capital max while honoring policyholder obligations; mutuals → owned by policyholders (surplus retained or returned via dividends/premium cuts). General account funds traditional-life & fixed-annuity liabilities (insurer bears investment risk); separate account for variable life/annuities (policyholder bears investment risk). Liabilities / horizonLife: long-duration payouts → historically 20–40y horizons. P&C: shorter duration, higher uncertainty (unpredictable high-payout events, e.g. disasters). Both perpetual as institutions, but the underwriting cycle (competition-driven profitability swings) affects horizon — intense competition/low underwriting profit → more appetite for investment risk. LiquidityInterest-rate-sensitive: ↑ rates → ↑ lapses/surrenders (policyholders on low-yield contracts surrender to reinvest → higher net outflows). P&C need ample cash/short-term FI (cash-flow uncertainty). General account splits into a reserve portfolio (meets policy liabilities → managed conservatively) & a surplus portfolio (generate higher returns, assume liquidity risk, allocate to alternatives). External constraintsLike banks, can be SIFIs; regulators ensure capital to absorb business + investment losses. US: NAIC (state regulators set accounting/reporting); Europe: Solvency II. Same 3 accounting systems; fully taxable → after-tax focus. Riskier investments → higher required reserves. ObjectivesLike banks: manage liquidity & reduce risk mismatches between the institution's assets & liabilities, considering general business conditions & the economy. Oversight by an investment committee responsible for all policies, reporting to regulators & stakeholders.
Quiz 10.5/10.6 Q1 & Q2. Q1 (capital requirements for banks/insurers set with reference to) → A (statutory reporting) — regulators use conservative statutory accounting, not GAAP/economic. Q2 (SAJ life insurer splits the general account into reserve + surplus portfolios) → A (correct): the general account (not separate account) is indeed split into a conservatively-managed reserve portfolio and a higher-return surplus portfolio. (Reasoning-derived; official keys not in photos.)
Module 10.6 · Balance-Sheet Management & Investment Considerations
LOS 10.hBalance-sheet considerations for banks & insurers — the three equity formulas
For both banks & insurers the overall objective is to maximize the market value of equity capital with high assurance that depositor/creditor/policyholder claims can be met. M = leverage multiplier = A/E. If E/A = 5%, M = 20 (assets funded $1 equity + $19 liabilities).
1. Percentage change in equity (%ΔE).
%ΔE = %ΔA × M − %ΔL × (M − 1) Example: E/A = 5% → M = 20. Liabilities rise 1.5%, assets stable: %ΔE = (0% × 20) − (1.5% × 19) = −28.5%
Read the terms: asset returns are magnified by leverage (M); the −(M−1) on liabilities reflects that rising liabilities cut equity, and (M−1) is the size of liabilities relative to equity. A tiny 1.5% liability rise wipes out 28.5% of equity because of 20× leverage.
2. Equity duration (DE).
DE = DA×M − DL×(M−1)×(Δi / Δy) Δi/Δy = expected move in liability yield per unit move in asset yield WellLife: E/A = 12.5% → M = 8; DA=3, DL=2, Δi/Δy = 0.70 DE = (3×8) − (2 × 7 × 0.70) = 24 − 9.8 = 14.2 • 25 bp FALL in asset yield → equity value ↑ ≈ 14.2 × 0.25% = +3.55% • If E/A raised to 10% → M = 10: DE = (3×10) − (2×9×0.70) = 17.4 (lower leverage cut... no — higher M→lower here? M fell 8→10? note E/A up 12.5%→10% is M UP 8→10 → DE rises)
Direction check: raising E/A from 12.5% to 10% actually lowers equity relative to assets → M rises 8→10 → equity duration rises 14.2→17.4 (more asset-rate sensitivity per unit of equity). DE = modified duration of equity; a 1% asset-yield move → ~DE% equity move.
3. Equity volatility (σE). A two-asset variance with weight M on assets and −(M−1) on liabilities:
σ²E = M²σ²A + (M−1)²σ²L − 2·M·(M−1)·σAσLρAL WellLife: M=8, σA=7%, σL=4%, ρAL=0.3 σ²E = (8²×0.07²) + (7²×0.04²) − (2×8×7×0.07×0.04×0.3) = 0.298 σE = √0.298 = 0.546 = 54.6% New regs: E/A = 20% → M=5, σA lowered to 5%, σL=4%, ρ=0.3 σ²E = (5²×0.05²) + (4²×0.04²) − (2×5×4×0.05×0.04×0.3) = 0.0641 σE = √0.0641 = 0.253 = 25.3%
Why σE collapses 54.6%→25.3%: two levers move together — lower leverage (M 8→5, i.e. more equity cushion) and lower asset volatility (7%→5%). Both shrink the magnified asset-risk term M²σ²A. The negative correlation term (asset/liability co-movement) partially offsets equity volatility.
Strategies for changing volatility (Fig 10.7) — each lever & its effect on σE:
StrategyImpact on factorσE
Hold diversified fixed incomeLowers σAFalls
Hold high-quality fixed incomeLowers σAFalls
Match asset/liability durations & borrower/claimant optionsIncreases ρALFalls
Hold common stockIncreases σA, lowers ρALRises (regulators require ~100% reserves vs stock)
Derivatives transparency & collateralizationLowers σA & σL, increases ρALFalls
Hold more liquid investmentsLowers σAFalls
Surrender penalties on insurance contractsLowers σLFalls (cushions losses when rates rise)
Prepayment penalties on debtIncreases ρALFalls (offsets rising liabilities in falling-rate env.)
Catastrophic insurance riskIncreases σLRises
Predictability of underwriting lossesDecreases σLFalls
Diversifying insurance businessDecreases σLFalls
Variable annuitiesIncreases ρALFalls (gains/losses pass through to policyholders)
SJT Bank switch (10.h worked example): switch HY corporate floating-rate → IG govt fixed-rate + a pay-fixed/receive-floating swap. (1) Addresses the two findings: lowers exposure to widening credit spreads (HY→IG) & improves the liquidity position (IG govt more liquid than HY, offsetting the loan-book/deposit stress). (2) Regulatory risk-based capital falls (IG govt lower risk weight than HY → lower RWA → less required capital). (3) Duration: floating→fixed raises asset duration, but the pay-fixed swap creates a synthetic liability raising liability duration — if tailored, the two offset → asset/liability profile unchanged. (4) Earnings & volatility: govt yields lower than corporate (no credit spread) → lower earnings, but more-liquid IG govt is less volatile → lower equity-capital volatility.
Quiz 10.5/10.6 Q3. Bank E/A = 20% → M = 5; σA=7%, σL=5%, ρAL=0.5.
σ²E = (5²×0.07²) + (4²×0.05²) − (2×5×4×0.07×0.05×0.5) = 0.1225 + 0.04 − 0.07 = 0.0925 → σE = √0.0925 = 30.4% → C. (Node-verified; official key not in photos.)
Trading Costs and Electronic Markets
READING 11 · Portfolio Construction
Execution costs (LOS 11.a)
TypeVisibilityExamples
ExplicitObservable & transparent ("get a receipt")Brokerage, taxes, fees. Large buy-side: trading staff (fixed). Small traders: variable commissions.
ImplicitNot readily discernible, estimated vs a benchmarkBid-ask spread, market/price impact, delay (slippage), opportunity cost
Implicit costs are the focus of this reading. They're measured as the result of a trade relative to a reference point (benchmark).
The four implicit costs
CostWhat it isDriver
Bid-ask spreadHighest potential cost for a small tradeMarket orders fill fast at posted bid/ask; patient traders trade between bid/ask but risk non-fill. Large trades walk down the book → higher cost.
Market / price impactCost of demanding liquidity (market-moving trades)Large buy → raise price to attract sellers; large sell → lower price to attract buyers. Breaking up reduces impact but raises delay/opportunity cost.
Delay cost (slippage)Adverse price move during the lag in executing a large tradeBreaking up a buy risks price rising over time; later batches fill at higher price.
Opportunity costFrom unfilled / failed ordersUnderpriced security rises; if higher price forces cancel of the unfilled part → lost profits.
The core tradeoff: market impact vs (delay + opportunity). Trade fast → high market impact. Wait patiently for a good price → the market may move out of your trading range (delay + opportunity cost). Most implicit-cost components compare actual execution price vs the price when the order was triggered; opportunity cost instead looks at the cost of lost (unfilled) trades.
Liquidity: demanding vs providing
Order typeLiquidityBehavior
Market orderDemands liquidityAccepts a posted bid/ask. Large ones "walk down" the limit order book, exhausting quantity at each level.
Limit orderProvides liquidityOffers to trade at a posted price; risk of non-execution.
Example: a buy order for 150,000 shares may hit several limit orders (at posted ask prices) until the cumulative quantity reaches 150,000.
Dealer quotes & the limit order book (LOS 11.b)
TermDefinition
Bid / inside bidHighest-posted bid price
Best ask / inside askLowest ask price
Inside spreadBest ask − best bid
MidquoteAverage of the bid & ask quoted by a single dealer
Limit order bookPosted bids & offers with quantities, sorted best → worst
Worked example — Figure 11.1 (XYZ order book)
BidsPrice / SizeAsksPrice / Size
P (9:31)32.25 / 3,000R (9:31)32.29 / 2,000
Q (9:41)32.24 / 2,500P (9:31)32.31 / 3,000
R (9:45)32.23 / 3,500Q (9:41)32.35 / 3,500
Market buy of 3,000 at 9:31: 2,000 @ 32.29 (inside ask, R) + 1,000 @ 32.31 (next, P) → the larger order had to split, costing $0.02 more per share on the second part (price impact moving down the book).
Standing limit order = trader posts her own quote → provides liquidity & trades at posted prices, but risks failure to complete. In a nonexchange market (no clearinghouse guarantee), a trader may choose a dealer other than the best price — creditworthiness/relationships matter in counterparty choice.
Quote-revision note: Dealer P may revise his quote higher once he sees the trade, so the 32.29 inside ask can disappear. To avoid missing the 32.31, a trader may execute the entire order with Dealer P.
Effective spread (LOS 11.b)
Uses the midquote as the benchmark.
Effective spread transaction cost = (side) × (transaction price − midquote) side = +1 for BUY, −1 for SELL effective spread = 2 × (effective spread transaction cost)
At the posted bid/ask → effective spread = quoted spread. At a better price → price improvement, effective spread < quoted spread.
Worked example — Spreads (Figure 11.1)
QuantityCalcResult
Spread quoted by Dealer Q32.35 − 32.24$0.11
Inside spread32.29 (best ask) − 32.25 (best bid)$0.04
Midquote Dealer R(32.23 + 32.29) / 2$32.26
Midquote Dealer P(32.25 + 32.31) / 2$32.28
Quoted spread Dealer P32.31 − 32.25$0.06
Effective spread (buy @ 32.29, P)2 × (+1) × (32.29 − 32.28)$0.02
Effective spread $0.02 < quoted spread $0.06 → there was price improvement on that trade.
Limitations of effective spread
MissesWhy
Price impact of split large ordersPoor indicator of trade performance when a large order is split into smaller orders
Slippage / delayDoesn't account for the unfilled portion, or delay from not routing to the best market; delay measured for the part unfilled by end of day
Opportunity costDoesn't capture lost profit when an unfilled part is abandoned after an adverse price move (e.g. analyst values stock $12.55, price runs past it, order abandoned)
Volume-weighted average price (VWAP / interval VWAP)
The weighted-average price at which all trades executed during the interval between the order being placed and executed. Easy to interpret — evaluates the trade's price vs other trades in the same period.
VWAP transaction cost = trade size × (side) × (trade VWAP − benchmark VWAP) side = +1 for BUY, −1 for SELL
Compare the trade VWAP to the benchmark VWAP (all market trades in the interval). If the entire order executed at one price, its VWAP = that price.
Worked example — VWAP (BNC)
Market trades in intervalSubject trade (buy 300)
10:00 — 100 @ 12.11100 @ 12.11
11:00 — 300 @ 12.00200 @ 12.00
11:30 — 600 @ 11.75—
Benchmark VWAP = (100/1000)×12.11 + (300/1000)×12.00 + (600/1000)×11.75 = $11.86 (total volume 1,000) Trade VWAP = (100/300)×12.11 + (200/300)×12.00 = $12.04 VWAP txn cost = 300 × (+1) × (12.04 − 11.86) = $54
Positive cost ($54) → the buy executed above the benchmark = unfavorable. A negative number would mean the trade beat the benchmark.
Limitations of VWAP transaction cost
LimitationWhy
Useless when the trade is a big part of volumeBenchmark VWAP & trade VWAP converge → measured cost skewed toward zero
Doesn't capture price impactA lone large buy at an above-normal price makes benchmark = trade VWAP → cost = 0, even though the price was bad
Bias-to-zero → popularity: the skew toward zero may explain why managers like VWAP — it highlights a low transaction cost. VWAP is appropriate to evaluate execution only when the trade is a SMALL part of overall trading volume.
Implementation shortfall (LOS 11.c)
Measures transaction cost as the difference between the value of the actual portfolio and the value of a hypothetical paper portfolio.
In the paper portfolio, the trade is fully executed at no cost, at the prevailing price when the order was placed — the decision price = arrival price = strike price, generally the midquote at order placement.
Captures all three implicit costs — price impact, slippage, and opportunity cost — so it fixes VWAP's shortfalls. Tradeoff: the computation is more complex.
Benchmark comparison — at a glance
BenchmarkReferenceCaptures
Effective spreadMidquote at executionSpread / price improvement only
VWAPInterval VWAP of market tradesRelative price vs interval; misses price impact, biased to zero
Implementation shortfallPaper portfolio at arrival/decision priceAll three implicit costs (impact + slippage + opportunity)
Effective spread calculator
Enter the trade. Effective spread transaction cost = side × (price − midquote); effective spread = 2 × that.
Textbook check: buy @ 32.29 with P's quotes (bid 32.25, ask 32.31) → midquote 32.28, effective spread $0.02 < quoted $0.06 = price improvement.
