Factors driving electronic trading systems (LOS 11.d)
#DriverDetail
1CostCheaper to operate than manual counterparts
2AccuracyPerform exactly as programmed → precisely enforce the exchange's order precedence & pricing rules
3Audit trailsGenerate & maintain records → investigators can examine the precise chain of events
4Fraud preventionKeep hidden orders hidden; don't leak information inadvertently or fraudulently
5Continuous marketNo breaks; operate continuously; unaffected by severe weather or events that hinder human traders
Mnemonic: CAAFC — Cost, Accuracy, Audit trails, Fraud prevention, Continuous market.
From the trader's perspective
Electronic systems can: quickly process vast amounts of data; exhibit perfect discipline (do exactly what programmed, no behavioral bias); maintain perfect records.
Bond markets remain OTC
While electronic systems greatly benefit stock traders, bond market trades remain largely over the counter. Many competing electronic bond exchanges exist, but they're used primarily by dealers.
Significant cost savings would result for public investors if they were given access to these systems by their brokers.
Market fragmentation (LOS 11.e)
Occurs when a security trades in multiple markets → significant liquidity differences between these electronic markets.
Example: a security may have several posted bids but few offers on one exchange, with the opposite on another. Fragmentation can lead to significant price and liquidity differences between markets.
Algorithms that overcome fragmentation
AlgorithmWhat it does
Liquidity aggregationCreates a "super book" displaying liquidity across all markets
Smart order routing (SOR)Sends orders to the markets with the best prices and sizes
Automated strategies for large orders seek out liquidity across all markets to minimize price impact — i.e. liquidity-seeking algos exist in response to market fragmentation.
Who uses electronic trading (LOS 11.f)
User groupIncludes
Proprietary tradersDealers, arbitrageurs, front runners (profit-seeking)
Buy-side tradersInvestment & risk managers
BrokersThat serve the above
Proprietary electronic traders include high-frequency traders (quick round-trips thousands of times/day) and low-latency traders (rely on speed receiving news & trading on it).
Latency = the time lapse between an event occurring and the execution of a trade based on that event.
News traders vs dealers — contrast
Electronic news tradersElectronic dealers
What they doAnalyze high-speed news feeds; submit market orders (not limit) on the analysisPost bid/offer to profit from the spread; profit depends on trading frequency
EdgeAI/NLP to trade against stale orders (posted limits not reflecting the news)Low inventory; quickly adjust positions; manage adverse-price risk by taking the opposite side fast
News behaviorProfit from acting on news firstSuspend quotes when news is released
Dealer quote-suspension tradeoff: suspending quotes on news → lost trading opportunities when the news turns out immaterial, BUT it protects the dealer from providing liquidity to news traders when the news is material (i.e. from being picked off on stale quotes). Low round-trip costs let news traders profit even if right only a fraction of the time.
Characteristics & uses — the need for speed (LOS 11.g)
Beyond lower trading costs, electronic systems give low-latency traders a competitive edge by jumping the order queue.
Queue-jump in...What it means
Order takingExecuting against a standing sell order when positive market news is revealed
Market makingTaking precedence when providing liquidity
Order cancelingCanceling when they no longer want to fill (e.g. trades at other exchanges make a posted quote ill-advised)
Bottom line: electronic traders must be faster than their competitors to capitalize on market opportunities.
Low-latency: 3 phases of a trade (LOS 11.g)
#Time gapLatency type
1Publication of actionable news → receipt by the traderCommunication
2Receipt of news → deciding the appropriate action (order)Computation
3Order determination → communicating the order to the exchangeCommunication
Mapping trap: phases 1 & 3 = communication speed; phase 2 = computation speed. Co-location / fiber-optic = communication; CPUs / OS / assembler = computation.
Communication speed
Minimize distance traveled. Invest in latest/fastest comms tech; site servers as close to the exchange as possible → co-location (servers inside the exchange, if offered).
Fairness: the exchange cannot selectively offer co-location to only a few traders.
Computation speed
LayerTechniques
HardwareOverclock fastest processors (souped-up cooling); fast memory vs hard disks (avoid disk-seeking time); multiple specialized processors
SoftwareLow-overhead simple/no-frills OS; key functions in assembler (high-level C++ compilers not specialized → slower)
Dynamic codeIf code updates with market conditions → use faster-to-write languages (Python) where deployment speed > processing speed
Pre-computationPre-run scenario analysis so the optimal action per scenario is predetermined → no delay once a scenario is observed
Advanced orders, tactics & algorithms (LOS 11.h)
ToolWhat it is
Advanced order typesLimit orders with a dynamic limit price that varies with a benchmark. E.g. pegged limit buy 1,000 at one tick below the lowest ask → as asks change, order is auto-canceled & replaced with a revised bid
Trading tacticsPlans submitting multiple orders (e.g. across multiple exchanges) to uncover hidden opportunities (hidden bids/asks), discretionary orders (limit ± a discretion amount), IOC orders; used at dark pools (venues hiding liquidity, select clientele). Reduce footprint via randomness in order size & time-to-cancel; often midspread orders (pegged to bid-ask midpoint)
Algorithms (algos)Programmed strategies using multiple orders, sequencing & tactics. E.g. a VWAP algo splits an order proportional to expected volume → reduces price impact. Good algos minimize total cost by using limit orders (offer liquidity) and market orders (minimize delay/opportunity cost)
Impact of electronic trading — strategies
#StrategyDetail
1Hidden ordersLimit orders hidden from all but the receiving exchange; remove the valuable option exposed standing orders give others. Electronic markets better suited (lower inadvertent exposure). Detected by pinging with small IOC orders → reveals existence (NOT size or side)
2LeapfrogBeating the best bid/ask. With large quoted spreads, a dealer posts a better price (lower ask / higher bid) → narrows the inside spread; frustrates others who must re-quote to keep precedence
3Flickering quotesExposed limit orders submitted & canceled almost immediately → deny others the option a standing order provides. To trade against one, submit a hidden limit order in anticipation of its return
5Machine learningData mining / statistical models that evolve on new data; rely on empirical data to fine-tune algos. Ineffective in extraordinary times (volatility spikes, past not a useful guide) → many traders shut down trading in high-risk periods
4. Electronic arbitrage — three types
TypeMechanismRisk
A. Take liquidity both sidesSimultaneous market buy & sell across markets to exploit mispricing of the same security (at posted ask/bid). Low latency critical so both legs fill at targetLowest — market orders fill fast
B. Offer liquidity one sidee.g. $100 bid / $105 offered in X & Y; place a bid at $95 in X; if it fills, immediately sell to the $100 bid in Y → $5 profitModerate — the offered leg may not fill
C. Offer liquidity both sidesPost limit orders inferior to best bid/offer in different markets to lower costs furtherHighest — if one leg fills & the other doesn't → exposed to adverse price movement
Electronic arbitrage calculator
Two markets, each with a best bid/ask and sizes. Take-liquidity-both-sides: buy at the lowest ask, sell at the highest bid; profit/share = best bid − best ask (only if > 0). Total = profit/share × the binding size.
MarketBest bidBid sizeBest askAsk size
1
2
Default = Stock ZZ example: buy @ 10.05 (Bravo), sell @ 10.06 (Alpha) → $0.01/share, $110 on 11,000. Quiz Philly/LA (16.13/16.14 sz 50k/48k; 16.09/16.11 sz 90k/100k) → $0.02 × 50,000 = $1,000.
Size trap: the binding quantity is the smaller of (the bid size you sell into) and (the ask size you buy from). For Philly/LA that's min(50,000 bid, 100,000 ask) = 50,000 → $1,000 (NOT $2,000 from using 100,000).
Risks of electronic trading (LOS 11.i)
RiskDetail
HFT arms raceFastest participants win → HFTs deploy the latest/most expensive state-of-the-art tech. Arms race offsets some cost benefits, acts as an entry barrier, playing field not level for smaller traders
Systemic riskCost of bad trades borne by parties other than the responsible one → less incentive to mitigate. Programming errors can cause market chaos with many casualties before being caught
HFT arms-race fix: introduce delays in trading at random intervals (cannot be forecast by HFT algos) → mitigates the speed advantage.
Common trading errors (under systemic risk)
ErrorDetail
Runaway algorithmsSeries of unintended orders. Flash crash of May 2010: an algo sold mini S&P 500 futures with orders proportional to trading volume (NOT a limit order) → more trading begat more volume → volatility spiral
Fat finger errorsInput errors; if large enough → dramatic volatility in an electronic market where human checks/balances are missing
Overlarge ordersMarket orders demanding liquidity significantly higher than what's available in the market they're sent to (the flash crash's large S&P 500 mini sell led to ripple effects)
Malevolent ordersCreated to specifically manipulate the market: e.g. aggrieved employees programming rogue trades, or denial-of-service attacks on competitors via excessive quote submission
Systemic-risk mitigation: ensure software is adequately backtested, strictly controlled, and supervised before deployment; brokers must scrutinize order appropriateness; markets should have limits / circuit breakers that trigger when volatility spikes.
Abusive practices surveillance may detect (LOS 11.j)
Real-time surveillance monitors electronic markets to detect abuses & potential crises as they unfold (faster response). Leans on the electronic audit trail to reconstruct the chain of events.
Front running
Low-latency trading ahead of known large trades. A front runner learning a large buy is being worked in pieces takes the best asks, then resells to the unsuspecting buyer at higher prices.
Legality nuance: illegal only if the information was obtained improperly. Often it's just inferred from market data — algos break large orders into pieces, and front runners use machine learning to sniff them out.
Market manipulation — produces false price/volume data
Manipulators deceive others into acting on misleading info, to the manipulator's advantage. Illegal in most jurisdictions, but enforcement is lax (hard to separate manipulative from genuine trades). Subtypes:
TacticMechanism
Trading for market impactTrades designed to move the price (up/down), sometimes at large cost, to influence others' perception of value
RumormongeringDisseminate fake info to affect the target's value assessment. Generally illegal; but biased reporting (highlighting one side) is not
Wash tradingTrading between commonly controlled accounts to create a false impression of liquidity → false sense of security about liquidity
Spoofing / layeringFake limit orders posted to create fake optimism/pessimism. E.g. post a hidden limit buy (low price) + exposed sell orders to convince others to sell low → fills the hidden buy
BluffingPrey on momentum traders (buy rising / sell falling). E.g. pump and dump (buy to raise price, sell back higher to momentum traders); sell-side analog = short and distort
Gunning the marketForce others into bad trades: e.g. rapid short selling collapses a security → triggers stop-loss orders the manipulator fills, repurchasing at a lower price
Squeezing & corneringControl resources needed to settle contracts, then withdraw → defaults; re-extend at higher price. Short squeeze: control lendable shares, lend to shorts, abruptly recall → shorts cover higher. Cornering (commodities): long futures + buy up spot supply, demand physical delivery the counterparty can't supply
Easy-to-confuse pair: Layering is risky — the exposed sell orders the spoofer intended to cancel may actually get filled. Bluffing targets momentum traders; analysts avoid falling for it by having a sound valuation basis (Standard V(A) Diligence & Reasonable Basis).
Patterns to fix
TrapCorrect frame
"Market impact" of a sub-tradeMeasured trade-on-trade: this trade's exec price − the previous trade's exec price. NOT vs the arrival midquote. (Arrival-midquote benchmark belongs to implementation shortfall, a different measure.)
ML model effectivenessBest in a well-understood / repeated market. Useless-or-worse in high volatility (few precedents) and unsuited to brand-new markets (no data history).
Leapfrog requires WIDE spreadsNarrow spread → NOT leapfrog. Wide spreads → dealers quote better prices and jump ahead.
Speed-preserving risk fixOnly trade halts keep the "faster than competitors" edge (pause everyone, then resume). Random delays & frequent call markets deliberately neutralize speed.
Market impact, trade-on-trade
5,000-share buy filled in 3 trades: T1 $25.20, T2 $25.22, T3 $25.27. Per-share market impact of Trade 2?
A — $0.02. Trade 1 executed at $25.20 and moved the price; Trade 2 executed at $25.22 → impact = 25.22 − 25.20 = $0.02 per share.
Don't use the arrival midquote here. (25.17+25.20)/2 = 25.185 → 25.22 − 25.185 = $0.035 ≈ B is the trap. That midquote method is implementation shortfall, not trade-on-trade price impact. C ($0.07) uses Trade 3's price (25.27 − 25.20) — wrong trade.
ML model environment
B — well-understood market environment. ML thrives on problems that repeat regularly. In high-volatility / uncharted conditions it has few precedents to learn from → useless or worse; traders often shut down. New markets lack the data history too.
Systemic-risk mitigation (testing + halts)
C — both. Exhaustive pre-launch testing curbs programming-error risk; mandatory trade halts on large price moves cap runaway spirals. Both reduce systemic risk.
Pattern-trading classification (BYYP)
Trader spots 500-share trades every 20 min for an hour (repeated across days), infers a large buy worked in pieces, and buys ahead of it.
B — front running. Order-anticipation: identifying predictable order-submission patterns and trading ahead of a liquidity demander. Not arbitrage (that's cross-market mispricing). Not quote matching (that trades ahead of liquidity suppliers).
No-standing-orders strategy (AXZ)
Narrow bid-ask spread, high volatility, strategy uses NO standing orders.
A — flickering quotes. Submit & cancel within ~1 second → the order never stands. Rules out B (ML fails in high volatility) and C (leapfrog needs wide spreads, this is narrow).
Speed-preserving structural change (2Fast)
B — trade halts. All three reduce systemic risk, but only halts preserve the "faster than competitors" edge: trading pauses for everyone and the fast trader is fast again on resumption. Random delays and once-a-second call markets deliberately neutralize speed.
Electronic-trader taxonomy — the discriminators
TypeTrades ahead of...Key tell
Front runnerLiquidity demandersDetects a large order worked in pieces (order-anticipation / predictable patterns) and trades ahead
Quote matcherLiquidity suppliers (standing orders)Exploits the option value of standing orders — buys relying on standing buy orders to exit; sells relying on standing sell orders
Arbitrageur— (cross-market)Buys undervalued / sells similar overvalued across markets; decision driven by mispricing, not order patterns
Front runner vs quote matcher = which side of liquidity they trade ahead of. Demander → front runner; supplier → quote matcher. If the prompt says a trader is "seeking/filling a large order" (demanding liquidity) → front running.
No-standing-order tactics: flickering quotes (submit/cancel <1s) and hidden orders — used when the trader wants others to see a willingness to trade without leaving a resting order that grants others a free option.

Module Quiz 11.2 (Q1–Q4)
C — market fragmentation. The drivers are cost, accuracy, audit trails, fraud prevention, and continuous market (CAAFC). Fragmentation is a market condition that algorithms respond to — not a driver of system development.
A — least accurate. Electronic trading mostly benefited stock traders; bond trades remain largely OTC and electronic bond exchanges are used primarily by dealers, not retail. B and C are both true.
A — market fragmentation. SOR and liquidity-aggregation algos exist to overcome fragmentation (uneven liquidity across markets). C is the opposite of the problem; B is unrelated.
A — front runners. They detect a large order being worked in pieces and trade ahead of it. Arbitrageurs exploit price differences; dealers profit from the spread.
Module Quiz 11.3 (Q1–Q3)
B — simple, no-frills operating systems. Computation speed = the decision/processing phase (hardware, OS, assembler). Co-location (A) and fiber optics (C) reduce communication speed (distance traveled), not computation.
C — advanced orders. These are limit orders with a dynamic limit price that varies with a benchmark (e.g. pegged orders). Discretionary = limit ± a discretion amount; IOC = immediate-or-cancel.
B — a large inside spread. Leapfrog = beating the best bid/ask; it occurs in the presence of large quoted spreads, where a dealer can post a better price and narrow the inside spread.
Module Quiz (arbitrage) Q4–Q5
A — take liquidity on both sides. Simultaneous market buy & sell fill fast and lock in the profit → lowest risk. Offering liquidity (B/C) risks one leg not filling → adverse-price exposure; offering on BOTH sides is the riskiest.
A — $1,000. Buy at the lowest ask (LA $16.11), sell at the highest bid (Philly $16.13) → $0.02/share. Binding size = min(Philly bid 50,000 ; LA ask 100,000) = 50,000 → 0.02 × 50,000 = $1,000.
Trap: using the 100,000 ask size gives $2,000 (B). The sell leg is capped by the 50,000 available at the $16.13 bid, so 50,000 is binding.
Module Quiz 11.4 — Storm & Kotak (Q1–Q3)
Storm I: ensure only authorized personnel can input orders. Storm II: algorithm updates must be signed off by supervisory personnel.
Kotak I: more concerned about traders conducting denial-of-service attacks on competitors via excessive quote submission. Kotak II: rapid short selling may collapse a security's market, triggering stop-loss orders.
A — both correct. Restricting order input to authorized personnel (I) and requiring supervisory sign-off on algo updates (II) are both valid systemic-risk checks and balances.
C — malevolent orders. Denial-of-service attacks on competitors via excessive quote submission = malevolent (rogue/aggressive) orders — a trading-error/risk category, not a manipulation tactic.
B — gunning the market. Rapid short selling to collapse a security and trigger stop-loss orders (then repurchasing cheaply) = gunning the market.
Q2 vs Q3 trap: both sound "aggressive." DoS-via-excessive-quotes = malevolent orders (an error/risk); short-selling-to-trip-stop-losses = gunning the market (a manipulation subtype).
Carry-over concept checks
B — the trade is a SMALL part of overall trading volume. When the trade is a big part of volume, benchmark and trade VWAP converge → cost skewed to zero, so VWAP is a poor measure.
C — implementation shortfall. It captures all three implicit costs by comparing the actual portfolio to a paper portfolio executed at the arrival/decision price.
Reading 11 · Trading Costs and Electronic Markets
Full-reading recap, module by module: execution-cost components (11.a), effective spread & VWAP (11.b), implementation shortfall (11.c), drivers of electronic trading (11.d), market fragmentation (11.e), types of electronic traders (11.f), characteristics/uses of electronic systems (11.g), low-latency advantages (11.h), electronic-trading risks & regulation (11.i), and market abuses & surveillance (11.j). Both calculation pieces — the effective spread and VWAP transaction cost — are node-verified and reproduced by the widget's calculators.
Where the marks are: (1) the sign convention on side (+1 buy / −1 sell) in every cost formula; (2) which benchmark each measure uses (ES → midquote; VWAP → interval VWAP; IS → decision/arrival price); (3) matching each electronic-trader type & each market abuse to its one-line definition.
Module 11.1 · Explicit & Implicit Trading Costs
LOS 11.aComponents of execution costs
Explicit costsBrokerage, taxes, fees — observable & transparent (you get a receipt). Large buy-side: trading staff & related expenses (fixed). Smaller traders: brokers & variable commissions. Implicit costsNot readily discernible — must be estimated vs a benchmark. Comprise the bid-ask spread, market/price-impact, delay (slippage), and opportunity costs.
The four implicit-cost components:
Bid-ask spreadHighest potential cost for a SMALL trade. Trades at posted bid/ask fill quickly; patient traders trade inside the spread but risk not filling. Larger, liquidity-demanding trades walk down the book → filled at worse prices. Market/price impactImpact of demanding liquidity (market-moving trades). A large buy must raise prices to attract sellers. Breaking a large order into smaller trades reduces price impact — but increases delay & opportunity cost. Delay cost (slippage)Cost of an adverse price move during the lag in executing a large trade. Breaking up a buy risks the price rising over time so later batches fill higher. Opportunity costFrom unfilled orders / failed opportunities. If an underpriced security rises and the higher price forces cancellation of the unfilled part, the lost profit is the opportunity cost. Only opportunity cost looks at lost opportunities on unfilled trades; the others compare actual execution vs the trigger price.
The central tradeoff: market-impact cost on one hand vs delay + opportunity cost on the other. Demand liquidity now → high impact; wait patiently for a good price → the market may move out of range (delay + opportunity). Liquidity-demanding = market orders taking a posted quote; limit orders provide liquidity.
LOS 11.bDealer quotes, effective spread & VWAP
Inside/best bidHighest-posted bid across dealers. Inside/best askLowest-posted ask. Inside spreadbest ask − best bid (across dealers). Quoted spreadask − bid for a single dealer. Midquote(bid + ask) / 2 — the ES benchmark. Standing limit orderA trader's own posted quote — provides liquidity, trades at posted price, but risks failure to complete. In non-exchange markets (no clearinghouse guarantee), dealer creditworthiness & relationships matter beyond price.
Calc 1 — Effective spread. Uses the midquote as benchmark.
Effective spread transaction cost = (side) × (transaction price − midquote) Effective spread = 2 × (effective spread transaction cost) side = +1 buy, −1 sell Dealer P (bid 32.25, ask 32.31); buy fills at 32.29: midquote = (32.25 + 32.31)/2 = 32.28 ES txn cost = (+1)(32.29 − 32.28) = 0.01 → effective spread = 2 × 0.01 = $0.02 quoted spread (P) = 32.31 − 32.25 = $0.06
Interpretation: if the trade fills at the posted bid/ask, effective spread = quoted spread. If it fills at a better price (as here, 0.02 < 0.06), there was a price improvement → effective spread < quoted spread. Worked spreads (Fig 11.1): Dealer Q spread = 32.35 − 32.24 = $0.11; inside spread = 32.29 − 32.25 = $0.04; Dealer R midquote = (32.23 + 32.29)/2 = $32.26.
Limitations of effective spread: (1) when a large order is split into smaller orders, ES is a poor indicator — it ignores price-impact cost; (2) it ignores slippage / delay cost (part of the order not filled at desired prices, or not routed to the best market); (3) it does not capture opportunity cost (unfilled part abandoned after an adverse move).
Calc 2 — VWAP transaction cost. Benchmark = the interval VWAP (volume-weighted average of all trades between order placement & execution).
VWAP txn cost = trade size × (side) × (trade VWAP − benchmark VWAP) BNC interval: 100@12.11, 300@12.00, 600@11.75 (total 1,000): benchmark VWAP = (100/1000)(12.11)+(300/1000)(12.00)+(600/1000)(11.75) = $11.86 Buy of 300 executed 100@12.11 + 200@12.00: trade VWAP = (100/300)(12.11)+(200/300)(12.00) = $12.04 VWAP txn cost = 300 × (+1) × (12.04 − 11.86) = $54
Limitations of VWAP: (1) not useful if the trade is a significant part of trading volume — benchmark & trade VWAP converge → measured cost skewed toward zero; (2) does not capture price-impact cost (a large buy that is the only trade sets both the benchmark and trade VWAP equal → measured cost zero even at a bad price). The bias-toward-zero may explain VWAP's popularity with managers wanting to look low-cost.
LOS 11.c — Implementation shortfall (IS). Measures transaction cost as the difference between the value of the actual portfolio and a hypothetical paper portfolio. In the paper portfolio the trade is fully executed at no cost, at the prevailing (decision/arrival/strike) price when the order was placed — generally the midquote at that time.
Why IS is the best measure: it addresses VWAP's shortfalls by capturing all three implicit costs — price impact, slippage (delay), and opportunity cost. The tradeoff: the computation is more complex. (Quiz 11.1 Q7 / carry-over: which measure captures price impact + slippage + opportunity cost → implementation shortfall.)
Module 11.2 · Electronic Trading Systems
LOS 11.dFactors driving the development of electronic trading systems
1. CostCheaper to operate than manual counterparts. 2. AccuracyPerform exactly as programmed → precisely enforce the exchange's order-precedence & pricing rules. 3. Audit trailsGenerate & maintain records → investigators can examine the precise chain of events. 4. Fraud preventionKeep hidden orders hidden; don't leak information inadvertently or fraudulently. 5. Continuous marketNo breaks; operate continuously; unaffected by severe weather or events that stop human traders.
From the trader's perspective: process vast data quickly, exhibit perfect discipline (no behavioral bias), maintain perfect records. Bond-market trades remain largely OTC — competing electronic bond exchanges exist but are used primarily by dealers; public investors would gain significant cost savings if given access via brokers. (Quiz 11.2 Q1: least likely a driver → market fragmentation is a consequence, not a driver. Q2 least accurate → electronic trading has NOT mostly facilitated retail bond trading — bonds are still OTC/dealer.)
LOS 11.eMarket fragmentation
DefinitionA security trades in multiple markets → liquidity differs across them (many bids in one venue, few offers in another). Leads to price & liquidity differences between markets. Smart order routingSends orders to the markets with the best prices & sizes. Liquidity aggregationCreates a "super book" displaying liquidity across all markets → overcomes fragmentation. (Quiz 11.2 Q3: liquidity-seeking algos across markets are a response to market fragmentation.)
LOS 11.fTypes of electronic traders
Latency = the time lapse between the occurrence of an event and the execution of a trade based on it. Proprietary traders include high-frequency traders (thousands of round-trips/day) & low-latency traders (rely on speed of receiving & acting on news).
Trader typeWhat they do / decisive detail
Electronic news tradersAnalyze high-speed news feeds & submit market orders; use AI / NLP to trade against stale limit orders (prices not yet reflecting news). Low round-trip costs mean they profit even if right only a fraction of the time.
Electronic dealersPost bid & offer to profit from the spread; profit depends on trade frequency. Keep low inventory of actively-traded securities; manage adverse-move risk by taking the opposite side. Monitor news & suspend quotes when news is material → lose trades to news traders on immaterial news, but protected on material news.
Electronic arbitrageursTrade in multiple markets to exploit price discrepancies. Arbitrage portfolios = long & short positions (legs) that minimize cost & risk.
Electronic front runnersUse AI to sniff out large trades (or many small trades) on the same side, then use low latency to trade ahead. Search for patterns (repeat order sizes/timing) & event relationships (e.g. orders after earnings). Most jurisdictions forbid dealers/brokers from front-running clients' orders (would be trading on inside info); brokers randomize buy-side clients' trades to hide patterns.
Electronic quote matchersUse standing limit orders as valuable options to trade while limiting risk. E.g. see a standing buy at 12.20, buy at 12.25; if price rises they profit, downside limited to $0.05 (the standing buy backstops them).
Buy-side tradersExecute trades for portfolio managers; use OMSs to track orders sent/filled; use electronic brokers offering advanced order-processing algos/tactics. Not the same as "buy orders" — buy-side traders process both buys & sells for their PMs.
Quiz 11.2 Q4. Traders using AI to sniff out large trades processed in small parts → front runners (A). Not arbitrageurs (multi-market mispricing) or dealers (spread capture).
Module 11.3 · Characteristics & Uses of Electronic Systems
LOS 11.g / 11.hThe need for speed & low-latency advantages
Jumping the order queue gives low-latency traders an edge: order-taking (execute against a standing sell on positive news), market-making (take precedence when providing liquidity), and order-canceling (pull a quote before it fills when it becomes ill-advised). Electronic traders must be faster than competitors to capitalize on opportunities.
Low-latency traders minimize latency in three phases of a trade:
1. News → receiptGap between publication of actionable news & the trader receiving it — a communication-speed issue. 2. Receipt → decisionGap between receiving news & deciding an action — a computation-speed issue. 3. Decision → exchangeGap between order determination & communicating it to the exchange — a communication-speed issue.
Communication speedMinimize distance traveled: latest/fastest tech & co-location (servers in the exchange). Fairness → the exchange cannot selectively offer co-location to only a few. Computation speedBest hardware: overclocked processors (souped-up cooling), fast memory vs hard disks (disc-seek time), multiple task-specialized processors. Low-overhead software: no-frills OS, assembler over C++ for critical functions. Dynamic codeIf code updates as markets change, use faster-to-write languages (e.g. Python) — deployment speed matters more than processing speed there. Pre-computationRun scenario analysis ahead of time so the optimal action per scenario is predetermined → no delay once the scenario occurs.
Quiz 11.3 Q1: achieving lower latency via computation speed → B (simple, no-frills operating systems). (Co-location & fiber-optic networks are communication speed.)
Advanced orders, tactics & algorithms:
Advanced ordersLimit orders with a dynamic limit price that varies with a benchmark. E.g. a pegged limit buy one tick below the lowest ask — as posted asks change, the order is auto-canceled & replaced. (Quiz 11.3 Q2: limit orders with dynamic prices → advanced orders, C.) Trading tacticsPlans to submit multiple orders across exchanges to uncover hidden liquidity. E.g. a limit buy at 18.01 may uncover hidden asks; a limit with a ± discretion amount; IOC (immediate-or-cancel) orders; trading at dark pools; midspread orders (pegged to the bid-ask midpoint). Randomize order size & time-to-cancel to reduce footprint. Algorithms (algos)Programmed execution strategies. A VWAP algo breaks an order into pieces proportional to expected trading volume → reduces price impact. Good algos minimize total transaction cost by judiciously using limit orders (offer liquidity) & market orders (minimize delay/opportunity cost).
Impact of electronic trading (strategy changes):
Hidden ordersLimit orders hidden from all but the exchange → remove the valuable option that standing orders give the market. Electronic markets are better suited to hidden orders (lower chance of inadvertent exposure). Detected by pinging (small IOC orders) — a fill reveals a hidden order exists (not its size or side). LeapfrogBeating the best bid/ask. With large quoted spreads, dealers post a better price (lower ask / higher bid) → narrows the inside spread & frustrates traders who must re-quote to keep precedence. (Quiz 11.3 Q3: leapfrog most likely during a large inside spread, B.) Flickering quotesExposed limit orders canceled almost immediately — used to remove the option standing orders give others. Traders anticipate the flickering quote's return & may submit a hidden limit order. Electronic arbitrage (3 types)(A) Take liquidity on both sides — market buy & sell simultaneously across markets; low latency critical; opportunities few. (B) Offer liquidity on one side — e.g. buy at 100-bid 105-offer, place a bid at 95; if filled, immediately sell to the 100 bid for a profit of 5. (C) Offer liquidity on both sides — post limit orders inferior to the best bid/offer in different markets; fraught with risk — if one leg fills and the other doesn't, exposed to adverse price moves. Machine learning(data mining) statistical models that evolve with new empirical data to fine-tune algos — but ineffective in extraordinary times when volatility spikes & the past is not a useful guide; many traders shut down then.
Khuslow arbitrage (11.g worked example). Alpha bid 10.06/ask 10.12; Bravo bid 10.02/ask 10.05. Take liquidity both sides: buy at best ask 10.05 (Bravo), sell at best bid 10.06 (Alpha) → $0.01/share (on 11,000 shares → $110). (a) Offer liquidity one side: post a limit buy at 10.04 in Bravo; if filled, sell at Alpha (10.06) → $0.02. (b) Offer liquidity both sides: limit buy 10.04 (Bravo) + limit sell 10.07 (Alpha) → $0.03 if both fill. Risk: quotes may go stale (lag between quote / receipt / action / communication) → a leg may not fill — failure-to-fill risk is highest when offering liquidity on both sides, lowest for market orders. (Quiz 11.4 Q5: Philly bid 16.13 / LA ask 16.11, take-liquidity both sides → 0.02/share × 50,000 available → ~$1,000, A.)
Module 11.4 · Risks & Surveillance of Electronic Trading
LOS 11.iRisks of electronic trading & how regulators mitigate them
HFT arms raceCompetitive edge to the fastest → HFTs must deploy the latest, most expensive tech. This arms race offsets the low-cost benefit of electronic trading & acts as an entry barrier (unlevel field for smaller traders). Calls to mitigate: random-interval trading delays (unforecastable by HFT algos). Systemic riskCost of bad trades borne by parties other than the responsible one → less incentive to prevent bad decisions. Programming errors can cascade to market chaos before being caught.
Common trading errors (subtypes of systemic risk):
Runaway algorithmsProduce a series of unintended orders. E.g. the May 2010 flash crash — a large market sell of mini S&P 500 futures, programmed to release orders proportional to trading volume; since it wasn't a limit order, the volume it created fed more selling → huge volatility spike. Fat-finger errorsInput errors; if large enough, dramatic volatility (where human checks/balances are missing). Overlarge ordersOrders larger than available liquidity in the market they're routed to. Malevolent ordersDeliberate abuse — e.g. traders seeking to DoS-attack competitors with excessive quote submission. (Quiz 11.4 Q2: "concerned about DoS attacks via excessive quotes" → malevolent orders, C.)
Regulatory mitigation: systemic risks can be managed — ensure only adequately backtested algos are used, controls are strict, software is tested before deployment. Brokers must scrutinize the appropriateness of orders; markets should have circuit breakers that kick in when volatility spikes.
LOS 11.jMarket abuses & real-time surveillance
Real-time surveillance detects abuses & potential manipulation. Major abuse categories:
AbuseDefinition / decisive detail
Front runningAn order being processed by an unsuspecting party is traded ahead of. Illegal if the info is obtained improperly. Detected: orders broken into smaller ones, then patterns sought.
Market manipulationTrading to create artificial prices; enforcement seeks genuine vs manipulative intent.
Wash tradingTrading between commonly controlled accounts to create false liquidity → false sense of security about a stock's liquidity.
Spoofing / layeringFake limit orders posted to create false optimism/pessimism. E.g. a buyer posts a hidden buy at a low price + exposed sell orders to convince others prices are falling → they sell into the hidden buy. Layering is risky — the exposed sells may actually fill.
BluffingPreying on momentum traders (who buy rising / sell falling). Post orders to influence perceived value. Pump-and-dump: buy to raise the price, sell higher to momentum traders (may use rumormongering / wash trading). Sell-side analogue = short-and-distort. Analysts need a sound basis for valuation (Standard V(A): Diligence & Reasonable Basis) to avoid falling for bluffing.
Gunning the marketForces other traders into bad trades. E.g. rapid short selling collapses a security → triggers stop-loss orders → manipulator repurchases at the lower price. (Quiz 11.4 Q3: "rapid short selling collapses market, triggers stop-losses" → gunning the market, B.)
Squeezing / corneringObtain control of resources needed to settle contracts, then withdraw them → trigger defaults, extend resources at a higher price. Short squeeze: take control of lendable shares, lend to shorts, recall abruptly → shorts cover higher. Cornering (commodities): long futures + buy up the spot supply → demand physical delivery counterparties can't supply. Illegal & prohibited by most futures exchanges.
Quiz 11.4 keys (Storm/Kotak).
Q1 Storm's two statements (only authorized personnel input orders; algo updates signed off by supervisors) → both are appropriate checks & balances → A (both correct).
Q2 Kotak I ("concerned about DoS attacks via excessive quote submission") → C (malevolent orders) — a deliberate trading-error/abuse of the system, not a price-manipulation tactic. (C circled in photo.)
Q3 Kotak II ("rapid short selling may collapse the market, triggering stop-loss orders") → B (gunning the market). (Reasoning-derived; not circled. Gunning = forcing others into bad trades via stop-loss triggering; distinct from bluffing, which preys on momentum traders via perceived-value orders.)
Quiz 11.1 answer summary (calc-verified). Q1 → B ($0.02) price impact of the 2nd lot (17.71 − 17.69). Q2 → C ($0.04) inside spread (17.69 − 17.65). Q3 → C ($44.70) benchmark VWAP. Q4 → B ($44.68) trade VWAP. Q5 → B ($25) VWAP txn cost = 1,500 × (44.68 − 44.70) ≈ −$25. Q6 → B (VWAP appropriate when the trade is a SMALL part of volume). Q7 → C (implementation shortfall) captures price impact + slippage + opportunity cost.
Portfolio Performance Evaluation
READING 13 · Performance Measurement
Two perspectives (framing)
PerspectiveCaptures
Fund sponsorALL value added or lost across the fund
ManagerOnly what that manager did to add/lose value
Setup: a large investor (pension, endowment, foundation) hires several managers. Evaluation deconstructs returns to quantify which decisions added or subtracted value.
Three interrelated components (LOS 13.a)
Each builds on the previous:
ComponentRoleQuestion
Performance measurementFoundation phase — calculates both return AND risk over specified periods. First determine: compared to a benchmark (relative) or a pre-specified target return % (absolute)?WHAT performance?
Performance attributionDetermines the key drivers of performance; expands on risk/return and explains how the return was achieved given the risk taken. Explains relative AND absolute returnsHOW achieved?
Performance appraisalDetermines whether performance was driven by investment decisions, the overall market, or chance; combines measurement + attribution into a judgment on qualitySKILL or LUCK?
Appraisal = the "chance/luck" component. If performance is attributed to luck, we cannot expect similar returns in the future. Don't confuse with attribution (the "how/drivers" component).
Attributes of an effective attribution process (LOS 13.b)
Must include
A reflection of 100% of the portfolio's return or risk exposure
The portfolio manager's current decision-making process
The active investment decisions taken by the PM
A full explanation of the portfolio's excess return and risk
Two non-negotiables: account for 100% of risk and return AND represent the PM's CURRENT process. If the investment process recently changed, the attribution must be updated to reflect it. An attribution that doesn't capture total risk/return is misleading and unreliable.
Return attribution vs risk attribution (LOS 13.c)
TypeAnalyzes impact of active decisions on...
Return attributionThe fund's investment returns
Risk attributionPortfolio risk (the parallel of return attribution)
Risk is generally compared to the appropriate benchmark (relative-based), but can be absolute (independent of a benchmark).
Matching trap: a relative-based risk attribution is NOT appropriate for a manager with a predetermined absolute target return goal. And a widely-quoted passive index (e.g. S&P 500) may or may not be an appropriate benchmark.
Why it matters more now: after a long bull market, attribution helps PMs justify performance & fees in negative-return periods. Bonus: a quality-control check — did the manager do what they said?
Macro vs micro attribution
LevelAnalyzesDetail
Micro attributionThe portfolio manager's levelVerifies the PM did what they said; explains the drivers of the portfolio's return
Macro attributionThe fund sponsor's levelCommon in institutional investing; quantifies sponsors' decisions to deviate from the strategic asset allocation and the timing of those decisions
Mnemonic: miCro → manager; maCro → sponsor (deviations from SAA + timing). Both possible because attribution is flexible across fund-sponsor and PM levels.
Three attribution methods (LOS 13.d)
MethodWhat it does
Returns-basedRegresses total portfolio returns against major risk factors (systematic, size, value) to identify the manager's active bets & their impact on active return
Holdings-basedUses beginning-of-period holdings to assess active sector/stock-selection bets & their contribution to active return. Does NOT adjust for changes during the period
Transactions-basedImproves on holdings-based by including the impact of any trades executed during the period
Figure 13.1 — advantages & disadvantages
MethodAdvantagesDisadvantages
Returns-basedEasy to implement; no holdings data needed (useful for private funds, e.g. hedge funds)Least accurate (ignores underlying holdings); returns data can be manipulated
Holdings-basedMore accurate than returns-based (considers holdings)Needs holdings data; trading-effect mismatch → not appropriate for high-turnover active funds with long evaluation periods
Transactions-basedMost accurateHighest data requirements; highest complexity
"Timing"/"trading" effect: holdings-based uses beginning-of-period holdings only, so for a high-turnover manager the output may not reconcile to overall portfolio returns. This mismatch is the timing/trading effect — reduced by using shorter evaluation periods.
Method choice is driven by: data nature/availability, the manager's investment process, and the analyst's need for accuracy. Accuracy ranking: returns < holdings < transactions.
Module Quiz 13.1
A — performance appraisal. Appraisal determines whether performance came from investment decisions, the overall market, or chance (skill vs luck). Attribution explains the drivers; measurement calculates return & risk.
C — transactions based. It's the most accurate because it includes trades executed during the period (at the cost of highest data needs/complexity). Returns-based is least accurate; holdings-based is in between.
Arithmetic vs geometric attribution (LOS 13.e)
ApproachActive returnProblem / property
ArithmeticR − B (single period)Single-period arithmetic active returns do NOT compound to the multi-period active return without a "smoothing" adjustment
GeometricG = (1+R)/(1+B) − 1Defines the periodic excess return as a RATIO; single-period geometric returns DO compound across periods
Two-period example (R = 5%,5% ; B = 3%,3%): R(2-period) = 1.05² − 1 = 10.25% B(2-period) = 1.03² − 1 = 6.09% ARITHMETIC 2-period active = 10.25% − 6.09% = 4.16% ...but each period's 2% does NOT give 4.16% (1.02²−1 = 4.04%) GEOMETRIC 2-period active = 1.1025 / 1.0609 − 1 = 3.92% each period 1.05/1.03−1 = 1.94%, and 1.0194²−1 = 3.92% ✓ compounds
Prof's note: all attribution models in this reading are arithmetic (the vast majority of practitioners use arithmetic attribution).
Arithmetic vs geometric calculator
Two single-period returns for portfolio and benchmark (in %).
Brinson-Hood-Beebower (BHB) method (LOS 13.h)
The Brinson model has two variants: BHB and Brinson-Fachler (BF). BHB breaks total active return into three components:
R = Σ wᵢRᵢ (portfolio) B = Σ WᵢBᵢ (benchmark) wᵢ,Rᵢ = PORTFOLIO weight/return in segment i Wᵢ,Bᵢ = BENCHMARK weight/return in segment i Allocation Aᵢ = (wᵢ − Wᵢ) × Bᵢ [active weight × passive segment return] Selection Sᵢ = Wᵢ × (Rᵢ − Bᵢ) [passive weight × active segment return] Interaction Iᵢ = (wᵢ − Wᵢ) × (Rᵢ − Bᵢ)
Memory hook: Allocation uses the active weight × benchmark return; Selection uses the benchmark weight × active return; Interaction multiplies both actives together. (BHB allocation uses Bᵢ directly — not Bᵢ−B; that's the BF tweak.)
Worked example (Fig 13.2)
Stylew (fund)R (fund)W (bm)B (bm)
Growth75%13%60%10%
Value25%19%40%20%
R = .75×13 + .25×19 = 14.5% B = .60×10 + .40×20 = 14.0% active = 0.5% Allocation: growth (.75−.60)×10 = +1.5% ; value (.25−.40)×20 = −3.0% ; total −1.5% Selection : growth .60×(13−10) = +1.8% ; value .40×(19−20) = −0.4% ; total +1.4% Interaction: growth (.75−.60)×(13−10)=+0.45% ; value (.25−.40)×(19−20)=+0.15% ; total +0.60% Total value added = −1.5% + 1.4% + 0.6% = 0.5% ✓
Interpretation: negative total allocation → overweighting growth/underweighting value was wrong in a period where value beat growth. Positive growth selection → manager's growth picks beat the growth benchmark.
Why interaction exists: allocation purely measures over/underweighting (ignores selection); selection purely measures picking (ignores weighting). The interaction captures their compounding — e.g. overweighting a style where your manager also outperformed.
Brinson-Fachler (BF) method
BF fixes a drawback of BHB: under BHB the sign of the allocation effect doesn't automatically tell you whether the over/underweight was correct.
BHB allocation: Aᵢ = (wᵢ − Wᵢ) × Bᵢ BF allocation: Aᵢ = (wᵢ − Wᵢ) × (Bᵢ − B) ← segment return RELATIVE to overall benchmark Selection & Interaction are calculated EXACTLY THE SAME in both models.
The whole point: overweighting growth (Bᵢ=10%) was a bad call because the overall benchmark returned 14%. BHB gives +1.5% (misleadingly positive). BF gives (.75−.60)×(10−14) = −0.6% — correctly negative, because you overweighted a segment that underperformed the overall benchmark.
BF worked example (same data, B = 14%)
growth allocation = (.75−.60)×(10−14) = −0.60% value allocation = (.25−.40)×(20−14) = −0.90% total allocation = −0.60% − 0.90% = −1.50% (same total as BHB)
StyleAllocationSelectionInteraction
Growth−0.60%1.80%0.45%
Value−0.90%−0.40%0.15%
Total−1.50%1.40%0.60%
The only difference between BF and BHB output is the individual growth/value allocation effects. Totals are identical. BF is the more popular model in practice.
Macro vs micro attribution (in the Brinson context)
LevelWhoWhat it attributes
Macro attributionFund sponsor = investment committee (sets strategic AA, oversees staff) + internal investment staff (tactical deviations, selects external managers)Value added by the sponsor's decision to over/underweight different styles of manager vs benchmark, and the sponsor's skill in selecting good managers within those styles
Micro attributionIndividual portfolio managers (internal or external)Their decisions to over/underweight segments (substyle / sector / geography) of their own portfolio to generate active return
The earlier BHB/BF growth-vs-value example was a macro attribution. Expanding the same example to size bets (large-cap vs small-cap) within each style is a micro attribution.
Micro attribution example — size bets (Fig 13.3, BF model, B = 14%)
SegmentwRWB
Large-cap growth50%15%30%8%
Small-cap growth25%9%30%12%
Large-cap value25%19%40%20%
GROWTH (BF alloc = (w−W)(Bᵢ−B); sel = W(R−Bᵢ); int = (w−W)(R−Bᵢ)): alloc: LC (.50−.30)(8−14)=−1.20% ; SC (.25−.30)(12−14)=+0.10% ; total −1.10% select: LC .30(15−8)=+2.10% ; SC .30(9−12)=−0.90% ; total +1.20% inter : LC (.50−.30)(15−8)=+1.40% ; SC (.25−.30)(9−12)=+0.15% ; total +1.55% VALUE (large-cap value only): alloc (.25−.40)(20−14)=−0.90% ; sel .40(19−20)=−0.40% ; inter (.25−.40)(19−20)=+0.15%
MICRO TOTALS: allocation −2.00% | selection +0.80% | interaction +1.70% | sum = 0.50% ✓
Key takeaways (exam-tested): • Growth alloc −1.10%: manager overweighted large-cap growth (50% vs 30%) when LC growth (8%) underperformed the overall benchmark (14%) → bad allocation. • Growth selection +1.20%: good large-cap picks (+2.10%) outweighed poor small-cap picks (−0.90%). • Micro per-segment effects differ from the macro numbers, but aggregate to the same 0.5% active return.
Two micro shortcuts & single-stock note
Shortcut (selection + interaction together): later attributions lump selection + interaction and compute it with actual portfolio weights: wᵢ × (Rᵢ − Bᵢ). E.g. LC growth: 0.50×(15−8) = 3.50% = 2.10% (selection) + 1.40% (interaction). (Selection alone uses benchmark weight Wᵢ.)
Single-stock micro attribution: when run on one stock, the allocation effect actually represents the selection effect (allocating to one security IS a stock-selection decision), and the selection effect represents the market-timing / transaction costs of the manager for that security.
Micro attribution can run on style, sector, OR geography — and a manager's allocation/selection effects differ depending on the segmentation. A manager could show negative aggregate selection by sector but positive by geography. The data show how the manager actually constructs the portfolio: if along geography, positive geo-selection → good stock picker; if the process is sector-based, negative sector-selection → poor stock picker.
Factor-based return attribution — the Carhart model
A fundamental factor model tests a portfolio's sensitivity to additional factors. The Carhart model calculates the excess return from active management via four factors; it lets practitioners remove the effects of known market factors to isolate excess returns from active decisions not explained by those factors.
RḚ − Rḫ = aḚ + bḚ₁·RMRF + bḚ₂·SMB + bḚ₃·HML + bḚ₄·WML + EḚ aḚ = alpha (return above expected for the portfolio's systematic-risk level) RMRF = market index: value-weighted equity index return above the 1-month T-bill SMB = small minus big (SIZE): avg return of 3 small-cap minus 3 large-cap portfolios HML = high minus low (VALUE): avg of 2 high book/price minus 2 low book/price portfolios WML = winners minus losers (MOMENTUM): past year's winners minus losers EḚ = error term (part of return unexplained by the model)
Four factors: (1) market RMRF, (2) size SMB, (3) value HML = book-to-price, (4) momentum WML. Don't confuse HML (value, book/price) with SMB (size).
Sample Carhart attribution (Fig 13.5)

Contribution to active return = factor sensitivity DIFFERENCE (col 3) × factor return (col 4) Factor tilts return = Σ contributions = 1.75% Active return = factor tilts (1.75%) + security selection (−0.10%) = 1.65%
Interpreting: benchmark RMRF sensitivity = 1.00 → diversified index; benchmark SMB = −1.00 → large-cap tilt; benchmark HML = 0, WML = 0 → large-cap blend (no value/growth tilt), no momentum. Portfolio HML diff +0.30 → a value tilt that contributed +1.29% (over 78% of active return). Security selection (stock picking) detracted slightly (−0.10%). Due diligence: if the prospectus says growth but the model shows a value tilt, investigate.

Fixed-income attribution — three methods (LOS 13.f)
Prof's note: candidates are NOT responsible for fixed-income attribution calculations — only for interpreting the results.
MethodWhat / sourcesData & complexityUsed by
Exposure decomposition (duration-based)Partitions portfolio & benchmark by weight into duration buckets (short/mid/long) × sectors (gov/corp); decomposes active return per bucket & sectorLowest data, simplest, clearly understandableMarketing & client reporting
Yield curve decomposition (duration-based)Decomposes total return into: yield/income, roll, shift, shape, spread, residualMore data & operational complexity than exposureAnalysts & PMs (not marketing)
Yield curve decomposition (full repricing)Most comprehensive/precise: reprices each bond using individual spot rates for each cash flow; broadest instrument rangeHighest — most complex, LEAST easily understoodAnalysts/PMs; least likely for client output
Active bets & the six yield-curve sources
Major active bets a fixed-income manager can take:
BetExample
DurationExpects curve to shift down → increase portfolio duration vs benchmark
Curve shapePosition for a change in slope/curvature (e.g. a steepening)
Sector selectionBelieves corporate spreads will narrow → increase corporate-sector exposure
Bond selectionOverweight individual bonds expected to outperform
Six sources (yield-curve decomposition): Yield/income – coupon income earned Roll – time passing, bond "rolling down" a stable yield curve Shift – parallel shift, via duration & convexity Shape – change in slope or curvature Spread – change in spread (sector or specific security) Residual – unexplained (estimation error in duration/convexity)
Yield, roll, and shift were the individual-bond total-return components from the fixed-income section. Interpretation example: a manager overweight in high-coupon, high-yield corporates expects a positive yield contribution (high coupon) and a positive spread contribution (expected spread narrowing). If holdings default or spreads widen, these turn negative → value lost vs benchmark.
Interpreting the exposure-decomposition example (Fig 13.8)
Portfolio total return 2.42% vs benchmark 2.56% → active = −0.14% Portfolio duration 4.84 vs benchmark 3.85 (overweight medium bucket 60% vs 44%) Overweight corporates 65% vs benchmark 45% (expected spread narrowing)
EffectValueInterpretation
Duration effect+0.33%Higher-duration position paid off → yield curve did indeed FALL (manager correct to extend duration)
Curve (shape) effect−0.39% (≈39 bps)Lost from curve shape: overweight high-duration assets while medium yields rose & short yields fell → a STEEPENING of the curve
Sector allocation−0.08% (≈8 bps)Lost from overweighting corporates → contrary to expectations, corporate spreads WIDENED (lower benchmark corporate returns confirm)
Bond selection0.00%Manager did not engage in active bond selection
Read the signs: +duration & curve fell = correct duration call; but −curve(shape) with overweight long + medium yields up/short down = a steepening that hurt; −sector = spreads widened against the manager. The duration-based exposure method is favored for client reporting (simple, low data).

Selecting a risk attribution approach (LOS 13.g)
Choosing the right risk metric needs an in-depth understanding of the manager's investment process — whether it's top-down or bottom-up — and a defined appropriate benchmark. Looking only at returns is insufficient; risk attribution identifies the sources of risk the manager took to produce the fund's returns.
Risk attribution must be combined with return attribution to fully understand the manager's active investment decisions. Return attribution alone tells you the "how" of returns; risk attribution tells you the "how" of risk.
Figure 13.9 — investment process × attribution type
The correct approach sits at the intersection of the process (row) and the attribution type (column).
Investment processRELATIVE (tracking risk)ABSOLUTE (total risk)
Bottom-upSecurity's marginal contribution to tracking risk (tracking error)Security's marginal contribution to total risk
Top-downAttribute tracking error to allocation & selectionFactor's marginal contribution to total risk and specific risk
Factor-basedFactor's marginal contribution to tracking error and active specific risk
Columns: RELATIVE attribution uses tracking risk / tracking error (objective: returns generated from active management vs the tracking risk assumed). ABSOLUTE attribution uses total risk, quantifying general risk (market, size, style exposures) + specific risk (stock picking); a common absolute risk measure is standard deviation.
Bottom-up vs top-down (the two relative rows)
ProcessHow relative risk is attributed
Bottom-upEach security has a marginal contribution to tracking risk, multiplied by its active weight to get its contribution to tracking risk
Top-downMore macro: attributes active return to allocation, then attributes tracking error to allocation & selection
ABSOLUTE / bottom-up example: • each security's marginal contribution to total risk = change in portfolio std dev from a small increase in that holding • sum the marginal contributions and divide by total portfolio risk → overall risk contribution due to selection decisions

B — yes, but only in technology. Consumer durables: 0.35×(2.00−3.00) = −0.35 → BAD (picks lagged the sector benchmark) Technology: 0.16×(2.60−(−2.00)) = +0.736 → GOOD (picks beat the sector benchmark)
Q4 — positive interaction (agricultural / utilities)?
Interaction = (w−W)×(Rᵢ−Bᵢ). Positive = good combined effect.
B — yes, in both. Agricultural: (0.04−0.06)×(−2.00−(−1.00)) = +0.02 → POSITIVE (underweighted & picks lagged: two negatives) Utilities: (0.12−0.10)×(4.00−(−2.00)) = +0.12 → POSITIVE (overweighted & picks beat benchmark)
Liability-based benchmarks (LOS 13.i)
Common in institutional investing when a firm has a specific future liability (e.g. a defined-benefit plan). It focuses on the cash flows needed to satisfy the liability, and frequently limits the investment choices available to the manager (e.g. equity & fixed income only).
Frequently used assets within a liability-based benchmark: nominal bonds, inflation-adjusted bonds, and high-quality stocks.
Plan features that shape the liability → asset choice
Feature
Years until the average worker retires
How many workers have already retired and are drawing cash
Impact of inflation on the liabilities
Correlation between the company's operating profit (EBIT) and plan assets
Whether the plan is frozen or has a terminal life
Actuarial assumptions: life expectancy & required discount rate
Seven asset-based benchmark types (LOS 13.j)
#TypeAdvantagesDisadvantages
1Absolute (return objective exceeding a minimum target, e.g. MAR in the Sortino ratio)Simple, straightforwardNot an investable benchmark
2Broad market index (e.g. S&P 500 for US stocks)Well recognized, easy to understand, widely available; unambiguous, investable, measurable, may be specified in advance; appropriate if it reflects the manager's current processManager's style may deviate from the index (S&P 500 wrong for a small-cap growth manager)
3Style index (LC growth, LC value, SC growth, SC value)Widely available/understood/accepted; appropriate if it reflects the manager's style & is investableMay contain weights in securities/sectors larger than prudent; differing style definitions produce very different returns
4Factor model (RḚ = aḚ + b₁F₁ + ... + bḤFḤ + ε); CAPM is a one-factor versionUseful in performance evaluation; gives insight into style via factor exposuresNot intuitive to all; data/modeling not always available & expensive; ambiguous (different models → different outputs → misspecification)
5Returns-based (regress account returns on style-index returns → allocation algorithm)Easy/intuitive; meets validity criteria; useful when only account returns are availableStyle indexes may not reflect actual holdings; needs enough monthly returns for a reliable pattern; won't work if the manager changes style
6Manager universes (the median manager/fund from a peer universe)MeasurableSurvivorship bias; relies on accurate compilation; can't be specified in advance → not investable → not an acceptable benchmark
7Custom security-based (designed to reflect the manager's security allocations & process)Meets all validity criteria; continual monitoring; lets sponsors allocate risk across teamsExpensive to construct/maintain; manager lack of transparency (e.g. hedge funds) can make it impossible
Three "not investable" traps: Absolute (#1, no holdings), Manager universes (#6, can't specify in advance + survivorship bias). The custom security-based benchmark (#7) is the gold standard — meets all validity criteria.
Tests of benchmark quality (LOS 13.k) — the 7 properties
A valid benchmark aligns the benchmark's style & risk with the manager's and gives an appropriate objective:
PropertyMeaning
Specified in advanceKnown to manager & sponsor at the start of the evaluation period
AppropriateConsistent with the manager's approach & style
MeasurableValue & return determinable on a reasonably frequent basis
UnambiguousClearly defined identities & weights of securities
Reflective of current opinionsManager has current knowledge/expertise of the securities in it
AccountableManager accepts applicability & agrees differences are due only to active management
InvestablePossible to replicate the benchmark and forgo active management
Mnemonic: SAMURAI — Specified in advance, Appropriate, Measurable, Unambiguous, Reflective, Accountable, Investable.
Decomposing portfolio return: P = M + S + A
P = M + S + A P = manager's portfolio return M = return on the MARKET index S = B − M = excess return to STYLE (style index B minus market M); can be + or − A = P − B = ACTIVE return (portfolio minus STYLE benchmark)
Had the manager taken a passive position in a broad market index, M would be the benchmark and S=0. Because the manager specializes in a style, we add (B>M, S>0) or subtract (B<M, S<0) the style-vs-market difference. A (active) is attributed to active management.
Example — test of benchmark quality
LC growth portfolio fell 11% (P = −11%) LC growth index fell 12% (B = −12%) Broad equity index fell 10% (M = −10%) S = B − M = −12% − (−10%) = −2% → growth STYLE out of favor (underperformed market) A = P − B = −11% − (−12%) = +1% → manager BEAT the style benchmark
Client concern (that a skillful manager should beat the broad market) is NOT valid. The manager performed well for a growth-style manager (active +1%); the underperformance vs the broad market is the style being out of favor (−2%), not poor active management.
Benchmarking alternative investments (LOS 13.m)
AssetBenchmark problems
Hedge funds3 candidate benchmarks all flawed: (1) broad market index — wide range of strategies, leverage/shorts/derivatives, low/no correlation, illiquidity → inappropriate; (2) risk-free + spread — only fits arbitrage strategies, but most carry systematic risk & leverage so spread must rise → unsuitable; (3) peer universe — backfill & survivorship bias, illiquid assets → current pricing inexact / appraisal-based → smoothing → reduces reported SD, inflates Sharpe, raises HF allocation
Real estateBenchmarks from a sample (not fully representative); high correlation to largest investments; self-reported returns (subjectivity/bias); value-based may bias to expensive properties; appraisal/infrequent pricing → smoothing & understated volatility; leverage inconsistency; indexes assume no transaction costs/full transparency/normal liquidity. Open-end funds → TWR (investor controls flows); closed-end funds → IRR (manager controls flows)
Private equityMetric usually IRR (all cash flows since inception + ending value). Problems: different valuation methods; IRR biased by early gains/losses; all results reported at one point in time though firms are at varying stages
CommoditiesBenchmarks usually based on futures, not actual assets → significant differences vs portfolio; differing leverage & exposure weightings reduce comparability
Managed derivativesStrategy-specific (e.g. Mount Lucas Management Index, a momentum strategy) or peer-group based; peer-group versions share HF issues like survivorship bias
Distressed securitiesIlliquidity/lack of marketability → almost impossible to determine an appropriate benchmark; recovery takes time; stale pricing valuation problems; indexes (e.g. Barclay Distressed Securities Index) span many strategies & value at erratic intervals so stale pricing persists
The recurring smoothing trap: illiquid/appraisal-priced alternatives (HF, real estate, distressed) produce smoothed returns → understated standard deviation → inflated Sharpe ratio → over-allocation. TWR for open-end (investor flows), IRR for closed-end / PE (manager flows).
Benchmark misspecification (LOS 13.l)
"Garbage in, garbage out." Useful performance evaluation (and all three components — measurement, attribution, appraisal) requires an appropriate fund benchmark. An incorrect benchmark makes performance measurement, attribution, and appraisal invalid, and produces misfit active return.
Misfit vs true active return (Euronext / CAC example)
Manager invests in large, liquid FRENCH stocks. Sponsor (wrongly) benchmarks vs the Euronext 100 (NL/Belgium/Portugal/Luxembourg + France). The CAC 40 (large liquid French) is the manager's true NORMAL portfolio. Portfolio P = 10% Euronext 100 (investor benchmark) = 12% CAC 40 (normal) = 9% Total active = P − investor benchmark = 10% − 12% = −2% TRUE active = P − normal portfolio = 10% − 9% = +1% MISFIT active = normal − investor = 9% − 12% = −3% Check: true + misfit = +1% + (−3%) = −2% = total active ✓
The point: measured vs the wrong (investor) benchmark the manager looks like a −2% underperformer. Measured vs the correct normal portfolio (CAC 40) the manager actually added +1% true active return. The −3% misfit comes purely from the misspecified benchmark, not the manager's skill.
Module Quiz 13.3 — Q1 (Rhombus, US small-cap, 2005)
Portfolio P = 8.9% Russell 2000 (style benchmark B) = 9.1% Wilshire 5000 (broad market M) = 8.5%
Return due to STYLE S = B − M = 9.1% − 8.5% = +0.6% Return due to ACTIVE A = P − B = 8.9% − 9.1% = −0.2% vs BENCHMARK (Russell 2000): underperformed by 0.2% (negative active management) vs MARKET (Wilshire 5000): outperformed by 8.9% − 8.5% = +0.4% → The small-cap STYLE was in favor (+0.6%), which carried the portfolio above the broad market, but the manager's ACTIVE decisions slightly DETRACTED (−0.2%) vs the proper style benchmark.
Q2 — Hexagon PLC (European equities): validity of "beat the median manager"?
A median-manager (manager-universe) benchmark is NOT valid. It fails key benchmark-validity tests: • Not specified in advance → the median manager is only known after ranking funds, so it's not investable • Survivorship bias → underperformers leave the universe, biasing the median upward • Ambiguous – constituents/weights not clearly identified ahead of time • Relies on accurate compilation by the universe provider It IS measurable, but failing "specified in advance / investable / unambiguous" makes it an unacceptable benchmark.
Performance appraisal — the seven measures (LOS 13.n)
Appraisal is the final stage of performance evaluation: are results more likely due to skill or luck? Should we hire/fire the manager? Active skill is evident when the manager outperforms an appropriate benchmark on a risk-adjusted basis consistently.
#MeasureNumeratorDenominator (risk)
1Sharpe ratioRḙ − rḚ (excess over risk-free)total risk σḙ (std dev)
2Treynor ratioRḙ − rḚsystematic risk βḙ (beta)
3Information ratioE(rḚ) − E(rᷱ) (vs benchmark)tracking risk σ(rḚ−rᷱ)
4Appraisal ratioα (alpha)residual risk σε (std error of regression)
5Sortino ratioE(rḚ) − rḢ (over MAR/target)downside risk σḋ (target semideviation)
6Capture ratios (up & down)Relative performance in up vs down markets
7Drawdown (max DD, duration)Peak-to-trough loss & recovery time
The first FIVE are risk-adjusted measures. Prof's note: with only a few years of data it's hard to separate luck from skill — many years of observations are needed to conclude at high confidence the manager truly has superior skill.
Sharpe · Treynor · Information ratio
Sharpe Sḙ = (Rḙ − rḚ) / σḙ (TOTAL risk) Treynor Tḙ = (Rḙ − rḚ) / βḙ (SYSTEMATIC risk) Info IR = [E(rḚ) − E(rᷱ)] / σ(rḚ − rᷱ) (TRACKING risk)
Sharpe drawback: the denominator (std dev) does not differentiate upside vs downside volatility — it penalizes ALL volatility, even "good" upside volatility. (Sortino fixes this.)
Treynor: uses beta → only systematic risk, so it assumes efficient markets and is only useful for well-diversified portfolios (no unsystematic risk). IR: numerator = mean port minus mean benchmark; denominator = tracking risk (variability of port vs benchmark).
Appraisal ratio (AR)
AR = α / σε α = active return (alpha) from a FACTOR-based regression σε = residual risk = "standard error of the regression" = volatility of the error term
A higher AR = more active return per unit of active (residual) risk → superior active manager. The AR is analogous to the IR (active return per unit of active risk); the only difference is the AR uses a factor-based regression to estimate active return & active risk.
Deriving σε from CAPM (single-factor): E(Rᵢ) = RḚ + βᵢ[E(Rḫ) − RḚ] α = forecast/actual return − CAPM fair return Total variance splits: σᵢ² = β²σḫ² + σε² → σε² = σᵢ² − β²σḫ² (remember to take the √ before using in AR!)
Worked example (textbook)
Port ret 8% | Port SD 20% | Port beta 1.2 | Mkt ret 6% | Mkt SD 16% | rf 1% CAPM fair = 1% + 1.2(6% − 1%) = 7% α = 8% − 7% = 1% σε² = 0.20² − (1.2² × 0.16²) = 0.003136 AR = 0.01 / √0.003136 = 0.01 / 0.056 = 0.18
Appraisal ratio calculator
Sortino ratio
SRḋ = [E(rḚ) − rḢ] / σḋ (ex-ante) SRḋ = (rḚ − rḢ) / σḋ (realized) rḢ = target rate of return = minimum acceptable return (MAR) σḋ = TARGET SEMIDEVIATION = std dev of returns BELOW the target
Sortino considers only downside risk — in contrast to Sharpe (all risk, upside AND downside). Positive upside volatility is "good" volatility. In practice clients care more about negative-return volatility, so Sortino can give a more meaningful risk-adjusted view.
Semideviation: sum the SQUARED distances of returns BELOW the target (ignore returns that beat it), divide by the TOTAL number of observations (incl. those above) → semivariance; √ → semistandard deviation. Example: avg port ret 7%, MAR 3%, semi-SD 5% → Sortino = (7% − 3%) / 5% = 0.80
Sortino > Sharpe (e.g. 0.75 vs 0.63) suggests the manager should earn greater returns relative to the downside-risk threshold (downside risk is lower than total risk). Comparability problem: the MAR is subjective & specific to each investor, so Sortino ratios aren't easily compared across investors. Negatively skewed strategies (higher semideviation) → lower Sortino; both pos- & neg-skewed lower the Sharpe. Sortino more appropriate for nonnormal/skewed distributions (hedge funds, options).
Capture ratios
Capture ratios measure the manager's relative performance in up vs down markets. Is the portfolio return above or below the benchmark when the benchmark is positive (up) or negative (down)?
Upside capture = port return / benchmark return (in an UP market, benchmark > 0) Downside capture = port return / benchmark return (in a DOWN market, benchmark < 0) CAPTURE RATIO = upside capture / downside capture
MarketBenchPortCaptureMeaning
Up4%5%125%outperform in up
Up4%3%75%underperform in up
Down−4%−5%125%underperform in down (captured MORE of the loss)
Down−4%−3%75%outperform in down (captured LESS of the loss)
Interpreting the capture ratio: • = 1 → symmetric return profile • > 1 → positively asymmetric / CONVEX (greater upside capture than downside) — desirable • < 1 → negatively asymmetric / CONCAVE (greater downside than upside capture) Ideally: capture as much of the upside, as little of the downside → maximize the capture ratio.
Example: up market mgr 7% / bench 8% → upside = 87.5% down market mgr −6% / bench −10% → downside = 60% capture ratio = 87.5% / 60% = 1.46 → positively asymmetric (convex)
Return profile: convex vs concave
Portfolio return (y) plotted against benchmark return (x). The 45° line is capture ratio = 1 (symmetric). A convex profile bows up (more upside, less downside); a concave profile bows down.
A manager with capture ratio > 1 sits on the convex line: in up markets the portfolio rises more than the benchmark, in down markets it falls less. That's the ideal — capture the upside, avoid the downside.
Capture ratio calculator
Drawdown (max drawdown & drawdown duration)
Drawdown = the maximum loss if an investor had bought at a peak valuation and sold at a trough. Drawdown duration = total time to fully recover: from when the drawdown commences up to when cumulative drawdown returns to zero.
Duration = drawdown phase + recovery phase. MAXIMUM drawdown occurs at the very END of the drawdown phase / very START of recovery — the point where cumulative drawdown is at its highest (in absolute terms).
Worked example (12-month stock)
MonthMonthly retCumulative drawdownComment
013.14%0.00%
02−2.55%−2.55%drawdown phase begins
03−2.71%−5.26%
04−4.66%−9.92%
05−4.91%−14.83%
06−0.73%−15.56%MAX drawdown; recovery begins
07–11+2.18% … +4.03%−13.38% → −0.14%recovery phase
124.14%0.00%drawdown recovered
Maximum drawdown = −15.56% (at month 06) Drawdown duration ≈ 11 months (02/20X8 begin → 12/20X8 full recovery)
Cumulative drawdown curve
Cumulative drawdown over the 12 months: it falls through the drawdown phase, hits the trough (max drawdown), then climbs back to zero through the recovery phase.
Duration spans the whole curve from the start of the drawdown (02) to full recovery at zero (12) ≈ 11 months. Max drawdown is the single lowest point (the trough at month 06), not the sum of the monthly losses.
Manager skill evaluation (LOS 13.p): attribution + appraisal
Skill is evaluated via attribution (country/stock decisions) AND appraisal (risk-adjusted vs peers).
ATTRIBUTION (Manager X vs Euronext 100, underperformed by 67 bps): • −12 bps from COUNTRY WEIGHTING (allocation): good call underweighting Netherlands (it lagged by 2.34%), but bad calls elsewhere (underweighted France which beat by 1.50%, overweighted Belgium which lagged by 1.87%) → net unsuccessful with country weighting • −56 bps from STOCK PICKING (selection): good picks in NL & Belgium (+32 bps) but France lost 81 bps → net unsuccessful; selection effect > allocation effect
Appraisal: Managers X / Y / Z vs benchmark (rf = 2%)
MeasureXYZBench
Return9.32%11.42%8.12%9.99%
Std dev11.65%13.76%10.11%11.98%
Sharpe0.630.680.610.67
Treynor0.070.080.060.08
Information ratio(0.22)0.41(0.72)—
Sortino (MAR 4%)0.750.780.630.87
• X's SD slightly below benchmark; lower than Y, higher than Z. Sharpe confirms (rf 2%): X 0.63 < Y 0.68 & Bench 0.67, but > Z 0.61 → X beat Z, lagged Y & benchmark, risk-adjusted • Sharpe conclusions match Treynor & IR. X & Z underperformed benchmark → negative IRs (X −0.22, Z −0.72); Y positive 0.41 → on systematic-risk basis X lagged Y & benchmark • X's Sortino 0.75 > X's Sharpe 0.63 → should earn greater returns vs the 4% downside threshold
Conclusion: X failed to show sufficient skill (poor country allocation + poor stock selection vs benchmark). On a risk-adjusted basis X beat Z but fell short of Y and the benchmark. Consider replacing X with a manager who can outperform on allocation, selection, AND risk-adjusted vs peers.
Module Quiz 13.4
It CAN be true: the Sharpe denominator is total standard deviation, which does not distinguish upside from downside volatility. If Mort's portfolio has lots of large positive (upside, "good") returns, those inflate the SD and penalize his Sharpe ratio even though they're desirable. Solution: use the Sortino ratio instead — it replaces total SD with the target semideviation (downside risk only, returns below the MAR), so "good" upside volatility no longer penalizes him.
C — 2.67. Upside capture = 4% / 3% = 1.333 Downside capture = −4% / −8% = 0.50 Capture ratio = upside / downside = 1.333 / 0.50 = 2.67 → > 1 = positively asymmetric (convex): captured the upside, avoided much of the downside.
Pattern 1 — "Where/when does RISK enter evaluation?"
Risk is NOT confined to performance appraisal. It enters across the process: measurement (calculates return AND risk), attribution (risk attribution is the parallel of return attribution), and appraisal (risk-adjusted measures).
Trap: "risk is considered only within performance appraisal" is FALSE. Risk attribution identifies the sources of risk the manager took — that's the attribution stage, not appraisal.
Pattern 2 — "Attribution explains HOW; APPRAISAL judges QUALITY"
Keep the three components in their lanes: measurement = WHAT (return+risk); attribution = HOW (break return/risk into explanatory components); appraisal = quality / skill vs luck.
Trap: "performance attribution draws conclusions about the QUALITY of the manager's decisions" is wrong — that's appraisal. Attribution explains how performance was achieved; effective attribution accounts for 100% of return/risk, reflects the decision process, quantifies the manager's active decisions, and fully explains excess return/risk.
Pattern 3 — pick the ratio by the RISK in the mandate
Mandate / objective wordingUseWhy
"return above a TARGET / MAR (e.g. rf + 1.5%)", "preserve capital", nonsymmetrical returnsSortinopenalizes returns below the specific target (downside semideviation)
excess over the risk-free rate, well-diversified, systematic riskTreynorpenalizes returns below rf; uses beta — won't measure a target-above-rf goal
performance vs a benchmarkInformation ratioactive return / tracking risk — relative to benchmark, not an absolute target
Trap: a "short-term return 1.5% above the risk-free rate" is a target return → Sortino. Don't grab Treynor (that's a below-rf penalty) or IR (that's vs-benchmark).
Pattern 4 — Brinson: separate the ALLOCATION decision from the NET contribution
A sector can have a positive net contribution (allocation + selection + interaction) while the allocation decision itself was bad. Judge the over/underweight on the allocation effect alone, not the net.
Trap (McNeil Statement 3): Consumer Goods net = −0.15% (alloc) + 0.56% (sel+int) = +0.41%. The +0.41 is real, but it came from SELECTION; the underweight (alloc −0.15%) was not beneficial. "Beneficial underweight given the +0.41 net" misattributes selection skill to the allocation call.
Also (Statement 1): the excess return's biggest driver was Technology sel+int 1.58%, not Financial 0.66% → "almost entirely financial" is false. (Statement 2 was true: underweighting Health Care, alloc −0.16%, was not beneficial.)
Pattern 5 — BF allocation sign: compare segment benchmark to the OVERALL benchmark
BF allocation Aᵢ = (wᵢ − Wᵢ)(Bᵢ − B). A weighting decision is good (positive) when you overweight a segment that beat the total benchmark OR underweight a segment that lagged the total benchmark.
Two-negatives rule: underweight (w−W < 0) × lagging segment (Bᵢ−B < 0) = positive allocation. That's why underweighting Developed Asia (12.85% < 22.67% total) was the only good call.
Q1 (AQI/Richard) — holdings-based residual term
Answer: A (correct). Richard's statement is right on both counts.
