The residual between portfolio and benchmark performance in holdings-based attribution (1) cannot be explained by a manager action, and (2) can result from transactions occurring more frequently than the holdings are measured — the timing/trading effect.
Context trap from the same vignette: Richard also said "risk is considered only within performance appraisal" — that part is FALSE (see Pattern 1). But this question only asked about the holdings-based residual.
Q2 (McNeil) — appraisal measure for the client mandate
Answer: A — Sortino ratio.
Mandate: moderate-high risk tolerance, short-term return 1.5% above the risk-free rate. A target above rf → Sortino (penalizes returns below that specific target).
B (Treynor) wrong: penalizes returns below rf only → can't measure a target-above-rf goal. C (IR) wrong: evaluates return relative to a benchmark, not an absolute target.
Q3 (Rao) — least accurate reason Sortino > Sharpe
Answer: C (Reason 3 is least accurate).
Reason 3 claimed Sortino's target return is "based on market conditions." Wrong — Sortino uses an investor-specific MAR (individual preferences), which is exactly why it has a comparability problem across investors.
Reasons 1 & 2 ARE accurate: Sortino suits a capital-preservation goal (penalizes below-MAR), and it handles nonsymmetrical distributions better (Sharpe assumes symmetry).
Q4 (Bragg) — which responses on effective attribution are correct
Answer: B — only Response 2.
Response 2 (attribution explains how performance was achieved by breaking return/risk into components) is correct. Response 1 (attribution "draws conclusions about the quality of decisions") describes appraisal, not attribution.
Effective attribution must: account for 100% of return/risk, reflect the decision-making process, quantify the manager's active decisions, and fully explain excess return/risk.
Q5 (Tolmach) — which region's over/underweight helped at the fund level (BF)
Answer: C — Developed Asia and Australasia.
BF allocation = (wᵢ − Wᵢ)(Bᵢ − B), total benchmark B = 22.67% North America = (10.84% − 7.67%)(16.47% − 22.67%) = −0.20% Greater Europe = (38.92% − 42.35%)(25.43% − 22.67%) = −0.09% Developed Asia/Aus. = (29.86% − 31.16%)(12.85% − 22.67%) = +0.13%
Only Developed Asia/Australasia is positive: the manager underweighted it (29.86% < 31.16%) and its benchmark lagged the total (12.85% < 22.67%) → underweighting a loser is a good call.
E1 (HCSF) — "Demonstrate which sectors contributed negatively" [left blank]
Answer: Automotive and Machinery. The command word is demonstrate → state each sector + the weighting decision + the relative return, in words. No full BHB calc required.
SectorWeight decisionHoldings vs benchmarkWhy it hurt
AutomotiveOVERweight +20% (30% vs 10%)UNDERperformed by 1.25% (7.85% vs 9.10%)overweighted a sector whose holdings lagged
MachineryUNDERweight (20% vs 35%)OUTperformed by 2.00% (7.65% vs 5.65%)underweighted a sector whose holdings beat the bench
The decision-vs-net trap (same as Pattern 4): the book grades the manager's decision, not the arithmetic net. By net BHB contribution Automotive is actually positive (+1.45%) because the +20% overweight on a 9.10% benchmark sector earns a big allocation term; what the book flags is that the selection/decision was bad — you overweighted a sector your holdings couldn't beat, and underweighted one they did beat. Answer at the level the verb asks for.
Note: the book prose says machinery was underweighted "by 10%," but Exhibit 1 gives 20% vs 35% = 15%. Treat as a book typo; the direction (underweight) is what matters.
E2 (Clark) — which attribution statement is correct + why the other two fail
You got the answer right (Statement 1) but the EXPLANATIONS for 2 & 3 were off.
Statement 1 correct: transactions-based attribution uses holdings AND the transactions (buys/sells) during the period, includes transaction costs → most accurate but most difficult / time-consuming.
MethodUsesAccuracyNote
Returns-basedtotal portfolio returns ONLYleast accurate, most manipulableeasiest to implement; use when holdings data is unavailable at needed frequency/detail
Holdings-basedbeginning-of-period holdingsimproves with shorter intervalsover long periods misses intra-period trades = the trading effect (residual)
Transactions-basedholdings + transactions + costsmost accuratehardest / most time-consuming
Your Statement 2 error: you wrote "returns-based uses IRR and is subject to manipulation." The IRR part is wrong — returns-based uses total portfolio returns. Its weakness is that it ignores the underlying holdings, making it the least accurate and most vulnerable to manipulation (Statement 2 claimed it was the most reliable / least vulnerable — the opposite).
Your Statement 3 error (right idea, imprecise): Statement 3 fails because holdings-based does NOT eliminate the trading effect and is NOT accurate for longer periods. It works for shorter intervals; over longer periods it fails to capture intra-period transactions, and that ignored residual IS the trading effect. So holdings-based includes/suffers the trading effect — it doesn't eliminate it.
Mastery checklist
Once a pattern is no longer being missed, it moves here as a confirmed mastery point.
Reading 13 · Portfolio Performance Evaluation
Full-reading recap: components of evaluation (13.a–b), return vs risk / macro vs micro attribution (13.c), returns- / holdings- / transactions-based methods (13.d), arithmetic vs geometric + BHB / BF / Carhart (13.e, 13.h), fixed-income attribution (13.f), risk attribution (13.g), benchmarks (13.i–m), and appraisal measures + skill (13.n–p). All figures node-verified against the Kaplan tables.
The master flow (memorize): Measurement (WHAT return & risk?) → Attribution (HOW was it achieved, given the risk taken?) → Appraisal (skill or LUCK?). Exam focus: interpret fixed-income attribution output — you are not responsible for computing it.
Module 13.1 · Performance Evaluation
LOS 13.aThree interrelated components
Measurement
Initial foundation phase — calculates both the return AND the risk of the fund over specified periods. Decide up front: compared to a benchmark (relative) or to a target return % specified in advance (absolute)?
Attribution
Determines the key drivers of performance — explains HOW the return was achieved given the risk taken. Can explain both relative and absolute returns.
Appraisal
Was performance driven primarily by investment decisions, the overall market, or chance? Combines measurement + attribution output. If performance = luck → don't expect it to repeat.
3 questions: 1) WHAT did the fund achieve? (measurement) 2) HOW did the manager achieve it? (attribution) 3) Skill or LUCK? (appraisal)
LOS 13.bEffective attribution process — 4 attributes
1) Reflects 100% of the portfolio's return or risk exposure — anything less is misleading and unusable · 2) reflects the manager's current decision-making process (update it if the process changed) · 3) reflects the active investment decisions taken · 4) provides a full explanation of excess return and risk.
LOS 13.cReturn vs risk attribution · macro vs micro
Return attribution
Impact of active management decisions on the fund's investment returns.
Risk attribution
The parallel of return attribution — impact of active decisions on portfolio risk. Risk is usually measured vs the benchmark but can be absolute: a manager with a predetermined absolute target → relative-based risk attribution is not appropriate.
Macro attribution
Decisions of the fund sponsor (investment committee + internal staff): deviations from strategic AA and their timing; overweighting styles of managers; selecting good managers.
Micro attribution
Decisions of the individual portfolio manager: overweight/underweight segments (substyle / sector / geography) to generate active return. Verifies the PM did what they said they would do.
Trap (13.c): a widely quoted passive index (e.g. S&P 500) may or may not be an appropriate benchmark for the portfolio — popularity ≠ appropriateness.
LOS 13.dReturns-based · holdings-based · transactions-based
MethodHowAdvantagesDisadvantages
Returns-basedRegresses total returns on major risk factors to identify active betsEasy to implement; no holdings data needed (useful for private funds, e.g. hedge funds)Least accurate (ignores holdings); returns data can be manipulated
Holdings-basedUses beginning-of-period holdingsMore accurate than returns-basedNeeds holdings data; timing / trading effect — ignores intra-period trades → not for high-turnover funds over long periods
Transactions-basedAdds the impact of trades executed during the periodMost accurateHighest data requirements; highest complexity
Tip: the timing/trading mismatch of holdings-based attribution is reduced by shorter evaluation periods — it is never “eliminated.”
Module 13.2 · Return Attribution
LOS 13.eArithmetic vs geometric attribution
Arithmetic active = R − B problem: single-period actives don't compound Geometric G = (1+R)/(1+B) − 1 → DOES compound across periods
Two periods, R = 5% and B = 3% each: wealth 100×1.05² = 110.25 vs 100×1.03² = 106.09 → two-period arithmetic active = 10.25% − 6.09% = 4.16%, but the two 2% single-period actives compound to only (1.02)²−1 = 4.04% ≠ 4.16%. Geometric: G = 1.05/1.03 − 1 = 1.94% per period, and (1.0194)²−1 = 3.92% = 1.1025/1.0609 − 1 ✓
Professor's note: all attribution models in this reading are arithmetic — the vast majority of practitioners use arithmetic attribution.
LOS 13.hBrinson — BHB method (asset owner vs manager)
R = ΣwiRi B = ΣWiBi active = R − B Allocation Ai = (wi − Wi) × Bi Selection Si = Wi × (Ri − Bi) Interaction Ii = (wi − Wi) × (Ri − Bi)
Allocation = WEIGHTING
Value added by over/underweighting a segment vs the benchmark — active weight × passive benchmark segment return. Ignores any selection ability.
Selection = PICKING
Value added by selecting investments different from the benchmark's — passive benchmark weight × active return in the segment. Ignores weighting.
Interaction = COMPOUNDING
Allocation and selection acting together — the first term of allocation × the second term of selection. Least intuitive but required: overweighting a style where the selected manager outperforms adds more than allocation + selection alone.
Fig 13.2 (growth 75/60 w R 13% B 10%; value 25/40 w R 19% B 20%): R = 14.5%, B = 14.0%, active = 0.5%. BHB: allocation +1.5% −3.0% = −1.5% · selection +1.8% −0.4% = +1.4% · interaction +0.45% +0.15% = +0.6% → sum = 0.5% ✓
LOS 13.hBrinson-Fachler (BF) — the sign fix
BF allocation Ai = (wi − Wi) × (Bi − B) ← segment return RELATIVE TO OVERALL benchmark
The WHY: under BHB the sign of Ai doesn't tell you whether the decision was correct. Growth: (0.75−0.60)×10% = +1.5% looks good — but overweighting a style returning 10% when the whole benchmark did 14% was a bad decision. BF: (0.75−0.60)×(10%−14%) = −0.60%; value (0.25−0.40)×(20%−14%) = −0.90%; total −1.50% = same aggregate as BHB, but each segment's sign now indicates decision quality.
Only allocation differs between BHB and BF — selection and interaction are calculated identically, and the total allocation effect is the same. In practice, BF tends to be the more popular model.
LOS 13.hMacro vs micro attribution · the shortcut · single stock
Macro = attribution on fund-sponsor decisions (the BHB/BF style-level examples above). Micro = attribution at the individual manager level (segments = substyle / sector / geography). Fig 13.3/13.4 (growth manager size bets): allocation −1.10% + selection +1.20% + interaction +1.55% = 1.65% — the same total as the growth manager under macro (−0.60 + 1.80 + 0.45 = 1.65%), even though the individual effects differ by segmentation. Grand total across styles: −2.00 + 0.80 + 1.70 = 0.50% ✓ (matches macro output).
Shortcut sel+int
Lumping selection + interaction = use the selection formula with portfolio weights: wi × (Ri − Bi). Check: 0.5 × (15%−8%) = 3.50% = 2.10% + 1.40% ✓
Single-stock micro
The allocation effect actually represents the selection decision (allocating to one security IS stock selection); the selection effect represents market timing + transaction costs on that security.
Segmentation matters
A manager can look like a good stock picker by geography and a poor one by sector. The verdict lies in the decision-making process: judge along the dimension the manager actually uses to construct the portfolio.
LOS 13.eCarhart 4-factor model (factor-based attribution)
Rp − Rf = ap + bp1RMRF + bp2SMB + bp3HML + bp4WML + Ep
RMRF
Market: value-weighted equity index return above the one-month T-bill.
SMB (size)
Small Minus Big: avg return of three small-cap portfolios − three large-cap portfolios. Negative sensitivity → large-cap tilt.
HML (value)
High Minus Low book-to-market: two high-B/M − two low-B/M portfolios. Positive → value tilt; zero → blend.
WML (momentum)
Winners Minus Losers: past year's winners − losers.
How to read Fig 13.5: benchmark sensitivities (RMRF = 1, SMB = −1, HML = 0, WML = 0.05) → the benchmark is a diversified, large-cap blend index that does not use momentum. Contribution to active return = (sensitivity difference) × factor return: the HML tilt contributed +1.29% = 78% of the 1.65% active return (a value tilt); security selection contributed −0.10%. Factor tilts total 1.75% + selection −0.10% = 1.65% ✓
Due-diligence trap: if the prospectus says growth but the attribution shows the value tilt drove returns → the strategy was not demonstrated in the model attribution — further due diligence required.
LOS 13.fFixed-income attribution — 3 methods (INTERPRET, don't calculate)
MethodMechanicsData / complexityUsed by / for
Exposure decomposition — duration basedPartition portfolio & benchmark into duration buckets, then sectors; decompose active return per bucket/sectorRelatively low data needs; simple presentationMarketing & client reporting — clearly understandable output
Yield curve decomposition — duration basedDecomposes active return into yield / roll / shift / shape / spread / residual using durations & YTMsMore data; more operational complexityAnalysts & portfolio managers (not client comms)
Yield curve decomposition — full repricingReprices individual cash flows with spot rates at different maturitiesMost complex; highest precision; broadest instrument coverageMost precise — but least likely to be understood by the recipient
4 active FI bets
Duration (expect curve shift DOWN → increase duration) · curve shape (position for steepening/flattening) · sector selection (expect corporate spreads to NARROW → overweight corporates) · bond selection (overweight individual bonds expected to outperform).
6 return sources (duration-based YC)
Yield (coupon income) · roll (rolling down a stable curve) · shift (parallel move, via duration & convexity) · shape (slope/curvature change) · spread (sector or security spread change) · residual (estimation error — mostly duration/convexity approximation).
Reading Fig 13.8 signs
Duration effect +0.33% → higher-duration bet paid → the yield curve did fall. Curve effect −0.39% with overweight in medium duration → medium yields rose while short yields fell → steepening. Sector −0.08% → corporate spreads widened, contrary to expectations. Bond selection 0.00% → no active bond picking. Total = 2.42% − 2.56% = −0.14% ✓
High-coupon high-yield overweight logic: expect positive yield contribution (high coupon) and positive spread contribution from expected narrowing; if issuers default on coupons or spreads widen instead → those effects flip negative.
LOS 13.gRisk attribution — selecting the approach (Fig 13.9)
Match the investment process (row) with the type of attribution (column). Relative attribution uses tracking risk; absolute uses total risk / standard deviation.
Investment processRelative (vs benchmark)Absolute
Bottom upSecurity's marginal contribution to tracking risk × active weightSecurity's marginal contribution to total risk
Top downAttribute tracking risk to relative allocation and selectionFactor's marginal contribution to total risk and specific risk
Factor basedFactor's marginal contribution to tracking risk and active specific risk
Why risk attribution at all: looking only at returns is insufficient — the risk the PM took must also be analyzed. Risk attribution identifies the sources of risk; it must be combined with return attribution to fully understand active decisions.
Module 13.3 · Benchmarking Investments and Managers
LOS 13.iLiability-based benchmarks
The more frequent benchmark in institutional investing — used by fund sponsors / PMs when the firm has a specific future liability (e.g. a DB plan). Focuses on the cash flows necessary to satisfy the liability; frequently limits the manager's investment choices (e.g. equity + fixed income only). Typical assets: nominal bonds, inflation-adjusted bonds, high-quality stocks.
Plan features shaping the liability
Years until the average worker retires · how many are already retired & drawing cash · inflation impact · correlation of company EBIT with plan assets · frozen / terminal life · actuarial assumptions (life expectancy, discount rate).
LOS 13.jSeven asset-based benchmark types
TypeKey advantageKey disadvantage
1. Absolute (e.g. MAR)Simple, straightforwardNot investable
2. Broad market indexWell recognized, unambiguous, investable, measurable, specified in advanceManager's style may deviate from the index (S&P 500 ≠ small-cap growth manager)
3. Style indexWidely available/understood; appropriate if it reflects the style & is investableWeightings may be imprudent; differing style definitions → very different returns
4. Factor modelUseful in evaluation; insight into style via factor exposuresNot intuitive; data/modeling costly; ambiguous (different models → different outputs → misspecification)
5. Returns-basedEasy, intuitive; meets validity criteria; works when only account returns are availableStyle indexes may not match what manager owns; needs many monthly returns; fails on style changers
6. Manager universes (median manager)Measurable — that's itSurvivor bias; not specified in advance; not investable; ambiguous; relies on compiler accuracy → not a valid benchmark
7. Custom security-basedMeets all validity criteria; continual monitoring; allocates risk across teamsExpensive to build/maintain; impossible without manager transparency (hedge funds)
LOS 13.kSeven tests of benchmark quality — “SAMURAI”
Specified in advance · Appropriate (consistent w/ style) · Measurable (reasonably frequent) · Unambiguous (identities & weights defined) · Reflective of current investment opinions · Accountable (manager accepts it) · Investable (replicable, can forgo active mgmt)
LOS 13.k/13.lP = M + S + A · benchmark misspecification
P = M + S + A S = B − M (style: style index − market) A = P − B (active: portfolio − style benchmark)
Test-of-quality example: portfolio −11%, style index −12%, market −10% → S = −12 − (−10) = −2% (growth style out of favor), A = −11 − (−12) = +1% → the manager BEAT the style benchmark. Client's complaint about underperforming the broad market is not valid — it is the style, not the manager, that underperformed.
Misspecification (garbage in, garbage out): manager holds large/liquid French stocks; investor benchmark = Euronext 100 (return 9%), normal portfolio = CAC 40 (return 12%), portfolio = 10%. Misfit active = 12% − 9% = +3% (benchmark vs benchmark); true active = 10% − 12% = −2%. With the wrong benchmark the manager looks like a +1% outperformer — the entire evaluation (attribution AND appraisal) becomes invalid.
Trap: misspecified benchmarks produce misfit active return — always separate misfit (style benchmark vs investor benchmark) from true active (portfolio vs normal portfolio).
LOS 13.mBenchmarking alternative investments — why it's hard
Hedge funds
3 candidates, all flawed: broad market indexes → strategies too diverse, leverage/shorts/derivatives, low correlation with the index → do not use. Risk-free rate + spread → only arbitrage-like strategies; most HFs carry systematic risk, leverage exacerbates it, low correlation with rf → unsuitable. Peer universes → risk/return objectives don't match a specific fund, backfill & survivorship bias, illiquidity → appraisal-based (stale) pricing → smoothing understates σ → inflates Sharpe and the allocation to HFs.
Real estate
Sample-based (not representative); index driven by largest holdings; self-reported returns; value-based indexes biased to expensive properties/areas; appraisal data → smoothing → understated volatility; leverage inconsistency; indexes assume no transaction costs/full transparency/normal liquidity. Return measure: TWR for open-end (investor controls flows) vs IRR for closed-end (manager controls flows).
Private equity
Metric is usually IRR since inception + ending value. Problems: managers use different valuation methods; IRR biased by early gains/losses; results reported at one common point despite varying stages of development.
Commodities
Benchmarks are futures-based, not actual assets → big differences vs the portfolio; leverage and exposure-weighting differences reduce comparability.
Managed derivatives
Strategy-specific (e.g. Mount Lucas Management Index — basic momentum) or peer-group benchmarks with the same survivorship issues as hedge funds.
Distressed securities
Illiquidity + severe lack of marketability → almost impossible to benchmark; stale pricing and erratic valuation intervals (Barclay Distressed Securities Index exists but mixes strategies).
Recurring exam trap: appraisal/stale pricing → smoothed returns → understated standard deviation → overstated Sharpe ratio → over-allocation to the asset class. Same mechanism for hedge funds, real estate, distressed.
Module 13.4 · Performance Appraisal
LOS 13.n/13.oSeven appraisal measures (first five are risk-adjusted)
MeasureFormulaRisk in denominatorKey point / limitation
1. Sharpe(R̄A − r̄f) / σ̂ATotal riskPenalizes ALL volatility, even “good” upside vol
2. Treynor(R̄A − r̄f) / β̂ASystematic onlyOnly for well-diversified portfolios (no unsystematic risk); benchmark universe limited to those assuming efficient markets
3. Information ratio[E(rp) − E(rB)] / σ(rp − rB)Tracking riskActive return per unit of benchmark-relative variability
4. Appraisal ratioα / σεResidual (active) risk from a factor regression“IR with a factor-based regression”; σε = standard error of the regression
5. Sortino[E(rp) − rT] / σDTarget semideviation (below MAR only)Better for nonnormal / skewed returns (hedge funds, options); MAR is subjective → comparability problem
6. Capture ratiosUC / DC—>1 = convex (positively asymmetric); <1 = concave
7. Drawdownpeak → trough loss—Max drawdown + drawdown duration (to full recovery)
Limitations (13.o) master point: most managers have only a few years of data → extremely difficult to separate luck from skill; require many years of observations at a high confidence level before concluding a manager truly has skill.
LOS 13.nAppraisal ratio & Sortino — the worked numbers
AR = α / σε σ²i = β²σ²m + σ²ε → σ²ε = σ²i − β²σ²m
Example (circled in photo): Rp 8%, σp 20%, β 1.2, Rm 6%, σm 16%, rf 1%. CAPM fair return = 1 + 1.2(6−1) = 7% → α = 8 − 7 = 1%. σ²ε = 0.20² − (1.2² × 0.16²) = 0.003136. AR = 0.01 / √0.003136 = 0.18.
Trap (professor's note): take the SQUARE ROOT of σ²ε before dividing — forgetting the root is the classic error.
Sortino: penalizes only returns below the MAR — sum squared distances below target, divide by TOTAL number of observations (including those above target), take the square root = semideviation. Example: (7% − 3%) / 5% = 0.80. Skew logic: higher σ lowers both Sharpe ratios, but only a negatively skewed strategy (higher semideviation) lowers the Sortino → Sortino discriminates between positive and negative skew.
LOS 13.nCapture ratios & drawdown
UC = Rp/RB in UP markets DC = Rp/RB in DOWN markets capture ratio = UC / DC
Up market: B +4%, P +5% → UC = 1.25 (outperformance); P +3% → UC = 0.75 (underperformance in an up market). Down market: B −4%, P −5% → DC = 1.25 = underperformance; P −3% → DC = 0.75 = outperformance during negative returns. UC 87.5% with DC 60% → ratio ≈ 1.46 = positively asymmetric (convex) profile. Ideal: capture the upside, avoid the downside → maximize the ratio.
Sign trap: in a DOWN market, DC > 1 is BAD (fell more than the benchmark) and DC < 1 is GOOD — the interpretation flips vs up markets. Quiz check: up P 4%/B 3%, down P −4%/B −8% → (4/3)/(−4/−8) = 1.333/0.5 = 2.67.
Drawdown: max loss from investing at a peak and liquidating at a trough. Drawdown duration = total time to fully recover (cumulative drawdown back to zero) = drawdown phase + recovery phase. Maximum drawdown occurs at the very end of the drawdown phase / very start of recovery — where cumulative drawdown is largest in absolute terms.
Table convention (node-verified): the cumulative drawdown column is the arithmetic sum of monthly drawdowns (−2.55 −2.71 −4.66 −4.91 −0.73 = −15.56%), capped at 0.00% once recovered.
LOS 13.pManager skill evaluation — attribution + appraisal together
1. Attribution read
Manager X vs Euronext 100: active = 9.32% − 9.99% = −0.67% = −12 bps country weighting (allocation) + −56 bps stock picking (selection + interaction). One good call (underweight Netherlands, which lagged by 2.34%) doesn't save it: bad weights in all other countries; France selection alone lost −81 bps. Selection damage > allocation damage.
2. Appraisal read
With rf = 2%: Sharpe X 0.63 < Y 0.68 and < benchmark 0.67, > Z 0.61 → X took less total risk but earned relatively less return per unit of risk. Treynor and IR agree (X and Z underperformed the benchmark → negative IRs). X's Sortino 0.75 > Sharpe 0.63 → X earns relatively more above the 4% MAR threshold (less “bad” volatility).
3. Conclusion pattern
Essay template: X showed insufficient skill (losses from poor country allocation AND poor stock selection vs benchmark); on a risk-adjusted basis X beat Z but fell short of Y and the benchmark; consider replacing X with a manager able to outperform on allocation, selection, and risk-adjusted peers comparison.
Quiz 13.4 essay answer (Sharpe complaint): a manager's σ can be “artificially inflated” by upside volatility — the Sharpe denominator penalizes good and bad vol alike. Solution: use the Sortino ratio (target semideviation below MAR only) so only downside volatility is penalized.
Investment Manager Selection
READING 14 · Performance Measurement
Due diligence — definition (LOS 14.a)
Due diligence = the analysis and investigation in support of an investment decision, action, or recommendation.
It must emphasize the sources AND reasons behind the actual returns generated in the past — not just the level of past returns. Then evaluate the probability of repeatedly earning sufficient or better returns in the future using the same investment process.
Decisive detail: DD is forward-looking judgment built on backward-looking evidence. The point is not "did returns happen" but why they happened and can the same process repeat them. An answer that stops at "past returns were good" is incomplete.
Three components of due diligence
ComponentWhat it doesPerformance assessed?
Manager universeBuild the pool of suitable managers; establish the role & risk fitNO — risk profile / fit only
Quantitative analysisObjective evaluation of the distribution of past returns; attribution + appraisal; capture ratio; drawdownsYES — this is where it happens
Qualitative analysisWill returns continue? Does the process capture all relevant risks? (4 Ps + risk assessment)Judgment on sustainability
Trap (stage placement): performance assessment does NOT happen at the universe stage — it happens later in quantitative analysis. At the universe stage the emphasis is purely the manager's risk profile and fit for the portfolio's requirements.
What makes a manager "suitable" for the universe
The universe contains only suitable managers. Suitable means they:
DriverRequirement
IPS fitFit the objectives and constraints of the IPS
Relevant styleInvest in the relevant portfolio style desired by the client (value / growth / mixed)
Active vs passiveManage with the appropriate balance between active and passive approaches
It is a process of elimination that balances having too many vs too few managers in the candidate pool. The purpose of the search is crucial (e.g., a new strategy, a new risk exposure, or a manager to complement existing holdings).
Subjectivity flag: the terms "best" and "complement" carry an aspect of subjectivity that must be judged in the context of the IPS — not in the abstract.
Establishing the role — defined by the benchmark
The search begins by establishing the potential manager's role within the portfolio, which is defined by the benchmark. The benchmark can be determined using one or more of:
MethodNote
Third-party categorizationFrom database/software providers — trap: the provider's definition may not match the definition needed for the role within your portfolio
Returns-based style analysis (RBSA)Examined in detail later (14.2)
Holdings-based style analysis (HBSA)Examined in detail later (14.2)
Manager experienceAscertained from analysis of holdings within the manager's portfolios as well as past returns
At the universe stage there should be no performance assessment — emphasis is on the manager's risk profile and whether it is a good fit for the portfolio's requirements. The universe is constantly changing as strategies change and managers come and go.
Quantitative analysis
Evaluate the manager objectively via the distribution of past returns. Components:
ToolPurpose
Attribution + appraisalDistinguish managerial skill vs luck (luck = external market factors)
Capture ratioExamines performance in both good AND weak market conditions
DrawdownsCheck for any significant drawdown = peak-to-trough decline (in %) over a specific time period
Qualitative analysis — the two issues
Two important issues arise:
(1) What is the likelihood the same level of returns will continue in the future? (2) Does the manager's investment process account for all the relevant risks?
Issue (1) → assessed via the four Ps. Issue (2) → assessed via risk assessment of the firm. (See "4 Ps & Risk" tab.)
Don't swap the stages. "Performing investment due diligence" is a qualitative activity. "Defining the universe" is the universe stage. Only evaluating a performance appraisal belongs to quantitative analysis — this is the Quiz 14.1 Q1 distinction.
Continuity of returns — the four Ps
Continuity of returns is assessed by looking at the four Ps:
PWhat it covers
PhilosophyFocuses on a specific area of market inefficiency to earn excess returns
ProcessDetermines whether the strategy is feasible
PeopleWhether it is possible to execute the strategy with the knowledge & skills of the employees
PortfolioMust be built congruent with the philosophy and process
Order of logic: philosophy (where's the edge?) → process & people (can we actually do it?) → portfolio (does the book match what we claim?).
Risk assessment (issue 2 — all relevant risks)
Risk assessment considers the firm and whether it is robust & performing well, and its likelihood of remaining a going concern. It examines:
Aspects such as the quality of the back office, the process and procedures of the firm. Ability to safeguard assets and to prepare useful, timely reports (operational due diligence). Going into such detail surfaces risks not evident in past returns — the focus is sustainability. The proposed investment vehicle and the terms of the manager contract must be assessed for suitability and must be reasonable and relevant. Finally, continual monitoring ensures the manager continues to be the appropriate one for the portfolio.
Q1. Quantitative analysis of the manager selection process includes:
Answer: B. Attribution and appraisal are the quantitative steps (skill vs luck from the distribution of returns). A = the universe stage (no performance assessment there). C = a qualitative activity.
Q2. The expected cost of Type I and Type II errors is:
Answer: B. The greater the difference in sample size & mean (wider dispersion between strong and weak managers), the easier it is to distinguish relative skill → less likely to make a Type I or II error → lower expected cost. Note A states the right relationship in the wrong direction (it's lower cost, not higher).
Q3. A return distribution of skilled managers that is not distinct from the return distribution of unskilled managers most likely implies a:
Answer: C. Indistinct distributions = you cannot tell skill apart, so you are more likely to wrongly pass on / not hire a skilled manager = a Type II error, whose cost is the opportunity (implicit) cost of not hiring skill — and here that cost is high. A is wrong: indistinct distributions point to an efficient market (small dispersion), not inefficient. B has the magnitude backwards.
The hypothesis setup (LOS 14.b)
H₀ (null): the manager adds NO value (no skill). To reject H₀, the calculated test statistic must be large enough — i.e., demonstrate value added on a statistically significant basis.
Reject H₀ → conclude there IS skill → hire/retain.   Fail to reject H₀ → conclude no skill → not hire / fire.
Figure 14.1 — tap any cell
Decision ↓   Realization →Realization (the truth)
Below expectations
(NO skill)		At/above expectations
(SKILL)
Hire / retain
Not hire / fire
Tap a cell to reveal whether it is Correct, Type I, or Type II — and why.
Memory hook: the error is named for the action you took on the wrong target. Type I = you acted (hired/retained) on a no-skill manager — a false positive, error of commission. Type II = you passed (didn't hire / fired) a skilled manager — a false negative, error of omission.
Type I vs Type II — full contrast
AttributeType IType II
Decision on H₀Reject H₀ when no value addedFail to reject H₀ when value WAS added
What you didHire / retain a manager with NO skillNot hire / fire a manager WITH skill
False...False positiveFalse negative
Error of...Commission (an active decision)Omission
Cost visibilityExplicit / visible costsImplicit / opportunity (less visible) costs
Easy to determine?Easier — measure vs a benchmarkDifficult — how do you judge a manager you never hired / fired?
Attention receivedMore attentionLess attention
Why Type I gets more attention: (1) regret aversion — commission errors produce explicit, visible costs; (2) Type I is easier to determine (measurable vs benchmark); (3) it impacts the decision-maker's compensation, so extra care is taken to reduce it; (4) it is more visible to clients, who can see an investment that underperformed.
Decisive detail under pressure: "errors of omission / opportunity cost / hard to see / hard to measure" → Type II. "errors of commission / explicit cost / visible / measurable / compensation-relevant" → Type I. Don't let "the manager has no skill" auto-trigger Type II — hiring a no-skill manager is Type I.
Costs of Type I and II errors
ErrorCost is...
Type ICost of retaining managers who are weak
Type IICost of not retaining managers who are strong
Dispersion → expected cost (the key driver chain)
Assume two groups of managers (strong and weak). Decompose the driver:
Driver movesEffect on distinguishing skillEffect on error likelihoodEffect on expected cost
Greater difference in sample size & mean (wider dispersion strong vs weak)Easier to distinguish relative skillLess likely Type I or IILOWER expected cost
Smaller dispersion (efficient market)Harder to distinguish skillMore likely Type I or IIHIGHER expected cost
Efficient market link: in an efficient market it is harder to achieve alpha through active management, so the dispersion of return distributions between strong and weak is smaller → this raises the cost of hiring/retaining weak managers (a Type I cost).
Direction trap: wider dispersion does NOT raise cost — it lowers it (easier to tell skill apart). The relationship is inverse: dispersion ↑ ⇒ expected error cost ↓.
Preventing Type II errors
An excessive number of Type II errors indicates a problem with the hiring and firing of managers. The obvious solution is to track the subsequent performance of managers who were not hired as well as those who were fired.
Compare characteristics of selected vs not-selected managers — are the selected ones consistent with the portfolio investment objectives? Compare characteristics of retained vs fired managers — are the retained ones consistent with the portfolio objectives?
Ultimate principle: do not hire or fire managers because of short-term performance or because of behavioral biases. Acting on either is exactly what generates excess Type II (and Type I) errors.
Style analysis — what it examines (LOS 14.c)
Style analysis examines the manager's risk exposures (e.g., industry, concentration, capitalization) in relation to an appropriate benchmark, and the changes in those exposures over time.
Risk exposures allow classification of managers by style (e.g., value, growth) for selection purposes.
TypeBased on
RBSA — returns-based style analysisThe manager's return series
HBSA — holdings-based style analysisThe manager's actual holdings
Once RBSA and HBSA are performed, congruence between the output and the investment process is crucial — to ensure the process can be replicated consistently in the future.
RBSA — what it is
RBSA estimates the portfolio's sensitivities to security market indexes for a set of key risk factors. It is top-down in nature.
Decisive detail: in RBSA the risk factors are estimated — NOT taken from predetermined style categories. That estimation is the "one complication" of RBSA.
RBSA — advantages
AdvantageWhy
Easy / low dataTop-down; little additional data needed → computationally relatively easy
Basic AND complexDetermines key risk factors & return drivers for basic and complex strategies
Objective + comparableUses objective data; allows comparability between managers and through time
TimelyCan be performed on a timely basis (e.g., right after data released)
RBSA — drawbacks (decompose)
DrawbackMechanism
Lacks precisionAssumes a static portfolio for the period → hard to ascertain impact of multiperiod decisions; could alter the breakdown of value-added sources
Stale pricesIlliquid securities → stale prices understate risk exposure
SD understated short-termWhen performance is based on appraisals of ongoing projects & IRR of cash distributions (VC, PE), short-term volatility may be understated → true SD best gauged over a longer period
Timeliness fallsReporting timeliness decreases with illiquid/nontraded securities (longer time to price)
HBSA — what it is
HBSA looks at the actual securities in the portfolio at one point in time. This allows estimating current risk exposures using a security-specific (bottom-up) approach.
Many advantages are the same as RBSA (key risk factors & return drivers, comparability between managers and through time, performed on a timely basis). Most appropriate for equity-based strategies.
HBSA — drawbacks (decompose)
DrawbackMechanism
Computational loadIncreases as complexity rises and transparency decreases
Point-in-time formatMay not be useful projecting forward, or if the portfolio has high turnover
Stale pricingLike RBSA, illiquid/nontraded securities → stale pricing understates risk exposure + decreases reporting timeliness
RBSA vs HBSA — the contrast that gets tested
DimensionRBSAHBSA
InputReturn seriesActual holdings
DirectionTop-downBottom-up (security-specific)
Time frameOver a period (assumes static portfolio)Point in time (current exposures)
Data / computationLess data, easierMore as complexity rises
PrecisionLacks precision (static assumption)More precise (security-specific)
Best forBasic & complex strategiesEquity-based strategies
High turnover—Weak — point-in-time snapshot misleads
Quiz 14.2 Q1 trap: "data required for HBSA is easier to obtain" is NOT an advantage — HBSA's computational/data requirement increases with complexity. HBSA's real advantages are more precise and better for equity.
Capture ratios (LOS 14.d)
Capture ratios determine how suitable a manager is with respect to the investor's risk tolerance and time horizon.
RatioMeasures capture when benchmark return is...Outperformance when...
Upside capture (UC)POSITIVEUC > 100% (higher = outperform). UC < 100% = underperform
Downside capture (DC)NEGATIVEDC < 100% (lower = outperform, lost less). DC > 100% = underperform
Inverse logic trap: for UC, higher is better. For DC, lower is better. They move in opposite directions on what counts as "good" — a high DC is BAD (lost more than the benchmark on the way down).
Capture ratio (CR) — calculator
CR = UC ratio / DC ratio.   CR > 1 = positive asymmetry (convex)  |  CR < 1 = negative asymmetry (concave).
Input (%)Value
Upside capture UC (%)
Downside capture DC (%)
Enter UC and DC, then Compute.
Convexity: natural vs manager skill
Source of positive asymmetryExample & signature
Naturally convex (strategy)Hedging: buy a series of OTM puts before severe downturns → many small losses (puts expire worthless → low DC) + far fewer large gains (high UC) → positive asymmetry comes from the structure, not skill
Manager skillLong-only equity needing active management to minimize losses & maximize gains → requires skill; may not give consistent positive asymmetry
Beta link: when betas are increasing (decreasing), momentum-driven strategies should have higher (lower) UC than value-driven. A low-beta (high-beta) strategy will have lower (higher) UC and DC. CRs can be used to confirm the stated investment strategy.
Drawdown (LOS 14.d)
TermDefinition
DrawdownTotal peak-to-trough loss for a specified time period
Maximum drawdownThe largest peak-to-trough loss during that period
Drawdown durationTotal time from when the drawdown begins to when it recovers to zero (achieved via offsetting gains)
Use: drawdowns help identify poor / poorly-executed strategies, weak internal controls, and operational problems. Large drawdowns are not appropriate for investors approaching the end of their horizon. Low-beta strategy may have lower absolute returns but lower drawdowns → better risk-adjusted returns.
Risk management vs self-preservation (the judgment call): significant/extended drawdowns can push a manager into self-preservationist tactics that harm investors. Selling unrealized-loss assets in a downturn may be prudent (losses could worsen) OR risky (if a reversal follows). The exam question: did the manager act per the IPS, for self-preservation, or as an overreaction?
Applying to the IPS: investors with shorter horizons and lower risk tolerance should invest with managers showing smaller and less extended drawdowns.
Detecting style drift
Monitoring RBSA and HBSA output over time can help detect style drift — whereby the manager's actions are deviating from the manager's stated style.
When is style analysis relevant / best?
Relevant when: comparisons can be made over time and between different managers; done on a timely basis; the risks analyzed are the key sources of the manager's risk & return; reported amounts are consistent with the manager's actual risk exposures. Works best for: publicly traded investments with frequent pricing data. Less liquid investments: style analysis can still be used to generate questions in the due diligence process.
A useful style analysis must be: meaningful, accurate, consistent, and timely.
Q1. Which statement is least likely an advantage of HBSA over RBSA?
Answer: C (least likely — it is the false statement). HBSA's computational/data requirement increases as complexity rises and transparency decreases, so the data is not easier to obtain. A is a true advantage (security-specific bottom-up → more precise). B is true (HBSA is most appropriate for equity-based strategies).
Q2. A manager whose relative performance is better during market upturns most likely has a capture ratio that is:
Answer: C. Better in upturns → strong upside capture (UC) relative to downside → CR = UC / DC > 1 = positive asymmetry (convex). A (=1) is symmetric; B (<1) is concave / better on the downside.
Investment philosophy (LOS 14.e)
The entire investment process should be driven by a succinct and precise investment philosophy.
Passive vs active — the core belief split
Passive viewActive view
Belief about marketsMarkets very efficient; active will underperform after costsMarkets inefficient; prices can deviate from intrinsic value
What they doExecute passive strategies; earn risk premiums insteadExploit inefficiencies when price ≠ intrinsic value
Extra belief—Value of diversification for risk mgmt; prices converge to intrinsic value → exploit incongruence before convergence
Risk premiums = returns earned above the risk-free rate for bearing undiversifiable risk (a.k.a. systematic / market risk). Passive strategies target specific systematic factors: equity, credit, liquidity, and volatility risk.
Congruence test (the exam hook)
Whatever the philosophy, the manager must convey the underlying assumptions clearly. Do the assumptions make sense and are they congruent with the investment process?
Classic incongruence: a belief in inefficient markets would NOT be congruent with a passive approach. The stated belief and the chosen process must line up — a mismatch is a red flag in due diligence.
Two broad types of inefficiencies (active managers exploit)
TypeCaused byHorizonExploitation
BehavioralMispricings from other investors' behavioral biases (e.g., trend-following)Short-termMust be quickly exploited (sometimes within seconds) before the market corrects
StructuralLaws and regulationsLong-termPersist because the structural cause persists
Decisive detail: the split is cause → horizon. Behavioral = investor biases = short-term = exploit fast. Structural = laws/regulations = long-term. Don't swap which one is short vs long-lived.
Investment decision-making process — 3 stages
StageWhat happensKey concern(s)
Idea generationAn investment signal = a piece of information used to establish a position exploiting an inefficiencyUse unique information for an informational advantage; act timely (short window); needs superior cognitive/interpretive skills
Idea implementationIdea → investment position (signal capture)Repeatability of process + congruence with philosophy; plus determination & approval of the position
Portfolio constructionDecide what kinds of securities build the portfolio (e.g., if derivatives used, is the manager knowledgeable/experienced enough to adapt?)Allocations (quant or qual) must make sense vs philosophy
Portfolio construction — the detail that gets tested
Congruence check: a passively managed portfolio should NOT have excessive turnover — high turnover in a "passive" book is a red flag. Account for manager views: performance maximization by overweighting expected outperformers and underweighting expected underperformers. Long & short allocation: if positions are paired, proper position sizing eliminates market risk while still allowing exploitation of inefficiencies before convergence. AUM: likely increases over time → underlying positions may need adjusting (e.g., liquidity constraints) to accommodate greater AUM.
Stop losses (risk management tool)
Stop losses = orders to sell a security once it reaches a certain price. Two types:
TypeBehavior when loss threshold is met
Hard stop lossAutomatic disposition when the specified loss threshold is met
Soft stop lossInvolves subjective evaluations when the threshold is met (not automatic)
Hard vs soft: hard = mechanical/automatic; soft = discretionary/subjective. Don't flip them — "automatic disposition" is always the hard stop.
Liquidity — net supplier or demander?
Determine whether the manager is a net supplier or net demander of liquidity. Ensure the portfolio reacts appropriately to changing market conditions and investor liquidity requirements.
Too many illiquid securities → high exit costs + risk of selling at depressed prices if funds are suddenly required.
Liquidity testReading
Can be liquidated in 5 days or lessMore liquid → greater flexibility
Needs more than 10 days to liquidateLess liquid → higher transaction costs
Average daily volume weighted by position sizeNecessary calculation
Firm owns > 5% of a security's total market capLiquidity problem flag if the entire position must be disposed of suddenly
Portfolio monitoring
Factor typeLooks at
ExternalGeneral economy & financial markets → impact on how the manager can exploit relevant inefficiencies
InternalHistorical returns, risk level, allocations
Check for significant deviations from the process (e.g., style drift) and ensure decisions are congruent with the most up-to-date client objectives.
Capacity of an inefficiency (LOS 14.e)
Assuming a valid inefficiency to exploit, capacity = the amount, repeatability, and sustainability of the inefficiency.
QuestionWhy it matters
Enough excess returns?Must cover transaction costs and fees
Leverage required?Then borrowing costs must be considered
Repeatable or one-time?Is the inefficiency repeatable or just a one-time opportunity?
Minimum asset level?What minimum asset level earns a sufficient return from the inefficiency
Sustainability driver: sustainability depends on market depth and liquidity, plus the amount of capital that can be set aside to exploit the inefficiency.
Behavioral biases among investment teams (LOS 14.f)
Many decisions are made by teams, not individuals. Using a group helps mitigate key person risk. But team performance can be adversely affected by three common behavioral biases:
BiasWhat it isResult / symptom
GroupthinkTeams minimizing conflict & dissent to reach/maintain consensusIndividuals withhold information / reluctant to share insights. Symptom = confirmation bias (new info, different interpretations, dissent minimized or discarded)
Authority biasDeferring decisions to members perceived as subject-matter experts or in authorityLack of perspectives & skills from other group members
Aversion to complexity
(Parkinson's law of triviality)		Too much attention on small/familiar issues rather than the important, difficult ones (asset allocation, manager selection)E.g., over-researching a familiar small position instead of analyzing a large, less-known one
Mitigation — due diligence inquiry (driver → bias mitigated)
InquiryBest practiceBias mitigated
How large is the team?3 to 5 is optimal; larger → coordination issues + higher groupthink oddsGroupthink
How are decisions made?Secret ballot preferable over open deliberationGroupthink + authority bias
How are meetings / agenda conducted?Agenda agreed in advance; most important topics discussed first with the most timeComplexity aversion + availability bias
How diverse is the team?Social & cognitive diversityGroupthink + errors (reduced)
Map the fix to the bias: team size 3–5 & diversity → groupthink; secret ballot → groupthink + authority; agenda-in-advance + most-important-first → complexity aversion + availability. Under pressure, don't give a generic "improve communication" — name the specific lever and the specific bias.
Two ways to execute a strategy (LOS 14.g)
VehicleStructureCustomization
Pooled investment vehicle
(mutual funds, ETFs, hedge funds)		Brings together funds from all investors into one portfolioNone for any specific investor
Separately managed account (SMA)Holds the funds of one investor in a separate accountYes — tailored to that investor
Key analysis for an SMA = the cost-benefit tradeoff of holding investments in a separate account. Also ensure the manager has the capability and resources to manage the SMA.
The core tradeoff
Decisive detail: compared to pooled investments, SMAs have higher transaction costs — that is the COST side. In exchange they provide control, customization, tax efficiency, separate reporting, and greater transparency — the BENEFIT side.
The 5 SMA benefits (decomposed)
BenefitWhat it means
ControlDirect & legal ownership of the underlying securities by the investor → extra protection in a liquidity event or bankruptcy of the manager; investor is not impacted by the redemption demands of other investors
CustomizationTailor to client-specific objectives and constraints
Tax efficiencyCould be higher in SMAs (see trap)
Separate reportingReporting specific to the one investor
Greater transparencyInvestor sees the actual holdings
Tax efficiency — realized vs unrealized (the trap)
VehicleTaxes paid on...
SMAOnly realized capital gains; strategies can be tailored to the investor's tax situation
PooledPayment of accrued taxes on unrealized gains may be required
Why SMAs are more tax-efficient: in a pooled vehicle you can inherit a tax bill on unrealized gains you never benefited from (driven by other investors). In an SMA you pay only on your own realized gains — and the strategy can be tailored to your tax position.
Contract types ranked by liquidity (LOS 14.h)
VehicleLiquidityWhy
Closed-end funds & ETFsHighestTraded intra-day
Open-end fundsAlmost as muchTraded on end-of-day NAV only
Hedge funds (LP)LowerRedemption frequency, notification periods, gates, lockups
Private equity / VC (LP)LowestCapital calls; returns only after ~5 yrs into ~10-yr life; manager may extend up to two one-year periods
SMADependsDetermined by liquidity of the underlying assets (securities can be sold any time)
Hedge fund liquidity terms (decompose)
TermMeaning
Redemption frequencyHow often the investor may withdraw funds
Notification periodAmount of advance notice required by the investor for a redemption
Lockup periodPeriod immediately after the initial investment where funds may NOT be withdrawn
GatesA limit on the redemption amount for any given redemption
Hard vs soft LOCK (don't confuse with stop losses): a hard lock does NOT permit redemptions; a soft lock permits redemptions for a fee. (Earlier, hard/soft stop losses were automatic vs subjective — different concept, same adjective.)
Limited partnership terms — advantages vs disadvantages
AdvantagesDisadvantages
Long investment horizon → investors don't overreact to short-term aberrationsImpaired ability to change allocations in response to the market
Earn illiquidity premiums by investing in illiquid assetsImpaired ability to meet sudden liquidity demands
Not forced to sell at depressed prices due to redemption requests—
Management fees (LOS 14.i)
Cover the manager's fixed & variable costs plus a profit. The asset-weighted expense ratio has declined over time as investors shifted to no-load and index funds. Often based on AUM; minimum balances sometimes required; structured as a fixed-dollar amount or a % of assets.
Principal-agent angle: fee structure matters for aligning manager & investor interests. Misalignment sources: investor doesn't see the full extent of the manager's work; differing views on time horizons or losses; performance has a luck element, so in theory the manager shouldn't be rewarded for it.
AUM-based fees — advantage vs disadvantages
AdvantageDisadvantages
Rewards the manager's skill & ability to grow the asset base; declining % for larger accounts reduces investor fees(1) Luck may drive short-term asset growth. (2) Once assets are attained, more incentive to retain them (safe strategies like indexing) rather than take risk for the investor's benefit
Performance-based fees = risk sharing
Performance-based fees are a form of risk sharing between investor and manager to align interests. Computed on total or relative return, via a sharing percentage, on total performance or performance in excess of a base.
The three basic forms
FormFee formulaKey property
Symmetrical
(full upside + downside)		Fee = base + performance sharing
(sharing can be negative)		Greatest alignment of incentives, but increased risk to manager (full downside exposure)
Bonus — full upside, limited downsideFee = greater of: (1) base, (2) base + sharing of positive performanceDownside floored at base; full upside
Bonus — limited upside & downsideFee = greater of: (1) base, (2) base + sharing of positive performance — within a limit (cap)Floored at base AND capped at a maximum
Common to ALL three: the base fee is paid even when the manager underperforms. That's the universal feature exam answers love.
Asymmetry & risk-measure trap: performance-based fees transform symmetrical gross active-return distributions into asymmetrical net distributions (lower relative variance on the upside vs downside). Using a symmetrical risk measure (SD) then leads to an underestimation of downside risk.
High-water marks, clawbacks, and PE structure
High-water mark / clawback provisions temper fees by offsetting prior-period negative returns against current positive returns (e.g., hedge funds). PE: investors = limited partners, manager = general partner. Beneficial term for LPs: repayment of principal + share of profits to the LPs BEFORE any performance fee is paid to the GP. Negotiation: only the most successful managers or those with limited capacity can command the highest base fees and/or sharing percentages.
Performance-fee calculator (all 3 forms)
InputValue
Form
Base fee (%)
Sharing (%)
Performance the sharing applies to (%)
net-of-base return, or active return — whatever the contract specifies
Max total fee / cap (%) (only for capped form)
Pick a form, set inputs, then Compute.
Setting up the "performance" input: for a fee on return net of base (Fund X style), enter gross − base. For a fee on active return (Fund Y style), enter gross − benchmark.
Call-option analogy (Fig 14.2 / 14.3)
Bonus fee structures ≈ the manager is long a call option on the portfolio's active return. The exercise price = the base fee. For the uncapped bonus (Schedule 1, Fig 14.2), the payoff to the manager is theoretically unlimited. Schedule 2 (Fig 14.3) adds a short position in a less valuable call (exercise price = the maximum fee) → this caps the payoff (limited upside + downside form).
Risk incentive (the recommendation): a net long call on active return makes the manager want more risk, because option-pricing theory says higher volatility increases option value. Therefore managers should be penalized for taking too much risk AND rewarded for higher risk-adjusted returns.
Sample fee schedule (LOS 14.j, Fig 14.4)
ParameterValue
Standard fee0.50%
Base fee0.25%
Sharing20%
Breakeven active return1.50%
Maximum annual fee0.75%
The billing rule (a bonus with limited upside + downside):
billed fee = base + perf fee perf fee = max( (active − base) × sharing , 0 ) ← floored at 0 billed fee = min( base + perf fee , max fee ) ← capped at max
Worked example — at the breakeven active return of 1.50%:
StepCalculationResult
Perf fee(1.50% − 0.25% base) × 20%0.25%
Billed fee0.25% base + 0.25% perf0.50%
Checkbilled = standard fee?0.50% = 0.50% ✓
The three regimes (this is all Panel B does — plug the active return into the rule):
Active returnPerf feeBilled feeWhy
≤ 0.25%0%0.25% (= base)Floor: perf fee can't go negative (nonnegativity constraint)
= 1.50% (breakeven)0.25%0.50% (= standard)Base + perf exactly equals the standard fee
≥ 2.75%0.50% (maxed)0.75% (= max)Cap: billed fee can't exceed the maximum annual fee
Where 2.75% comes from: the cap binds once perf fee hits its max of 0.50%. Solve (active − 0.25%) × 20% = 0.50% → active − 0.25% = 2.50% → active = 2.75%. Above that, extra active return earns the manager nothing more.
Q1. Which investment fund generally has the least amount of liquidity?
Answer: C. PE/VC has the lowest liquidity (capital calls; returns only ~5 yrs into a ~10-yr life; life extendable). B closed-end funds are the most liquid (intra-day). Hedge funds sit between.
Q2. Which fee structure most likely has no impact on the volatility of a portfolio's net returns?
Answer: B. A flat management fee is symmetric — it doesn't change the risk-taking incentive, so it has no impact on net-return volatility. Incentive/performance fees create the call-option payoff → manager wants more volatility → they DO affect volatility (so A and C are wrong).
Q3. Fund X earns −3% gross. Fee = base 2% + 20% sharing of both positive and negative performance, based on return net of the base fee. Total management fee?
Answer: A (1.0%). This is the symmetrical form (shares both up AND down). Performance net of base = −3% − 2% = −5%. Sharing = 20% × (−5%) = −1%. Total fee = base 2% + (−1%) = 1.0%. C (2.0%) is the trap if you forget the negative sharing reduces the fee.
Q4. Fund Y earns 12% gross, benchmark 3%. Fee = higher of base 0.4% OR base + 20% sharing of positive performance, max 2.9%, sharing on active return. Total management fee?
Answer: A (2.2%). This is the bonus with cap form. Active return = 12% − 3% = 9%. Option 2 = 0.4% base + 20% × 9% = 0.4% + 1.8% = 2.2%. Higher of (0.4%, 2.2%) = 2.2%, and 2.2% < 2.9% cap so the cap doesn't bind. C (2.9%) is the trap if you wrongly assume the max binds.
Patterns
Recurring mistake patterns from mocks land here.
MCQ Misses
Mock-exam MCQ misses, each with the decisive detail that was dropped. Re-test these cold before the exam.
M1 — ABC high-water mark fee (picked C 4.55%, ans A 4.15%)
ABC = symmetrical (base 2.5%, 10% sharing net of base), HWM recapture of prior loss required. Year 2 = −4%, Year 3 gross = 23%.
Step 1 (HWM, BEFORE the formula): recover Y2 loss adjusted return = 23% − 4% = 19% Step 2 (symmetrical fee on adjusted return): perf = (19% − 2.5% base) × 10% = 1.65% fee = 2.5% + 1.65% = 4.15%
Decisive detail: the HWM adjusts the return first (it's a pre-step), THEN the normal fee formula runs on the adjusted number. Trap C (4.55%) = skipped HWM (used 23%). Trap B (4.40%) = forgot to net the base fee before sharing.
M2 — Universe stage: what to AVOID (picked C, ans A)
Question: when defining the manager universe, the process should avoid ___. Answer = excluding managers based on historical risk-adjusted returns.
Decisive detail: the universe stage has NO performance assessment — screen on role/fit only. So screening on past risk-adjusted returns is the thing to avoid. Identifying a benchmark (= the role) and using third-party categorization are both legitimate universe-building tools. The trap: you picked a correct practice (C) as the thing to avoid — the question was inverted.
M3 — Style output inconsistent w/ philosophy (picked A, ans B)
Style analysis (RBSA/HBSA) results not consistent with the manager's stated philosophy/process → implies the investment process may not be repeatable (or not consistently implemented) → manager should NOT be included.
Decisive detail — the fork:
• output inconsistent with stated philosophy → repeatability red flag (exclude).
• output tracks over time but drifts from stated style → style drift.
"Absence of style drift" (A) is wrong — inconsistency isn't the absence of anything, it's a repeatability problem.
M4 — Greatest risk incentive: Red Grass (picked Blue Water, ans A)
Red Grass = uncapped, higher-of base or base + sharing of positive performance → unlimited upside, no downside penalty. Blue Water = same shape but capped at 2.50%.
Decisive detail: no maximum fee + positive-only sharing = unlimited call option = greatest risk incentive. A cap truncates the upside → it removes the incentive. Blue Water's 2.50% cap is exactly why it's NOT the answer. Don't let a high sharing % distract from the cap.
M5 — Yellow Wood 2016 fee (picked A 3.00%, ans B 4.20%)
Yellow Wood = symmetrical (base 1.5%, 20% sharing net of base). 2016 gross = 15%.
perf = 20% × (15% − 1.5% base) = 20% × 13.5% = 2.70% fee = 1.5% + 2.70% = 4.20%
Decisive detail (your #1 repeat error): sharing always applies to (return − base fee), never raw return. Trap A 3.00% = 20% × 15% with the base-fee netting skipped — the same omission as trap B in M1. Always subtract the base before applying the sharing %.
★ Cross-cutting pattern (fees)
Two recurring fee mistakes to drill:
(1) Net the base fee before applying the sharing % — missed in M1-trap and M5.
(2) HWM is a pre-step — adjust the return for recouped losses BEFORE the fee formula (M1).
(3) Cap kills risk incentive — "greatest incentive" = uncapped + upside-only (M4).
Essay Misses
Constructed-response misses. Most were partial credit — right idea, missing a second required reason or the decisive mechanism. Re-drill the starred fee card.
★ E1 — Schwinn net active return (you 2.55%, ans 2.60%) — REPEAT ERROR
return subject to sharing = 3.50% − 0.25% base = 3.25% ← NET of base sharing fee = 3.25% × 20% = 0.65% billed fee = 0.25% base + 0.65% = 0.90% net active = 3.50% − 0.90% = 2.60%
Your 2.55% = sharing applied to GROSS 3.50% (0.20×3.50=0.70), billed 0.95%. This is the exact same base-netting error as MCQ M1-trap and M5 — now three times. Sharing is ALWAYS on (active return − base fee), never on gross. This is your #1 fee mistake — check it on every fee question.
★ E2 — Circue fee schedule (NO answer) — the 4-regime calc
Base 0.20%, sharing 25% on active beyond base, standard 0.35%, breakeven 1.25%, max 0.90%.
Gross activeBilled feeNet active = gross − billedNote
≤ 0.20%0.20% (base only)0.00% (at 0.20)No sharing — at/below base
0.75%0.20 + (0.75−0.20)×25% = 0.3375%0.41%0.75 − 0.3375 = 0.4125
