The breakeven is the point where the performance schedule is set to equal the standard fee. Use the standard fee directly there.
E3 — Aspen consistent philosophy? (got reason 1, missed reason 2)
You got: passive label contradicts active strategy (exploiting structural inefficiencies / mispricings = active). ✓
Missed second reason: Aspen states its strategy/philosophy has evolved over time in response to fund and market performance → it is reacting to markets, not following a consistent philosophy → results may not be repeatable. Two-reason questions need both: (1) the passive/active contradiction, (2) the changing-over-time reactivity.
E4 — Lyon Detail 1 paired long/short (you "drawback", ans benefit)
Decisive detail: paired long & short positions are a BENEFIT — if well-matched and sized correctly, proper position sizing offsets/eliminates market risk while capturing alpha as prices converge. (This is the same "paired → eliminates market risk" point from the Decision Process tab.) Detail 2 (relies on unique info) = drawback (hard to keep an edge when regulation reduces info asymmetry). Detail 3 (AUM grew, positions unchanged) = drawback (should adjust positions for the larger AUM).
E5 — Yang best fund (you Beta, ans Gamma)
Decisive detail: Yang retires in 3 years + hates losses → short horizon, low risk tolerance → she needs the shallowest AND shortest drawdown — that's Gamma (28% loss, 12 months). You chose Beta on capture ratio, but the binding constraint here is drawdown, not capture. When the stem stresses short horizon + loss aversion, drawdown depth/duration is the decision driver, not the capture ratio.
E6 — Patnode best manager (you Alcanfor, ans Laurbær)
Decisive detail: Patnode needs predictable ongoing income → favor the manager whose edge is repeatable / evolving to stay ahead. Laurbær invests in new themes & measures each one's contribution, and recognizes its edge can be arbitraged away → more likely to evolve and sustain returns. Alcanfor (your pick) judges itself on sector mispricing but measures against overall market benchmarks — a mismatch (not testing success in its own selection domain). Mylesten is ad-hoc / chases sentiment → not repeatable. Don't pick "mispriced securities" reflexively — check whether the manager measures itself in the right domain and can sustain the edge.
E7 — Parade: SMA vs Diversified by characteristic (partial)
You got: Transparency → SMA; Investor behavior → (you said SMA "not subject to investor behavior"); Liquidity → SMA. Transparency and Liquidity are correct.
CharacteristicBest vehicleWhy
TransparencySMAReal-time position-level detail; pooled may be delayed
Investor behaviorDiversified (pooled)NOT susceptible to investor micromanagement; manager sets decisions
CostDiversified (pooled)Pooled is cheaper (economies of scale)
LiquiditySMAOwns securities directly; not hit by other investors' redemptions
Tracking riskDiversified (pooled)Lower tracking risk; SMA customization raises it
Decisive detail: Investor behavior → pooled (the pooled fund is protected from investor micromanagement; an SMA investor CAN meddle). You assigned it to SMA — backwards. Also memorize: Cost & Tracking risk → pooled; Transparency & Liquidity → SMA.
E8 — Circue vehicle choice (you Hedge fund, ans Open-end + incentive fee)
Decisive detail — the closet-indexing driver: Circue has heightened sensitivity to closet indexing → needs an incentive fee to motivate the manager (mutual-fund assets are "sticky" → managers coast → closet index). Open-end + incentive fee gives daily liquidity (Circue tolerates some illiquidity) AND the incentive. Hedge fund (your pick) is wrong twice: least liquid, and a soft lock charges a redemption fee → conflicts with Circue's moderate fee sensitivity. Closed-end has no incentive fee → doesn't fix closet indexing. Match each IPS priority to a feature: closet-indexing→incentive fee; fee sensitivity→avoid soft-lock fee.
E9 — Smith downside-risk under bonus fee (got incentive, missed the mechanism)
You got: bonus (full upside, limited downside) incentivizes the manager to increase portfolio risk to raise the bonus. ✓ (partial credit)
The decisive mechanism the book wanted: performance-based fees convert symmetrical gross active-return distributions into asymmetrical net distributions (variability reduced on the upside but NOT the downside). So a single SD on that net series leads to underestimation of downside risk. Phrase it as "estimated risk is misestimated / downside underestimated," not just "manager takes more risk."
E10 — Carpenter = call option (NO answer)
Answer: Carpenter Management. A bonus-style fee with a maximum = the close equivalent of a manager's call option on active return: exercise price = base fee (18 bps), long a call struck at the base/min fee, minus a short (less valuable) call struck at the maximum fee (the cap). Hidden Lake is symmetrical (full up + down exposure) → NOT option-like. The tell for "call option" = bonus/asymmetric structure, usually with a cap.
E11 — Vaudreuil (AUM) vs Pourtir (perf) adv/disadv (NO answer)
ManagerAdvantage to clientDisadvantage to client
Vaudreuil (AUM-based)Fee impact lower as assets grow in a rising marketOnce assets are large, manager may coast to retain sticky assets → lower returns than another structure
Pourtir (performance-based)Aligns interests (both share results); client pays lower fees when active returns are low; manager may work harderClient pays base even if underperform; may misestimate risk / incentivize higher risk; bonus-style misaligns; may hold assets to realize a profit even when client should sell
One adv + one disadv each is enough for credit, but know both sides of each.
E12 — Grimmett qual/quant considerations (over-narrow)
You got valid quant: attribution + appraisal (skill vs luck), capture ratio (up vs down). ✓ Could add drawdown as the third quant tool.
Qualitative was too narrow: you gave only the 4 Ps (philosophy/portfolio). The book splits qualitative into (1) investment due diligence (the 4 Ps: philosophy, process, people, portfolio) AND (2) operational due diligence (firm/infrastructure: track-record accuracy, back-office processes, investment vehicle suitability, contract terms, ongoing monitoring, firm profitability/culture/going-concern). For "two qualitative considerations," pick process-and-people + operational due diligence — not two flavors of the same 4 Ps.
E13 — Grimmett preparatory steps (incomplete)
You said: due diligence (manager universe, quant, qual). That's the selection process itself, not the preparatory steps the question asked for.
The three preparatory steps BEFORE manager selection: (1) decide that outside support is necessary; (2) complete an IPS; (3) determine the appropriate asset allocation. Without these you can't identify managers that fit, confirm IPS suitability, or trust they'll implement the right allocation. "Preparatory steps" = IPS + asset allocation come first; due diligence is what you do after.
★ Essay cross-cutting patterns
Drill list:
(1) Base-netting — sharing on (active − base), never gross (E1, +MCQ M1/M5). Your single biggest leak.
(2) Breakeven = standard fee anchor, not base+sharing (E2).
(3) Two-reason questions — always give the SECOND reason (E3 Aspen, Patnode domain+sustainability).
(4) Match the binding constraint to the stem — short horizon→drawdown not capture (E5); closet-indexing→incentive fee (E8); income+repeatable→evolving manager (E6).
(5) SMA vs pooled map — Transparency/Liquidity = SMA; Cost/Tracking/Investor-behavior = pooled (E7).
(6) Paired long/short = benefit (offsets market risk) (E4).
(7) Operational due diligence is a distinct qualitative bucket from the 4 Ps (E12); IPS + asset allocation are preparatory (E13).
Mastery checklist
Once a pattern is no longer being missed, it moves here as a confirmed mastery point.
Reading 14 · Investment Manager Selection
Full-reading recap: selection process & due diligence (14.a), Type I / II errors (14.b), RBSA vs HBSA style analysis (14.c), capture ratios & drawdowns in selection (14.d), philosophy & decision-making process (14.e), team behavioral biases (14.f), pooled vs SMA (14.g), liquidity terms (14.h), fee forms (14.i) and the sample performance-based fee schedule (14.j). Fee figures node-verified.
Exam focus: the reading is primarily qualitative. The named key areas: Type I / II errors, capture ratios & drawdowns, and computing performance-based fees.
Module 14.1 · Manager Selection Process
LOS 14.aDue diligence = universe → quantitative → qualitative
Manager universe
Only managers suitable for the IPS objectives/constraints, the desired style (value/growth/mixed), and the right active vs passive balance. A process of elimination — not too many, not too few. The role is defined by the benchmark, determined via third-party categorization (trap: provider's style definition may differ from yours), returns-based and holdings-based style analysis, and manager experience. NO performance assessment at this stage — focus on risk profile & portfolio fit.
Quantitative
Evaluate the distribution of past returns objectively: attribution & appraisal distinguish skill vs luck; the capture ratio tests both good and weak markets; check for significant drawdowns (peak-to-trough % decline over a period).
Qualitative
Two questions: (1) will the same level of returns continue? (2) does the process account for all relevant risks? Continuity via the four Ps: Philosophy (which market inefficiency), Process + People (is the strategy feasible & executable with the team's skills), Portfolio (built congruent with philosophy & process).
Risk assessment
The firm: robust, a going concern? Operational due diligence: back-office quality, safeguarding assets, timely useful reports → firm sustainability. The investment vehicle must suit the strategy; contract terms reasonable & relevant; continual monitoring that the manager remains appropriate.
LOS 14.bType I vs Type II errors (H0: no value added)
DecisionBelow expectations (no skill)At/above expectations (skill)
Hire / retainType ICorrect
Not hire / fireCorrectType II
Type I = COMMISSION
Hire/retain a manager with no skill (reject H0 wrongly). Gets more attention: linked to regret aversion; an active decision with explicit, visible costs; easier to determine (relative performance measured vs a benchmark — also feeds the decision maker's compensation, so extra care to avoid it); clients can easily see underperformance.
Type II = OMISSION
Do not hire / fire a manager who had skill (fail to reject H0 wrongly). Costs are implicit / opportunity costs (less visible); difficult to determine — clients rarely monitor how not-hired or fired managers would have performed.
Preventing Type II
Track the subsequent performance of managers who were NOT hired and those who were fired; compare characteristics of selected vs non-selected, retained vs fired, against portfolio objectives. Ultimately: don't hire or fire on short-term performance or behavioral biases.
Costs logic
Bigger difference in mean returns between skilled & unskilled → greater the cost of an error. But wider dispersion between strong and weak → easier to distinguish skill → errors less likely → lower expected cost. In an efficient market the dispersion is smaller (alpha is harder) → lessens the cost of hiring/retaining weak managers (Type I).
Quiz traps (reasoning-derived): “expected cost of Type I and II” → higher the greater the difference between mean returns of skilled/unskilled. Skilled distribution not distinct from unskilled → low opportunity cost of not hiring a skilled manager (small mean gap → small cost — NOT “highly inefficient market”).
Module 14.2 · Approaches to Manager Analysis
LOS 14.cStyle analysis — RBSA vs HBSA
Style analysis examines the manager's risk exposures vs an appropriate benchmark and their changes over time → classify managers by style, verify congruence between output and stated process, and detect style drift. Useful style analysis is meaningful, accurate, consistent, timely. Works best with publicly traded, frequently priced investments; for illiquid ones it still generates due-diligence questions.
RBSA (returns-based)HBSA (holdings-based)
ApproachTop-down: regress returns on market indexes; risk factors estimated, not predeterminedBottom-up: actual securities held at a point in time → current, security-specific exposures
StrengthsLittle data needed; computationally easy; works for basic AND complex strategies; objective & comparable across managers/time; timely (right after data release)Same comparability/timeliness benefits; more precise on current exposures; most appropriate for equity-based strategies
WeaknessesLacks precision — assumes a static portfolio for the period; can't isolate multiperiod decisions; illiquid holdings → stale prices → understated risk; VC/PE appraisal-and-IRR-based data → short-term σ understated (true σ needs long periods); illiquidity delays reportingComputational burden grows with complexity while transparency falls; point-in-time snapshot projects poorly (esp. high turnover); same stale-pricing / reporting-timeliness issues
Quiz trap: “data required for HBSA is generally easier to obtain” is the false advantage — RBSA is the low-data method; HBSA needs full holdings.
LOS 14.dCapture ratios & drawdowns in manager evaluation
UC = capture when benchmark return > 0 (>100% = outperformance) DC = capture when benchmark return < 0 (lower = better; <100% = outperformance) CR = UC / DC >1 positive asymmetry (convex) <1 negative asymmetry (concave)
Suitability tool
Capture ratios determine how suitable a manager is for the investor's risk tolerance and time horizon.
Convexity: strategy or skill?
Ask whether convexity is natural to the strategy or comes from manager skill. Structural example: hedging by buying series of OTM puts before severe downturns — many small losses as puts expire worthless, but protection when it matters. Skill example: long-only equity actively minimizing losses & maximizing gains — requires skill and may not be consistent.
Beta & strategy check
Rising (falling) betas → momentum-driven strategies should show higher (lower) UC than value-driven. A low-beta strategy → lower UC and DC (high-beta → higher both). Use CRs to confirm the stated investment strategy.
Drawdown in selection
Total peak-to-trough loss over a period; max drawdown = largest; duration = time until cumulative drawdown recovers to zero via offsetting gains. Large drawdowns are not appropriate for investors near the end of their horizon; IPS link: shorter horizon / lower risk tolerance → pick managers with smaller, less extended drawdowns.
What drawdowns reveal
Useful for identifying poor or poorly executed strategies, weak internal controls, operational problems. Fine line between risk management (prudent selling on fundamental change) and self-preservation (overreaction) — judge whether the manager acted per the IPS. A low-beta strategy can beat a long-only on a risk-adjusted basis via lower drawdowns despite lower absolute returns.
Quiz: manager whose relative performance is better during market upturns → capture ratio greater than one.
Module 14.3 · Evaluating Managers
LOS 14.eInvestment philosophy — passive vs active, inefficiencies, capacity
Passive philosophy
Markets efficient; active underperforms after costs → earn risk premiums = returns above rf for bearing undiversifiable (systematic) risk. Target factors: equity, credit, liquidity, volatility risk.
Active: 2 inefficiency types
Behavioral: mispricings caused by other investors' biases (e.g. trend-following) — very short-term, must be exploited quickly (sometimes within seconds) before correction. Structural: caused by laws & regulations — can be long-term. Exploit incongruence before prices converge to intrinsic value.
Repeatability test
Assumptions conveyed clearly & congruent with the process? Philosophy constant over time — and if it changed, was the change logical given market shifts or merely reactionary to short-term performance? Informational advantages are short-term & less repeatable; structural inefficiencies are long-term & more repeatable.
Capacity
Amount / repeatability / sustainability of the inefficiency: must cover transaction costs and fees; leverage → add borrowing costs; repeatable or one-time?; minimum asset level needed for sufficient return; sustainability depends on market depth and the capital that can be set aside.
LOS 14.eInvestment decision-making process — the 4 stages
1. Idea generation
Signal exploiting an inefficiency requires unique information (informational advantage), used on a very timely basis (windows are short), plus superior cognitive/interpretive skills.
2. Idea implementation
Transform idea into a position (signal capture). Two concerns: repeatability of the process and congruence with the philosophy + determination & approval of the position.
3. Portfolio construction
Which securities? (derivatives → is the manager sufficiently knowledgeable?). Allocations quant or qual but must fit the philosophy — a passive portfolio should not have excessive turnover. Long/short: paired (proper sizing eliminates market risk, isolates the inefficiency) or determined separately. Growing AUM → adjust for liquidity constraints. Stop losses: hard = automatic disposition at a loss threshold; soft = subjective evaluation when threshold hit. Hedging: which instruments, how implemented, hedge ratios.
3b. Liquidity checks
Net supplier or demander of liquidity? Too many illiquid securities → high transaction costs + high exit costs / depressed prices if funds are suddenly required. Tests: how much liquidates in ≤5 days (liquid, flexible) vs needing >10 days; average daily volume weighted by position size; flag any security where the firm owns >5% of its market cap.
4. Portfolio monitoring
External: economy & markets vs the exploited inefficiencies. Internal: historical returns, risk level, allocations; check for deviations from the process (style drift) and congruence with up-to-date client objectives.
LOS 14.fBehavioral biases in investment teams + mitigation
Groupthink
Teams minimize conflict/dissent to keep consensus → individuals withhold information or won't share insights. Symptom: confirmation bias (new info, different interpretations & dissent get discarded).
Authority bias
Deferring to members perceived as experts or in authority → loses the perspectives and skills of other members.
Aversion to complexity
= Parkinson's law of triviality: too much attention to small, familiar issues instead of the important, difficult ones (asset allocation, manager selection) — e.g. over-researching a familiar small position vs analyzing a large unfamiliar one.
Mitigation (due-diligence Qs)
Team size 3–5 is optimal (larger → coordination issues + groupthink odds ↑). Secret ballot preferable to open deliberation (reduces groupthink AND authority bias). Agendas agreed in advance, most important topics first with the most time (mitigates complexity aversion + availability bias). Team diversity (social & cognitive) is shown to reduce groupthink and errors. Using a group at all mitigates key person risk.
LOS 14.gPooled vehicles vs separately managed accounts
Pooled (mutual funds, ETFs, hedge funds)SMA
StructureAll investors' funds in one portfolio; no customizationOne investor's funds in a separate account; manager needs capability & resources to run it
CostsLowerHigher transaction costs
BenefitsSimplicity, scaleControl = direct legal ownership of securities → extra protection if the manager has a liquidity event / bankruptcy, and not impacted by other investors' redemptions; customization to client objectives/constraints; tax efficiency (pay only on realized gains; pooled may require paying accrued taxes on unrealized gains); separate reporting; greater transparency
Module 14.4 · Manager Contracts and Fees
LOS 14.hLiquidity spectrum of vehicles
MOST liquid closed-end funds & ETFs (intraday) > open-end funds (end-of-day NAV) > hedge funds (LP terms) > PE / VC (capital calls) LEAST liquid SMAs: liquidity = liquidity of the underlying assets (sellable any time)
Hedge fund LP terms
Redemption frequency (how often you can withdraw) · notification period (advance notice required) · lockup period (post-investment freeze): hard lock = no redemptions, soft lock = redemptions for a fee · gates = cap on the amount redeemable at any given redemption.
PE / VC = lowest
Capital calls; returns only ~5 years into the ~10-year average life; manager may extend the life by up to two one-year periods → even less liquidity.
LP terms: + / −
Advantages: long horizon (investors can't overreact to short-term noise), earn illiquidity premiums, no forced selling at depressed prices on redemptions. Disadvantages: impaired ability to change allocations as markets move, impaired ability to meet sudden liquidity demands.
Quiz: least liquidity → private equity fund (capital calls + 10-year life beat even hedge-fund lockups).
LOS 14.iManagement fees & the 3 performance-based forms
AUM fees
Cover fixed + variable costs + profit; average expense ratios have declined (shift to no-load & index funds). + rewards skill in growing the asset base; declining % for larger accounts reduces investor fees. − luck drives short-term growth; once assets are attained the incentive is to retain them (safe strategies, e.g. indexing) rather than take risk for the investor — principal-agent misalignment.
3 basic performance forms
1. Symmetrical (full upside + downside): fee = base + performance sharing → greatest alignment of interests but most risk transferred to the manager. 2. Bonus, full upside / limited downside: fee = greater of (base) or (base + sharing of positive performance). 3. Bonus, limited upside AND downside: fee = greater of (base) or (base + sharing of positive performance, within a limit).
Key consequences
Performance fees transform symmetrical gross active-return distributions into asymmetrical net distributions (lower relative variance on the upside) → a symmetric risk measure like σ underestimates downside risk. Investors benefit (pay less when active returns are low vs a fixed fee); managers benefit (incentives, higher compensation). All three forms: the base fee is paid even when the manager underperforms. Tempering tools: high-water marks / clawbacks (offset prior negative periods); PE waterfall: LPs receive principal + profit share before any GP performance fee. Only the most successful / capacity-constrained managers command the highest base fees and sharing percentages.
Call-option analogy
A bonus structure = manager long a call on active return with exercise price = base fee; payoff theoretically unlimited. Limited upside adds a short call struck at the maximum fee. A net long call incentivizes more risk-taking (higher volatility → higher option value) → recommended to penalize excessive risk and reward risk-adjusted returns.
Quiz trap: which fee structure has no impact on the volatility of net returns? → Management fees only (a flat % shifts the distribution; incentive fees reshape it asymmetrically).
LOS 14.jSample performance-based fee schedule (Fig 14.4) — node-verified
Panel APanel BAR ≤ 0.25%AR = 1.50%AR ≥ 2.75%
Standard fee0.50%Billed fee0.25%0.50%0.75%
Base fee0.25%Net active return≤ 0.00%1.00%≥ 2.00%
Sharing (on AR beyond base fee)20%Bonus with limited upside (max billed fee) and limited downside (min billed fee); symmetric within the 0.25%–2.75% active-return range, centered on the 1.50% breakeven.
Breakeven active return1.50%
Maximum annual fee0.75%
Breakeven check: (1.50% − 0.25%) × 20% = 0.25% performance fee → + 0.25% base = 0.50% = the standard fee ✓ Floor: AR ≤ 0.25% → performance fee = 0 (nonnegativity constraint) → billed = base = 0.25% Cap: AR ≥ 2.75% → performance fee maxed at 0.50% → billed = 0.75% maximum
Fee-quiz worked answers (reasoning-derived): Fund X: gross −3%, base 2%, 20% sharing of both positive and negative performance, on return net of the base fee → fee = 2% + 20% × (−3% − 2%) = 2% − 1% = 1.0%. Fund Y: gross 12%, benchmark 3%, fee = higher of 0.4% base or base + 20% of active return, capped at 2.9% → 0.4% + 20% × 9% = 2.2% < cap → 2.2%.
Read the sharing base carefully: “on active return beyond the base fee” vs “on active return” vs “net of the base fee, both signs” — the three quiz variants above each use a different base. Identify (1) what's shared, (2) one-sided or symmetric, (3) floor/cap, before computing.
Overview of the GIPS Standards
READING 15 · Performance Measurement
What the GIPS standards are
Ethical & professional standards for the presentation of investment performance results.
PropertyDetail
VoluntaryFirms choose to adopt; not legally mandated
Two fundamental principlesFull disclosure + fair representation of performance results
A minimumNot all-encompassing — view as a minimum set; firms should always add additional info to help clients understand results
PurposeLets clients/prospects/consultants fairly assess historical performance & compare across firms
Decisive detail: GIPS is voluntary and a minimum standard for presentation — not a legal requirement, not exhaustive. Firms add information beyond the minimum; they don't treat GIPS as the ceiling.
2020 edition — three sets of standards
For whomWhich standards they use
Investment management firmsGIPS Standards for Firms
Asset owners who compete for businessGIPS Standards for Firms
Asset owners who do NOT compete for businessGIPS Standards for Asset Owners
Verifiers (third parties)Provide verification that a firm complies
The competing-for-business fork: an asset owner uses the Firms standards if it competes for business, and the Asset Owners standards if it does not. The LOS focus is the standards for investment management firms.
The GIPS Report
When a firm claims compliance, it must calculate & present compliant returns in a GIPS Report, provided to ALL (not just some) prospective clients & investors.
Contains required + additional disclosures; should be up to date and comparable to reports from other compliant firms.
The 5 objectives of GIPS (LOS 15.a)
#Objective
1Advance the interests of investors & increase their confidence in the investment industry
2Provide accurate and comparable data to investors
3Create a globally accepted standard for the determination & presentation of performance
4Facilitate fair competition among global investment managers
5Encourage self-regulation in the global investment industry
Memory hook: C-C-G-F-S — Confidence, Comparable data, Global standard, Fair competition, Self-regulation.
Who may claim compliance
Only investment management firms and asset owners who compete for business may claim compliance to the GIPS Standards for Firms.
Key terminology (memorize the definitions)
TermDefinition
CompositeA collection of portfolios with similar investment mandates, objectives, or strategies
Segregated accountA portfolio owned by a single investor (a.k.a. an SMA)
Pooled fundA portfolio NOT owned by a single investor
Broad distribution pooled fund (BDPF)Subject to regulation, available to the general public (e.g., mutual funds)
Limited distribution pooled fund (LDPF)NOT available to the general public (e.g., hedge funds)
Client vs investor: a client invests via a segregated account; an investor invests in a firm's pooled funds. (The reading often uses the two interchangeably.)
Scope rules
Firmwide only: GIPS compliance can be claimed only on a firmwide basis — NOT for just some products, and NOT for only specific composites/funds/portfolios. All, not some: to claim compliance a firm must comply with ALL applicable requirements. Requirements vs recommendations: requirements are mandatory; recommendations are optional but consistent with best practice. The standards evolve over time.
What a claim of compliance indicates
RequirementDetail
Compliant calcsThe firm's data inputs, processes, and return calculations are compliant
Segregated accountsALL fee-paying segregated accounts assigned to at least one composite
LDPFAll limited distribution pooled funds included in a composite appropriate to their characteristics
BDPF (the exception)Only required to be in a composite IF their strategy is also offered in separate accounts
"Can't be halfway" rule: to be compliant — all customers get a report, all products compliant, all standards followed.
The one exception = BDPF: they often need NOT be in a composite, because BDPF are government-regulated → investor protections already established.
Watch the trap: "fee-paying segregated accounts → at least one composite" is required. A non-fee-paying account is not forced in. And BDPF only join a composite when the strategy is also run in separate accounts.
Benefits to prospective clients & investors
BenefitWhy
ComparableStandardizes determination & presentation → manager performance more comparable
ReliableManager performance is more reliable when the firm is GIPS compliant
Benchmark discussionGIPS benchmark requirements facilitate a discussion of the strategy's past & targeted future performance
Benefits to investment managers (firms)
Firms incur costs to comply; in return GIPS may provide:
BenefitNote
Investor confidenceIn the industry & the firm — especially if verified by a third party
Attract investorsMany investors prefer or require GIPS-compliant managers
Compete internationallyFirm performance is comparable across borders
Internal controlsStrengthened via the recordkeeping & reporting GIPS requires
Operational insightAdditional info about operations via the technology adopted to comply
Definition of the firm (LOS 15.b)
Firm = an investment firm, subsidiary, or division held out to clients or potential clients as a distinct business entity. Distinct business entity (DBE) = a unit, division, department, or office that is organizationally or functionally separated from others, retains discretion over the assets it manages, and should have autonomy over the investment decision-making process.
Why it matters: compliance is claimed at the firm level, so how you draw the firm boundary determines what must comply. (Ties to the "can't be halfway" rule from 15.1.)
Characteristics — more likely a DBE if it has a distinct:
8 distinguishing characteristics
Legal organization (e.g., a separate subsidiary)
Market
Client base
Investment process
Investment strategy
Investment staff (portfolio managers, analysts)
Physical location
Chain of command
Judgment call — the shared trading desk
Two divisions share the same trading desk. Whether they're still distinct depends on what the desk does:
Desk does...Distinct business entities?
Only buys & sells securities (pure execution)Still can be distinct — sharing execution doesn't break separation
Helps value securitiesLess likely distinct — the desk is now part of the investment process
Decisive detail: shared execution is fine; shared valuation (part of the investment process) undermines distinctness. Judgment is required — the characteristics are indicators, not a checklist.
Total firm assets (at fair value)
The firm definition is used to determine the fair value of total firm assets. Fair value = the value at which willing & knowledgeable parties would exchange an asset (most easily = market value of identical assets in liquid markets).
INCLUDESEXCLUDES
Discretionary AND nondiscretionary assetsAdvisory-only assets (firm advises but has no trading authority)
Fee-paying AND non-fee-paying assetsUncalled, committed capital (pledged but not yet drawn)
Net of leverage used—
Only actual (not simulated) assets—
Total firm assets INCLUDE nondiscretionary; composite assets do NOT. When calculating composite assets (not total firm assets), nondiscretionary assets are excluded — performance the manager doesn't control shouldn't be attributed to the manager. This firm-vs-composite split is a classic exam trap.
Discretionary vs nondiscretionary
TypeDefinition
DiscretionaryManager has control of the investment strategy. Includes subadviser assets IF the manager selects the subadviser.
NondiscretionaryClient constraints materially affect the manager's ability to execute the strategy.
Subadviser nuance: assets run by a subadviser are still discretionary to the firm as long as the firm chose the subadviser — the firm is exercising control over strategy by that selection.
The test for nondiscretionary: it's not "client has some rules" — it's that the constraints materially affect the manager's ability to execute the strategy. Material interference = nondiscretionary.
Other compliance fundamentals
FundamentalDetail
Initial track recordTo initially claim compliance: minimum of 5 years — or since inception if the firm has existed less than 5 years
Policies & proceduresMust establish, update on a timely basis, and document P&P for meeting GIPS — including for any recommendations voluntarily adopted and any error corrections
Conflict with local lawIf GIPS conflicts with local laws/regulations → comply with local law AND disclose the conflict
No false/misleading infoMust not present false or misleading performance info — whether or not it pertains to GIPS
Local law conflict: you do NOT abandon GIPS or ignore the law — you follow local law AND disclose the conflict. Both actions, not one.
Return calculation requirements (LOS 15.c)
GIPS requires comparable calculation methods by all firms to facilitate comparison.
RuleDetail
FrequencyNonprivate market portfolios: returns calculated monthly; geometrically linked to an annual return
Total return basisCalculate on a total return basis (income + capital gains/losses)
No interim ECFIf no interim external cash flows: R = (EV − BV) / BV
R_t = (EV − BV) / BV (no interim ECFs)
Why ECFs are a problem: interim external cash flows (client withdrawals = outflows; contributions = inflows) distort the calc — large interim flows affect EV and it becomes unclear how much return is from client cash flows vs manager performance.
Exact (true) TWRR
Ideally, to eliminate ECF distortion, the portfolio is valued each time an ECF occurs; subperiod returns are geometrically linked.
R_TWRR = (1+R₁)(1+R₂)(1+R₃) × ... × (1+R_t) − 1
Because of the interim valuations, this is called a true / exact TWRR — not distorted by the ECFs.
Worked example — Rooney account (ECF at end of each subperiod)
BV $2,500,000; EV $2,700,000. Inflows: $45,000 Day 7, $25,000 Day 19. Values (incl. CF): $2,555,000 (Day 7), $2,575,000 (Day 19). 30-day month.
Sub 1 (Days 1-7): (2,555,000 − 2,500,000 − 45,000) / 2,500,000 = 0.4% Sub 2 (Days 8-19): (2,575,000 − 2,555,000 − 25,000) / 2,555,000 = −0.2% Sub 3 (Days 20-30): (2,700,000 − 2,575,000) / 2,575,000 = 4.9% TWRR = (1.004)(0.998)(1.049) − 1 = 5.1%
Subperiod numerator: when the ECF lands at the end of a subperiod, subtract the ECF in that subperiod's numerator (it's not manager-generated). The denominator is the subperiod's beginning value.
When approximations are allowed
If a firm doesn't value portfolios every day AND the ECFs are relatively small, approximations of the monthly return give a close estimate of the true TWRR.
SituationMethod
Daily valuation doneDaily returns geometrically linked → monthly true TWRR
No daily valuation, ECFs smallApproximation (no interim valuation needed): Modified Dietz or MIRR
ECFs largePortfolio must be valued at the time of the ECF to calculate a subperiod return
Large vs small ECF: the firm defines "large" per composite (and must document it). A large ECF forces an actual valuation at the flow; a small one permits an approximation. The larger the ECFs & the more volatile the market, the bigger the gap between true TWRR and the approximation.
Modified Dietz return
R_MD = (EV − BV − ECF) / (BV + adjusted ECF)
Numerator logic: subtract ECFs (manager shouldn't get credit for client contributions). Denominator logic: add the day-weighted ECF (manager had use of the cash for part of the period).
Weight W = (days in period − day of ECF) / days in period Rooney: ECF +45k Day7 → W = 23/30 → adj 34,500 ECF +25k Day19 → W = 11/30 → adj 9,167 R_MD = (2,700,000 − 2,500,000 − 70,000) / (2,500,000 + 34,500 + 9,167) = 5.1%
Sign of the ECF: inflows are positive; outflows (client withdrawals) get a negative sign in both numerator and the weighted denominator term.
MIRR (modified internal rate of return)
An IRR that adjusts for the timing of ECFs. Solve for the rate r that equates EV to the future value of BV and the ECFs. Like Modified Dietz, each ECF is weighted by the days of the month.
2,700 = 2,500(1+r) + 45(1+r)^0.77 + 25(1+r)^0.37 MIRR = 5.1% (exponents: 23/30 = 0.77, 11/30 = 0.37)
Modified Dietz and MIRR typically give similar values — both adjust for daily-weighted ECFs. With small ECFs and a path of returns that doesn't vary much by subperiod, all three (true TWRR, Mod Dietz, MIRR) are close.
Modified Dietz calculator
InputValue
Beginning value (BV)
Ending value (EV)
Days in period
ECF 1 amount (+ in / − out)
ECF 1 day
ECF 2 amount (0 if none)
ECF 2 day
Set inputs and Compute. (Defaults = Rooney example → 5.1%)
Outflows: enter client withdrawals as negative amounts. The calculator day-weights each flow as (days − ECF day)/days.
When money-weighted return (MWR) is allowed
Normally GIPS requires TWRR (removes the client's cash-flow timing). But where the firm controls the timing & size of ECFs, an MWR better represents the manager's skill. MWR can be used instead of TWRR IF:
Both conditions
(1) The firm has control of the timing of ECFs
(2) The portfolios are closed-end, fixed-life, fixed-commitment, OR have a significant amount of illiquid assets
MWR is an IRR calculation; portfolios must be valued at least annually.
Quiz hook (15.3 Q5): MWR over TWRR is most likely when the manager controls the timing of ECFs — NOT because the account is large or nondiscretionary. Control of cash-flow timing is the decisive condition.
Valuation frequency by portfolio type
Portfolio typeValuation / return frequency
Nonprivate marketMonthly (daily return geometrically linked if daily valuation done)
Private market (real estate, PE, illiquid)Quarterly
Pooled funds not in a compositeAt least annually — AND valued + subperiod return at the time of subscriptions/redemptions
Other return calculation requirements
RequirementDetail
Trade dateUse trade date, not settlement date, prices
No annualizing partial yearPartial-year returns cannot be annualized (= representing simulated as actual returns — not allowed)
Total returnsInclude income + capital gains/losses; income-generating (e.g., bonds) use accrual accounting
Cash returnsReturns must reflect the manager's allocations to cash & cash equivalents — even if an outside firm manages the cash
Cash equivalents = money market instruments and fixed-income securities with maturities less than a year.
The "can't be halfway" theme again: total returns must be used (not price-only), partial-year can't be annualized, and cash returns count even when outsourced. A manager may dislike the low cash return showing up, but excluding it isn't fair representation.
Gross-of-fees, transaction costs & bundled fees
ItemTreatment
Gross-of-fees returnMust be calculated AFTER the deduction of transaction costs
Transaction costsCosts of buying/selling (brokerage commissions, spreads, exchange fees; PE: legal/advisory). Can be estimated only if unknown
Custody feesNOT included (not a transaction cost)
Bundled / all-in feesIf they include trading + mgmt + custody + admin: reduce gross-of-fees by the portion due to transaction costs; OR by the ENTIRE bundled fee if transaction costs can't be separated out
Decisive detail: gross-of-fees is still net of transaction (trading) costs — it's "gross" of investment management fees, not of trading costs. Custody fees are excluded entirely. Net-of-fees (which also removes mgmt fees) is recommended to also be shown, and investors should get a fee schedule.
Q1. Firm Z sweeps excess cash into a money market fund it does NOT manage, and excludes that cash from its total return calc. Is claiming GIPS compliance acceptable? (essay)
NOT acceptable. Returns must reflect the manager's allocations to cash & cash equivalents — even if an outside firm manages the cash. Excluding the swept cash from the total return understates the cash drag and is not fair representation. Firm Z cannot claim compliance while excluding the cash portion.
Q2. Growth & income composite quarterly returns: Q1 3.00%, Q2 4.15%, Q3 3.75%, Q4 3.15%. Calculate the annual return under GIPS.
Annual = (1.0300)(1.0415)(1.0375)(1.0315) − 1 = 14.80%
Geometric linking, not addition. The trap is summing to 14.05%. GIPS requires subperiod returns be geometrically linked → 14.80%.
Q3. JIM creates 5 composites covering 60% of its fee-paying discretionary portfolios and claims compliance "for most of the assets." Acceptable? (essay)
NOT acceptable. Compliance is firmwide, all-or-nothing — it cannot be claimed for "most" or only some composites/portfolios. ALL fee-paying segregated accounts must be in at least one composite. A "for most of the assets" claim is a prohibited partial claim ("can't be halfway").
Q4. Kenzo Fund ($m): Sep1 BV 50.0; Sep10 51.5 before, +5.0 CF, 56.5 after; Sep20 59.0 before, −2.0 CF, 57.0 after; Sep30 EV 55.0. 30-day month.
(a) Modified Dietz: net ECF = +5.0 − 2.0 = +3.0 adj ECF = 5.0×(30−10)/30 + (−2.0)×(30−20)/30 = 5.0×20/30 + (−2.0)×10/30 = 3.333 − 0.667 = 2.667 R_MD = (55.0 − 50.0 − 3.0) / (50.0 + 2.667) = 2.0 / 52.667 = 3.80% (b) Exact TWRR (revalue at every ECF): Sub1: (51.5 − 50.0)/50.0 = 3.00% Sub2: (59.0 − 56.5)/56.5 = 4.42% Sub3: (55.0 − 57.0)/57.0 = −3.51% TWRR = (1.0300)(1.0442)(0.9649) − 1 = 3.78%
Two methods, two numbers: Mod Dietz 3.80% (day-weighted approximation) vs exact TWRR 3.78% (reval at each ECF). Close because ECFs are small. In (b), each subperiod's denominator is the value after the prior CF.
Q5. MWR could most likely be used instead of TWRR if the:
Answer: C. MWR is allowed when the firm/manager controls the timing of ECFs (and the portfolio is closed-end/fixed-life/fixed-commitment or has significant illiquid assets). Account size (A) and nondiscretionary status (B) are irrelevant to the TWRR-vs-MWR choice.
What a composite is (LOS 15.e)
Composite = a grouping of one or more portfolios with similar investment mandates, objectives, or strategy.
Composite returns are essential for communicating with investors, so GIPS requires composite returns be calculated at least monthly (except private market: quarterly; pooled funds not in a composite: annually).
Must / must NOT be in a composite
Must be in ≥1 compositeMust NOT be in a composite
All actual, fee-paying, discretionary segregated accountsNondiscretionary accounts
Pooled funds also offered as segregated accounts (limited- or broad-distribution with a separate-account version)Pooled funds not also offered as segregated accounts (e.g., a broad-distribution fund — typically government-regulated)
—Simulated portfolios
Optional inclusions: Non-fee-paying discretionary segregated accounts MAY be included with additional disclosure (disclose the % of composite assets they represent).
The three discriminators: a "must include" account is actual + fee-paying + discretionary + segregated. Drop any one and it changes: non-fee-paying → optional w/ disclosure; nondiscretionary → excluded; simulated → excluded.
Model / simulated portfolios & seed money
TypeTreatment
Simulated / model / theoretical / backtestedCannot be in a composite. Performance only as supplemental info (labeled, must not contradict GIPS disclosures)
Seed money (firm's own funds for a new strategy)These are actual portfolios — can be in existing/new composites; subject to non-fee-paying disclosure rules
Actual vs simulated is the line: backtested model = supplemental only. Seed money is real money → allowed in a composite (just disclose as non-fee-paying).
Three ways to calculate a composite return (LOS 15.e)
#MethodHow
1Asset-weight by beginning-of-period (BOP) valuesEach portfolio return × its BOP weight (simplest)
2Asset-weight by BOP values + ECFsSame, but weights use the Modified Dietz denominator (BOP + day-weighted CF)
3Aggregate methodTreat the whole composite as one portfolio; apply Modified Dietz to total values & flows
Methods 2 & 3 weight the ECFs (familiar from Modified Dietz). In many cases methods 2 and 3 produce the same result.
Worked example — 3-portfolio equity composite (October, 31 days, $m)
Port30-Sep BVECF (day)31-Oct EVMod Dietz
A110.00−10.10 (19th)109.208.77%
B167.80−11.10 (13th)166.906.32%
C344.20+22.00 (3rd)345.10−5.80%
Total622.00—621.20—
a) Per-portfolio Mod Dietz — note A's EV < BV but return is positive (client withdrew 10.10); C contributed 22.00 so its return is negative even though EV > BV. The flow direction flips the intuition.
b) Method 1 — BOP weights
Weights: A 110/622 = 17.68% B 167.80/622 = 26.98% C 344.20/622 = 55.34% Composite = 0.1768(8.77%) + 0.2698(6.32%) + 0.5534(−5.80%) = 1.5505% + 1.7051% − 3.2097% = 0.05%
c) Method 2 — BOP + ECF weights (Mod Dietz denominators)
Denominators (BOP + weighted CF): A 106.09, B 161.35, C 364.07 → total 631.51 Weights: A 16.80%, B 25.55%, C 57.65% Composite = 0.1680(8.77%) + 0.2555(6.32%) + 0.5765(−5.80%) = −0.25%
Why method 2 < method 1 here: Portfolio C's contribution came early (3rd) so its Mod-Dietz denominator (and weight) is larger → C's negative return gets more influence → composite turns slightly negative. Timing of the flow changes the weight.
d) Method 3 — aggregate method
Treat composite as one portfolio (Mod Dietz on totals): numerator uses total EV, BV, and total CF from bottom row; denominator = total BOP + total weighted CF (= 631.51) R = (621.20 − 22 − −11.10 − −10.10 − 622) / 631.51 = −1.60 / 631.51 = −0.25%
Methods 2 and 3 both give −0.25% here — the second and third methods frequently produce the same result.
Composite return calculator (all 3 methods)
Up to 3 portfolios. Enter BV, EV, days, and up to 2 ECFs each (inflows +, outflows −; leave amount 0 if none). Defaults = the equity example.
PortBVEVCF1day1CF2day2
A
B
C
Days in period:   (set a portfolio's BV to 0 to exclude it)
Defaults = equity example → M1 +0.05%, M2/M3 −0.25%
"Discretionary" in composite construction (LOS 15.f)
A key determinant of inclusion is whether the manager has discretion — whether the manager's ability to implement the investment strategy is intact. If performance doesn't reflect the manager's decisions (nondiscretionary), the portfolio is excluded from composite returns.
The purpose of the construction rules is partly to prevent managers from excluding poorly performing portfolios from composites (cherry-picking).
IPS constraints — degrees of discretion
A client IPS specifies risk preferences & constraints (benchmark, sector/credit limits, derivatives use, ESG, restrictions on selling company stock, low-basis-stock limits, legal e.g. domestic-only). None of these automatically make a portfolio nondiscretionary — there are degrees of discretion.
Guidance: is the manager's ability to use professional judgment materially constrained?
Constraint is...Manager action
Immaterial (e.g., IPS bans derivatives the manager wouldn't use anyway)Portfolio is discretionary → place in composite with similar unconstrained portfolios
MaterialEither group with similar constrained portfolios, OR exclude from all composites
Restricted assets & ECF-driven nondiscretion
SituationManager may...
Restrictions on particular assets (e.g., can't sell low-basis stock)(1) treat the entire portfolio nondiscretionary; OR (2) remove the restricted assets and put the remainder in a composite; OR (3) treat the entire portfolio discretionary if restricted-asset value is below a stated % threshold
ECFs indicate nondiscretion (client makes large withdrawals forcing a large cash balance)Restricts the manager's ability to invest in equity → may render the portfolio nondiscretionary (same as any constraint)
Discretion is a judgment, not a checklist: the test is whether professional judgment is materially constrained. A constraint that doesn't bite (manager wouldn't act differently) leaves the portfolio discretionary.
Inclusion & exclusion of portfolios (LOS 15.h)
Firms must have documented policies, applied consistently & on a composite-by-composite basis, for: inclusion, exclusion, switching, cash flows from new investments/liquidations, and the minimum asset level.
EventRule
New portfolio inclusionInclude at the beginning of the next full measurement period (funded with cash July 6, monthly composite → include Aug 1). Firm has discretion to wait longer if it takes time to invest (illiquid/emerging markets, or must sell other securities first)
Terminated portfolio exclusionInclude through the last full measurement period the firm had discretion. (Client says June 4 they leave July 9 → include only through May 31)
The asymmetry: new portfolios join at the start of the next full period; terminated ones stay through the last full period of discretion (the partial final period is dropped). For the June-4/July-9 case the last full month of discretion ends May 31.
Switching portfolios between composites
TriggerDetail
Client changes mandate/objective/strategye.g., client now allows derivatives → switch to a composite that allows them
Firm redefines the compositeShould be highly unusual — in most cases the firm should create a new composite instead
History stays put: when a portfolio is switched to a new composite, its past performance must remain in the OLD composite's historical record — you don't retroactively move history (that would enable cherry-picking).
Significant cash flows
Significant cash flow = one large enough that it impedes the firm from implementing the strategy on a timely basis (e.g., a contribution/withdrawal too large to invest/divest quickly in an illiquid market). The firm documents what counts as "significant."
To prevent composite performance being distorted by a significant CF, a firm can:
OptionDetail
1. Temporarily exclude the portfolioRemove from the composite while the flow is being invested/divested
2. Temporary new account (outside the composite)Holds cash contributions until invested, OR securities until divested
Example — Account #207 (illiquid fixed income, large infusion Apr 12, ~60 days to invest)
ApproachWhat happens
Best solutionPut funds in a temporary subaccount 207T (not in any composite); keep reporting 207 in its composite. Once 207T is invested per objectives, merge 207T into 207. Client still gets reports on 207T + 207 (Standards of Professional Conduct); 207T is only excluded from GIPS reporting
AlternativePut funds directly into 207, but temporarily exclude 207 from the composite until invested. If done by June 15, exclude 207 for April, May, June (monthly composites)
Minimum asset levels
RuleDetail
Exclude if too smallA portfolio may be excluded if its size is so small it can't be invested appropriately
Add/remove thresholdsMin level must be specified in advance; add when size rises above (e.g., €5m), remove when it falls below (e.g., €4.5m)
History preservedPortfolios removed for falling below the minimum cannot have their prior performance removed from the composite's historical record
Recurring "history stays" theme: whether a portfolio is terminated, switched, or removed for min-asset reasons — its prior performance always stays in the composite history. This blocks cherry-picking.
Role of mandate/objective/strategy (LOS 15.g)
Per GIPS, composites must:
Composites must...
Be determined by investment mandate, objective, or strategy
Contain all portfolios that match the composite definition
Be based on criteria documented in P&P
Be defined so clients can compare one firm to another
Be representative of the firm's products & consistent with its marketing strategy
Too narrow vs too broad
DefinitionConsequence
Too narrow (e.g., small-cap value frontier-market stocks)Too few portfolios in each → unnecessary costs, jeopardizes client confidentiality
Too broadDisparate performance among composite portfolios (not comparable)
Bases for composite construction: equity style; the benchmark; equity/bond sector; risk-return profile (e.g., tracking error); active vs passive vs core-plus; investment strategy (sector rotation, fundamental analysis, etc.).
A portfolio can be in more than one composite (e.g., a value portfolio in both a value composite and a small-cap-value composite, if it meets both definitions) — but the firm must not double-count its assets in total firm value.
Q1. RRC runs a long-short strategy but never intends to market it, so excludes those portfolios from all composites. Acceptable if claiming GIPS compliance? (essay)
NOT acceptable. ALL actual, fee-paying, discretionary segregated accounts must be in at least one composite — regardless of whether the firm markets that strategy. "We don't market it" is not an exemption. (A composite need not be presented to a given prospect, but the portfolios still must be assigned to a composite.)
Q2. TIM builds an aggressive-growth composite from hypothetical assets + a backtested allocation, and wants to show those model results in its presentation. Acceptable? (essay)
NOT acceptable. Simulated / model / backtested portfolios cannot be in a composite. Their performance may only be shown as supplemental information (clearly labeled, not contradicting GIPS disclosures) — not as composite results.
Q3. For each, choose may-be-included vs must-be-excluded and explain. (i) significant liquidity needs + large cash position; (ii) client pays no fees; (iii) client requests strictly following an index.
(i) Must be EXCLUDED. A large forced cash position from significant liquidity needs materially constrains the manager's ability to implement the strategy → nondiscretionary.
(ii) MAY be included. Non-fee-paying discretionary accounts may be included with additional disclosure (disclose % of composite assets) — not required, not forbidden.
(iii) MAY be included. "Strictly follow an index" is a defined passive mandate, not a loss of discretion — the manager still implements the (indexing) strategy. Group it in a composite of similar index/passive portfolios.
Q4. JIM uses monthly valuation. When is it appropriate to remove a portfolio from JIM's composite if it's terminated on July 15, 2015? (essay)
Keep it through the last full measurement period of discretion = through June 30, 2015. The partial month (July 1–15) is dropped because it's not a full measurement period. The portfolio's prior performance stays in the composite history.
Q5. UK composite, 2 portfolios, April (30-day, £m). A: BV 400, +25 (12th), +10 (22nd), EV 467. B: BV 200, −13 (20th), EV 224. Total BV 600, EV 691. Compute (i) per-portfolio Mod Dietz, (ii) BOP-weighted, (iii) BOP+CF, (iv) aggregate.
(i) Mod Dietz: A: adj CF = 25×18/30 + 10×8/30 = 15 + 2.667 = 17.667 R = (467 − 400 − 35)/(400 + 17.667) = 7.66% B: adj CF = −13×10/30 = −4.333 R = (224 − 200 − −13)/(200 − 4.333) = 18.91% (ii) BOP weights A 400/600 = 66.67%, B 33.33% Composite = 0.6667(7.66%) + 0.3333(18.91%) = 11.41% (iii) BOP+CF denoms A 417.67, B 195.67 → tot 613.33 weights A 68.10%, B 31.90% Composite = 0.6810(7.66%) + 0.3190(18.91%) = 11.25% (iv) Aggregate: net CF = 25 + 10 − 13 = 22; adj CF = 15 + 2.667 − 4.333 = 13.333 R = (691 − 600 − 22)/(600 + 13.333) = 11.25%
Methods (iii) and (iv) match (11.25%) — the BOP+CF and aggregate methods frequently give the same answer. Method (ii) differs (11.41%) because it ignores the cash-flow timing in the weights.
GIPS Reports (LOS 15.i)
When marketing a strategy, firms must make every reasonable effort to provide a GIPS Report to prospective clients and limited-distribution pooled fund investors.
Two report typesFor
GIPS Composite ReportComposite (segregated-account) strategies — the curriculum's focus
GIPS Pooled Fund ReportPooled funds
The exam focuses on the composite time-weighted return report requirements (below).
Performance history requirement
RuleDetail
On adoptionPresent GIPS-compliant annual performance for at least 5 years
Younger compositeOr since inception if the composite has existed < 5 years
Build-upThen extend each year until the firm has a 10-year GIPS-compliant track record
5 → 10: start at a minimum of 5 years (or since inception), then add a year annually until you reach a 10-year compliant history. Don't confuse the 5-year start with the 10-year target.
Returns & size measures the report must include
Must include
Time-weighted returns for the composite AND the benchmark
The amount of firm assets
The amount of composite assets
The number of portfolios in the composite — only if there are 6 or more
Two number-of-portfolios traps: (1) you only report the count if ≥ 6 portfolios; (2) but there is NO minimum number of portfolios for a composite to be formed — a composite can hold just one portfolio. "Need 6 to report the count" ≠ "need 6 to have a composite."
Risk: three dispersion measures
The report must include annual measures of: internal composite dispersion, benchmark dispersion, and composite dispersion as a whole.
MeasureWhat it showsScale
Internal dispersionVariability of portfolio returns within the composite — how consistent performance is across portfoliosMicro
Benchmark dispersion + composite-as-a-wholeCompare the composite's historical risk against a benchmarkMacro
Large internal dispersion may indicate the firm wasn't consistent in implementing the strategy, and/or the composite definition is too broad.
Internal dispersion — eligibility & methods
Only portfolios in the composite for the ENTIRE year can be included in internal dispersion. (Figure 15.1: A, C, E were in all 4 quarters → included; B, D, F lack a full year → excluded.)
Acceptable internal-dispersion methodsNote
High & low returns; RangeSimplest, easy to interpret; but an extreme value skews them and they're not stand-alone risk measures
Equal-weighted standard deviationMost widely accepted measure of within-composite dispersion
Asset-weighted standard deviationWeights each portfolio by its market weight
Another firm-chosen measureIf it fairly represents the composite's internal dispersion
The "≥6 to report" link: Figure 15.1 leaves only 3 full-year portfolios → below 6, so no dispersion need be reported. The full-year rule and the 6-portfolio reporting threshold both gate dispersion.
The two SD formulas (reference)
Equal-weighted SD of composite: σ_C = sqrt[ Σ(R_i − meanR)² / (n − 1) ] R_i = return on portfolio i; meanR = equal-weighted mean; n = # portfolios (n or n−1 both defensible; firm should disclose which) Asset-weighted SD: dispersion = sqrt[ Σ w_i (R_i − C_ASSET)² ] w_i = market weight of portfolio i; C_ASSET = Σ w_i R_i (asset-wtd return)
Composite & benchmark dispersion (the macro measures)
RuleDetail
MeasureEx post standard deviation
FrequencyEach annual period
Of whatThe composite AND the benchmark
WindowUsing the previous 3 years of data, annualized
3-year annualized ex post SD is the macro risk measure presented each year — distinct from the within-year internal dispersion (range / equal- or asset-weighted SD across portfolios).
Portability of performance (LOS 15.j)
When a firm acquires/joins another firm, manager group, or manager, the new firm can link to the previous firm's historical performance ONLY IF ALL 4 conditions hold:
#Condition
1Substantially all the investment decision-makers are retained by the new firm
2The decision-making process remains substantially intact & independent within the new firm
3The new firm has records that document the previous firm's performance
4There is no break in the performance record between the new and previous firm
The "garden" exception & the 1-year grace period
ScenarioResult
Only the first 3 conditions met (e.g., previous firm's employees take a garden / temporary leave at acquisition)Previous history can still be used to represent the new firm's, BUT the records may not be LINKED — assets aren't managed during the garden period → a break in the presented record
New firm is GIPS-compliant but the previous firm was notNew firm has 1 year to bring the assets into compliance for future reporting
Condition 4 is the linking switch: all 4 → link the history (continuous record). Only 1–3 (a break exists) → you can use/represent the history but not link it. "Use" ≠ "link." And a non-compliant acquired firm = 1 year grace to get compliant.
Advisory-only & uncalled committed capital reporting
Advisory-only assets and uncalled-but-committed capital cannot be in total firm assets. But the firm can report info on them separately or combined with composite/firm assets — if combined, it must also report separately for the advisory-only / uncalled-committed portion, and in any case must clearly label those assets.
Ties back to 15.2: total firm assets exclude advisory-only and uncalled committed capital. Here's the disclosure mechanics if a firm chooses to show them.
Fair value & accrued income
RuleDetail
Fair valueThe amount an asset would be sold for in an arm's-length transaction between willing & knowledgeable parties
Accrued incomeFair value should include accrued income for bonds & other income-generating assets
Cash incomeFor cash, income may be accounted for on a cash OR accrual basis
DocumentationFirms must document the valuation process & methodologies (composite- or pooled-fund-specific)
Recommended valuation hierarchy (LOS 15.d)
Descending order of usage — a level lower in the hierarchy is used only when all higher levels are unavailable.
#LevelExample / note
1Quoted price for an IDENTICAL asset in a LIQUID market, same dayThe gold standard
2Quoted price for a SIMILAR asset in a liquid market, same day—
3Quoted price for identical/similar assets in markets that are NOT activee.g., a stock trades infrequently — last price is days old
4A value based on market inputse.g., apply a comparable P/E to the firm's earnings
5Subjective, unobservable valueLast resort — only when observable inputs/prices aren't available/appropriate; if used, disclose these assets as a % of composite assets
The two collapsing dimensions: price moves from identical→similar and market moves from liquid/active→inactive→model→subjective. Level 1 = identical + liquid + same day. Drop to a lower level only if every level above is unavailable. Level 5 (subjective) triggers a %-of-composite-assets disclosure.
Q1(i). Tribon: returns are gross-of-fees, but GIPS requires net-of-management-fees. Guptar agrees to recalculate to net. Is Tribon correct? (essay)
Tribon is INCORRECT. GIPS permits gross-of-fees presentation (gross is still net of transaction costs). Net-of-management-fees is only recommended, not required. Guptar should NOT "fix" a presentation that is already acceptable — gross-of-fees is compliant.
Q1(ii). Excerpt 2: assets directed to client-appointed subadvisers. Guptar says GIPS requires including them in total firm assets. Is Guptar correct? (essay)
Guptar is CORRECT. A client-appointed subadviser means the firm did NOT select it → those assets are nondiscretionary to the firm. But total firm assets INCLUDE nondiscretionary assets (only composite assets exclude them). So they must be included in total firm assets.
The firm-vs-composite trap again: nondiscretionary → IN total firm assets, OUT of composite assets. Don't reflexively exclude "nondiscretionary."
Q2. PMG's 8 actions — compliant or not, and why?
ActionVerdictWhy
1. S&P 500 as benchmark for all 3 composites (fixed income, equity, balanced)NOT compliantBenchmark must reflect the composite's mandate; S&P 500 doesn't fit a fixed-income or balanced composite
2. Accrual accounting BUT book values for fixed-income returnsNOT compliantMust use fair (market) value, not book value
3. Accrued income included for fixed-incomeCompliantFair value should include accrued income for bonds
4. Fee schedule NOT includedNOT compliantInvestors must be provided a fee schedule
5. Asset-weighted composite using end-of-period weightingsNOT compliantMust weight by beginning-of-period values (± CF), not end-of-period
6. Composites only actual AUM, not linked to simulated/modelCompliantSimulated/model can't be in composites
7. Equal-weighted (CF-adjusted) returns for portfolio returnsNOT compliantPortfolio/composite returns must be asset-weighted; equal-weighting is for internal dispersion, not the return itself
8. Performance after deduction of actual trading expensesCompliantGross-of-fees must be net of transaction costs
Pattern: the non-compliant ones each violate a specific rule — benchmark-must-match-mandate (1), fair-value-not-book (2), provide-fee-schedule (4), BOP-not-EOP weighting (5), asset-weight-not-equal-weight portfolio returns (7). The compliant ones (3, 6, 8) are accrued income, no-simulated, and net-of-transaction-costs.
Q3. A security has no observable quoted market price in an active market. The next best valuation basis per the GIPS hierarchy is:
Answer: C. Levels 1–2 (active-market quotes for identical/similar) are unavailable. The next level down (3) is a quoted price in an INACTIVE market for the same or similar security. Only below that come market inputs (B, level 4) and subjective unobservable (A, level 5, last resort). "Next best" = level 3 = C.
What verification is (LOS 15.k)
Verification = the process whereby an independent, outside party assesses the firm's: (1) P&P for composite/pooled-fund construction & maintenance, (2) performance calculation, (3) performance presentation, (4) distribution of performance.
AspectDetail
PurposeProvide greater confidence to investors & the firm in its GIPS-compliance claim; based on the GIPS principle of fair presentation & full disclosure
What it does NOT doDoes NOT assure that the construction, calculation, & presentation for any particular portfolio or composite is accurate
Required?No — voluntary, but recommended & consistent with best practices
Three things people get wrong: (1) verification is voluntary, not required; (2) it gives confidence but does not assure accuracy of any particular portfolio/composite; (3) it is not part of the GIPS-compliant presentation itself.
Benefits to the firm
Beyond confidence in the compliance claim
Increased knowledge of performance-presentation personnel
Better quality presentations
Better internal processes & procedures
Possible marketing benefits
Scope — firmwide only
Verification must follow the GIPS Standards for Verifiers and be issued firmwide. It cannot be provided for a single portfolio, composite, or pooled fund. A firm can't say a portfolio/fund/strategy is "in compliance" — verification is for the entire firm, and a firm must meet ALL requirements (no compliance "except for").
The exception: a firm CAN have a verifier do a detailed performance examination on one or more composites/pooled funds, then state that a performance examination was issued on that specific composite/fund. (Verification = firmwide; performance examination = single composite.)
"Can't be halfway" again: verification = firmwide, all-or-nothing. The single-composite deep-dive is a performance examination, a different deliverable. Don't conflate the two.
Choosing a verifier — fit to the firm
A firm should weigh its operations, products & needs. Different firm pairs need different verifiers, e.g.:
These pairs have different needs
Large global firm vs small local firm
Tax-exempt investor (pension fund) vs a firm focused on managing portfolio taxes
Quantitative manager using derivatives vs a direct real-estate investor
Info to request from potential verifiers
Request
A description of the verifier (personnel & organizational structure)
Services offered & previous projects completed
The verifier's project management, sampling & testing procedures
References from previous clients
Fees, proposal & timeline
The verification process
The GIPS Standards for Verifiers set the procedures. Focus: planning, sample selection, testing.
StageDetail
PlanningVerifier gathers info on the firm — all products, calculation methodologies, GIPS P&P
SamplingVerification is asserted firmwide, but verifiers often use samples. When choosing samples, consider: firm & composite size, internal controls & methods, number of portfolios, number of years verified, etc. Deficiencies found → larger samples / additional procedures
Sampling is the key nuance: verification is firmwide, yet it's done via samples — so it is NOT a "detailed analysis of every product." If the verifier finds deficiencies, it expands the sample.
Testing areas
Verifiers test whether the firm satisfies requirements in:
Recordkeeping
Policies & procedures
Firm definition
Thoroughness of the firm's list of composites & limited-distribution pooled funds
Calculation of total firm assets
Input data (e.g., portfolio inflows/outflows — verifiable vs custodial statements & third-party docs)
Construction & maintenance of composites: classification of portfolios as discretionary/nondiscretionary; assignment of portfolios to appropriate composites (outlier returns may flag calc errors or misassignment)
Content of the firm's GIPS Report & any marketing material
Q1. Which statement about verification is LEAST accurate? Verification is:
Answer: C (least accurate = the false one). Verification is voluntary (A true) and recommended / best practice (B true). It is NOT required, and it is not part of the GIPS-compliant presentation. C is false on both counts.
Q2. Which statement about verification is MOST accurate?
Kaplan's answer: A. In planning, the verifier must gather info on all the firm's products to assert compliance on a firmwide basis. B is false (verification is firmwide, NOT single-portfolio/composite/fund — that would be a performance examination).
Watch the A-vs-C tension: statement C is also a true sentence (it's verbatim curriculum — verification doesn't assure any particular portfolio is accurate). Kaplan keys A because the question targets the firmwide/all-products scope; but note A slightly overstates ("detailed analysis of all") since verification actually uses samples. If the exam pits A against C, read the stem: a scope question → A; an "assurance/limitations" question → C. Both describe true features of verification.
