Reading 15 · Overview of the Global Investment Performance Standards
Full-reading recap: objectives / scope / benefits (15.a), compliance fundamentals & firm definition (15.b), return calculations (15.c), composites & asset weighting (15.e–h), presentation & reporting (15.i), portability (15.j), valuation hierarchy (15.d), and verification (15.k). All calculation figures node-verified against the Kaplan examples.
Exam focus: GIPS sits inside Performance Measurement (5–10% of the exam), usually item sets, occasionally constructed response. Like Ethics: know the principles, then apply them to spot compliance / noncompliance. There is a surprising number of calculation issues — work the practice questions. Master heuristic: GIPS can't be halfway.
Module 15.1 · GIPS Overview
LOS 15.aObjectives, scope, benefits
Nature
Voluntary, ethical minimum standards for performance presentation, built on full disclosure and fair representation; firms should add any information that helps clients understand results. 2020 edition: three sections — firms, asset owners, verifiers. Asset owners who compete for business use the Standards for Firms.
5 objectives
Advance investor interests & confidence · accurate, comparable data · a globally accepted standard for determining AND presenting performance · fair competition among global managers · encourage industry self-regulation.
Vocabulary
Composite = collection of portfolios with similar mandates/objectives/strategies. Segregated account (SMA) = portfolio owned by a single investor. Pooled fund = not owned by a single investor: broad distribution = regulated, general public (mutual funds); limited distribution = not available to the general public (hedge funds).
Scope: FIRMWIDE only
Compliance can be claimed only on a firmwide basis — never for some products, specific composites, pooled funds, or portfolios. Must comply with all applicable requirements (recommendations optional, best practice). The GIPS Report must go to ALL prospective clients and investors.
Compliance claim means
Data inputs, processes & return calcs compliant · all fee-paying segregated accounts in ≥1 composite · all limited distribution pooled funds in an appropriate composite · broad distribution pooled funds only required in a composite if the strategy is also offered as separate accounts (why: they're government-regulated — investor protections already exist).
Benefits
To clients/investors: standardized determination & presentation → comparability; more reliable performance; benchmark requirements facilitate strategy discussion. To managers: investor confidence (especially with third-party verification), attracts new investors, compete internationally, stronger internal controls from recordkeeping, extra operational insight from adopted technology — against the costs of compliance.
Module 15.2 · Compliance Fundamentals
LOS 15.bFirm definition, total firm assets, discretion basics
Firm = “an investment firm, subsidiary, or division held out to clients as a distinct business entity” — a unit organizationally/functionally separated that retains discretion over the assets it manages and should have autonomy over investment decisions. More likely distinct if it has its own: legal organization, market, client base, investment process, strategy, investment staff, physical location, chain of command. Judgment case: two divisions sharing a trading desk — if the desk only executes, they can still be distinct; if it helps value securities, less likely.
Total firm assets INCLUDETotal firm assets EXCLUDE
Discretionary AND nondiscretionary assets · fee-paying AND non-fee-paying · net of leverage · actual assets only · assets run by a subadviser IF the firm selects the subadviserAdvisory-only assets (no trading authority) · uncalled committed capital · simulated assets
Trap pair: total FIRM assets include nondiscretionary; COMPOSITE assets exclude nondiscretionary (performance not controlled by the manager isn't attributed to the manager). And subadviser assets count only if the firm selects the subadviser — client-appointed subadviser assets are OUT (the Guptar quiz excerpt is incorrect on exactly this).
Other fundamentals
Initial claim: minimum 5 years of compliance (or since inception if younger) · establish, update timely, and document policies & procedures (incl. voluntarily adopted recommendations & error correction) · GIPS vs local law conflict → comply with local law and disclose the conflict · never present false/misleading performance info (GIPS-related or not) · annual GIPS-compliant report to all existing clients of their composites · benchmarks must be total return (not price-only) · disclose all material errors to clients & verifiers · maintain data + a list of composites for the last five years.
Module 15.3 · Return Calculations
LOS 15.cTWRR, Modified Dietz, MIRR — the toolkit
No interim ECFs: Rt = (EV − BV) / BV Exact TWRR: value at EVERY ECF → chain-link: R = (1+R₁)(1+R₂)…(1+Rₖ) − 1 Modified Dietz: RMD = (EV − BV − ECF) / (BV + adjusted ECF) adjusted ECF = Σ Wᵢ×ECFᵢ, Wᵢ = (days remaining)/(days in month) MIRR: solve r: EV = BV(1+r) + Σ ECFᵢ(1+r)^{Wᵢ} (daily-weighted, like Mod Dietz; typically similar values)
Rooney example (node-verified): subperiods +0.4%, −0.2%, +4.9% → exact TWRR = 5.1%; Modified Dietz with adjusted ECFs $34,500 (23/30 × 45k) and $9,167 (11/30 × 25k) → 5.1%; MIRR → 5.1%. Approximations are close when ECFs are small; the larger the ECFs and the more volatile the market, the greater the gap vs true TWRR. Inflows are positive, outflows (withdrawals) negative.
Valuation frequency
Non-private-market portfolios: returns monthly; if daily valuations, geometrically link dailies to a monthly true TWRR; monthly returns geometrically linked to annual. Private market (RE, PE, illiquid): at least quarterly. Pooled funds not in a composite: at least annually + valued and subperiod return at subscriptions/redemptions.
Large ECFs
Definition is set by each firm for each composite (generally: large enough to affect the return) and the policy must be documented. Small ECFs → approximations OK without interim valuation; large ECFs → the portfolio MUST be valued at the ECF time for a subperiod return.
MWR instead of TWR
Allowed when the firm controls the timing and size of the ECFs AND the portfolio is closed-end, fixed life, fixed commitment, or holds significant illiquid assets. The MWR (an IRR) must be calculated and portfolios valued at least annually.
Other requirements
Trade date (not settlement) · partial-year returns cannot be annualized (= presenting simulated as actual) · total returns (income + capital gains/losses); income-generating assets use accrual accounting · returns must reflect cash & cash equivalents (money-market instruments, FI maturities < 1yr) even if an outside firm manages the cash.
Fees
Gross-of-fees return must be after deducting transaction costs (brokerage commissions, spreads, exchange fees; private markets: also legal/advisory). Custody fees NOT included. Transaction costs may be estimated only if unknown. Bundled/all-in fees: reduce the gross return by the transaction-cost portion, or by the entire bundled fee if it can't be separated. Net-of-fees returns recommended; a fee schedule must be provided to investors.
Quiz patterns (reasoning-derived): Firm Z ignoring the swept cash in returns → NOT acceptable (returns must reflect cash even if managed externally). ADA quarterly returns → geometric link: (1.03)(1.0415)(1.0375)(1.0315) − 1 = 14.80%. Kenzo: Modified Dietz → 2 / 52.667 = 3.80%; exact TWRR (3.0%, 4.425%, −3.509%) → 3.78%. MWR-over-TWR condition → manager controls the timing of ECFs.
Module 15.4 · Composites
LOS 15.eComposite returns — 3 asset-weighting methods
Composites = groupings of portfolios with similar mandates/objectives/strategies. Composite returns are essential to investor communication → calculated at least monthly (except private market investments). Three acceptable methods:
MethodWeightsWorked example (A/B/C, node-verified)
1. BOP valueswᵢ = BVᵢ / ΣBV (simplest)17.68% × 8.77 + 26.98% × 6.32 + 55.34% × (−5.80) = +0.05%
2. BOP values + ECFswᵢ = Modified Dietz denominator (BV + adjusted ECFs)106.09 / 631.51, 161.35 / 631.51, 364.07 / 631.51 → −0.25%
3. AggregateTreat the composite as ONE portfolio; Modified Dietz on totals(621.20 − 622.00 − net ECFs) / 631.51 = −0.25%
Why methods 1 and 2 differ: Portfolio C received a large early-month inflow ($22 on Oct 3) → the ECF-adjusted weight of C is bigger (57.65% vs 55.34%) → C's negative return (−5.80%) drags the composite negative. Methods 2 and 3 often produce the same result. Also note the Mod Dietz sign logic: a positive return despite EV < BV means the client withdrew; a negative return despite EV > BV means the client contributed.
LOS 15.fDiscretion — what goes in a composite
MUST be in ≥1 compositeMust NOT be in a composite
All actual, fee-paying, discretionary segregated accounts · pooled funds also offered as segregated accounts (limited distribution + broad distribution whose strategy is offered via separate account)Nondiscretionary accounts · pooled funds not also offered as segregated accounts (typical broad distribution fund) · simulated portfolios
Non-fee-paying discretionary accounts MAY be included — if included, disclose the % of composite assets that is non-fee-paying. Intent of the rules: prevent managers from excluding poorly performing portfolios (cherry-picking). Key test: does performance reflect the manager's decisions? If not → nondiscretionary → excluded from composite returns.
IPS constraints
Benchmark, risk controls (sector weights, credit quality, derivatives limits), ESG preferences, restrictions on company-stock sales, low-basis-stock limits (tax), legal restrictions. NONE automatically makes a portfolio nondiscretionary — there are degrees of discretion; the test is whether professional judgment is materially constrained (e.g. a derivatives limit on a manager who doesn't use them anyway → still discretionary).
Materiality routing
Constraint immaterial → composite with similar unconstrained portfolios. Constraint material → group with similar constrained portfolios OR exclude from all composites.
Restricted assets
3 options: treat the entire portfolio nondiscretionary; remove the restricted assets and composite the remainder; or keep it discretionary if restricted assets < a policy-stated % of the portfolio.
ECF-driven
Large repeated withdrawals forcing a big cash balance can make a portfolio nondiscretionary (manager can't invest like the composite's other portfolios).
Model portfolios
Simulated / hypothetical / model / backtested portfolios cannot be in a composite — only supplemental info (labeled, not conflicting with required disclosures). But seed money (firm's own funds) creates an ACTUAL portfolio → can join composites, with non-fee-paying disclosures. (TIM quiz: backtested model composite in the presentation → NOT acceptable.)
LOS 15.gComposite construction
Composites must: be determined by investment mandate, objective, or strategy · contain ALL portfolios matching the definition · be based on criteria documented in policies & procedures · let clients compare firms · be representative of the firm's products and consistent with its marketing. Bases: equity style, benchmark, equity/bond sector, risk-return profile (tracking error), active/passive/core-plus, strategy (sector rotation, fundamental…).
Goldilocks trap: definition too narrow (small-cap value frontier markets) → too few portfolios per composite, unnecessary cost, potential client-confidentiality risk. Too broad → disparate performance within the composite. A portfolio can sit in multiple composites (a small-cap value portfolio → both the value composite AND the small-cap value composite) — but don't double-count its assets in total firm value.
LOS 15.hInclusion, exclusion, switching, SCFs, minimum asset levels
Firms must have policies for: inclusion · exclusion · switching between composites · cash flows from new investments/liquidations · minimum asset level — set composite-by-composite, applied timely & consistently (unethical managers might otherwise steer best performers into a favored composite).
Inclusion
New portfolios enter at the beginning of the next full measurement period (funded July 6, monthly calc → in composite August 1). Firm has discretion to allow longer when investing takes time: illiquid securities (EM) or funding with securities that must be sold first — documented policy may vary by composite.
Exclusion
Terminated portfolios stay in through the last full measurement period in which the firm had discretion (client stops trading June 4, leaving July 9 → include only through May 31). Terminated portfolios' history stays in the composite record.
Switching
Only on client mandate/objective/strategy change (e.g. client now allows derivatives) or a firm redefinition of the composite — which should be highly unusual (create a new composite instead). Performance to date remains in the OLD composite's history.
Significant cash flows
= large enough to impede implementing the strategy on a timely basis; the firm documents what's “significant.” Options: temporarily exclude the portfolio, or use a temporary new account (outside the composite) holding contributions until invested / securities until divested. Account #207 example: best = temporary subaccount 207T, excluded from GIPS reporting only, merged into 207 once invested; alternative = exclude 207 itself for April–June until invested. Either way the client still gets full reports (Standards of Professional Conduct).
Minimum asset level
A portfolio too small to be invested appropriately may be excluded. Size limits for adding/removing per firm policy (add > €5M, remove < €4.5M). Must be specified in advance; removed portfolios keep their prior performance in the composite history.
Quiz (reasoning-derived): monthly valuation, portfolio terminated July 15 → include through June 30. Client with significant liquidity needs/cash → MAY be included (judgment / degrees of discretion). Non-fee-paying → MAY be included (with disclosure). Client demands strict index tracking → nondiscretionary → MUST be excluded.
Module 15.5 · Presentation & Reporting
LOS 15.iGIPS Reports — history, returns, size, risk
Two report types
GIPS Composite Report and GIPS Pooled Fund Report — every reasonable effort to deliver to prospects & limited-distribution pooled fund investors when marketing a strategy. Curriculum focus: composite time-weighted return reports.
Performance history
On adoption: GIPS-compliant annual performance for at least 5 years (or since composite inception if younger), then extend each year up to a 10-year compliant history.
Returns & size
TWRs for composite AND benchmark · amount of firm assets · amount of composite assets · number of portfolios if six or more. No minimum number of portfolios to form a composite.
Risk measures
Internal composite dispersion (micro: variability of portfolio returns WITHIN the composite) + benchmark dispersion and composite dispersion as a whole (macro: compare composite's historical risk vs benchmark) — ex post standard deviation, each annual period, using the previous 3 years annualized.
Internal dispersion
Shows consistency. Very large dispersion → firm not consistently implementing the strategy AND/OR composite definition too broad. Only full-year portfolios enter the calc (Fig 15.1: A, C, E in; B, D, F out); six or more portfolios required to report dispersion. Acceptable measures: high/low, range (simple but skewed by extremes, not standalone risk measures), equal-weighted σ (most widely accepted; n or n−1 both defensible — disclose), asset-weighted σ, or another fair measure.
equal-weighted: σC = √[ Σ(Rᵢ − MEAN(R))² / (n−1) ] asset-weighted: dispersion = √[ Σ wᵢ(Rᵢ − CASSET)² ] CASSET = Σ wᵢRᵢ
LOS 15.jPortability — the 4 conditions
On acquisition/joining, the new firm can LINK the previous firm's history if: 1) substantially all investment decision makers retained; 2) decision-making process substantially intact & independent within the new firm; 3) records documenting the history exist; 4) no break in the performance record. Only 1–3 met → the old history can represent the new firm but cannot be linked (e.g. garden leave at acquisition → break for that period). New firm compliant but the acquired firm isn't → 1 year to bring the assets into compliance.
Module 15.6 · Valuation Hierarchy
LOS 15.dRecommended fair-value hierarchy (descending)
Fair value = amount in an arm's-length transaction between willing, knowledgeable parties; includes accrued income for bonds and other income-generating assets (cash income: cash or accrual basis). Valuation process documented, composite- or pooled-fund-specific. Use a lower level only when all higher levels are unavailable:
Quiz: no observable quoted price from an active market → next best = quoted prices from an INACTIVE market for the same or similar security (level 3) — NOT market-based inputs (level 4). If level 5 is used, disclose those assets as a % of composite assets.
Advisory-only & uncalled committed capital: never in total firm assets, but the firm CAN report them separately or combined with composite/firm assets — if combined, it must ALSO report the advisory-only and uncalled-committed amounts, always clearly labeled.
Module 15.7 · GIPS Verification
LOS 15.kPurpose, scope, process
What it is
An independent third party assesses the firm's: policies & procedures for composite / pooled fund construction & maintenance; performance calculation; presentation; distribution. Purpose: greater confidence in the compliance claim.
Three exam facts
1. Verification is NOT required — voluntary, recommended, best practice. 2. It does NOT assure that the construction, calculation, and presentation of any particular portfolio or composite is accurate. 3. Firmwide only — never for a single portfolio, composite, or pooled fund; no compliance “except for.” BUT a firm can commission a performance examination on specific composites/funds and state that an examination was issued on them.
Benefits to the firm
More knowledgeable presentation personnel · better-quality presentations · better internal processes & procedures · possible marketing benefits.
Selecting a verifier
Match to operations/products/needs (large global vs small local; tax-exempt pension vs tax-focused; quant-derivatives vs direct real estate). Request: verifier description (personnel, org structure), services & past projects, project-management / sampling / testing procedures, client references, fees-proposal-timeline.
Process
Planning: gather all products, calculation methodologies, GIPS policies. Sampling (assertion is firmwide but samples are used): consider firm & composite size, internal controls & methods, number of years verified; deficiencies → larger samples. Testing: recordkeeping, policies & procedures, firm definition, thoroughness of the composite / limited-distribution-fund list, total firm assets calc, input data (vs custodial statements), composite construction & maintenance (discretionary classification, portfolio assignment, outlier returns = possible calc errors or misassignment), GIPS Report content & marketing material.
Quiz (circled in photo): least accurate about verification = “a requirement noted in a GIPS-compliant presentation” (it's voluntary); most accurate = “does not assure accuracy of any particular portfolio or composite.”
DrillCompliance spot-check patterns (essay-style, reasoning-derived)

Composites covering only 60% of fee-paying discretionary portfolios + “compliant for most assets” statement (JIM)Not acceptableFirmwide or nothing — no partial compliance language
Presenting gross-of-fees returns (Tribon excerpt)AcceptableGross returns are fine if after transaction costs; net-of-fees is recommended, not required → Tribon incorrect
Payer vs Receiver swap — leg by leg
▪ Payer swap = pay fixed, receive floating (MRR), on a notional principal.   ↳ floating leg gains when realized floating rates > rates expected at initiation → payer swap value ↑   ↳ floating rates below expectations → payer swap value ↓ ▪ Receiver swap = the counterparty: receive fixed, pay floating. Mirror image. ▪ Netting: payments are netted at each settlement — the party owing the larger amount pays the difference (reduces credit risk). ▪ First settlement: the floating payment for the first settlement date is known at initiation; later ones are not (set by the MRR at each reset).
Capital-market replication: payer swap = issue a fixed-rate bond + buy an FRN. Receiver swap = issue an FRN + buy a fixed-rate note. This replication is what drives swap duration (next tab).
Converting exposures — interactive (Fig 17.2)
Pick the existing exposure; the required swap and its drivers are decomposed below.

Trap: the locked-in cost is swap fixed rate + FRN margin — NOT the fixed rate alone. ABC pays 2% + 0.25% = 2.25% regardless of the realized MRR. Dropping the margin is the classic dropped-leg error.
Why a payer swap has NEGATIVE duration — two-leg decomposition
▪ Payer swap = issue fixed-rate note + buy FRN   ↳ leg 1: SHORT fixed-rate note → short a long-duration instrument → contributes negative duration   ↳ leg 2: LONG FRN → duration ≈ time to next reset (small) → contributes ≈ 0   ↳ net: MDₛ < 0 → payer swap gains value when rates rise ▪ Receiver swap = mirror → MDₛ > 0 → gains when rates fall (like a long bond) ▪ Portfolio effect: add payer swap → portfolio duration ↓  |  add receiver swap → portfolio duration ↑
Professorʼs note: all of this uses modified duration, which implicitly assumes a flat yield curve and parallel shifts.
Notional principal for a target duration
NPₛ = [ (MDₜ − MDₚ) / MDₛ ] × MVₚ NPₛ = notional swap principal MDₜ = target modified duration MDₚ = current portfolio MD MDₛ = modified duration of swap MVₚ = market value of portfolio
Target duration MDₜ
Portfolio duration MDₚ

Portfolio MV (millions)
Direction first, formula second: MDₜ > MDₚ → need duration ↑ → receiver swap (MDₛ = +). MDₜ < MDₚ → payer swap (MDₛ = −). Textbook: increase 4.5 → 6 on £120m with MDₛ = 2 → receiver swap, NPₛ = £90m.
FRA mechanics — who takes which side
▪ Future BORROWER (fears rates ↑) → LONG FRA   ↳ if realized MRR > forward rate → receives payment → offsets higher borrowing cost   ↳ if realized MRR < forward rate → pays → offsets cheaper borrowing → cost still locked ▪ Future LENDER (fears rates ↓) → SHORT FRA ▪ Key rule: long FRA value ↑ when rates rise; short FRA value ↑ when rates fall.
2×6 FRA timeline (Fig 17.3)
Trap: the FRA settlement is the present value of the rate difference, discounted from the end of the loan period back to FRA expiry — it is exchanged at expiry (T60), not at T180.

STIR / Eurodollar futures — IMM pricing decomposed
▪ Price convention: futures price = 100 − annualized forward rate (IMM Index)   ↳ forward rates fall → price rises → LONG futures gains ▪ Contract size: $1 million deposit, 90-day rate, quarterly maturities ▪ Tick value: 1 bp = $1m × 0.0001 × 90/360 = $25 per contract ▪ Contracts needed: amount to hedge / $1 million
TRAP — direction flip vs FRA: a LONG Eurodollar futures gains when rates FALL (price = 100 − rate), while a LONG FRA gains when rates RISE. Future depositor/lender → long futures. Future borrower → short futures (or long FRA). The exam loves this inversion.
Futures vs FRA: futures are standardized, exchange-traded, marked to market with margin; FRAs are dealer-customized (not liquid) and carry counterparty risk. Both price off the same forward rate (no-arbitrage).

Fixed-income futures — mechanics decomposed
▪ Notional bond: Treasury futures are priced off a notional government bond with a 6% coupon. ▪ Conversion factor (CF): clean price of $1 face of the eligible bond discounted at YTM 6%   ↳ coupon = 6% → CF = 1  |  coupon > 6% → CF > 1  |  coupon < 6% → CF < 1 ▪ Delivery option: the SHORT chooses which eligible bond to deliver (e.g. any UST 15–25y).
principal invoice price = (futures settlement / 100) × $100,000 × CF total invoice amount = principal invoice price + accrued interest profit/(loss) on delivery = [(settlement × CF) + AIₜ] − (CTD clean + AIₜ)
▪ CTD identification — two equivalent methods:   ↳ 1. highest implied repo rate on a cash-and-carry trade   ↳ 2. lowest basis (basis = spot price − futures price); lowest basis ↔ highest implied repo
CF bias trap: CFs assume a flat 6% term structure. Yields below 6% → bias to short-duration (high coupon, low maturity) bonds as CTD. Yields above 6% → bias to long-duration bonds.
Professorʼs note: with mark-to-market, the short does not receive the initial futures price at expiry — daily P/L (FPₜ − FPₜ₋₁) settles via margin; at maturity the short receives final settlement × CF (+ AI).

Hedging with Treasury futures — the logic chain
▪ rates ↑ → bond prices ↓ → futures price ↓ → SHORT futures gains → short futures hedge a long bond portfolio ▪ short futures → portfolio duration ↓  |  long futures → portfolio duration ↑ ▪ futures price tracks the CTD: Δfutures price = ΔCTD / CF (CTD and futures share the same duration)
ΔP = HR × Δfutures price HR = (ΔP / ΔCTD) × CF BPVHR (full hedge) = [ −BPVₚₒₙₜ / BPV⁋ₜ₃ ] × CF BPVHR (target) = [ (BPVₜₐₙₒₜ − BPVₚₒₙₜ) / BPV⁋ₜ₃ ] × CF BPVₚₒₙₜ = MDₚ × 0.0001 × MVₚ BPVₜₐₙₒₜ = MDₜ × 0.0001 × MVₚ BPV⁋ₜ₃ = MD⁋ₜ₃ × 0.0001 × MV⁋ₜ₃ MV⁋ₜ₃ = (CTD price / 100) × $100,000
Two classic dropped details: (1) MV⁋ₜ₃ uses the CTD price scaled to $100,000 face, not the raw quote. (2) The result is × CF at the END — multiply, never divide. Negative BPVHR = SELL that many contracts.

Why the hedge is imperfect — 3 factors
▪ 1. CTD switch: the hedge is built on the CTD; if the level or slope of the term structure changes significantly, the CTD bond — and hence the futures duration — may change. ▪ 2. Convexity ignored: duration is a linear approximation of price/yield; it ignores the convexity of the bonds. ▪ 3. Shaping risk: modified duration only captures parallel shifts; nonparallel changes (steepening, flattening, curvature) are unhedged. ▪ Plus basis / spread risk: portfolio bonds and the CTD are not perfect substitutes — mismatch between Δportfolio and Δhedge value.
Currency swap — mechanics decomposed
▪ Structure: each party pays periodic interest on a notional in ONE currency; the two notionals are equivalent at the inception FX rate. ▪ Purpose — synthetic borrowing: a firm without good access to foreign capital markets borrows domestically and swaps → effectively borrows in the foreign currency, hedging the FX risk of foreign cash flows. ▪ Cross-currency basis swap: the variant where notionals are exchanged at the beginning AND re-exchanged at the end. ▪ Typical legs: fixed or floating, but the standard market swap is floating-for-floating. ▪ Interest direction: each counterparty pays variable interest on the currency it initially received.
Terminology trap: in the euro-company example, the European company is the dollar payer and the dealer the euro payer — the label refers to the interest flows and final principal payment, NOT to the swap of initial principal.
No FX risk on principals: at expiration the notionals re-exchanged are the SAME amounts as at initiation — changes in the exchange rate over the life of the swap do not affect the principal flows.
Cross-currency basis swap — 3 phases (€ company, €50m @ 1.1236)
Cross-currency basis — what it is, why it exists
▪ CIRP: under covered interest rate parity, borrowing USD directly = borrowing foreign currency + hedging with a currency swap. Held well for 3 decades pre-2008. ▪ Definition: basis = the additional cost of borrowing dollars synthetically (via swap) relative to direct USD cash-market borrowing. ▪ Convention: basis is quoted from the foreign-currency perspective, not the USD perspective. ▪ Negative basis = synthetic USD cost > direct USD cost. Most currencies have shown a negative basis vs USD since the crisis.   ↳ implication: the USD borrower must accept a lower rate on the foreign-currency interest it receives. ▪ Why CIRP fails since 2008 — three drivers:   ↳ 1. stricter capital adequacy rules → covered interest arbitrage became much more costly for banks   ↳ 2. high demand for USD loans   ↳ 3. USD lending via swaps has attracted a premium since the crisis
USD investor angle: when a foreign currency shows a negative basis, a USD investor can swap USD → foreign currency, buy foreign-currency bonds, and use the swap to convert returns back — earning MORE than direct USD bonds (the basis is harvested as extra yield).

All-in synthetic rate decomposed: pays €ref + spread on the loan; receives €ref + basis on the swap → net € outflow = spread − basis; pays $ref on the swap → all-in = $ref + (spread − basis). Spread 60, basis −20 → $ref + 80 bp. A negative basis ADDS to the cost — the sign here is the classic dropped detail.
Currency forwards vs futures
▪ Forwards: customized — tailored to the exact quantity AND the exact date of the expected foreign-currency flow. ▪ Futures: standardized quantity and delivery dates; limited currency-pair range; greater liquidity attracts investors and dealers. ▪ Direction: expecting to RECEIVE foreign currency → SELL futures on it (promise to deliver). Having to PAY foreign currency → BUY.
HR = amount of currency to be exchanged / futures contract size
Settlement-date mismatch — risk decomposed:
▪ futures settle BEFORE the currency arrives → exchange-rate risk from settlement until receipt
▪ futures settle AFTER → position closed early at the then-futures price ≠ spot → basis risk (more or less USD than delivery would have given)

Equity swaps — structure decomposed
▪ Purpose: synthetic exposure to stocks — the economic benefits of ownership without the cost and expense of ownership. ▪ 3 main types:   ↳ 1. pay fixed, receive equity return   ↳ 2. pay floating, receive equity return   ↳ 3. pay another equity return, receive equity return (e.g. pay Nasdaq, receive S&P 500) ▪ Equity return basis: single stock | basket of equities | equity index ▪ Return type: price return (typical) or total return (price + dividends) ▪ To REDUCE exposure: pay equity return, receive floating/fixed = synthetic sell equity + invest in money markets
Equity swap vs physical stock (Fig 17.4)
AdvantagesDisadvantages
▪ gain exposure when physical participation is restricted
▪ avoid tax on physical ownership (e.g. stamp duty)
▪ avoid custody fees
▪ avoid monitoring costs of corporate actions (dividends, splits, buybacks, M&A)		 ▪ typically require collateral
▪ illiquid
▪ no voting rights

Equity futures & forwards — uses and mechanics
▪ Futures: exchange-traded, standardized, margin, low transaction costs; on indexes and single stocks. ▪ Uses: tactical allocation (SELL → reduce / BUY → increase equity exposure), diversification, international exposure, directional bets. ▪ Forwards: same advantages but illiquid, no mark-to-market, counterparty credit risk (no clearinghouse); major advantage = customization. ▪ Multiplier: actual futures value = quoted points × multiplier (S&P 500: $250 | FTSE 100: £10).
number of contracts (hedge) = monetary value to hedge / (futures price × multiplier) number of futures required = [ (βₜ − βₚ) / βₒ ] × [ MVₚ / F ] F = futures price × multiplier full hedge: βₜ = 0
Trap: negative result = SELL contracts. And a hedged-but-rounded HR leaves a small residual (FTSE example: net −£300 from rounding 821.9 → 822).

Cash equitization — concept decomposed
▪ Problem: cash yields less than equity/FI → cash drag → risk of underperforming the benchmark. ▪ Solution: BUY index futures to replicate the index return on the cash balance. ▪ Why futures: liquidity + low transaction costs vs direct equity investment. ▪ Aliases: cash securitization, cash overlay. ▪ Alternative: buy calls + sell puts, same strike & expiry = synthetic forward position. ▪ Setup in the beta formula: βₚ = 0 (cash), βₜ = 1 (match the index), MVₚ = cash position.

VIX — what it actually measures
▪ Definition: implied volatility of the S&P 500 over a forward period of 30 days — a weighted average inferred from traded S&P 500 calls AND puts with avg expiration of 30 days.   ↳ NOT actual/realized volatility — it is the expected volatility priced into options ("fear index / fear gauge"). ▪ Interpretation: annualized SD of expected ±% moves over the next 30 days, at 68% confidence. ▪ Rules of thumb: < 20 = low-risk environment | > 30 = high-risk. Very low → excessively bullish market; very high → excessively bearish. ▪ Two empirical properties: (1) mean reversion — spikes do not last; (2) negative correlation with stock returns, even more pronounced in downturns → VIX derivatives can offset equity losses. ▪ Other indexes: VSTOXX (EURO STOXX 50), VFTSE (FTSE 100), VDAX-NEW (DAX 30); US: S&P 100, DJIA, Nasdaq, Russell 2000.
Calculator — reading a VIX level
VIX level
VIX futures — how they differ from every other future
▪ No cost-of-carry pricing: impossible to invest directly in spot VIX → the cost-of-carry model cannot determine fair value. ▪ Price meaning: expected S&P 500 volatility in the 30-day period AFTER the futures expiration date. ▪ LONG VIX futures = tail-risk protection: vol ↑ in a crash → equity portfolio ↓ but VIX futures ↑. ▪ SHORT VIX futures = short volatility: captures the volatility risk premium embedded in S&P 500 options — but large losses if expected volatility spikes. ▪ History: CBOE futures 2004, options 2006 → volatility became a separate, tradeable asset class (pure-play bets).
VIX options
▪ Cash-settled, European-style — exercisable only at contract maturity. ▪ Value driven by expectations of VIX at contract expiry (not spot VIX today): calls gain when expected volatility at maturity ↑; puts gain when it ↓.
Contango vs backwardation — decomposed
▪ Basis = spot − futures price. Negative basis defines contango (longer-dated > short-dated): market expects 30-day vol to RISE. Typical when VIX is low (textbook: 18 Jul 2011, spot 20.95, upward curve). ▪ Backwardation: downward curve — market expects vol to FALL back. Typical after a spike (textbook: 9 Aug 2011, spot 35.06 after the S&P US-debt downgrade of 5 Aug 2011). ▪ Convergence: VIX futures settle against spot VIX → futures price converges to spot at expiration; the basis moves toward zero over the life of the contract.   ↳ contango: futures price declines toward spot → long loses on the roll   ↳ backwardation: futures price rises toward spot → long gains on the roll ▪ Roll yield = the P/L generated as basis → 0. Steeper short end of the curve → roll yield magnified.
Roll yield — interactive (position × term structure)
Position
Term structure
Variance swap — structure decomposed
▪ Payoff basis: variance (σ²), not volatility (SD). ▪ Fixed leg: implied variance over the period = variance strike — known at initiation. ▪ Variable leg: realized variance of the underlying over the swap life — known only at maturity. ▪ Long (purchaser): RECEIVES realized variance, PAYS the strike. Gains when realized > implied. Pure play on realized vs expected variance. ▪ Mechanics: NO notional exchange at initiation, NO interim settlements — one single payment at expiration. Value = 0 at initiation (implied vol = best ex ante estimate of realized). ▪ Any underlying works as long as it is traded with a record of daily prices.
settlementₜ = variance notional × (realized variance − variance strike) N₍ₐₙ = vega notional / (2 × K) profit/(loss) = N₍ₐₙ × (σ² − K²) = N₌ₒ₏ₐ × (σ² − K²) / (2K) realized: Rᵢ = ln(Pₜ / Pₜ₋₁) daily variance = Σ Rᵢ² / (N − 1) annualized = daily × 252
Two squaring traps: (1) both σ and K are quoted as volatilities (SD) — square them before any payoff computation (strike 20 → K² = 400). (2) Market quotes vega notional, not variance notional — divide by 2K first.
Professorʼs notes: (1) realized variance does NOT deduct the mean — movement is measured regardless of direction, which makes variances perfectly additive (one-year variance = two equal six-month pieces). That additivity is what powers the MTM valuation. (2) Vega = Δpremium/Δvolatility — why vega notional is the natural market quote.
Convexity — why hedgers love variance swaps
▪ Payoff is in variance, strike in volatility → payoff is convex in volatility (like bond price vs yield).   ↳ realized vol BELOW strike → losses smaller than a linear volatility derivative   ↳ realized vol ABOVE strike → gains greater than the linear derivative ▪ Tail-risk appeal: when equities crash and vol explodes, the swap profit increases at an accelerating rate.
Valuing a variance swap during its life — 3 steps
Step 1: expected variance at maturity (time-weighted, thanks to additivity) E[var] = σₜ² × (t/T) + K²₍ₜ₋ₜ₎ × ((T−t)/T) σₜ² = realized vol (initiation → valuation date), squared K₍ₜ₋ₜ₎ = implied vol quoted NOW for the REMAINING period, squared Step 2: expected payoff at maturity payoff = N₍ₐₙ × (E[var] − original strike²) Step 3: discount back to the valuation date value = payoff / (1 + r × remaining/12)
Dropped-detail watch: Step 2 uses the ORIGINAL strike (squared), not the currently quoted strike — the current quote only feeds the remaining-period leg of Step 1. And the discount rate is unannualized over the remaining months only.

Inferring market expectations — which derivative for what
ApplicationDerivative
Inferring expectations of FOMC movesFed funds futures
Inferring expectations of inflationCPI swaps
Inferring expectations of future volatilityVIX futures and options
Market expectations are derived from market prices — and can change rapidly after a market shock.
Fed funds — the two rates, decomposed
▪ Federal funds rate: rate deposit institutions charge each other on overnight interbank loans. The FFE (Fed funds effective) = weighted average of rates actually charged. ▪ Federal funds target rate: set by FOMC governors (8 meetings/year), as a range (e.g. 2.25%–2.50%), driven mainly by inflation and GDP growth. ▪ Control mechanism: the Fed does NOT directly set the FFE — it steers it into the range via open-market operations and interest paid on bank reserves. ▪ Fed funds futures: trade on the CME; price = 100 − expected average FFE at contract maturity; monthly maturities out to 36 months.
Probability of a target-rate change
% probability of rate change = (FFE implied by futures − current target rate) / (target rate assuming the change − current target rate) = (implied FFE − current target) / expected size of change current target = MIDPOINT of the target range
Trap: "current Fed funds target rate" in the formula = the midpoint of the range (1.50–1.75 → 1.625), not the bottom or top of the range.

Reading 17 · Swaps, Forwards, and Futures Strategies
Full-reading recap, module by module: interest rate risk — swaps, FRAs, futures (17.1 / LOS 17.a), currency exposure (17.2 / 17.b), equity risk (17.3 / 17.c), derivatives on volatility (17.4 / 17.d), and portfolio uses — targeted exposures, asset allocation, inferring market expectations (17.5 / 17.e–17.f). Every calculation below is node-verified against the Schweser figures.
Where the marks are: (1) picking the right instrument & direction — payer vs receiver, long vs short, buy vs sell — from the exposure and the rate/market view; (2) the four hedge-sizing formulas: NPS (swap duration), BPVHR (bond futures), β-adjustment contracts (equity futures), NVAR = Nvega/2K (variance swaps); (3) sign conventions — negative answer = sell/short; (4) cash-flow direction on every leg of every swap.
Module 17.1 · Managing Interest Rate Risk
LOS 17.aInterest rate swaps — payer vs receiver
Payer swapPay fixed, receive floating on a notional principal. Value rises if future floating rates come in above what was expected at initiation; falls if below. Counterparty holds the receiver swap (receive fixed, pay floating). NettingIn practice payments are netted — the party owing the larger amount pays the difference — to reduce credit risk. Floating leg timingThe floating payment for the first settlement date is known at initiation; later ones are not. A quarterly-pay swap settles on the quarterly MRR (market reference rate). ReplicationPayer swap ≡ issue a fixed-rate bond + buy an identical FRN. Receiver swap ≡ issue an FRN + buy a fixed-rate note. Same cash flows via a capital-market trade.
Existing exposureConvertingSwap requiredBeneficial when
Floating-rate liabilityFloating → fixedPayerFloating rates expected to rise
Fixed-rate liabilityFixed → floatingReceiverFloating rates expected to fall
Floating-rate assetFloating → fixedReceiverFloating rates expected to fall
Fixed-rate assetFixed → floatingPayerFloating rates expected to rise
⚠ Liability vs asset flips the swap. A floating liability is fixed with a payer swap, but a floating asset is fixed with a receiver swap. Read which side of the balance sheet the exposure sits on before naming the swap.
Example — converting a floating-rate liability to fixed (ABC, Inc.)
ABC issued $30M 4-yr semiannual FRNs at 6-mo MRR + 25 bp, expects rates to rise, and enters a 3-yr payer swap: fixed 2%, notional $30M, same settlement dates. MRR at initiation = 1.5%; at date 1 = 3%.
Date 1 (MRR was 1.5%) Step 1 swap fixed paid ..... $30M × 2% × 180/360 = $300,000 Step 2 swap floating rec ... $30M × 1.5% × 180/360 = $225,000 Step 3 swap net ............ 225,000 − 300,000 = −$75,000 Step 4 FRN coupon .......... $30M × (1.5% + 0.25%) × 180/360 = $262,500 Step 5 total paid .......... 262,500 + 75,000 = $337,500 Date 2 (MRR was 3%) swap net = 450,000 − 300,000 = +$150,000; FRN = $487,500 total paid = 487,500 − 150,000 = $337,500 (identical) Lock check: $30M × (2% + 0.25%) × 180/360 = $337,500 = swap fixed + FRN margin
The FRN floating coupon and the swap floating receipt offset exactly (same MRR, same dates), leaving swap fixed rate + FRN margin regardless of realized MRR. This kills both the downside and the upside of floating exposure.
Using swaps to alter portfolio duration
Swap durationsFixed-rate note has greater MD than an identical FRN ⇒ payer swap has negative duration (gains when rates rise); receiver swap has positive duration (loses when rates rise). Effect on portfolioAdd payer ⇒ portfolio duration falls. Add receiver ⇒ duration rises. Notional formulaNPS = [(MDT − MDP) / MDS] × MVP — target MD, current portfolio MD, swap MD, portfolio market value. Which MDSIf increasing duration, use the receiver swap’s (positive) MD; if reducing, the payer swap’s MD (negative signs then take care of direction).
Example (£120M U.K. bonds, MD 4.5 → 6; payer MD = −2, receiver MD = +2) Step 1 duration must rise ⇒ receiver swap Step 2 NPₛ = [(6 − 4.5) / 2] × £120M = £90 million
⚠ Professor’s Note: the whole analysis uses modified duration — it implicitly assumes a flat yield curve and parallel shifts. Non-parallel moves (shaping risk) are not captured.
LOS 17.aForward rate agreements (FRAs)
What’s hedgedUncertainty about a future short-term borrowing or lending rate (e.g., borrowing a lump sum for 60 days, 30 days from now). DirectionLong FRA ⇒ hedges a future borrower; gains when rates rise. Short FRA ⇒ hedges a future lender; gains when rates fall. Payoff (long)(floating rate − fixed FRA rate) × days/360 × NP, computed for the loan period. NP = anticipated loan amount. Settlement timingPayment is based on end-of-loan-period interest, but is discounted back and exchanged at FRA expiry (the loan start date). NamingA 2×6 FRA: expires in 2 months, on the rate covering months 2→6 (a 120-day rate discovered at T60).
Example — Smithies Plc borrows £1M for 180d, 90d from now, at MRR + 50 bp; long FRA @ 5% MRR = 7% at expiry: loan cost ......... 7.5% × 180/360 × £1M = £37,500 FRA receipt ....... (7% − 5%) × 180/360 × £1M = +£10,000 net ............... £27,500 MRR = 3% at expiry: loan cost £17,500; FRA pays −£10,000 → net £27,500 Lock check: 5.5% × 180/360 × £1M = £27,500 = FRA rate + 50 bp spread
Short-term interest rate (STIR) futures — Eurodollar
ContractBased on $1M deposits for 90 days starting at futures expiry; standardized maturities (typically quarterly); hedgers usually close out with an offsetting trade. IMM pricingPrice = 100 − annualized forward rate. Futures prices rise when forward rates fall. Tick value1 bp move = $25 per contract: $1M × 0.0001 × 90/360. vs FRA directionLong Eurodollar futures gains when rates FALL — the opposite of a long FRA. A future depositor/lender goes long futures; a future borrower goes short futures. vs FRA structureFutures: standardized, exchange-traded, margined / marked-to-market, liquid. FRAs: dealer-customized, not liquid, counterparty risk. Both prevent arbitrage by pricing off the same forward rate.
Example — Luard: $20M inheritance in 120d, 90-day deposit at MRR − 25 bp; futures @ 95, long 20 contracts A. MRR = 3.5% in 120 days: deposit interest ... $20M × (3.5% − 0.25%) × 90/360 = $162,500 contracts .......... $20M / $1M = 20 futures at expiry .. 100 − 3.5 = 96.5 → gain 150 bp × $25 × 20 = +$75,000 total .............. $237,500 B. MRR = 6.5%: interest $312,500; futures 93.5 → −$75,000; total $237,500 Lock check: $20M × (5% − 0.25%) × 90/360 = $237,500
⚠ Long futures ≠ long FRA. Long FRA gains when rates rise; long STIR futures gains when rates fall (price = 100 − rate). Exam answers hinge on this inversion.
Fixed-income (Treasury) futures — CF, invoice price, CTD
Delivery optionShort party may deliver any eligible bond (U.S. T-bond futures: maturity 15–25 yrs). Longer-maturity bonds are usually hedged with bond futures (best liquidity). Conversion factorFutures price is quoted vs a notional 6% coupon bond. Each deliverable gets a CF = clean price of $1 face discounted at 6% YTM. Coupon > 6% ⇒ CF > 1; coupon < 6% ⇒ CF < 1. Invoice priceprincipal invoice = (futures settlement / 100) × $100,000 × CF; total invoice = principal invoice + accrued interest. CTDCF bias (flat 6% curve assumed) ⇒ one bond gives the short the greatest gain / smallest loss at delivery = cheapest-to-deliver. Found via highest implied repo rate or lowest basis (basis = spot − futures price). Delivery P&Lprofit/(loss) = [(settlement × CF) + AIT] − (CTD clean price + AIT). Yield biasYields < 6% ⇒ CTD biased to short-duration (high coupon, low maturity); yields > 6% ⇒ biased to long-duration.
Example — identifying the CTD (settlement 148.75, AI = 0) Bond 1: invoice 148.75 × 0.9422 = 140.15 ; dirty 141.13 → loss −$980 per $100,000 Bond 2: invoice 148.75 × 0.9719 = 144.57 ; dirty 145.10 → loss −$530 ⇒ Bond 2 is CTD (smallest delivery loss)
Professor’s Note (MTM): daily P&L on futures = FPt − FPt−1, credited/debited to margin. To avoid double counting, the short receives final settlement price × CF at maturity, not the initial futures price.
Hedging interest rate risk with Treasury futures — BPVHR
DirectionTo hedge a long bond portfolio, sell futures: rates ↑ ⇒ bond prices ↓, short futures gain. Short futures reduce duration; long futures increase it. Why CTD-basedFutures prices track the CTD most closely (lowest basis) ⇒ Δfutures price = ΔCTD / CF; futures and CTD share the same duration. BPVBPV = expected value change for a 1 bp yield move: BPVportfolio = MDP × 0.0001 × MVP; BPVCTD = MDCTD × 0.0001 × MVCTD, with MVCTD = CTD price / 100 × $100,000. Full hedgeBPVHR = (−BPVportfolio / BPVCTD) × CF = number of futures (negative ⇒ short). Target durationBPVHR = [(BPVtarget − BPVportfolio) / BPVCTD] × CF, with BPVtarget = MDtarget × 0.0001 × MVP. Full hedge = special case BPVtarget = 0. Basis / spread riskPortfolio and CTD are imperfect substitutes ⇒ mismatch between asset value change and hedge value change = basis (spread) risk.
Example — immunizing £60M (MD 10.75) with Long Gilt futures (CTD: price 139.56, CF 1.0709, MD 9.7) Step 1 BPVₚ = 10.75 × 0.0001 × £60M = £64,500 Step 2 BPV₡ₜₖ = 9.7 × 0.0001 × (139.56/100 × £100,000) = £135.37 Step 3 BPVHR = (−64,500 / 135.37) × 1.0709 = −510.25 → sell 510 Target MD 8.7 instead: BPVₜ = 8.7 × 0.0001 × £60M = £52,200 BPVHR = [(52,200 − 64,500) / 135.37] × 1.0709 = −97.30 → sell 97
⚠ Three reasons hedges are imperfect: (1) the CTD can change if the level/slope of the curve moves — futures duration then changes too; (2) duration ignores convexity; (3) MD only captures parallel shifts — steepening/flattening/curvature = shaping risk.
Module Quiz 17.1 — answers (reasoning-derived, node-verified)
Q1 → CQuarterly floating payments are set in advance, paid in arrears: the Day-270 payment uses the 90-day MRR observed at Day 180. Q2 — receiver swapSharma holds a floating asset (FRN) and fears falling rates ⇒ receiver swap (receive 4% fixed, pay floating) on $4M. Settlement 1 (MRR 3.5%): net = 4M × (4% − 3.5%) × 0.5 = +$10,000; FRN coupon $78,000 → total $88,000. Settlement 2 (MRR 2.5%): net +$30,000; FRN $58,000 → total $88,000. Locked at swap rate + 40 bp margin: 4M × 4.4% × 0.5 = $88,000 per period. Q3 → ABPVₚ = 12 × 0.0001 × $200M = 240,000; BPVₜ = 8 × 0.0001 × $200M = 160,000; BPV₡ₜₖ = 14.54 × 0.0001 × (126.39/100 × 100,000) = 183.77. BPVHR = (160,000 − 240,000)/183.77 × 0.7689 = −334.7 → sell 335 contracts.
Module 17.2 · Managing Currency Exposure
LOS 17.bCurrency swaps & cross-currency basis swaps
Currency swapEach party makes periodic interest payments on a notional in a different currency; notionals are equivalent at the inception FX rate. Enables synthetic borrowing in a foreign currency when direct access is poor/expensive. Cross-currency basis swapNotionals exchanged at start AND re-exchanged at maturity at the same amounts ⇒ no FX risk on principal. Typical legs: floating-for-floating, quarterly. Who pays whatEach counterparty pays variable interest on the currency it received at initiation. The company borrowing locally passes the swap-received interest to service its bank loan. Naming trap“Dollar payer” / “euro payer” refers to the interest flows and final principal payment, NOT the initial principal exchange.
Cross-currency basis
CIRP baselineUnder covered interest rate parity, borrowing USD directly costs the same as borrowing foreign currency + swapping. Frictionless market ⇒ zero basis. Why it failsSince the GFC: stricter capital rules raise arbitrage costs + high demand for USD ⇒ USD lending via swaps commands a premium; basis ≠ 0. Negative basisViewed from the foreign currency: if synthetic USD (via swap) costs more than direct USD borrowing, the foreign currency shows negative basis. Most currencies since the crisis. The USD borrower accepts a lower rate on the foreign-currency interest it receives. USD investor playWhen basis is negative, a USD investor can swap USD → foreign currency, buy foreign bonds, swap returns back, earning more than USD bonds.
Example — Boivis: needs $50M 4 yrs; direct USD = $ref + 100 bp; instead borrows € at €ref + 60 bp + basis swap (−20 bp); spot $1.1815; €ref 1.5%, $ref 2.0% → 1.6% / 1.9% at settle 1 Step 1 € principal ......... $50M / 1.1815 = €42,319,086 (re-exchanged at maturity) Step 2 pays € loan ......... 42,319,086 × (1.5% + 0.6%) × 90/360 = €222,175 Step 3 pays $ swap ......... $50M × 2.0% × 90/360 = $250,000 Step 4 receives € swap ..... 42,319,086 × (1.5% − 0.2%) × 90/360 = €137,537 Step 5 direct $ cost ....... $50M × 3.0% × 90/360 = $375,000 synthetic $ cost .... $50M × (2.0% + 0.6% + 0.2%) × 90/360 = $350,000 net benefit ......... $25,000 = $50M × (1% − 0.8%) × 90/360 Settle 2 (1.6%/1.9%): loan €232,755; $ swap $237,500; rec €148,117; direct $362,500 vs synthetic $337,500 → benefit $25,000 Locked cost = $ref + 80 bp (60 bp loan spread + 20 bp negative basis)
⚠ The −20 bp basis is SUBTRACTED from the € interest Boivis receives on the swap — it doesn’t reduce what it pays. Synthetic cost = $ref + loan spread (60) + basis paid away (20) = +80 bp, still 20 bp cheaper than direct (+100 bp).
Currency forwards & futures
Forwards vs futuresForwards: customized (exact quantity + date). Futures: standardized quantity & delivery dates, limited pairs, but greater liquidity. Hedge ratioHR = amount of currency to be exchanged / futures contract size. DirectionReceiving foreign currency later ⇒ sell its futures (deliver it at the locked rate). Paying foreign currency later ⇒ buy its futures. Basis riskIf futures settlement date ≠ cash-flow date, the hedge is imperfect: futures closed early trade at a price ≠ spot ⇒ more or less domestic currency than a matched delivery.
Example — U.S. firm receives €20M in 90d; EUR-USD futures 1.3150, size €125,000 HR = €20,000,000 / €125,000 = sell 160 contracts At settlement: deliver €20M, receive 20M × 1.3150 = $26,300,000
Module Quiz 17.2 — answers (reasoning-derived, node-verified)
Q1 → ANZD trades at a positive cross-currency basis vs USD ⇒ a USD investor picks up the basis by swapping USD for NZD and investing in NZ government securities. GBP’s negative basis would cost a USD-based investor; C starts from GBP, not USD. Q2 — long 160 EUR futuresWood owes €20M in 30d (GBP-based) ⇒ buy 20M/125,000 = 160 EUR-GBP futures @ 0.8989. Unhedged cost = 20M × 0.9034 = £18,068,000. Hedged: futures gain = (0.9054 − 0.8989) × 125,000 × 160 = +£130,000 → net cost £17,938,000. Futures expire in 40d (> 30d) ⇒ closed early at 0.9054, leaving basis risk. Q3 — saves 25 bpABC borrows $30M × 1.2000 = $36M at $ref + 40 bp, swaps into £30M paying £ref − 15 bp, receiving $ref. Settle 1 ($2.5% / £1.5%): pays loan 36M × 2.9% × 0.5 = $522,000; receives swap $450,000; pays £30M × 1.35% × 0.5 = £202,500. Settle 2 ($2.25% / £1%): loan $477,000; receives $405,000; pays £127,500. Synthetic £ cost = £ref + 40 − 15 = £ref + 25 bp vs direct £ref + 50 bp ⇒ saves 25 bp ≈ £37,500 per semiannual period (30M × 0.25% × 0.5).
Module 17.3 · Managing Equity Risk
LOS 17.cEquity swaps
PurposeCreate synthetic exposure to equities — the economic benefits of ownership without the cost of holding shares. Return may be on a single stock, a basket, or an index; price return (typical) or total return (price + dividends). Three types(1) pay fixed, receive equity return; (2) pay floating, receive equity return; (3) pay one equity return, receive another (e.g., pay Nasdaq, receive S&P 500). PaymentsUsually a series at periodic settlement dates; some swaps settle with a single payment at maturity. Negative return trapIf the index falls, the equity-return receiver pays BOTH legs: the floating rate and the negative equity return.
Advantages vs physical stockDisadvantages
Gain exposure where physical participation is restrictedTypically require collateral
Avoid tax on physical ownership (e.g., stamp duty)Swaps are illiquid
Avoid custody feesNo voting rights
Avoid monitoring costs from corporate actions (dividends, splits, buybacks, M&A)
Example — German pension fund, €200M tracking DAX 30 (12,400), wants +40% exposure: swap NP €80M, pay floating + 30 bp, receive index; semiannual, 6-mo rate 6% Scenario 1 — DAX → 13,020 (+5%): portfolio ....... €200M × 5% = +€10M equity leg ...... €80M × 5% = +€4M floating leg .... €80M × (6% + 0.3%) × 180/360 = −€2.52M swap net ........ +€1.48M = €80M × [0.05 − 0.063 × 180/360] position ........ +€11.48M Scenario 2 — DAX → 11,780 (−5%): swap net = −4M − 2.52M = −€6.52M → position −€16.52M
The swap is the synthetic equivalent of borrowing €80M at floating + 30 bp and investing it in the index tracker. To reduce equity exposure instead: pay the equity return, receive floating/fixed = synthetic sale of equity into the money market.
Equity futures & forwards
UsesTactical allocation (selling futures reduces equity exposure, buying increases it); diversification; international exposure; directional bets. Futures vs forwardsFutures: exchange-traded, standardized, margined, low transaction costs. Forwards: customizable but illiquid, no clearinghouse ⇒ counterparty credit risk. MultiplierActual futures price = quoted points × multiplier. S&P 500 = $250/pt; FTSE 100 = £10/pt. Contracts to hedgeN = monetary value of position to be hedged / (futures price × multiplier), negative for a hedge (short).
Example — hedge 30% of a £200M FTSE tracker; Sep futures 7,300, £10/pt Step 1 N = −£60M / (7,300 × £10) = −821.9 → sell 822 FTSE +5% (futures 7,665): futures ......... (7,665 − 7,300) × £10 × (−822) = −£3,000,300 portfolio ....... 1.05 × £200M = £210M → net £206,999,700 hedged slice .... −3,000,300 + 60M × 5% = −£300 (rounding only) FTSE −5% (futures 6,935): futures +£3,000,300; portfolio £190M → net £193,000,300; slice +£300
Achieving a target portfolio beta
Formulanumber of futures = [(βT − βP) / βF] × (MVP / F), with F = futures price × multiplier. Negative ⇒ sell. DriversβT target beta; βP current beta; βF futures (index) beta, usually 1; MVP portfolio value. Short futures cut beta, long futures raise it. Full hedge: βT = 0. Effectiveness checkrealized β = % change in portfolio / % change in index.
Example — $60M, β 1.2 → 0.8; S&P futures 2,984 × $250; index −1.5% over 6 mo Step 1 F = 2,984 × $250 = $746,000 Step 2 N = [(0.8 − 1.2)/1] × (60M / 746,000) = −32.17 → sell 32 Step 3 portfolio: $60M × [1 − (0.015 × 1.2)] = $58,920,000 Step 4 futures: 2,984 × 0.985 = 2,939.24 → 2,939 (nearest 0.5 pt) profit = (2,984 − 2,939) × $250 × 32 = +$360,000 Step 5 net $59,280,000 → return −1.2% Step 6 realized β = −0.012 / −0.015 = 0.8 ✓
⚠ The portfolio moves by index move × its OWN beta (−1.5% × 1.2 = −1.8%), not by the index move. The futures leg then drags the combined return to target β × index move.
Cash equitization (cash securitization / cash overlay)
ProblemCash yields less than equity/FI ⇒ cash drag, risk of underperforming the benchmark. FixBuy index futures replicating the return the cash would earn in the index — liquid, low transaction cost. Alternative: buy calls + sell puts (same strike/expiry) = synthetic forward. SizingSame beta formula with βP = 0 (cash) and βT = 1 (or the fund’s target): N = (βT/βF) × (cash / F).
Example — $8M cash, S&P futures 2,780 × $250, β 1 F = $695,000 ; N = (1/1) × (8M / 695,000) = 11.51 → buy 12 contracts

Module 17.4 · Derivatives on Volatility
LOS 17.dThe VIX Index
What it measuresImplied (expected) volatility priced into S&P 500 options over a forward 30-day window — a weighted average across traded calls & puts averaging 30 days to expiry. NOT actual/realized volatility. A.k.a. the fear index/gauge. InterpretationVIX = annualized SD of expected ±% S&P moves over next 30 days. VIX 20 ⇒ ±20% over a year with 68% confidence ⇒ 30-day range ± 20/√12 = 5.77%. Rules of thumb< 20 low-risk environment; > 30 high-risk. Extremes flag sentiment: very low VIX = excessively bullish; very high = excessively bearish. Spikes mean-revert. CorrelationVIX vs stock returns: negative, stronger in downturns ⇒ VIX-based derivatives can offset equity losses when vol spikes. Other indexesU.S.: S&P 100, DJIA, Nasdaq, Russell 2000. Europe: VSTOXX (EURO STOXX 50), VFTSE (FTSE 100), VDAX-NEW (DAX 30).
VIX futures & options
PricingSpot VIX is not investable ⇒ cost-of-carry does NOT apply. Futures price = expected S&P vol in the 30 days after the futures expiration. Tail hedgeBuy VIX futures to protect equities from extreme downturns: vol ↑ ⇒ equities ↓ but VIX futures ↑. Selling VIX futures = short vol, harvesting the vol premium in S&P options — large losses if expected vol spikes. Term structureContango (typical, VIX low): longer futures > spot; basis (spot − futures) negative. Backwardation (post-shock, VIX high): futures < spot. Shape reflects expected 30-day vol at future dates. Convergence & rollFutures settle against spot VIX ⇒ basis → 0 over life. P&L from that drift = roll yield, magnified when the short end of the curve is steeper than the long end. VIX optionsEuropean, cash-settled, exercisable only at maturity ⇒ valued off expected VIX at expiry. Calls gain if expected vol at maturity ↑; puts gain if it ↓.
PositionTerm structureRoll yield
Long futuresContangoNegative
Short futuresContangoPositive
Long futuresBackwardationPositive
Short futuresBackwardationNegative
Variance swaps
Payoff basisVariance (σ²), not volatility. Fixed leg = variance strike = implied volatility², known at initiation. Variable leg = realized variance of the underlying over the swap’s life, known only at maturity. Long / shortLong (purchaser) receives realized variance, pays the strike. Realized vol > strike ⇒ long profits; realized vol < strike ⇒ long loses. Pure play on realized vs implied variance. StructureNo notional exchanged, no interim settlements, single payment at expiration: settlementT = variance notional × (realized variance − variance strike). Value = 0 at initiation (implied vol = best ex ante estimate). Notional conversionQuoted as vega notional; NVAR = Nvega / (2 × K). profit/(loss) = NVAR × (σ² − K²) = Nvega × (σ² − K²)/(2K). Both σ and K quoted in vol (SD) terms ⇒ square them. Realized varianceRᵢ = ln(Pₜ/Pₜ₋₁); daily variance = ΣRᵢ²/(N−1) — mean NOT deducted (movement regardless of direction; makes variances time-additive). Annualized = daily × 252. ConvexityPayoff convex in volatility: vs a linear vol derivative, losses smaller below strike, gains greater above ⇒ attractive tail-risk hedge (gains accelerate as vol explodes). Mark-to-marketValue drifts as realized & implied diverge. Expected variance at maturity = time-weighted average: (σₜ² × t/T) + (K²(T−t) × (T−t)/T), using annualized realized vol so far and the implied vol quoted for the remaining term.
MTM in 3 steps Step 1 expected variance to maturity = (σₜ² × t/T) + (K²ᾐₜ₋ₜᾑ × (T−t)/T) Step 2 expected payoff at maturity = Nₖₐₘ × (expected variance − original strike²) Step 3 discount to valuation date at the unannualized rate
Example — Luke Amos: 1-yr S&P variance swap, Nₖₓₐ = $100,000, strike 20; after 9 mo realized vol 21; 3-mo strike now 22; r = 2% Step 1 EV = (21² × 9/12) + (22² × 3/12) = 330.75 + 121 = 451.75 Step 2 Nₖₐₘ = 100,000 / (2 × 20) = $2,500 payoff = (451.75 − 20²) × 2,500 = $129,375 Step 3 r = 2% × 3/12 = 0.5% → value = 129,375 / 1.005 = $128,731 gain to the long (purchaser), loss to the seller
⚠ Time weights use elapsed/remaining over TOTAL: t/T = 9/12 on realized, (T−t)/T = 3/12 on the 3-month re-quoted strike — and everything is squared before weighting. Forgetting to square K (20 → 400) is the classic error.

Q1 → BLeast accurate: VIX measures implied, not realized, volatility. A and C are true statements. Q2 → Bprofit/(loss) = notional variance × (σ² − K²). Vega notional needs the /2K conversion first. Q3 — −€3,678,447 to QuarkNₖₐₘ = 150,000/(2 × 15) = €5,000. EV = (28² × 3/12) + (32² × 9/12) = 196 + 768 = 964. Payoff = (964 − 15²) × 5,000 = €3,695,000. Discount 0.6% × 9/12 = 0.45%: 3,695,000 / 1.0045 = €3,678,447 — a gain to the long and a loss to Quark (the seller), who posts margin accordingly.
Module 17.5 · Uses of Derivatives in Portfolio Management
LOS 17.eTargeted equity exposure with a total return swap
Example — Seago: 80,000 ABC shares @ €6.00 (can’t sell: tax); fears decline; 1-yr total return swap: pay ABC total return, receive floating 0.95%; NP = 80,000 × €6.00 = €480,000 Stock −5% + €0.05 dividend: total return = (5.70 + 0.05)/6.00 − 1 = −4.1667% Seago receives [0.0095 − (−0.041667)] × 480,000 = +€24,560 Stock +5% + €0.05: total return = (6.30 + 0.05)/6.00 − 1 = +5.8333% Seago receives (0.0095 − 0.058333) × 480,000 = −€23,440 (pays)
Paying the total return (price + dividend) and receiving floating removes the concentrated exposure without triggering a taxable sale — she keeps positive carry only if the stock underperforms the floating rate.
Cash equitization at scale (Barbet)
£60M cash + £300M equities (β 1.2 vs FTSE); 6-mo futures 7,348.50 × £10 (β 1); cash rate 0.86% Step 1 F = 7,348.50 × 10 = £73,485 Step 2 N = (1.2/1) × (60M / 73,485) = 979.79 → buy 980 Scenario: FTSE +6%, futures → 7,642 equities ....... £300M × [1 + 0.06 × 1.2] = £321.6M → +£21.6M cash interest .. 60M × 0.0086 × 180/360 = +£258,000 futures ........ (7,642 − 7,348.5) × £10 × 980 = +£2,876,300 total .......... £24,734,300 → return 24,734,300 / 360M = 6.87%

Changing allocations with swaps (Weber, ¥21.58B)

LOS 17.fInferring market expectations — Fed funds futures
Inferring expectations of…Derivative
FOMC rate movesFed funds futures
InflationCPI swaps
Future volatilityVIX futures & options
FFE vs targetFFE rate = weighted average of overnight interbank rates (the Fed influences it via open-market ops + interest on reserves, doesn’t set it). Target rate = range set by the FOMC (8 meetings/yr), e.g., 2.25%–2.50%. ContractCME; price = 100 − expected average FFE at contract maturity; monthly maturities out to 36 months. Use the nearest contract after the next FOMC meeting. Probability% prob of change = (implied FFE − current target midpoint) / (target assuming change − current midpoint) = (implied FFE − midpoint) / expected size of change.
Example — Stokes: futures 98.1625; current target 1.50%–1.75%; 25 bp hike? Step 1 implied FFE = 100 − 98.1625 = 1.8375% Step 2 midpoint = (1.50 + 1.75)/2 = 1.625% ; post-hike = 1.875% Step 3 prob = (1.8375 − 1.625) / (1.875 − 1.625) = 0.2125/0.25 = 85%
⚠ Work from the MIDPOINT of the target range, and put the expected size of the move (25 bp, 50 bp…) in the denominator. Futures price falling = implied FFE rising = market pricing hikes.

Price & Base Currency
A quote P/B reads: the base currency B is the denominator, priced in units of the price currency P (numerator). Unless clearly identified otherwise, "buy" and "sell" refer to the BASE currency.
Sell spot 1,000,000 at CAD/USD 0.9800 → sell (deliver) USD 1,000,000 & buy (receive) CAD 980,000 Buy 500,000 USD/CHF 6-mo forward at 1.07 → buy CHF 500,000 vs sell USD 535,000 (settles in 6 months)
Technique (Prof's note): always think base = denominator, and be ready to read the quote from either perspective (base or price currency).
Bid/Ask Rules — the 4 interpretations
Smaller number first (bid), larger second (ask). The ask can be read as the sale of one currency vs the purchase of the other. The spread is the dealer's margin: the customer always pays it — buy base at ask, sell base at bid. Quote: 0.9790 / 0.9810 CAD/USD (base = USD).
Spot vs Forward & Forward Points
Spot = immediate settlement (T+2 by convention, usually ignored — the FX swap is the exception). Forward = price agreed today for delayed settlement. Forward points adjust the spot: move the decimal LEFT by the number of decimals in the spot quote.
Spot quotePointsAdjustedForward price
1.33 (2 dec)1.11.1 / 100 = 0.0111.33 + 0.011 = 1.341
2.554 (3 dec)−9.6−9.6 / 1,000 = −0.00962.554 − 0.0096 = 2.5444
0.7654 (4 dec)13.6713.67 / 10,000 = 0.0013670.7654 + 0.001367 = 0.766767
Myth: points are NOT always /10,000 — that only works for 4-decimal spots. 5 decimals on the right → /100,000. Count the decimals.

Mark-to-Market of a Forward — 3 steps
MTM value = present value of the gain/loss locked in by an offsetting position to the same maturity date.
Step 1 Offset = OPPOSITE trade, SAME maturity date → all-in forward = current spot ± remaining-tenor points → pick the side you trade ON THE OFFSET (buy base → ask) Step 2 Gain/loss = (rate difference) × notional, settled at expiry Step 3 Discount at the market reference rate of the REMAINING period, unannualized: ÷ [1 + R × (days/360)]

The FX Swap (rollover)
An FX swap is not a currency swap (and not a "swap" in the usual sense). It rolls over a maturing forward: a spot transaction offsets the maturing contract, and a new forward re-establishes the position.
Kaplan example — long ZAR 10,000,000 3-mo fwd at ZAR/USD 9.4518 2 days before expiry, extend 30 days: Leg 1 SELL spot ZAR 10,000,000 (spot settles T+2 = same day the forward matures → offsets the maturing contract) Leg 2 BUY ZAR 10,000,000 new 30-day forward (rolls the position over)
The T+2 settlement convention — ignored everywhere else — matters here: it's what makes the spot leg land exactly on the forward's maturity date.
Option Basics — delta anatomy
Call = right to buy the underlying; gains as it rises above strike, Δ → 1.00 (100-delta); loses below, Δ → 0.00. Put = right to sell; gains below strike, Δ → −1.00 (the sign is assumed, "100-delta"); loses above, Δ → 0.00.
Pair rule: call + put with identical parameters (expiry, strike, underlying): |Δcall| + |Δput| = 1.00 (100-delta).
🎯 Interactive — where is the underlying?
Pick the price region of the base currency; see moneyness + delta of both options.
Currency Options — every option is two options
Two currencies → a call on one currency IS a put on the other. Unless otherwise specified, the option is read from the base currency perspective.
Call to buy GBP 10,000,000 at strike ZAR/GBP 14.56 = right to buy GBP 10,000,000 and sell ZAR 145,600,000 = PUT on ZAR: right to sell ZAR 145,600,000, buy GBP 10,000,000 Put to sell EUR 100,000 at MXN/EUR 20.1 = right to sell EUR 100,000 and buy MXN 2,010,000 = CALL on MXN: right to buy MXN 2,010,000, sell EUR 100,000
Reflex: notional of the other side = notional × strike. Restating the option from the other currency's perspective flips call ↔ put.
Domestic-Currency Return — the two sources
TermMeaning
RFCReturn of the foreign asset in its local (foreign) currency — "local market return"
RFX% change in the value of the foreign currency — quote must have the FOREIGN currency as BASE
RDCReturn in the investor's domestic currency, combining both
Equation 1: R DC = (1 + R FC)(1 + R FX) − 1 = R FC + R FX + (R FC × R FX) R DC ≈ R FC + R FX (approximation)
Prof's note — 3 ways to get R DC, the case facts decide: (1) approximation R FC + R FX when precision isn't needed; (2) exact compounding when R FX is known — the default; (3) when R FX isn't simple (hedged currency, unknowable ending units), compute directly: R DC = (EV − BV) / BV in domestic units.

⚠️ The R FX base-currency trap
R FX must be computed with the foreign currency as base (denominator). Doing it on the inverted quote gives the wrong number — appreciation of one currency is not the negative of the other's depreciation.
Foreign (EUR) as base: 1.339 / 1.300 − 1 = +3.000% ✓ R FX Domestic (USD) as base: 0.74683 / 0.76923 − 1 = −2.912% ✗ (USD depreciation ≠ −EUR appreciation)
Prof's note: label every number domestic/foreign or foreign/domestic, take reciprocals if needed, then solve EV / BV − 1 = R FX on the foreign-as-base quote.
Multiple Foreign Investments
Equation 2: R DC = Σ wᵢ × R DC,ᵢ wᵢ = weight (in DOMESTIC currency terms) of market i R DC,ᵢ = domestic-currency return of investment i
Compute each R DC,ᵢ first (each with its own R FX, foreign as base), then weight.
