Risk of R DC — two sources, one correlation
Two sources of risk: fluctuation of the foreign currency and fluctuation of the foreign asset price. Single foreign asset → weights = 1.0:
Equation 3 (approx): σ²(R DC) ≈ σ²(R FC) + σ²(R FX) + 2 σ(R FC) σ(R FX) ρ(R FC, R FX)
ρ positive → R FX amplifies R FC → volatility to the domestic investor increases ρ negative → R FX dampens R FC → volatility decreases (→ minimum-variance hedge ratio topic)
Prof's note: Equation 3 is an approximation (ignores the (R FC)(R FX) cross product). True variance would need every correlation pair: 2 foreign assets + 2 currencies = 4 variables = 6 pairs; 3 foreign assets → 15 pairs — unrealistic, false precision.
Special case — R FC is RISK-FREE
If the foreign asset is risk-free, σ(R FC) = 0 and its correlation with R FX is 0: R FX is the only source of risk, and the calculation becomes direct and precise:
Equation 4: σ(R DC) = σ(R FX) × (1 + R FC)
Exam trap: Equation 4 is a special case — it cannot be derived from Equation 3. Spot the words "risk-free foreign asset" and switch formulas.
Hedge or not? — the two camps
Arguments for NOT hedgingArgument for ACTIVE management
• Avoid the time and cost of hedging/trading
• Long run: currency effects are a zero-sum game (one appreciates, another depreciates)
• Long run: currencies revert to theoretical fair value		• Short run: currency moves can be extreme
• Inefficient pricing: many FX trades are dictated by international trade or central-bank policy, not fair value → prices can be exploited for return
The 4 strategies — discretion decomposed
StrategyDiscretionMechanismGoal
Passive hedgingNone — rule-basedMatch the portfolio's currency exposure to the benchmark's; periodic rebalancing to maintain the matchEliminate currency risk vs benchmark
Discretionary hedgingModest — e.g. ±5% around benchmark exposureDeviate from passive within a specified bandReduce risk + modest incremental return
Active managementGreater deviations allowedManager expected to take positions vs benchmark exposuresAlpha, not risk reduction
Currency overlayBroad — outsourcedOutside specialist; at the extreme treats currency as an asset class (e.g. short SEK with zero SEK exposure)Pure alpha, pure risk reduction, or hybrid — per mandate
IPS must specify: target hedge % • allowable discretion around it • rebalancing frequency • benchmarks for evaluating currency decisions • allowed/prohibited hedging tools. Relevant IPS sections: objectives (risk tolerance), horizon, liquidity needs, benchmark.
Why rebalance with no trades? (Kaplan example)
US client and index both 10% UK equities, GBP sold forward. Over the month, benchmark UK stocks fall (−R FC) while portfolio UK stocks rise (+R FC): the index reduces its GBP short, the manager must increase his. Rebalancing reflects not just explicit trades but R FC differentials between index and portfolio.
Short-term performance focus → match or deliberately deviate from index currency exposure; "currency doesn't matter long-run" is inappropriate. Low liquidity needs → reduces the need to hedge (less risk of liquidating foreign assets at depressed values).
Strategic Diversification Issues
⏲ Long run: currency volatility is lower than short run → less need to hedge for long-horizon portfolios ρ(R FC, R FX) positive → more R DC volatility → more need to hedge; negative → natural dampening → less need ρ varies by period → a varying hedge ratio is appropriate 💰 Bonds: asset–currency correlation tends higher than equities → more reason to hedge bond portfolios Hedge ratio (the % of exposure hedged) varies by manager preference
Strategic Cost Issues — hedging isn't free
CostDriver
Transaction costsSingle bid/ask small, but repeated trades add up — full hedging + frequent rebalancing is costly
Option premiumPaid upfront; lost if the option expires OTM
Rollover (FX swap)Forwards shorter than the hedge period → rollovers realize gains/losses → cash-flow volatility; financing outflows costly when rates are high
OverheadBack office, trading infrastructure, multi-currency cash accounts for settlements/margin
Opportunity cost100% hedge forgoes all favorable moves → some "split the difference" with a 50% strategic ratio
Managers generally choose partial hedges: hedge/rebalance monthly rather than daily, or accept some negative currency return rather than zero.
LOS 18.c — factors pushing toward FULLY HEDGED
• Short time horizon for portfolio objectives • High risk aversion • Client unconcerned with opportunity cost of missing positive currency returns • High short-term income & liquidity needs • Significant foreign-currency BOND exposure • Low hedging costs • Client doubts the benefits of discretionary management
Reverse any factor → argument for benchmark-neutral / more discretion. Classic essay LOS: justify from case facts.
Strategic vs Tactical (LOS 18.d)
The strategic decision sets the portfolio's normal hedging policy. Within allowed discretion, the manager makes tactical decisions to increase return — every one of them requires a view or prediction. Four broad approaches: fundamentals, technical, carry trade, volatility trading — and none works consistently.
Economic Fundamentals — convergence to fair value
Assumes long-term currency value converges to fair value, e.g. purchasing power parity sets long-run rates:
PPP: basket costs 100 units of A's currency, 200 units of B's → exchange rate A to B = 100/200 = 0.50 A/B
Short/intermediate path of convergence — a currency APPRECIATES when it is/has:
1. More undervalued relative to its fundamental value 2. The greatest rate of increase in its fundamental value 3. Higher real or nominal interest rates 4. Lower inflation relative to other countries 5. A decreasing risk premium
Opposite conditions → declining currency value. Exam reflex: scan the vignette for these 5 drivers and their direction.
When drivers contradict (real vs nominal, #3 vs #4): these are 5 separate channels, not one story — apply the one the vignette tests.

1. Real beats nominal. A high nominal rate is ambiguous: nominal = real + expected inflation. High nominal because of high inflation → PPP erodes the ccy → depreciation. A high real rate → attracts capital → appreciation. If inflation is given, reason in real terms.

2. Horizon splits the channels. Short/intermediate term = rate differentials & capital flows drive the path (#3); long term = convergence to PPP / fair value drives the destination (#4). "Short/intermediate path of convergence" is the module's own framing.

Reflex: expansionary monetary policy → rates DOWN → ccy depreciates (the false INR statement). Don't combine all 5 — pick the channel the question hands you.
Technical Analysis — the 3 principles
1. Past price data predicts future prices — prices already reflect fundamentals and all relevant info, so no need to analyze it 2. Fallible humans react to similar events in similar ways → past price patterns tend to repeat 3. Unnecessary to know what the currency should be worth — only where it will trade
FX technical analysis focuses on price trends (volume data generally less available) and works best in markets with identifiable trends.
Patterns — overbought, support, resistance
PatternWhat it isExpected behavior
Overbought / oversoldMarket has gone up (down) too farPrice likely to reverse
Support levelSubstantial bids from customers to buyPrice falling to it bounces higher as purchases execute
Resistance levelSubstantial offers from customers to sellPrice rising to it bounces lower as sales execute
Sticky... until broken: at support/resistance the price becomes "sticky" — but if the market moves through the level, it can accelerate and continue in the same direction.
Kaplan example — support for GBP at 1.70 USD/GBP: Traders place LIMIT BUY orders at 1.70 + STOP-LOSS SELL orders between 1.70 and 1.69 GBP falls to 1.70 → buy orders execute → price supported ("sticky price behavior") GBP breaks lower → stop-loss sells execute → drives GBP further down through support
Moving averages — the crossover rule
Shorter-term MA crossing a longer-term MA triggers a signal:
50-day MA rises ABOVE 200-day MA → BUY signal 50-day MA falls BELOW 200-day MA → SELL signal
Carry Trade — the 3 issues
Borrow the lower-rate currency, invest in the higher-rate currency.
IssueContent
1. CIRP
holds by arbitrage		F₀ − S₀ reflects the periodic rate differential.
Higher-rate currency → forward discount (F₀ < S₀)
Lower-rate currency → forward premium (F₀ > S₀)
2. UCIRP
does NOT hold		Asserts the CIRP forward is an unbiased estimate of future spot: higher-rate currency would depreciate by the differential, lower-rate appreciate by it. If true, a carry trade earns zero.
3. Forward rate bias
what carry exploits		Historically: the higher-rate currency usually depreciates less than IRP predicts (or even appreciates) → profit. But a small % of the time it depreciates far more → large losses.
Profitability condition: the carry trade is profitable if the spot of the higher-rate currency declines LESS than predicted by the forward rate.
Figure 18.1 — two equivalent readings
The carry trade...Lower-yield / fwd premium sideHigher-yield / fwd discount side
Is implemented byBorrow + sell spot the lower-yield currencyBuy + invest in the higher-yield currency
Is trading the forward rate biasSell spot the currency at a forward premiumBuy spot the currency at a forward discount
Funding currencies = lower-rate, developed economies. Investing currencies = higher-rate, emerging economies.
Crash risk: profitable in normal conditions, but in financial distress the high-yield EM currencies depreciate sharply → large losses. Stress = rising FX volatility → traders exit carry trades when volatility rises significantly.
🧮 Calculator — Carry trade (BRL/USD, Kaplan)
Spot (high/low)
Rate high-yield %
Rate low-yield %
Borrow (low ccy)
Unhedged by definition: hedging with the forward would lock in CIRP → zero profit. The primary risk is the ending value of the high-yield currency: decline beyond the rate differential → trade unprofitable.
Prof's note — the forward is NOT a forecast
Under IRP the higher-rate currency trades at a forward discount; UCIRP claims that discount predicts the future spot. The L3 curriculum rejects this: evidence shows the higher-rate currency tends to appreciate, not depreciate, and the carry trade exists precisely because spot moves less than UCIRP suggests. The forward rate is a hedging tool, not a predictor — "unless you want a very short career as a currency manager."
Vol Trading — delta, vega, delta-neutral
GreekMeasuresKey property
DeltaChange in option value for a change in the underlyingDirection exposure — what delta hedging removes
VegaChange in option value for a change in volatilityPositive for both puts and calls — higher expected vol raises both
Delta hedging creates a delta-neutral position (delta = 0): no gain/loss on small moves in the underlying, but it gains or loses as implied volatility changes — a pure bet on vol.
Prof's note: deltas change as the underlying moves → the position must be continually rebalanced to stay delta-neutral.
🎯 Interactive — your volatility view
Straddle vs Strangle
StraddleStrangle
LegsATM call + ATM putOTM call + OTM put, same |Δ|
Initial costHigherLower
Move needed for intrinsic valueSmallerLarger
Likely profitHigherLower — "similar but more moderate payoffs"
Expectation → Action (LOS 18.e)
Active = risky: the manager forms expectations; wrong view or uncovered transaction costs → return reduced.
ExpectationAction
Relative currencyAppreciationReduce the hedge (short position) OR increase the long position in the currency
DepreciationIncrease the hedge or decrease the long position
VolatilityRisingLong straddle (or strangle)
FallingShort straddle (or strangle)
Market conditionsStableCarry trade
CrisisDiscontinue the carry trade
Subtle variations: (1) a carry trade can bundle several funding/investing currencies with unequal weights — overweight the long (or cut the short) in the currency expected to gain the most; (2) delta-neutral positions can be "tilted": expect appreciation → net positive delta, depreciation → net negative delta.
7 tips to sort through currency questions
#Tip
1What exposure needs hedging? Typically the portfolio's exposure to fluctuation in a foreign currency's value.
2Easier when the foreign currency is the base. Quote given as B/P → take the reciprocal to make it P/B.
3Assume statements refer to the base currency unless indicated — but be explicit in answers and state the currency.
4Buy or sell the base?
• Buy forwards/futures or buy calls on base → increases exposure to base
• Sell forwards/futures or buy puts on base → decreases exposure
• Call on base = put on pricing ccy; put on base = call on pricing ccy
5Hedging is not free
• Forwards: no/minimal initial cost, high opportunity cost (upside eliminated)
• Bought options: high initial cost, upside retained (protective put)
• Lowering cost = giving up downside protection or upside, via: writing options (premium inflow), adjusting strikes, adjusting notional, adding exotic features
6Discretionary hedging: deviating from policy-neutral can lower costs and enhance return, but increases underperformance risk.
7The IPS defines the strategic policy-neutral hedge — generally a 100% hedge matching the benchmark's currency exposure.
Why forwards beat futures for FX hedging (LOS 18.f)
Customizable vs standardized futures Available for almost any currency pair vs limited futures listings Futures require margin → operational complexity + periodic cash flows FX forward/swap volume dwarfs futures → better liquidity
Static vs Dynamic — CHF 10m → 11m (Kaplan)
Static = established and held to expiration. Dynamic = periodically rebalanced. EUR-based manager hedges CHF 10,000,000; one month later the asset is worth CHF 11,000,000.
Option 1 — 1-month forward, roll at expiry Rollover realizes gain/loss + cash flow; new contract can be resized to 11m → static within the month, dynamic at rollover. Via FX swap (2 days before expiry): near leg: BUY CHF 10m SPOT (covers maturing short) far leg: SELL CHF 11m FORWARD (rolls + resizes) → "MISMATCHED" FX swap: near spot leg ≠ far forward leg CHF fell EUR 0.01? short fwd pays 0.01 × 10m = EUR 100,000 cash Option 2 — 3-month forward, look at month 1 Underhedged: short 10m vs asset 11m a. Static → do nothing b. Dynamic → SELL extra CHF 1m fwd (2 months) → short 11m nothing closed → all gains/losses DEFERRED to month 3
Choice of approach: shorter contracts / dynamic hedges = more frequent rebalancing → more transaction costs but better hedge results. Higher risk aversion → more frequent rebalancing. Lower risk aversion + strong views → more discretion around the strategic policy.
Roll Yield — the hedge's hidden carry
Return from the forward price converging toward spot over time = the P&L on the contract if spot is unchanged at expiry. Sign depends on two factors: (1) forward premium or discount, (2) contract bought or sold.
Roll yield (held to expiry) = (F₀ − S₀) / S₀ for the short Mini example: sell CHF 1m 6-mo fwd at 1.05, spot 1.04 → premium → short earns it: deliver at 1.05 what costs 1.04 gain USD 10,000 ; unannualized roll = 0.01/1.04 = 0.96%
Prof's note (convergence): F₀ > S₀ and base sold forward → FT = ST at expiry whatever spot does → positive roll for the short regardless of spot direction. Positive roll for the short = negative roll for the long. Roll yield ≠ total return: total ΔF = unknown spot change + known-in-advance roll yield.

Two traps: (1) F > S = forward premium → selling that currency forward earns positive roll (EUR, USD) — but roll yield is only one factor: USD's +3.41% expected appreciation beats the +0.34% locked by the hedge → leave USD unhedged. (2) The hedged return IS the implied roll yield: (F₀ − S₀)/S₀ — for CHF, 1,257.89/1,265.22 − 1 = −0.58%; hedging locks the forward as the end-of-period rate.
The trade-off (LOS 18.g)
Perfect hedging is expensive: forwards have opportunity cost (upside eliminated), insuring downside while keeping upside costs more. Every cost reduction = less downside protection or less upside, moving away from a 100% hedge ratio and/or toward more active decisions. Context: manager hedges long CHF exposure, quotes EUR/CHF (CHF = base). Roll-yield lever: increase trades earning positive roll, reduce trades earning negative roll.
The ladder — highest → lowest initial option cost
#StrategyLegsKey trade-off
1Over/underhedge with forwards
(view-driven, low cost)		Adjust hedge ratio: CHF↑ expected → hedge less; CHF↓ → hedge more than full exposureIf right: "positive convexity" — gains increased, losses reduced
2ATM protective put
(portfolio insurance)		Buy 50-delta putAsymmetric: ALL downside removed, ALL upside kept. Only time value → highest initial cost, zero opportunity cost
3OTM putBuy 35-delta (or 25-delta, further OTM) putCheaper, but exposed down to the strike
4CollarBuy 35-delta put + sell 35-delta callCall premium cuts initial cost, but upside capped (opportunity cost ↑)
5Put spreadBuy 35-delta put + sell 25-delta putProtection only between the two strikes — lost below the sold strike
6Seagull spreadPut spread + sell 35-delta callLess cost than put spread, same downside protection, upside limited
Delta vocabulary: ATM put ≈ −0.50 = "50-delta" (sign ignored). OTM puts have |Δ| < 0.50: a 35-delta put is OTM, a 25-delta put further OTM — cheaper, less protective.
Risk reversal (collar's mirror): the counterparty who buys the OTM call and sells the OTM put is LONG the risk reversal — profits above the call strike, loses below the put strike. The collar user (sells the call, buys the put) is SHORT the risk reversal.
Notional variations & exotic options
1×2 put spread: buy 100 40-delta puts, SELL 200 30-delta puts → extra premium cuts initial cost → but DOUBLES downside risk below the 30-delta strike
ExoticFeature
Knock-inPlain vanilla that only comes into existence if the underlying first reaches a prespecified level
Knock-outStandard option that ceases to exist if the underlying reaches a prespecified level
Binary / digitalPays a fixed amount, regardless of the strike-vs-underlying distance
Prof's note: endless combinations and odd names — what matters is how each strategy moves the three dials: cost of the hedge • downside protection • upside potential.

Selecting a hedge — the 6 steps
#Step
1Determine the base in the P/B quote. USD/CHF: CHF is base — quoted price ↑ (↓) = CHF appreciates (depreciates).
2Base bought or sold? Bought + price ↑ = gain (price ↓ = loss). Sold + price ↑ = loss (price ↓ = gain).
3Need to BUY the base to hedge → buy forwards or calls. Buying OTM calls or writing options cuts cost but cuts downside protection or upside.
4Need to SELL the base → sell forwards or buy puts. Same cost lever: OTM puts / writing options.
5Higher risk tolerance + stronger manager views → less likely a simple 100% hedge.
6Combinations of options, strikes, and sizes can cut initial cost even to zero — but only by giving up downside protection or upside.
Hedging Multiple Currencies — natural hedges
International portfolios hold several foreign currencies; hedging each exposure individually is unnecessary, expensive, and time-consuming.
European investor: UNDERWEIGHT AUD, OVERWEIGHT NZD Mechanical fix: long AUD + short NZD to neutral weights But AUD & NZD: very similar economies → strong POSITIVE correlation → the two positions are NATURAL HEDGES Equal over/underweights → possibly NO additional hedging needed
The follow-up (Module 18.6): when the correlation is imperfect, the residual is cross-hedge risk — little, but not zero, for AUD/NZD.
Cross Hedge (proxy hedge) — LOS 18.h
Hedging with an instrument not perfectly correlated with the exposure (e.g. S&P futures vs a non-identical diversified US portfolio). Generally unnecessary in FX — forwards exist for virtually all pairs — but can improve hedging efficiency.
Imperfect correlation → residual risk increases AUD/NZD: high positive correlation → hedging an AUD underweight with an NZD overweight has little, but not zero, cross-hedge risk Historical correlation is no guarantee: corr → 0 → hedge underperforms; performance can benefit OR suffer from a correlation change
Macro Hedge — portfolio-wide factors
A type of cross hedge targeting portfolio-wide risk factors rather than individual assets. Bond portfolio illustration:
Risk factorMacro-hedge instrument
Interest rate riskBond futures (modify duration)
Credit riskCredit derivatives
Volatility riskVolatility trading
Currency version: a derivative on a fixed basket of currencies. The basket won't precisely match the portfolio's exposures, but it's cheaper than hedging each currency individually.
The trade-off to state on the exam: accepting higher residual currency risk versus lower cost.
Minimum-Variance Hedge Ratio
Mathematical hedge ratio: regress past changes in R DC on past changes in the hedging instrument's value to minimize tracking error. The hedge ratio = beta (slope coefficient) of that regression.
Kaplan highlight: the MVHR is based on historical returns — if the correlation between portfolio returns and hedging-instrument returns changes, the hedge will not perform as expected.
#Practical implication
1Direct hedges need no MVHR: long CHF 1m hedged by selling CHF 1m forward — CHF vs its own forward, corr ≈ 1.00 → one-for-one.
2Cross/macro hedges are "indirect": correlation may not be 1.00 → MVHR may not be one-for-one.
3The MVHR jointly optimizes over R FX and R FC to minimize the volatility of R DC.
🎯 Why MVHR ≠ 1.0 — the economy type

Managing Emerging Market Currency (LOS 18.i)
Most investable assets and FX flow through the six largest developed-market currencies. Everything else brings two core problems: (1) higher transaction costs ("high markups") and (2) higher probability of extreme events. The mechanisms:
ChallengeMechanism
Wider bid/ask spreadsLow trading volume → dealers charge more; spreads widen further in crisis
Asymmetric liquidityCostlier to exit than enter: carry traders accumulate long EM positions, then mass-exit in crisis → EM currency driven below fundamental value, trading disrupted
EM-to-EM pairs costlier stillFew dealers make direct markets: a MYR/HUF quote is actually executed as EUR/MYR + EUR/HUF component trades
Non-normal returnsHigher extreme-event probability, negative skew → strategies and risk measures assuming normality are flawed
Negative roll yieldHigher EM yields → large forward discounts → negative roll for investors who must sell forward (hedgers)
ContagionIn crisis, EM correlations (markets and currencies) converge toward +1.0 → diversification disappears exactly when needed
Tail riskGovernments intervene → long artificial stability, then sharp moves when market forces overwhelm them → negative events more frequent than the normal distribution assumes
Non-Deliverable Forwards
EM governments often restrict currency movement in/out of the country (BRL, CNY, RUB). NDFs replace deliverable forwards: cash settlement of the gain/loss in a developed-market currency — no exchange of notionals.
Benefit: lower credit risk — no notional delivery; only the gain to one party is paid at settlement Caveat: NDFs exist because the government restricts the market — policy changes can cause sharp currency moves (tail risk)
🧮 Calculator — NDF cash settlement (RUB/EUR, Kaplan)
Trader buys the base (EUR) forward; the NDF settles at the ending spot, in the developed currency.
Notional (base)
Forward rate
Spot at expiry
Settlement trap: the gain accrues in the restricted currency but is paid in the developed currency, converted at the ENDING spot — divide by ST, not by the forward. Only the net amount changes hands.
1 — Quotes & Forwards
P/B: base = denominator; buy/sell refer to the BASE Client buys base → ASK ; sells base → BID (spread always paid) Points: ÷ 10^(# decimals of spot) ; all-in = spot + points (bid+bid / ask+ask) B/P given? take the reciprocal → P/B
2 — Forward MTM (3 steps)
1. Offset = opposite trade, same maturity (side of the OFFSET!) 2. P&L = Δrate × notional, at original expiry 3. MTM = P&L / [1 + R × (days/360)] (remaining tenor, unannualized)
3 — Returns & Risk
Eq1: R DC = (1+R FC)(1+R FX) − 1 ≈ R FC + R FX Eq2: R DC = Σ wᵢ R DC,ᵢ (compound each leg FIRST) R FX: FOREIGN currency as base — invert if needed, then EV/BV − 1 Eq3: σ²(R DC) ≈ σ²FC + σ²FX + 2σσρ (ρ+ amplifies, ρ− dampens) Eq4 (risk-free R FC): σ(R DC) = σ(R FX)(1 + R FC) — not from Eq3
4 — Carry Trade
F = S × (1+iₕ)/(1+iₖ) ; CIRP holds, UCIRP doesn't Borrow low → convert → invest high → convert back → repay Spot unchanged → profit = differential ; profitable if high-rate ccy falls LESS than the forward predicts ; EXIT when volatility spikes
5 — Roll Yield & Hedge Decision
Roll (short, to expiry) = (F₀ − S₀)/S₀ IRP precise: [(1+iₚ)/(1+iₘ)]^t − 1 (analyzed ccy in denominator) LONG asset + premium → +roll, encourages hedge ; discount → −roll SHORT asset: flip the signs Decision: hedge if F₀/S₀ − 1 > E[ST]/S₀ − 1
6 — Options Ladder (cost ↓)
ATM put → OTM put → collar → put spread → seagull (fwd over/underhedge: ≈ free, "positive convexity" if right) Every euro saved = downside protection or upside given up Collar = SHORT the risk reversal ; 1×2 spread doubles tail risk
7 — MVHR & NDF
MVHR: regress R DC on instrument → hedge = exposure × β Import-dependent (+ρ) → β > 1 ; export-dependent (−ρ) → β < 1 Past data → correlation drift = underperformance NDF: settle = (ST − F) × N / ST in the DM ccy, at ENDING spot
8 — Tactical table
Appreciation → hedge↓ / long↑ Depreciation → hedge↑ / long↓ Vol↑ → long straddle Vol↓ → short straddle Stable → carry trade Crisis → discontinue carry
9 — Essay add-ons (mock gaps)
MVHR from stats: h = ρ × σ(R DC) / σ(R FX) ; hedge = h × exposure Currency contribution = R DC − Σw·R FC (= Σw·R FX + cross terms) R FX sign reflex: R FX > 0 = FOREIGN appreciated = domestic fell Negative carry: borrow HIGH, invest LOW — profitable only if fwd FX return (F/S − 1) > net borrowing cost (iₙ − iₖ) Trading costs: bid/ask churn | option premium | roll cash flows | overhead (opportunity cost = a SEPARATE bucket) Band width: ±5% discretionary | ±25% active | rule-based passive

Reading 18 · Currency Management: An Introduction
Full-reading recap, module by module: managing currency exposure — currency math, RDC, risk, strategic choices (18.1 / LOS 18.a–18.c), active strategies: fundamentals & technical (18.2 / 18.d), carry & volatility trading (18.3 / 18.d), implementation & forwards: tactical decisions, hedge ratios, roll yield (18.4 / 18.e–18.f), implementation & options: reducing hedge cost (18.5 / 18.g), and advanced issues: cross/macro hedges, MVHR, emerging markets, NDFs (18.6 / 18.h–18.i). Every calculation node-verified against the Schweser figures.
Where the marks are: (1) base currency in the denominator — every buy/sell, call/put, premium/discount statement refers to the base unless stated; (2) RFX must be computed with the foreign currency as base (invert if needed, EV/BV − 1); (3) forward points ÷ 10decimals of the spot quote; (4) the hedge-cost ladder in 18.5 — what each tweak gives up (downside protection vs upside); (5) roll yield sign → hedge or don’t.
The map — how the six modules are one pipeline
Where you saw it firstWhere it comes backSame idea, new seat

Eq 3 correlation term (18.1)Hedge-more/less list (18.1c) & MVHR (18.6)ρ as risk → ρ as policy → ρ as hedge ratio

How to use this: for any exam vignette, walk the pipeline left to right — What’s the exposure? What does the IPS permit? What’s the view and which of the 4 sources produced it? Which instrument, and what does the rate differential do to its cost? Can the cost be engineered down, and what friction remains? Every LOS in R18 answers exactly one of those questions.
Module 18.1 · Managing Currency Exposure
Price & base currencies, bid/ask, forward points
P/B conventionQuote = price currency / base currency (denominator). “Buy” and “sell” refer to the base. Sell 1,000,000 at CAD/USD 0.9800 = sell USD 1M, buy CAD 980,000. Settlement convention: spot = 2 business days. Bid/ask rulesSmaller number first. Dealer’s margin = the spread; customer pays more / receives less. A 0.9790/0.9810 CAD/USD quote: buy 1 USD → deliver 0.9810 CAD (dealer’s ask); sell 1 USD → receive 0.9790 CAD (bid). Four equivalent phrasings per side. Forward pointsAdjustment to spot: move the decimal left by the number of decimals in the spot quote. 1.33 + 1.1 pts → 1.33 + 0.011 = 1.341; 2.554 − 9.6 → 2.5444; 0.7654 + 13.67 → 0.766767. ÷10,000 only when spot has 4 decimals; 5 decimals ⇒ ÷100,000.
Example — AUD/EUR spot 1.2571/1.2574; 30d pts −1.0/−0.9; 90d pts +11.7/+12.0 30-day quotes: 1.2571 − 0.00010 = 1.25700 ; 1.2574 − 0.00009 = 1.25731 90-day quotes: 1.2571 + 0.00117 = 1.25827 / 1.2574 + 0.00120 = 1.25860 Manager sells AUD 1,000,000 90d forward (delivers AUD, receives EUR): delivering the base’s counterpart ⇒ deals at the ask 1.25860 receives 1,000,000 / 1.25860 = EUR 794,533.61 in 90 days
⚠ Which side of the quote? The customer always gets the worse side: delivering more AUD / receiving fewer EUR here means both bid and ask work against you — identify what you deliver vs receive before picking bid or ask.
Offsetting transactions & mark-to-market
ConceptForwards have no interim cash flows, but the position can be marked to market: MTM value = PV of the gain/loss locked in by an offsetting contract for the remaining term. MechanicsOffset a short with a matching-maturity long (and vice versa); both settle on the original date; discount the locked-in difference at the market reference rate of the P&L currency for the remaining days.
Example — sold EUR 10,000,000 90d forward at AUD/EUR 1.25827; 30 days later: Step 1 offset: buy EUR 10M 60d forward at the ask: 1.3191 + 0.00105 = 1.32015 Step 2 in 60 days: receive 10M × 1.25827 = AUD 12,582,700 pay 10M × 1.32015 = AUD 13,201,500 locked-in loss = −AUD 618,800 (= 0.06188/€ × 10M) Step 3 MTM = −618,800 / [1 + 0.012 × 60/360] = −AUD 617,564.87 (60-day AUD reference rate 1.20%)
⚠ Discount at the 60-day rate of the P&L currency (AUD), unannualized as rate × days/360 — the loss settles 90 days after inception but only 60 days after the valuation date.
FX swap — rolling a forward
What it isNot a currency swap: an FX swap rolls a maturing forward via a spot transaction + a new forward — the existing forward is “swapped” for another. MechanicsTwo days before expiry (spot settlement window), take the spot position that offsets the maturing leg, and enter the new forward. Mismatched sizes on near/far legs ⇒ “mismatched” FX swap (used for dynamic re-sizing).
Example — long ZAR 10,000,000 3-mo forward at ZAR/USD 9.4518; extend 30 days: • sell spot ZAR 10,000,000 (offsets the maturing purchase; both settle T+2) • enter a new 30-day forward to buy ZAR 10,000,000 vs USD → trade rolled
Option & currency-option basics
DeltasCall delta 0 → +1.00 as underlying rises through the strike; put delta 0 → −1.00 as it falls (sign usually dropped: “100-delta”). ATM ≈ 50-delta. Same-parameter call + put: |Δcall| + |Δput| = 1.00. Two-currency dualityA call on the base = a put on the pricing currency. Call on 10M at ZAR/GBP 14.56 = right to buy GBP 10M and sell ZAR 145.6M = put on ZAR 145.6M. Unless specified, options are read from the base currency perspective.
As the base currency rises…Call on the basePut on the base
From 0 to the strikeOTM, rising in value; Δ 0.0 → 0.5ITM, falling; Δ −1.0 → −0.5
At the strikeATM; Δ ≈ 0.5ATM; Δ ≈ −0.5
Above the strikeITM, rising; Δ 0.5 → 1.0OTM, falling; Δ −0.5 → 0.0
LOS 18.aEffects of currency on portfolio return — RDC
DefinitionsRFC = foreign asset return in its local currency; RFX = % change in value of the foreign currency (foreign = base!); RDC = return in the investor’s currency. Equation 1RDC = (1 + RFC)(1 + RFX) − 1 = RFC + RFX + RFCRFX ≈ RFC + RFX. Approximation OK for well-spaced MC answers; use the compounded form when precision matters; hedged currency ⇒ determine the precise RFX from the hedge. Equation 2Multiple foreign assets: RDC = Σ wᵢ × RDC,i, with weights in domestic currency terms. Risk-free special caseNaive hedge sells the beginning number of FC units forward; the true ending number isn’t knowable for a risky asset ⇒ F₀/S₀ comparison ≠ true RFX. Direct route: RDC = (EV − BV)/BV in domestic units.
Example — USD investor, EUR stocks +5%; USD/EUR 1.300 → 1.339 Rₖₓ = 1.339/1.300 − 1 = +3% R₌ₛ = 1.05 × 1.03 − 1 = 8.15% (≈ 5 + 3 = 8%) Two-market example (EUR investor, 75% GBP / 25% USD) GBP leg: 1.12 × (1.1437/1.1666) − 1 = 9.80% (GBP fell ≈2% vs EUR) USD leg: quotes given USD/EUR → INVERT: 1/1.332 = 0.7508; 1/1.324 = 0.7553 1.05 × (0.7553/0.7508) − 1 = 5.63% Portfolio: 0.75 × 9.80 + 0.25 × 5.63 = 8.76%
⚠ RFX needs the FOREIGN currency as base. Using USD/EUR quotes to measure USD (0.74683/0.76923 − 1 = −2.912%) gives the USD’s depreciation — NOT the negative of the EUR’s appreciation (+3.000%). Invert first, then EV/BV − 1.
Risk of RDC
Equation 3σ²(RDC) ≈ σ²(RFC) + σ²(RFX) + 2σ(RFC)σ(RFX)ρ(RFC,RFX) — single foreign asset, weights = 1.0. Positive ρ amplifies volatility; negative ρ dampens it (→ MVHR). Why approximateIgnores the (RFC)(RFX) cross term; a “precise” formula would demand every correlation pair (2 assets → 6 pairs; 3 → 15) — false precision. The CFA text uses the approximation. Equation 4If RFC is risk-free: σ(RDC) = σ(RFX) × (1 + RFC) — a special case NOT derivable from Eq 3.
LOS 18.bStrategic decisions in currency management
Don’t hedge argsAvoid time & cost; long-run currency effects are a zero-sum game; currencies revert to fair value in the long run. Active argsShort-run moves can be extreme; inefficient pricing exists — many FX trades (international trade, central banks) aren’t motivated by fair value. Passive hedgingRule-based; matches the benchmark’s currency exposure; periodic rebalancing; goal = eliminate currency risk vs the benchmark. DiscretionaryModest deviations allowed (e.g., ±5% around the matched ratio); goal = risk reduction first, plus modest incremental return. ActiveLarger deviations permitted; manager is expected to generate alpha from currency, not just reduce risk. Currency overlayOutsourced currency management; at the extreme, currency = separate asset class, positions independent of portfolio assets (e.g., short SEK with no SEK exposure). Mandates range from pure risk reduction to pure alpha. IPS contentsTarget hedge %, allowable discretion around it, rebalancing frequency, evaluation benchmarks, allowed/prohibited tools.
Choosing-an-approach example: client fully hedges to a global index, rebalances monthly, low liquidity needs, short-term evaluation ⇒ either (A) manager lacks currency skill: fully hedge and rebalance monthly, add value elsewhere; or (B) manager has currency views: over/underweight currencies expected to appreciate/depreciate. Short-term focus ⇒ can’t assume “currency doesn’t matter”; rebalancing must reflect RFC differentials between portfolio and index, not just explicit trades.
LOS 18.cDiversification, cost, and the hedge decision
DiversificationLong run: currency vol is lower ⇒ less need to hedge long-horizon portfolios. Positive ρ(RFC,RFX) raises σ(RDC) ⇒ hedge more; negative ρ dampens ⇒ hedge less. ρ varies by period ⇒ varying hedge ratio appropriate. Bond portfolios: asset–currency correlation typically higher than equities ⇒ more reason to hedge bonds. CostsBid/ask (small per trade, adds up); option premiums (lost if OTM); rolling short-dated forwards (FX swaps) ⇒ realized cash-flow volatility; overhead (back office, multi-currency accounts, margin); 100% hedging = opportunity cost (zero favorable moves) ⇒ some adopt a 50% strategic ratio; partial hedges / monthly rebalancing are common. Toward full hedgeShort time horizon; high risk aversion; client unconcerned with opportunity cost; high short-term income/liquidity needs; significant foreign bond exposure; low hedging costs; client doubts discretionary value.

Modules 18.2 / 18.3 · Active Strategies
LOS 18.dFour active approaches (none work consistently)
Economic fundamentalsLong term, currency converges to fair value (e.g., PPP). Appreciation associated with: more undervalued currencies; fastest rise in fundamental value; higher real/nominal rates; lower inflation; decreasing risk premiums. Technical analysis3 principles: past prices predict (prices reflect all info); humans repeat patterns; fair value irrelevant — only where it will trade. FX = price trends (volume scarce). Support = bids cluster, price bounces up; resistance = offers cluster, bounces down; through a sticky level ⇒ move accelerates. Moving averages: 50-day crossing above 200-day = buy signal; below = sell. Carry tradeBorrow the low-rate (funding) currency, invest in the high-rate (investing) currency — typically fund in developed, invest in EM. Volatility tradingTrade vega, not direction (next card).
The carry trade — CIRP, UCIRP, forward rate bias
CIRP (holds)Arbitrage forces F₀ vs S₀ to reflect the rate differential: higher-rate currency trades at a forward discount (F₀ < S₀); lower-rate at a premium (F₀ > S₀). UCIRP (fails)Asserts the CIRP forward is an unbiased forecast of the future spot (high-rate currency depreciates by the differential). If true, carry earns zero. Empirically the high-rate currency depreciates less than predicted or even appreciates ⇒ carry profits — = trading the forward rate bias. Small % of the time: crashes ⇒ large losses. Figure 18.1Implemented by: borrow & sell spot the lower-yield currency, buy & invest in the higher-yield. Forward-rate-bias view: sell the currency at a forward premium; buy the one at a forward discount. Crash riskProfitable in calm markets; big losses in financial distress / rising vol as investors flee high-yield currencies ⇒ traders exit carry when FX vol spikes.
Example — BRL/USD spot 2.41; rates 6% (BRL) / 1% (USD) Step 1 1-yr forward ≈ 5% below spot: 2.41 × (1.06/1.01) = BRL/USD 2.529 (forward measured as BRL price of USD rises = BRL at a discount) Step 2 trade: borrow USD @1% → convert to BRL @2.41 → invest @6% Step 3 unchanged spot: borrow 100 → owe 101; BRL 241 → 255.46 convert back: 255.46/2.41 = 106.00 → profit USD 5.00 per 100 (= the 5% rate differential, spot unchanged) Step 4 primary risk: unhedged — BRL falling > 5% makes it unprofitable
⚠ Professor’s Note: the curriculum does NOT support the forward rate as a predictor of the future spot. The forward is for hedging; empirically the higher-rate currency tends to appreciate, not depreciate — that violation IS the carry trade.
Volatility trading
GreeksDelta = Δoption/Δunderlying; vega = Δoption/Δimplied vol, positive for both puts and calls. Delta hedgingDelta-neutral position: no P&L from small underlying moves; gains/loses on changes in implied vol ⇒ a pure vol bet. Deltas drift ⇒ must be continually rebalanced. Long straddleExpect vol ↑: buy ATM call + ATM put (equal, opposite deltas ⇒ neutral) = buying volatility. Short straddleExpect vol ↓: sell both; repurchase cheaper if vol declines. StrangleOTM call + OTM put, same |delta|: cheaper, needs a bigger move, more moderate cost AND likely profit than a straddle.
Module Quiz 18.2, 18.3 — answers (circled in photo)
Q1 → C (circled)Carry works when investing-currency yields are higher and volatility is stable — rising vol (B) is when carry trades are exited. Q2 → C (circled)Rising euro-zone real rates ⇒ euro expected to appreciate ⇒ a delta-neutral book can be tilted net long the euro. A is false (falling vol favors staying in carry); B false (a collar’s premium income makes it cheaper than a protective put as vol rises).
Module 18.4 · Implementation & Forwards
LOS 18.eTactical trading decisions
ExpectationAction
Relative currencyAppreciationReduce the hedge (short) OR increase the long
DepreciationIncrease the hedge or decrease the long
VolatilityRisingLong straddle (or strangle)
FallingShort straddle (or strangle)
Market conditionsStableCarry trade
CrisisDiscontinue the carry trade
Variations: carry bundles need not be equally weighted (overweight the currency with the strongest expected gain); delta-neutral books can be tilted net positive/negative delta on a directional view.
Exam tips (1–7)(1) identify the exposure to hedge; (2) make the foreign currency the base — given B/P, take the reciprocal; (3) statements refer to the base unless stated — be explicit in answers; (4) buy base risk ⇒ buy forwards/calls; sell base risk ⇒ sell forwards/buy puts; call on base = put on pricing; (5) hedging isn’t free — forwards: no upfront cost, high opportunity cost; options: high upfront, keep upside; cheapen via writing options / strikes / notional / exotics; (6) discretion lowers cost, raises underperformance risk; (7) the IPS defines the policy-neutral hedge — generally 100% of benchmark exposure.
LOS 18.fForwards, FX swaps, and hedge-ratio adjustment
Forwards preferredCustomizable; nearly every pair; futures require margin + periodic cash flows; FX forward/swap volume dwarfs futures ⇒ better liquidity. Static vs dynamicStatic = hold to expiry; dynamic = periodically rebalanced (frequency specified by the strategy). Rolling (1-mo)EUR manager short CHF 10M 1-mo; asset → 11M. At rollover: realized gain/loss + cash flow; new size can match the new value (dynamic at rollover). Via mismatched FX swap: buy CHF 10M spot (covers the maturing short) + sell CHF 11M forward — near and far legs unequal. Spot vs initial-forward gap ⇒ EUR cash flow (CHF −0.01 ⇒ gain EUR 100,000 on 10M). 3-mo alternativeOne month in, underhedged 10M vs 11M: static ⇒ do nothing; dynamic ⇒ sell CHF 1M more 2-mo forward (total 11M); nothing closes ⇒ all gains/losses deferred to the end. Choice driversShorter/dynamic ⇒ more transaction costs, better hedge; higher risk aversion ⇒ more frequent rebalancing; lower risk aversion + strong views ⇒ more discretion.
Roll yield
DefinitionReturn from the forward price converging to spot; profit/loss if spot unchanged at expiry. Held to expiry: roll yield = (initial forward − spot)/initial spot. Depends on (1) forward premium/discount and (2) bought or sold. Known vs unknownTotal forward return = Δforward price = unknown Δspot + known-in-advance roll yield. Roll yield is a hedging cost/benefit: positive roll → hedge; negative roll → think twice. Quick exampleSell CHF 1M 6-mo fwd @1.05, spot 1.04: sells at a premium ⇒ short earns as F rolls down: gain USD 10,000; roll = 0.01/1.04 = 0.96%. IRP shortcutFP/B = SP/B (1+iₚ)/(1+i⃀); % premium/discount = (F−S)/S; with parity spot 1/1: % roll = (1+iₚ)/(1+i⃀) elevated to the period, −1. Analyzing currency X ⇒ X in the denominator of every term.
Example — ZAR exposure, USD investor; iₖₛₖ 2.8%, iₛₐₘ 3.6%, 6-mo hedge (sell ZAR fwd) approx: +2.8%/2 − 3.6%/2 = −0.4% (ZAR at a forward discount) precise: (1.00)(1.028/1.036)⁰⋅⁵ − 1 = −0.387% selling ZAR at a discount ⇒ negative roll: hedging costs ≈0.39%/6 mo
Position in foreign asset (B)HedgeF > S, i⃀ < iₚ (fwd premium)F < S, i⃀ > iₚ (fwd discount)
Short the foreign assetLong forward in BNegative roll → discourages hedgingPositive roll → encourages hedging
Long the foreign assetShort forward in BPositive roll → encourages hedgingNegative roll → discourages hedging
Worked set — hedging & roll yield (KRW portfolio, node-verified)
Reporting currency KRW; assets in EUR, USD, CHF. Spot / 6-mo forward / manager forecast: KRW/EUR 1,483.99 / 1,499.23 / 1,450.87; KRW/USD 1,108.78 / 1,112.56 / 1,146.63; KRW/CHF 1,265.22 / 1,257.89 / 1,212.55.
Unhedged (forecast/spot − 1)Hedged (forward/spot − 1)Decision
EUR−2.23%+1.03%Hedge
USD+3.41%+0.34%Don’t hedge
CHF−4.16%−0.58%Hedge
Q1/Q2EUR & USD trade at a forward premium (F > S) ⇒ selling them forward earns positive roll. Q3Active manager compares columns → hedge EUR and CHF (hedged > unhedged); leave USD (expected appreciation beats the +0.34% locked hedge). Q4Positive roll from selling USD/EUR forward reduces hedging cost — but roll is only one input: for USD, expected appreciation dominates. Q5Implied roll on the CHF hedge = (F₀ − S₀)/S₀ = 1,257.89/1,265.22 − 1 = −0.58% = the hedged currency return.
Two views, one number: positive (negative) roll reduces (increases) hedging cost; equivalently, hedging locks the forward as the end-of-period exchange rate.
Module 18.5 · Implementation & Options
LOS 18.gReducing hedging cost — the strategy ladder (long CHF, EUR/CHF quotes)
#StrategyBuildGives up / keeps
1Over/underhedge with forwardsCHF ↑ expected ⇒ hedge <100%; CHF ↓ ⇒ hedge >100%“Positive convexity” if right; low cost
2ATM protective put (portfolio insurance)Buy 50-delta put on CHFHighest initial cost
3OTM putBuy 35- or 25-delta putCheaper; unprotected down to the strike
4CollarBuy 35Δ put + sell 35Δ callPremium income; caps upside
5Put spreadBuy 35Δ put, sell 25Δ putProtection only between the strikes
6SeagullPut spread + sell 35Δ callCheapest; put-spread protection AND capped upside
Risk reversalBuy OTM call + sell OTM put = long risk reversal (profits if underlying rises). The collar seller side (sell call, buy put) = short the risk reversal. 1×2 ratio spreadBuy 100 40Δ puts, sell 200 30Δ puts: extra premium cuts cost but doubles downside risk below the sold strike. ExoticsKnock-in: comes into existence only if a level is hit; knock-out: ceases to exist at a level; binary/digital: fixed payout regardless of moneyness depth. Hedge-selection steps(1) find the base in the P/B quote — quoted price ↑ = base appreciates; (2) will the base be bought or sold?; (3) buying base risk ⇒ forwards/calls, OTM or written options cheapen it; (4) selling base risk ⇒ sell forwards / buy puts; (5) higher risk tolerance + stronger views ⇒ less likely a plain 100% hedge; (6) cost can reach zero — only by giving up protection or upside.
Module 18.6 · More Advanced Implementation Issues
LOS 18.hCross hedges, macro hedges, MVHR
Cross (proxy) hedgeHedge with an instrument imperfectly correlated with the exposure. Rare in FX (forwards exist for nearly all pairs) but can improve efficiency. Residual risk rises when correlation is imperfect or shifts — e.g., AUD/NZD natural hedge: equal over/underweights may need no extra hedging, but cross-hedge risk > 0. Macro hedgeCross hedge of portfolio-wide risk factors (e.g., a fixed currency-basket derivative) — cheaper than hedging each currency, but the basket ≠ portfolio ⇒ higher residual currency risk vs lower cost. MVHRRegression of RDC on the hedging instrument’s returns; hedge ratio = the beta (slope). Minimizes tracking-error variance; jointly optimizes over RFX AND RFC. Based on historical data ⇒ if correlation changes, the hedge underperforms. When MVHR ≠ 1Direct hedges (long CHF 1M, sell CHF 1M forward): corr ≈ 1.00 ⇒ no MVHR needed. Import-dependent economy: +RFX ⇒ +RFC (strong positive ρ) ⇒ volatility amplified ⇒ hedge ratio > 1.0. Export-dependent: +RFX ⇒ −RFC (negative ρ) ⇒ natural damping ⇒ ratio < 1.0.
Example — U.S. portfolio long EUR 2,000,000; regression on weekly data: Rₖₛ = 0.12 + 1.25 (%ΔSₖₛₖₔₑₖₚ) + ε (ρ = 0.75) hedge = 2,000,000 × 1.25 = short EUR 2,500,000 effectiveness: cross-hedge on past correlation; 0.75 isn’t perfect and can change ⇒ hedge may perform better or worse than expected
LOS 18.iEmerging market currency & NDFs
Two core problems(1) higher transaction costs (“high markups”); (2) increased probability of extreme events. SymptomsLow volume ⇒ wide bid/ask, wider in crises; exit costlier than entry (carry unwinds crush EM currencies together); EM–EM pairs routed through EUR legs; return distributions non-normal, negatively skewed ⇒ normal-based risk measures flawed; high yields ⇒ large forward discounts = negative roll for sellers; contagion: correlations → +1.0 exactly when diversification is needed; tail risk from government intervention — long artificial stability, then sharp moves. NDFsFor restricted currencies (BRL, CNY, RUB): cash settlement of the gain/loss in the developed-market currency, no exchange of notionals ⇒ lower credit risk (only one party’s gain moves). They exist BECAUSE markets are restricted ⇒ policy changes = tail risk.
Example — buy EUR 1,000,000 6-mo NDF at RUB/EUR 39; spot at expiry 40 agreed: “sell” RUB 39,000,000 for EUR 1,000,000 → EUR now worth RUB 40,000,000 gain = RUB 1,000,000, but settled in EUR at ending spot: 1,000,000 / 40 = EUR 25,000 received net from the counterparty
Module Quiz 18.4, 18.5, 18.6 — answers (circled in photo; node-verified)
Q1 → B (circled)Reduce downside protection to cut cost while staying a put-based hedge ⇒ put spread: buy 40Δ put, sell 20Δ put. C (collar) reduces upside, not downside; A is a straddle, not a hedge-cost reduction. Q2 → B (circled)Direct hedge = notional GBP 1,000,000; minimum-variance = 1,000,000 × slope 1.25 = GBP 1,250,000. Q3 → C (circled)Short CNY 2,000,000 NDF at CNY/USD 6.1155 ⇒ locked to receive 2,000,000/6.1155 = USD 327,038. Ending spot USD/CNY 0.1612 ⇒ CNY/USD 6.2035 ⇒ market value 2,000,000/6.2035 = USD 322,400. Gain to the short ≈ USD 4,638 → closest: USD 4,650 gain, cash-settled in USD.

📌 Read the Command Word
Global essay method · applies to every reading
Before writing an essay answer, read the command verb — it tells you the SHAPE a full-credit answer must take. After writing, count your slots against that shape. This replaces "do I feel done?" (which only tracks whether you said something TRUE) with a structural check (did I fill every slot?).
The 20-second check, every answer
1. Circle the command verb in the prompt
2. Name the shape it demands (concede+challenge? chain? list of N? delta?)
3. Count your slots against the shape — short means incomplete
4. Scan for trigger words you read past
Trigger words = slots the grader put there on purpose: all / every · only / never · over and above / in addition to · two / main / persistent / relative to. Each one is a deliberate instruction. Reading past them is how essay points get silently lost.
Why this works: you're not summoning missing content from nowhere — you're using the PROMPT'S structure to flag an empty slot, which then cues the retrieval. "Describe wants a cause — what's the cause here?" is a far better memory prompt than staring at a blank feeling like you forgot something.
The 17 CFA command words
Official definitions · grouped by the answer shape each one demands
STATE / RECALL — short, precise, no argument needed
DefineTo state exactly the meaning of
IdentifyTo recognize, to correctly pick out or name
CalculateTo compute, to determine by mathematical processes
DemonstrateTo show practical mastery of
FormulateTo express in a precise form; to devise
LAY OUT FEATURES — the describe-shape: a chain or a list of characteristics
DescribeTo state characteristic features of something, to portray it in words
ExplainTo make clear and intelligible, provide insight into
AnalyzeTo examine the constituent parts of something and how the parts relate to each other and to the whole
InterpretTo explain the meaning or implications of something, to reach a conclusion about something by application of knowledge
COMPARE / CONTRAST — two-sided: watch whether they want similarities too
CompareTo state the similarities and differences between
ContrastTo state the differences between
JUDGE / CONCLUDE — the highest bar: reach a position and back it
DiscussTo examine critically from various points of view, considering pros and cons and relevant details
EvaluateTo reach a conclusion about something by application of knowledge and judgment
JustifyTo provide good reasons for, to show to be valid or appropriate
DetermineTo decide on through analysis of alternatives, to find or ascertain definitely
RecommendTo advise as suitable or fit for purpose
EstimateTo determine an approximate value for something; to reach an informed but possibly imprecise evaluation of something
Definitions are the official CFA Institute command-word glossary, verbatim. The grouping maps each verb to the answer shape from the decoder above.

⚡ TRIGGER SHEET — read the cue, fire the formula
Organized by the phrase in the question, not by reading. Column 3 is where marks die.
The five sign traps, before anything else: (1) a negative contract count = SELL/short — state the direction; (2) RFX needs the foreign currency as base — given B/P, invert 1/x first; (3) variance swaps: square both vols (K 20 → 400); (4) buy/sell & premium/discount statements refer to the base (denominator); (5) forward points ÷ 10^(decimals of the spot quote) — not always 10,000.
