“DISADVANTAGES OF EQUITY INDEX DERIVATIVES” (asset allocation / rebalancing)
The trade-off: index derivatives are cheap, fast, and preserve the underlying portfolio (adjust exposure without selling holdings) — BUT they give you market beta, not your alpha, and carry the frictions below.
✓ CFA answer-key ADVANTAGES (3 pts — identify ONE): (1) can quickly adjust factor exposures at low cost; (2) trade in liquid markets; (3) make it easy to leverage the portfolio.
✓ CFA answer-key DISADVANTAGES (identify TWO): (1) finite expirations → must be rolled at/near expiry → extra transaction costs; (2) position limits → full coverage may not be possible; (3) specialty needs may not be met by existing exchange-traded offerings; (4) OTC derivatives introduce counterparty risk; (5) basis risk (e.g. futures) may increase tracking error.
General (any equity index derivative):
Basis risk
The derivative tracks the index, not your actual holdings. If your portfolio ≠ the index (active managers), the hedge/exposure won’t move exactly with your book.
Beta, not alpha
Delivers only the broad market return — can’t replicate stock-specific or factor bets. A blunt tool for anything but market exposure.
No ownership rights
Not the actual shares → no voting rights, dividends only embedded in pricing (not directly received). Bad for stewardship/engagement mandates.
Futures-specific:
Roll risk
Short-dated → must roll to the next contract repeatedly → transaction costs + roll yield (contango can make rolling expensive).
Standardized sizing
Fixed contract sizes → often can’t match the exact notional → slightly over/under-hedged.
Margin / MTM
Daily settlement → margin calls force posting cash on adverse moves (a liquidity drain) even before closing; ongoing margin management.
Limited maturities
Liquid only for near-dated, major indices — long-horizon or niche exposures unavailable.
Swap-specific (OTC):
Counterparty risk
Bilateral OTC → exposed to counterparty default (no clearinghouse, unlike exchange-traded futures).
Illiquidity
Customized → hard to exit/unwind before maturity; no continuous market price.
Less transparency
Bespoke terms → opaque pricing + dealer spread.
Exam one-liner: cheap, fast, preserves the portfolio — but disadvantages cluster into basis risk (index ≠ your holdings), roll/margin/sizing frictions (futures), counterparty & illiquidity risk (swaps), and no ownership rights. You get market beta, not your alpha. Plus: tracking error, operational/expertise burden, and possible IPS/regulatory limits.
“WHAT MOVES ACTIVE SHARE vs ACTIVE RISK” (active equity / portfolio construction)
Two different things. Active Share = ½Σ|w_p − w_b| — a holdings-based measure (0 to 1) of how different your weights are; fully controllable by the manager. Active risk (tracking error) = std dev of active returns — depends on holdings AND volatilities/correlations, so it involves forecasts and is NOT fully controllable.
ActionASARWhy (the mechanism)
Hold more securities / smaller deviations↓↓Weights move toward benchmark → smaller |w_p−w_b|; AS-driven active risk is inversely ∝ number of securities (more names diversify the deviations).
Concentrate (fewer, larger bets)↑↑Bigger over/underweights → larger |w_p−w_b| (AS up) AND fewer positions to diversify → bigger return deviations (AR up).
Hold securities NOT in benchmark↑↑A non-benchmark name is a 100% active weight (w_b=0) → AS up; it also adds return that can diverge from the benchmark → AR up (usually).
Bigger systematic factor tilts (sector/beta/style)↑ (somewhat)↑↑Factor bets are correlated across many holdings → deviations move together, don’t cancel → active risk rises sharply even for modest AS.
Take idiosyncratic (stock-specific) bets↑↑ modestlyUncorrelated bets → deviations partly cancel out (diversify) → AS can be high while active risk grows only slowly.
Higher benchmark / market volatility—↑AS depends only on weights (unchanged), but active return = std of (R_p−R_b) scales with market vol → AR up.
Higher correlation among active positions—↑Weights unchanged (AS same), but correlated deviations reinforce instead of cancelling → AR up.
The key split: Active Share is about WHAT you hold (weights vs benchmark) — you control it exactly. Active risk adds HOW those bets covary (volatility + correlation) — forecast-based, not fully controllable. Two portfolios can have the same Active Share but very different active risk: concentrated factor bets → high active risk; diversified stock-specific bets → lower active risk for the same Active Share.
⚠ Active risk from Active Share is inversely proportional to the number of securities; active risk rises with factor & idiosyncratic risk levels. Benchmark-agnostic managers usually have higher Active Share AND higher active risk. A closet indexer = low Active Share & low active risk (looks active, isn’t).
“SECTOR-NEUTRALIZED PRICE MOMENTUM FACTOR” (active equity / factors)
Price momentum
Winners keep winning. Rank stocks by past return — typically trailing 12-month return skipping the last month (“12-1”), since the most recent month tends to reverse. Long past winners, short past losers.
The problem
Sectors move together → raw momentum loads up on whichever sectors have been hot. Your “momentum” bet secretly becomes a sector bet (e.g. massively overweight tech just because tech rose) — not what you wanted.
The fix
Rank each stock’s momentum only against its OWN-sector peers: within each sector, demean/standardize the scores (center each sector on zero), then build the long/short book from those within-sector ranks.
Result
Long winners & short losers inside every sector → portfolio holds ≈ the benchmark’s sector weights → net sector exposure ≈ 0. What’s left is pure stock-selection momentum.
Why do it: (1) isolates the momentum signal from sector timing — you’re paid for picking the right stocks within sectors, not for guessing which sector runs; (2) cuts unintended risk — raw-factor returns can be dominated by a few sector swings; neutralizing makes the factor cleaner & more attributable to the anomaly. (Same idea generalizes: neutralize to sector, size, country, or beta.)
One-line: ranks each stock’s past-return momentum only against its own-sector peers (long winners / short losers within each sector), so the portfolio carries no net sector tilt — pure within-sector momentum instead of an accidental bet on whichever sector has been running.
“WHICH RETURN MODEL? — Gordon vs Grinold-Kroner vs Singer-Terhaar” (CME Part 2)
“Justify with one reason” questions: pick the model by the one distinguishing feature that matches the data/asset given. Read the trigger words in the vignette.
If the data / asset gives you…UseBecause (your one reason)
Mature market, dividend yield + a single stable long-run growth rateGordon growthAssumes a single constant perpetual growth rate — fits a stable/mature market
Expected ΔP/E (repricing) and/or buybacks/issuance (%ΔS)Grinold-KronerOnly G-K captures repricing (%ΔP/E) and net share change (−%ΔS)
Market’s volatility, correlation w/ global, degree of integration (EM, or new/illiquid asset)Singer-TerhaarOnly S-T weights integrated vs segmented RPs by integration (and can add a liquidity premium)
One-line router: P/E change or buybacks → Grinold-Kroner. Integration / correlation / EM / new-or-illiquid asset → Singer-Terhaar. Mature market, one steady dividend growth rate → Gordon growth.
Model-answer phrasing — “[Model] is most appropriate because [the one distinguishing feature]”:
Singer-Terhaar: “…most appropriate because the country is an emerging market that is only partially integrated with global markets, and only Singer-Terhaar weights the integrated and segmented risk premiums by the degree of integration.” Grinold-Kroner: “…most appropriate because the forecast specifies an expected change in the P/E ratio (repricing), which the Gordon growth model cannot incorporate.” Gordon growth: “…most appropriate because the market is mature with a single stable long-run dividend growth rate, which is exactly the model’s assumption.”
“FX FORECASTING — THE TWO APPROACHES (full checklist)” (CME Part 2)
Two lenses on the same question. Trade approach = the goods side (what a country buys/sells). Capital approach = the money side (where investors put assets). Capital flows dominate in the short/medium term; trade/CA in the long run.
Approach 1 · Trade in goods & services — 3 pieces:
Net trade flows
How large are exports/imports relative to the economy and to other (larger) financing/investment flows. Small unless unfinanced.
PPP / inflation
Expected %ΔFX ≈ difference in inflation rates (lower inflation → appreciates).
CA sustainability
Sustainability of current-account imbalances — reflects national saving vs investment.
Approach 2 · Capital flows & capital mobility — 4 pieces:
Risk-adj return
Capital seeks the highest risk-adjusted return.
5 differentials
Expected %ΔFX reflects differences in asset characteristics: relative short-term rates + TERM, CREDIT, EQUITY, LIQUIDITY premiums.
Hot money
Hot-money flows (capital chasing rate differentials).
Portfolio role
FX is the across-the-board mechanism for adjusting the relative sizes of each country’s asset portfolio.
Memory: Trade approach = flows + PPP + CA sustainability (3). Capital approach = risk-adjusted return + the 5 differentials + hot money + portfolio-rebalancing role (4).
“ESSAY: WHICH COUNTRY’S CURRENCY STRENGTHENS?” (judge each factor INDEPENDENTLY)
Prompt style: for each observation independently, which country shows a strengthening currency? Do NOT net them — each row is its own answer.
ObservationStrongerWhy
Inflation: X 2.0% / Y 3.0%XLower inflation → PPP appreciation
ST gov rate: X ↓ / Y ↑YHigher rate attracts capital
Expected GDP growth: X 2.0% / Y 3.3%YStronger growth → higher risk-adjusted returns → inflows
New FDI-enabling laws: X yes / Y noXOpens market to foreign capital inflows
Current account: X +8% / Y −1%XSurplus supports the currency
The split: X strengthens on inflation, FDI laws, CA surplus. Y strengthens on higher ST rate & higher growth. Each factor judged independently — don’t net them into one answer.
⚠ The growth row uses the short-run capital-inflow view (growth → inflows → strengthens). The long-run portfolio-balance view says the opposite (growth → currency’s share ↑ → weakens, unless home bias / productivity / EM). Both are curriculum — match the view the question is testing.
“FX WATCH-LIST — the traps to re-read before the exam” (CME Part 2)
PPP direction
Higher inflation → currency depreciates; favor the lower-inflation currency.
PPP limits
Works long-term / large inflation gaps, NOT short-term; ignores capital flows, trade barriers, non-traded goods.
Current account
LENGTH of the imbalance matters more than its SIZE.
Capital-mobility sign
Positive E(%ΔS_d/f) = domestic DEPRECIATES by that %.
Overshooting
3 phases: appreciate → expect reversal → revert (depreciate).
UIP
Only the interest-rate differential matters (not the premium terms).
Carry trades
Contradict UIP — their success confirms risk premiums exist.
Hot money
3 issues (policy effectiveness, short-term financing risk, overshoot) + central-bank sterilized intervention.
Portfolio balance
Growth → currency’s share ↑ → currency weakens (unless home bias / productivity / EM).
“WHICH COUNTRY IS MOST VULNERABLE? — capital composition” (CME Part 2)
Key idea: not all foreign capital is equally “sticky.” The type of capital a country relies on determines how fast it can flee in a crisis. Rank by how supportive (committed / hard to withdraw) each is.
HoldingSupportivenessWhy
Private equity (Country A)MOST supportiveLong-term committed capital — locked up, illiquid, doesn’t flee.
Public equity (Country B)MiddleMore mobile than private (traded daily), but less flight-prone than debt — no repayment obligation.
Public debt (Country C)LEAST supportive → MOST vulnerableMust be serviced + repaid/refinanced — each rollover depends on market confidence → can trigger a crisis.
Ranking hook (most → least supportive): Private equity > Public equity > Public debt. “Most vulnerable” = LEAST supportive = the majority-public-debt country (C). Debt has to be paid back; equity doesn’t.
⚠ The trigger word is vulnerable / crisis-prone → flip to least supportive → whichever country’s inflows are mostly debt. Equity (esp. private/FDI) is patient capital; debt is the flighty, must-be-refinanced kind that sparks currency crises.
“BUILDING-BLOCK EXPECTED RETURN” (CME Part 2 — fixed income)
Stack the premiums on top of the risk-free rate. Each layer compensates for one extra risk the instrument carries.
Worked — Lou Bee: 1-yr gov (rf 2.5%) & 5-yr AA corp; term 60bp, credit 30bp, liquidity 25bp; equal-weight corp E(R) = 2.50 + 0.60 + 0.30 + 0.25 = 3.65% ; gov E(R) = 2.50% Q2 portfolio E(R) = (2.50 + 3.65)/2 = 3.075% → closest 3% (B) gov risk premium above rf = 0 ; corp risk premium = 0.60+0.30+0.25 = 1.15% Q3 portfolio risk premium = (0 + 1.15)/2 = 0.575% → closest 0.6% (A)
⚠ The government bond’s risk premium above the risk-free rate is zero — it is the risk-free asset over its horizon. Don’t accidentally give it a term premium in the equal-weight average.
“GRINOLD-KRONER (equity expected return)” (CME Part 2)
E(R_e) ≈ D/P + (%ΔE − %ΔS) + %ΔP/E D/P = dividend yield %ΔE = expected % change in total earnings %ΔS = expected % change in shares outstanding %ΔP/E = expected % change in the P/E ratio
Regroup into three intuitive components:
1 · Income return
D/P − %ΔS — current yield adjusted for buybacks (−%ΔS adds return) / issuance (dilutes).
2 · Earnings growth
%ΔE = real earnings growth + expected inflation (nominal, like NOI growth in real estate).
3 · Repricing
%ΔP/E = expected change in the P/E multiple (re-rating up or down).
“EQUITY RISK PREMIUM — TWO DEFINITIONS” (CME Part 2)
DefinitionERP =Approach
Relative to risk-freeequity return − risk-free rateA single premium for equity
Relative to bondsequity return − expected return on a default-free bondBuilding-block (bond return already stacks term premium onto rf)
“SINGER-TERHAAR (equilibrium / CAPM-based ERP)” (CME Part 2)
Idea: a market’s risk premium depends on how integrated it is with global markets. Blend a fully-integrated RP (uses correlation with the global market) and a fully-segmented RP (local market is its own reference, ρ = 1), weighted by the degree of integration.
FULL INTEGRATION: RP_i = ρ_i,global × σ_i × (global Sharpe) (+ illiquidity for EM) FULL SEGMENTATION: RP_i = σ_i × Sharpe (ρ = 1; use LOCAL Sharpe if given) (+ illiq) WEIGHTED: RP = (integ)(RP_int) + (1 − integ)(RP_seg) E(R) = Rf + RP
Worked — Market A (developed) & B (emerging); global Sharpe 0.29; Rf 5.0%; EM illiq 2.30%:
InputMarket AMarket B
Volatility σ17%28%
Correlation w/ global0.820.63
Degree of integration80%65%
Illiquidity premium0%2.3%
Local Sharpe (segmentation)—0.40
INTEGRATED RP_A = 0.82 × 0.17 × 0.29 = 4.04% RP_B = 0.63 × 0.28 × 0.29 + 0.0230 = 7.42% SEGMENTED RP_A = 0.17 × 0.29 = 4.93% RP_B = 0.28 × 0.40 + 0.0230 = 13.50% WEIGHTED RP_A = 0.80 × 4.04 + 0.20 × 4.93 = 4.22% RP_B = 0.65 × 7.42 + 0.35 × 13.50 = 9.55% E(RETURN) R_A = 5% + 4.22% = 9.22% R_B = 5% + 9.55% = 14.55%
⚠ Segmentation detail: under full segmentation the local market is the reference (ρ = 1.0), and if a local Sharpe is given, use it (here B’s 0.40), NOT the global 0.29. The EM illiquidity premium is added in both the integrated and segmented legs.
“CAP RATES (real estate valuation)” (CME Part 2)
cap rate = current NOI ÷ property value (an earnings yield) ⇒ value = NOI ÷ cap rate — HIGHER cap rate = LOWER valuation (riskier / lower-growth) Analogous to the Gordon-model denominator (E(R) − growth): cap rate = E(R_re) − NOI growth rate E(R_re) = cap rate + NOI growth (infinite horizon) E(R_re) = cap rate + NOI growth − %Δcap rate (finite horizon)
NOI growth ≈ GDP
In stable periods long-run NOI growth ≈ GDP growth. Like G-K, it’s nominal = real growth + inflation.
Competition
Cap rate is sensitive to competition — e.g. the mall cap-rate gap between high- & low-productivity malls grew 1.2% (2008) → 3.2% (2018) (a 2.0% widening) with online retail.
Rates & vacancy
Cap rates positively related to interest rates & vacancy (a long-term risk discount rate).
Credit availability
Lenders less willing → higher perceived risk → cap rates inversely related to credit/debt-financing availability. Countercyclical credit spreads mitigate cap-rate cyclicality.
The “gap” intuition: the gap = how far apart the market prices a strong vs weak mall (in cap-rate points). Online retail made weak malls much riskier (cap rate up, value down) while sparing strong ones, so the gap more than doubled 1.2% → 3.2% — proof cap rates move with competitive pressure, and the pressure hits vulnerable assets hardest.
“REAL-ESTATE RISK PREMIUMS” (CME Part 2)
Term premium
For holding a long-term asset (RE has high duration).
Credit premium
For the risk of tenant non-payment (a lease ≈ a corporate bond).
Equity risk premium
Above corporate-bond returns — for fluctuation in RE values, leases, vacancies.
Liquidity premium
RE (incl. REITs) can’t always be sold quickly at fair value — sellable only at periodic times. 2%–4% for commercial RE.
⚠ Combined RE risk premium is higher than corporate bonds but lower than equities. Using an equilibrium model (Singer-Terhaar) for RE needs two adjustments: (1) remove smoothing from the data, (2) add a liquidity premium. Also treat RE as local, not global.
“FORECASTING EXCHANGE RATES — A. TRADE CHANNELS” (CME Part 2)
FX is especially hard to forecast — managers either fully hedge or accept the volatility. Currencies are the unit of account for asset prices: an FX move reprices all assets in one currency vs others. Three trade-in-goods channels:
1 · Trade flows
Net trade flows have a relatively small FX impact if they can be financed. Large trade flows without financing flows → likely a crisis.
2 · PPP
Expected FX move follows expected inflation differentials (expected change in the real rate = 0). Works poorly short-term, better long-term & when inflation gaps are large (money-supply driven). Breaks with trade barriers, non-traded goods, capital flows.
3 · Competitiveness
Current-account sustainability drives FX (see capital-mobility channels).
“FORECASTING EXCHANGE RATES — B. CAPITAL FLOWS” (CME Part 2)
1 · Capital mobility — expected % FX change: E(%ΔS_d/f) = (r^d − r^f) + (Term^d − Term^f) + (Credit^d − Credit^f) + (Equity^d − Equity^f) + (Liquid^d − Liquid^f) Positive E(%ΔS_d/f) → the DOMESTIC currency DEPRECIATES by that %.
2 · UIP
FX change should equal the nominal rate differential only (no premium terms). BUT carry trades (borrow low-rate, lend high-rate) succeed because a risk premium exists — confirming the premium terms in the capital-mobility equation.
3 · Portfolio balance
Strong growth → that currency’s share in the global market portfolio rises → investors must be induced (higher returns) to raise allocations.
⚠ Hot money (capital chasing rate differentials) creates policy problems: (1) limits central-bank policy effectiveness; (2) firms use short-term financing for long-term investment → ↑ financial-market risk; (3) FX overshoots → business disruption. CBs counter via sterilized intervention.
Sterilized intervention — get the DIRECTION right: the open-market bond trade is always OPPOSITE the FX trade — that opposite trade is what neutralizes the liquidity effect (leaves money supply unchanged).
FlowCurrency pressureFX tradeSterilizing bond trade
INFLOW (hot money in)currency over-appreciatesCB BUYS FX (injects liquidity)CB SELLS domestic bonds (drains it back)
OUTFLOW (hot money out)currency under downward pressure / depreciatesCB SELLS FX reserves (drains liquidity)CB BUYS domestic bonds (re-injects it)
Exam reflex: read the bond trade to identify the country. CB “buys domestic bonds” → it’s re-injecting liquidity it lost selling FX → the OUTFLOW country. CB “sells domestic bonds” → draining liquidity it gained buying FX → the INFLOW country. Sterilization = the offsetting open-market trade, always.
“CURRENT ACCOUNT & FX — MITIGATING FACTORS” (CME Part 2)
What matters
Current-account balances hit FX hardest when persistent & sustained — the length of the imbalance matters more than its size. Structural sources: fiscal imbalances, demographics/trade preferences, resource abundance/scarcity, investment-opportunity availability, terms of trade.
High trend-growth mitigants
Growth weakens currency & raises risk premiums, BUT offset by: home-country bias (locals absorb new assets); growth from productivity funded by FDI/financial flows; high-trend countries tend to be smaller EMs (raising their weight doesn’t much weaken the currency).
Large-deficit mitigants
Deficits from large investment spending are easier to finance if expected profitable; small deficits in reserve currencies (incl. USD) supply global liquidity & benefit the system.
“FORECASTING VOLATILITY — 4 VCV METHODS” (CME Part 2)
One asset’s variance is easy; many assets need a variance-covariance (VCV) matrix. Four methods:
1 · Sample VCV
Variances/covariances from sample statistics. Rule: observations ≥ 10× the number of assets; assets cannot exceed observations or the result is meaningless (a big portfolio can falsely appear riskless).
2 · Factor-based
Multifactor models cut the observations needed — correlations come from a few common factors; variances add an asset-specific factor.
3 · Shrinkage
Weighted average of the sample VCV and a target (e.g. factor-based) matrix → more precise, less estimation error.
4 · Smoothed returns
Adjust for data smoothing that understates risk & overstates diversification.
“FACTOR-BASED VCV — THE COUNT ADVANTAGE” (CME Part 2)
Return: r_i = α_i + Σ β_ik F_k + ε_i (k = 1..K) Variance: σ²_i = ΣΣ β_im β_in ρ_mn + ν²_i (m,n = 1..K) Covariance: σ_ij = ΣΣ β_im β_jn ρ_mn (m,n = 1..K) ρ_mn = covariance between factors m and n ν²_i = variance of asset i’s unique factor ε_i
Element count (N = 50 assets, K = 6 factors): full sample VCV : N(N−1)/2 = 50×49/2 = 1,225 covariances factor model : N×K = 50×6 = 300 sensitivities + K(K+1)/2 = 6×7/2 = 21 factor var/cov
⚠ Two factor-VCV shortcomings: (1) biased — factor inputs are estimated, so the matrix is biased and isn’t the true predictor even on average; (2) inconsistent — doesn’t converge to the true matrix as sample grows. By contrast the sample VCV is consistent AND unbiased. (Factors must not be redundant / have no zero terms, so portfolios don’t falsely appear riskless.)
“SHRINKAGE & SMOOTHED RETURNS” (CME Part 2)
Shrinkage = sample VCV blended with a target (e.g. factor) matrix, same weights for all elements → smaller error. Even a biased target can help — its lower variance can win the bias-variance trade-off. Example: sample cov = 220, target = 180, weights 60% target / 40% sample estimate = 180 × 0.60 + 220 × 0.40 = 196
Smoothed returns understate risk & overstate diversification. Adjust via a weighted average of the true current and prior observed return: R_t = (1 − λ) r_t + λ R_(t−1) (0 ≤ λ ≤ 1) var(r) = [(1 + λ)/(1 − λ)] · var(R) > var(R) Example λ = 0.6 : (1+0.6)/(1−0.6) = 1.6/0.4 = 4× the observed variance → true SD = √4 = 2× the observed SD
⚠ The true current return isn’t directly observable — proxy it (e.g. with an asset index). Smoothing makes illiquid assets look deceptively safe & diversifying.
“ARCH MODELS (volatility clustering)” (CME Part 2)
Returns show periods of high & low volatility — volatility clustering — captured by autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH). Usable for multi-asset VCV. Simplest form:
σ²_t = γ + α σ²_(t−1) + β η²_t = γ + (α + β) σ²_(t−1) + β(η²_t − σ²_(t−1)) α, β, γ ≥ 0 and (α + β) < 1 η_t = unexpected return component
⚠ Higher (α + β) → more weight on past information → more volatility clustering. The constraint (α+β) < 1 keeps variance from exploding (mean-reverting).
“THE ADJUSTMENT PLAYBOOK — how each signal shifts the allocation” (CME Part 2)
SignalDo this
Trend growth ↑Favorable to equities (long-term earnings growth); unfavorable to bonds (higher rates). Shift equity↔bond weights using country + global VCV.
Integration ↑Required returns fall as markets integrate (Singer-Terhaar) → increase allocations to EMs expected to integrate more; decrease from already-highly-integrated markets.
Trough of cycleEquities do well (valuations & earnings rising) → ↑ equity (G-K for ERP). Curve steep w/ high credit & term premiums but rates set to rise → ↓ bonds & duration; a barbell may be optimal (↑ short + long, ↓ medium).
Peak of cycleReverse the trough: ↓ equity, ↑ bond exposure & duration.
PolicyFocus on structural changes (tax code, QE), NOT policy already reflected in prices.
Current accountThe long-term trend matters. Rising deficits → rising required returns → falling asset prices + more capital flows to fund the deficit (moving currencies).
CurrencyHigher risk-adjusted return → capital inflow → upward currency pressure. Judge whether it still has room to appreciate or is at its peak.
“Trough” and “peak” are TURNING POINTS, not phases — you position AT THE TURN, not mid-phase. At the trough, everything cheap is about to rise → buy equities, cut bonds/duration (rates about to rise). At the peak, everything expensive is about to fall → sell equities, add bonds/duration (rates about to fall).
Trough → curve 19
Curve is steep (short rates cut to the bottom) → the playbook’s “steep curve, high premiums, but rates set to rise → barbell, reduce duration.”
Peak → curve 19
Curve is flat / inverted (short rates hiked to the top) → the reverse: reduce equity, add duration.
One-liner: trough = bottom turning point (contraction ending → recovery); peak = top turning point (late expansion ending → slowdown). They’re the hinges of the cycle where you flip your allocation — not the phases on either side of them.
“EM HEALTH CHECKLIST — THRESHOLDS & WHY THEY MATTER” (CME / EM debt)
The unifying story: EM crises are almost always foreign-currency debt + short maturities + reliance on foreign capital. Every threshold below is really one question: if foreign investors suddenly stop lending or the currency falls, can this country still pay?
MetricThresholdWhy it matters / what goes wrong
Fiscal deficit / GDP> 4% = substantial credit riskGov’t keeps borrowing to cover the shortfall. EMs borrow short & refinance repeatedly → each rollover needs markets to stay willing to lend. A big deficit compounds the debt pile → higher odds the market balks at some rollover → non-payment risk rises. (The flow that feeds the stock.)
Debt / GDP70–80% troublesome for EMsIt’s not the SIZE of the debt that triggers an EM crisis — it’s that EM debt is foreign, short, and held by flighty investors, sitting on weak revenue, so serviceability breaks at a lower ratio than in a developed market. 70–80% is where investors start to doubt the country can keep paying.
Real growth rateexpect ≥ 4%(1) Growth lets a country grow out of its debt (GDP outpaces debt → ratios fall). (2) EM risk → investors demand ≥ 4% as compensation. Below 4% signals a slowing economy → weaker tax revenue, harder debt service, risk premium not earned.
Current account deficit / GDP> 4% = warningCountry imports/spends more than it earns → must fund the gap with foreign capital every year → dependent on continued inflows. If sentiment turns (a “sudden stop”), the currency drops & financing dries up. Above ~4% the external funding need is dangerously large.
Foreign debt / GDP> 50%, or outpacing serviceabilityDebt in a foreign currency is the dangerous kind — can’t print $/€ to repay, and if the local currency falls the debt gets more expensive in local terms (vicious loop). Above ~50%, or a large share being short-term foreign debt, a currency slide or refinancing freeze can trigger a crisis.
FX reserves / short-term debt< 100% concern; > 200% strongThe liquidity lifeline — can it cover near-term foreign obligations without new borrowing? Reserves repay short-term foreign debt & defend the currency. < 100% = reserves don’t even cover what’s due soon → vulnerable to a run. > 200% = ample buffer. Often the single most-watched crisis-vulnerability ratio.
⚠ The “borrow short, refinance often” trap: because EMs roll over debt frequently, they face not just solvency risk (can they ever pay?) but liquidity / rollover risk (can they pay right now, at this refinancing, if markets are jittery?). That’s why FX reserves / short-term debt is so decisive — it measures whether they survive the next rollover, not the eventual total.
“STEEP CURVE = BULLISH FOR CREDIT → BARBELL” (CME / credit)
Why a steep curve is bullish for a credit manager: you’re paid two fat premiums at once — a high credit premium AND a high term premium — at exactly the moment defaults are about to fall. Paid a lot, for risk that’s about to shrink.
High OAS
OAS = pure compensation for credit risk (spread over Treasuries, options stripped out). High OAS → market pays a lot to hold credit → big credit premium.
Steep Treasury curve
Signals expansion ahead (short rates cut to stimulate; both policies expansive — card 19) → firms improve → default rates decline. So the high OAS is overcompensating for a risk that’s falling.
Big term premium too
Steep = long yields >> short yields → extending maturity (duration/term risk) earns a large term premium. So a steep curve pays generously for credit AND duration risk together.
The trade — a BARBELL (hold both ends, skip the middle), sourcing each premium where it’s safest:
EndTake this riskWhy it’s the safe place for it
SHORT maturitiesCREDIT risk (grab the high OAS)Short horizon → less time for a firm to deteriorate & default; near-term default visibility is good, and defaults are falling anyway.
LONG maturitiesDURATION risk (grab the term premium)Take it in high-quality long bonds (Treasuries / high-grade). Long-dated credit is dangerous (20–30 yrs = lots of time to fail) → want long duration, NOT long credit.
⚠ The whole point is matching each risk to the maturity where it’s least punishing: credit risk SHORT (short window = little default danger), duration risk LONG (from safe issuers = term premium without long-term default exposure). You harvest both premiums a steep curve offers while avoiding the worst combo — long-dated credit risk. Skip the risky middle.
“WHAT PREDICTS CREDIT-SPREAD CHANGES? (& why the spread isn’t a default forecast)” (CME)
Unifying principle: spread changes are predicted by forward-looking, market-priced, firm-value signals — NOT by backward-looking, lagged, lumpy realized data. Markets price the future; macro data reports the past.
PredictorStrong / weak?Why
Stock returnsSTRONGEquity & credit are claims on the same firm. Stock rises → bigger equity cushion → default risk falls → spreads tighten (Merton: bond ≈ short a put on firm assets).
Stock volatilitySTRONGHigher firm-value volatility = higher chance value hits the default boundary → wider spreads. Volatility is practically a direct input to credit risk.
Risk-free rateSTRONGForward-looking, market-priced, cycle-driven. Rising rates (good times) → spreads narrow; falling rates (cuts in downturns) → spreads widen. Reliable inverse co-movement.
GDP growthWEAKBackward-looking & lagged — reported late and revised; markets already priced the outlook long before the print. Stale data can’t predict a forward-looking price.
Default-rate changesWEAKLumpy, clustered & lagging — defaults peak after the recession; the spread already reacted to the risk before defaults materialize.
Why the yield spread is NOT a good predictor of future default rates:
Premiums uneven
The realized credit premium isn’t earned smoothly — many small gains, then occasional large losses (a bad recession year). Lumpy, not steady, so one year’s spread is a poor guide to what you’ll actually earn.
Defaults cluster
Defaults are serially correlated — long stretches of low defaults (calm expansions), then a sudden cluster of high defaults in recessions. They come in waves, not evenly spread.
So the spread is…
Compensation for bearing lumpy, clustered, hard-to-time risk (plus liquidity), NOT an unbiased forecast of defaults. A tight spread is not “safe” — it’s often the calm before the cluster; a wide spread reflects current fear, not a clean forecast.
⚠ The exam split: to predict spread changes → use stocks, stock vol, risk-free rate (forward-looking market signals). Do NOT lean on GDP or realized defaults (lagged, lumpy). And never read today’s spread as the market’s default forecast — it’s a risk premium for timing risk, earned unevenly.
“ARE BONDS A RECESSION HEDGE? → TERM PREMIUM” (CME Part 1)
The insurance logic: an asset is a hedge if it pays off when you need it most (in a recession). Good insurance → investors accept a LOW expected return (low term premium). Bad insurance (does badly in bad times) → investors demand a HIGH return. So the term premium hinges on one thing: do bonds do well or badly in a recession? — which depends on why inflation moves.
Inflation caused by…Inflation vs growthBonds in a recessionBond return vs growthRecession hedge?Term premium
DEMAND shocks (agg. demand)moves WITH growth (boom→inflation up, recession→inflation down)rise (inflation falls → CB cuts → yields fall)NEGATIVELY correlated (bonds gain when growth is bad)GOOD hedgeLOW
SUPPLY shocks (agg. supply)moves AGAINST growth (stagflation: inflation up + growth down)fall (inflation high → CB can’t cut → yields stay high)POSITIVELY correlated (bonds lose when growth is bad)POOR hedgeHIGH
The two chains, end to end: DEMAND inflation → recession brings LOW inflation → rate cuts → bonds RISE → bonds are insurance → investors pay up → LOW term premium SUPPLY inflation → recession brings HIGH inflation → no cuts → bonds FALL → bonds fail you in the downturn → demand extra → HIGH term premium
⚠ The hinge is the CORRELATION SIGN, and it flips with the source of inflation. Demand-driven → bonds negatively correlated with growth → good hedge → low premium. Supply-driven (stagflation) → positively correlated → bad hedge → high premium. Don’t memorize the answer — ask “does a recession bring low inflation (demand) or high inflation (supply)?” and the rest follows.
“CURRENCY PEGS, RATE DIFFERENTIALS & THE TRILEMMA” (CME Part 1)
Master idea: capital chases the best risk-adjusted return, so the interest rate, the currency, or both must adjust until investors are indifferent. A peg removes the currency as a shock absorber → rates absorb everything.
The Impossible Trinity (trilemma) — a country can hold at most 2 of 3; the third must give:
Fixed FX?Capital flowsMonetary policyWhich corner
FixedUnrestricted (free)DEPENDENT — must follow the anchorGive up MP independence
FixedRestricted (controls)INDEPENDENTCapital controls buy back MP
FloatingUnrestrictedINDEPENDENTLet the currency float
Read it as: fixed FX + free capital → you LOSE monetary independence (you must import the anchor’s policy). To keep independent MP with a fixed rate, you must restrict capital. Or float the currency and keep both.
WITH a peg (small economy pegs to a larger anchor):
Cycles converge
To hold the peg the country must mimic the anchor’s monetary policy → monetary conditions & business cycles converge. If it doesn’t follow, investors favor one currency → the peg fails.
Rate differential
Pegged-currency rates generally exceed the anchor’s — the gap is a risk premium on the peg surviving. High confidence → small differential; doubt → large differential. It’s a live confidence meter.
Defending the peg
If confidence cracks and the currency starts to fall, the country raises short-term rates to attract capital and hold the peg (rates are the only lever left once the currency can’t move).
WITHOUT a peg (floating) — the differential & currency reflect fundamentals:
Overvalued currency
If substantially overvalued & expected to decline → bond rates likely higher, to compensate foreign investors for the expected currency loss on conversion (UCIRP logic).
Relative bond yields
Both nominal & real yields rise with strong economic activity & rising demand for funds.
Real rates
Driven by savings/investment decisions & capital productivity. They differ across countries but tend to move together — global saving & investing are linked through the current account.
⚠ The link between the two halves: same law, two regimes. Pegged = currency can’t move, so the rate differential (and rate hikes) do ALL the adjusting. Floating = the adjustment splits between the currency’s move and the rate differential (an overvalued, expected-to-fall currency pays a higher yield to hold investors). The rate differential is always the market pricing the risk of holding that currency.
“But rate moves influence the currency — isn’t that still independent MP?” No. Having the rate tool ≠ monetary independence. Independence = using rates for your own domestic goals (inflation, growth). Under a peg with open capital, every rate decision is consumed defending the currency, leaving nothing for domestic goals.

Independent MP: look at the domestic economy → set the rate you want → accept whatever the currency does.
Pegged MP: look at the currency → set whatever rate holds the peg → accept whatever that does to the economy.

One-line resolution: under a peg, MP acts but does not choose — you can touch rates, but only in service of the peg, never in service of your economy. Defending a falling currency by hiking when a weak economy would want a cut is the proof: the peg chose, not the central bank.
“YIELD CURVE AS AN ECONOMIC PREDICTOR” (CME Part 1 — policy mix)
The yield curve = relationship between interest rates and maturity. It’s sensitive to government actions (monetary + fiscal) and to current / expected conditions. Its shape encodes the policy mix:
MonetaryFiscalCurve shapeSignal
ExpansiveExpansiveSharply upward (steep) — short < longEconomy likely to expand
RestrictiveRestrictiveDownward / inverted — short > longEconomy likely to contract
RestrictiveStimulativeFlatImplications less clear
StimulativeRestrictiveModerately steepImplications less clear
The curve morphing through the cycle:
Curve over the cycle: typically steep at the bottom of the cycle → flattens toward expansion → flat / inverted at the top → re-steepens during contraction (bull steepener as short rates get cut). Use the curve to read the state of the economy and the future path of rates — but the relationships may not always hold.
⚠ The two clear signals are the “both same” cases: both expansive → steep → expand; both restrictive → inverted → contract. When monetary and fiscal pull opposite ways (one tight, one loose), the curve is flat/moderate and the signal is ambiguous — don’t over-read it.
“HOW DOES FISCAL POLICY WORK?” (CME Part 1 — countercyclical policy)
To STIMULATE (loose fiscal): ↓ taxes or ↑ government spending → larger budget deficit To REIN IN growth (tight fiscal): ↑ taxes or ↓ spending → smaller deficit / surplus
⚠ It’s the CHANGE, not the level. The size of the deficit does NOT stimulate — an increase in the deficit does. A large but steady deficit is not stimulative. This is the single most common fiscal-policy trap.
Cyclical ≠ policy (automatic stabilizers don’t count). Deficit changes that happen naturally over the cycle are neither stimulative nor restrictive:
PhaseWhat happens automaticallyDeficitCounts as stimulus?
ExpansionTax receipts ↑, transfer payments (unemployment, welfare) ↓Deficit fallsNo — automatic
RecessionTax receipts ↓, transfers ↑Deficit risesNo — automatic
DiscretionaryGovernment deliberately cuts taxes / raises spendingDeficit rises by policyYes — real stimulus
Exam trap (state it exactly): a large deficit by itself does not stimulate; only a discretionary increase in the deficit does. Automatic-stabilizer swings (deficit falling in expansion, rising in recession) are not stimulus or restraint — they’re the cycle working on the budget, not policy working on the cycle.
“HOW DOES MONETARY POLICY WORK?” (CME Part 1 — countercyclical policy)
Central banks use monetary policy as a countercyclical force, balancing price stability against economic growth. Goal: keep growth near its long-run sustainable rate — growth persistently above it → inflation. Late-expansion inflation → CBs turn restrictive; risk: overtighten and cause a recession (policy is better at slowing than accelerating).
Lower rates (easing) transmit to: ↑ consumer spending ↑ business spending / investment ↑ stock prices ↑ bond prices (yields fall) lower domestic currency → ↑ exports (cheaper goods abroad) Raising rates (tightening) = the mirror on every line.
⚠ Level matters, not just direction. Rates raised 4% → 6% to fight inflation may still be low vs the country’s historical average → policy is still growth-permissive even though it’s tightening. Direction ≠ the whole story — always compare the rate to the neutral rate and the country’s norm before calling policy “tight” or “loose.”
Neutral (equilibrium) rate = the policy rate that balances growth & inflation — neither stimulative nor restrictive:
Neutral rate = real trend growth component + inflation (target) component (+ judgment) e.g. inflation target 3% + trend growth 2% → neutral ≈ 5% policy is EASY when actual rate < neutral | TIGHT when actual rate > neutral
Exam reflex: to judge if a central bank is stimulative or restrictive, don’t look at the last move — compare the actual rate to the neutral rate (real growth + target inflation). A 6% rate is loose if neutral is 7%, tight if neutral is 5%.
“INFLATION, THE BUSINESS CYCLE & ASSET RETURNS” (CME Part 1 — LOS 1.g)
1) Inflation & the business cycle — the 5 phases and what markets do:
PhaseInflationShort rates / bond yieldsStocks & cyclicals
Initial recoveryFalling / lowShort rates & yields low, bottoming; curve steepStocks may rise strongly; cyclicals (small caps, HY, EM) do well
Early expansion (upswing)Low, stable, creeping upShort rates rising; long yields stable / slightly upStocks trending up; profits rise rapidly
Late expansion (upswing)Rising (accelerating)Rates rise, yield curve flattensStocks up but volatile; cyclicals underperform, inflation hedges outperform
SlowdownStill rising / accelerating (does NOT peak yet)Short rates at/near peak; govt yields peak then may fall sharply; curve may invert; credit spreads widen (weak credits)Stocks may fall; interest-sensitive & “quality” stocks perform best
Contraction (recession)Peaks, then falls (the peak lives HERE)Rates & yields drop; easing policy → curve steepens (bull steepener)Stocks drop initially but rise well before recovery (bottom ~3–6 mo before the economy)
Business-cycle analysis is most reliable/actionable in the 2–3 year range. Central banks are better at slowing than accelerating → they prefer persistent positive inflation. The real rate on cash is procyclical around the target.
⚠ Classic trap — the inflation peak: inflation keeps accelerating right through Slowdown and only peaks in the Contraction/Recession phase. Candidates wrongly place the peak at Slowdown because short rates peak there — but rates peak before inflation does (the central bank is still fighting rising prices). Rate peak = Slowdown; inflation peak = Recession.
2) Inflation vs expectations — effect by asset class (the exam’s core LOS grid):
AssetAt expectationsAbove expectations (rising)Below / deflation
CashNeutral — floating real rate, ~zero duration, inflation-protectedPositive: rates rise with inflation → cash attractive in a rising-rate environmentRates fall toward zero → cash return ↓. BUT deflation + ZLB → cash’s REAL return turns positive (see below)
BondsLittle effect (priced in)Capital losses: yields rise with the inflation premium. Out-of-range → long yields move mostGains: yields fall. Persistent deflation helps highest-quality bonds (real value of fixed CFs ↑) but impairs low-quality credit (default risk ↑)
EquitiesLittle effect (revenues & costs both scale)Mixed / headwind if it overshoots — margin pressure, higher discount rate. Firm-specificNegative: weak demand, pricing power lost, real debt burden ↑
Real estateNeutralPositive — a real asset / inflation hedge; rents & values track pricesNegative: deflation suppresses rents & values; if levered, equity value falls faster (does NOT outperform in deflation)
One-line mnemonic: rising inflation → real assets win (real estate, cash, inflation hedges), bonds lose, equities mixed. Deflation → high-quality bonds & cash win, everything real (RE, equities, low-quality credit) loses.
3) Why cash has a POSITIVE real return in deflation (nominal rate bound at 0)
real return on cash = nominal (floored at ~0%) − inflation in deflation inflation < 0 → real return = 0 − (−x%) = +x% (positive!)
1. Cash becomes attractive vs bonds / risky assets in deflation. Normally cash is the drag (negative real return when inflation is positive — the “cash drag” from equitization). Flip inflation negative and cash quietly becomes a positive-real-return holding — one reason deflation is pernicious: it incentivizes hoarding cash instead of spending/investing, deepening the downturn.

2. It’s the floor that makes deflation dangerous for policy (the ZLB trap). Because nominal rates can’t go below zero, the central bank can’t make cash unattractive enough to force money out — real rates stay positive (or can’t fall enough), monetary stimulus loses traction.

3. Asset-allocation / liability context: when discounting or comparing returns, cash’s real return isn’t zero in deflation — it’s positive, which changes the relative attractiveness of holding cash vs locking into low-yielding bonds.
⚠ The exam nuance: deflation makes cash attractive only if the zero lower bound is binding on the nominal rate. Otherwise deflation is simply a component of the required short-term real rate (the nominal rate would just go negative and cash wouldn’t be special). And real estate does NOT outperform in deflation — suppressed rents feed straight into valuations, worse if levered.
“P&L ON A CDX / CDS INDEX POSITION?” (Credit strategies)
⚠ Do NOT use ΔSpread × duration × notional for a CDX index. That single-duration shortcut lands on a decoy answer. Use the index price at each date, each with its OWN spread duration.
Index price = 1 + (Coupon − Spread) × Spread Duration CDX HY fixed coupon = 500 bp (5%) | CDX IG = 100 bp (1%) TOTAL P&L (buyer) = price change − coupon paid price change = (Price₀ − Price₁) × N (buyer is short the index → gains as price falls) coupon paid = Coupon × N (the buyer PAYS the fixed premium all period) Seller: mirror — price change = (Price₁ − Price₀) × N, and the seller RECEIVES the coupon.
PositionCredit riskGains when…
Buy protectionShort credit riskSpreads widen → index price falls (buyer is short the index)
Sell protectionLong credit riskSpreads tighten → index price rises (seller is long the index)
Worked — fund buys $10M CDX HY protection; recession view right (Mock 3 Q53) Inception: spread 350 bp, spread duration 4.66 12 mo on: spread doubled to 700 bp, spread duration 3.77 Price₀ = 1 + (0.05 − 0.0350) × 4.66 = 1 + 0.06990 = 1.0699 Price₁ = 1 + (0.05 − 0.0700) × 3.77 = 1 − 0.07540 = 0.9246 price change = (1.0699 − 0.9246) × $10M = +$1,453,000 coupon paid = 0.05 × $10M = −$500,000 TOTAL P&L = 1,453,000 − 500,000 = $953,000 gain
The two decoys this generates: • $1,453,000 = the price change but forgot to subtract the coupon the buyer pays — the most tempting trap; • $1,631,000 = ΔSpread × beginning SD (4.66), no coupon at all. Correct = price change (each leg at its own SD) MINUS the coupon paid over the period.
Two reflexes: (1) buy protection = short the index = short credit risk → profits when spreads widen (recession view); seller is the mirror. (2) Always net the coupon: the buyer PAYS the fixed premium (a cost), the seller RECEIVES it — “total return including the coupon outflow” is the exam’s phrase for the correct answer.
“EVERYTHING THAT MOVES A CURRENCY” — full driver list (R18 + economics foundation)
Master principle: a currency appreciates when capital flows toward it, and capital flows toward the highest risk-adjusted expected return. Every driver below is just a channel that raises or lowers that risk-adjusted return. (CFA Institute: capital flows respond to high nominal rates, lower inflation expectations, a lower risk premium, and an upward revision of long-run fair value.)
FactorCurrencyWhy (the mechanism)
THE FOUR CANONICAL R18 FUNDAMENTAL DRIVERS (exam-quotable)
Undervalued vs fair valueAppreciatesMean-reversion toward the PPP/equilibrium anchor; also fastest rise in fundamental value pulls it up.
Higher real (or nominal) interest rateAppreciatesAttracts foreign capital chasing the higher return → demand ↑. Must ideally be real (net of inflation) to be a genuine draw.
Lower (expected) inflationAppreciatesPPP: slower erosion of value → currency must appreciate to keep the basket equal; also raises the real rate. (card 13 has the 3 channels.)
Lower country / risk premiumAppreciatesDiscipline, stability, reform → lower required compensation to hold → more attractive. Rising premium → depreciates.
BROADER MACRO / BALANCE-OF-PAYMENTS FACTORS (feed the four above)
Current account surplusAppreciates (slow)Exports > imports → foreigners must buy the currency to pay for its goods → net demand ↑. Deficit → net selling → depreciation pressure. Slow: imbalances persist for years before adjusting.
Capital / financial account inflows (FDI, portfolio)AppreciatesForeign investment requires buying the local currency → demand ↑. Can offset a current-account deficit: the deficit country attracts capital with higher yields. In the short/medium run these flows dominate the current account.
Higher expected GDP growthAppreciatesNot a standalone curriculum driver — works through higher expected earnings / real returns → attracts inflows, and signals lower risk. Feeds the “risk-adjusted return” channel.
Higher risk-adjusted expected return on the country’s assetsAppreciatesThe unifying idea: capital moves to the highest risk-adjusted return → that flow bids up the currency. Real rates, growth, and low risk premium all roll up into this.
Fiscal / monetary discipline, structural reform, political stabilityAppreciatesLowers the risk premium and inflation expectations → capital responds positively.
Persistent large fiscal deficit / rising govt debtDepreciatesRaises inflation & default-risk expectations, may force monetary financing → higher risk premium, weaker currency.
Two must-remember caveats: (1) current account vs capital account tension — a deficit pushes the currency down through trade but can pull it up by attracting capital with higher yields; net effect = whichever flow dominates (short run: capital wins). (2) These are all long-run relationships — short run, currencies overshoot and reverse, which is exactly why the reading says none of the four active approaches works consistently.
⚠ Dornbusch (1976) overshooting — the “higher return → appreciate” exception: a currency with a higher expected return does rise, but it overshoots — it jumps past its new long-run equilibrium because capital moves faster than goods markets adjust. From that overshot peak it is now above fair value, so it depreciates back down going forward.

The exam split: • initial / reaction direction → appreciate (the driver list above holds); • longer-term / going-forward direction, after the overshoot → weaken / depreciate back to equilibrium.
The tells: the words “longer-term” / “going forward” and an explicit Dornbusch / overshooting reference → answer depreciate, even when the currency has the higher risk-adjusted return. Don’t reflexively answer “higher return = appreciate” on a longer-horizon question.
“WHY DOES A CURRENCY APPRECIATE?” — economic fundamentals (R18)
Long run, a currency converges to fair value. Appreciation is associated with currencies that are more undervalued, have the fastest rise in fundamental value, higher real/nominal rates, lower inflation, and decreasing risk premiums. The one that trips people up — lower expected inflation → appreciation — has three channels:
ChannelWhy lower inflation → stronger currency
Purchasing power parityThe exchange rate reflects relative price levels. If a country’s prices rise slower, its goods get relatively cheaper → to keep the same basket costing the same everywhere, its currency must appreciate. Inflation is the erosion rate of a currency — less erosion = more value.
Real interest rateNominal ≈ real + expected inflation. Same nominal rate but lower expected inflation → higher real return → capital chases real yield → demand for the currency rises.
Credibility / risk premiumLow, stable inflation signals a disciplined central bank → lower currency risk premium → more attractive to hold.
One-line memory: inflation = how fast a currency loses value; lower expected inflation = slower erosion = appreciation. But these are the long-run fundamental drivers — short term, currencies routinely move the other way, which is why the reading says none of the four active approaches (fundamentals / technical / carry / vol) work consistently.
“REBALANCING A PORTFOLIO WITH ILLIQUID ASSETS?” (Asset Allocation / endowment)
ThemeItemWhat it means / how it works
Why it’s hardCore problemIlliquids (PE, RE, VC, HF) can’t trade cheaply/quickly — wide spreads, market impact, stale appraised prices, long time-to-transact, exit penalties. Physical rebalancing = forced selling at bad prices.
Denominator effectIn a drawdown, liquid assets fall while illiquids stay at stale marks → the illiquid % mechanically rises above target though you did nothing. Rebalancing back = selling illiquids when you least can.
Appraisal / stale pricingIlliquid values come from periodic appraisals, not live markets → reported weights lag, drift is understated, rebalancing signals arrive late.
Assess liquidity needsCash-flow projection / liquidity budgetingProject inflows (distributions, income) vs outflows (spending draw ≈5%, capital calls on unfunded commitments) period by period → net liquidity requirement; enough liquid assets without forced sales.
Stress testing / scenariosAdverse cases (crash; calls spike while distributions dry up; denominator effect) → reveals the shortfall in the tail that base-case projection misses.
Liquidity classification (bucketing)Sort holdings by time-to-liquidate (<1 week / <1 month / >1 year) → compare liquid buckets vs near-term needs.
How to rebalanceCash-market approachPhysically buy/sell the underlying → for illiquids: high cost, market impact, forced sales, losses/penalties. The problem, not the solution.
Derivatives overlay (preferred)Adjust market exposure synthetically with index futures/swaps → illiquids stay untouched. Low cost, high liquidity, margin only (not full capital), fast to execute/reverse, preserves the illiquid sleeve, keeps exposure at target between dates. (R17 cash-equitization / overlay logic.)
When to rebalanceCalendar rebalancingFixed schedule (monthly/quarterly). Simple; ignores how far the portfolio has actually drifted.
Percentage-range / corridor (automatic mechanism)Pre-set tolerance bands around each target (e.g., 60% ±5%). Trades trigger automatically when a band is breached → back to target or the near edge. Rules-based, no discretion.
Benefits of the automatic rule(1) Discipline / removes behavioral bias — forces sell-high/buy-low, takes timing out of human hands; (2) tighter tracking of the SAA / risk control — catches drift (incl. denominator effect) continuously, not at the next meeting; (3) lower monitoring cost.
Setting corridor widthWider bands when: illiquid / high transaction cost, high correlation with the rest, higher risk tolerance. Narrower when: liquid, low cost, tight risk control needed.
Value illiquid assetsMarketable comparable + option dataValue illiquid Y from a marketable twin X via put-call parity: Vᵧ = Sₓ − (C − P) = PV(strike). The (C − P) spread = the illiquidity discount (value of the tradability Y lacks). MUE: 100 − (13.02 − 8.15) = $95.13.
Through-line: illiquid assets make rebalancing costly → (a) assess liquidity needs before committing, (b) rebalance the exposure with derivatives, not physicals, (c) automate the trigger with corridors so drift — especially the denominator effect — gets caught without forced sales.
“COMPARE SAA vs TAA” / “HOW IS THE ALLOCATION BUILT?” (R4 / R8)
SAA — strategicTAA — tactical
DefinitionLong-term target weights per asset class from the IPS + long-run CMEs; the policy portfolio, rebalanced back to targetsDeliberate short-term deviations from SAA weights, within allowed ranges, to exploit perceived mispricings; return to SAA after
How it’s builtInputs (R1–R2): long-run E(r), σ, ρ. Then an optimizer (R4): MVO (max U = E(r) − 0.005λσ²) · reverse optimization / Black-Litterman (market weights → implied returns + views; fixes MVO input sensitivity) · resampled MVO · Monte Carlo path testing · risk budgeting / risk parity · liability-relative (surplus) or goals-basedTwo families (R8): discretionary — judgment on macro, valuation, cycle, policy, sentiment, flows · systematic — rule-based signals with documented premiums: value (incl. the FX carry / forward rate bias, R18) and momentum/trend (time-series momentum, 50d/200d MA crossovers = R18 technicals)
Return sourceBeta — long-run risk premiumsAlpha — forecasting skill
AdvantagesDiscipline vs behavioral errors; low turnover → low costs & taxes; captures the reliable premiums; clean benchmark for everything elseAdds value if views are right; flexibility in changing conditions; cheap to implement with futures/ETFs (R17 overlay)
ShortcomingsIgnores short-term opportunities; hostage to CME estimation error; can go stale between reviews; rebalancing costTrading costs + tax drag; tracking error vs policy; skill rarely persistent; concentration reduces diversification
EvaluationObjectives met? Periodic / life-event reviewSharpe vs the SAA’s Sharpe; information ratio; plot vs the SAA on the risk/return frontier
“HOW DOES THIS DB-PLAN FEATURE AFFECT THE LIABILITY / IPS?” (R10 / P4)
DB characteristicLiab. PVLiab. dur.HorizonRisk tol.LiquidityObjective / constraintWhy (one line)
More retired livespaid down, near-weighted↓↓↓↑LDI / match payoutsBenefits flow out now — cash flows are close, discounting barely shrinks them, cash must be on hand.
Older active workforce↑↓↓↓↑ soonDe-risking glide pathAccruals become payments at near-peak salaries — little time to recover a drawdown.
Younger employees↓↑↑↑↓Growth assets OKPayments are decades away: heavy discounting shrinks the PV, and decades of runway absorb volatility.
Extended time to retirement↓↑↑↑↓Longer glide pathRaising the retirement age pushes every payout further out — same effect as a younger workforce.
Plan frozen / closedgrowth stops↓ over time↓↓↑ over timeImmunize → annuitizeNo new accruals: the liability is a fixed, shrinking bond — hold the bond that matches it.
Early-retirement / lump-sum options↑, unpredictable↓↓↓↑↑Liquidity buffer; no illiquidsMembers hold an option against the plan: money can leave sooner, and the plan can’t schedule it.
Higher funded status———ability ↑, used to de-risk—Protect the funded ratioSurplus is a cushion you could risk — but sponsors lock the win: losing a surplus hurts more than growing it helps.
Strong sponsor———↑—More return-seekingA deficit is a small call on a big healthy balance sheet — contributions can fix mistakes.
Sponsor ↔ plan correlation high———↓↑ in stressDiversify away from sponsorThe plan needs cash exactly when the sponsor can least contribute — one shock hits both.
Discount rate ↓↑↑ (≈ BPVₗ × Δy)↑ (convexity)—↓ (funded status falls)—Duration hedge: Nₖ = (BPVₗ − BPVₐ)/BPVₖThe liability is a short bond: rates down = its PV up — unhedged, the funded ratio falls with no change in benefits.
Longevity ↑ / wage growth ↑↑↑↑——Return ≥ discount rateMore years of payments at higher final salaries — the promise itself grows, not just its price.
Mirror rule: younger workforce / raised retirement age = exact inverse of retired lives / early retirement — every column flips (PV ↓, duration ↑, horizon ↑, tolerance ↑, liquidity ↓). And funded status is the hinge: it drives both the ability to take risk and the glide path that removes it.
